sections.heading: Automatic Purge of Expired Keys
sections.text:
Expired enrollment keys are hard-deleted automatically by a daily sweep that runs at **04:00 UTC**. A key is only purged once it has been expired for a grace period of `ENROLLMENT_KEY_PURGE_AFTER_DAYS` days (default **7**), so a recently expired key remains visible long enough to audit or rotate. Keys with no expiration date are never auto-purged. Set `ENROLLMENT_KEY_CLEANUP_ENABLED=false` to disable the sweep entirely.

A key is also skipped by the sweep — even past its grace period — while it still has a live, unexhausted [installer bootstrap token](#installer-bootstrap-tokens) outstanding, so an installer whose token lives up to 30 days cannot be purged out from under itself before its own token expires or is fully consumed.

Installer bootstrap tokens and deployment invites that reference a purged key are cascade-deleted along with it.

sections.heading: Bulk-Deleting Expired Keys
sections.text:
You can also delete all expired keys on demand, without waiting for the grace period:

```bash
curl -X POST https://breeze.yourdomain.com/api/v1/enrollment-keys/purge-expired \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

The endpoint requires the same `organizations:write` permission + MFA as single-key deletion, deletes every expired key in the caller's scope (the caller's org, all accessible orgs for partner scope, or all orgs for system scope), and returns `{ "success": true, "deletedCount": N }`. Keys without an expiration are never matched.

In the dashboard, this is surfaced as a **Delete expired** button above the key list, with a confirmation dialog before anything is removed.

---

sections.heading: How Agent Enrollment Uses the Key
sections.text:
When an agent starts for the first time, it presents the enrollment key to the API. The full flow is:

1. The agent sends `POST /api/v1/agents/enroll` with the raw enrollment key, hostname, OS type, architecture, and agent version.
2. In production, the API first validates the static **enrollment secret** (from the `AGENT_ENROLLMENT_SECRET` env var or `x-agent-enrollment-secret` header).
3. The API hashes the enrollment key with SHA-256 + pepper and looks up the matching record.
4. The API checks that the key has not expired (`expiresAt > NOW()`) and has remaining usage (`usageCount < maxUsage`).
5. `usageCount` is atomically incremented.
6. The API verifies the key has a `siteId`. If not, the enrollment is rejected and the usage increment is rolled back.
7. A device record is created (or updated if the hostname already exists in the same org + site) with a new `agentId` and `agentTokenHash`.
8. Hardware and network inventory from the enrollment payload is stored.
9. An mTLS certificate is issued if Cloudflare mTLS is configured for the organization.
10. The API returns the `agentId`, `deviceId`, `authToken` (a `brz_`-prefixed bearer token), `orgId`, `siteId`, and heartbeat configuration.

```json
// Successful enrollment response (201)
{
  "agentId": "hex-agent-id",
  "deviceId": "uuid",
  "authToken": "brz_a1b2c3d4...",
  "orgId": "uuid",
  "siteId": "uuid",
  "config": {
    "heartbeatIntervalSeconds": 60,
    "metricsCollectionIntervalSeconds": 30
  },
  "mtls": null
}
```

  The `authToken` is only returned once. The agent stores it in `secrets.yaml` (`/etc/breeze/secrets.yaml` on Linux, `/Library/Application Support/Breeze/secrets.yaml` on macOS, `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\secrets.yaml` on Windows) with `0600` permissions. The main config (`agent.yaml`) uses `0644` so the Helper can read it. The API stores only the SHA-256 hash.

---

sections.heading: Peppered Hashing
sections.text:
Enrollment keys are hashed using SHA-256 with a server-side pepper before storage. `ENROLLMENT_KEY_PEPPER` itself is required in production — the server refuses to start unless it is set, at least 32 characters, and not a known placeholder/insecure value. New keys are always hashed with `ENROLLMENT_KEY_PEPPER`; there is no acceptable substitute.

`APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `SSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `JWT_SECRET`, and `SESSION_SECRET` are consulted only as legacy fallbacks on the *read* path, so enrollment keys hashed before `ENROLLMENT_KEY_PEPPER` became mandatory still match after an upgrade — they are never used to hash a newly created or rotated key.

Installer bootstrap tokens (the short token embedded in a downloaded installer's filename or bundle) are also stored only as a hash keyed by `ENROLLMENT_KEY_PEPPER`. They have **no** legacy-pepper fallback: rotating `ENROLLMENT_KEY_PEPPER` invalidates every outstanding installer link and every downloaded installer that has not enrolled yet, so re-issue installers after a rotation.

The hash is computed as:

```
SHA-256( pepper + ":" + rawKey )
```

This means that even if the database is compromised, the raw enrollment keys cannot be recovered without knowledge of the pepper.

sections.heading: Dual Gate: Secret + Key
sections.text:
The enrollment endpoint uses two layers of protection:

| Layer | Purpose | Scope |
|-------|---------|-------|
| **Enrollment secret** (`AGENT_ENROLLMENT_SECRET`) | Static gating token validated at the start of the request. Required in production if set. | Global -- same for all enrollments. |
| **Enrollment key** | Per-deployment token that determines org, site, and usage limits. | Per-key -- each deployment batch gets its own key. |

The enrollment secret can be passed as the `enrollmentSecret` field in the request body or via the `x-agent-enrollment-secret` header.

sections.heading: Re-enrollment
sections.text: If an agent with the same hostname already exists in the same org and site, the enrollment endpoint updates the existing device record rather than creating a duplicate. This supports scenarios like OS reinstalls or agent upgrades. If the existing device has been **decommissioned**, re-enrollment is still allowed — the API creates a *fresh* device record (new id, new tokens) rather than reviving the decommissioned row, so the old row's audit history stays intact and the new agent is treated as a distinct asset. The only case that's blocked is when the decommissioned row's token was also suspended for a security reason (for example, a cross-tenant access probe) — that returns a `409 Conflict` until an administrator clears the suspension. See [Reusing a hostname for a decommissioned device](/agents/enrollment/#reusing-a-hostname-for-a-decommissioned-device) for the full behavior.

sections.heading: Audit Trail
sections.text:
Every enrollment key operation is recorded in the audit log:

| Action | Trigger |
|--------|---------|
| `enrollment_key.create` | New key created. |
| `enrollment_key.rotate` | Key material regenerated. Includes previous and new `maxUsage`, `expiresAt`, and `usageCount`. |
| `enrollment_key.delete` | Key permanently deleted. |
| `enrollment_key.purge_expired` | Bulk deletion of expired keys. Includes the `deletedCount`. |
| `enrollment_key.bootstrap_token_issued` | A single-use bootstrap token was minted from this key (dashboard "generate installer" flows). |
| `enrollment_key.installer_link_created` | A public installer link or short link was generated for this key. |
| `enrollment_key.installer_download` | A pre-configured installer (Windows MSI or macOS zip) was built and downloaded from the dashboard for this key. |
| `enrollment_key.installer_build_failed` | Installer build failed after usage was already reserved; logged so the failure is traceable. |
| `enrollment_key.public_download` | An anonymous download via a public or short installer link. Logged with the requester's IP and a sentinel anonymous actor id (no logged-in user). |
| `installer.bootstrap_redeemed` | A downloaded installer redeemed its bootstrap token and received a child enrollment key. Logged per device with the token id, parent and child enrollment key ids, source IP, and `consumedCount` / `maxUsage` / `remainingUsage`. Failed redemptions are not audited. |
| `agent.enroll` | Agent successfully enrolls using a key. Logged with `actorType: agent`. |

---

sections.heading: Multi-Tenant Access Control
sections.text:
Enrollment key management respects the Breeze multi-tenant hierarchy:

| User Scope | Behavior |
|------------|----------|
| **Organization** | Can only manage keys for their own organization. `orgId` is inferred automatically. |
| **Partner** | Can manage keys for any organization they have access to. Must provide `orgId` when managing multiple orgs. If the partner has exactly one org, `orgId` is inferred. |
| **System** | Can manage keys for any organization. Must provide `orgId`. |

All management endpoints require `organizations:read` for listing/viewing and `organizations:write` + MFA for creating, rotating, and deleting.

---

sections.heading: Partner & Organization Enrollment Defaults
sections.text:
Partners and organizations can configure three settings that shape enrollment link and installer TTLs without touching environment variables per-deployment. All three live under `settings.defaults` on the partner or organization record.

| Setting | Scope | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `defaultEnrollmentTtlMinutes` | Partner default, **inherit-with-override** by org | Pre-selects the link/installer expiry in the **Add Device** dialog. A partner sets a house default; an individual organization may override it with its own default. The product fallback when neither is set is 30 days. |
| `defaultEnrollmentDeviceCount` | Partner default, **inherit-with-override** by org | Same inherit-with-override pattern, for the default device count on a new link. The product fallback when neither is set is 50 devices. |
| `maxEnrollmentLinkTtlMinutes` | **Partner only** | A hard ceiling on enrollment key/installer lifetime for every organization under that partner. An organization cannot raise it — there is no org-level equivalent field. |

Partners configure all three from their partner settings page (`PATCH /partners/me`); organizations override the first two from their own org settings page (`PATCH /orgs/organizations/:id`). See [Partner Management](/reference/partner-management/#updating-partner-settings-self-service) for the general settings-PATCH mechanics.

**The cap is a ceiling on key lifetime, not just on requests:**
  `maxEnrollmentLinkTtlMinutes` bounds how long any key or token minted under that partner may remain usable — it is not merely a limit on what an admin is allowed to type into a form. If a partner sets a one-hour cap, **nothing** minted under any of that partner's organizations — an explicit `ttlMinutes` from an admin, a redemption-time child key, an installer bootstrap token, or an MCP-generated deployment invite — stays valid for longer than an hour, regardless of which code path created it.

sections.heading: Rejected vs. clamped
sections.text:
The cap is enforced two different ways, depending on whether there's an interactive caller present to show an error to:

- **An explicit request above the cap is REJECTED with 400, not silently reduced.** `POST /enrollment-keys`, `POST /enrollment-keys/:id/rotate`, the installer / installer-link download routes, and the device onboarding-token route all validate an explicit `ttlMinutes` (or `expiresAt`) against the partner's cap before doing anything else. A caller asking for more than the cap allows gets `400` with `{ "error": "ttlMinutes exceeds the partner maximum of <N> minutes" }` — the key is never created with a shorter TTL as a fallback.
- **A system-picked TTL is CLAMPED to the cap instead of rejected**, because there is no request to reject and no user to show an error to. This applies to:
  - the fresh child enrollment key minted when an installer is redeemed (`/s/:code`, `/bootstrap`),
  - the child enrollment key embedded in an installer download or installer link when the admin didn't pass an explicit `ttlMinutes` (`GET /enrollment-keys/:id/installer/:platform`, `POST /enrollment-keys/:id/installer-link`) — it falls back to the deployment default, which is then clamped,
  - the base TTL of a freshly-issued [installer bootstrap token](#installer-bootstrap-tokens) when the admin didn't choose an explicit expiry, and
  - deployment invites generated by the AI/MCP `send_deployment_invites` tool.

  In the dashboard, the **Link expires in** picker in the Add Device modal also hides any preset longer than the effective cap (for example, a 24-hour cap removes the 7-day/30-day/90-day/1-year options), so most admins never hit the 400 path at all — it exists for direct API/script callers and forged requests.

sections.heading: The practical consequence: this also shortens the completion window, not just the download window
sections.text:
A short cap doesn't just limit how long an installer link is downloadable. After an installer is run, it redeems its embedded bootstrap token and is issued a brand-new, single-use child enrollment key — and that child key's TTL is *also* clamped to the same partner cap. So a one-hour cap gives a machine **one hour from redemption** to complete the actual `POST /api/v1/agents/enroll` call, on top of however long the bootstrap token itself was valid for download.

In normal operation that gap is seconds. It stops being seconds — and starts producing "invalid or expired enrollment key" support tickets — whenever something delays the agent's first enrollment call after the installer runs: disk-imaging pipelines, a reboot baked into the install sequence, MDM-staged rollouts, or a machine that sits offline for a while right after setup. If enrollment fails on a machine that "was definitely installed within the download window," check whether a partner cap is also clamping the post-redemption completion window.

sections.heading: "Never expires" is not offered
sections.text:
There is no option to mint a key or installer link that never expires, by design. `installer_bootstrap_tokens.expires_at` is `NOT NULL` with a `CHECK (expires_at > created_at)` constraint at the database level — supporting "never" would need a migration to make the column nullable, plus null-handling added through issuance, the `/bootstrap` consume path, the daily purge sweep, and the expiry countdown in the dashboard UI. That is tracked as a follow-up, not implemented here.

---

sections.heading: Environment Variables
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `ENROLLMENT_KEY_DEFAULT_TTL_MINUTES` | `43200` | Default time-to-live for new enrollment keys when `expiresAt` is not specified. |
| `CHILD_ENROLLMENT_KEY_TTL_MINUTES` | `43200` | Fresh TTL (minutes) given to a "child" enrollment key minted at installer-download, installer-link, or short-code redemption time, measured from mint time rather than the parent key's remaining lifetime. Clamped to the partner's `maxEnrollmentLinkTtlMinutes` cap. |
| `INSTALLER_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN_TTL_MINUTES` | `10080` | Base TTL (minutes) for a freshly-issued [installer bootstrap token](#installer-bootstrap-tokens) when no explicit `ttlMinutes` is supplied. Maximum `43200` (30 days); a larger value is clamped, with a warning at API startup. The token's own expiry, not the parent enrollment key's, governs how long an installer has to complete enrollment. |
| `INSTALLER_PARENT_MIN_REMAINING_SECONDS` | `60` | Minimum remaining lifetime (seconds) a parent enrollment key must have to be used as an installer source. Guards against building an installer from a parent that expires before the download reaches the target machine. |
| `ENROLLMENT_KEY_PEPPER` | -- | Pepper used for SHA-256 hashing of enrollment keys. **Required in production** (at least 32 characters, not a placeholder value) — the server refuses to start without it. `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `SSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `JWT_SECRET`, and `SESSION_SECRET` are only consulted as legacy fallbacks when matching keys hashed before this requirement took effect. |
| `AGENT_ENROLLMENT_SECRET` | -- | Static secret that gates the enrollment endpoint in production. If empty or unset, the gate is skipped in non-production environments. |
| `ENROLLMENT_KEY_CLEANUP_ENABLED` | `true` | Set to `false` to disable the daily sweep that purges expired keys. |
| `ENROLLMENT_KEY_PURGE_AFTER_DAYS` | `7` | Grace period (in days past expiry) before the daily sweep hard-deletes an expired key. |

---

sections.heading: API Reference
sections.text:
All routes are prefixed with `/api/v1/enrollment-keys` and require JWT authentication.

| Method | Path | Permission | Description |
|--------|------|------------|-------------|
| `GET` | `/enrollment-keys` | `organizations:read` | List enrollment keys with pagination and filters. |
| `POST` | `/enrollment-keys` | `organizations:write` + MFA | Create a new enrollment key. Returns the raw key once. |
| `GET` | `/enrollment-keys/:id` | `organizations:read` | Get metadata for a single enrollment key (raw key not included). |
| `POST` | `/enrollment-keys/:id/rotate` | `organizations:write` + MFA | Regenerate key material, reset usage count. Returns the new raw key. |
| `DELETE` | `/enrollment-keys/:id` | `organizations:write` + MFA | Permanently delete an enrollment key. |
| `POST` | `/enrollment-keys/purge-expired` | `organizations:write` + MFA | Delete all expired enrollment keys in the caller's scope. Returns the number of keys deleted. |
| `GET` | `/enrollment-keys/:id/installer/:platform` | `organizations:read` | Download a pre-configured MSI or PKG installer. |
| `POST` | `/enrollment-keys/:id/installer-link` | `organizations:write` | Generate a public download link for an installer. |
| `GET` | `/enrollment-keys/public-download/:platform` | Token (public) | Download an installer via a public link token. |
| `GET` | `/s/:code` | Public (short code) | Auto-detects platform and redirects to the matching installer download. Increments enrollment-key usage atomically. |

The agent enrollment endpoint is separate:

| Method | Path | Auth | Description |
|--------|------|------|-------------|
| `POST` | `/api/v1/agents/enroll` | Enrollment secret + enrollment key | Register a new agent. No JWT required. |

---

sections.heading: Enrollment key rejected (401)
sections.text:
All enrollment-key rejections share the `401` status code, but each carries a distinct `reason` field and error message so you can tell them apart without guessing:

| `reason` | Error message | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| `enrollment_key_not_found` | "Enrollment key not recognized" | The SHA-256 hash of the provided key did not match any record — the key was rotated (an old value is still baked into an installer) or mistyped. This is also what you'll see if the server pepper changed since the key was created. |
| `enrollment_key_expired` | "Enrollment key has expired — regenerate the key or installer link and retry" | The `expiresAt` timestamp has passed. The default TTL is 30 days. |
| `enrollment_key_exhausted` | "Enrollment key has reached its maximum usage count — regenerate a fresh key or installer link" | `usageCount` has reached `maxUsage`. Check the key details via `GET /enrollment-keys/:id`. |
| `enrollment_key_race_lost` | "Enrollment key was just exhausted or expired — regenerate a fresh key or installer link" | Two agents enrolled with the same key at the same instant and this request lost the race for the last remaining use. |

All four stay on HTTP `401` (rather than `404`/`410`/`409`) for backward compatibility with older agents that don't parse the `reason` field.

sections.heading: "Enrollment secret required" (403)
sections.text: The `AGENT_ENROLLMENT_SECRET` environment variable is set in production but the agent did not provide it. Pass the secret via the `enrollmentSecret` field in the JSON body or the `x-agent-enrollment-secret` HTTP header.

sections.heading: "Invalid enrollment secret" (403)
sections.text: The provided enrollment secret does not match the configured `AGENT_ENROLLMENT_SECRET`. The comparison uses timing-safe equality to prevent timing attacks. Verify the secret value in your deployment configuration.

sections.heading: "Enrollment key must be associated with a site" (400)
sections.text: The enrollment key was created without a `siteId`. The enrollment endpoint requires every key to specify which site agents should be placed into. Delete this key and create a new one with a `siteId`.

sections.heading: "Device has been decommissioned" (403)
sections.text: This is not an enrollment-key error. Enrolling a new agent on a hostname whose prior device row was decommissioned now succeeds and creates a fresh device record — see [Re-enrollment](#re-enrollment). You'll see this 403 instead if an *already-enrolled* agent tries to connect (WebSocket, heartbeat, or Helper) using a token for a device that has since been decommissioned. Re-run `breeze-agent enroll` with a valid enrollment key to get a new device record and token.

sections.heading: "Organization context required" (403)
sections.text: An organization-scoped user attempted a key management operation without a valid `orgId` in their session. This usually indicates a misconfigured user account.

sections.heading: "No enrollment key pepper configured" (server startup)
sections.text: `ENROLLMENT_KEY_PEPPER` must be set in production — at least 32 characters and not a known placeholder/insecure value — or the server refuses to start. The legacy fallback variables (`APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `SSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `JWT_SECRET`, `SESSION_SECRET`) are only used to verify keys hashed before this requirement took effect; they do not satisfy the startup check. Without `ENROLLMENT_KEY_PEPPER`, enrollment key hashes would be vulnerable to rainbow table attacks.

sections.heading: Key appears valid but agent fails to connect after enrollment
sections.text:
- Verify the `authToken` returned by enrollment is stored correctly in the agent config file.
- Check that `secrets.yaml` permissions are `0600` (owner read/write only) and `agent.yaml` is `0644`.
- Ensure the agent is connecting to the correct WebSocket URL (`/api/v1/agents/:id/ws`) with the `Authorization: Bearer brz_...` header.

title: Enrollment
description: How Breeze agent enrollment and authentication works, covering the enrollment flow, brz_ token generation, SHA-256 hashed storage, and validation.
headings: Reusing a hostname for a decommissioned device

sections.heading: Enrollment Flow
sections.text:
```
Agent                                 API Server
  │                                      │
  │─── POST /api/v1/agents/enroll ──────►│
  │    { enrollmentKey, hostname,        │
  │      osType, architecture,           │
  │      enrollmentSecret }              │
  │                                      │
  │    Validate enrollment secret        │
  │    Create device record              │
  │    Generate brz_ token               │
  │    Hash token (SHA-256) → store      │
  │    Issue mTLS cert (if configured)   │
  │                                      │
  │◄── 201 { authToken, deviceId,   ─────│
  │         orgId, siteId, mtls? }       │
  │                                      │
  │    Store config to disk              │
  │    Connect WebSocket                 │
  │                                      │
  │─── WS /agents/:id/ws ──────────────►│
  │    Authorization: Bearer brz_...     │
  │                                      │
  │◄── { type: "connected" } ────────────│
  │                                      │
  │─── { type: "heartbeat", ... } ──────►│
  │                                      │
```

sections.heading: Full Enrollment Response
sections.text:
The `201` response carries more than the `authToken` shown in the diagram above. In full, it is:

```json
{
  "agentId": "uuid",
  "deviceId": "uuid",
  "authToken": "brz_...",
  "watchdogAuthToken": "brz_...",
  "helperAuthToken": "brz_...",
  "orgId": "uuid",
  "siteId": "uuid",
  "backupServerUrl": "https://backup.example.com",
  "config": { "heartbeatIntervalSeconds": 60, "metricsCollectionIntervalSeconds": 30 },
  "mtls": { "...": "..." },
  "manifestTrustKeys": [ "..." ],
  "manifestKeyDelegations": [ "..." ]
}
```

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `watchdogAuthToken` | Separate `brz_` token for [`breeze-watchdog`](/agents/building/#other-agent-binaries) to authenticate its own restart-monitoring calls. |
| `helperAuthToken` | Separate token for the [Helper](/agents/helper/) process -- distinct from the agent's own `authToken`. |
| `backupServerUrl` | Present only when `AGENT_BACKUP_SERVER_URL` is configured server-side; tells `breeze-backup` where to ship vault data. |
| `manifestTrustKeys` / `manifestKeyDelegations` | The current release-artifact signing trust keyset and any active key delegations, used to verify signed agent updates. See [Sign Your Own Agent Packages](/deploy/sign-your-own-packages/). |

sections.heading: Token Security
sections.text:
Agent tokens follow the `brz_` prefix convention:

- **Generation**: Cryptographically random, 32-byte hex string with `brz_` prefix
- **Storage (server)**: Only the SHA-256 hash is stored in the `agentTokenHash` column
- **Storage (agent)**: The raw token is stored in `secrets.yaml` with `0600` permissions (the main `agent.yaml` config uses `0644` so the Helper can read it)
- **Validation**: API hashes incoming tokens and compares against stored hash
- **Same pattern as API keys** (`apiKeyAuth.ts`)

  The `agentTokenHash` column is nullable to support migration of pre-existing devices. New enrollments always populate the hash.

sections.heading: Enrollment Keys
sections.text:
Enrollment keys are created in the dashboard and can be scoped to:

- **Organization** — devices enroll into a specific org
- **Site** — devices enroll into a specific site within an org
- **Expiry** — keys expire after a configurable TTL (default: 30 days, via `ENROLLMENT_KEY_DEFAULT_TTL_MINUTES`)
- **Usage limit** — keys can be limited to a number of uses

sections.heading: Bulk Enrollment
sections.text:
For deploying agents at scale from a script:

```bash
# Keep the enrollment secret out of the command line / shell history.
# BREEZE_AGENT_ENROLLMENT_SECRET is the only environment variable the
# agent reads — there is no server-URL env var.
export BREEZE_AGENT_ENROLLMENT_SECRET=your-secret

breeze-agent enroll YOUR_ENROLLMENT_KEY --server https://breeze.yourdomain.com
```

The enrollment key is a required positional argument, and the server URL must
come from the `--server` flag (or an existing `agent.yaml` on a pre-staged
image — see
[Pre-Staging Without Enrollment](/agents/advanced-install/#pre-staging-without-enrollment)).
The site is determined by the enrollment key on the server side. The agent
reads `BREEZE_AGENT_ENROLLMENT_SECRET` from the environment when the
`--enrollment-secret` flag isn't provided.

For fleet-wide rollout recipes (GPO, Intune, JAMF, Ansible), see the
[Mass Deployment guide](/migration/mass-deployment/).

sections.heading: Re-enrollment
sections.text:
If an agent's token is compromised or the device needs to be reassigned:

1. **Revoke the device** in the dashboard (invalidates the token hash)
2. **Delete the config** on the device:
   - Linux: `sudo rm /etc/breeze/agent.yaml /etc/breeze/secrets.yaml`
   - macOS: `sudo rm "/Library/Application Support/Breeze/agent.yaml" "/Library/Application Support/Breeze/secrets.yaml"`
   - Windows: `Remove-Item C:\ProgramData\Breeze\agent.yaml, C:\ProgramData\Breeze\secrets.yaml`
3. **Re-enroll**: `sudo breeze-agent enroll YOUR_ENROLLMENT_KEY --server ... --enrollment-secret ...`

sections.heading: Reusing a hostname for a decommissioned device
sections.text:
When a device row is **decommissioned** in the dashboard, the original device id is retired but the hostname is free to be claimed again. Running `breeze-agent enroll` from a new install on the same hostname creates a fresh device record (new id, new token) rather than failing with a hostname collision. The decommissioned row stays in audit history for compliance — the new device is treated as a distinct asset from day one.

The only exception is if the decommissioned device's token was suspended for a security reason (for example, a cross-tenant access probe). In that case re-enrollment is blocked with a `409 Conflict` until an administrator reviews the previous incident. The response includes the reason so the technician on-site knows to escalate rather than retry.

title: Breeze Helper
description: System tray companion app for end users with AI chat, vision-based screen analysis, computer control, and self-service troubleshooting tools.
headings: How the Helper receives its token

sections.text:
The Breeze Helper is a companion application that runs in the end user's desktop session alongside the Breeze agent service. It provides a system tray icon with status indicators, an AI-powered chat interface for self-service troubleshooting, vision-based screen analysis, and computer control capabilities. The Helper bridges the gap between the background agent service (which runs as SYSTEM/root in Session 0) and the interactive user session where display, input, and notification APIs are available.

The Helper is designed for **end users**, not IT administrators. It speaks in simple, non-technical language and uses a filtered subset of AI tools appropriate for the permission level configured by the organization. Destructive operations always require explicit approval before they reach the device.

  The Helper requires the Breeze agent to be enrolled and connected. It authenticates to the API using its own helper-scoped `brz_`-prefixed token — issued alongside, but distinct from, the agent's own token — and communicates with the agent service over a local IPC socket. Each request also re-checks the device credential's lifecycle state (suspended, decommissioned, quarantined, or an inactive tenant), and the Helper's database access is scoped to its own organization only, with no partner-wide access.

---

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
The Helper serves three audiences:

| Audience | Use Case |
|----------|----------|
| **End users** | Self-service troubleshooting, AI chat for common IT questions, disk cleanup, service restarts |
| **IT administrators** | Remote vision-based diagnostics, screenshot capture, computer control for hands-free remediation |
| **MSPs / Partners** | White-labeled tray presence on customer machines, org-level feature toggles |

Key capabilities:

- **AI Chat** -- conversational interface powered by Claude, scoped to the local device
- **Vision Troubleshooting** -- screenshot capture and AI analysis of what is on screen
- **Computer Control** -- AI-driven mouse and keyboard interaction for guided fixes
- **Self-Service Tools** -- disk cleanup, service management, alert viewing, security posture checks
- **System Tray** -- persistent status indicator with contextual menu items
- **Desktop Notifications** -- IT-initiated notifications delivered to the user's session

---

sections.heading: Installation
sections.text:
The Helper can be deployed automatically via config policy or installed manually. On Windows, the agent downloads the MSI installer, runs it silently, and the session broker spawns the Helper into the user's desktop session. On macOS, the agent downloads the DMG, mounts and copies the app to `/Applications`. On Linux, the agent downloads the AppImage. The agent also detects headless mode (macOS LaunchDaemon, Linux systemd) and routes desktop commands through IPC to the Helper instead of attempting direct screen capture.

  **Windows:**

The Helper is spawned automatically by the Breeze agent service when a user logs in. The session broker (`sessionbroker/spawner_windows.go`) detects active user sessions and launches the Helper process using `CreateProcessAsUser` with a SYSTEM token, targeting the user's desktop session ID.

No manual installation is required. The Helper binary is bundled with the agent installer.

```
C:\Program Files\Breeze Helper\Breeze Helper.exe
```

  **Linux:**

Install the user helper and enable it as a user-level systemd service:

```bash
sudo make install-user-helper
systemctl --user enable breeze-agent-user
systemctl --user start breeze-agent-user
```

The Helper connects to the agent service via a Unix domain socket at `/var/run/breeze/agent.sock`.

  **macOS:**

On macOS, the Helper auto-installs the first time a remote desktop connection is initiated -- no manual setup is needed. The agent downloads and configures the Helper automatically.

For manual installation, use the LaunchAgent:

```bash
sudo make install-user-helper
# LaunchAgent auto-starts at login
```

The LaunchAgent plist is installed to `/Library/LaunchAgents/com.breeze.agent-user.plist` and starts automatically when the user logs in.

sections.heading: Verifying the Helper Is Running
sections.text:
The Helper announces its capabilities to the agent service immediately after authenticating over IPC. Check the agent logs for confirmation:

```
user helper connected and authenticated agentId=<device-id>
```

The IPC authentication handshake includes:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `ProtocolVersion` | IPC protocol version for compatibility checks |
| `UID` / `SID` | Unix UID or Windows SID of the logged-in user |
| `Username` | Current username |
| `SessionID` | Unique helper session identifier (`helper-<username>-<pid>`) |
| `DisplayEnv` | Display server: `windows`, `quartz`, `x11:<DISPLAY>`, or `wayland:<WAYLAND_DISPLAY>` |
| `PID` | Helper process ID |
| `BinaryHash` | SHA-256 hash of the Helper binary for integrity verification |
| `WinSessionID` | Windows session ID (for Session 0 routing) |

After authentication, the Helper sends a capabilities message reporting what it can do in the current session:

| Capability | Description |
|------------|-------------|
| `CanNotify` | Desktop notifications available (requires display) |
| `CanTray` | System tray icon available (requires display) |
| `CanCapture` | Screen capture available (requires display) |
| `CanClipboard` | Clipboard access available (requires display) |
| `DisplayServer` | Active display server string |

sections.heading: Console User Tracking (macOS)
sections.text:
On macOS, the Helper tracks console user changes and automatically tears down stale sessions when the active user switches. This ensures that remote desktop sessions, screen captures, and input actions are always routed to the correct user session -- even on shared machines where multiple users log in throughout the day.

No configuration is required. The Helper detects user switches via the system console and cleans up automatically.

---

sections.heading: AI Chat
sections.text: The Helper provides a conversational AI interface for end users. Chat sessions are powered by Claude and scoped to the single device where the Helper is running. The AI assistant can view device details, analyze performance metrics, check security posture, manage alerts, browse files, and more -- all through natural language.

sections.heading: Creating a Chat Session
sections.text:
1. Click the Breeze tray icon and select **Chat** (or open the Helper window).

2. The Helper authenticates to the API using the agent's bearer token and creates a new AI session.

3. Type a question or describe an issue. The AI responds using real device data from the tools available at your permission level.

4. Sessions persist for 24 hours. You can resume a previous session or start a new one.

sections.heading: Session Architecture
sections.text:
```
User types message
  → Helper app (Tauri frontend)
  → POST /helper/chat/sessions/:id/messages
    Authorization: Bearer brz_<helper-token>
  → API validates helper token (SHA-256 hash lookup)
  → Pre-flight: session validity, rate limit, budget check, input sanitization
  → Streaming session manager invokes Claude with filtered tool set
  → SSE stream returns AI response chunks + tool execution events
  → Helper renders response in chat UI
```

Each session is stored in the `ai_sessions` table with a `contextSnapshot` that records the source as `helper`, the device ID, hostname, OS type, permission level, and optionally the logged-in username (`helperUser`).

sections.heading: Session Constraints
sections.text:
| Constraint | Value |
|------------|-------|
| Maximum session age | 24 hours |
| Rate limit | 30 messages per 60 seconds per device |
| Maximum message length | 10,000 characters |
| Turn limit | Configured per session (default from `ai_sessions.maxTurns`) |
| Model | The partner's or platform's default AI model, resolved when the session is created (Claude Sonnet 5.5 by default from v0.120.0); an existing session keeps its model |
| Budget | Org-level AI budget applies; sessions are rejected when budget is exhausted |

sections.heading: Tool Permission Levels
sections.text:
The Helper uses a tiered tool whitelist that controls which AI tools are available. The permission level is set when creating a session and stored in the session's `contextSnapshot`. Every tool available to the Helper is single-device — org-wide enumeration tools like `query_devices` or `get_fleet_health` are never available here, no matter the permission level, because the Helper's identity is pinned to the one device it runs on.

| Tool | Basic | Standard | Extended |
|------|:-----:|:--------:|:--------:|
| `get_device_details` | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `analyze_metrics` | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `analyze_disk_usage` | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `get_cis_device_report` | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `get_security_posture` | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `take_screenshot` | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `analyze_screen` | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `search_logs` | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `get_active_users` | -- | Yes | Yes |
| `get_user_experience_metrics` | -- | Yes | Yes |
| `manage_alerts` | -- | Yes | Yes |
| `manage_services` | -- | Yes | Yes |
| `disk_cleanup` | -- | Yes | Yes |
| `file_operations` | -- | Yes | Yes |
| `computer_control` | -- | -- | Yes |
| `execute_command` | -- | -- | Yes |
| `security_scan` | -- | -- | Yes |
| `s1_isolate_device` | -- | -- | Yes |
| `network_discovery` | -- | -- | Yes |
| `apply_cis_remediation` | -- | -- | Yes |

  The **extended** permission level grants access to `computer_control`, `execute_command`, `security_scan`, `s1_isolate_device`, `network_discovery`, and `apply_cis_remediation`. `security_scan` and `network_discovery` are Tier 3; `execute_command` is Tier 2 for a handful of read-only command types (`list_processes`, `file_list`, `event_logs_list`) and Tier 3 for everything else — but on the Helper path, PAM governs any Tier ≥ 2 tool call regardless of that split, so all of these still require explicit approval before execution here. Only enable extended mode for trusted environments where end users should be able to trigger device commands.

The default permission level is `basic`. Organizations can raise it via a configuration policy's **Breeze Assist** feature link, applied at the partner, organization, site, device-group, or device level (most specific wins). There is no way to set it directly through the Helper configuration endpoint — `GET /helper/config` reports the resolved level but does not accept writes.

---

sections.heading: Vision Troubleshooting
sections.text: The Helper can capture the user's screen and send it to the AI for analysis. This is useful when an end user describes a visual problem ("my screen looks weird", "there's an error dialog I don't understand") and the AI needs to see what they see.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.text:
1. The AI invokes the `take_screenshot` tool during a chat conversation.

2. The Helper captures the screen using platform-native APIs (DXGI on Windows, Core Graphics on macOS, X11 on Linux -- Wayland-only sessions are not supported yet). These APIs are only available in the user session, not in Session 0 -- this is why the Helper exists.

3. The screenshot is uploaded to the API via `POST /helper/screenshots` as a base64-encoded image.

4. The AI receives the screenshot and analyzes it using vision capabilities to identify error dialogs, misconfigurations, or UI anomalies.

5. The AI explains what it sees in plain language and suggests next steps.

sections.heading: Screenshot Storage
sections.text:
| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `deviceId` | Device the screenshot was captured on |
| `orgId` | Organization scope |
| `sessionId` | AI session that triggered the capture (optional) |
| `capturedBy` | Always `helper` for Helper-initiated screenshots |
| `retentionHours` | 24 hours (auto-deleted after expiration) |
| `maxSize` | 2 MB (base64 encoded, ~1.5 MB raw) |

  Screenshots are stored with a 24-hour retention policy and automatically deleted. They are scoped to the organization and device, and are not accessible outside the originating AI session.

sections.heading: Screen Analysis
sections.text:
The `analyze_screen` tool goes beyond simple screenshot capture. It interprets the visual content and provides structured analysis:

- Identifies error dialogs, warning banners, and notification toasts
- Reads text from UI elements (application titles, status bars, error messages)
- Recognizes common application states (loading screens, login prompts, crash dialogs)
- Suggests remediation steps based on what it observes

---

sections.heading: Computer Control
sections.text:
When enabled (extended permission level only), the AI can interact with the user's desktop by controlling the mouse and keyboard. This allows the AI to perform guided fixes -- clicking buttons, typing commands, navigating menus -- while explaining each step to the user.

Computer control commands are dispatched from the API to the agent service, then forwarded over IPC to the Helper process running in the user's session. The Helper executes the commands using platform-native input APIs (SendInput on Windows, Core Graphics events on macOS, XTest on Linux).

  Computer control is a powerful capability. The AI always explains what it intends to do before acting, and destructive operations require user approval. The `computer_control` tool is only available at the `extended` permission level -- it is not available at `basic` or `standard`.

sections.heading: Supported Actions
sections.text:
| Action | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| Mouse move | Move cursor to specific screen coordinates |
| Mouse click | Left, right, or middle click at coordinates |
| Mouse double-click | Double-click at coordinates |
| Keyboard input | Type text or press key combinations |
| Scroll | Scroll up or down at current position |

sections.heading: Command Flow
sections.text:
```
AI decides to click a button
  → tool call: computer_control { action: "click", x: 450, y: 320 }
  → API sends command to agent via WebSocket
  → Agent forwards to Helper via IPC (TypeCommand)
  → Helper executes ComputerAction in user session
  → Result returned through IPC → WebSocket → AI
```

---

sections.heading: Self-Service Tools
sections.text:
At the **standard** permission level and above, end users can perform common IT tasks through the AI chat without contacting their IT team:

| Task | Tool | What It Does |
|------|------|-------------|
| Check disk space | `analyze_disk_usage` | Shows what is consuming disk space with cleanup candidates |
| Clean up disk | `disk_cleanup` | Previews and removes temp files, browser cache, trash |
| View alerts | `manage_alerts` | Lists active alerts for this device, acknowledges them |
| Restart a service | `manage_services` | Lists, starts, stops, or restarts system services |
| Browse files | `file_operations` | Lists and reads files (write/delete requires extended level) |
| Check security | `get_security_posture` | Shows device security score and recommendations |
| View metrics | `analyze_metrics` | Analyzes CPU, RAM, disk, and network trends |
| Search logs | `search_logs` | Searches agent diagnostic logs |

All self-service actions are scoped to the single device where the Helper is running. The AI uses the device ID from the Helper's authentication context and cannot access other devices in the organization.

---

sections.heading: Organization Controls
sections.text: Organizations can enable or disable the Helper on a per-org basis. The toggle is delivered to agents through the heartbeat response, so changes take effect within 60 seconds without requiring an agent restart.

sections.heading: Enabling / Disabling Helper Chat
sections.text:
The Helper toggle is managed through organization settings or the **Deploy Breeze Assist to devices** toggle on a configuration policy's **Breeze Helper** feature (the policy takes precedence when one applies). A newly created Breeze Helper policy feature starts with the toggle on. When a device's effective Helper setting is off, the agent stops and removes a Helper it installed on its next heartbeat, and the Helper API refuses every request from that device with `403` and code `helper_disabled` ("Breeze Helper is disabled for this device by policy"), so a client can tell it apart from a credential failure.

```bash
# Check current helper settings (returned in heartbeat response)
# The heartbeat response includes:
{
  "helperEnabled": true | false
}
```

The agent reads `helperEnabled` from each heartbeat response. When the effective setting turns off, the agent stops the Helper in every user session and uninstalls it, provided the agent installed it.

The agent records each Helper install it makes. A Helper installed another way (Intune, a software policy, or by hand) is left alone while the setting is off: the agent does not start, update or remove it, and the device page reports it as not installed by Breeze (`helperInstallIssue: unmanaged_install`). Turning the setting on adopts that copy when the agent installs the next Helper version the server offers.

On Windows the agent also checks the WebView2 Runtime before it starts the Helper. If the runtime is older than the installed Helper build needs, the agent does not start the Helper and the device reports `webview2_outdated`; update the WebView2 Runtime on the device to clear it. A Helper that keeps closing right after it starts is reported as `crash_loop`, with the exit codes in the agent log, and the agent tries it again after 6 hours or when a new Helper version is installed.

The device page's **Breeze Assist** row shows the last reported state: **Installed**, **Not deployed**, or **Unavailable** with the reason (`webview2_outdated`, `crash_loop` or `unmanaged_install`). In the device list these three show as **Assist unavailable**, with the reason in the tooltip, because Assist is on disk in each case. All of this needs agent 0.125.0; an older server shows the new reasons as unknown.

**Known issue in v0.125.0:**
  Crash-loop detection does not fire yet: a crash-looping Helper keeps restarting and is not reported as `crash_loop` ([#10302](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/issues/10302)).

sections.heading: Window and Tray Behavior
sections.text:
The Helper always runs in the user's session and always shows its tray icon. Its main window starts **hidden**: the agent launches the Helper at logon, after agent or Helper updates, and whenever its session watcher restarts an exited Helper, and none of these put a window on screen. The user opens the window by clicking the tray icon or choosing **Open Breeze Assist** from the tray menu (always present, even when a policy turns off every other item). On macOS, re-opening the app from the Dock or Finder also shows it. Closing the window hides it back to the tray.

The tray menu has no **Exit** item. The agent restarts an exited Helper within about 30 seconds, so Exit only made the window come back. Launching the Helper by hand (Start menu, Dock, double-click) opens the window. The agent always passes `--config`, and a launch without it counts as manual; `--show` forces the window open in either case. On Windows, launching it again while it already runs in the tray shows the running instance's window instead of starting a second copy.

Policies saved before this change may still store `showTrayIcon` in the Breeze Assist inline settings. The key is ignored and dropped the next time the policy is saved.

sections.heading: Configuration Endpoint
sections.text:
The Helper retrieves its configuration on startup:

```
GET /helper/config
Authorization: Bearer brz_<helper-token>
```

**Response:**

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `enabled` | boolean | Always `true` today -- this field does not yet reflect the org's Helper chat toggle. See [Enabling / Disabling Helper Chat](#enabling--disabling-helper-chat), which uses a separate `helperEnabled` flag on the agent heartbeat response instead. |
| `permissionLevel` | string | The resolved permission level for this device: `basic`, `standard`, or `extended` (see [Tool Permission Levels](#tool-permission-levels)) |
| `allowScreenCapture` | boolean | Always `true` today -- not currently configurable |
| `sessionRetentionHours` | number | Always `24` today -- not currently configurable |

---

sections.heading: Process Model
sections.text:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│  Agent Service (Session 0)      │
│  - Runs as SYSTEM / root        │
│  - WebSocket to API server      │
│  - Heartbeat, commands, patching│
│  - IPC server (Unix socket /    │
│    named pipe)                  │
├─────────────┬───────────────────┤
│             │ IPC               │
│             ▼                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ Helper (User Session)   │   │
│  │ - System tray icon      │   │
│  │ - AI chat UI            │   │
│  │ - Screen capture (DXGI/ │   │
│  │   CoreGraphics/X11)     │   │
│  │ - Input injection       │   │
│  │ - Desktop notifications │   │
│  │ - Script execution      │   │
│  │   (user context)        │   │
│  └─────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────┘
```

sections.heading: Windows Helper Lifecycle (Always-On vs. On-Demand)
sections.text:
On Windows the agent service starts the helper processes itself, one per interactive session, in two roles: a **SYSTEM helper** (screen capture, input, the PAM approval dialog and consent-prompt handling) and a **user helper** (tray, chat, notifications, user-context scripts). How many it keeps running depends on the lifecycle mode:

| Mode | Behavior |
|------|----------|
| `always-on` | A SYSTEM helper and a user helper in every eligible session, all the time. Default on workstations and on Windows Server without the RD Session Host role. |
| `on-demand` | No helpers at rest. A helper is started when an operation needs one (a remote desktop connection or a script targeted at a session) and stopped about two minutes after the operation ends. Default on RD Session Hosts, where one helper per session per user adds up. |

**PAM on on-demand hosts.** While the device's effective PAM policy has UAC interception enabled, an on-demand host also keeps a SYSTEM helper in every session a user is signed into. The SYSTEM helper shows the elevation dialog and handles `consent.exe`, and a UAC prompt can appear at any time. Sessions at the logon screen and disconnected sessions get no PAM helper. User helpers stay on-demand. When the policy turns interception off, those SYSTEM helpers are stopped on the next reconcile. If an elevation request arrives before the helper for that session is up (for example, right after the user signs in), the agent starts one for that session and waits up to 30 seconds for it. If no helper comes up, the agent logs an error. When it gives up on the request (the session exists but is not active or connected, or the helper did not start: crash cooldown, repeated failures, or not ready within the 30-second wait, after which the user's UAC prompt is no longer being handled), it reports that to the server. When it cannot tell (the session could not be resolved, the session check itself failed or the session was not in the list, the session dropped out of the list while the agent waited, the helper lease was refused, the helper came up but the agent could not find it, or the agent is still starting and its helper manager is not up yet), it leaves the request pending for the stale-request expiry (`PAM_PENDING_REQUEST_TTL_MINUTES`, 15 minutes by default) rather than close a request it might still handle. A request still waiting for a technician is then closed as expired, so nobody can approve it, and the PAM requests list shows that the device could not act under its Expired or All filter, with the agent's reason as a tooltip. Agents older than this report leave the request pending until the stale-request expiry closes it.

**Choosing the mode.** The agent resolves the mode in this order:

1. **Local agent config.** `helper_lifecycle_mode` in `agent.yaml`, or the `BREEZE_HELPER_LIFECYCLE_MODE` environment variable. Values: `always-on`, `on-demand`, or `auto`. Use this when you need to override the mode on one machine. It always wins, so the policy setting below has no effect on that device. Restart the agent service after changing it.
2. **Configuration policy.** The **Helper lifecycle on RD Session Hosts** setting on the policy's Breeze Helper feature (`auto`, `always-on`, `on-demand`). Applied live from the heartbeat.
3. **Auto-detection.** With neither set (or both `auto`), RD Session Hosts run on-demand and every other machine runs always-on.

```yaml
# agent.yaml: force a helper in every session on this host
helper_lifecycle_mode: always-on
```

The agent logs the resolved mode at startup (`helper lifecycle mode resolved`, with `mode`, `rdsHost`, and `override` fields) and reports it in its heartbeat.

sections.heading: IPC Message Types
sections.text:
The Helper communicates with the agent service over a local IPC connection (Unix domain socket on Linux/macOS, named pipe on Windows). Messages are typed envelopes with JSON payloads.

| Message Type | Direction | Description |
|-------------|-----------|-------------|
| `auth_request` | Helper -> Agent | Authentication handshake with user identity and binary hash |
| `auth_response` | Agent -> Helper | Accepted/rejected with session key and allowed scopes |
| `capabilities` | Helper -> Agent | Report display, notification, capture, clipboard capabilities |
| `command` | Agent -> Helper | Execute a command in the user session (scripts, screenshots, computer actions) |
| `command_result` | Helper -> Agent | Command execution result with status, output, and error |
| `notify` | Agent -> Helper | Show a desktop notification to the user. May carry a list of buttons, in which case the Helper draws a real modal dialog rather than a passing toast |
| `notify_result` | Helper -> Agent | Whether the notification was delivered, and which button the user pressed |
| `tray_update` | Agent -> Helper | Update tray icon status, tooltip, and menu items |
| `desktop_start` | Agent -> Helper | Start a remote desktop capture session |
| `desktop_stop` | Agent -> Helper | Stop a remote desktop capture session |
| `desktop_input` | Agent -> Helper | Forward mouse/keyboard input to the user's desktop |
| `clipboard_get` | Agent -> Helper | Read clipboard contents from the user session |
| `clipboard_set` | Agent -> Helper | Write content to the user session clipboard |
| `sas_request` | Helper -> Agent | Request Ctrl+Alt+Del (Secure Attention Sequence) via the SCM service |
| `sas_response` | Agent -> Helper | SAS request result |
| `ping` / `pong` | Bidirectional | Keepalive (5-second interval) |
| `disconnect` | Either | Graceful shutdown signal |

**Restart prompts on Linux do not use the Helper:**
  The end-user restart prompt described in [Patch Management](/features/patch-management/) is drawn by the Helper on Windows and macOS, through the `notify` message above. There is no Helper binary for Linux — on a Linux endpoint the agent itself draws the dialog in the signed-in user's graphical session using `zenity`, and falls back to a plain `notify-send` notification (which the user cannot postpone from) when `zenity` is not installed.

sections.heading: Session Security
sections.text:
- **Authentication**: The Helper sends its UID/SID, username, PID, and a SHA-256 hash of its own binary. The agent service validates these against expected values.
- **Session key**: After authentication, the agent issues a hex-encoded session key used for subsequent message integrity.
- **Scoped access**: The agent controls which IPC message types the Helper is allowed to receive via `AllowedScopes`.
- **API authentication**: Chat requests to the API use a dedicated helper-scoped `brz_` bearer token -- issued at enrollment alongside, but distinct from, the agent's own token -- validated by SHA-256 hash lookup against the `devices.helperTokenHash` column (not `agentTokenHash`).
- **Org isolation**: All API queries include an organization condition derived from the device's `orgId`, ensuring the Helper cannot access data from other organizations.

sections.heading: How the Helper receives its token
sections.text:
The agent hands the helper-scoped token to the Helper over the authenticated local IPC channel, and the Helper prefers that copy (v0.119.0+). On disk the token is kept only in the agent's protected secrets file (`secrets.yaml`, readable by SYSTEM/Administrators on Windows and by root on Linux and macOS). It is no longer written to `agent.yaml` on any platform (v0.120.0+).

- **Windows:** the IPC channel is the only way the Helper gets its token. When an upgraded agent first starts, it moves any token an older agent left in `agent.yaml` into `secrets.yaml` and then rotates the token once, on its next successful heartbeat. The Helper keeps working through the rotation: the agent keeps delivering the old token until the server confirms the new one, then pushes the new one.
- **macOS and Linux:** unchanged. The Helper also receives the token over IPC, with the `breeze`-group `helper_token.yaml` file as its on-disk fallback.

**Windows: Breeze Assist works only in the console session:**
  On Windows the agent delivers the token only to the Helper running in the **active console session**. A Helper running in an RDP or other non-console session does not receive it and shows a message that it has not received its credentials. This is a known limitation in v0.120.0.

  A Helper older than v0.119.0 that starts after the agent upgrade reports that it is still setting up until the Helper update installs; one that was already running keeps working.

---

sections.heading: Helper Chat
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| POST | `/helper/chat/sessions` | Create a new AI chat session |
| GET | `/helper/chat/sessions` | List chat sessions for this device |
| POST | `/helper/chat/sessions/:id/messages` | Send a message and receive SSE response stream |
| GET | `/helper/chat/sessions/:id/messages` | Load message history for a session |
| POST | `/helper/chat/sessions/:id/tool-results` | Report the outcome of a client-declared tool call (see below) |
| POST | `/helper/chat/sessions/:id/flag` | Flag a session for admin review, with an optional `reason` |
| DELETE | `/helper/chat/sessions/:id` | Close a chat session |

Some tools run on the end-user's machine rather than the server -- for example, a client-side confirmation dialog. For those, the SSE stream's `tool_use` event parks the call instead of resolving it immediately, and the Helper process reports the result back via `POST /helper/chat/sessions/:id/tool-results` with `{ toolUseId, output }` (or `{ toolUseId, error }` on failure). The server persists the outcome as a `tool_result` message so it renders the same way on reload as a server-executed tool.

sections.heading: Helper Configuration & Screenshots
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| GET | `/helper/config` | Get Helper configuration for this device |
| GET | `/helper/device-info` | Get basic device details (hostname, OS, status, agent version) for the authenticated device |
| POST | `/helper/screenshots` | Upload a screenshot for AI analysis |

  All Helper endpoints require a valid helper bearer token (`Authorization: Bearer brz_...`) -- a separate credential from the agent's own token, issued to the device at enrollment time. The token is validated by hashing with SHA-256 and matching against the `helperTokenHash` column in the `devices` table. Decommissioned and quarantined devices are rejected with 403, and so is a device whose effective Helper setting is off (`helper_disabled`).

sections.heading: Creating a Session
sections.text:
```bash
POST /helper/chat/sessions
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer brz_<helper-token>

{
  "helperUser": "jsmith"
}
```

`helperUser` is optional and associates the session with a specific logged-in user for filtering. Permission level is not a request field -- the request body accepts only `helperUser` and `clientTools`. The level is always resolved server-side from the device's configuration-policy assignment (see [Tool Permission Levels](#tool-permission-levels)); a `permissionLevel` field sent in the body is silently ignored.

**Response (201):**

```json
{
  "id": "uuid",
  "orgId": "uuid"
}
```

sections.heading: Sending a Message
sections.text:
```bash
POST /helper/chat/sessions/:id/messages
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer brz_<helper-token>

{
  "content": "Why is my computer running slowly?"
}
```

The response is an SSE stream. Events include:

| Event | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `text_delta` | Incremental text from the AI response |
| `tool_use` | AI is invoking a tool (includes tool name and parameters) |
| `tool_result` | Tool execution result |
| `approval_required` | A Tier 2+ tool call is waiting on PAM approval (see below) |
| `title_updated` | Session title was auto-generated from the first message |
| `done` | Stream complete |
| `error` | An error occurred during processing |

sections.heading: Tool Approval
sections.text:
The end user does not approve tool calls from inside the Helper chat -- there is no endpoint for that. When the AI wants to run a Tier 2+ tool, it opens a PAM (Privileged Access Management) elevation request instead: the `approval_required` event above lets the Helper UI show a "waiting for approval" state, and an administrator decides the request out-of-band via `POST /pam/elevation-requests/:id/respond` (or the PAM Requests tab in the dashboard). See [PAM](/security/pam/) for the full elevation-request lifecycle.

---

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**Helper tray icon does not appear.**
The Helper requires a display server to show the tray icon. On Linux, verify that `DISPLAY` or `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` is set in the user session. On Windows, the Helper is spawned by the session broker -- check agent logs for "starting helper in session" messages. If the agent service is not running, the Helper cannot start.

**"Invalid agent credentials" when Helper tries to chat.**
The Helper authenticates to the API using its own helper-scoped `brz_` token, separate from the agent's own token. If the device was re-enrolled or the token was rotated, the Helper's cached token may be stale. Restart the agent service to pick up the new token. Also verify the device is not in `decommissioned` or `quarantined` status.

**Breeze Assist says it has not received its credentials (Windows).**
On Windows the Helper gets its token only over IPC from the agent, and only in the active console session. If the user is connected over RDP or another non-console session, Assist cannot get a token there (a known limitation). In a console session, confirm the agent service is running and the Helper is v0.119.0 or later; an older Helper reports that it is still setting up until its update installs.

**AI chat returns "Rate limit exceeded."**
The Helper enforces a rate limit of 30 messages per 60 seconds per device. Wait for the window to reset before sending another message. If multiple users share a device, they share the same rate limit.

**AI chat returns "Unable to verify budget."**
The organization's AI budget may be exhausted or the budget service is temporarily unavailable. Contact your IT administrator to check the org AI budget in **Settings > AI Configuration**.

**Screenshot capture fails.**
Screen capture requires display access. On Windows, DXGI requires the Helper to be running in the user's desktop session (not Session 0). On Linux, the Helper needs access to an X11 display; Wayland-only sessions cannot be captured yet -- the device page shows **Wayland Unsupported**, or, where XWayland is running, capture attaches to it and shows only X11 application windows (see [Supported Linux Distributions](/agents/installation/#supported-linux-distributions)). Check that `CanCapture` is `true` in the capabilities message logged at startup.

**Computer control actions have no effect.**
Input injection requires the Helper to have appropriate permissions. On Windows, the Helper runs with a SYSTEM token that can `OpenInputDesktop(GENERIC_ALL)` for UAC and lock screen access. On Linux, `XTest` extension must be available. On macOS, the Helper needs Accessibility permissions in System Preferences > Privacy & Security > Accessibility.

**Helper chat is not visible despite being installed.**
The organization may have disabled Helper chat. Check the heartbeat response for `helperEnabled: false`. An administrator can re-enable it through organization settings. The change takes effect within 60 seconds (next heartbeat cycle).

**Session expired after 24 hours.**
Helper chat sessions have a 24-hour maximum lifetime. Expired sessions cannot receive new messages. Start a new session to continue the conversation. Previous session history is preserved and can be listed via `GET /helper/chat/sessions`.

title: Agent Installation
description: Install the Breeze agent on Linux, macOS, and Windows. Download the single Go binary, enroll with an enrollment key, and run it as a system service.

sections.text: The Breeze agent is a single Go binary (~8 MB) with no runtime dependencies. It runs as a system service and communicates with your Breeze server over HTTPS/WSS. Deploying to a whole fleet with GPO, Intune, or JAMF? See the [Mass Deployment guide](/migration/mass-deployment/).

sections.heading: Supported Platforms
sections.text:
| Platform | Architecture | Binary |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | amd64 | `breeze-agent-linux-amd64` |
| Linux | arm64 | `breeze-agent-linux-arm64` |
| macOS | amd64 (Intel) | `breeze-agent-darwin-amd64` |
| macOS | arm64 (Apple Silicon) | `breeze-agent-darwin-arm64` |
| Windows | amd64 | `breeze-agent-windows-amd64.exe` |

sections.heading: Supported Windows Versions
sections.text:
The agent requires **Windows 10 or Windows Server 2016 or later**. This is a
hard floor set by the Go toolchain the agent is built with (Go 1.22+ dropped
support for older Windows kernels) -- it is not a Breeze-specific choice and
cannot be worked around by an older agent build.

| Windows version | Supported |
|---|---|
| Windows 10 / 11 | Yes |
| Windows Server 2016 / 2019 / 2022 / 2025 | Yes |
| Windows 8.1 / Server 2012 R2 and earlier | No |
| Windows 7 / Server 2008 R2 | No |

Legacy boxes are not silently accepted: the MSI installer refuses to run
below this floor (`Breeze Agent requires Windows 10 or Windows Server 2016 or
later.`), and the PowerShell quick-install command checks the same floor
before it downloads anything, so an unsupported machine fails fast with a
clear message instead of installing a binary that can't run.

**MSI installs on Windows 10/11 failed in v0.110.0 – v0.111.1:**
  Agent MSIs published with those releases refused **every fresh install** on
  Windows 10, Windows 11 and Server 2016+ with the legacy-OS message above.
  Windows Installer reports the Windows 8.1 version number to MSI packages on
  every newer Windows by design, so the floor check tripped on supported
  machines. From **v0.112.0** the MSI reads the Windows version from the
  registry instead, which is not affected. Already-enrolled agents were never
  affected (self-update does not run the MSI), and repair, upgrade and
  uninstall of an installed agent are never blocked by the floor check. If you
  handed out installer links or MSIs from those releases, replace them with the
  current ones.

  Monitoring a Windows 7 / Server 2008 R2 fleet? There's no supported Breeze
  agent path today. Agentless coverage (SNMP/WMI from a modern jump-box
  agent) and a legacy build track are both open roadmap questions, not
  shipped features -- reach out if this is blocking you.

sections.heading: Supported Linux Distributions
sections.text:
The Linux agent is a statically linked binary, so it runs on any amd64 or
arm64 distribution, and it is installed as a **systemd** service. What works
beyond that depends on the distribution's package manager and display server:

| Capability | Debian, Ubuntu | RHEL, Fedora, Rocky, AlmaLinux | openSUSE | Arch, other systemd distributions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Install, enrollment, heartbeat, monitoring, alerts | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Remote terminal, scripts, automations | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Software inventory | Yes (dpkg) | Yes (rpm) | Yes (rpm) | No (pacman not collected) |
| OS patch management | Yes (apt) | Yes (dnf/yum) | No (zypper) | No (pacman) |
| Disk encryption (LUKS) and firewall (ufw, firewalld) status | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Remote desktop and screenshots | X11 sessions only | X11 sessions only | X11 sessions only | X11 sessions only |

**Wayland sessions:**
  Remote desktop and screenshots require an X11 session. Wayland-only
  sessions -- the default GNOME and KDE sessions on current Ubuntu and Fedora
  releases, and compositors such as Hyprland and Sway -- are not supported
  yet. When no X11 display exists the device page reports **Wayland
  Unsupported** and **Connect Desktop** is disabled; on compositors that run
  XWayland the agent may attach to that display instead and show only X11
  application windows. Everything else works normally. Where the login
  screen offers an X11 session, selecting it restores remote desktop.

Distributions without systemd (for example Alpine with OpenRC) can run the
binary but are not supported by the service installer. There is no `.deb`,
`.rpm`, or Arch package -- see [Mass Deployment](/migration/mass-deployment/)
for the script-based fleet install.

sections.heading: Quick Install
sections.text:
**Linux:**
```bash
    # Download the agent
    curl -fsSL -o breeze-agent \
      https://breeze.yourdomain.com/api/v1/agents/download/linux/amd64
    chmod +x breeze-agent

    # Enroll and install as a service
    sudo ./breeze-agent enroll YOUR_ENROLLMENT_KEY \
      --server https://breeze.yourdomain.com \
      --enrollment-secret YOUR_ENROLLMENT_SECRET

    sudo ./breeze-agent service install
```

  **macOS:**
```bash
    # Download the agent
    curl -fsSL -o breeze-agent \
      https://breeze.yourdomain.com/api/v1/agents/download/darwin/arm64
    chmod +x breeze-agent

    # Enroll and install as a LaunchDaemon
    sudo ./breeze-agent enroll YOUR_ENROLLMENT_KEY \
      --server https://breeze.yourdomain.com \
      --enrollment-secret YOUR_ENROLLMENT_SECRET

    sudo ./breeze-agent service install
```

  **Windows:**
```powershell
    # Check the minimum supported OS before downloading anything
    $osv = [System.Environment]::OSVersion.Version
    if ($osv.Major -lt 10) {
      throw "Breeze: Windows 10 or Windows Server 2016 or later is required (detected $($osv.Major).$($osv.Minor))"
    }

    # Older PowerShell/.NET defaults (e.g. Windows Server 2016) can omit
    # TLS 1.2, which makes Invoke-WebRequest fail outright.
    [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = `
      [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol -bor [Net.SecurityProtocolType]::Tls12

    # Download the agent into a temp directory. Do not download into
    # C:\Windows\system32 (an elevated PowerShell's default directory):
    # Defender's ASR rule "Block use of copied or impersonated system tools"
    # then blocks the service binary that `service install` copies out of it.
    Set-Location (New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$env:TEMP\breeze-install")
    Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://breeze.yourdomain.com/api/v1/agents/download/windows/amd64" `
      -OutFile "breeze-agent.exe"

    # Enroll (run as Administrator)
    .\breeze-agent.exe enroll YOUR_ENROLLMENT_KEY `
      --server https://breeze.yourdomain.com `
      --enrollment-secret YOUR_ENROLLMENT_SECRET

    # Install as a Windows Service
    .\breeze-agent.exe service install
```

    Alternatively, use the MSI installer for silent deployment:
```powershell
    msiexec /i breeze-agent.msi /qn `
      SERVER_URL=https://breeze.yourdomain.com `
      ENROLLMENT_KEY=YOUR_ENROLLMENT_KEY
```

    The MSI installer enrolls the agent by invoking `breeze-agent.exe enroll` directly during installation — there is no PowerShell wrapper script in the install path. If enrollment fails, the installer surfaces the underlying agent error message instead of a generic Windows error.

**Self-hosted server with a self-signed or internal-CA certificate?:**
  The agent and every installer verify the server certificate against the machine's trust store. If your server uses Caddy's internal CA (`CADDY_LOCAL_CERTS`, a bare IP or `localhost`) or any other private CA, install its root certificate on each endpoint first. Otherwise the MSI, the PowerShell one-liner and `breeze-agent enroll` all fail before enrollment. See [Trusting the internal CA on agents](/deploy/tls/#trusting-the-internal-ca-on-agents).

sections.heading: Pre-Configured Installers
sections.text:
Instead of running manual enrollment commands, you can download a ready-to-run installer from the Breeze dashboard.

1. Open the **Add Device** dialog from the Devices page.
2. Stay on the **Download Installer** tab, choose the platform (**Windows (.msi)** or **macOS (.zip)**) and the **Site**.
3. Set a **device count** to control how many devices can enroll with this installer.
4. Click **Download Installer** (or **Generate Link** to get a shareable download link), then run the installer on the target machine. The agent enrolls automatically with the correct organization and site -- no enrollment commands needed.

  Each installer is pre-loaded with the enrollment key and site assignment. Just distribute the file and run it.

  **Windows agent packages in the public release are published unsigned by design**, so that you can sign them under your own certificate. Expect a SmartScreen prompt on an interactive install unless you deploy them silently through your existing tooling, or sign them yourself first -- see [Sign Your Own Agent Packages](/deploy/sign-your-own-packages/). The Viewer and Helper installers *are* signed.

sections.heading: Public Installer Links
sections.text:
You can generate a shareable download URL for an enrollment key so that site contacts can install the agent without needing access to the Breeze dashboard.

- From the enrollment key details, click **Copy Public Link** or use the API (`POST /enrollment-keys/:id/installer-link`).
- Share the link with on-site contacts via email, chat, or documentation.
- Links are token-authenticated and rate-limited to prevent abuse.

sections.heading: Short Enrollment Links
sections.text:
Public installer links can also be issued as short, human-friendly URLs of the form `https://breeze.yourdomain.com/s/<code>`. The short link automatically delivers the right installer for the requester's platform (Windows MSI or macOS PKG), respects the enrollment key's usage limits, and is one-time-use by default.

Short codes are issued alongside long-form public links — copy the short URL from the enrollment key details page and share it however you like. Each visit increments the underlying enrollment key's usage count atomically, so you cannot exceed the configured `maxUsage`.

sections.heading: macOS GUI Installer
sections.text:
For onboarding Macs the same way you'd install any other native macOS app, Breeze provides a Swift-based GUI installer (`Breeze Installer.app`). A site contact opens the app, confirms the install with **Touch ID**, and the agent is enrolled and started — no Terminal commands.

The GUI installer uses bootstrap tokens generated server-side from an enrollment key, so the same usage-limit and site-pinning guarantees as MSI/PKG installers apply.

sections.heading: Windows MSI Zero-Config Enrollment
sections.text:
Windows MSI installers downloaded from the dashboard or via a public link also auto-enroll with zero configuration. The enrollment token is embedded directly in the downloaded filename as a `(TOKEN@HOST)` block — for example:

```
Breeze Agent (ABCD1234XY@breeze.example.com).msi
```

The installer parses this block at runtime using a regex search anywhere in the filename, so a browser-added dedup suffix such as `(1)` — producing `Breeze Agent (ABCD1234XY@breeze.example.com) (1).msi` — does not break enrollment. Just run the file as downloaded. (Older installer downloads used square brackets, `[TOKEN@HOST]`; the installer still recognizes that legacy form too.)

  If you rename the MSI before deploying it, preserve the `(TOKEN@HOST)` block exactly as downloaded. Removing the block causes the installer to fall back to requiring the enrollment key and server URL entered manually during setup.

sections.heading: Linux/macOS One-Liner (CLI Commands Tab)
sections.text:
There is no downloadable pre-configured installer for Linux, so the **Add Device** dialog's **CLI Commands** tab generates a copy-paste install command instead.

1. Open **Add Device** from the Devices page and switch to the **CLI Commands** tab (the dialog opens on it by default when Linux is the detected platform).
2. Pick the **Site** the new devices should join. Under **Step 1 — Copy your installation token**, set **Number of devices** and **Link expires in**, then click **Generate token**. Opening the tab does not create a key — nothing is minted until you click. Use **Generate new token** if you change any of the three afterwards; the line under the token names the site it enrolls into.
3. Under **Step 2 — Run the install command**, copy the one-liner shown for the Linux/macOS tab. The command and its copy button appear only after a token exists; until then the box reads **Generate a token first**.
4. Paste and run it on the target machine.

The generated command downloads and runs the same `install.sh` used by [Quick Install](#quick-install) above, with `--token` and `--server` filled in for you. Generating a token requires MFA on your account. Behind the scenes, the token is a short-lived **enrollment key** minted specifically for this dialog (`POST /devices/onboarding-token`) — not the same bootstrap-token mechanism the macOS GUI installer uses above — scoped to the site, device count and expiry you chose, up to 1000 devices and 365 days. API callers that omit `siteId` get the organization's oldest site they can access (by creation time).

The same tab also shows a **Windows** command for an elevated PowerShell. It downloads the agent into a private temporary folder, checks its checksum and signature, enrolls the device, then installs the service, which starts it. Since v0.122.1 it enrolls before installing the service and no longer ends with a separate `service start`.

The `--server` address in these commands comes from the API's `PUBLIC_API_URL` setting (or `API_URL` when that is unset). If your dashboard and API are served from different hosts, set `PUBLIC_API_URL` on the API so the command points agents at the API.

---
