sections.heading: Pre-Provisioning Devices
sections.text:
For deployments where you want a device row to exist in the dashboard before the agent has ever talked to the server — for example, building out an asset list ahead of a hardware shipment — admins can pre-create the row with `POST /devices/provision`. The endpoint accepts the device's hostname, target organization, and site, and returns a single-use enrollment payload that can be baked into the installer.

Pre-provisioned devices land in `status: 'pending'` and stay there until the agent's first heartbeat arrives. They show up in the device list with a "Pending enrollment" indicator so it's clear which rows are placeholders versus active devices.

---

sections.heading: What Gets Installed
sections.text:
All platform installers (MSI, PKG, and manual service install) include these components:

| Component | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| **Breeze Agent** | The main service that communicates with the Breeze server, runs commands, and reports device status. |
| **Watchdog** | A companion service that monitors the agent and automatically restarts it after crashes or hangs. |
| **Desktop helper** (macOS) | A per-user helper that runs in the logged-in user's session so features like screen sharing work. Installed at `/usr/local/bin/breeze-desktop-helper`. |

The watchdog runs alongside the agent as a separate process. You do not need to configure it -- it starts automatically with the agent service. See the [Watchdog documentation](/features/watchdog) for details.

When running `breeze-agent service install` manually, the agent fetches the matching-version watchdog binary from GitHub releases if one is not already present next to the agent executable. If you need to skip this (for example on an air-gapped host), pass `--no-watchdog`:

  **Linux / macOS:**
```bash
    sudo ./breeze-agent service install --no-watchdog
```

  **Windows:**
```powershell
    .\breeze-agent.exe service install --no-watchdog
```

`--no-watchdog` is remembered. It writes a marker file named `watchdog.disabled` in the agent's config directory (`/etc/breeze` on Linux, `/Library/Application Support/Breeze` on macOS, `C:\ProgramData\Breeze` on Windows). A later plain `service install`, for example from an upgrade script, keeps honouring the opt-out and prints `watchdog install skipped: opted out (use --watchdog to re-enable)`. The agent's automatic watchdog repair (below) also stays off while the marker exists.

To re-enable the watchdog, run `service install --watchdog`. It removes the marker, resets the retry state, and installs the watchdog. `--watchdog` and `--no-watchdog` cannot be combined.

  **Linux / macOS:**
```bash
    sudo ./breeze-agent service install --watchdog
```

  **Windows:**
```powershell
    .\breeze-agent.exe service install --watchdog
```

Hosts that ran `--no-watchdog` with an agent version older than this behaviour have no marker file. On air-gapped fleets that deliberately run without a watchdog, re-run `service install --no-watchdog` once after upgrading so the opt-out is recorded.

On macOS the desktop helper is resolved the same way: `breeze-agent service install` uses a `breeze-desktop-helper` binary staged next to the agent if there is one, and otherwise downloads the matching-version signed binary from GitHub releases. If neither is available (for example on an air-gapped host), the install prints a warning and continues -- the agent service is still installed and running, and only the helper's features are unavailable until you place the binary next to `breeze-agent` and re-run `service install`. The agent binary is never installed under the helper's name: doing so would give the helper the agent's code-signing identity, and macOS would drop the Screen Recording and Accessibility grants once a real helper replaced it. The macOS `.pkg` always ships the signed helper, so this only affects raw-binary installs.

When a macOS agent updates itself (v0.122.1+), it downloads the installer package from your own Breeze server first and falls back to the GitHub release only if that fails. Either way, the package must match the signed release checksum before it is installed.

If the watchdog could not be installed during `service install` (for example because the download failed), you no longer need to re-run the command on an enrolled host. The running agent installs the watchdog later by itself when the Breeze server offers a watchdog version for the device. See [Automatic repair of a missing watchdog](/features/watchdog#automatic-repair-of-a-missing-watchdog) for what it does, when it stays off, and the retry schedule.

`service install` still exits `0` when the watchdog bootstrap fails, because the agent itself installed. It prints a machine-readable `BREEZE_WATCHDOG_INSTALL=deferred reason=<class>` line on stdout so scripts can detect the deferral. Pass `--strict-watchdog` to make it exit `78` instead. See [`service install` exit codes](/agents/advanced-install#service-install-exit-codes).

Air-gapped hosts, and any host that should run without a watchdog, must use `--no-watchdog`. Without it, the agent keeps trying to install the watchdog on its bounded schedule, and the device page reports that it gave up once the attempts are used.

The Linux and macOS install scripts (`install-linux.sh`, `install-darwin.sh`) copy and register a watchdog only when the package bundles one. When the package has no watchdog binary and none is installed yet, they print `Warning: no watchdog bundled; the agent installs one after enrollment when the control plane offers a watchdog build for this platform` and continue. They do not install the watchdog themselves; the enrolled agent does.

You can still re-run `breeze-agent service install` yourself to add the watchdog immediately. It records whether the agent service was running before the install, rewrites and re-enables the unit, and starts the service again if it was running before or the host is already enrolled -- a fresh, unenrolled host is left stopped until you enroll it. If the service was stopped for the install and can't be started again, the command now fails with recovery instructions instead of exiting successfully. It also registers the missing watchdog, which is always restarted so a newly staged binary takes over. To add *only* the watchdog without touching the agent service, run `breeze-watchdog service install` directly.

On agent v0.110.0 and earlier, `service install` stopped the service and did not start it again. On those versions, follow it with `sudo systemctl restart breeze-agent breeze-watchdog` (Linux), or prefer the in-band auto-update instead.

---

sections.heading: What Enrollment Does
sections.text:
During enrollment, the agent:

1. Sends system information (hostname, OS, architecture) to the API
2. Validates the enrollment secret
3. Receives a unique `brz_` bearer token
4. Stores configuration in `/etc/breeze/agent.yaml` (Linux), `/Library/Application Support/Breeze/agent.yaml` (macOS), or `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\agent.yaml` (Windows)
5. Stores secrets in a separate `secrets.yaml` file with `0600` permissions
6. Sets file permissions: `0755` for directory, `0644` for config file (`agent.yaml`), `0600` for secrets file (`secrets.yaml`)

  The enrollment secret (`AGENT_ENROLLMENT_SECRET`) is different from the agent's bearer token. The enrollment secret is a shared secret used once during registration. The bearer token is unique per device and used for all subsequent communication.

sections.heading: Verifying Installation
sections.text:
```bash
# Check service status
sudo systemctl status breeze-agent  # Linux
sudo launchctl list | grep breeze   # macOS
Get-Service BreezeAgent              # Windows

# Check agent version
breeze-agent version

# View agent logs
sudo journalctl -u breeze-agent -f  # Linux
sudo log show --predicate 'process == "breeze-agent"' --last 1h  # macOS
```

The device should appear in your Breeze dashboard within 60 seconds of enrollment.

sections.heading: Configuration File
sections.text:
After enrollment, the agent stores its configuration at:

| OS | Config Path | Secrets Path |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | `/etc/breeze/agent.yaml` | `/etc/breeze/secrets.yaml` |
| macOS | `/Library/Application Support/Breeze/agent.yaml` | `/Library/Application Support/Breeze/secrets.yaml` |
| Windows | `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\agent.yaml` | `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\secrets.yaml` |

**Windows: no links under ProgramData\Breeze (agent 0.118.0+):**
  The agent keeps `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\data` and `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\logs` as real directories that only SYSTEM and Administrators can write to. If either is a junction or symbolic link (for example, one that redirects logs to another drive), the installer and the agent replace it with a real directory. Files in the old link target are not moved or copied. If the link cannot be removed, the agent refuses to start and writes the reason to `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\logs\agent-start-failed.txt`; remove the link by hand, then start the service.

```yaml
# agent.yaml (0644 — readable by Breeze Helper)
server_url: "https://breeze.yourdomain.com"
agent_id: "hex-agent-id"
auth_token: "brz_..."
org_id: "uuid-..."
site_id: "uuid-..."
```

```yaml
# secrets.yaml (0600 — root only)
auth_token: "brz_..."
```

  The `secrets.yaml` file contains the agent's bearer token and is restricted to `0600` (owner-only read/write). The `auth_token` is intentionally duplicated in `agent.yaml` (which uses `0644` permissions) so the Breeze Helper process can discover the token without needing root access to `secrets.yaml`. Do not change these permissions.

title: macOS Permissions
description: Grant Full Disk Access, Accessibility, and Screen Recording to the Breeze agent using MDM PPPC profiles or System Settings.
headings: Zero-Touch Grants with a PPPC Profile

sections.text: macOS gates access to the screen, input events, and protected files behind per-app privacy permissions (TCC). The Breeze agent and its desktop helper need three of these permissions for full functionality. Apple does not allow applications to grant these permissions to themselves -- the supported paths are an MDM-delivered PPPC (Privacy Preferences Policy Control) configuration profile for zero-touch deployment, or a manual grant in System Settings.

sections.heading: Permissions Overview
sections.text:
| Permission | Binary | Used For | How to Grant |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Full Disk Access** | `/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent` or `/Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent` (see [agent path](#agent-path-usrlocalbin-or-librarybreezebin)), `/usr/local/bin/breeze-desktop-helper` | System data collection, backup features | MDM PPPC profile (zero-touch) or manual System Settings grant |
| **Accessibility** | `/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent` or `/Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent` (see [agent path](#agent-path-usrlocalbin-or-librarybreezebin)), `/usr/local/bin/breeze-desktop-helper` | Remote input (mouse and keyboard) during remote desktop sessions | MDM PPPC profile (zero-touch) or manual System Settings grant |
| **Screen Recording** | `/usr/local/bin/breeze-desktop-helper` | Remote desktop screen capture | **User approval only.** MDM cannot pre-grant it -- a PPPC profile can only allow standard (non-admin) users to approve it themselves, via the `ScreenCapture` service's `AllowStandardUserToSetSystemService` authorization (macOS 11+) |

  Apple does not permit MDM to silently grant Screen Recording. The best available automation is the `AllowStandardUserToSetSystemService` key, which lets a logged-in standard user click **Allow** without needing admin credentials. The end user still has to approve the prompt once.

sections.heading: Agent Path: /usr/local/bin or /Library/Breeze/bin
sections.text:
macOS ties Full Disk Access for a bare (non-bundle) binary to its file path, not just its code-signing identity, so which path the agent runs from decides where you grant FDA.

From agent 0.118.3:

- The agent and watchdog **stay in `/usr/local/bin`** when `/usr/local/bin` and every directory above it are owned by root and not writable by group or other -- the stock macOS state. Nothing moves, and existing Full Disk Access and other privacy grants keep working.
- The agent **moves to `/Library/Breeze/bin`** only when `/usr/local/bin` is unsafe for a root daemon: the binary or a directory above it is not owned by root, or is group- or world-writable. The known case is Homebrew on Intel Macs, which hands `/usr/local/bin` to an admin user. Only in this case do you need to re-grant Full Disk Access, for `/Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent`. The agent logs a warning when it moves.
- Agents 0.118.0 through 0.118.2 moved **every** install, safe or not, which is why fleets on those versions saw Full Disk Access break widely. 0.118.3 does not move an install back to `/usr/local/bin` once it has moved -- a re-grant you already made for `/Library/Breeze/bin` keeps holding. Move any Mac still on 0.118.0-0.118.2 to 0.118.3 or later; do not promote those versions to Macs you cannot touch.
- The `.pkg` installer (used for installs and for macOS agent updates) always installs to wherever the existing install lives, so it never moves an install back and forth on its own. `breeze-agent service install` (manual CLI install) and the dev install script install to `/Library/Breeze/bin` directly.
- The desktop helper is never moved -- it always stays at `/usr/local/bin/breeze-desktop-helper`.

For an MDM-managed fleet, the simplest zero-touch approach is a PPPC profile that lists both paths (see below) so it covers a Mac regardless of which one it runs from.

See [After an agent relocation](#after-an-agent-relocation) for what changes on a Mac that does move, and how to confirm the grant landed.

sections.heading: Zero-Touch Grants with a PPPC Profile
sections.text:
If the Mac is enrolled in an MDM (Jamf, Mosyle, Kandji, Intune, etc.), deploy a PPPC configuration profile that grants Full Disk Access and Accessibility to both Breeze binaries. This is the recommended path for fleet deployments -- no on-device interaction is required for those two permissions.

The profile identifies each binary by its installed path plus a code-signing requirement, so the grant only applies to a genuine, Developer ID-signed Breeze binary at that path.

**Cover both agent paths:**
  From agent 0.118.3, most Macs keep running the agent from `/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent`; only Macs where that directory is unsafe for a root daemon (see [Agent Path](#agent-path-usrlocalbin-or-librarybreezebin)) move to `/Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent`. A path-based PPPC grant for one path does not cover the other, so list both `/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent` and `/Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent`, each with the same code requirement, as the sample profile below does. That way the profile grants the permission wherever a given Mac's agent runs, with no need to know in advance which path applies. The desktop helper is never moved -- it always stays at `/usr/local/bin/breeze-desktop-helper`.

  PPPC payloads are only honored when delivered through a user-approved or supervised MDM enrollment. Installing the same `.mobileconfig` by double-clicking it does not apply the privacy grants.

The following profile is ready to import into your MDM (most consoles accept a raw `.mobileconfig` upload):

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>PayloadContent</key>
  <array>
    <dict>
      <key>PayloadType</key>
      <string>com.apple.TCC.configuration-profile-policy</string>
      <key>PayloadIdentifier</key>
      <string>com.breezermm.pppc.privacy</string>
      <key>PayloadUUID</key>
      <string>7D3F2A91-5B4C-4E8D-9A16-C2E7F0B83D54</string>
      <key>PayloadVersion</key>
      <integer>1</integer>
      <key>PayloadDisplayName</key>
      <string>Breeze Agent Privacy Preferences</string>
      <key>Services</key>
      <dict>
        <key>SystemPolicyAllFiles</key>
        <array>
          <dict>
            <key>Identifier</key>
            <string>/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent</string>
            <key>IdentifierType</key>
            <string>path</string>
            <key>CodeRequirement</key>
            <string>(identifier "breeze-agent-darwin-arm64" or identifier "breeze-agent-darwin-amd64") and anchor apple generic and certificate leaf[subject.OU] = D8W6N2JYMA</string>
            <key>Allowed</key>
            <true/>
          </dict>
          <dict>
            <key>Identifier</key>
            <string>/Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent</string>
            <key>IdentifierType</key>
            <string>path</string>
            <key>CodeRequirement</key>
            <string>(identifier "breeze-agent-darwin-arm64" or identifier "breeze-agent-darwin-amd64") and anchor apple generic and certificate leaf[subject.OU] = D8W6N2JYMA</string>
            <key>Allowed</key>
            <true/>
          </dict>
          <dict>
            <key>Identifier</key>
            <string>/usr/local/bin/breeze-desktop-helper</string>
            <key>IdentifierType</key>
            <string>path</string>
            <key>CodeRequirement</key>
            <string>(identifier "breeze-desktop-helper-darwin-arm64" or identifier "breeze-desktop-helper-darwin-amd64") and anchor apple generic and certificate leaf[subject.OU] = D8W6N2JYMA</string>
            <key>Allowed</key>
            <true/>
          </dict>
        </array>
        <key>Accessibility</key>
        <array>
          <dict>
            <key>Identifier</key>
            <string>/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent</string>
            <key>IdentifierType</key>
            <string>path</string>
            <key>CodeRequirement</key>
            <string>(identifier "breeze-agent-darwin-arm64" or identifier "breeze-agent-darwin-amd64") and anchor apple generic and certificate leaf[subject.OU] = D8W6N2JYMA</string>
            <key>Allowed</key>
            <true/>
          </dict>
          <dict>
            <key>Identifier</key>
            <string>/Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent</string>
            <key>IdentifierType</key>
            <string>path</string>
            <key>CodeRequirement</key>
            <string>(identifier "breeze-agent-darwin-arm64" or identifier "breeze-agent-darwin-amd64") and anchor apple generic and certificate leaf[subject.OU] = D8W6N2JYMA</string>
            <key>Allowed</key>
            <true/>
          </dict>
          <dict>
            <key>Identifier</key>
            <string>/usr/local/bin/breeze-desktop-helper</string>
            <key>IdentifierType</key>
            <string>path</string>
            <key>CodeRequirement</key>
            <string>(identifier "breeze-desktop-helper-darwin-arm64" or identifier "breeze-desktop-helper-darwin-amd64") and anchor apple generic and certificate leaf[subject.OU] = D8W6N2JYMA</string>
            <key>Allowed</key>
            <true/>
          </dict>
        </array>
        <key>ScreenCapture</key>
        <array>
          <dict>
            <key>Identifier</key>
            <string>/usr/local/bin/breeze-desktop-helper</string>
            <key>IdentifierType</key>
            <string>path</string>
            <key>CodeRequirement</key>
            <string>(identifier "breeze-desktop-helper-darwin-arm64" or identifier "breeze-desktop-helper-darwin-amd64") and anchor apple generic and certificate leaf[subject.OU] = D8W6N2JYMA</string>
            <key>Authorization</key>
            <string>AllowStandardUserToSetSystemService</string>
          </dict>
        </array>
      </dict>
    </dict>
  </array>
  <key>PayloadDescription</key>
  <string>Grants Full Disk Access and Accessibility to the Breeze agent and desktop helper, and allows standard users to approve Screen Recording.</string>
  <key>PayloadDisplayName</key>
  <string>Breeze RMM - macOS Privacy Permissions</string>
  <key>PayloadIdentifier</key>
  <string>com.breezermm.pppc</string>
  <key>PayloadScope</key>
  <string>System</string>
  <key>PayloadType</key>
  <string>Configuration</string>
  <key>PayloadUUID</key>
  <string>E19C6B0F-8A72-4D35-B6E4-1F5A9D27C803</string>
  <key>PayloadVersion</key>
  <integer>1</integer>
</dict>
</plist>
```

The code requirements match both the Apple Silicon (`-darwin-arm64`) and Intel (`-darwin-amd64`) builds, so a single profile covers a mixed fleet. The agent entry is listed twice, once per path, so the same profile grants the permission whether a given Mac's agent runs from `/usr/local/bin` or `/Library/Breeze/bin` (see [Agent Path](#agent-path-usrlocalbin-or-librarybreezebin)). You can verify the signing identity of an installed binary at any time, using whichever path the agent currently runs from:

```bash
codesign -dvvv /usr/local/bin/breeze-agent 2>&1 | grep -E '^Identifier|TeamIdentifier'
# or, on a Mac where the agent moved:
codesign -dvvv /Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent 2>&1 | grep -E '^Identifier|TeamIdentifier'
# Identifier=breeze-agent-darwin-arm64
# TeamIdentifier=D8W6N2JYMA
```

  If your MDM builds PPPC payloads from its own UI (for example Jamf's PPPC editor), enter the binary path with identifier type **path**, paste the matching code requirement string, and enable **App or Service: SystemPolicyAllFiles, Accessibility** for both binaries plus **ScreenCapture → Allow Standard Users to Allow Access** for the desktop helper.

**Forward compatibility:**
  Starting with macOS Tahoe 26.2, privacy permissions configured via device management are visible in **System Settings > Privacy & Security**. At WWDC 2026 Apple introduced a new declarative privacy framework to replace PPPC, and the `com.apple.TCC.configuration-profile-policy` payload keys are deprecated -- but not removed -- in macOS 27. Existing PPPC profiles like the one above continue to work through the macOS 27 cycle. Expect to migrate to the declarative mechanism in a future release; watch Apple's device management documentation for the timeline.

sections.heading: Manual Grants in System Settings
sections.text:
Without an MDM, grant the permissions on the device under **System Settings > Privacy & Security**:

1. **Full Disk Access** -- open **Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access**, click **+**, press <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>G</kbd> in the file picker, and add `/usr/local/bin/breeze-desktop-helper` plus the agent binary at whichever path it runs from -- `/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent` on most Macs, or `/Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent` if it has moved (see [Agent Path](#agent-path-usrlocalbin-or-librarybreezebin)). Run `ls /Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent` first if you are not sure which one applies.

2. **Accessibility** -- open **Privacy & Security > Accessibility** and add the same two binaries.

3. **Screen Recording** -- open **Privacy & Security > Screen & System Audio Recording** (labeled **Screen Recording** on macOS 12-14) and enable `breeze-desktop-helper`. The helper never captures the screen to check this permission, so it may not appear in the list until you add it with **+** (`/usr/local/bin/breeze-desktop-helper`). On macOS 12-15 the helper asks macOS for the grant once a day while it is missing, and a remote desktop connection is refused (with a `missing_permission` reason in the console) until it is granted; on macOS 26 the first connection is allowed and its own capture decides.

Changes to Full Disk Access take effect after the agent service restarts:

```bash
sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.breeze.agent
```

After granting Screen Recording or Accessibility, restart the desktop helper as the logged-in user (run in that user's Terminal, without `sudo`) so it re-reads its permissions:

```bash
launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.breeze.desktop-helper-user
```

Remote desktop needs **both** Screen Recording and Accessibility for the desktop helper -- with either one missing, the device reports remote desktop as unavailable.

sections.heading: After an agent relocation
sections.text:
This applies only to a Mac where `/usr/local/bin` was unsafe for a root daemon and the agent moved to `/Library/Breeze/bin` (see [Agent Path](#agent-path-usrlocalbin-or-librarybreezebin)). Most Macs never hit this.

- **Grant Full Disk Access at the new path.** Add `/Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent` in **System Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access**, or push the PPPC update, if you have not already covered both paths as shown above.
- **How to tell a Mac needs this.** Until the grant lands, the device's Full Disk Access status still shows as missing, and the agent's self-health reports a `macos_fda_relocation` warning naming the old and new path (from `GET /devices/{id}/health`). The warning clears on its own once Full Disk Access is granted for the new path -- there is no separate UI panel for it.
- **Leftover binaries are cleaned up automatically.** After moving, the agent removes the old `breeze-agent`, `breeze-watchdog` and `breeze-backup` copies left behind in `/usr/local/bin` on its next start.
- **A PPPC profile covering both paths needs zero further action.** If your profile already lists both `/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent` and `/Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent` with the same code requirement (as in the sample profile above), the grant applies automatically regardless of which path the agent ends up on.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**A permission "disappears" after an agent update.**
For a bare (non-bundle) binary like the agent, macOS keys a TCC grant to the binary's file path, not just its code-signing identity, so a grant made for one path does not carry over if the binary starts running from a different one -- see [After an agent relocation](#after-an-agent-relocation) if that is what happened. Within a stable path, official Breeze binaries are Developer ID signed with a stable identity, so grants survive ordinary updates. If a grant stops applying after an update at the same path, check that the binary is still properly signed:

```bash
codesign -dvvv /usr/local/bin/breeze-agent
# or /Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent, whichever path the agent runs from
```

Expect `Authority=Developer ID Application: LanternOps LLC (D8W6N2JYMA)` and `TeamIdentifier=D8W6N2JYMA`. An ad-hoc or unsigned binary -- typical of a manual or development build -- gets a new identity on every build, so macOS treats each update as a brand-new app and drops the grant. Reinstall an official signed release, or re-grant after each build for development installs.

**The PPPC profile is installed but permissions are not granted.**
Confirm the profile arrived through MDM (`profiles list` should show it under a device channel). PPPC payloads are ignored when the profile is installed manually. Also verify the code requirement matches the installed binary, at whichever path it runs from: `codesign -d -r- /usr/local/bin/breeze-agent` (or the `/Library/Breeze/bin` path) prints the designated requirement to compare against.

**Remote desktop connects but shows a black screen.**
Screen Recording has not been approved for `breeze-desktop-helper`. This permission always requires a one-time user approval -- see the table above.

**macOS keeps asking to let `breeze-desktop-helper` record the screen (macOS 15+).**
On macOS 15 and later, ScreenCaptureKit can show its own "record this computer's screen and audio" approval, and for the bare helper binary macOS may not keep that approval. macOS 15 also shows a separate acknowledgement alert ("`breeze-desktop-helper` can record this computer's screen") for the first screen capture in each 30-day window, by any API. The desktop helper's permission checks (at startup, on every connect, and in its periodic TCC loop) never capture the screen and never use ScreenCaptureKit; only a remote desktop session captures, so that alert can appear only while a technician is connecting. A helper restart on its own shows nothing.

Where macOS reports the Screen Recording grant unreliably (macOS 26 can say "not granted" while it is), the helper reads other non-capturing signals instead: whether other apps' window titles are visible to it, and whether an earlier remote desktop session captured successfully on this agent version and macOS build. The agent log's `TCC permissions received` line carries `screenRecordingState` (`granted`, `denied` or `unknown`); `unknown` still allows a session, whose own capture decides. If ScreenCaptureKit cannot capture in a session (the user declines its prompt, or it produces no frames) while Screen Recording is granted, the helper switches to CoreGraphics capture and records that, so later sessions and helper restarts don't ask again. The record lapses when the agent updates, macOS updates, or the Screen Recording grant changes. Run these as the logged-in user, without `sudo`:

```bash
breeze-desktop-helper capture-backend                    # show the recorded verdict
breeze-desktop-helper capture-backend pin-coregraphics   # never use ScreenCaptureKit for this user
breeze-desktop-helper capture-backend reset              # forget it; the next session tries ScreenCaptureKit
```

From a root shell, such as a Breeze remote terminal, use `launchctl asuser <uid> sudo -u '#<uid>' /usr/local/bin/breeze-desktop-helper capture-backend ...`.

`breeze-desktop-helper probe` reports the non-capturing check as `captureAccess` and then takes one real capture (it is the only permission check that does); it doesn't call ScreenCaptureKit unless you pass `--sck`. macOS charges a probe's capture to whatever launched it: Terminal, or `breeze-agent` from a Breeze script or remote terminal. The launchd helper's grants are separate, so the probe can't show them. For the helper's real permission state, look for the `TCC permissions received` line in the device's agent logs.

**Remote desktop is unavailable even though the device shows Online.**
The desktop helper runs alongside the agent and can briefly lose its connection to it — after an agent update, or when the Mac sleeps and wakes. The helper now reconnects on its own when that happens, so this should clear within moments. Earlier agent versions left the helper stopped until it was relaunched or the user logged out and back in; if you are seeing that, update the agent.

title: Migrating to the Self-Host Agent Edition
description: Move devices off hosted-edition agent builds and onto the self-host agent edition for self-hosted Breeze servers.

sections.text:
If your self-hosted Breeze dashboard shows a persistent banner saying some of
your devices are running the **hosted agent edition**, this page explains what
that means and how to migrate those devices. The banner is shown to
administrators only and clears on its own once every affected device has been
migrated.

sections.heading: What the banner means
sections.text:
Breeze ships the agent in two editions:

- **Self-host edition** — the standard build published on GitHub Releases,
  which is also what your own server's install links and downloads serve by
  default (see [Agent Binary Distribution](/deploy/binaries/)). It connects to
  any Breeze server. This is the edition every device on a self-hosted server
  should run.
- **Hosted edition** — built exclusively for the Breeze-hosted cloud and
  restricted to hosted control-plane servers.

A device is counted in the banner when its agent reports that it is a
hosted-edition build talking to your self-hosted server. This usually means the
agent was originally installed from an installer or download link that came
from the hosted service, rather than from your own server.

Hosted-edition agents currently keep working against a self-hosted server —
they only report the mismatch. Future hosted-edition releases enforce the
restriction and will refuse to run against a non-hosted server. Migrate
affected devices before updating them.

sections.heading: Migrate a device
sections.text:
On macOS and Linux, migration is an in-place reinstall with the self-host
edition: the device's enrollment, identity, and history are preserved — the
agent keeps its existing configuration and does not re-enroll. On Windows, the
two MSI editions carry different product identities and **refuse to install
over each other**, so the hosted MSI must be uninstalled first (back up the
agent's configuration to keep the device's identity — see step 2).

1. Get the self-host agent from **your own server**: use the install command or
   installer download from **Devices → Add Device** in your dashboard. Anything
   your server hands out is the self-host edition.

2. Install it on the affected device:

   - **Windows** — the self-host MSI will not upgrade a hosted-edition install
     in place (the installer blocks with *"A different edition of the Breeze
     Agent is already installed."*). To migrate while keeping the device's
     enrollment: first back up `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\agent.yaml` and
     `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\secrets.yaml` (uninstalling removes them), then
     uninstall the hosted agent MSI, install the self-host MSI, restore the two
     files, and restart the **Breeze Agent** service. If you skip the backup,
     the agent re-enrolls as a new device record instead.
   - **macOS / Linux** — run the install script over the existing
     installation, or replace the binary and run
     `breeze-agent service install`, which reinstalls the binary and, because
     the device is already enrolled, starts the service again automatically
     without re-enrolling. (On agent v0.110.0 and earlier, `service install`
     stopped the service without restarting it — on those versions, follow it
     with `sudo systemctl restart breeze-agent breeze-watchdog`, or prefer the
     in-band auto-update instead.) See
     [Agent Installation](/agents/installation/) for the full commands.

3. Let the device check in. The agent reports its edition on every check-in,
   so the flag clears automatically the first time the self-host build starts.

On **macOS and Linux**, do not uninstall the agent, decommission the device, or
re-enroll with a new enrollment key — none of that is needed. On **Windows**,
uninstalling the hosted MSI is required, but back up the configuration files
first as described above; re-enrolling is only appropriate when you
intentionally want a new device record.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
The banner's device count drops as each migrated device checks in, and the
banner disappears when the count reaches zero. There is nothing to acknowledge
or dismiss manually.

sections.text:

title: Third-Party Backup Providers
description: Connect N-able Cove Data Protection to Breeze so third-party backup status appears in backup health, device pages, attention items and alerts.

sections.text:
If some of your customers are protected by a third-party backup product, Breeze can read that product's status and show it alongside Breeze's own backups. A device protected by the provider counts as covered, so it no longer shows up as "no backup" just because Breeze did not run the job.

**N-able Cove Data Protection** is the supported provider today.

The integration is **read-only**. Breeze reads backup status from Cove; it never changes settings, starts backups, or restores data in Cove. Restores are still done in the Cove console.

---

sections.heading: Before You Start
sections.text:
- **Partner accounts only.** Connections belong to your MSP (partner) account and cover every organization under it. Organization-scoped users cannot see or manage them.
- **Who can manage a connection.** Adding, editing, testing, syncing, deleting and mapping customers requires a partner user with organization write permission, access to *all* organizations, and MFA. Partner users with access to only selected organizations can view the connection but not change it.
- **A Cove API user.** In the Cove Management Console, go to **Management → Users → API Users**, select your **top-level customer** in the Customer list, and click **Add API User**. Give it a login name (for example, `breeze-sync`) and the most restrictive role that can still read customers and backup statistics. Copy the token when it is shown — Cove displays it only once; if you lose it, delete the API user and create a new one. An API user cannot sign in to the console, so two-factor authentication does not apply to it.

sections.heading: Connecting Cove
sections.text:
1. Go to **Integrations** and open the **Backup** tab. (The old address `/settings/integrations/backup` redirects here.)
2. Click **Add connection** and choose **Cove Data Protection**.
3. Enter a **Connection name** (for example, *Main Cove account*). For **Cove partner name**, enter the name of the customer the API user was created under, exactly as Cove shows it. Enter the API user's login name as the **Username** and its token as the **Password**.
4. Optionally turn on **Show the provider name in the client portal**. It is off by default, so customer-facing views use the generic label *Managed cloud backup* instead of the vendor name.
5. Save. Breeze signs in to Cove before saving anything — if the login fails, nothing is created and the error is shown. On success, the first sync starts right away.

The password is stored encrypted and is never shown again. To change it, use **Re-enter credentials** on the connection card; the new password is tested before it replaces the old one, so a failed change never leaves the connection without a working login.

sections.heading: Connection card actions
sections.text:
| Action | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| **Test connection** | Signs in to Cove and reports the account name and how many customers are visible. |
| **Sync now** | Queues an immediate sync instead of waiting for the next scheduled one. |
| **Active** toggle | Turning a connection off stops syncing and resolves its open alerts. |
| **Delete** | Removes the connection and its synced devices and history from Breeze. Cove itself is untouched. Open alerts from the connection are resolved. |

The card also shows the last sync time, customer and device counts, how many devices are linked or ambiguous, and how many devices sit under unmapped customers.

sections.heading: Mapping Customers to Organizations
sections.text:
Each Cove customer must be mapped to a Breeze organization before its devices appear anywhere in Breeze. Devices under an unmapped customer are counted on the connection card but never stored.

On each sync Breeze maps a new customer automatically only when the Cove customer's **external code** is set to a Breeze organization ID.

A customer whose name exactly matches one organization name (ignoring case) is **not** mapped automatically. It stays unmapped until you map it yourself. Before v0.118.0 such name matches were mapped on sync; mappings made that way are not changed by the upgrade, but check them. To have customers map themselves, set each Cove customer's external code to its Breeze organization ID.

An organization is only auto-mapped to one customer. Auto-mapped rows show an **Auto** badge.

To map a customer yourself, pick an organization in the **Customer mapping** list, or choose **Unmapped (kept)** to deliberately leave it out. Manual choices are never overridden by auto-mapping. Re-mapping a customer immediately removes its devices, history and open alerts from the old organization and starts a sync so they reappear under the new one.

sections.heading: Device Matching
sections.text:
Within a mapped organization, Breeze links each Cove device to a Breeze device automatically:

- A Cove device whose computer name matches exactly one Breeze device's hostname or display name (ignoring case) is linked.
- If several devices share that name, Breeze narrows the match by MAC address.
- If there is still no single match, or the matching device is already linked to another provider device, the Cove device stays unlinked and is counted as **Ambiguous** on the connection card.

Decommissioned devices are never matched, and Microsoft 365 backup accounts are shown as accounts rather than linked to a device. If an automatic link is wrong, click **Unlink** on the device's external backup card (below). The Cove device stays in Cove and can be linked again later.

sections.heading: Sync, History and Alerts
sections.text:
Each connection syncs **every 30 minutes**. A connection whose login Cove rejects is marked **Credentials rejected** and stops syncing until you use **Re-enter credentials** with a working login. If a connection has not synced for more than two sync intervals, its devices show as **Unknown** health and the backup health view shows a banner that provider data is out of date.

Breeze keeps a **daily history** for each provider device (the worst status seen that day), shown as the *Last 28 days* strip. History older than 60 days is pruned.

Alerts are raised only for provider devices **linked to a Breeze device**:

| Condition | Severity |
|-----------|----------|
| Backup failed | High |
| Backup over quota | High |
| No backups recorded | High |
| No successful backup in 48 hours | High |
| Backup completed with errors (or interrupted) | Medium |
| Nothing selected for backup | Medium |

To avoid noise from one bad poll, an alert is raised only when the **same condition is seen on two consecutive syncs**. It resolves automatically on the **first sync where the condition no longer holds**, with the note *Condition cleared by provider sync*.

sections.heading: Where Provider Data Appears
sections.text:
- **Backup overview → Backup health.** One table of every managed device plus every device the provider reports, with status, last successful backup, data sources, selected and used size, errors and the 28-day history. Filter by health, by source (Breeze or provider), or search by device or organization. Summary counts show coverage, provider-only endpoints and Microsoft 365 accounts. Partner users in **all-organizations** mode see this health view across every organization.
- **Device → Backup tab.** An **External backup** card sits above Breeze's own backup sections, showing the Cove device name, status, last successful backup, last session, provider customer, data sources, sizes, errors and the 28-day history.
- **Attention items.** A device covered by a recent provider backup is no longer listed as overdue.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text:
- Status only: no restores, backup runs, or configuration changes through Breeze.
- Cove Data Protection is the only supported provider.
- Cove users with two-factor authentication cannot be used for the connection.
- Microsoft 365 backup accounts are shown in backup health but never raise device alerts.

sections.heading: Related
sections.text:
- [Monitoring Backups](/backup/monitoring/)
- [Backup Overview](/backup/overview/)

title: Bare Metal Recovery
description: Boot the Breeze recovery media, enter a one-time code, and rebuild a Linux machine from a whole-machine snapshot onto a blank disk — or, as the fallback, reinstall an OS yourself and recover files or OS state into it with a recovery token.
headings: Known limits of the media path
Alternative: recover into a freshly installed OS
What a Recovered Machine Is — and Isn't
Rebuilding a Linux disk from scratch (`breeze-backup rebuild`)

sections.text:
Bare Metal Recovery (BMR) has two modes.

- **Recover from Breeze recovery media** (Linux). Download the release-built Linux ISO, boot the target machine from it, and enter a one-time nine-character code from the console. The media partitions the blank disk from the layout recorded with the snapshot, restores a whole-machine snapshot into it, applies the OS state offline, installs the bootloader and reboots into the rebuilt system. Progress is reported live on the recovery's timeline in Breeze. This is the path for a dead disk or replacement hardware; see [Recover from Breeze recovery media](#recover-from-breeze-recovery-media).
- **Reinstall-then-recover** (all platforms). You put a working OS on the target machine yourself, then run the `breeze-backup` recovery binary with a one-time token. A `file` snapshot restores its files onto whatever is booted; a `system_image` snapshot downloads the OS-state artifacts collected at backup time, verifies each one, and **applies them to the booted OS** (registry hives, `/etc`, packages, services, firewall rules, scheduled tasks — see [What gets applied](#what-a-system_image-recovery-applies)). There is no WinPE/WinRE environment yet: on Windows and macOS this is the only mode, and you provide the booted OS before recovery starts. See [Alternative: recover into a freshly installed OS](#alternative-recover-into-a-freshly-installed-os).

Both modes share the same rebuild engine, [`breeze-backup rebuild`](#rebuilding-a-linux-disk-from-scratch-breeze-backup-rebuild), which is also available as a command-line tool for scripted or unusual recoveries.

A recovery token is scoped to **one snapshot**. A `file`-mode snapshot recovers data; a `system_image`-mode snapshot applies OS state. To recover both for one machine, generate two tokens (one per snapshot) and run `bmr-recover` twice, or back the machine up with a [Whole machine profile](/backup/profiles/#whole-machine-templates) so one snapshot carries both — a whole-machine profile is a single `system_image` selection that also walks the OS root, so it produces exactly one snapshot with files, layout, and system state together, not a separate file snapshot plus a files-less `system_image` snapshot.

  Recovering from an **incremental** snapshot — one that reuses files unchanged since an earlier snapshot instead of re-uploading them — works the same as recovering from a full snapshot, in every mode on this page. Breeze resolves those cross-snapshot references automatically at recovery time.

---

sections.heading: Recover from Breeze recovery media
sections.text: This is the fully guided path. It needs a whole-machine snapshot that Breeze marked **Bare-metal restorable** (see [Is the snapshot bare-metal restorable?](#is-the-snapshot-bare-metal-restorable)) and a target machine that boots UEFI with one blank disk at least as large as the source disk.

sections.heading: 1. Get the media
sections.text:
1. Open **Backup → Recovery Bootstrap**. The **Boot media** list shows the current release's `breeze-recovery-linux-amd64.iso` and `breeze-recovery-linux-arm64.iso` with their SHA-256 checksums. The same files are attached to each [GitHub release](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/releases) and served by your Breeze server at `/download/recovery-iso/linux/<arch>`.
2. Write the ISO to a USB stick (`dd if=breeze-recovery-linux-amd64.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress`, Rufus in DD mode, or balenaEtcher), or attach it as a virtual DVD to a VM.
3. Keep the media current. The server enforces a minimum media version at code exchange, so an ISO from an older release is refused with `This recovery media (vX) is older than the server requires (vY); download the current ISO.`

The media is a Debian live system with the `breeze-backup` binary and nothing else of yours on it: no server address, no credentials, no snapshot data. Everything is fetched at recovery time with the code.

sections.heading: 2. Create a recovery code
sections.text:
1. Still on **Recovery Bootstrap**, in the **Bare-metal recovery** panel, pick the snapshot to rebuild from. Only snapshots marked **Bare-metal restorable** are listed.
2. Choose the **Device identity**:
   - **Original device** — the rebuilt machine keeps its machine ID, hostname and agent enrollment, and the recovery completes when it checks in for the first time. Use this to bring the same device back on repaired or identical hardware.
   - **New device** — the machine ID is regenerated, the hostname gets a `-restored` suffix and the agent identity is stripped, so it enrolls as a brand-new device if you install an agent. Use this for rehearsals, VMs, or when the original is still in service.
3. Click **Create recovery code**. The code (`XXX-XXX-XXX`) is shown once, expires after **15 minutes**, and can be used **once**. Create it right before you boot the media.

  One recovery at a time per device. While a recovery is anywhere between `created` and `rebooted`, creating another for the same device is refused with `recovery_in_progress`; it clears once the recovery reaches a terminal state (`checked_in`, `completed`, `failed` or `refused`).

  **Recovery media too old.** If this snapshot's files reference objects
  stored under an earlier snapshot, the console needs recovery media that
  supports cross-snapshot references. An older ISO is refused with a
  message telling you to download the current recovery media and boot
  again — the target disk is never touched.

  Recovery media and recovery tools older than v0.120.0 are refused at
  code exchange and authentication with **This recovery tool is too old to
  check backup integrity.** Rebuild or download current media before you
  need it. Recovering from a **Not verified** (unattested) snapshot also
  needs a technician's two-factor confirmation; see
  [Integrity checks on restore](/backup/restoring/#integrity-checks-on-restore).

  **Preparing file index.** The first time you recover from an incremental
  snapshot, Breeze may need a few seconds to a few minutes to verify which
  older-snapshot objects it references. The console retries automatically
  and shows "Breeze is preparing the file index for this snapshot…" while
  it waits — this is expected and does not consume one of your three code
  attempts.

sections.heading: 3. Boot and follow the console
sections.text:
1. Boot the target machine from the media. GRUB starts the live system automatically after 5 seconds; the console also mirrors to the first serial port (`ttyS0`, 115200 8N1) for headless servers reached over IPMI or SOL.
2. **Breeze server URL** — enter your server's `https://` address. Plain `http://` is refused unless the media was booted with `breeze.insecure=1` on the kernel command line (development only).
3. **Recovery code** — enter the code. You get three attempts. On success the console downloads the plan: the device, snapshot time, source disk layout, the detected target disk with model, size and serial, and the identity mode.
4. If more than one candidate disk is found, choose one by number. Disks that are mounted or hold the live system are never offered.
5. **Confirm** by typing the target disk's serial number exactly as shown, or `ERASE` when the disk reports no serial (common for virtual disks). Anything else cancels without touching the disk.
6. The seven rebuild phases run with progress on screen: preflight, provision, restore, boot, identity, encryption, validate. Each phase is also posted to Breeze, so the recovery's timeline on the **Recovery Bootstrap** panel moves through `Media booted → Planned → Restoring → Validated → Rebooted`.
7. `Restored. Rebooting in 10 s (press any key to stay).` Remove the media. With **Original device** the recovery becomes `Checked in` on the restored agent's first heartbeat; with **New device** it is `Completed` as soon as validation passes.

If a phase fails or the snapshot is refused, the reason stays on screen with a `[r]etry  [s]hell  [p]oweroff` prompt, and the same reason is recorded on the recovery in Breeze. `[s]hell` drops to a root shell on the live system for inspection. Re-running the same recovery resumes: phases already completed are skipped and restore progress is kept.

**Unattended boot options:**
  The kernel command line accepts `breeze.server=`, `breeze.code=`, `breeze.target=`, `breeze.confirm=` and `breeze.after=poweroff` to pre-answer the prompts. These exist for Breeze's own CI and for lab automation; a code on a command line is a code in a boot log, so do not use them for production recoveries.

sections.heading: Known limits of the media path
sections.text:
- **Linux only today.** There is no Windows or macOS recovery media. For those, use [reinstall-then-recover](#alternative-recover-into-a-freshly-installed-os), or rebuild a Windows snapshot onto a VHDX with [Restore as VM](#restore-as-vm) or a [DR rehearsal](/backup/disaster-recovery/).
- **One blank UEFI/GPT disk** at least as large as the source disk, from a snapshot marked **Bare-metal restorable**. Multi-disk, BIOS/MBR, LVM, LUKS, RAID, btrfs and ZFS layouts are named at backup time and not rebuilt.
- **No driver injection.** The rebuilt system boots with the drivers its own image carries; see [Windows fidelity](#windows-fidelity) for the Windows side.
- **Rehearsal is not production.** DR rehearsals and Restore as VM rebuild into a disk image on a rebuild host and prove the snapshot can be rebuilt; only a recovery from the media brings a real machine back (with **Original device** it counts as done once the machine checks in).

Every rebuild outcome, with its measured duration, also feeds the device's [recovery readiness](/backup/verification/#bare-metal-rebuild-evidence) — a failed or stale rebuild shows up as a risk factor on the Verification tab.

---

sections.heading: Alternative: recover into a freshly installed OS
sections.text:
Use this mode on Windows and macOS, on Linux machines whose layout is not bare-metal restorable, or when you only need data or configuration back on a machine that already boots.

1. Get a working OS onto the target machine by installing one normally.
2. Generate a **recovery token** from a backup snapshot and download the recovery bundle (the `breeze-backup` binary, a launch script, and `bootstrap.json`).
3. On the target machine, run the recovery binary with the token — no Breeze enrollment needed.
4. It downloads the snapshot: for a `file` snapshot, files are restored to their original paths; for a `system_image` snapshot, every OS-state artifact is downloaded, its size and SHA-256 checksum are verified against the snapshot's manifest, and the platform restorer applies it.
5. A post-restore validation probe runs and reports pass/fail; nothing reboots the machine for you.

sections.heading: Generating a Recovery Token
sections.text:
1. Find the snapshot you want to recover from (via the Backup dashboard or device backup tab).
2. Select **Bare Metal Recovery** from the restore options.
3. Configure the recovery:
   - **Snapshot** — the single backup to recover from (one snapshot per token)
   - **Token lifetime** — how long the token remains valid, 1–168 hours
   - **Restore type** — Full, Selective, or Bare Metal
   - **Target configuration** — optional `source=target` path remappings applied on the recovery machine
4. Click **Generate Token**.
5. The token is displayed **once**. Copy it immediately — it's stored as a SHA-256 hash and cannot be retrieved later.

Once a token exists, download the recovery bundle (the helper binary and a launch script) for the target platform from the **Recovery Bootstrap** tab. Bootable media is no longer built per token; use the release ISO described above.

sections.heading: Recovery bundle signing
sections.text:
**v0.118.0+.** Before it runs the helper binary, a recovery bundle's launch script downloads that binary's signature from your Breeze server (authenticated with the recovery token) and checks it with `minisign`. It checks against the public key written into the bundle when it was built, never a key fetched at run time. The script refuses to run the helper when:

- the bundle was built without recovery signing configured on the server, so it carries no key;
- `minisign` (or, on Linux and macOS, `curl`) is not installed on the recovery machine;
- the server has no signature for the binary, or the signature does not match.

To build bundles that run, set `RECOVERY_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY` and `RECOVERY_SIGNING_PUBLIC_KEY` on the API, and make a `minisign` binary available to it (see [Environment Variables → Backup](/deploy/environment/#backup-enterprise-agent-backup)). **Rebuild bundles you downloaded before upgrading to v0.118.0**, and install `minisign` on the machine you recover.

  Recovery tokens are shown only once at creation time. Store the token securely and use it promptly. If lost, generate a new one.

  Recovering data and OS state for one machine takes two tokens and two runs unless the snapshot came from a profile with both **Files** and **System image** enabled: one against the device's `system_image` snapshot, one against its `file` snapshot.

---

sections.heading: Running the Recovery
sections.text:
1. Get the target machine to a booted OS by installing one normally.
2. Install `minisign` (and `curl` on Linux and macOS) on the target machine; the launch script needs it to [verify the helper](#recovery-bundle-signing). Download and extract the recovery bundle for the target platform/architecture, then run the launch script (`run-recovery.sh` / `run-recovery.ps1`) or the binary directly:
```
   breeze-backup bmr-recover --token <recovery-token> --server <breeze-server-url>
```
   Add `--target-path <source>=<target>` (repeatable) to remap individual file paths from the snapshot onto different locations on the recovery machine; anything not remapped restores to its original path. `Ctrl+C` (SIGINT/SIGTERM) stops the run cleanly and reports `recovery interrupted by signal`.
3. The recovery agent authenticates with the token and downloads the snapshot manifest.
4. For a `system_image` snapshot, the recovery binary downloads the system-state manifest and each artifact into a temporary staging directory, verifies every artifact's size and checksum, and then applies them — see [What a `system_image` recovery applies](#what-a-system_image-recovery-applies). Any artifact that fails verification is discarded and reported as a warning, and the run's `stateApplied` result is `false`.
5. For a `file` snapshot, files are downloaded and written to their original paths (or their `--target-path` remapping). Files, symbolic links, empty directories, ownership and permission bits are restored when the snapshot recorded them (see [File backup fidelity](/backup/policies/#file-backup)); ownership and setuid/setgid/sticky bits are applied only when the recovery runs as root, otherwise one summary warning is printed.
6. A post-restore validation probe checks network reachability, presence of critical files, and service status, and reports the result — it does not repair or retry anything it finds wrong.

#### Reading the result

The run ends with a status and a short result summary (`filesRestored`, `failedFiles`, `bytesRestored`, `stateApplied`, `validated`, `warnings`, and an optional result `code`). The same fields are recorded against the recovery in Breeze, and the **Recovery Bootstrap** tab shows any code as **Result code: …** — for example an integrity code such as `checksum_mismatch` (see [Integrity checks on restore](/backup/restoring/#integrity-checks-on-restore)). Advisory warnings (unattested snapshot, vault fallback, files-only Windows recovery) are shown as warnings, never as the failure reason.

For an attested snapshot, the recovery checks the manifest, the system-state manifest and every file against the attestation before using them, and stages each file privately (readable only by root, or SYSTEM and Administrators) before moving it into place, keeping the replaced file's owner, mode and permissions. A snapshot that failed its integrity check is refused.

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `completed` | Every file restored and, for a `system_image` snapshot, the system state was found, verified and applied (`stateApplied: true`). |
| `partial` | Some files restored or the state was applied, but something else failed — read `warnings`. A `system_image` run whose state manifest was found but could not be applied (missing required step, failed checksum) is never reported as `completed`. |
| `failed` | Nothing was restored. Also the outcome when the token's snapshot advertised system state that could not be found, or a step the snapshot marks as **required** was never collected. |

A snapshot counts as advertising system state when its backup type is `system_image` **or** it recorded a state manifest — so a `system_image` snapshot whose state collection failed is held to the same rule rather than recovering "successfully" with files only. The same gate applies to [`breeze-backup rebuild`](#rebuilding-a-linux-disk-from-scratch-breeze-backup-rebuild) and the recovery media, which refuse such a snapshot before touching the disk.

**Before v0.112.0, a completed system_image recovery applied nothing:**
  Snapshots taken before v0.112.0 published their OS-state artifacts under a location the recovery binary never looked at, so a `system_image` recovery downloaded them, applied nothing and still reported `completed` with `stateApplied: false`. Both halves are fixed in v0.112.0 — the agent publishes state where the consumer reads it, and the consumer refuses to report `completed` when advertised state was not applied — but only for snapshots **taken by a v0.112.0 or later agent**. To recover OS state, take a fresh `system_image` backup after upgrading.

---

sections.heading: What a `system_image` recovery applies
sections.text: The artifacts are collected by the agent at backup time and applied by the platform restorer on the booted OS. Steps run in order; a failing step is logged and the remaining steps still run. **Linux** | Step | What is applied | |---|---| | `/etc` | Copied onto the live `/etc` — regular files, symlinks, modes and timestamps. **Excluded**, so the booted OS keeps its own identity and networking: `fstab`, `machine-id`, `hostname`, `netplan/`, `network/interfaces`, `NetworkManager/system-connections/`. The skipped paths are logged. | | Packages | The captured package list is reinstalled — `dpkg --set-selections` + `apt-get dselect-upgrade` on Debian/Ubuntu, `dnf install` on RHEL-family. Needs working package repositories. Entries are validated first: on RHEL-family an invalid package name is skipped with a warning; on Debian/Ubuntu a selections list with any invalid line is not applied at all, with a warning. | | Services | Every unit the source machine had **enabled** is re-enabled with `systemctl enable`. | | Firewall | `iptables-restore` of the captured rules. | | Scheduled tasks | Per-user crontabs are reinstalled with `crontab -u `. The system `/etc/crontab` is deliberately left alone. | Permissions and ownership inside the restored `/etc` currently reflect the staging copy (`0600`/`0700`, root-owned), not the source machine. Review anything that must be world-readable (for example `/etc/hosts`, `/etc/ssl/certs`) after a Linux recovery. **Windows** — **v0.120.0+: `bmr-recover` on Windows restores files only.** It no longer imports registry hives, the BCD store, certificates, firewall policy or drivers into the running system. The result carries `stateApplied: false`, the code `system_state_requires_rebuild` and a warning saying so; this is not a failure, and the **Recovery Bootstrap** tab shows the note **System state is applied by a bare-metal rebuild**. To apply a Windows snapshot's system state, rebuild it with the rebuild engine instead — for example [Restore as VM](#restore-as-vm) — which applies the hives, boot configuration and the rest offline. Earlier agents imported the `SYSTEM`, `SOFTWARE`, `SAM` and `SECURITY` hives with `reg restore`, the BCD store with `bcdedit /import`, the certificate store with `certutil -restoreDB`, firewall policy with `netsh advfirewall import`, and staged captured driver packages with `pnputil /add-driver … /install`, each best-effort. Since v0.120.0 the Windows agent flushes the loaded registry hives to disk just before it takes the VSS snapshot for a system-state backup, so registry changes made shortly before the backup (a newly created service, for example) are included. Earlier backups could miss changes that were still only in memory. **macOS** — preference plists into `/Library/Preferences`, LaunchDaemon/LaunchAgent items into `/Library/LaunchDaemons` and `/Library/LaunchAgents`, and the network configuration into `SystemConfiguration/preferences.plist` (followed by a `configd` restart). Best-effort, warnings only. On macOS the apply steps never fail the run, so a `stateApplied: false` there always means an artifact failed download or verification — check `warnings` for which one. On Windows, `stateApplied: false` is expected from v0.120.0 on (files only, see above). ---

sections.heading: What a Recovered Machine Is — and Isn't
sections.text:
A machine recovered with a `file` snapshot is: the OS you installed or booted, plus the recovered files, otherwise unchanged. A machine recovered with a `system_image` snapshot on Linux or macOS is: the OS you installed or booted, with the source machine's configuration layered back on top — its registry hives or `/etc`, services, firewall rules, scheduled tasks and (Linux) package set — while keeping the booted OS's own disk layout, boot identity, hostname, machine ID and network configuration. Neither snapshot type produces a byte-identical clone of the original machine: `bmr-recover` does no disk or partition imaging, and kernel and driver binaries come from the OS you installed. For a from-scratch rebuild of a Linux disk, use [`breeze-backup rebuild`](#rebuilding-a-linux-disk-from-scratch-breeze-backup-rebuild) instead.

---

sections.heading: Is the snapshot bare-metal restorable?
sections.text:
Every `system_image` backup taken by a v0.112.0 or later agent on Linux or Windows also records the machine's **disk layout** (disks, partition table, filesystems, boot mode, fstab) alongside the snapshot, and Breeze assesses whether that layout is one the rebuild engine can reproduce. The verdict is shown in the [Snapshot Browser](/backup/restoring/#browsing-snapshots) header as a **Bare-metal restorable** or **Not bare-metal restorable** badge — hover the amber badge for the reasons — and is included as a warning on the backup run.

A layout is restorable when the machine boots **UEFI**, its OS lives on **one GPT disk** with an EFI system partition, and the root filesystem is **ext4, xfs or ntfs**. Anything else is named at backup time rather than discovered at recovery time:

- BIOS/MBR boot (only UEFI with GPT is supported)
- the OS tree spread across more than one disk
- LVM volumes, LUKS/dm-crypt encrypted volumes, software RAID members
- a btrfs root filesystem, or ZFS anywhere in the OS tree
- no disk layout captured at all (macOS backups, or a collection error)

The badge governs only the `rebuild` path below. A snapshot marked *not* restorable can still be used with `bmr-recover` onto an OS you install yourself.

---

sections.heading: Rebuilding a Linux disk from scratch (`breeze-backup rebuild`)
sections.text:
`breeze-backup rebuild` is the from-scratch counterpart to `bmr-recover`: instead of restoring onto an OS you installed, it takes a **blank disk (or a raw image file)**, provisions the partitions recorded in the snapshot's layout manifest, restores a whole-machine snapshot into them, applies the system state offline, installs a bootloader and validates the result. It ships in the same `breeze-backup` binary as the recovery bundle, and — as of this release — runs on Windows rebuild hosts too: a Windows snapshot rebuilds on a Windows host, a Linux snapshot on a Linux host. The steps below (partition provisioning, offline restore, bootloader install) apply to both; where a step is platform-specific, that's called out.

**Scope:**
  Run from a booted host matching the snapshot's platform — a Linux snapshot
  rebuilds on Linux, a Windows snapshot on Windows (Breeze checks this and
  refuses the pair otherwise); the snapshot must be marked **Bare-metal
  restorable** and the target must be UEFI/GPT. The [recovery media](#recover-from-breeze-recovery-media)
  runs it for you; the command below is for scripted or unusual recoveries
  and does not appear in the device's command history. [Restore as VM](#restore-as-vm)
  and [DR bare-metal rebuild steps](/backup/disaster-recovery/#bare-metal-rebuild-step)
  also run this engine, targeting a VHDX image instead of a disk.

```
breeze-backup rebuild \
  --snapshot <snapshot-id> \
  --target disk:/dev/sdb        # or image:/path/to/disk.img with --image-size 40G
  --provider-config provider.json \
  [--identity original|new] [--marker-file marker.json] \
  [--dry-run] [--result-json result.json]
```

| Flag | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `--snapshot` | The `system_image` snapshot to rebuild from (must carry a layout manifest). |
| `--target` | `disk:/dev/…` for a real block device, `image:/path.img` for a raw image file (created sparse; `--image-size` is required when the file does not exist yet), or `vhdx:<path>` for a VHDX disk image. A mounted disk, or the one backing the running system, is refused. On a **live Windows host**, only `vhdx:` is supported — `disk:` needs a WinPE-booted environment, which doesn't ship until the Windows recovery media (W07). |
| `--provider-config` | JSON file with the backup destination credentials, as used by the recovery bundle. |
| `--identity` | `original` (default) keeps the machine ID, hostname and agent enrollment and writes a recovery marker; `new` clears the machine ID, appends `-restored` to the hostname and strips the agent's device identity so it re-enrolls as a new device. |
| `--dry-run` | Run the preflight only — fetch and verify the layout, plan the partitions, check the target — and print the plan without writing anything. |
| `--state-dir` | Where the resumable state file lives (default `/var/lib/breeze/rebuild`). |
| `--force-reprovision`, `--allow-partial`, `--no-initramfs` | Re-partition even if a previous run already did; continue when some files failed to restore; skip the initramfs regeneration. |
| `--expect-system-state` | `auto` (default), `true` or `false`: whether the snapshot must carry system state that the rebuild applies. `auto` says yes for a `system_image` snapshot (the recovery media and `--token` mode take this from the server's bootstrap; `--provider-config` mode infers it from a `layout.json` or state manifest in the snapshot). `false` rebuilds a file-only snapshot with a warning. |

The rebuild runs seven phases in order — **preflight → provision → restore → boot → identity → encryption → validate**:

1. **Preflight** downloads `layout.json`, refuses a snapshot that is not restorable or whose platform doesn't match the rebuild host's, checks the target is safe and large enough, plans the partitions, and downloads and checksum-verifies the snapshot and system-state manifests. Nothing is written. A `system_image` snapshot whose `system-state/manifest.json` is missing (or lists no artifacts) is **refused** here — the rebuild never proceeds files-only when system state was expected.
2. **Provision** wipes the target, recreates the GPT partitions with their original type codes, GUIDs, names and filesystem UUIDs/labels, and formats them.
3. **Restore** mounts the new partitions, restores the file snapshot into them, then applies the system state **offline** into that tree. On Linux, unlike a live `bmr-recover`, `/etc` is restored **without** the identity/network excludes (`fstab`, `machine-id`, `hostname` and network configuration do land, because the rebuilt disk is the original machine), services are enabled with `systemctl --root`, crontabs are written straight into the spool, and firewall rules are written to `/etc/iptables/rules.v4` (or `/etc/breeze/recovery/iptables.rules` with a warning if `iptables-persistent` is absent); package reinstall is skipped offline. On Windows, registry hives, the certificate store and firewall policy are applied offline into the mounted tree — see [Windows fidelity](#windows-fidelity) below for exactly what that covers.
4. **Boot** installs GRUB for UEFI on Linux (Debian/Ubuntu via `grub-install` + `update-grub`, RHEL-family via `grub2-mkconfig` + `efibootmgr`), regenerates the initramfs, and always writes the removable-media fallback loader (`EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI` / `BOOTAA64.EFI`); other Linux distribution families are not supported. On Windows, `bcdboot` regenerates the EFI system partition, run as the **rebuild host's own** `System32` binary, resolved by absolute path, never anything from the restored tree. Driver injection is not supported yet — see [Windows fidelity](#windows-fidelity).
5. **Identity** applies the `--identity` choice.
6. **Encryption** is a no-op in this release — encrypted layouts are refused at preflight, and a BitLocker-protected Windows source restores in plaintext with a recorded re-encryption intent (see [Windows fidelity](#windows-fidelity)).
7. **Validate** spot-checks a sample of restored files against their checksums, confirms the bootloader (`grub.cfg` on Linux, the BCD store on Windows) exists, cross-checks filesystem UUIDs/volume identifiers against the new partitions, then syncs and unmounts. When system state was expected, it also fails with `system state not applied` if the restore phase did not apply it.

The result JSON carries `stateManifestFound` and `stateApplied` alongside `status`; a rebuild is never `completed` unless `stateApplied` is `true` whenever system state was expected.

Progress is checkpointed to `<state-dir>/rebuild-<snapshot>-<target>.json` after every phase. If a run is interrupted, re-running the same command **resumes**: phases already completed are skipped, the partitions are re-attached rather than re-created, and the state file is removed only on success.

---

sections.heading: Restore as VM
sections.text:
The **VM Restore Wizard**'s **Rebuild engine** option runs the same [rebuild engine](#rebuilding-a-linux-disk-from-scratch-breeze-backup-rebuild)
described above, but writes the result straight to a **VHDX** disk image
instead of a physical disk on a platform-matched rebuild host. On a Windows
rebuild host it can also create (but does not start) a Hyper-V VM from that
VHDX — only when you ask for one in step 6; otherwise, and always on Linux,
you attach the VHDX to a VM yourself. It's offered alongside **Full Restore** and
**Instant Boot** whenever the selected snapshot carries a layout manifest
(the same **Bare-metal restorable** snapshots the recovery media uses).

1. Open the restore workflow for the device and choose **Restore as VM**.
2. Select the backup snapshot to restore.
3. On the **Restore mode** step, choose **Rebuild engine**.
4. Pick a **rebuild host** running the same platform as the snapshot — an
   online device running the Breeze helper with enough free disk space for
   the image. On Linux the host also needs `qemu-utils`; the engine's
   preflight refuses the run if `qemu-img` is missing or the free space is
   short. A Windows host writes the VHDX natively, so the rebuild itself
   needs no Hyper-V role — only the optional VM in step 6 does, and without
   it that step fails as described there.
5. Enter an absolute **output path** on the rebuild host ending in `.vhdx`
   (a POSIX path on Linux, a drive-letter path on Windows — a path in the
   other host's style is refused with `output_path_host_mismatch`).
6. On a Windows rebuild host, optionally name a Hyper-V VM and virtual
   switch — Breeze creates a Generation 2 VM from the finished VHDX, with
   no network adapter unless you name a switch, and leaves it off for you
   to start. If VM creation fails, the rebuild still completes, the VHDX is
   kept, and the failure is reported rather than hidden: it is the first
   warning on the restore job (shown as its error summary in the restore
   history) and is recorded on the recovery's result as `vmCreated: false`
   with the reason in `vmError`.
7. Click **Start Rebuild**.

The rebuilt image always gets a **new machine identity** — a new machine ID,
a `-restored` hostname, and no agent enrollment — since it's building a
standalone copy, not reclaiming the original device.

---

sections.heading: Windows fidelity
sections.text:
What a Windows whole-machine rebuild preserves, and what it doesn't yet:

**Preserved:**
- NTFS security descriptors (owner, group, DACL) for every file and
  directory, so a rebuilt `C:\Windows\System32\config` keeps its original
  ACLs rather than inheriting Authenticated-Users-Modify from a fresh
  volume — this closes the class of issue behind CVE-2021-36934.
- Partition GUIDs, the EFI boot configuration, and (best-effort) boot-start
  storage driver settings for the disk controller the target machine
  actually has.
- The machine's SID is never regenerated.

**Not yet restored:**
- Driver injection is not supported yet: the rebuilt system boots with the
  drivers its own image carries. Boot the restored machine and install any
  other drivers from Windows. `breeze-backup rebuild --drivers` is refused
  with that message rather than ignored.
- Hard links, alternate data streams, and EFS-encrypted file contents.
- Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) partition contents — the partition
  is recreated and formatted but left empty; `reagentc` is not run.
- A BitLocker-protected source volume restores in **plaintext**. Breeze
  records the intent to re-encrypt on first boot; the executor for that
  intent ships with the Windows recovery media (W07).
- A domain controller source is refused at preflight — recovering a DC
  this way risks a broken AD replication topology; use your normal DC
  recovery procedure instead. The refusal can only be overridden from the
  command line (`breeze-backup rebuild --allow-domain-controller`), after
  reading the DC recovery guidance; the recovery console, Restore as VM
  and DR rehearsals never override it.

---

sections.heading: When to Use BMR
sections.text:
| Scenario | Approach |
|----------|----------|
| **Hard drive failure (Linux, UEFI/GPT)** | [Boot the Breeze recovery media](#recover-from-breeze-recovery-media) and enter a recovery code for a **Bare-metal restorable** whole-machine snapshot. |
| **Hard drive failure (other)** | Install/boot an OS on the new disk, recover data with a `file` snapshot, then apply configuration with a `system_image` snapshot. |
| **Machine replacement** | Install a base OS on the replacement hardware, then recover data and system state with BMR. Drivers and hardware-specific configuration come from the OS you installed; `rebuild` targets identical or compatible hardware. |
| **Disaster recovery** | BMR as part of a [DR plan](/backup/disaster-recovery/). |
| **Migration** | Recover data onto different hardware, then decide whether to apply the `system_image` snapshot — it brings the old machine's services, firewall rules and (Linux) package set with it. |

For recovering individual files or databases onto an already-enrolled device, use the standard [restore workflow](/backup/restoring/) instead — it's faster and doesn't require a recovery token.

---

sections.heading: Recovery Token Security
sections.text:
- Tokens authenticate recovery agents the same way JWT authenticates regular users — they grant time-limited access to a specific snapshot
- Tokens are hashed (SHA-256) at rest and cannot be retrieved after creation
- Each token is scoped to a single snapshot and organization
- Expired tokens are automatically invalidated
- A token is consumed by the first recovery that completes (fully or with some files failed). A run that fails before completing — for example a network drop mid-download — is recorded against the token but does not consume it, so you can rerun `bmr-recover` with the same token until it expires. Revoke the token from the console if you no longer want it usable.

title: Cloud-to-Cloud Backup
