description: Back up Microsoft 365 mailboxes, OneDrive, and SharePoint plus Google Workspace Drive data, with delta sync for incremental backups.

sections.text:
Cloud-to-Cloud (C2C) backup is designed to protect your organization's SaaS data — Microsoft 365 mailboxes, OneDrive files, SharePoint sites, and Google Workspace Drive content — using delta sync for incremental updates. You can connect a Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace tenant and define a backup configuration today, but syncing and restoring data is not yet implemented — see [Running a Sync](#running-a-sync) below.

---

sections.heading: Connecting Microsoft 365
sections.text:
Two authentication modes are available depending on your Breeze deployment:

  **Multi-tenant app (recommended):**
    If your Breeze instance has `C2C_M365_CLIENT_ID` and `C2C_M365_CLIENT_SECRET` configured, the one-click consent flow is available.

    1. Go to the **C2C** section in Breeze.
    2. Click **Grant Access** (or **Connect Microsoft 365**).
    3. You're redirected to Microsoft's admin consent screen.
    4. Sign in with a Microsoft 365 admin account and grant the requested permissions.
    5. Microsoft redirects back to Breeze. The connection is created automatically.

  **Manual credentials:**
    If the platform app isn't configured, the connection wizard prompts you to register an Azure AD app manually.

    1. In the Azure portal, register a new app and grant the required Graph API permissions.
    2. In Breeze, open the C2C connection wizard.
    3. Enter the **Client ID**, **Client Secret**, and **Tenant ID** from your Azure AD app.
    4. Click **Connect**.

---

sections.heading: Connecting Google Workspace
sections.text:
Google Workspace backup requires a service account with domain-wide delegation.

1. In the Google Cloud Console, create a service account and enable domain-wide delegation.
2. In your Google Workspace admin console, authorize the service account's client ID with the required scopes.
3. In Breeze, open the C2C connection wizard and select **Google Workspace**.
4. Upload the service account key file.
5. Click **Connect**.

---

sections.heading: Managing Connections
sections.text:
Once connected, your C2C connections appear in the connections list showing:
- Provider (Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace)
- Connection status
- Last sync time
- Number of accounts/sites backed up

---

sections.heading: Configuring Backup Scope
sections.text:
After connecting, create a backup configuration to define what gets backed up:

1. Click **Add Backup Config** in the C2C section.
2. Select the connection to use.
3. Choose what to include:
   - **Mailboxes** — select specific users or all users
   - **OneDrive / Google Drive** — file storage for selected users
   - **SharePoint sites** — select specific sites (Microsoft 365 only)
4. Set a sync schedule (how often to pull changes).
5. Click **Save**.

---

sections.heading: Running a Sync
sections.text:
Sync execution is not yet implemented. Clicking **Run Now** (or waiting for the schedule) creates a sync job, but that job immediately fails with `c2c_sync_not_implemented`. No mailbox, OneDrive, SharePoint, or Google Workspace data is actually transferred by a C2C sync today.

---

sections.heading: Restoring C2C Data
sections.text: Restore execution is not yet implemented. Triggering a restore creates a job that immediately fails with `c2c_restore_not_implemented`. There is currently no way to recover C2C data through Breeze.

title: Disaster Recovery Plans
description: Build disaster recovery plans with ordered recovery groups, RTO and RPO targets, test and live execution types, and execution history tracking.

sections.text:
Disaster Recovery (DR) plans let you define how to bring your systems back online after a major incident. You organize devices into ordered recovery groups, set overall RTO/RPO targets, and rehearse the plan before you need it.

---

sections.heading: Creating a DR Plan
sections.text:
1. Navigate to the **Disaster Recovery** section.
2. Click **Create Plan**.
3. Enter the plan details:
   - **Name** — descriptive label (e.g., "Primary site failover")
   - **Description** — operator notes explaining the plan's scope and assumptions
   - **RPO target** — maximum acceptable data loss in minutes
   - **RTO target** — maximum acceptable recovery time in minutes
4. Click **Save**.

---

sections.heading: Adding Recovery Groups
sections.text:
Recovery groups define which devices to recover and in what order. Groups execute sequentially — group 1 completes before group 2 starts.

1. Open your DR plan.
2. Click **Add Recovery Group**.
3. Configure the group:
   - **Name** — e.g., "Domain Controllers", "Database Servers", "Application Tier"
   - **Devices** — select which devices belong to this group
   - **Step type** — how to restore each device in the group; see [Step Types](#step-types) below
   - **Sequence order** — execution priority (lower numbers run first)
   - **Dependencies** — optionally set a group to depend on another group completing first
4. Repeat for each recovery tier.

sections.heading: Step Types
sections.text:
Every recovery group has one step type, which determines how its devices are restored:

| Step type | What it does |
|---|---|
| VM restore from backup | Restores the snapshot as a new Hyper-V virtual machine. |
| VM instant boot | Boots a VM directly from backup storage while data migrates to the host in the background. |
| Hyper-V restore | Restores a Hyper-V export/backup back onto a Hyper-V host. |
| SQL Server restore | Restores a SQL Server backup chain. |
| Bare-metal recover (boot media) | Boots the device from [Breeze recovery media](/backup/bare-metal-recovery/#recover-from-breeze-recovery-media) and enters a recovery code. |
| Bare-metal rebuild (rebuild engine) | Runs the [rebuild engine](/backup/bare-metal-recovery/#rebuilding-a-linux-disk-from-scratch-breeze-backup-rebuild) against a rebuild host running the same platform as the snapshot. See [Bare-metal rebuild step](#bare-metal-rebuild-step) below. |

**Steps never store credentials (v0.118.0+):**
  A step's restore settings cannot include a recovery token or storage credentials. Breeze resolves the storage destination from the snapshot when the step runs. Saving a step that includes one is rejected. Steps saved on an earlier release that stored one **fail when they run**; the v0.118.0 upgrade removes those keys, so open each such step and save it again.

#### Bare-metal rebuild step

The **bare-metal rebuild** step type behaves differently depending on the execution type:

- **Rehearsal** — rebuilds each group device's latest **bare-metal restorable** snapshot into a VHDX image on a rebuild host, without touching production hardware. Configure:
  - **Rebuild host** — an online device running the same platform as the group's snapshots (Linux: `qemu-utils` installed; Windows: Hyper-V role) that runs the rehearsal rebuilds. A mismatched pairing is refused.
  - **Output directory** — where the rebuild host writes one VHDX image per device; defaults to a per-OS path on the rebuild host (`/var/lib/breeze/rebuild/out` on Linux, `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\rebuild\out` on Windows) when left blank.
  - Rehearsals only write the VHDX — they never create a Hyper-V VM automatically, even on a Windows rebuild host; that automatic VM creation is a **Restore as VM** feature (see [Restore as VM](/backup/bare-metal-recovery/#restore-as-vm)).
- **Failover** and **Failback** — boot each group device from Breeze recovery media instead, restoring it in place with its original device identity. The rebuild host and output directory settings are only used for rehearsals.

The **Wait timeout (minutes)** setting applies to all three execution types. It is how long each device's recovery may run before the step marks that device failed and cancels its recovery. For a failover or failback, this includes the time before someone boots the recovery media. The default is **1440** (24 hours), which is also the maximum. A whole-machine rebuild can take several hours: in testing, a Windows rebuild of about 133,000 files (20.6 GB) took over 5 hours. Steps saved on an earlier release stored the old default of **240** (4 hours) and keep it. On such a plan, a large rehearsal is cancelled at 4 hours, so open the step and raise the value.

Each device recovers from its own latest snapshot marked **Bare-metal restorable**; a device with no such snapshot fails the step with a specific "no restorable snapshot" error rather than a generic one. During execution, the per-device recovery status is shown in the execution view, where you can also **Reissue code** (rotate an unused recovery code) or **Cancel recovery** for a device that's in progress.

##### Rebuild host requirements

| | Linux rebuild host | Windows rebuild host |
|---|---|---|
| OS | Any Linux with the tools below; same distro family is not required | Windows Server or Windows 10/11 with Hyper-V |
| Tools | `util-linux`, `sgdisk`, `dosfstools`, `e2fsprogs`/`xfsprogs`, `grub-efi`, `efibootmgr`, `qemu-utils` (used to convert a raw image to VHDX) | Built-in `bcdboot.exe`, `dism.exe`, `format.com`; Hyper-V role for automatic VM creation |
| Target snapshot platform | Must match the rebuild host's OS — Breeze refuses the pair otherwise | Must match the rebuild host's OS — Breeze refuses the pair otherwise |

sections.heading: Example Recovery Order
sections.text:
| Order | Group | Devices | Why |
|-------|-------|---------|-----|
| 1 | Domain Controllers | DC01, DC02 | Authentication must be online first |
| 2 | Database Servers | SQL01, SQL02 | Applications need their data layer |
| 3 | Application Servers | APP01–APP04 | Now that auth and data are up |
| 4 | File Servers | FS01 | Lower priority, can wait |

  Model your recovery groups after your service dependency chain. If Application Server depends on Database Server, put the database in an earlier group.

---

sections.heading: Execution Types
sections.text:
| Type | What happens | When to use |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| **Rehearsal** | Validates recovery steps without modifying production systems | Regular DR testing (quarterly recommended) |
| **Failover** | Live execution — actually restores systems according to the plan | Real disaster or planned migration |
| **Failback** | Returns services to the primary environment after a failover | After the original site is repaired |

---

sections.heading: Running a DR Plan
sections.text:
1. Open the plan and click **Execute**.
2. Select the execution type: **Rehearsal**, **Failover**, or **Failback**.
3. Confirm to start.
4. Recovery groups execute in sequence order. Track progress in the execution detail view.
5. To stop a running execution, click **Abort**.

If a group can't start, the execution error names the specific missing prerequisite — for example, no restorable snapshot for a device, or no valid recovery source — instead of a generic error, so you know exactly what to fix before retrying.

DR plan steps that restore a backup also follow the [restore integrity checks](/backup/restoring/#integrity-checks-on-restore): each target device needs a v0.120.0 or later agent, and a plan cannot restore a **Not verified** (unattested) snapshot, because that needs a technician's two-factor confirmation. Restore such a snapshot from the console instead.

sections.heading: Viewing Execution History
sections.text:
Past executions are listed on the plan detail page, showing:
- Execution type (rehearsal/failover/failback)
- Start and end times
- Status (running, completed, failed, aborted)
- Per-group results

---

sections.heading: DR Testing Best Practices
sections.text:
- **Rehearse quarterly** at minimum. Real disasters are not the time to discover your plan doesn't work.
- **Start with a rehearsal** before relying on a plan for production failover.
- **Review after each rehearsal** — update device assignments, sequence orders, and targets based on what you learned.
- **Keep plans current** — when you add or decommission servers, update the recovery groups.
- **Combine with SLA monitoring** — your [SLA policies](/backup/sla/) track whether RPO/RTO targets are achievable day-to-day, giving you confidence before a DR event.

title: Encryption Key Management
description: How backup data is actually encrypted at rest today (S3 server-side encryption), and the early-access client-managed key manager for a future client-side encryption model.
headings: How to Actually Protect Backup Data Today

sections.text:
Backup data at rest is protected by your storage destination's own encryption, not by a Breeze-managed cipher on the agent. Today that means **S3 server-side encryption (SSE)** — there is no agent-side encryption step, and no client-managed key is currently used to encrypt or decrypt any live backup.

---

sections.heading: What's Actually Enforced
sections.text:
Encryption is a toggle on your [storage configuration](/backup/storage/), and it's only enforceable for **Amazon S3** (or S3-compatible) destinations:

- **SSE-S3 (AES-256)** — set `serverSideEncryption` to `AES256` in the provider config. S3 encrypts every object with an AWS-managed key.
- **SSE-KMS** — set `serverSideEncryption` to `aws:kms` and provide a `kmsKeyId` (or `keyArn`). S3 encrypts objects using your own KMS key.

If you enable encryption on a **Local/NAS** destination, or on S3 without a recognized `serverSideEncryption` value, Breeze rejects the configuration as unsupported — there is no client-side fallback cipher for those cases.

---

sections.heading: Encryption Keys Manager (Early Access)
sections.text:
Go to **Backup > Device Backup > Encryption** to see the key manager.

  This page is early access and is **not wired to any live backup data**. Creating, rotating, or deactivating a key here does not encrypt, protect, or otherwise affect any actual backup or snapshot today — the agent has no encryption capability of its own to apply these keys to. It exists ahead of a planned client-side (envelope) encryption model.

The key list shows:
- Key name
- Key type (AES-256 or RSA-2048)
- Status: **Active** (green), **Rotated** (gray), or **Deactivated** (red)
- Created date
- Expiry date (if set)

1. Click **Create New Key**.
2. Enter a descriptive name (e.g., "Production AES Key 2026").
3. Select the key type (AES-256 or RSA-2048).
4. Click **Create**.
5. The key's fingerprint (SHA-256 hash) is displayed once, at creation time.

Keys can also be rotated (the old key moves to **Rotated**, a new one becomes **Active**) or deactivated. Rotation is manual only — there is no scheduled or automatic rotation.

---

sections.heading: How to Actually Protect Backup Data Today
sections.text:
- **In transit** — all backup data is transferred over HTTPS (TLS 1.2+)
- **At rest** — for S3 destinations, enable server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) on the storage configuration, as described above
- For Local/NAS destinations, rely on your own disk/volume-level encryption — Breeze does not encrypt data written to a local path

title: HTTPS for Backups
description: Backups to S3 storage are written through a short-lived storage session over HTTPS. The minimum agent version, what a self-hosted install needs, and how to replace and disable the storage keys used before.
headings: Replacing and disabling old storage keys

sections.text:
Backups to **S3 or S3-compatible storage** (MinIO, Wasabi, Backblaze B2 and so on) are written through a short-lived, write-scoped **storage session**. The session is bound to one backup job, one device and one snapshot identifier that Breeze issues for that job. The device uploads each object with a signed link that Breeze issues for that object only. No backup command carries the storage destination or its access keys. This covers file and system image backups, SQL Server backups and Hyper-V backups, whether scheduled or run on demand.

There is no fallback. If a requirement below is missing, the backup is refused with a message that names what to change.

Local and NAS destinations are paths, not credentials. They back up the same way as before, on any agent version.

sections.heading: Requirements
sections.text:
A backup to S3 storage needs all of these:

| Requirement | Why | If it is missing |
|---|---|---|
| The device runs the **v0.119.0 agent or later** | Older backup components cannot write through a storage session. | `Update the Breeze agent on this device, then try again. Backups now require secure storage access, and the backup component on this device has not reported support for it.` (HTTP 409 from the SQL Server and Hyper-V backup routes; scheduled backups fail with the same message.) |
| Agents reach the Breeze API over **HTTPS**, and `PUBLIC_API_URL` is set to that address | The device redeems the storage session at this origin. It accepts only a bare `https://` origin that matches the server it is enrolled with. | `Backups to S3 storage require agents to reach Breeze over HTTPS.` or `Set PUBLIC_API_URL to the address agents use.` |
| The backup destination's **storage endpoint uses HTTPS** | Signed upload links are only issued for an HTTPS endpoint. | `Backups to S3 storage require the storage endpoint to use HTTPS.` |
| The destination is **S3-compatible or local** | Only these providers can be written through a storage session. | `This backup destination uses a storage provider that backups no longer support.` |

An empty endpoint (AWS S3) counts as HTTPS. So does an endpoint entered without a scheme: `minio.example.com:9000` is treated as `https://minio.example.com:9000`.

A device that has just enrolled and has not yet reported its agent version waits for its first report (a few minutes at most) before a backup is started or refused.

**Check before you upgrade:**
Update every device that backs up to S3 storage to the v0.119.0 agent or later, and move `http://` storage endpoints and `http://` agent API addresses to HTTPS, **before** you upgrade the server to a release that includes this change. After that upgrade, backups from older agents and to `http://` endpoints are refused. There is no setting that turns the old path back on.

If you run the API and background workers as separate services (see [Worker split](/deploy/worker-split/)), upgrade them together: the storage key list assumes every service runs the same version from the upgrade on.

The steps for moving the agent API and MinIO to HTTPS are the same as for restores: see [HTTPS for Restores](/backup/https-restores/#moving-the-agent-api-to-https).

sections.heading: Replacing and disabling old storage keys
sections.text:
Storage keys that devices received before backups used storage sessions keep working until you disable them with your storage provider. Breeze lists every such key until there is evidence it no longer works.

Open **Configuration Policies**, choose a policy with a **Backup** feature, and look at the **Destination** section. While any key needs attention, a card titled **Replace and disable the storage keys used before <date>** lists each one with the destination it belongs to.

1. **Create a new key** with your storage provider for the same bucket. Give it only the permissions Breeze needs on that bucket: read, write, delete and list objects, and multipart uploads.

2. **Replace the key on the destination.** Edit the destination in Breeze, enter the new access key and secret key, and save. The old key moves to **Replaced** on the card. Run **Test connection**, then a backup and a restore, to confirm the new key works.

3. **Disable the old key** with your storage provider. Deleting it is best: only a key that no longer exists can be checked conclusively.

4. **Check the old key.** Select **Check old key** on the card. Breeze tries to list one object with the old key:
   - If storage answers that the key no longer exists, the key is recorded as disabled and leaves the card.
   - If it still works, the card says so. Disable it with your provider, then check again.
   - If storage refuses the key for listing (access denied, or a signature error), nothing is recorded: a key without permission to list may still be able to upload. Delete the key with your provider and check again, or confirm that you disabled it.
   - If the storage provider cannot be reached, nothing is recorded. Try again later.

Breeze keeps what it needs to check a replaced key for 30 days. After that, or if the check cannot reach your storage, disable the key with your provider and select **I disabled this key**. Breeze records your confirmation. It is weaker evidence than a check that shows the key no longer works.

When one key is used by several destinations of the same organization, deleting it with your provider and checking it on one of them records it as disabled on every destination where it was replaced. A destination that still uses the key must be given a new key first.

Checks are limited to 10 per organization every 10 minutes. Checking a key, confirming it and changing a destination's keys are recorded in the audit log.

sections.heading: Other refusal messages
sections.text:
| Message | What to do |
|---|---|
| `This backup job has already finished or been cancelled.` | Nothing. Run the backup again if you need it. |
| `The backup was not started: a secure storage session could not be issued for it. Run the backup again.` | Run the backup again. If it keeps failing, check the API logs. |
| `This backup was queued by an earlier version of Breeze and can no longer be delivered. Start it again.` | Start the backup again. |
| `The backup destination encryption settings changed after this backup was queued. Start it again.` | Start the backup again. |

See [Backup Troubleshooting](/backup/troubleshooting/) for other failures.

title: HTTPS for Restores
description: Restores and backup verification read from S3 storage through a short-lived storage session over HTTPS. What a self-hosted install needs, and how to move plain-HTTP MinIO or a plain-HTTP agent API to HTTPS.
headings: Moving the agent API to HTTPS
Moving MinIO (or another S3-compatible store) to HTTPS

sections.text:
Restores, test restores and backup verification that read from **S3 or S3-compatible storage** (MinIO, Wasabi, Backblaze B2 and so on) use a short-lived, read-only **storage session**. The session is bound to one command and one device. The device never receives the storage destination or its access keys for a read. Backups to S3 storage have the same requirements and are written through a storage session too: see [HTTPS for Backups](/backup/https-backups/).

Since v0.119, Breeze has no fallback for a read that cannot use a storage session. If a requirement below is missing, the restore is refused with a message that names what to change. Before v0.119, such a restore fell back to sending the storage destination to the device.

Local and NAS destinations are paths, not credentials. They restore the same way as before, on any agent version.

sections.heading: Requirements
sections.text:
A restore, test restore or verification from S3 storage needs all three of these:

| Requirement | Why | If it is missing |
|---|---|---|
| The device runs the **v0.118 agent or later** | Older backup components cannot use a storage session. | `Update the Breeze agent on this device, then try again.` (HTTP 409 from the restore, MSSQL, Hyper-V and verification routes, before anything is queued.) |
| Agents reach the Breeze API over **HTTPS**, and `PUBLIC_API_URL` is set to that address | The device redeems the storage session at this origin. It accepts only a bare `https://` origin that matches the server it is enrolled with. | `Restoring or verifying backups requires agents to reach Breeze over HTTPS.` or `Set PUBLIC_API_URL to the address agents use.` |
| The backup destination's **storage endpoint uses HTTPS** | Signed object URLs are only issued for an HTTPS endpoint. | `Restoring or verifying backups requires the storage endpoint to use HTTPS.` |

An empty endpoint (AWS S3) counts as HTTPS. So does an endpoint entered without a scheme: `minio.example.com:9000` is treated as `https://minio.example.com:9000`.

**Check before you upgrade:**
If your storage configuration uses an `http://` endpoint, or your agents connect to an `http://` API address, **every S3 restore and verification is refused after the upgrade to v0.119.** There is no setting that turns the old path back on. Move to HTTPS first, then upgrade.

sections.heading: Moving the agent API to HTTPS
sections.text:
Put Breeze behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy. The shipped Caddy configuration already does this. See [TLS & Reverse Proxy](/deploy/tls/).

1. Serve the API at an `https://` address with a certificate the devices trust. See the note on certificates below.

2. Set `PUBLIC_API_URL` to exactly that address, for example `https://rmm.example.com`, and restart the API.

3. Make sure the agents connect at that address. Agents enrolled against an `http://` URL keep using it. Re-enroll them, or update `server_url` in the agent config, so they use the `https://` address.

sections.heading: Moving MinIO (or another S3-compatible store) to HTTPS
sections.text:
Breeze records which endpoint **host and port** and which bucket each backup was written to, and it only restores a backup from that same location. The scheme is not part of it: `http://minio.example.com:9000` and `https://minio.example.com:9000` are the same location, but `https://minio.example.com` (port 443) is a different one. A backup written before the change and read from a different host or port is refused with `This backup was written to a different bucket or endpoint than its backup configuration now uses.`

So keep the host and port your existing backups were written to:

- **TLS on MinIO itself (recommended).** Put `public.crt` and `private.key` in MinIO's certificate directory (`~/.minio/certs` by default, or the directory passed with `--certs-dir`) and restart MinIO. It then serves HTTPS on the same port, and existing backups stay restorable.
- **A reverse proxy in front of MinIO.** Terminate TLS at Caddy or Nginx and proxy to MinIO's HTTP port, passing the `Host` header through unchanged (S3 request signatures cover it). The proxy has to listen on the **same host and port** the backups were written to, or those backups cannot be restored. If it cannot, only backups taken after the change are restorable.

Then edit the storage configuration in Breeze and change only the scheme of the endpoint to `https://`.

Run a **Test connection** on the updated configuration before relying on it.

**Certificates:**
The device checks the storage and API certificates against its operating system's trust store. Use a certificate from a public CA, or an internal CA certificate that you have deployed to every device's trust store. A self-signed certificate that the devices do not trust fails the same way it would in a browser.

sections.heading: Other refusal messages
sections.text:
| Message | What to do |
|---|---|
| `The storage location of this backup has not been confirmed yet.` | Wait for the next storage check, or run a new backup. |
| `The backup's file list was still being prepared for a secure restore.` | Nothing. The restore is held and delivered automatically once the file list is ready. |
| `This restore was queued by an earlier version of Breeze and can no longer be delivered.` | Start the restore again. |

See [Restoring Data](/backup/restoring/) for the restore workflow and [Backup Troubleshooting](/backup/troubleshooting/) for other failures.

title: Hyper-V VM Backup
description: Discover, back up, and restore Hyper-V virtual machines with application-consistent or crash-consistent snapshots.

sections.text:
Breeze can discover, back up, and restore Hyper-V virtual machines directly from the Backup dashboard. Every backup is a full `Export-VM` of the VM, in either application-consistent or crash-consistent mode — there is no incremental backup and no use of Resilient Change Tracking (RCT).

---

sections.heading: Discovering VMs
sections.text:
Before you can back up VMs, Breeze needs to discover what's running on your Hyper-V hosts.

1. Go to **Backup > Device Backup > Hyper-V**.
2. Click **Discover VMs** for the host device you want to scan.
3. Breeze queries the Hyper-V host and populates the VM list.

  Discovery is not automatic. A profile protects every VM on an assigned host, but only against the **discovered** inventory — scheduled runs don't query the host themselves. Run **Discover VMs** again after creating a new VM, or it won't be backed up until you do.

The VM list shows:

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **VM name** | The virtual machine's display name |
| **State** | Running (green), Off (gray), Paused/Saved (yellow) |
| **CPU count** | Number of virtual processors assigned |
| **Memory** | Allocated memory in MB |
| **VHD count** | Number of virtual hard disks |

Use the search box and state filter to find specific VMs. There's no VM pick-list for backup — a profile protects everything discovered on its assigned hosts minus whatever you exclude (see [Scheduled Backup](#scheduled-backup) below).

---

sections.heading: Manual Backup
sections.text:
1. On the **Hyper-V** tab, find the VM you want to back up.
2. Click the **Backup** button on the VM row.
3. Select the consistency type:
   - **Application-consistent** (default) — uses Hyper-V's own VSS integration. Because the running VM's memory state is captured as part of the export, a VM restored from an application-consistent backup comes back in **Saved** state, not Off.
   - **Crash-consistent** — for a running VM, the agent saves it (`Save-VM`), exports it, then resumes it (`Start-VM`), minimizing how long the source VM is paused. A VM that is **Off** or **Saved** is already consistent on disk, so it is exported as-is and left in that state. A **Paused** VM is saved and exported, then left **Saved** rather than resumed, so the guest doesn't run without you; the job records a warning. A VM in a transitional state (starting, stopping, saving, …) or a critical state is refused; retry once it settles.
4. Confirm to start the export.

The backup job appears in the Recent Jobs feed on the Overview tab.

**No export destination path:**
  There's no field to choose where the export goes. Breeze stages it on the Hyper-V host's **system drive**, under the Windows system temp folder, before uploading — so a VM export needs free space on the system drive roughly equal to the VM's size. A configurable path and cleanup of the staging directory are tracked in [issue #5460](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/issues/5460).

sections.heading: Scheduled Backup
sections.text:
To back up VMs automatically, create a [backup policy](/backup/policies/) with the **Hyper-V** mode. By default, every VM on an assigned host is included; there's no VM pick-list. Add VMs to the policy's exclude list to skip specific ones (e.g., test or development VMs).

  Hyper-V mode uses **all-by-default targeting**, but it's all-by-default against the **discovered** inventory, not a live scan of the host — see the discovery note above. A VM created after the last discovery scan isn't protected by a scheduled run until you discover it.

---

sections.heading: Viewing Checkpoints
sections.text:
Expand a VM row to see its checkpoint (snapshot) tree. Each checkpoint shows its name and creation timestamp, arranged in a hierarchy that reflects the checkpoint chain.

---

sections.heading: Restoring a VM
sections.text:
1. On the **Hyper-V** tab, find the VM and click **Restore**.
2. The restore dialog walks you through:
   - **Select snapshot** — choose which backup snapshot to restore from
   - **Target host** — pick the Hyper-V host to import the VM onto (can be a different host)
   - **VM name and ID** — keep the original name or rename. Toggle whether to generate a new VM ID (on by default).
3. Review the settings and confirm.

The restore runs in the background. Starting it queues the import on the host and returns straight away; follow its progress and final result like any other restore job — see [Monitoring a Restore](/backup/restoring/#monitoring-a-restore). Before v0.117.0 a Hyper-V restore that ran longer than 10 minutes was reported as failed even though the host was still importing.

The restore does an `Import-VM -Copy` into the target host's **default** virtual machine and virtual hard disk paths — there's no option to import somewhere else today. Budget roughly **twice** the VM's size in free space on the host's system drive: the export is downloaded, then copied into place. The imported VM comes back in whatever state its backup captured — **Saved** for an application-consistent backup, **Off** for a crash-consistent one — start it manually when you're ready.

From v0.118.0 (with the 0.118 agent), the restore refuses a VM name that already exists on the target host. Rename the VM in the restore dialog, or remove the existing VM first.

sections.heading: Restore as New VM
sections.text:
You can also restore a backup snapshot as a new VM from the Restore Wizard. This lets you adjust hardware specs (CPU count, memory, disk size) and select a virtual switch before creating the VM.

From v0.118.0 (with the 0.118 agent), a restore as new VM that cannot place every file fails before any VM is created. Earlier releases could report it as completed.

A restore as new VM copies the snapshot's files onto the new disk and leaves the restored Windows installation as it was: no drivers are added to it on the Hyper-V host. The VM is Generation 2, which needs a Windows 8 / Windows Server 2012 or later guest, and those already include the Hyper-V storage and network drivers. Install any other drivers from inside the running VM.

sections.heading: Instant Boot
sections.text:
For fast recovery validation, use **Instant Boot** to boot a VM directly from a snapshot without fully restoring it. This lets you verify that the backup is usable without waiting for a full import. Instant boot status is tracked on the Hyper-V tab.

From v0.118.0 (with the 0.118 agent), the background sync runs inside the instant-boot command and must finish within the command's run time. If it does not finish in time, the VM keeps running, is reported as **degraded**, and the partial staging data is removed.

Instant boot writes the VM's boot files with the host's own `bcdboot.exe`. If `bcdboot` fails, the instant boot fails before any VM is created, and the job's error shows `bcdboot`'s exit code and output. Earlier agents logged the failure and reported the VM as booted.

---

sections.heading: VM Power State Control
sections.text: From the Hyper-V tab you can manage VM power state — start, stop, save, or pause VMs on managed hosts. This is useful for pre-backup preparation or post-restore validation.

title: Monitoring Backups
description: Track backup health across the fleet: dashboard metrics, job history and lifecycle, storage usage trends, per-device status, and on-demand backup runs.

sections.text:
The Backup dashboard gives you a real-time view of protection coverage, job activity, and storage consumption across your organization. Navigate to **Backup > Device Backup** to access it.

---

sections.heading: Overview Tab
sections.text: The **Overview** tab is your primary monitoring surface. It includes:

sections.heading: Metrics Cards
sections.text:
At the top of the dashboard, summary cards show:

| Metric | What it means |
|--------|---------------|
| **Total Jobs** | Number of backup jobs created |
| **Snapshots** | Total point-in-time snapshots stored |
| **Success Rate (24h)** | Percentage of jobs in the last 24 hours that produced a restore point (**Completed** or **Completed with errors**). Color-coded: green (90%+), yellow (70–89%), red (below 70%) |
| **Devices Protected** | Devices assigned to at least one backup policy |
| **Storage Used** | Bytes stored across all providers. For each device's backup chain, the oldest retained snapshot counts at its full size and each later incremental counts only the data it uploaded — unchanged files an incremental references from an earlier snapshot are not counted again. It is an estimate from backup results, not a figure reported by the storage provider |

sections.heading: Recent Jobs
sections.text:
A live feed of the latest backup activity. Each job card shows:
- Device name and configuration
- Status: **Completed** (green), **Partial** (amber), **Running** (blue), **Failed** (red), **Queued** (gray), **Canceled**
- Start time, duration, and data size

Click **View all** to see the full job history with filters for status, device, and date range.

sections.heading: Storage by Provider
sections.text: A breakdown of storage usage per provider (S3, Local) with usage bars and a 14-day trend chart. Useful for tracking growth and planning capacity.

sections.heading: Devices Needing Backup
sections.text: Cards highlighting devices with overdue backups, showing the device name, when it was last backed up, and how many days overdue it is. Address these first.

sections.heading: Attention Items
sections.text:
Issues requiring admin action — failed jobs, configuration errors, or policy gaps — listed with severity indicators.

---

sections.heading: All Devices
sections.text: Click the **Run all backups** button at the top of the Overview tab. A confirmation dialog shows how many devices will be included and lists any jobs already in progress. Confirm to trigger immediate backups across your fleet.

sections.heading: Single Device
sections.text:
To back up one device:

1. Navigate to the device's detail page.
2. Open the **Backup** tab.
3. Click **Run Backup Now**.

The job appears immediately in the dashboard's Recent Jobs feed.

If the device is offline, Breeze returns an error immediately and does not create a backup job. If queue dispatch fails after job creation, the job is marked **Failed** with the dispatch error so the history stays accurate.

---

sections.heading: Per-Device Backup Status
sections.text:
Each device's detail page includes a **Backup** tab showing:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Protection status** | Whether the device is assigned to a backup policy |
| **Last successful backup** | Timestamp of the most recent completed job |
| **Next scheduled backup** | Computed from the policy schedule |
| **Recent jobs** | List of recent backup/restore jobs for this device |
| **VSS writer status** (Windows) | Health of Volume Shadow Copy writers — Stable, Failed, or Waiting |

---

sections.heading: Job Lifecycle
sections.text:
Backup and restore jobs move through these statuses:

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **Pending / Queued** | Created and waiting to be dispatched to the agent |
| **Running** | Actively in progress on the device |
| **Completed** | Finished and every file was read; a snapshot was created |
| **Completed with errors** | A snapshot was created and can be restored from, but one or more files could not be read or uploaded (for example, permission denied or a locked file). The failures stayed within 10% of the run. The job shows how many files failed and which ones, so check it before relying on the snapshot for those files. |
| **Partial** | A snapshot was created and can be restored from, but a disproportionate share of the run failed — more than 10% of the scanned bytes, or more than 10% of the attempted files. Check the error log for which files were skipped. |
| **Failed** | Encountered an error (check the error details) |
| **Canceled** | Explicitly stopped by a user before completion |

Jobs are triggered either **automatically** by a policy schedule, **manually** via the Run Backup button, or as part of a **restore** operation.

**Completed with errors** is new in v0.118.0; earlier releases reported these runs as **Completed**. API consumers see the status value `completed_with_errors`. It counts as a successful backup for "no successful backup" checks and is not a failure for "consecutive failures" checks. To be alerted on it, add a **Backup continuity** [monitor](/features/monitors/) with the **Completed with file errors** check, which fires when a device's latest backup ended in that state.

  Only jobs in the **Running** or **Queued** status can be canceled. Canceling a running job stops the operation, but data already transferred to the storage target remains.

  Restore jobs also use the same durable command pipeline. If a restore command times out, Breeze marks the device command failed and propagates the timeout into the restore job result so it does not remain stuck in **Pending** or **Running** forever.

---

sections.heading: Storage Usage History
sections.text:
Track storage growth over time from the **Overview** tab's storage section. The usage chart shows cumulative stored bytes by provider over the past 14 days, starting from what was already stored before the window, so its last point matches **Storage Used**. The series reflects the restore points retained now: when the oldest one expires, the next one takes over its full size, so earlier days can shift after retention runs (configurable from 3 to 90 days via the API).

If storage is growing faster than expected, check whether large datasets were recently added to backup scope. Expired restore points are removed from Breeze immediately and their storage is reclaimed by the periodic reclamation sweep (see the [storage page](/backup/storage/) for timing and safety windows) — allow for the grace period and the next scheduled sweep before usage reflects the drop.

---

sections.heading: Audit Trail
sections.text:
All backup operations are recorded in the [audit log](/reference/audit-logs/):

| Event | When it's logged |
|-------|-----------------|
| Configuration created/updated/deleted | Storage target changes |
| Configuration tested | Connectivity checks |
| Policy created/updated/deleted | Schedule or targeting changes |
| Manual backup triggered | On-demand backup runs |
| Job canceled | Admin stops a running/queued job |
| Restore initiated | Data recovery operations |

Each entry includes the organization, resource, and user who performed the action.

title: Backup Overview
description: Centralized backup management for your fleet — file, system image, Hyper-V, and SQL Server backups with cloud and local storage options.

sections.text:
Device Backup gives you centralized control over backups across your managed fleet. From the **Backup** dashboard you can configure where backups are stored, schedule what gets backed up, monitor protection coverage, and restore data when you need it — whether that's a single file, an entire system, a Hyper-V VM, or a SQL Server database.

---

sections.heading: What You Can Back Up
sections.text:
**Files & Folders:**
    Back up selected directories with include/exclude path rules. Uses Volume Shadow Copy (VSS) on Windows for application-consistent snapshots.

  **System Images:**
    Full system state capture including OS configuration, drivers, registry (Windows), and boot configuration.

  **Hyper-V VMs:**
    Export virtual machines with application-consistent or crash-consistent snapshots. Supports Resilient Change Tracking (RCT) for incremental backups.

  **SQL Server Databases:**
    Full, differential, and transaction log backups with LSN chain tracking for point-in-time recovery.

---

sections.heading: Where Backups Are Stored
sections.text:
Breeze supports two storage providers:

| Provider | Best for |
|----------|----------|
| **Amazon S3** (or S3-compatible) | Primary cloud storage — works with MinIO, Wasabi, Backblaze B2, and other S3-compatible services by setting a custom endpoint |
| **Local / NAS** | Fast restores from on-site storage, USB drives, or SMB shares |

You can configure multiple storage targets and assign different ones to different policies. For example, critical servers might back up to S3 with a local vault mirror, while workstations use local NAS only.

---

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.text:
Backup is organized around five core concepts:

1. **Storage configurations** — where backups go (S3 bucket, local path, etc.)
2. **Policies** — what gets backed up, on what schedule, and how long to keep it. Managed through [Configuration Policies](/features/configuration-policies/) for hierarchical assignment.
3. **Jobs** — individual backup or restore executions. Created automatically by schedules or triggered manually.
4. **Snapshots** — point-in-time archives produced by completed backup jobs. You can browse their contents file-by-file.
5. **Restore operations** — recover data from a snapshot to the original device or a different target.

---

sections.heading: The Backup Dashboard
sections.text:
Navigate to **Backup > Device Backup** in the sidebar to reach the backup dashboard. It has ten tabs:

| Tab | What it shows |
|-----|---------------|
| **Overview** | Protection coverage, success rates, storage trends, recent activity, devices needing attention |
| **Verification** | Backup integrity checks, test restores, recovery readiness scores |
| **Profiles** | Reusable backup profiles defining what gets backed up — see [Backup Profiles](/backup/profiles/) |
| **Snapshots** | Browse snapshots across the organization without going through a specific device |
| **SQL Server** | Discovered SQL instances, databases, backup chains |
| **Hyper-V** | Virtual machines, checkpoint trees, VM backup/restore |
| **Vault** | Local and network vault mirrors for fast offline recovery |
| **SLA** | RPO/RTO targets, compliance tracking, breach alerts |
| **Encryption** | Encryption key management (early access — see [Encryption](/backup/encryption/)) |
| **Recovery Bootstrap** | Create, inspect, and revoke bare metal recovery tokens for manual recovery environments |

If some customers are protected by N-able Cove Data Protection, you can connect it so those devices show as covered in the Overview's backup health view and on each device's Backup tab — see [Third-Party Backup Providers](/backup/backup-providers/).

sections.heading: The Device Backup Tab
sections.text:
Each device also has its own **Backup** tab (on the device detail page) for single-device actions:

- **Run backup now** — triggers an immediate backup for that one device. It's disabled when the device is offline or has no backup policy assigned, and if a backup is already running it shows a friendly "already running" message instead of starting a second job. This is different from the dashboard's **Run all backups**, which fans out a run across every protected device.
- **Next run** and **Last success** are shown in the device's effective timezone (with the zone label), matching the schedule you set in the policy editor — not your browser's local time. A schedule set for "03:00 in the device's timezone" reads as `03:00 AM` on the tab, not shifted to wherever your browser happens to be.

---

sections.heading: Quick Start
sections.text:
New to Breeze Backup? Here's the fastest path to protecting your first device:

1. **Add a storage target.** From the Overview tab, open the storage configuration wizard. Pick a provider (S3 is recommended), enter your credentials, set a schedule and retention policy, and publish the configuration. See [Storage Configuration](/backup/storage/) for details.

2. **Create a backup policy.** Go to **Settings > Configuration Policies**, create a new policy, and add a **Backup** feature link. Choose your backup mode (file, Hyper-V, MSSQL, or system image), select the storage configuration you just created, and assign the policy to devices, sites, or groups. See [Backup Policies](/backup/policies/) for details.

3. **Verify it works.** Back on the Backup dashboard, click **Run all backups** to trigger an immediate run across every protected device (or use **Run backup now** on a single device's Backup tab). Watch the job appear in Recent Jobs. Once it completes, go to the **Verification** tab and run an integrity check. See [Verification & Recovery Readiness](/backup/verification/) for details.

---

sections.heading: Backup Binary Architecture
sections.text:
Enterprise backup operations (Hyper-V, SQL Server, system image, cloud-to-cloud) run in a dedicated `breeze-backup` helper process that communicates with the main agent over HMAC-signed IPC. This keeps the core agent lightweight (~15 MB) while the backup binary includes the heavier cloud SDKs and backup tooling. The backup binary is bundled by the Windows MSI, the macOS .pkg, and the Linux and macOS shell-script service installs — so every supported install path can run backups out of the box. (Previously only the MSI and .pkg bundled it, which meant hosts set up with the shell-script installer couldn't run backups until the helper was placed manually.)

As of v0.105.0, the helper's version is slaved to the agent's: when the agent auto-updates, it downloads and atomically swaps `breeze-backup` in the same upgrade, so the helper no longer stays at whatever version the installer shipped. A periodic reconcile also re-fetches the helper if it turns up missing or stale.

  The backup binary is installed automatically and kept up to date alongside the agent. No additional setup is needed unless you're building from source.

title: Backup Policies
description: Schedule backups through configuration policies. Covers file, Hyper-V, MSSQL, and system image modes, storage targets, GFS retention, and assignment.

sections.text:
Backup scheduling is managed through [Configuration Policies](/features/configuration-policies/). You create a policy, add a **Backup** feature link, configure the backup mode and targets, then assign it at any level of the hierarchy — organization, site, device group, or individual device. The policy system resolves which devices get which backup settings using the same precedence rules as other features.

---

sections.heading: Creating a Backup Policy
sections.text:
1. Go to **Settings > Configuration Policies**.

2. Click **Create Policy** (or edit an existing one).

3. In the policy editor, click **Add Feature** and select **Backup**.

4. Configure the backup settings:

   **Backup Mode** — choose one per policy:

   | Mode | What it backs up |
   |------|-----------------|
   | **File** (default) | Selected directories and files with include/exclude path rules |
   | **Hyper-V** | Virtual machines on Hyper-V hosts |
   | **MSSQL** | SQL Server databases |
   | **System Image** | Full system state capture |

   **Storage Configuration** — select which storage target to use (created in [Storage Configuration](/backup/storage/)). The list shows the destinations of the organization that owns the policy. If there are none yet, the tab shows **Backups need a destination first** with a **New destination** button, so you can create one without leaving the policy.

   **Schedule** — frequency (daily, weekly, monthly), time of day, timezone, and optionally day-of-week or day-of-month.

   **Retention** — Grandfather-Father-Son (GFS) settings:
   - Daily snapshots to keep
   - Weekly snapshots to keep
   - Monthly snapshots to keep
   - Yearly snapshots to keep (for compliance)

5. **Assign the policy** to organizations, sites, device groups, or individual devices.

6. Click **Save**.

---

sections.heading: How Policy Assignment Works
sections.text:
Backup policies follow the same hierarchical precedence as all configuration policies:

```
Device (most specific) > Device Group > Site > Organization (least specific)
```

A device-level assignment overrides a site-level one. If a device has no direct assignment, it inherits from its device group, then site, then organization.

  Assign backup policies at the site or organization level to protect new devices automatically as they enroll. Use device-level overrides only for exceptions (e.g., a server that needs more frequent backups than the site default).

---

sections.heading: File Backup
sections.text:
The default mode. Specify which paths to include and exclude:

- **Include paths** — directories to back up (e.g., `C:\Users`, `/home`)
- **Exclude paths** — skip specific subdirectories or patterns (e.g., `C:\Users\*\AppData\Local\Temp`)

On Windows, file backups automatically use Volume Shadow Copy (VSS) to capture application-consistent snapshots of open files.

**Exclude patterns** follow gitignore-style rules (Windows `\` separators are accepted and treated as `/`):

| Pattern shape | Matches |
|---|---|
| No slash — `*.tmp`, `Thumbs.db` | The **name** of any file or folder at any depth. |
| Contains a slash, no leading `/` — `node_modules/**`, `AppData/Local/Temp/**` | That relative path **at any depth** below the backup root. |
| Leading `/` — `/proc/**`, `/swapfile` | **Only** that path directly under the backup root (root-anchored). Since v0.112.0; previously a leading `/` was ignored and the pattern matched at any depth. |

`**` matches zero or more path segments, a pattern that matches a folder skips the whole subtree, and matching is case-insensitive on Windows only. A trailing `/` carries no special meaning (`foo/` is the same as `foo`). Invalid patterns are logged and ignored rather than failing the backup.

**What a file backup preserves** (agent v0.112.0 and later): regular files, symbolic links (as links, never followed), empty and specially-permissioned directories, owner and group, and the full permission bits including setuid/setgid/sticky. Sockets, FIFOs and device nodes are skipped. Ownership and the special bits are reapplied on restore only when the restore runs as root (never on Windows); otherwise the restore prints one summary warning and keeps the files. A snapshot that records any of these extras is written in a newer manifest format that **older agents cannot restore correctly** — restore it with a v0.112.0 or later agent. Snapshots containing only plain files are unchanged.

sections.heading: Hyper-V Backup
sections.text:
Targets Hyper-V virtual machines. Uses **all-by-default targeting** — newly discovered VMs are automatically included on the next scheduled run. You can configure exclude lists to skip specific VMs.

Two consistency modes:
- **Application-consistent** (default) — uses Hyper-V's VSS integration for clean VM snapshots
- **Crash-consistent** — saves VM state before export, faster but less clean

sections.heading: SQL Server Backup
sections.text:
Targets SQL Server databases. Like Hyper-V, new databases are automatically included. Supports three backup types in a chain:
- **Full** — complete database backup
- **Differential** — changes since last full backup
- **Log** — transaction log for point-in-time recovery

sections.heading: System Image
sections.text:
Captures the OS state needed to rebuild a machine's configuration — registry hives, boot configuration, certificate store, drivers, services and firewall policy on Windows; `/etc`, the package list, enabled services, firewall rules and crontabs on Linux; preferences, launch items and network configuration on macOS — plus, on Linux and Windows, the disk layout used to judge whether the snapshot is [bare-metal restorable](/backup/restoring/#browsing-snapshots). Used for [bare metal recovery](/backup/bare-metal-recovery/); turning on whole-machine backup for this source also walks the root filesystem in the same snapshot (the **Whole machine** [profile templates](/backup/profiles/#whole-machine-templates) do this) for a full rebuild in one snapshot.

---

sections.heading: Bandwidth and Scheduling Controls
sections.text:
Policies support additional controls for managing backup impact:

| Setting | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| **Backup window** | Time range during which backups are allowed to run |
| **Bandwidth limit** | Maximum throughput in Mbps to avoid saturating the network |
| **Priority** | Controls ordering when multiple devices are scheduled simultaneously |

---

sections.heading: Monitoring Policy Coverage
sections.text:
The Backup dashboard **Overview** tab shows:
- **Devices Protected** — count of devices assigned to at least one backup policy
- **Devices Needing Backup** — devices with overdue or missing backups

Individual device status is visible on each device's **Backup** tab, showing the assigned policy, last successful backup, and next scheduled run.

title: Backup Profiles
description: Build a reusable backup profile once, choose which sources it protects, and apply it across organizations, including partner-wide profiles for every org.
headings: Applying a Profile in a Policy

sections.text:
A **backup profile** is a reusable, named definition of *what to protect* on a class of devices — for example a "Server" profile or a "Windows Workstation" profile. You build the profile once, then apply it to as many organizations as you like instead of re-selecting the same folders and data sources policy by policy.

A profile deliberately answers only *what* gets backed up. *Where* backups are stored, *when* they run, and *how long* restore points are kept are set separately, where the profile is assigned. That separation is what lets a single "Server" profile be reused across many customers that each have their own storage destination and schedule.

  A profile defines what gets protected. Schedules, retention, and destinations are set where the profile is assigned.

---

sections.heading: What a Profile Protects
sections.text:
A profile enables any combination of the following data sources — at least one must be enabled:

| Source | What it captures |
|--------|------------------|
| **Files** | One or more folder paths, with optional exclusion patterns. File backups require at least one path. |
| **System State** | Registry hives, boot configuration, certificate store, drivers, services and firewall policy on Windows; `/etc`, the package list, enabled services, firewall rules and crontabs on Linux; preferences, launch items and network configuration on macOS. On Linux and Windows the machine's disk layout is recorded too, so the snapshot can be judged [bare-metal restorable](/backup/restoring/#browsing-snapshots). |
| **SQL Server** | Discovered SQL Server databases, with a full / differential / log backup type and optional database excludes. |
| **Hyper-V** | Virtual machines, with an application- or crash-consistency setting and optional VM excludes. |

  Cloud-synced folders such as OneDrive and Dropbox are offered as opt-in **exclusion** chips on the Files source, so you can skip re-backing-up data that already lives in the cloud. They are not a separate backup source.

---

sections.heading: Org-Owned vs. Partner-Wide Profiles
sections.text:
Every profile is owned in exactly one of two ways, chosen when you create it:

- **This organization** — the profile belongs to a single organization and is only assignable there.
- **All organizations** (partner-wide) — the profile belongs to your partner and is assignable in **every** organization you manage, including organizations you create later.

Partner-wide profiles carry an **All orgs** badge in the profile list. Because a partner-wide profile reaches across all your customers, creating, editing, or deleting one requires full partner access.

  Ownership is fixed at creation. You can rename a profile or change what it protects, but you cannot later convert an organization profile into a partner-wide one (or vice versa) — create a new profile instead.

---

sections.heading: Managing Profiles
sections.text:
Profiles live on the **Profiles** tab of the **Backup** dashboard.

1. Open **Backup → Profiles**. Each profile shows its owner badge, the sources it enables, and how many policies currently use it ("Used by N policies").
2. Click to create a profile. Start from a template card — **Server**, **Windows Workstation**, **macOS Workstation**, **Linux Server**, or **Blank** — which pre-fills the editor. Everything remains editable.
3. Choose the owner scope (**This organization** or **All organizations**), name the profile, and enable the sources it should protect.
4. Save. The profile is now available to assign from any configuration policy's Backup tab.

A profile that is in use by one or more policies cannot be deleted until it is unlinked from them — the delete is blocked inline and names the policies that still reference it.

---

sections.heading: Applying a Profile in a Policy
sections.text:
Profiles are applied to devices through a **configuration policy's Backup tab**, which has been redesigned into four clearly titled groups:

| Group | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| **Source** | What to back up on each device. |
| **Destination** | Where backups are stored. |
| **Schedule & retention** | When backups run and how long restore points are kept. |
| **Protection** | Legal hold / immutability (snapshot protection). |

In the **Source** group you choose between **Use a profile** — selecting one of your reusable profiles from a set of cards — and **Custom selection**, which keeps the older per-policy source editor for one-off cases.

sections.heading: Whole machine templates
sections.text:
When you create a profile, the first two templates in the list are **Whole machine (Linux)** and **Whole machine (Windows)**. Each enables a single **System State** source with whole-machine backup turned on, so ONE snapshot carries everything [bare-metal recovery](/backup/bare-metal-recovery/) needs — the whole root filesystem (`/` or `C:\`), the OS state, and the disk layout — and seeds a root-anchored exclude list for the paths that must never be backed up:

- **Linux:** `/proc/**`, `/sys/**`, `/dev/**`, `/run/**`, `/tmp/**`, `/var/tmp/**`, `/mnt/**`, `/media/**`, `/snap/**`, `/var/cache/apt/archives/**`, `/swapfile`, `/swap.img`, `**/lost+found/**`
- **Windows:** `/pagefile.sys`, `/hiberfil.sys`, `/swapfile.sys`, `/$Recycle.Bin/**`, `/System Volume Information/**`, `/Windows/Temp/**`, `/Windows/SoftwareDistribution/Download/**`, `**/AppData/Local/Temp/**`

The leading `/` anchors each pattern to the backup root — see [exclude patterns](/backup/policies/#file-backup). Edit the list freely after choosing the template.

sections.heading: OS Presets (Quick Start)
sections.text:
When building a custom file selection, one-click **presets** seed sensible paths and exclusions that you can then edit freely:

- **Windows user data** — backs up `C:\Users`, skips temp files, browser caches, and the Recycle Bin.
- **macOS user data** — backs up `/Users`, skips caches, Trash, and local iPhone backups.
- **Linux home + config** — backs up `/home` and `/etc`, skips caches and Trash.

Presets are combinable for mixed-OS fleets — apply more than one and paths that do not exist on a given device are simply skipped when the backup runs.

sections.heading: Destination Cards
sections.text: The **Destination** group presents each configured storage destination as a selectable card showing its provider, bucket or path, and its enabled, encrypted, and object-lock (WORM) status. You can edit or test the selected destination in place. Storage destinations hold provider credentials and are shared infrastructure — one destination can be reused by many policies.

sections.heading: Org Default Destination
sections.text:
You can mark one destination per organization as its **default**. Policies that don't name an explicit destination — and every **partner-wide** policy — fall back to each device's org default at backup time.

  A partner-wide backup policy relies on each organization having a default destination. If an organization has none, its backups fail with a loud error rather than being silently skipped. Set a default destination under each organization's backup destinations before rolling out a partner-wide policy.

---

sections.heading: Per-Selection Job Fan-Out
sections.text:
When a profile enables more than one source, Breeze runs **one backup job per enabled source** on each device, rather than a single combined job.

This matters in practice: a device covered by Files **and** System State **and** SQL Server now produces three independent backup jobs, each succeeding or failing on its own. Previously a device with several sources selected could end up with only one working backup. The Backup tab states this directly — "A policy using this profile runs one backup job per enabled source." Jobs run in a fixed order (Files, then System State, then SQL Server, then Hyper-V) and are de-duplicated per device and source.

---

sections.heading: Integrator Reference
sections.text:
For automation, backup profiles are exposed under the backup API (`/api/v1/backup`). All mutations require the `backup:write` permission and a completed MFA challenge; reads require `backup:read`.

| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `GET` | `/backup/profiles` | List profiles (`includeInactive`, `orgId` query parameters). Each profile includes an in-use policy count. |
| `GET` | `/backup/profiles/:id` | Retrieve a single profile. |
| `POST` | `/backup/profiles` | Create a profile (`name`, `ownerScope`, `orgId`, `selections`, ...). Partner scope requires full partner access. |
| `PATCH` | `/backup/profiles/:id` | Update a profile's name, description, sources, or active state. Ownership is immutable. |
| `DELETE` | `/backup/profiles/:id` | Delete a profile. Returns `409` with the referencing policies if it is still linked. |

title: Restoring Data
description: Restore individual files or full snapshots from Breeze backups. Covers browsing snapshots, full and selective (file-level) restores, cross-device restore, and bare metal recovery.

sections.text:
Breeze supports several restore methods depending on what you need to recover — from a single file to a complete system.

**S3 restores need HTTPS:**
Restores and verification from S3 or S3-compatible storage need the v0.118 agent or later, an HTTPS agent API and an HTTPS storage endpoint. See [HTTPS for Restores](/backup/https-restores/).

---

sections.heading: Browsing Snapshots
sections.text:
Before restoring, you can inspect what a snapshot contains:

1. Go to **Backup > Device Backup**.
2. Find the device in the job list or device backup tab.
3. Open the **Snapshot Browser** and select a snapshot from the dropdown.
4. Navigate the file tree — expand folders to see their contents, including file names, sizes, and modification dates.

  Non-file snapshots are badged by type in the browser — a system-state snapshot shows a **System image** badge in both the snapshot selector and the detail header, so you can tell it apart from a file backup at a glance.

A `system_image` snapshot taken by a v0.112.0 or later agent on Linux or Windows also carries a restorability verdict in the detail header: a green **Bare-metal restorable** badge, or an amber **Not bare-metal restorable** badge whose tooltip lists why (BIOS/MBR boot, LVM, LUKS, RAID, btrfs root, ZFS, multi-disk OS, or no layout captured). The verdict tells you whether [`breeze-backup rebuild`](/backup/bare-metal-recovery/#rebuilding-a-linux-disk-from-scratch-breeze-backup-rebuild) can reproduce the machine's disk from that snapshot; ordinary restores and `bmr-recover` are not affected by it. File-only and macOS snapshots show no badge.

  Always browse a snapshot before restoring to confirm the files you need are present. This is especially useful when deciding between a full restore and a selective one.

---

sections.heading: Restore Types
sections.text:
| Type | What it recovers | When to use |
|------|-----------------|-------------|
| **Full restore** | Everything in the snapshot | Replacing a failed drive or rebuilding a system |
| **Selective restore** | The files and folders you choose | Recovering accidentally deleted files or folders |
| **Bare metal recovery** | Files and/or OS state (registry or `/etc`, services, firewall, scheduled tasks, packages) onto a machine that reinstalls or boots its own OS — or, on Linux, a full disk rebuild from a whole-machine snapshot | Replacing a dead machine entirely. See [Bare Metal Recovery](/backup/bare-metal-recovery/) |

---

sections.heading: Full Restore
sections.text:
1. Go to **Backup → Restore** in the console to open the **Restore Wizard**.
2. Choose the device whose backup you want to restore, then select one of its snapshots. The wizard lists one device's snapshots at a time and selects nothing until a device is chosen (it picks the device for you only when you arrive from the **Snapshots** tab or the organization has a single backed-up device). The review step names the source device.
3. Choose **Full Restore**.
4. Choose the destination:
   - **Staging folder on the device** — the default. Files are restored under the device's system temp directory (`breeze-restore/<original path>`); the originals are never overwritten. (Earlier releases labelled this option "Original location", which it never was.) To restore in place — overwriting the originals — choose **Alternate path** and type in the original root path yourself.
   - **Alternate path** — specify a directory (e.g., `/var/restore` or `D:\Restored`); files are written there preserving their relative structure.
5. Review the summary and click **Restore**. The restore always runs on the device that owns the snapshot — the wizard does not offer a way to target a different device (see [Cross-Device Restore](#cross-device-restore) below).

sections.heading: Selective Restore
sections.text:
1. Go to **Backup → Restore** in the console to open the **Restore Wizard**. (The **Snapshots** tab links to it from the snapshot file list.)
2. Choose the device, then select the snapshot. Arriving from the **Snapshots** tab, the snapshot and its device are already selected.
3. Choose **Selective Restore**.
4. Browse the file tree and check the files and folders you want to recover. Each folder shows how many backed-up files it holds. Checking a folder selects every file indexed beneath it, and a partly selected folder shows a partial checkmark. When the selection covers more than 1,000 files, Breeze asks you to confirm.
5. Choose the destination path (see the staging-folder default above).
6. Review and click **Restore**.

  A selected folder is expanded to the files the snapshot indexed beneath it, matched on whole folder names: selecting `/home/alice` never includes a sibling such as `/home/alice2`. One restore can expand to at most 10,000 files; a larger selection is refused with the count, so split it into several restores. The same rules apply when you restore a folder through the API or the AI assistant.

---

sections.heading: Monitoring a Restore
sections.text:
After you start a restore, the job appears in restore history and on the target device's Backup tab. You can track it from:

- The **Backup** dashboard's Recent Jobs section
- The target device's **Backup** tab

Completed restore jobs show the final status, restored file count, restored byte count, and any structured warnings or errors reported by the agent.

If the target device is offline, Breeze rejects the restore request immediately instead of creating a pending restore that cannot run.

---

sections.heading: How restores reach storage
sections.text:
**v0.118.0+.** Restore commands no longer carry your storage credentials. This covers file restores, verification and test restores, SQL Server restores and verification, Hyper-V restores, restore as VM, and instant boot. Breeze looks up the storage destination when it delivers the command, not when you start it.

With the 0.118 backup helper, the device does not receive the storage destination at all. Instead:

1. Breeze issues a short-lived, read-only storage session for that one command on that one device.
2. For each file it needs, the helper asks Breeze for a download link. Breeze checks that the file belongs to the snapshot being restored, then returns a link that expires within minutes.
3. The helper downloads the file directly from storage over that link, and renews the session for as long as the restore runs.

Breeze uses this path when all of these hold:

- the device's backup helper is 0.118.0 or later;
- the snapshot is on S3-compatible storage reached over HTTPS, and its storage location still matches the destination's current settings;
- the server address the device uses is HTTPS;
- Breeze has a verified file list for the snapshot (it builds one automatically when it is missing), or, for SQL Server, the snapshot's manifest and backup file.

Otherwise the restore uses the previous path, where the device receives the storage destination with the command. This is the case for devices whose backup helper predates 0.118 until they update. Restores keep working either way.

  A backup, restore or verify command still queued when its device moves to another organization, including during an organization merge, is not delivered. It is expired with a reason. Run it again after the move.

  Self-hosted operators can see which path each restore took from the `breeze_backup_read_dispatch_total` metric on `/metrics`. Its `mode` label is `brokered` (storage session) or `legacy` (previous path), and its `reason` label says why.

---

sections.heading: Integrity checks on restore
sections.text:
**v0.120.0+.** Every restore, verification, test restore, SQL Server restore, Hyper-V restore, restore as VM, instant boot and bare-metal recovery carries what Breeze knows about the snapshot's **attestation**: the exact size and SHA-256 of its manifest (and, for whole-machine snapshots, its disk layout and system-state manifest), or why the snapshot has none.

**Attested snapshots.** With a v0.120.0 or later backup helper on the device:

- The manifest, layout and system-state manifest are checked against the attestation before they are read.
- Every restored file must match its manifest entry exactly, size and SHA-256. A file whose entry has no checksum fails (`missing_checksum`).
- Each file is downloaded to a staging file next to its destination and moved into place only after it passes, so a file that fails is never written over anything.
- If a [vault](/backup/vault/) copy does not match, the helper reads the file from primary storage instead and adds a warning (`vault copy differs from backup; restored from primary storage`).

A failed check is reported with a result code such as `checksum_mismatch`, `size_mismatch`, `integrity_mismatch`, `missing_checksum` or `not_attested`, shown on the restore as **Result code: …**.

**Snapshots that failed their integrity check are refused.** If a snapshot's stored objects did not match its attestation, Breeze will not deliver any restore, verification or VM restore from it. The command fails with `This backup did not match its integrity record and cannot be read from storage.` (or `The stored backup does not match its integrity record…`). A restore already running from such a snapshot is stopped at its next storage request. If only the snapshot's file list was built before its attestation existed, Breeze rebuilds the list and the message says so; run the restore again afterwards.

**Restores require a backup helper that checks attestations.** A restore that writes, imports or boots a backup (file restore, SQL Server restore, Hyper-V restore, restore as VM, instant boot, bare-metal recovery and rebuild) is sent only to a device whose backup helper reports it checks restores against attestations (Breeze agent v0.120.0 or later). An older device is refused when you start the restore, and again if the device was downgraded before the command was delivered: **Update the Breeze agent on this device, then try again.** Bare-metal recovery media and recovery tools older than v0.120.0 are refused at code exchange and authentication: **This recovery tool is too old to check backup integrity. Download current recovery media or the current recovery tool, then try again.** Verification and test restore are not affected.

**Unattested snapshots need a confirmation.** A snapshot with no attestation (taken before attestations existed, or by an older helper) is labelled **Not verified** in the restore wizards, which badge each snapshot **Verified**, **Checking**, **Not verified** or **Failed integrity check**. Restoring it requires a technician to confirm it with two-factor authentication (or, on a deployment with two-factor authentication disabled, an explicit confirmation). A technician who has not set up a second factor is asked to set one up first (an authenticator app or a passkey, from their profile), then retries the restore and confirms it. Text-message codes don't count: an account with only SMS codes must add an authenticator app or a passkey. The confirmation applies to that one snapshot, target device and restore type, is recorded in the audit log as `backup.restore.unattested_override` (with the confirmation method), and the restore result carries the warning **Unattested snapshot: files were not checked against a snapshot attestation.** The same confirmation is needed to restore a backup kept on a device's own disk onto a different device. AI-initiated restores and DR plan executions cannot confirm and are refused for such snapshots; start them from the console.

**Snapshots still being checked wait.** A restore of a snapshot whose attestation is still being verified is refused with **This backup is still being checked. Try again in a few minutes.**; a queued restore waits for the check.

Verification and test restore of an unattested snapshot still run without confirmation; their result says the snapshot is unattested.

  Self-hosted operators can track this from the `breeze_backup_restore_integrity_total` metric on `/metrics`. Its `type` label is the command type (or `recovery_bootstrap`), `status` is `attested`, `unattested`, `override`, `refused` or `absent`, and `reason` says why.

---

sections.heading: Cross-Device Restore
sections.text:
The restore API (`POST /backup/restore`) accepts a target `deviceId`, so a snapshot can be restored to a different device than the one it was taken from — both devices must be in the same organization. This is **API-only today**: the Restore Wizard in the web UI never sends a `deviceId`, so any restore started from the wizard runs on the device that owns the snapshot. To restore to a different device, call the API directly with the target `deviceId`.

Cross-device restores also require the destination device to be online when you start the restore. If Breeze cannot queue the restore command, the restore job is marked failed with the dispatch error instead of remaining stuck in a pending state.

---

sections.heading: What Is and Isn't Preserved
sections.text:
- **Preserved** — file content byte-for-byte; on Linux and macOS, Unix mode permission bits and the original modification time (mtime) are reapplied to each restored file.
- **Not preserved** — symlinks are skipped entirely, both in the backup and on restore; empty directories are not recreated; setuid/setgid/sticky bits are dropped (only the base permission bits are restored).
- **Open files.** On Windows, files locked by running applications may fail to restore. Stop the relevant services first, or restore to an alternate path.
- **Windows names.** A path component that contains `:`, ends in `.` or a space, or is a reserved device name (`CON`, `NUL`, `COM1`, …) is refused with `invalid_windows_name`. This applies to file restores, bare-metal recovery, VM file restore and Hyper-V restore.
- **Windows permissions.** A recorded security descriptor is applied only when every owner, group and access-list account is one the machine recognises (a well-known account, the local machine, its domain or a trusted domain).
