Otherwise, or when the recorded descriptor cannot be read, the item gets a restrictive access list: owner Administrators, access for SYSTEM and Administrators only. The restore result shows **N items restored with a restrictive access list** with the affected paths (up to 100 listed); review and reassign their permissions. When only an auditing (SACL) entry names an unknown account, the descriptor is applied without its auditing entries. A whole-machine rebuild applies descriptors as recorded.

---

sections.heading: Restore Considerations
sections.text:
- **Destination path.** See the staging-folder default above — an explicit destination path is the only way to control where files land, including restoring in place.
- **Permissions.** See "What Is and Isn't Preserved" above. If restoring to a different device or OS, permissions may need adjustment regardless.
- **Disk space.** Ensure the target device has enough free space for the restore. The snapshot's total size is shown in the Restore Wizard summary.
- **Download speed.** With a v0.122.1 or later agent, file restores and bare-metal recovery download up to 8 files at a time from storage, while still putting files in place in the snapshot's manifest order.

title: SLA Management
description: Define RPO and RTO targets for backup-protected devices, track compliance from the SLA dashboard, and get alerts when backup SLAs are breached.

sections.text:
SLA Management lets you define recovery objectives for your backup-protected devices and automatically alerts you when those objectives aren't met. Set RPO (how much data loss you can tolerate) and RTO (how quickly you need to recover) targets, then let Breeze monitor compliance.

---

sections.heading: Key Terms
sections.text:
| Term | Definition |
|------|-----------|
| **RPO** (Recovery Point Objective) | Maximum acceptable time between the last backup and a failure. An RPO of 60 minutes means you can lose at most 60 minutes of data. |
| **RTO** (Recovery Time Objective) | Maximum acceptable time to restore from backup. An RTO of 30 minutes means the restore must complete within 30 minutes. |

---

sections.heading: Creating an SLA Policy
sections.text:
1. Go to **Backup > Device Backup > SLA**.
2. Click **Add SLA Config**.
3. Fill in the configuration:
   - **Name** — descriptive label (e.g., "Tier 1 Servers — 1hr RPO")
   - **RPO target** — maximum minutes between backups (minimum 1)
   - **RTO target** — maximum minutes to restore (minimum 1)
   - **Scope** — choose **Target Devices** or **Target Device Groups**, then select from the dropdown
   - **Alert on breach** — enable to receive notifications when an SLA is violated
   - **Active** — toggle on/off
4. Click **Save**.

---

sections.heading: SLA Dashboard
sections.text: The SLA tab shows:

sections.heading: Compliance Metrics
sections.text:
- **Overall compliance %** — percentage of SLA checks that passed
- **Active breaches** — count of currently violated SLAs
- **Average RPO/RTO** — actual recovery metrics across your fleet

sections.heading: SLA Configurations
sections.text:
A table of your SLA policies showing:
- Policy name
- RPO and RTO targets (in minutes)
- Number of devices affected
- Active/inactive status
- Edit and delete actions

sections.heading: SLA Events
sections.text:
A chronological list of SLA events:
- **Device name** — which device triggered the event
- **Event type** — RPO Breach (red), RTO Breach (yellow), or Missed Backup (gray)
- **Detected time** — when the breach was identified
- **Resolved time** — when the breach was cleared (if applicable)

---

sections.heading: How Breach Detection Works
sections.text:
Breeze continuously monitors backup activity against your SLA policies:

1. **RPO check** — compares the time since the last completed backup to the RPO target. If more time has passed than the target allows, an RPO breach event is created.
2. **RTO check** — measures actual restore times from test restores and verification runs. If the measured time exceeds the RTO target, an RTO breach is recorded.
3. **Missed backup** — if a scheduled backup didn't run at all (agent offline, policy misconfigured), a missed backup event is created.

Breach detection runs automatically — no manual action needed.

---

sections.heading: Recommended SLA Targets
sections.text:
| Device tier | RPO | RTO | Rationale |
|-------------|-----|-----|-----------|
| **Tier 1** (domain controllers, databases) | 15–60 min | 15–30 min | Critical infrastructure — minimal data loss and fast recovery |
| **Tier 2** (application servers, file servers) | 4–8 hours | 1–2 hours | Important but can tolerate some downtime |
| **Tier 3** (workstations, dev machines) | 24 hours | 4–8 hours | Lower priority — daily backup is sufficient |

  Start with conservative (longer) targets and tighten them as you build confidence in your backup infrastructure. It's better to have achievable SLAs than to create constant breach noise.

title: SQL Server Backup
description: Discover SQL Server instances and run full, differential, and transaction log backups.

sections.text:
Breeze can discover, back up, and restore SQL Server databases directly — no third-party SQL backup tool required. The agent connects as its own Windows service identity and runs native `sqlcmd` commands to produce standard `.bak` and `.trn` backup files; the `sqlcmd` shipped with SQL Server 2022 and 2025 is supported.

**Windows Authentication only:**
  Breeze always connects locally over Windows Authentication, as the agent's service identity (**LocalSystem**) — there is no SQL Authentication option. Instances configured for SQL-Authentication-only logins are not supported. Grant the service identity **sysadmin**, or the combination of **db_backupoperator** + **dbcreator** + **VIEW SERVER STATE**, so it can back up and restore databases.

---

sections.heading: Discovering Instances
sections.text:
1. Go to **Backup > Device Backup > SQL Server**.
2. Click **Discover Instances** for a device to scan it for SQL Server installations.
3. Discovered instances appear in the list.

  Discovery is not automatic. A profile protects every database on a discovered instance, but only against the **discovered** inventory — scheduled runs don't rescan the instance themselves. Run **Discover Instances** again after creating a new database, or it won't be backed up until you do. There's also no per-database pick-list: a profile protects everything minus whatever you exclude.

Each instance shows:
- Instance name, version, and edition
- Authentication type and port — informational only; Breeze always connects locally over Windows Authentication regardless of what's shown here
- Status (Online / Offline)

Expand an instance to see its databases, including:
- Database name and size
- Recovery model (Simple, Full, Bulk-logged)
- TDE (Transparent Data Encryption) status
- Compatibility level

---

sections.heading: Backup Types
sections.text:
SQL Server supports three backup types:

| Type | What it captures | File extension | Frequency |
|------|-----------------|----------------|-----------|
| **Full** | Complete database | `.bak` | Weekly (typical) |
| **Differential** | Changes since last full backup | `.bak` | Daily (typical) |
| **Transaction Log** | Log entries since last log backup | `.trn` | Every 15–60 min (typical) |

**No chain orchestration:**
  Breeze doesn't track an LSN chain or offer a point-in-time picker. Each restore is a single `RESTORE DATABASE ... FROM DISK` against **one** backup file — there's no automatic full → differential → log replay. To reconstruct a specific point in time, restore the full backup `WITH NORECOVERY`, then apply the differential/log backups in order yourself (outside Breeze), finishing the last one `WITH RECOVERY`.

---

sections.heading: Running a Manual Backup
sections.text:
1. On the **SQL Server** tab, find the database you want to back up.
2. Click the **Backup** action.
3. Select the backup type: **Full**, **Differential**, or **Log**.
4. Optionally select a storage configuration for cloud upload.
5. Confirm to start the backup.

There's no field to choose the output path. Breeze runs `BACKUP DATABASE ... TO DISK` into the instance's **default backup directory**, under a `breeze` subfolder, then uploads the resulting `.bak`/`.trn` file and deletes the local copy — it doesn't accumulate on the SQL Server host. Backups are compressed except on **Express Edition**, which doesn't support backup compression.

sections.heading: Scheduled Backups
sections.text:
Create a [backup policy](/backup/policies/) with the **MSSQL** mode to automate SQL Server backups. Like Hyper-V, MSSQL mode uses **all-by-default targeting** against the discovered inventory — see the discovery note above. Use exclude lists for databases that don't need backup (e.g., `tempdb`).

  Scheduling a combination — weekly full + daily differential + frequent log — gives you the raw backups needed to reconstruct a point in time, but Breeze doesn't chain them for you; see the caution in [Backup Types](#backup-types) above. The backup policy schedule controls the primary backup type; you may want separate policies for different backup frequencies.

---

sections.heading: Restoring a Database
sections.text:
1. On the **SQL Server** tab, find the database and click **Restore**.
2. The restore dialog walks you through:
   - **Source** — select the instance and source database
   - **Backup to restore** — pick one specific backup (full, differential, or log) from the list; there's no point-in-time picker — each restore applies exactly one backup file
   - **Target database** — name of the database to restore into; it can differ from the source name
   - **No Recovery mode** — optionally leave the database in a restoring state so you can apply additional log backups before bringing it online
3. Review and confirm.

The restore runs in the background. Starting it queues the command on the device and returns straight away; Breeze does not wait for SQL Server to finish, which on a large database can take hours. Follow its progress and final result like any other restore job — see [Monitoring a Restore](/backup/restoring/#monitoring-a-restore). Before v0.117.0 a SQL Server restore that ran longer than 10 minutes was reported as failed even though the agent was still working.

  Restoring a database overwrites the target database if it already exists (`WITH REPLACE`). Restoring under a **different** name while the source database is still attached is not supported today — Breeze doesn't relocate the backup's data/log file paths (no `MOVE` clause), so the new database's files would collide with the original's. To restore a copy alongside the original, restore onto a different **instance** instead.

---

sections.heading: Security
sections.text: All SQL Server backup and restore commands use strict input validation to prevent T-SQL injection. Instance names, database names, and file paths are validated against allowed patterns before being passed to `sqlcmd`.

title: Storage Configuration
description: Set up backup storage targets for S3 (and S3-compatible services like MinIO, Wasabi, and Backblaze B2) or local NAS, with connectivity testing and multiple configurations.
headings: Recommended bucket settings for S3-compatible storage

sections.text:
Before you can run backups, you need at least one storage configuration that tells Breeze where to send backup data. You can create multiple configurations — for example, an S3 bucket for off-site cloud storage and a local NAS for fast restores.

---

sections.heading: Creating a Storage Configuration
sections.text:
The storage configuration wizard walks you through four steps:

1. **Select a provider.** Choose Amazon S3 or Local/NAS. Each option shows a brief description to help you decide.

2. **Enter provider settings.** The fields change based on your provider:

     **Amazon S3:**
       - **Region** — AWS region (e.g., `us-east-1`)
       - **Bucket Name** — the S3 bucket to store backups in
       - **Path Prefix** — optional key prefix within the bucket (e.g., `breeze-backups`). New snapshots are stored under `<prefix>/snapshots/`; see [Key prefix](#key-prefix) below
       - **Access Key** and **Secret Key** — IAM credentials with `s3:PutObject`, `s3:GetObject`, `s3:ListBucket`, and `s3:DeleteObject` permissions (scoped to `<prefix>/*` when you set a prefix)

       Also works with S3-compatible services like MinIO, Wasabi, and Backblaze B2 — just set the endpoint URL accordingly. Enter the endpoint as a host (`s3.example.com`) or host and port (`minio.local:9000`), optionally prefixed with `http://` or `https://`; a scheme-less endpoint is treated as `https://`. Other schemes (such as `s3://` or `ftp://`) are rejected with a validation error rather than failing later at backup time.

     **Local / NAS:**
       - **Local Path** — mount point or UNC path (e.g., `/mnt/backups` or `\\nas\breeze`)
       - **Retention Tier** — storage tier classification

3. **Set a schedule.** Choose how often backups run:
   - **Daily** — pick a start time and backup window duration
   - **Weekly** — pick days of the week, start time, and timezone
   - **Cron** — enter a custom cron expression for advanced scheduling

4. **Configure retention.** Choose a preset or customize:
   - **Standard** — 30 days, 5 versions
   - **Extended** — 90 days, 10 versions
   - **Compliance** — 365 days, 20 versions
   - **Custom** — set your own day count and version count

   Optionally enable encryption. This is only enforceable for S3 destinations with server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) configured — see [Encryption](/backup/encryption/) for details. Local/NAS destinations do not support enabling this toggle.

   **What retention removes today:**
     When a restore point passes its retention window, Breeze removes it from the snapshot list — it can no
     longer be restored or verified — and marks its data for reclamation. A background storage sweep then
     deletes the restore point's exclusive data from the storage target on its next scheduled run. Data
     another surviving restore point still depends on (for example, a file shared with an incremental backup)
     is never deleted, no matter how old it is. A short safety grace period (48 hours by default) additionally
     protects any loose object that might still be mid-upload before it is considered for deletion at all. An
     upload that never finished, or whose record could not be reconciled, is reclaimed once it has sat idle
     for about 9 days — giving Breeze time to recognize and finish adopting it first.

     If a device's Breeze backup helper predates version 0.112.0, storage reclamation beyond an expired
     snapshot's own row stays deferred on that device's destination until every device sharing it has
     upgraded — update the agent to enable full reclamation.

     Permanently deleting (purging) a device or erasing an organization removes its restore points from
     Breeze, but from v0.122.1 it does **not** reclaim their storage: the backup files stay in the storage
     target, and the storage sweep never deletes them later, including data already past its retention
     window. They are kept until an explicit backup-deletion feature ships. A legal hold on a snapshot,
     on the backup policy it ran under, or in a configuration policy's backup settings blocks a device purge
     (`409`, `BACKUP_PROTECTED`) and an organization erasure until the hold is released.

Click **Publish Configuration** to make it active, or **Save as Draft** to finish later.

---

sections.heading: How Backup Data Is Stored
sections.text:
File backups are written to the target as one object per file, under a `snapshots/<snapshot-id>/files/` prefix. Every file object's name ends in `.gz`, but whether the bytes are compressed depends on the provider:

| Provider | Object name | Stored bytes |
|----------|-------------|--------------|
| **Amazon S3 and S3-compatible** (MinIO, Wasabi, Backblaze B2) | ends in `.gz` | **Not compressed.** The object is the original file, byte for byte. |
| **Local / NAS** | ends in `.gz` | gzip-compressed, decompressed again on restore |

On S3 storage the `.gz` suffix is only part of the object name. Expect an S3 target to use roughly as much space as the files you protect, and size buckets and quotas on that basis. If you download a file object directly from the bucket, it is the original file. Rename it to drop the `.gz` instead of running `gunzip` on it, which fails with `not in gzip format`.

Breeze relies on this layout: restores, bare-metal recovery media, integrity verification and older agents all read S3 objects as raw bytes. Don't rename, compress or recompress objects in the bucket.

sections.heading: Key prefix
sections.text:
An S3 destination's **Path Prefix** decides where its new snapshots are written:

| Destination | New snapshot objects |
|-------------|----------------------|
| No prefix | `snapshots/<snapshot-id>/...` at the bucket root |
| Prefix `msp/acme` | `msp/acme/snapshots/<snapshot-id>/...` |

Each snapshot records the location it was written to, and Breeze reads, verifies, restores and cleans it up there for its whole life. As a result:

- **Existing snapshots are never moved.** Snapshots taken before you set or changed the prefix stay where they are and keep restoring normally.
- **Changing the prefix makes the next backup a full backup.** An incremental never builds on a snapshot stored under a different prefix, so the first run scheduled after a change uploads everything again. An incremental run that was already scheduled against a base under the old prefix when you changed it fails with a message saying so; the next scheduled run takes the full backup.
- **Several organizations can share one bucket** with a prefix each. The storage cleanup sweep lists and deletes under one prefix at a time and never touches another prefix's objects.
- **Scope IAM policies to the prefix.** A policy that only allows `bucket/snapshots/*` stops working once a prefix is set; allow `bucket/<prefix>/*` instead. **Test connection** writes a probe object under the prefix, so it catches this before the first backup fails.

A valid prefix is at most 256 characters, made of `/`-separated segments that use only letters, digits and `! _ . * ' ( ) -`. Leading and trailing slashes are ignored. Empty segments (`a//b`), `.` and `..` are not allowed, and no segment may be `snapshots` (in any letter case), so one prefix can never contain another prefix's snapshots. The form flags an invalid prefix as you type and the API rejects it on save. A destination saved with an invalid prefix by an older version is not backed up to the bucket root instead: its backups fail with a message asking you to correct the prefix, and **Test connection** fails naming the rule the prefix breaks.

Bare-metal recovery of a snapshot stored under a prefix always downloads through Breeze (token-mode download), which is the default for recovery media. Agent-side tools that read a bucket directly with a hand-supplied configuration (the `breeze-backup rebuild --provider-config` command and the `agent.yaml` backup manager) do not apply the prefix.

sections.heading: How destination credentials are stored
sections.text:
From v0.121.0, the credentials in a storage configuration (access keys, secret keys, session tokens, and the equivalent Azure, Google Cloud Storage and Backblaze B2 fields) are stored encrypted with your instance's application encryption key. Bucket, region, endpoint and prefix stay readable. Existing configurations are encrypted by a background sweep on the first start after the upgrade, which logs one `[startup] Backup destination credentials sealed: …` line.

**Roll forward only:**
  Once that sweep has run, do not roll back to a release older than v0.121.0. Older releases would hand the encrypted values to agents as storage credentials and S3 backups would fail. If you rotate `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, follow [Secret Rotation](/security/secrets/#rotating-app-encryption-key); the re-encryption script covers these credentials.

sections.heading: Recommended bucket settings for S3-compatible storage
sections.text:
When backups go to a bucket you or your customer own on an S3-compatible service (AWS S3, Wasabi, Backblaze B2, iDrive e2 and similar), set the bucket up so that backup data cannot be silently removed with the same key Breeze uses to write it:

- **Turn on Object Lock, or at least versioning.** Object Lock (often called immutable or WORM storage) keeps each object version for a retention period you choose, even if a delete request arrives. Most providers only let you enable it when the bucket is created, so decide before the first backup. If your provider or plan has no Object Lock, enable bucket versioning instead, so a deleted or overwritten object leaves a recoverable previous version.
- **Add a lifecycle rule for old versions.** With Object Lock or versioning on, Breeze's retention sweep still sends deletes for expired restore points, but on a versioned bucket a delete only hides the object and the data is kept as a noncurrent version. Add a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after the number of days you want to keep them (no shorter than your Object Lock retention), or storage use keeps growing.
- **Use a key scoped to that one bucket.** Create a dedicated access key for Breeze that can only reach the backup bucket (and, if you set one, its base path), with the object permissions listed above and nothing else: no access to other buckets, no permission to change bucket settings, Object Lock configuration or lifecycle rules, and no permission to bypass retention. If you use provider-enforced immutability on individual snapshots, the key also needs to read the bucket's Object Lock configuration and set object retention (`s3:GetBucketObjectLockConfiguration` and `s3:PutObjectRetention` on AWS).

Breeze does not create buckets or manage these settings: it does not turn on Object Lock or versioning, write lifecycle rules, or create or scope access keys. Configure them in your storage provider's console. When Object Lock is already enabled on the bucket and a snapshot is made immutable with provider enforcement, by its backup policy or by hand (`POST /backup/snapshots/:id/immutability` with `"enforcement": "provider"`), Breeze places a Governance-mode retention date on that snapshot's objects. If the bucket does not have Object Lock enabled, the manual request is refused with `409`, and a policy-driven snapshot falls back to Breeze's own application-level immutability and records the reason on the snapshot (`immutabilityFallbackReason`).

---

sections.heading: Testing Connectivity
sections.text:
After creating a configuration, test that Breeze can reach the storage target:

1. Find the configuration in your storage list.
2. Click the **Refresh** (test) action on the configuration row.
3. A success or failure message appears. The configuration's **Last Tested** timestamp updates on success.

  Always test connectivity after creating or updating a configuration. This catches credential errors or network issues before your first scheduled backup fails.

---

sections.heading: Editing a Configuration
sections.text:
Click the **Edit** action on any configuration to reopen the wizard. Changes are merged — updating a single field (like the bucket name) won't erase your other settings.

---

sections.heading: Deleting a Configuration
sections.text:
Click **Delete** on a configuration to remove it. Configurations that are actively referenced by a backup policy should have the policy reassigned first.

**Destinations with job history:**
  A configuration that has any backup job history can't be deleted: Breeze returns `409` and names what blocks it (v0.120.0 returned a server error instead). Disable it — reassign its policies, then set `"enabled": false` with `PATCH /backup/configs/:id`.

  Deleting a storage configuration does not delete the backup data already stored at that target. The data remains in S3 or your local path until you remove it manually.

---

sections.heading: Multiple Configurations
sections.text:
You can create different configurations for different use cases:

| Use case | Recommended setup |
|----------|-------------------|
| **Critical servers** | S3 (off-site) + local vault (fast restore) |
| **Workstations** | Local NAS with 30-day retention |
| **Compliance** | S3 with 365-day retention and server-side encryption |
| **Development/test** | Local storage with minimal retention |

Assign each configuration to the appropriate devices through [backup policies](/backup/policies/).

  From v0.118.0, a bucket, endpoint or local path that an organization under **another partner** already uses is refused. Organizations under the same partner can still share one.

title: Backup Troubleshooting
description: Fixes for common backup issues: stuck or failing jobs, empty snapshot browses, VSS writer failures, SQL Server chain breaks, and recovery token errors.
headings: Backup job fails with "backup helper exited unexpectedly"
Backup waits for the backup component to report
Restore refused: "did not match its integrity record"
Restore refused: "Update the Breeze agent on this device"
Restore includes more files than I selected
Restore or verification will not start
Whole-machine restore looks stuck for a long time
DR plan execution or save fails with a generic error
Bare-metal recovery fails with no reason shown
Post-restore validation flags healthy services as failed

sections.heading: No backup configuration available
sections.text:
**Symptom:** Manual backup fails with "No backup config available."

**Cause:** No storage configuration exists for your organization, or no policy targets the device.

**Fix:**
1. Create a [storage configuration](/backup/storage/) if you haven't already.
2. Create a [backup policy](/backup/policies/) that targets the device, or ensure at least one storage configuration exists in the organization (the system falls back to any available config).

---

sections.heading: Job stuck in Queued status
sections.text:
**Symptom:** A backup job stays in **Queued** and never starts.

**Cause:** The job was created but the agent hasn't picked it up.

**Fix:**
1. Verify the target device is online (check the device list for connectivity status).
2. Confirm the Breeze agent is running on the device.
3. Check that Redis is operational — backup jobs are dispatched through the job queue.

If a manual backup request cannot be queued at all, Breeze now marks the job **Failed** immediately with the dispatch error instead of leaving it queued forever.

---

sections.heading: Job fails immediately
sections.text:
**Symptom:** Job moves to **Failed** status within seconds.

**Cause:** Typically a storage connectivity issue or permission error.

**Fix:**
1. Open the failed job to read the error message.
2. Test the storage configuration connectivity (click Refresh/Test on the config).
3. Verify storage credentials haven't expired or been rotated.
4. Check that the agent has network access to the storage target.

A backup is also stopped and marked failed if the device moves to another organization, or its backup configuration is edited, while the backup is being sent to the device. Run the backup again once the move or edit is done.

---

sections.heading: Backup job fails with "backup helper exited unexpectedly"
sections.text:
**Symptom:** A backup job that was running normally suddenly fails, with an error mentioning the backup helper exiting unexpectedly — most often on a small or busy device during a large backup.

**Cause:** Under sustained load, the agent's internal health check can time out and trigger an agent restart, which also stops any backup helper process that was in progress.

**Fix:** Re-run the backup — Breeze resumes from where it left off using its checkpoint journal instead of starting over. If this happens repeatedly on the same device, reduce load on it during the backup window or narrow the backup scope.

---

sections.heading: Backup waits for the backup component to report
sections.text:
**Symptom:** A backup or restore stays queued with a note naming the backup component, or a backup fails with "The backup was not started because the backup component on this device hasn't reported which storage features it supports yet. If the device is online, update or reinstall the Breeze agent, then run the backup again."

**Cause:** Each heartbeat reports which storage features the device's backup helper supports. When the agent cannot ask the helper (not installed yet, crashed, timed out, unreadable output), it reports **unknown** rather than "no support". A device that already reported support keeps its last known value; a device with no report yet waits — for up to 10 minutes — instead of being treated as an older helper. The agent retries the check after 1, 2 and 4 minutes, then every 5 minutes.

**Fix:** Usually none: the next successful check releases the work. If the message persists while the device is online, update or reinstall the Breeze agent on the device, then run the backup again.

---

sections.heading: Restore refused: "did not match its integrity record"
sections.text:
**Symptom:** A restore, verification or VM restore fails with `This backup did not match its integrity record and cannot be read from storage.`

**Cause:** The snapshot's stored objects did not match its attestation when they were checked. Breeze will not read such a snapshot. See [Integrity checks on restore](/backup/restoring/#integrity-checks-on-restore).

**Fix:** Restore from a different snapshot. Investigate the storage target for tampering or corruption. If the message instead says the file list `is being rebuilt from storage`, wait a few minutes and run the restore again.

---

sections.heading: Restore refused: "Update the Breeze agent on this device"
sections.text:
**Symptom:** Starting a file, SQL Server, Hyper-V, restore-as-VM, instant boot or bare-metal restore fails with **Update the Breeze agent on this device, then try again.** Or recovery media fails at the recovery code with **This recovery tool is too old to check backup integrity.**

**Cause:** Restores that write, import or boot a backup need a backup helper that checks snapshot attestations (Breeze agent v0.120.0 or later). Recovery media and recovery tools older than v0.120.0 are refused too. Verification and test restore are not affected.

**Fix:** Update the agent on the target device and start the restore again. For bare-metal recovery, download current recovery media or the current recovery tool and boot it again. See [Integrity checks on restore](/backup/restoring/#integrity-checks-on-restore).

---

sections.heading: Deleting a backup destination fails
sections.text:
**Symptom:** Deleting a backup destination that has ever run a backup returns a server error.

**Cause:** Known issue in v0.120.0: a destination with job history cannot be deleted.

**Fix:** Stop using the destination instead of deleting it: reassign the policies that point at it, then disable it (`PATCH /backup/configs/:id` with `"enabled": false`).

---

sections.heading: Snapshot browse returns empty
sections.text:
**Symptom:** A snapshot exists but the file browser shows no contents.

**Cause:** The agent didn't report file-level metadata during the backup, or the browsing index was pruned while the snapshot record remains.

**Fix:** This is expected for some backup types (e.g., system image or Hyper-V exports). File-level browsing is available for file-mode backups. For other types, restore the full snapshot to inspect contents.

---

sections.heading: Restore goes to wrong device
sections.text:
**Symptom:** Data was restored to the original device instead of the intended target.

**Cause:** The target device wasn't explicitly specified in the restore wizard.

**Fix:** When restoring, explicitly select the target device in the destination step. If omitted, the restore defaults to the snapshot's original device. Both devices must be in the same organization.

---

sections.heading: Restore includes more files than I selected
sections.text:
**Symptom:** A selective restore of one file also restores other, unrelated files that happen to share the start of the same name or path (for example, restoring `report.txt` also restores `report.txt.bak` and `report.txt2`).

**Cause:** Selective restore currently matches a selected path as a text prefix rather than an exact path, so any file whose path starts with a selected path is included.

**Fix:** This is a known issue with no workaround yet. For an in-place restore, avoid selecting individual files that have similarly-named siblings — restore to an alternate path instead and copy back only the file you intended.

---

sections.heading: Restore or verification will not start
sections.text:
**Symptom:** Starting a restore or verification returns an error immediately.

**Cause:** The target device is offline, disconnected, or the command pipeline could not queue the agent command.

**Fix:**
1. Confirm the destination device shows as **Online** in Breeze.
2. Verify the Breeze agent service is running and can reach the API.
3. If the error mentions queue or dispatch failure, check Redis and API logs for command queue errors.
4. Retry after the connectivity or queue issue is resolved.

Breeze does not create simulated verification records or silent pending restores in this case. The action fails explicitly so operators can correct the underlying issue first.

---

sections.heading: No verification history
sections.text:
**Symptom:** The Verification tab shows **No verification history. Run a verification to check backup integrity.**

**Cause:** No completed live verification has run yet for that device, or all recent attempts were skipped because the device was offline.

**Fix:**
1. Bring the device online.
2. Run an **Integrity Check** or **Test Restore** manually.
3. Review scheduled verification logs if the device is frequently offline during verification windows.

---

sections.heading: Dashboard shows 0 protected devices
sections.text:
**Symptom:** Backup dashboard reports no devices are protected, but policies exist.

**Cause:** The protection count is based on direct device assignments in policies. Devices targeted only through site or device group assignments are resolved at runtime and may not appear in this count.

**Fix:** If you need accurate coverage reporting, ensure policies include explicit device assignments. Alternatively, check individual device backup tabs to confirm they have a policy assigned.

---

sections.heading: VSS writers in Failed state
sections.text:
**Symptom:** The device backup tab shows one or more VSS writers as **Failed**.

**Cause:** A Windows service that provides a VSS writer is not running or is in an error state (common with SQL Server, Exchange, or Hyper-V writers).

**Fix:**
1. On the Windows device, run `vssadmin list writers` to see writer status.
2. Restart the service associated with the failed writer.
3. If the writer is not needed for your backup scope, it can be ignored — file backups will fall back to file-level copy if VSS is unavailable.

---

sections.heading: SLA breach alerts firing unexpectedly
sections.text:
**Symptom:** Receiving RPO or RTO breach notifications when backups appear to be running normally.

**Cause:** The SLA target may be tighter than the actual backup frequency, or test restore times are exceeding the RTO target.

**Fix:**
1. Review the [SLA configuration](/backup/sla/) — ensure RPO targets are compatible with your backup schedule (e.g., a 30-minute RPO requires backups at least every 30 minutes).
2. For RTO breaches, check whether the measured restore time in [verification results](/backup/verification/) exceeds the target. Consider faster storage (local vault) or smaller backup scope.

---

sections.heading: SQL Server backup chain broken
sections.text:
**Symptom:** Differential or log backups fail with a chain continuity error.

**Cause:** A full backup is needed to start a new chain. This happens after a database restore, a backup to a different tool, or a missed full backup.

**Fix:** Run a manual **Full** backup for the affected database from the [SQL Server tab](/backup/sql-server/). Subsequent differential and log backups will chain from it.

---

sections.heading: Hyper-V export fails
sections.text:
**Symptom:** VM backup job fails during export.

**Cause:** Common causes include insufficient disk space at the export path, the VM being in an unsupported state, or Hyper-V integration services not running in the guest.

**Fix:**
1. Check available disk space at the export destination.
2. Verify the VM state — exports work best when the VM is **Running** or **Off**.
3. For application-consistent exports, ensure Hyper-V integration services are installed and running in the guest OS.
4. Try a **crash-consistent** export if application-consistent fails — but not for a VM that is **Off**. Known issue in v0.120.0: a crash-consistent backup of a powered-off VM fails with `failed to save VM state … Save-VM`; use **Application-consistent** for powered-off VMs.

---

sections.heading: Whole-machine restore looks stuck for a long time
sections.text:
**Symptom:** A bare-metal rebuild, bare-metal recovery, VM restore, or SQL Server restore is still "in progress" after an hour or more.

**Cause:** These restores move a lot of data. For bare-metal rebuild and recovery a v0.122.1 or later agent downloads and verifies up to 8 files at a time (older agents one at a time). Real hardware and large disks still commonly take one to several hours — that alone isn't a failure. Breeze allows up to **24 hours** before treating a whole-machine restore as stalled.

**Fix:** Let it continue; check the recovery's timeline (or the device's command history) for phase progress. If it's genuinely stuck, it's automatically marked failed once it exceeds 24 hours — investigate storage throughput or network connectivity to the target at that point.

---

sections.heading: DR plan execution or save fails with a generic error
sections.text:
**Symptom:** Running a DR plan fails immediately, or saving a plan reports failure without saying what's wrong.

**Cause:** A recovery group is missing a prerequisite — commonly a bare-metal rebuild group with no bare-metal-restorable snapshot, no valid rebuild host, or a device reference that no longer resolves to anything, or a rebuild step's output directory isn't a valid absolute path.

**Fix:** The execution error now names the specific missing prerequisite (for example "no restorable snapshot") instead of a generic error — resolve that and retry. Saving a plan now validates group configuration before writing anything, so an invalid step is refused with nothing changed; if a save still fails partway through a multi-group plan, Breeze reports it as a **partial save** and refreshes the plan list automatically rather than leaving it out of sync with the server.

---

sections.heading: Bare-metal recovery fails with no reason shown
sections.text:
**Symptom:** A bare-metal recovery (boot media or rebuild engine) reports **Failed**, but the recovery details in the **Recovery Bootstrap** tab show nothing beyond "failed."

**Cause:** Older agents didn't always report *why* a system-state artifact failed to apply during recovery.

**Fix:** Current agents record the specific failure reason (for example, which artifact failed verification) and show it directly on the recovery. If you still see a blank reason, update the recovering agent and retry.

---

sections.heading: Post-restore validation flags healthy services as failed
sections.text:
**Symptom:** After a bare-metal recovery, the post-restore validation probe lists a template-style unit (e.g. `getty@.service`) or a one-shot systemd unit as unhealthy, even though the recovered system is fine.

**Cause:** Earlier validation probes checked template and one-shot units the same way as regular long-running services, even though those are never continuously "running" on a healthy system.

**Fix:** This is fixed in current agents — the probe now skips template units and evaluates one-shot units by their actual state, so only real regressions are flagged. Update the agent if you still see this.

---

sections.heading: Recovery token not working
sections.text:
**Symptom:** Bare metal recovery agent rejects the recovery token.

**Cause:** The token may have expired, been used already, or was copied incorrectly.

**Fix:** Generate a [new recovery token](/backup/bare-metal-recovery/). A token is consumed once a recovery completes with it and stops working when it expires; a recovery that failed before completing does not consume it, so `Token is used` means a recovery already finished with that token. Ensure you copy the full token string without trailing whitespace.

---

sections.heading: Generating bootable recovery media fails
sections.text:
**Symptom:** Building bootable recovery media (ISO) or a recovery bundle for a token, from the **Recovery Bootstrap** tab, shows a **Failed** status.

**Cause:** On some deployments, building recovery media runs out of temporary disk space on the server.

**Fix:** Retry the request — transient load can also cause a failure. If it fails consistently, contact your Breeze administrator; the server's temporary storage may need to be increased. This affects both the ISO and the downloadable recovery bundle.

  For persistent issues, check the device's diagnostic logs via the device detail page. Filter by the `backup` component to see agent-side backup logs.

title: Local Vaults
description: Mirror backup snapshots from cloud storage to a local vault, NAS share, or USB drive for fast offline recovery, with incremental sync and retention.

sections.text:
A local vault mirrors your backup snapshots from cloud storage to a local location — a NAS share, an external drive, or a local disk. This gives you fast, offline recovery when the cloud is unreachable or when you need to restore large datasets without waiting for a download.

---

sections.heading: Creating a Vault
sections.text:
1. Go to **Backup > Device Backup > Vault**.
2. Click **Add New Vault**.
3. Fill in the vault configuration:
   - **Device** — which device the vault is attached to
   - **Vault path** — local mount point, SMB share, or USB drive path
   - **Type** — Local Disk, SMB Share, or USB Device
   - **Retention count** — number of snapshots to keep locally (1–100)
4. Click **Save**.

The vault appears in the list with a **Never synced** status.

---

sections.heading: Syncing a Vault
sections.text:
Click the **Sync** button on a vault to trigger an immediate sync. The sync process:

1. Compares local vault contents against the latest cloud snapshots
2. Downloads only missing files (incremental sync)
3. Removes snapshots that exceed the retention count
4. Updates the vault status and last sync timestamp

  Vaults sync intelligently — they only download files that aren't already present locally. After the initial sync, subsequent syncs are fast and bandwidth-efficient.

---

sections.heading: Vault Status
sections.text:
| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **Syncing** | A sync operation is in progress |
| **Completed** | Last sync finished successfully |
| **Failed** | Last sync encountered an error — check the vault path and connectivity |
| **Never synced** | Vault was created but hasn't been synced yet |

---

sections.heading: Managing Vaults
sections.text:
- **Deactivate** — temporarily disables the vault without deleting its configuration. No further syncs will run. Reactivate at any time.
- **Delete** — removes the vault configuration. Does not delete the data already on the local storage.

---

sections.heading: When to Use Vaults
sections.text:
| Scenario | Recommendation |
|----------|---------------|
| **Critical servers** | Pair cloud backup with a local vault for sub-minute restore times |
| **Remote offices with slow WAN** | Vault to local NAS so restores don't depend on internet bandwidth |
| **Compliance** | Keep an offline copy on USB or air-gapped storage |
| **Disaster recovery** | Local vaults provide a second restore option if the cloud provider is down |

title: Verification & Recovery Readiness
description: Verify backup integrity with checksum checks and test restores, review verification history, and track per-device recovery readiness scores in Breeze.

sections.text:
A backup you can't restore is worthless. The Verification tab helps you continuously validate that your backups are recoverable and measure how prepared each device is for a recovery scenario.

  Verification is a live agent operation. The target device must be online and connected to Breeze before an integrity check or test restore can start.

---

sections.heading: Verification Types
sections.text:
Go to **Backup > Device Backup > Verification** to access verification controls.

| Type | Duration | What it checks | Impact |
|------|----------|----------------|--------|
| **Integrity check** | Fast (minutes) | Downloaded object size and SHA-256 checksum compared against the manifest, plus file counts and manifest consistency | None — no data is restored |
| **Test restore** | Medium (10+ min) | Extracts the full snapshot to a temporary location, verifies each object against the manifest, and measures restore time | Low — uses temp space, no production impact |

  Both checks genuinely detect corruption — an object whose bytes or length no longer match the manifest fails verification (reported as **Failed** or **Partial** with the specific file listed), rather than passing on a presence check alone. Snapshots taken before checksums were recorded still verify via the size comparison.

**Attested snapshots (v0.120.0+):**
  For a snapshot with an attestation, a v0.120.0 or later backup helper also checks the manifest itself against the attestation, and every file must match its manifest entry exactly. A snapshot that already failed its integrity check cannot be verified or test-restored: the command fails with `This backup did not match its integrity record and cannot be read from storage.` A new verification of such a snapshot fails straight away, and one already waiting fails as soon as the snapshot is marked. An unattested snapshot still verifies, with an advisory **Unattested snapshot** warning. See [Integrity checks on restore](/backup/restoring/#integrity-checks-on-restore).

sections.heading: Running a Verification
sections.text:
1. Go to **Backup > Device Backup > Verification**.
2. Click **Run Integrity Check** or **Test Restore**.
3. Confirm the action in the dialog.
4. The verification appears in the history table with a status of **Running**.
5. When complete, the status updates to **Passed**, **Failed**, or **Partial**.

If the device is offline, Breeze shows `Device is offline. Verification requires a connected agent.` and the verification buttons stay disabled. If command dispatch fails for another reason, Breeze shows the dispatch error and lets you retry after the underlying issue is fixed.

sections.heading: Verification History
sections.text:
The history table shows all past verifications with:
- Verification type
- Status (Pending, Running, Passed, Failed, Partial)
- Start time and duration
- Files verified and files failed
- Total size checked

---

sections.heading: Automated Verification
sections.text:
Breeze runs verifications automatically on a schedule:

| Check | Frequency | What it does |
|-------|-----------|-------------|
| **Post-backup integrity** | Every 10 minutes | Validates the most recent completed backup when the device is available |
| **Weekly test restore** | Sundays at 03:38 UTC | Runs a restore test for recent backups when the device is available |
| **Readiness score recalculation** | Daily at 02:18 UTC | Updates recovery readiness scores for all devices |
| **Timeout detection** | Every 5 minutes | Flags verifications that have been running too long |

No setup is needed — automated verifications run as soon as backup is configured. If a device is offline when a scheduled verification window arrives, Breeze skips that run and logs the skip instead of creating a synthetic verification record.

---

sections.heading: Recovery Readiness Score
sections.text:
Each device gets a readiness score from 0 to 100, visible on the Verification tab:

| Score | Rating | Meaning |
|-------|--------|---------|
| **85–100** | High | Device is well-protected and verified |
| **70–84** | Acceptable | Minor gaps — review risk factors |
| **Below 70** | Low | Significant recovery risk — take action |

The score is calculated from:
- **Recency** — how fresh the latest snapshot is (within 30 days)
- **Verification success rate** — recent integrity and restore test results
- **RTO/RPO compliance** — whether estimated recovery times meet SLA targets
- **Risk factor assessment** — missing backups, failed verifications, or expired snapshots

sections.heading: Risk Factors
sections.text:
The Verification tab lists specific risk factors for each device, color-coded by severity:

| Risk factor | Severity | What to do |
|-------------|----------|------------|
| No recent backups | High (red) | Check policy assignment and agent connectivity |
| Verification failures | High (red) | Investigate the failed verification — storage may be unreachable |
| SLA breaches | Medium (orange) | Review SLA targets or increase backup frequency |
| Data change accumulation | Medium (orange) | Large volume of unprotected changes — run a backup |
| Immutable backup gaps | Low (yellow) | Consider enabling immutability on your storage configuration |

sections.heading: Bare-metal rebuild evidence
sections.text:
When a device has been through a real [bare-metal rebuild](/backup/bare-metal-recovery/) — from Breeze recovery media, a DR rehearsal or Restore as VM — the outcome feeds its readiness. Only settled rebuilds count: a recovery that is still running, was refused before touching a disk, or was cancelled before it started is neither proof nor failure. Breeze looks at the device's ten most recent settled rebuilds.

- **Measured recovery time.** The time from the start of the restore to validation is the rebuild's measured duration. The device's estimated RTO becomes the slower of this and the test-restore estimate, so the [SLA](/backup/sla/) RTO check compares against a figure a full rebuild actually produced.
- **Rebuild risk factors.**

| Risk factor | Severity | When it appears |
|-------------|----------|-----------------|
| Latest bare-metal rebuild failed | High (red) | The most recent settled rebuild failed. The score also drops by 10 points. |
| Earlier bare-metal rebuilds failed | Medium (orange) | A rebuild failed, but a later one succeeded. |
| Last successful rebuild is old | Medium (orange) | The last successful rebuild is more than 90 days old. |
| Rebuild slower than 60 minutes | Medium (orange) | The slowest recent successful rebuild exceeded 60 minutes. |

A rebuild that finishes (or checks in) or fails refreshes the device's readiness straight away; you do not have to wait for the daily recalculation. A device with no rebuild history is not penalized: rebuild evidence only adds information, it never replaces the verification-based score. If the rebuild history cannot be read when readiness is calculated, the score reflects verification only and shows a low-severity "evidence unavailable" risk factor until the next recalculation.

  A **DR rehearsal** and a **Restore as VM** rebuild into a disk image on a rebuild host, so they prove the snapshot can be rebuilt and how long it takes; they do not prove the physical machine's hardware. A recovery from recovery media with the **Original device** identity is the production path and is only counted as successful once the restored machine has checked in.

---

sections.heading: Organization Backup Health
sections.text:
The Verification tab also shows an organization-wide health summary:

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **Healthy** | All devices have recent, verified backups |
| **Degraded** | Some devices have low readiness scores or recent failures |
| **Critical** | Multiple devices are unprotected or have failed verifications |

Use this as a quick indicator of overall backup posture.

If the overview shows **No verification history**, that means Breeze has no completed live verification for the device yet. Run a real verification once the device is online to populate readiness and recent-failure history.

title: Antivirus Exceptions
description: Antivirus and security software exclusions for the Breeze agent, plus how to report a false positive on a signed binary.
headings: Step 1: Confirm the binary is actually signed
Step 3: Report the false positive to the vendor

sections.text:
Endpoint protection software may flag, quarantine, or block the Breeze agent. This guide covers the exclusions needed for each platform, and what to do when a *signed* binary is flagged.

  Unsigned binaries are common during development, self-hosted builds, and early deployments, and are the most common cause of AV interference. As of v0.105.0, this includes the **public release's Windows agent artifacts** — see the note below. For production fleets, consider signing your binaries to avoid the need for broad AV exclusions. See [Sign Your Own Agent Packages](/deploy/sign-your-own-packages/) for the supported path.

  **Not every Breeze binary is signed the same way.** macOS agent binaries are codesigned and notarized by Breeze. On Windows, the **Viewer and Helper** installers are Authenticode-signed by LanternOps, but as of v0.105.0 the **Agent** artifacts (`breeze-agent.exe`, `breeze-agent.msi`, and the backup/watchdog/user-helper `.exe`s bundled with it) are published **unsigned** in the public self-host release, as signing inputs for deployments that sign under their own certificate — `Get-AuthenticodeSignature` reporting `NotSigned` on those is expected, not a red flag. See [Code Signing](/deploy/code-signing/) for the full breakdown. If a **signed** binary (macOS agent, or the Windows Viewer/Helper) is being quarantined, exclusions are a workaround rather than the fix — see [Signed Binaries Flagged as Malware](#signed-binaries-flagged-as-malware) below.

sections.heading: Why Exclusions Are Needed
sections.text:
The Breeze agent is a single Go binary that:

- Runs as a **system service** with elevated privileges
- Opens **persistent WebSocket connections** to your Breeze server
- Executes **scripts and commands** on behalf of remote administrators
- Spawns **child processes** (terminal sessions, user helper, discovery scans)
- Reads **hardware and software inventory** from the system

These behaviors overlap with patterns that heuristic-based antivirus engines flag as suspicious. Without code signing, there is no publisher reputation to offset the heuristic score.

sections.heading: Signed Binaries Flagged as Malware
sections.text: Agent binaries published in official Breeze releases are codesigned and notarized on macOS. On Windows, the **Viewer and Helper** installers are Authenticode-signed by LanternOps; the **Agent** installer and executables are published **unsigned** in the public release as of v0.105.0 (self-host signing inputs), unless you've signed them under your own certificate — see [Code Signing](/deploy/code-signing/) and [Sign Your Own Agent Packages](/deploy/sign-your-own-packages/). A signed binary being quarantined is a **false positive**, and adding an exclusion treats the symptom rather than the cause.

sections.heading: Step 1: Confirm the binary is actually signed
sections.text:
Do this before anything else. This applies to macOS agent binaries and the Windows Viewer/Helper installers. A publicly-released Windows **Agent** binary is expected to report `NotSigned` unless you've signed it yourself — that's normal, not a broken build.

```powershell
# Windows Helper (the Windows component Breeze itself signs alongside the Viewer)
Get-AuthenticodeSignature "C:\Program Files\Breeze Helper\breeze-helper.exe" | Format-List Status, SignerCertificate
```

```bash
# macOS agent (runs from /usr/local/bin/breeze-agent on most Macs; from
# /Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent if it moved there -- see macOS Permissions)
codesign --verify --deep --strict --verbose=2 /usr/local/bin/breeze-agent
spctl --assess --type execute --verbose /usr/local/bin/breeze-agent
```

If the Windows Helper/Viewer reports `NotSigned`, or macOS reports the binary is not signed, that binary did not come from an official release. Reinstall from an official release before pursuing a false-positive report.

sections.heading: Step 2: Read the detection name
sections.text:
Machine-learning verdicts end in `!ml` (for example `Trojan:Script/Wacatac.B!ml`). These are heuristic scores, not signature matches, and are the detection class most likely to be a false positive on a legitimate RMM agent.

Several normal agent behaviors contribute to that score: writing PowerShell scripts to a temporary directory and executing them with `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass`, downloading a replacement binary during self-update, and running as SYSTEM while spawning processes into user sessions. Every remote management tool does some version of this.

sections.heading: Step 3: Report the false positive to the vendor
sections.text:
Reporting it is what actually fixes the problem, for you and for everyone else running the same version. Include the detection name, the agent version, and the file hash.

| Vendor | Submission channel |
|---|---|
| Microsoft Defender | [Microsoft Security Intelligence submission portal](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/filesubmission) — choose **Software developer** and note that the file is signed |
| CrowdStrike Falcon | Support portal detection review, or ask your CS rep for a certificate-based exclusion |
| SentinelOne | Support ticket referencing the signing certificate |
| Other vendors | Most maintain a "submit a false positive" form; search for the vendor name plus "false positive submission" |

Please also open an issue on the [Breeze repository](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/issues) with the detection name and agent version, so the same submission can be made centrally.

sections.heading: Step 4: Add a temporary exclusion
sections.text:
Use the platform sections below to unblock the fleet while the vendor submission is processed, then remove the exclusion once the detection is retired.

  **Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules do not honour standard AV exclusions.** If Defender is blocking the agent through an ASR rule rather than real-time protection, the exclusions in this guide will have no effect. Check the Windows Defender operational event log for ASR block events (event IDs 1121 and 1122) and configure a per-rule exclusion instead. The rules most likely to fire are "Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands" and "Block credential stealing from LSASS".

sections.heading: Agent Binary
sections.text:
| OS | Default Path |
|---|---|
| Linux | `/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent` |
| macOS | `/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent` on most Macs; `/Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent` if the agent has moved there (see [macOS Permissions](/agents/macos-permissions/#agent-path-usrlocalbin-or-librarybreezebin)) -- exclude both paths |
| Windows | `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-agent.exe` |

sections.heading: Companion Windows Executables
sections.text:
The agent installer also stages a watchdog, a per-user helper, and a backup binary in the **same directory** as the agent (`C:\Program Files\Breeze\`). Exclude these by process name alongside `breeze-agent.exe`:

| Binary | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `breeze-watchdog.exe` | Runs as its own service (`BreezeWatchdog`) and restarts the agent if it stops responding |
| `breeze-user-helper.exe` | GUI-subsystem sibling of the agent, spawned into the interactive user session for prompts and remote-desktop UI |
| `breeze-desktop-helper.exe` | Per-user desktop-session helper process used by remote access |
| `breeze-backup.exe` | Enterprise backup binary (Hyper-V, MSSQL, system image) — see [Binary Distribution](/deploy/binaries/#backup-binary) |

sections.heading: Configuration Directory
sections.text:
| OS | Path |
|---|---|
| Linux | `/etc/breeze/` |
| macOS | `/Library/Application Support/Breeze/` |
| Windows | `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\` |

sections.heading: Log Directory
sections.text:
| OS | Path |
|---|---|
| Linux | `/var/log/breeze/` |
| macOS | `/Library/Application Support/Breeze/logs/` and `~/Library/Logs/Breeze/` (user-session helper logs) |
| Windows | `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\logs\` |

sections.heading: User Helper (if installed)
sections.text:
| OS | Path |
|---|---|
| Linux | `/usr/local/bin/breeze-helper` |
| macOS | `/Applications/Breeze Helper.app/Contents/MacOS/breeze-helper` |
| Windows | `C:\Program Files\Breeze Helper\breeze-helper.exe` |

sections.heading: Microsoft Defender
sections.text:
**PowerShell:**
    Run as Administrator:

```powershell
    # Process exclusions
    Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess "C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-agent.exe"
    Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess "C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-watchdog.exe"
    Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess "C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-user-helper.exe"
    Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess "C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-desktop-helper.exe"
    Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess "C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-backup.exe"
    Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess "C:\Program Files\Breeze Helper\breeze-helper.exe"

    # Path exclusions (config, logs, working directories)
    Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath "C:\Program Files\Breeze"
    Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath "C:\Program Files\Breeze Helper"
    Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath "C:\ProgramData\Breeze"

    # Verify
    Get-MpPreference | Select-Object -ExpandProperty ExclusionProcess
    Get-MpPreference | Select-Object -ExpandProperty ExclusionPath
```

  **Group Policy:**
    For fleet deployment via GPO:

      1. Open **Group Policy Management** and create or edit a GPO linked to the target OU.
      2. Navigate to **Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → Windows Components → Microsoft Defender Antivirus → Exclusions**.
      3. Under **Path Exclusions**, add:
         - `C:\Program Files\Breeze`
         - `C:\Program Files\Breeze Helper`
         - `C:\ProgramData\Breeze`
      4. Under **Process Exclusions**, add:
         - `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-agent.exe`
         - `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-watchdog.exe`
         - `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-user-helper.exe`
         - `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-desktop-helper.exe`
         - `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-backup.exe`
         - `C:\Program Files\Breeze Helper\breeze-helper.exe`
      5. Run `gpupdate /force` on target machines or wait for the next policy refresh.

  **Intune:**
    For Microsoft Intune-managed devices:

      1. Go to **Endpoint security → Antivirus → Create policy**.
      2. Select **Windows 10/11** and **Microsoft Defender Antivirus exclusions**.
      3. Add the following exclusions:

         | Type | Value |
         |---|---|
         | Process | `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-agent.exe` |
         | Process | `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-watchdog.exe` |
         | Process | `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-user-helper.exe` |
         | Process | `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-desktop-helper.exe` |
         | Process | `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-backup.exe` |
         | Process | `C:\Program Files\Breeze Helper\breeze-helper.exe` |
         | Folder | `C:\Program Files\Breeze` |
         | Folder | `C:\Program Files\Breeze Helper` |
         | Folder | `C:\ProgramData\Breeze` |

      4. Assign the policy to the appropriate device groups.

sections.heading: Windows SmartScreen
sections.text:
SmartScreen may block the initial download or execution of an unsigned `.exe`. To bypass for a single file:

1. Right-click the binary → **Properties** → check **Unblock** → **OK**
2. Or run from an elevated PowerShell: `Unblock-File "C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-agent.exe"`

For MSI deployments via GPO/SCCM/Intune, SmartScreen does not interfere since the installer runs silently under SYSTEM.

sections.heading: Third-Party Antivirus (Windows)
sections.text:
For products like CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Sophos, Bitdefender, etc., add **both process and path exclusions**:

| Exclusion Type | Value |
|---|---|
| Process / Application | `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-agent.exe` |
| Process / Application | `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-watchdog.exe` |
| Process / Application | `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-user-helper.exe` |
| Process / Application | `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-desktop-helper.exe` |
| Process / Application | `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-backup.exe` |
| Process / Application | `C:\Program Files\Breeze Helper\breeze-helper.exe` |
| Directory | `C:\Program Files\Breeze\` |
| Directory | `C:\Program Files\Breeze Helper\` |
| Directory | `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\` |

  Some EDR products (CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne) require exclusions configured in their **cloud console**, not locally. Check your vendor's documentation for the correct procedure.

#### CrowdStrike Falcon

1. In the Falcon console, go to **Configuration → Prevention Policies**.
2. Select the relevant policy → **Machine Learning Exclusions**.
3. Add a pattern: `C:\Program Files\Breeze\**`
4. Under **IOA Exclusions**, add the process path for `breeze-agent.exe`.

#### SentinelOne

1. In the management console, go to **Sentinels → Exclusions**.
2. Add a **Path** exclusion: `C:\Program Files\Breeze\`
3. Add a **Signer Identity** or **Hash** exclusion if the binary hash is stable across your builds.

#### Sophos

1. In Sophos Central, go to **Global Settings → General → Global Exclusions**.
2. Add exclusions for the process and directory paths listed above.

sections.heading: Gatekeeper
sections.text:
macOS Gatekeeper blocks unsigned binaries downloaded from the internet. See the [installation guide](/agents/installation/) for the `xattr` command to remove the quarantine flag.

For MDM-managed fleets, deploy the binary via your MDM profile to bypass Gatekeeper entirely.

sections.heading: XProtect
sections.text:
XProtect performs signature-based malware checks. It does not typically flag custom Go binaries, but if it does:

```bash
# Check if the binary is quarantined (use /Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent
# instead if the agent has moved there -- see macOS Permissions)
xattr -l /usr/local/bin/breeze-agent

# Remove all extended attributes
sudo xattr -c /usr/local/bin/breeze-agent
```

sections.heading: Third-Party Antivirus (macOS)
sections.text:
For products like CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, or Jamf Protect, add these exclusions:

| Exclusion Type | Value |
|---|---|
| Process | `/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent` and `/Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent` (the agent runs from one or the other depending on the Mac -- see [macOS Permissions](/agents/macos-permissions/#agent-path-usrlocalbin-or-librarybreezebin)) |
| Process | `/Applications/Breeze Helper.app/Contents/MacOS/breeze-helper` |
| Directory | `/Library/Breeze/bin/` (only needed if the agent runs from there; do not exclude all of `/usr/local/bin/`, since that directory holds unrelated binaries too) |
| Directory | `/Library/Application Support/Breeze/` |
| Directory | `/Applications/Breeze Helper.app/` |
| Directory | `/etc/breeze/` (if symlinked) |

sections.heading: MDM Configuration Profile
sections.text:
For managed fleets, deploy a configuration profile to suppress Gatekeeper and TCC prompts:

```xml
<!-- Gatekeeper: allow identified developers + unsigned -->
<key>AllowIdentifiedDevelopers</key>
<true/>
<key>EnableAssessment</key>
<false/>
```

  A better approach is to deploy a **PPPC (Privacy Preferences Policy Control)** profile that pre-approves the Breeze binary. See the [macOS Permissions section](/agents/installation/#macos-permissions) of the installation guide.

sections.heading: Linux
sections.text: Linux antivirus is less common but increasingly used in enterprise environments.

sections.heading: SELinux
sections.text:
If SELinux is in **enforcing** mode, the agent may be blocked from binding sockets, executing scripts, or accessing certain paths. Create a custom policy module:

```bash
# Generate a policy from audit denials
sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent | audit2allow -M breeze-agent

# Install the module
sudo semodule -i breeze-agent.pp

# Verify
sudo semodule -l | grep breeze
```

Alternatively, label the binary with an appropriate SELinux type:

```bash
sudo semanage fcontext -a -t bin_t "/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent"
sudo restorecon -v /usr/local/bin/breeze-agent
```

sections.heading: AppArmor
sections.text:
On Ubuntu/Debian systems with AppArmor, create a permissive profile if the agent is blocked:

```bash
# Create a basic profile
sudo aa-autodep /usr/local/bin/breeze-agent

# Set to complain mode (log but don't block)
sudo aa-complain /usr/local/bin/breeze-agent

# After verifying logs, enforce if desired
# sudo aa-enforce /usr/local/bin/breeze-agent
```

sections.heading: ClamAV
sections.text:
If ClamAV's on-access scanner flags the binary:

```bash
# Add to /etc/clamav/clamd.conf
ExcludePath ^/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent$
ExcludePath ^/etc/breeze/
ExcludePath ^/var/log/breeze/
```

Restart the ClamAV daemon after changes: `sudo systemctl restart clamav-daemon`

sections.heading: Third-Party EDR (Linux)
sections.text:
For CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, or similar:

| Exclusion Type | Value |
|---|---|
| Process | `/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent` |
| Directory | `/etc/breeze/` |
| Directory | `/var/log/breeze/` |

sections.heading: Verifying Exclusions
sections.text:
After configuring exclusions, verify the agent runs without interference:

```bash
# Check agent service status
sudo breeze-agent service status

# Watch logs for AV-related errors
# Linux
sudo journalctl -u breeze-agent -f

# macOS
sudo tail -f "/Library/Application Support/Breeze/logs/agent.log"

# Windows (PowerShell)
Get-Content "C:\ProgramData\Breeze\logs\agent.log" -Wait
```

Common symptoms of AV interference:

| Symptom | Likely Cause |
|---|---|
| Agent binary deleted or moved to quarantine | Real-time scan flagging the binary — if it is signed, see [Signed Binaries Flagged as Malware](#signed-binaries-flagged-as-malware) |
| Agent service starts then stops immediately | On-execution scan blocking the process |
| Intermittent WebSocket disconnections | Network inspection blocking persistent connections |
| Script execution failures | Behavior-based detection blocking child processes |
| High CPU usage from agent process | On-access scanning of agent I/O operations |

  If the agent is repeatedly quarantined before you can add exclusions, temporarily disable real-time protection, install the agent, add the exclusions, then re-enable protection.

sections.heading: Minimum Exclusion Summary
sections.text:
For quick reference, here are the minimum exclusions needed per platform:

  **Windows:**
    **Processes:**
    - `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-agent.exe`
    - `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-watchdog.exe`
    - `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-user-helper.exe`
    - `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-desktop-helper.exe`
    - `C:\Program Files\Breeze\breeze-backup.exe`
    - `C:\Program Files\Breeze Helper\breeze-helper.exe`

    **Directories:**
    - `C:\Program Files\Breeze\`
    - `C:\Program Files\Breeze Helper\`
    - `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\`

  **macOS:**
    **Processes:**
    - `/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent` (most Macs)
    - `/Library/Breeze/bin/breeze-agent` (Macs where the agent has moved -- see [macOS Permissions](/agents/macos-permissions/#agent-path-usrlocalbin-or-librarybreezebin))
    - `/Applications/Breeze Helper.app/Contents/MacOS/breeze-helper`

    **Directories:**
    - `/Library/Breeze/bin/` (only if the agent runs from there)
    - `/Library/Application Support/Breeze/`
    - `/Applications/Breeze Helper.app/`

  **Linux:**
    **Processes:**
    - `/usr/local/bin/breeze-agent`

    **Directories:**
    - `/etc/breeze/`
    - `/var/log/breeze/`

title: Binary Distribution
description: How Breeze serves agent and viewer downloads. Covers GitHub Releases mode, local disk with optional S3 offload, and the release manifest trust root.

sections.text: Breeze serves agent binaries and viewer installers through its own API. The download source is configurable via `BINARY_SOURCE`, so downloads work regardless of how you deploy.

sections.heading: Binary Source Modes
sections.text:
Set `BINARY_SOURCE` to control where downloads come from:

| Mode | Description | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| `github` (default) | Agents download directly from GitHub Releases CDN | Most deployments |
| `local` | Serve from disk, with optional S3 offload | Distribute binaries from your own infrastructure |

sections.heading: GitHub Mode (Default)
sections.text:
No local binaries needed. Download requests redirect to GitHub Releases:

```
GET /api/v1/agents/download/linux/amd64
→ 302 https://github.com/lanternops/breeze/releases/download/v0.11.3/breeze-agent-linux-amd64
```

The release version is determined by `BINARY_VERSION` or `BREEZE_VERSION`. If neither is set, redirects to the `latest` release.

  **The pinned release has to be published on GitHub, not merely tagged.** Boot-time sync asks for that exact release; if it does not exist yet -- for example your server images rolled ahead of the public release -- the sync fails loudly, registers no agent binaries for that version, and deliberately does *not* fall back to `latest`. Agents then get a 404 when they try to download. The API still starts, and the log line tells you the fix: set `BINARY_VERSION` to the last published release until the newer one is out.

The repository itself is configurable: `BINARY_GITHUB_REPOSITORY` (default
`lanternops/breeze`) controls where downloads redirect and where release
sync reads from. Self-hosters who [sign their own agent
packages](/deploy/sign-your-own-packages/) point this at their signing
repository and set `RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS` to their own
manifest key.

On startup, the API calls GitHub's Releases API to register the current version's checksums in the `agent_versions` table, so agents know when a new version is available.

  In both modes, registering a release also promotes it to the fleet upgrade target by default — and boot-time sync only registers the release matching your own `BREEZE_VERSION`/`BINARY_VERSION`, never a newer public release. Set `AGENT_AUTO_PROMOTE=false` to register binaries without promoting them, then promote explicitly once you've verified — see [Controlled agent fleet rollout](/deploy/upgrades/#controlled-agent-fleet-rollout).

#### Manifest trust root

In production, GitHub mode requires the `RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS` env var. This is the base64 SPKI of the Ed25519 public key that signs our release manifests. The API verifies every fetched manifest against this key before trusting its checksums, so a compromised GitHub release alone can't deliver tampered binaries.

For the official Breeze releases, use the published trust anchor:

```bash
RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS=yzx8ftmcls6uBetFC5SYnZhBo+cbur3IX50TbBthTso=
```

This is a public key (also embedded in the agent and CI), so it is safe to commit. Only override it if you build and sign your own binaries. The API refuses to start in production without it. During a signing-key rotation you can trust multiple keys at once by comma-separating them (`RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS=old,new`).

**Rotation on the server doesn't retire trust on agents:**
  Comma-separating keys makes the *server* trust both. Each agent still only
  trusts the key(s) it pinned at enrollment and keeps trusting a retired key
  indefinitely — there's no remote revocation yet. Treat rotation as a fleet
  re-enrollment: see [Key
  rotation](/deploy/sign-your-own-packages/#key-rotation).

#### Unsigned signing inputs

Official releases also publish `*-unsigned` build outputs with manifest entries marked `intendedUse: "signing-input"` and `platformTrust: "none"`. These exist solely as inputs for self-signing and are never registrable or downloadable through the API.

Manifest entries for the Windows assets that *are* Authenticode-signed (the Viewer and Helper installers) additionally record which certificate authority signed them, so the provider behind a given build is auditable from the signed manifest itself.

macOS package entries record `signingIdentity` and `signingTeamId`. The release
workflow adds these fields only after `pkgutil` reports the exact expected
Developer ID Installer leaf identity and Apple Team ID for those package bytes.

sections.heading: Local Mode
sections.text:
Binaries are served from disk. The API reads from these directories:

| Variable | Default | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `AGENT_BINARY_DIR` | `./agent/bin` | Agent binaries (e.g. `breeze-agent-linux-amd64`) |
| `VIEWER_BINARY_DIR` | `./viewer/bin` | Viewer installers (e.g. `breeze-viewer-macos.dmg`) |
| `HELPER_BINARY_DIR` | `AGENT_BINARY_DIR` | Helper binaries (e.g. `breeze-helper-windows.msi`). When unset it uses the same directory as `AGENT_BINARY_DIR` (v0.120.0+; earlier releases used `./agent/bin` regardless of `AGENT_BINARY_DIR`). The bundled `docker-compose.yml` overrides this to `/data/binaries/helper`, alongside the other two directories under the shared `binaries` volume. |

macOS agent packages and `Breeze Installer.app.zip` are privileged installers.
Local mode serves them only when the release's original
`release-artifact-manifest.json` and `.ed25519` signature are staged at the
parent of `AGENT_BINARY_DIR` and verify with
`RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS`. A deployment-generated manifest that
merely signs whatever bytes happen to be on the volume is not a source-authenticity
substitute.

Breeze Assist (Helper) installers are verified the same way, but always against
the public release's manifest entry (`edition: "self-host"`, whatever
`BINARY_EDITION` is): the API looks for the manifest pair in `HELPER_BINARY_DIR`
first, then, on a self-host deployment, at its parent. A deployment with
`BINARY_EDITION=hosted` must stage the public release's manifest pair inside
`HELPER_BINARY_DIR`; it never falls back to the manifest at the volume root.

On startup, the API:
1. Scans `AGENT_BINARY_DIR` for agent binaries
2. Computes SHA-256 checksums and registers each binary in the `agent_versions` table
3. Marks them as the latest version
4. If S3 is configured, syncs both directories to your S3 bucket

  If the API detects a version mismatch between the binaries volume and `BREEZE_VERSION` (e.g. the init container wasn't refreshed during an upgrade), it automatically falls back to GitHub Releases so agents still get the correct binary.

sections.heading: Docker Compose Setup
sections.text:
The `docker-compose.yml` includes a **binaries init container** that bundles agent and viewer binaries into a shared volume:

```yaml
services:
  binaries-init:
    image: ${BREEZE_BINARIES_IMAGE_REF:?Set BREEZE_BINARIES_IMAGE_REF to a digest-pinned image ref}
    pull_policy: always
    volumes:
      - binaries:/target
    restart: "no"

  api:
    volumes:
      - binaries:/data/binaries:ro
    environment:
      BINARY_SOURCE: ${BINARY_SOURCE:-github}
      AGENT_BINARY_DIR: /data/binaries/agent
      VIEWER_BINARY_DIR: /data/binaries/viewer
      HELPER_BINARY_DIR: /data/binaries/helper
depends_on:
      binaries-init:
```
