sections.heading: Background retention sweeps
sections.text:
Breeze prunes its own operational tables nightly so a long-running instance does not accumulate delivery queues and diagnostic history forever. Every one of these is optional — the defaults are sensible and nothing needs setting on a normal deployment. Each sweep runs in batches so it never holds a long transaction; raise `*_MAX_BATCHES` only if a sweep repeatedly stops before it has caught up.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `TICKET_OUTBOX_RETENTION_DAYS` | `14` | Days to keep delivered or exhausted ticket-email delivery records, clamped to 1–365 |
| `TICKET_OUTBOX_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `5000` | Rows deleted per batch |
| `TICKET_OUTBOX_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `50` | Maximum batches per nightly run |
| `INTENT_OUTBOX_RETENTION_DAYS` | `14` | Days to keep delivered approval/action-intent delivery records, clamped to 1–365 |
| `INTENT_OUTBOX_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `5000` | Rows deleted per batch |
| `INTENT_OUTBOX_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `50` | Maximum batches per nightly run |
| `METRIC_ANOMALY_INCIDENT_RETENTION_DAYS` | `14` | Days to keep resolved metric-anomaly incidents, clamped to 1–365 |
| `METRIC_ANOMALY_INCIDENT_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `5000` | Rows deleted per batch |
| `METRIC_ANOMALY_INCIDENT_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `50` | Maximum batches per nightly run |
| `AGENT_LOG_RETENTION_DAYS` | `7` | Days to keep uploaded agent diagnostic logs, clamped to 1–365 |
| `AGENT_LOG_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `10000` | Rows deleted per batch |
| `AGENT_LOG_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `200` | Maximum batches per nightly run |
| `AI_INVOCATIONS_RETENTION_DAYS` | `400` | Days to keep AI invocation ledger rows, capped at 3650 |
| `AI_INVOCATIONS_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `5000` | Rows deleted per batch |
| `AI_INVOCATIONS_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `200` | Maximum batches per daily run |
| `LLM_EGRESS_EVENTS_RETENTION_DAYS` | `90` | Days to keep raw LLM egress audit rows before they are folded into per-org daily summaries, capped at 3650 |
| `LLM_EGRESS_EVENTS_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `5000` | Rows folded per batch |
| `LLM_EGRESS_EVENTS_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `200` | Maximum batches per daily run |
| `CHANGE_LOG_RETENTION_DAYS` | `90` | Days to keep processed device change-log entries, clamped to 1–365 |
| `CHANGE_LOG_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `10000` | Rows deleted per batch |
| `CHANGE_LOG_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `200` | Maximum batches per nightly run |
| `IP_HISTORY_RETENTION_DAYS` | `90` | Days to keep device IP-address history, clamped to 1–365 |
| `IP_HISTORY_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `10000` | Rows deleted per batch |
| `IP_HISTORY_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `200` | Maximum batches per nightly run |
| `RESTORE_POINT_ATTEMPT_RETENTION_DAYS` | `90` | Days to keep System Restore checkpoint attempts (the device's System Restore tab), clamped to 1–365. An attempt still awaiting the device is kept until its command can no longer report back, whatever this is set to |
| `RESTORE_POINT_ATTEMPT_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `5000` | Rows deleted per batch |
| `RESTORE_POINT_ATTEMPT_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `50` | Maximum batches per sweep, per nightly run |
| `WEBHOOK_DELIVERY_RETENTION_DAYS` | `90` | Days to keep delivered and failed webhook delivery records, clamped to 1–365. Pending and retrying deliveries are never deleted. Runs daily at 22:13 UTC; the first run after upgrading to v0.124.0 removes every delivered or failed record older than the window |
| `WEBHOOK_DELIVERY_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `1000` | Rows deleted per batch |
| `WEBHOOK_DELIVERY_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `100` | Maximum batches per nightly run |
| `DNS_SECURITY_RETENTION_DAYS_DEFAULT` | `90` | Days to keep DNS security events and daily statistics for an integration that has no `retentionDays` of its own, clamped to 1–365. Runs daily at 22:18 UTC; the first run after upgrading removes every event and statistic older than the window. See [DNS Security](/features/dns-security/#data-retention) |
| `DNS_SECURITY_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `5000` | Rows deleted per batch (also used by the background integration delete) |
| `DNS_SECURITY_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `400` | Maximum batches per table, per integration, per nightly run (and per background-delete job before it re-queues itself) |
| `PAM_EVIDENCE_RETENTION_ENABLED` | on when empty | **v0.124.0+.** Nightly deletion of PAM request chains on **held organization-merge shells** only, never on a live organization, so a hold can release once its evidence has aged out. `false` skips the job |
| `PAM_EVIDENCE_RETENTION_DAYS` | `400` | Days a held shell's PAM evidence is kept, measured from its newest activity. Values below 30 are clamped to 30 |
| `AI_TOOL_OUTPUT_RETENTION_CRON` | `33 4 * * *` | **v0.124.0+.** When the nightly AI tool-output scrub runs (UTC). The window itself is not set here: it is the per-partner (and per-organization) **Keep AI tool outputs for** setting under AI Features, 30 days by default and blank for "keep forever". See [AI](/features/ai/) |
| `AI_TOOL_OUTPUT_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `1000` | Rows replaced per batch, per organization and table |
| `AI_TOOL_OUTPUT_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `50` | Maximum batches per organization and table, per nightly run |
| `SNMP_METRICS_RETENTION_DAYS` | `7` | Days to keep raw SNMP-polled metrics, clamped to 1–365 |
| `SNMP_METRICS_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `10000` | Rows deleted per batch |
| `SNMP_METRICS_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `200` | Maximum batches per nightly run |
| `PROCESS_SAMPLE_RETENTION_DAYS` | `7` | Days to keep per-process monitoring samples, clamped to 1–14. Not batch/max-batches tunable — this sweep loops in fixed 10,000-row batches until caught up. |
| `SERVICE_PROCESS_CHECK_RESULTS_RETENTION_DAYS` | `14` | Days to keep service/process watch check results, clamped to 1–365. Not batch/max-batches tunable — same fixed-batch-loop shape as the process-sample sweep above. |
| `RELIABILITY_HISTORY_RETENTION_DAYS` | `120` | Days to keep device reliability-scoring history, floored at 30 |
| `RELIABILITY_HISTORY_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `10000` | Rows deleted per batch |
| `RELIABILITY_HISTORY_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `50` | Maximum batches per nightly run |
| `ML_OUTPUT_RETENTION_DAYS` | `365` | Days to keep stored ML model outputs, floored at 30 |
| `ML_OUTPUT_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `5000` | Rows deleted per batch |
| `ML_OUTPUT_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `50` | Maximum batches per nightly run |
| `USER_RISK_RETENTION_DAYS` | `90` | Days to keep resolved user-risk signal history, floored at 30 |
| `USER_RISK_RETENTION_BATCH_SIZE` | `5000` | Rows deleted per batch |
| `USER_RISK_RETENTION_MAX_BATCHES` | `50` | Maximum batches per nightly run |

Audit-log retention is **not** set here — it is a per-organization policy an operator saves in the app. See [Audit Logs → Retention](/reference/audit-logs/#retention-policies).

sections.heading: Metric history retention (`metric_rollups`)
sections.text:
Device history charts, capacity trends, AI performance tools and anomaly detection read the `metric_rollups` table. It stores each metric at three resolutions: 5-minute, hourly and daily buckets. Each resolution has its own retention window, and each month of data is stored as one partition per resolution. When a resolution's window passes a whole month, the maintenance job drops that month's partition for the resolution. Dropping a partition returns its disk space to the operating system immediately. No row-by-row `DELETE` is involved, and no `VACUUM FULL` is needed.

| Variable | Default | Minimum | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `METRIC_ROLLUP_5M_RETENTION_DAYS` | `90` | `30` | Days to keep 5-minute buckets. About 92% of the table, so this window sets most of its size. |
| `METRIC_ROLLUP_HOURLY_RETENTION_DAYS` | `548` | `365` | Days to keep hourly buckets. Raised to at least the 5-minute window. |
| `METRIC_ROLLUP_DAILY_RETENTION_DAYS` | `1095` | `730` | Days to keep daily buckets. Raised to at least the hourly window. Past this, the whole month is dropped. |
| `METRIC_ROLLUP_MAINTENANCE_CRON` | `13 3 * * *` | — | When the daily maintenance job runs (partition creation, retention, compaction). |
| `METRIC_ROLLUP_MAINTENANCE_ENABLED` | `true` | — | Set to `false` to stop the job. Retention then stops too, and the table grows without limit. |
| `METRIC_ROLLUP_PARTITION_MONTHS_AHEAD` | `3` | `1` | How many months of partitions to create in advance. |
| `METRIC_ROLLUP_DELETE_BATCH_SIZE` | `5000` | `100` | Batch size for the one remaining row delete, on `metric_rollups_default`. That partition only holds rows written for a month that had no partition, and is normally empty. |

Values below the minimum are raised to the minimum. Retention runs at whole-month granularity: a month is dropped once all of it is older than the window. With the 90-day default, you keep between 90 and about 120 days of 5-minute data. Disk use for `metric_rollups` levels off once each window has filled.

#### Upgrading an existing install

Before this change, each month was one partition that held all three resolutions. 5-minute rows were removed by a capped `DELETE`, which never gave the space back. On upgrade:

- The migration converts empty pre-created future months to the new per-resolution layout. New data lands in the new layout from the next month onwards.
- Months that already hold data keep the old layout and keep working. Once a month's 5-minute data is past `METRIC_ROLLUP_5M_RETENTION_DAYS`, the maintenance job rewrites it. The job copies only the hourly and daily rows, about 8% of the month, into the new layout, then drops the old table. That frees the month's whole footprint, including the dead space left by the old deletes.
- To reclaim space sooner, lower `METRIC_ROLLUP_5M_RETENTION_DAYS`, down to the minimum of 30, and restart. The next maintenance run compacts every older month.

Each compaction runs in its own transaction and only blocks writes to the month being rewritten; reads continue throughout. The final switch takes a short exclusive lock on `metric_rollups`, `devices` and `organizations`, waits at most 5 seconds for it, and only changes catalog entries. If it cannot get the lock in time it rolls back, and the next nightly run retries it. A failed step fails the `metric-rollup-maintenance` job with the month named, so it shows up in job monitoring.

sections.heading: Audit chain
sections.text:
Two nightly jobs protect the tamper-evident audit chain described in [Audit Logs → Tamper Evidence](/reference/audit-logs/#tamper-evidence). The verifier (04:15 UTC) re-checks the chain. It is bounded rather than walking the whole table every night. The anchor job (04:45 UTC) records each organization's chain head in the append-only `audit_chain_anchors` table, so a chain rebuilt after rows were deleted is caught. Both jobs are on by default.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `AUDIT_CHAIN_VERIFY_ENABLED` | `true` | Set to `false` to turn nightly verification off. From v0.110.0 this also stops a sweep that is already running, not just the schedule — previously, restarting the API with the flag off could hand the in-flight sweep to the fresh container and re-run it from the beginning |
| `AUDIT_CHAIN_VERIFY_MODE` | `incremental` | `incremental` verifies new rows since the last anchor plus one rolling slice of history per night. Set to `full` to restore the old whole-table walk — expect substantially more database I/O |
| `AUDIT_CHAIN_VERIFY_RESCAN_SLICES` | `30` | How many nightly slices the historical portion of the chain is divided into. At the default, every historical row is re-verified at least once a month |
| `AUDIT_CHAIN_ANCHOR_ENABLED` | `true` | Set to `false` to stop scheduling the daily anchor job. Leave it on: the anchor is the only check that catches a chain rebuilt after a `DELETE`. |
| `AUDIT_ANCHOR_SIGNING_KEY` | — | Signs each anchor with Ed25519. The value is a **base64-encoded 32-byte seed**. When unset, anchors are still written but unsigned: `signature` and `signing_key_id` are `NULL`. A value that does not decode to exactly 32 bytes makes every anchor write fail and is logged as an error. See [Anchor signing](#anchor-signing) below. |
| `AUDIT_ADMIN_DATABASE_URL` | — | `postgres://` URL for a `breeze_audit_admin` login, used only by audit retention. This keeps the delete permission off the API's request connection. When unset, retention falls back to the legacy shared-credential path and the API logs a `SECURITY` warning at boot. Set the role's password first (`ALTER ROLE breeze_audit_admin PASSWORD '…'`). The full runbook is in `apps/api/migrations/2026-06-11-e-audit-retention-revoke-breeze-app.sql`. |

Up to and including v0.119.0, the shipped compose files did not pass these six variables to the API container, so setting them in `.env` had no effect. If you set any of them before, they take effect once you upgrade, so check them first.

#### Anchor signing

An unsigned anchor guards against the API's own database role, which can insert anchors but never change or delete them. It does not guard against someone who can write to the database directly, because that person can also rewrite the anchors. A signed anchor that you keep **outside** the database closes that gap: nobody can forge one without the seed, and the seed is not stored in the database.

1. Generate a seed and add it to `.env`:

```bash
   echo "AUDIT_ANCHOR_SIGNING_KEY=$(openssl rand -base64 32)" >> .env
```

   Treat it like `JWT_SECRET`. Keep a copy somewhere other than the server, because a new seed means a new public key.

2. Restart the API (and the worker, if you run one). At boot the API logs the key id and the public key:

```text
   [AuditChainAnchor] Anchor signing enabled: keyId=anchor-1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b publicKey(SPKI DER, base64)=MCowBQYDK2VwAyEA…
```

   Record the public key with whatever verifies your anchors. You can read it again from any later boot log.

3. Keep the anchors off the server. Each anchor is also written to the API container's stdout as one JSON line tagged `"evt":"audit_chain_anchor"`. The line contains `canonical` (the exact signed message), `signature` (base64) and `signingKeyId`. Breeze does not ship these lines anywhere by itself. To keep a copy outside the server, forward the API container's stdout with a log shipper such as Vector, Fluent Bit or promtail.

The in-database check (`audit_chain_verify_anchor`) compares chain heads only and does not read the signature. The signature is useful only for a copy you keep somewhere else. To check a forwarded line, verify `signature` over the `canonical` string with the public key you recorded:

```js
// verify-anchor.mjs: node verify-anchor.mjs '<anchor JSON line>' '<public key, base64>'
import { createPublicKey, verify } from 'node:crypto';

const [line, publicKeyB64] = process.argv.slice(2);
const anchor = JSON.parse(line);
const key = createPublicKey({ key: Buffer.from(publicKeyB64, 'base64'), format: 'der', type: 'spki' });
const ok = verify(null, Buffer.from(anchor.canonical, 'utf8'), key, Buffer.from(anchor.signature, 'base64'));
console.log(ok ? 'valid' : 'INVALID');
```

Verify the `canonical` string exactly as it was forwarded. Do not rebuild it from a database row, because the timestamp formatting can differ. A line with `"signed":false` has no signature. This happens when no key was set, or when the chain head moved while the anchor was being signed. The next day's anchor covers that case.

A signature proves that the anchor came from a server that held the seed. It does not protect you if the whole host is compromised, because the seed is in the API's environment. If you change the key, older anchors keep their old `signingKeyId`, so keep the old public keys to check older anchors.

sections.heading: Event-loop lag monitor
sections.text:
The API samples its own event-loop delay so that a stalled main thread shows up
as a stalled main thread. Without it, a stall surfaces as unrelated downstream
errors — most confusingly a Postgres `write CONNECT_TIMEOUT <host>:<port>`, which
names the database even though the database and the network were both healthy.
The monitor runs by default; you do not need to set any of these.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `EVENT_LOOP_MONITOR_INTERVAL_MS` | `1000` | Sampling interval for event-loop delay. Values above `EVENT_LOOP_STARVATION_WARN_MS` leave a blind spot one interval wide — stalls shorter than one interval cannot be observed and are reported as cause `unknown`. The API logs a startup warning if you configure it that way. |
| `EVENT_LOOP_STARVATION_WARN_MS` | `1000` | Lag at or above which a reading counts as starvation. Drives the `[event-loop] Main thread blocked…` warning and the `breeze_nodejs_eventloop_starved` gauge. |
| `EVENT_LOOP_MONITOR_DISABLED` | — | Set to `1`, `true`, `yes`, or `on` to turn the monitor off. With it off, every Postgres `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` is classified `unknown`, because starvation can be neither ruled in nor out. |

At startup the API prints one line stating whether it can see its own loop and at
what settings — `[event-loop] Lag monitor started (interval …ms, warn threshold
…ms, CONNECT_TIMEOUT attribution threshold …ms)`, or a warning if the monitor is
disabled. The two thresholds can differ: `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` attribution caps its
own threshold at the 10s connect budget, so raising the warn threshold above 10s
cannot cause a timeout to be mis-attributed.

Lag is exported on `/metrics/scrape` (see [Monitoring Stack](/monitoring/stack/#event-loop-metrics)).
It is deliberately **not** reported by `/health/ready`: that endpoint is
unauthenticated, and a live load gradient plus the configured threshold would let
an unauthenticated prober measure whether its own traffic is starving the
instance. Readiness is also not gated on lag — starvation is a load symptom, and
failing readiness under load would shift traffic onto peers and starve those too.

sections.heading: Agent admission control
sections.text:
When the API falls behind — its event loop is slow, or requests queue for a
database connection — it can refuse low-priority agent work before that work
costs anything, and pace how fast agents reconnect their WebSockets. Refused
requests get `503` with a `Retry-After`, which every agent since v0.64.3 honours;
the agent keeps the data where it would on any failed send. Heartbeats, command
results, event logs, token rotation and uninstall are never refused.

`observe` is the default: the API computes everything and counts what it
*would* refuse (`breeze_admission_decisions_total{outcome="would_shed"}`) but
refuses nothing. Switch to `enforce` once those counters look right for your
fleet. `off` disables it. `breeze_admission_rise_suppressed_total` counts the
short spikes that would have raised the level if it did not require
sustained pressure.

Any database pool-acquire timeout or RLS-prologue timeout in the last 30
seconds holds the level at 2 or higher and blocks recovery below it. Only
agent WebSocket requests that carry `Upgrade: websocket` are paced; other
requests to the WebSocket path are not counted against the connection budget.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `BREEZE_ADMISSION_MODE` | `observe` | `off`, `observe` or `enforce`. |
| `BREEZE_ADMISSION_LAG_MS` | `200,250,600` | Median event-loop lag (ms) that raises the level to 1, 2 and 3. |
| `BREEZE_ADMISSION_DB_WAIT_MS` | `150,200,600` | Time requests wait for a database connection (ms) that raises the level to 1, 2 and 3. |
| `BREEZE_ADMISSION_RISE_TICKS` | `3` | Consecutive one-second checks a signal must stay over a threshold before the level rises (1–10). A single blip never raises the level. |
| `BREEZE_ADMISSION_LEVEL1_HOLD_MS` | `5000` | How long level 1 stays on once both signals are below 60 % of their level-1 thresholds (1000–60000). Levels 2 and 3 step down after 15 seconds. |
| `BREEZE_ADMISSION_EMERGENCY_MS` | `1000` | A single stall, or a database wait, this long jumps straight to level 3, without waiting for `BREEZE_ADMISSION_RISE_TICKS`. |
| `BREEZE_ADMISSION_BULK_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` | `15` | Inventory-type uploads processed at once. Applies in `enforce` mode only; `observe` counts but never refuses. |
| `BREEZE_ADMISSION_WS_RATE_PER_SEC` | `10` | Agent WebSocket connections accepted per second at level 0 (halved at 1, a fifth at 2, a twentieth at 3). |
| `BREEZE_ADMISSION_WS_BURST` | `20` | How many WebSocket connections can arrive at once before pacing starts. |
| `BREEZE_ADMISSION_WS_MAX_SETUPS` | `8` | WebSocket connections being set up at the same time. |

Level 1 refuses inventory-type uploads (hardware, software, disks, network,
process samples, agent logs, UniFi). Level 2 also refuses periodic status
uploads (security status, sessions, patches, monitoring results). Level 3 only
paces WebSockets harder — if an instance stays at level 3 it needs more
capacity, not more shedding. Invalid values fall back to the default with a
startup warning; they never stop the API from booting.

sections.heading: Database pool-health watchdog
sections.text:
The API's Postgres driver (postgres.js) can leave a pooled connection permanently
unable to reconnect if that connection's socket dies while a write is still
buffered. The affected pool slot then retries forever, failing every time with
`write CONNECT_TIMEOUT` — **against a database that is completely healthy**. Slots
are lost one at a time, so the pool decays over hours until most queries fail at
connect. Nothing in the API can repair it: only restarting the API process
recovers the pool.

The watchdog exists because that failure is very easy to misread as a database
outage. When the `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` rate breaches the threshold, it opens **one
brand-new connection** to the same database, outside the pool. A fresh connection
is unaffected by the defect, so the result separates the two causes:

- the fresh connection **succeeds** → the database is fine and the **pool** is
  broken. Restart the API.
- the fresh connection **also fails** → a genuine database, network, TLS, or auth
  fault. Restarting the API will not help.

The full verdict — with counts, rates and probe timing — is written to the
container log. Sentry receives a throttled event carrying the
`db_pool_health_verdict` tag only; Breeze strips message text and structured
extras from every outgoing Sentry event, so treat Sentry as the alert channel
and the log or `/metrics` as the detail. The numbers are exported on
`/metrics/scrape`:

| Series | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `breeze_db_pool_health{verdict="…"}` | `1` for the current verdict, `0` for the others. Verdicts are `below-threshold`, `pool-degraded`, `database-unreachable`, `unknown`. |
| `breeze_db_connect_timeouts_total{cause="…"}` | Connect timeouts by diagnosed cause (`connectivity`, `event-loop-starvation`, `unknown`). |
| `breeze_db_connect_timeout_rate_per_min` | The rate the watchdog evaluates. |
| `breeze_db_pool_health_last_check_timestamp_seconds` | When the last evaluation completed. `0` = never. |
| `breeze_db_pool_health_check_failures` | Evaluations that threw before producing a verdict. |
| `breeze_db_pool_health_probe_close_failures` | Probe clients whose close failed — each a possible leaked connection. |
| `breeze_db_pool_admission_permits` / `_in_use` / `_waiting` | Request-transaction permits configured, held and waited for. `-1` when the process has no request pool. |
| `breeze_db_pool_admission_abandoned` / `_effective_permits` | Permits held by transactions abandoned at their connection-setup deadline or after the pool-acquire budget expired (see `[db-pool-acquire]` and `[db-wedged-backend]` logs), and the permits actually available (`permits − abandoned`). |
| `breeze_db_pool_admission_cancelled_waiters_total` | Requests that gave up waiting for a permit before ever reaching the database. |
| `breeze_db_pool_admission_abandoned_total`, `breeze_db_pool_admission_abandoned_returned_total{how="…"}` | Permits abandoned, and returned by `rollback` (the slow statement finished) or `connection-closed` (a wedged connection was reclaimed). |
| `breeze_db_pool_acquire_timeouts_total{timer="…"}`, `breeze_db_prologue_deadline_expiries_total{timer="…"}` | Pool-acquire and connection-setup timeouts; `timer="late"` means the API's event loop was stalled at the deadline. |

**Alert on `breeze_db_pool_health{verdict="pool-degraded"} == 1`.** There is
deliberately no `healthy` verdict: the quiet one is `below-threshold`, because
the underlying count only sees timeouts that reach an error handler and the
watchdog never observes pool slot occupancy. It can tell you something is wrong;
it cannot certify that nothing is. For the same reason, all verdict series read
`0` before the first evaluation and after a failed one — never infer health from
the absence of a bad verdict, and pair any alert with a freshness check on
`breeze_db_pool_health_last_check_timestamp_seconds`.

The watchdog runs by default; you do not need to set any of these.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `DB_POOL_HEALTH_INTERVAL_MS` | `60000` | How often the watchdog evaluates. Floored at 5000. |
| `DB_POOL_HEALTH_WINDOW_MS` | `300000` | Trailing window the `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` count is taken over. Floored at 30000. |
| `DB_POOL_HEALTH_MIN_TIMEOUTS` | `10` | Timeouts within the window that trigger the fresh-connection probe. Below this, no probe runs and no connection is opened. |
| `DB_POOL_HEALTH_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS` | `5000` | Hard bound on the probe. Keep it well under the interval so a slow probe cannot overlap the next tick. |
| `DB_POOL_HEALTH_CAPTURE_THROTTLE_MS` | `900000` | Minimum gap between Sentry captures of the same verdict. A degraded pool stays degraded until restart, so an unthrottled capture would report it every tick. `0` disables the throttle. Console logging is never throttled. |
| `DB_POOL_HEALTH_DISABLED` | — | Set to `1`, `true`, `yes`, or `on` to turn the watchdog off. With it off, a poisoned pool decays silently until someone notices the 503s. |

Like event-loop lag, these figures are kept off the unauthenticated
`/health/ready` for the same reason — they describe how close the instance is to
falling over.

sections.heading: Redis memory watchdog
sections.text:
**v0.117.0+.** The bundled Redis runs with `maxmemory-policy noeviction` (size set
by `REDIS_MAXMEMORY`, default `256mb`): when it fills, writes fail loudly rather
than silently evicting queue or session data. Before this watchdog, the first
sign of a full Redis was a failed login or a stuck queue. The API now reads
Redis memory usage on an interval and logs a warning (and reports to Sentry,
throttled) once usage crosses a threshold, so you can raise `REDIS_MAXMEMORY`
ahead of an incident. It only observes; it never changes the Redis eviction
policy. If Redis has no `maxmemory` limit at all, it logs that on every check
instead, because no usage ratio can be computed.

It publishes these series on `/metrics`:

| Metric | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `breeze_redis_used_memory_bytes` | Redis `used_memory` from the last check. |
| `breeze_redis_maxmemory_bytes` | Redis `maxmemory`; `0` means unbounded. |
| `breeze_redis_memory_used_ratio` | `used_memory / maxmemory`. `-1` when Redis is unbounded, or when the last check failed or has not run yet. |
| `breeze_redis_memory_last_check_timestamp_seconds` | When the last successful check completed. `0` = never. |
| `breeze_redis_memory_check_failures` | Checks that failed before producing a reading, since process start. |
| `breeze_redis_memory_check_skipped_total` | Ticks skipped because the previous check was still running. |

Pair any alert on the ratio with a freshness check on
`breeze_redis_memory_last_check_timestamp_seconds`. A broken watchdog reports
`-1`, not a stale healthy value.

The watchdog runs by default; you do not need to set any of these.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `REDIS_MEMORY_MONITOR_INTERVAL_MS` | `60000` | How often Redis memory is checked. |
| `REDIS_MEMORY_WARN_RATIO` | `0.8` | Usage ratio (greater than `0`, at most `1`) at which the warning fires. Any other value falls back to `0.8`. |
| `REDIS_MEMORY_CAPTURE_THROTTLE_MS` | `900000` | Minimum gap between Sentry reports of the same condition. `0` disables the throttle. Console logging is not throttled. |
| `REDIS_MEMORY_MONITOR_DISABLED` | — | Set to `true` to turn the watchdog off. |

sections.heading: Readiness probe tuning
sections.text:
`/ready` and `/health/ready` answer a real readiness question — are Postgres,
Redis and the background consumers this process needs actually up — as distinct
from `/health`, which is liveness only and answers 200 well before that. Point a
load balancer or Compose healthcheck that should hold traffic back at `/ready`.
See [Health Monitoring](/monitoring/health/) for the response shapes and for the
worker container's own variant of the endpoint.

Neither of these needs setting; the defaults suit every deployment we know of.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `READINESS_CACHE_TTL_MS` | `5000` | How long a readiness verdict is reused before the probes run again, so a busy load balancer cannot turn a healthcheck into a database workload. Accepted range is `0`–`10000` minus the probe timeout below. |
| `READINESS_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS` | `3000` | Hard bound on each individual Postgres and Redis probe. Clamped to `100`–`5000` — a wedged dependency reports not-ready rather than hanging the healthcheck. |

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `OFFLINE_DETECTOR_WORKER_CONCURRENCY` | `5` | How many offline-sweep jobs the offline detector processes at once. Clamped to `1`–`20`; anything unparseable falls back to `5`. Raise it only if offline detection visibly lags on a very large fleet. |

sections.heading: Sentry
sections.text:
Both API and web Sentry integrations are off by default. Leave the DSN variables blank to disable. See [Error Tracking & Privacy](/security/error-tracking/) for what gets collected and how scrubbing works.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `SENTRY_DSN` | — | API Sentry DSN. Leave blank to disable server-side error tracking. |
| `SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT` | `production` | Sentry environment tag. In a **multi-region** deployment use a region-qualified value (`production-us`, `production-eu`) — a bare `production` on every region makes them indistinguishable in Sentry, and `server_name` is a per-deploy container hash, so nothing else can attribute an error to a region. |
| `SENTRY_RELEASE` | — | Sentry release tag (e.g. git SHA) |
| `SENTRY_TRACES_SAMPLE_RATE` | `0.1` | Sentry performance trace sample rate (0.0-1.0) |
| `SENTRY_PROFILES_SAMPLE_RATE` | — | API performance-profiling sample rate (0.0-1.0). Leave blank to disable profiling. |
| `PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN_WEB` | — | Web Sentry DSN. Leave blank to disable browser error tracking and on-error session replay. Inlined into the web bundle at build time. |
| `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN` | — | Sentry auth token used during the web build to upload source maps. If unset, source map upload is skipped and the build still succeeds. |

sections.heading: Rate Limiting
sections.text:
Most per-endpoint rate limits (MFA, dashboard usage) are fixed in code and not configurable via environment variables. A few are deployment-tunable: the per-org agent cap, which bounds how much traffic a single tenant's fleet can generate even with thousands of agents, plus the account lockout and refresh-token limits on the login path.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `AGENT_ORG_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN` | `600` | **Floor** for the per-organization sliding-window rate limit on agent-authenticated endpoints. The effective ceiling scales with the org's enrolled device count (see `AGENT_ORG_RATE_LIMIT_PER_DEVICE`), so this value only applies to small orgs. Returns `429` with a `Retry-After` derived from the window reset. Not mapped in the stock compose file — to change it, add it to the `api` service `environment:` block as well as `.env`. |
| `AGENT_ORG_RATE_LIMIT_PER_DEVICE` | `12` | Requests per minute allowed per enrolled device when sizing the per-organization ceiling. A steady-state agent uses ~2 req/min, so the default leaves roughly 6x headroom for synchronized bursts, manual scans and command traffic. |
| `AGENT_ORG_RATE_LIMIT_MAX` | `20000` | Hard platform ceiling for the per-organization limit, regardless of device count. Keeps the per-tenant guardrail meaningful for very large fleets. |
| `LOGIN_ACCOUNT_LOCKOUT_MAX` | `5` | Consecutive failed password attempts (keyed per account, not per IP) before the account is locked for the window below. Set to `0` to disable lockout entirely. Not mapped in the stock compose file — add it to the `api` service `environment:` block as well as `.env`. |
| `LOGIN_ACCOUNT_LOCKOUT_WINDOW_SECONDS` | `900` | Lockout duration once `LOGIN_ACCOUNT_LOCKOUT_MAX` is reached. Not mapped in the stock compose file — add it to the `api` service `environment:` block as well as `.env`. |
| `AUTH_REFRESH_RATE_LIMIT` | `60` | Requests per window allowed on `POST /auth/refresh`, keyed per refresh-token family (roughly one browser session chain). |
| `AUTH_REFRESH_RATE_WINDOW_SECONDS` | `60` | Window for `AUTH_REFRESH_RATE_LIMIT`. |

  Earlier `.env.example` files carried `RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS`, `RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS`, `SESSION_MAX_AGE`, and `ENABLE_API_DOCS` entries. None of these were ever read by the API — they are gone from `.env.example` as of v0.99.0 and can be safely deleted from your `.env`.

sections.heading: Agent traffic and ingest budgets
sections.text:
**v0.118.0+.** These limits keep one device, or one organization's fleet, from using more than its share of the API. The defaults sit well above normal fleet traffic, so you do not need to set any of them. None is mapped in the stock Compose files: to change one, add it to `.env` **and** to the `api` service `environment:` block (and the `worker` block if you run the [worker split](/deploy/worker-split/)).

**Agent WebSocket messages.** Each agent connection has a message budget: a burst capacity plus a steady refill rate. Messages over budget are dropped. A connection that keeps sending after this many dropped messages in a row is closed. Command results and update-status messages have their own budgets.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `AGENT_WS_MESSAGE_BUDGET_CAPACITY` | `300` | Burst capacity, in messages, for general agent WebSocket traffic. |
| `AGENT_WS_MESSAGE_BUDGET_REFILL_PER_SECOND` | `60` | Messages per second added back to the general budget. |
| `AGENT_WS_MESSAGE_BUDGET_CLOSE_THRESHOLD` | `200` | Dropped messages in a row, on any budget, before the connection is closed. |
| `AGENT_WS_COMMAND_RESULT_MESSAGE_BUDGET_CAPACITY` | `600` | Burst capacity for command-result messages. |
| `AGENT_WS_COMMAND_RESULT_MESSAGE_BUDGET_REFILL_PER_SECOND` | `120` | Refill rate for command-result messages. |
| `AGENT_WS_UPDATE_STATUS_MESSAGE_BUDGET_CAPACITY` | general capacity | Burst capacity for update-status messages. |
| `AGENT_WS_UPDATE_STATUS_MESSAGE_BUDGET_REFILL_PER_SECOND` | general refill rate | Refill rate for update-status messages. |

**Daily ingest budgets.** Agent log, event-log and change-log uploads are counted per device and per organization per day. An upload over budget is refused with `429`.

| Variable | Default |
|---|---|
| `AGENT_LOG_MAX_ROWS_PER_DEVICE_PER_DAY` | `2000000` |
| `AGENT_LOG_MAX_BYTES_PER_DEVICE_PER_DAY` | `524288000` (500 MiB) |
| `AGENT_LOG_MAX_ROWS_PER_ORG_PER_DAY` | `20000000` |
| `AGENT_LOG_MAX_BYTES_PER_ORG_PER_DAY` | `5368709120` (5 GiB) |
| `AGENT_EVENTLOG_MAX_BYTES_PER_DEVICE_PER_DAY` | `2147483648` (2 GiB) |
| `AGENT_EVENTLOG_MAX_ROWS_PER_ORG_PER_DAY` | `2000000` |
| `AGENT_EVENTLOG_MAX_BYTES_PER_ORG_PER_DAY` | `10737418240` (10 GiB) |
| `AGENT_CHANGES_MAX_ROWS_PER_DEVICE_PER_DAY` | `500000` |
| `AGENT_CHANGES_MAX_BYTES_PER_DEVICE_PER_DAY` | `209715200` (200 MiB) |
| `AGENT_CHANGES_MAX_ROWS_PER_ORG_PER_DAY` | `5000000` |
| `AGENT_CHANGES_MAX_BYTES_PER_ORG_PER_DAY` | `2147483648` (2 GiB) |

Event-log rows per device are already limited by the event-log policy's hourly rate, so there is no per-device row budget for event logs.

**Other limits.**

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `HELPER_SCREENSHOT_RATE_LIMIT` | `12` | Screenshot uploads per device from Breeze Helper per window. |
| `HELPER_SCREENSHOT_RATE_WINDOW_SECONDS` | `60` | Window for `HELPER_SCREENSHOT_RATE_LIMIT`. |
| `SCREENSHOT_MAX_BYTES` | `1600000` | Largest single screenshot stored. |
| `SCREENSHOT_MAX_PER_DEVICE` | `20` | Stored (unexpired) screenshots per device. |
| `SCREENSHOT_MAX_BYTES_PER_DEVICE` | count × size above | Total stored screenshot bytes per device. |
| `LOG_FORWARDING_MAX_JOB_BYTES` | `1048576` | Largest batch of events one log-forwarding job may carry. |
| `LOG_FORWARDING_MAX_PENDING_PER_ORG` | `2000` | Log-forwarding jobs one organization may have queued at once. A slow destination for one organization no longer holds up the others. |
| `LOG_FORWARDING_MAX_WAITING_GLOBAL` | `10000` | Instance-wide ceiling on waiting log-forwarding jobs. |
| `TENANT_TOOL_MAX_IN_FLIGHT_PER_ORG` | `8` | Concurrent calls one organization (or partner, for partner-owned tools) may have in flight across all its connected tool sources. |
| `TURN_CREDENTIAL_MINT_LIMIT_PER_WINDOW` | `30` | TURN credentials one user may request per window. Over the limit, the request returns `429`. `0` turns the limit off. |
| `TURN_CREDENTIAL_MINT_WINDOW_SECONDS` | `600` | Window for `TURN_CREDENTIAL_MINT_LIMIT_PER_WINDOW`. |
| `PUBLIC_DOWNLOAD_KEY_MAX_TTL_MINUTES` | `1440` (24 h) | Longest lifetime of the short-lived download key an installer link hands out. |

sections.heading: Upgrade and rollout controls
sections.text:
**v0.118.0+.** All optional and not mapped in the stock Compose files; add any you set to the `api` service `environment:` block as well as `.env`.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `BREEZE_LEGACY_ALERTING_SWEEP` | on | Set to `false` to skip converting and retiring leftover legacy alert rules and service/process watches at boot. The API still counts and logs what is left. See the [v0.118.0 upgrade notes](/deploy/upgrades/#v01180--legacy-alerting-retired-network-checks-become-monitors). |
| `AGENT_ROLLBACK_DENYLISTED_VERSIONS` | unset | Comma-separated agent versions that an agent rollback may never target. Unset means no restriction. |
| `AGENT_ROLLBACK_MIN_VERSION` | unset | Lowest agent version a rollback may target. An invalid version is ignored. Unset means no restriction. |
| `EMAIL_DOMAINS_ADOPT_EXISTING_ALLOWLIST` | unset | Comma-separated sending domains that may be adopted when they already exist at the email provider without the `_breeze-verify.<domain>` TXT record. Only needed for a migration. See [Custom Sender Addresses](/deploy/custom-sender-addresses/). |

The four `OFFLINE_DETECTOR_REEVAL_*` variables were removed in v0.118.0. The job that read them was retired with legacy alerting, so you can delete them from `.env`.

sections.heading: Agent connection switches
sections.text:
**v0.123.0+.** Both are server-wide kill switches, on by default and mapped in both shipped Compose files. Each accepts only `true` or `false`; any other value stops the API from booting.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `AGENT_ECH_ENABLED` | `true` | Lets agents that detect an ISP security filter on the TLS port connect with [Encrypted Client Hello](/agents/advanced-install/#encrypted-client-hello-ech). Agents receive the value in their heartbeat response. **Treat `false` as a last resort:** live connections stay up, but the next dial is plain, so a device that can only reach the API over ECH goes offline and cannot receive the setting back until it is on an unfiltered network. |
| `PROMPT_HOST_ENABLED_KINDS` | unset | **v0.125.0+, groundwork.** The on-device prompt kinds the server enables, sent to agents in each heartbeat. Unset uses the built-in list, which is empty in this release, so nothing uses it yet. An explicitly empty value is the kill switch. Mapped in both Compose files as `${PROMPT_HOST_ENABLED_KINDS-default}`, so leaving it out of `.env` keeps the built-in list. |
| `HEARTBEAT_RETAIN_STATE_ENABLED` | `true` | An agent that supports it keeps its current PAM, Breeze Assist and remote-management state on a heartbeat where the server could not decide that setting (for example, a policy lookup failed), instead of being told to turn it off. `false` sends every agent the older heartbeat payload, as an earlier API would. |

sections.heading: Database
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `DB_POOL_MAX` | `30` | Maximum postgres-js connection pool size. Tune up if you see cascading 504s during heartbeat storms; confirm Postgres `max_connections` has headroom (default 100 is fine for a single API replica). |

sections.heading: Remote Sessions & Storage
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `MAX_ACTIVE_REMOTE_SESSIONS_PER_ORG` | `10` | Concurrent remote sessions per org |
| `MAX_ACTIVE_REMOTE_SESSIONS_PER_USER` | `5` | Concurrent remote sessions per user |
| `PATCH_REPORT_STORAGE_PATH` | `./data/patch-reports` | Patch compliance report storage |
| `PATCH_REPORT_RETENTION_DAYS` | `30` | Days a generated patch compliance report file is kept after it completes (minimum `1`). A daily job then removes the file and marks the report `expired`. A value that is not a plain integer falls back to the default. |
| `PATCH_REPORT_ORPHAN_MIN_AGE_MS` | `3600000` (1 hour) | How old a `<uuid>.csv` file in `PATCH_REPORT_STORAGE_PATH` that no report owns (for example, left behind when an organization was erased and the file could not be removed at the time) must be before the daily job removes it. Never below 10 minutes. |
| `TUNNEL_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE` | unset | Serves Network Proxy content from a dedicated origin per tunnel (host mode), in the form `https://{id}.<suffix>`. Unset keeps path mode. The suffix must be on a different registrable domain from every app, API, portal, WebAuthn and CORS origin; a malformed template, or one that shares a registrable domain with any of them, stops the API from booting. Each partner also opts in under **Settings → Partner → Remote Access**. See [Network Proxy Dedicated Origin](/deploy/network-proxy-tunnel-origin/). |
| `TUNNEL_FRAME_ANCESTOR` | origin of `PUBLIC_APP_URL` (else `DASHBOARD_URL`) | Exact `https://` origin allowed to frame tunnel content when `TUNNEL_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE` is set. Boot fails if it is unset and neither default exists. |
| `TUNNEL_SITE_ADDRESS` | `http://tunnel-disabled.invalid` (matches nothing) | Caddy site address for the tunnel domain, for example `*.us.tunnel.example.net, *.*.us.tunnel.example.net` (use `http://` forms behind Cloudflare Tunnel). Must be on a different registrable domain from `CADDY_SITE_ADDRESS`. Never set it empty. |
| `TUNNEL_HOST_SUFFIX` | `tunnel-disabled.invalid` (matches nothing) | Caddy: the bare tunnel suffix (`<region>.<tunnel-domain>`). Tunnel-domain hosts that miss the wildcards get `421` instead of being served as the app. Never set it empty. |
| `TUNNEL_TLS_DIRECTIVE` | empty | Caddy: a full `tls <cert> <key>` line when Caddy terminates TLS for the tunnel domain with your own certificate. |

sections.heading: Rollout Modes
sections.text:
**Required in production** (and when `DEPLOYMENT_ENV=staging`). The API refuses to
boot without them, and the shipped compose files use `${VAR:?}` so the container
stops before it starts. In development they fall back to the defaults shown.

Full explanation of what each one is for: [Rollout Modes & Compatibility Switches](/deploy/rollout-modes/).

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `EVENT_PERMISSION_EPOCH_MODE` | `compat` | `compat` accepts event-WebSocket tickets from pre-upgrade servers; `enforce` rejects them. Move to `enforce` ≥60s after the last old server stops. A malformed value falls back to `enforce` (fails closed). |
| `REMOTE_WS_AUTH_MODE` | `post_upgrade` | `post_upgrade` accepts remote-session tickets minted by pre-upgrade servers; `pre_upgrade` rejects them and applies full authorization before the WebSocket upgrade. Stay on `post_upgrade` until every legacy viewer token has expired. |
| `REMOTE_ACCESS_ADMISSION_MODE` | `open` | Remote-access barrier. `closed` returns `503` for every terminal/desktop/VNC/tunnel endpoint at the proxy. Used during the lease cutover and for maintenance. |
| `REMOTE_WS_REDIS_TOPOLOGY` | `standalone-single-primary` | Attestation that Redis is a single primary with AOF on, `noeviction`, cluster disabled. Only accepted value. Sentinel/Cluster/HA Redis will freeze remote admission by design. |
| `REMOTE_WS_LEGACY_TICKET_WRITER_DRAINED_AT` | — | Timestamp the last pre-upgrade ticket writer stopped. Used to compute the barrier-reopen deadline. |
| `REMOTE_WS_LEGACY_VIEWER_ISSUER_DRAINED_AT` | — | Timestamp the last legacy viewer-token issuer stopped. Gates the move to `pre_upgrade`. |
| `REMOTE_DESKTOP_FENCE_REQUIRED` | `true` | Remote desktop refuses to start (`503 agent_upgrade_required`, "Remote desktop needs an agent update on this device") on any agent that has not declared the durable start/terminal fence capability (`desktopFenceProtocolVersion=1`). Agents v0.114.0 and later declare it. Set `false` only as a temporary opt-out while older agents finish updating; any other value refuses boot. |
| `OAUTH_AUTH_EPOCH_ENFORCE_AFTER` | — | **Required when MCP OAuth is enabled in production/staging.** Absolute UTC timestamp ending the compatibility window for access tokens issued before the live-revocation release. Must be ≥1800s after new token writers start. Choose once; never extend on restart. |

sections.heading: Security Enforcement (opt-in)
sections.text:
These ship **disabled**. Nothing changes on upgrade — each is a separate decision
with its own rollout gate. See [Rollout Modes](/deploy/rollout-modes/).

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `AGENT_MTLS_BINDING_MODE` | `off` | `audit` counts certificate/device binding mismatches without denying; `enforce` denies them. Requires a validating proxy. Never inferred from `NODE_ENV`/`IS_HOSTED`/`CF_MTLS_*`. |
| `MANAGED_SOFTWARE_POLICY_MODE` | `compat` | `enforce` requires an upgraded agent for every managed-software command, public destinations included. Check your not-yet-upgraded device count first — they are denied outright. |
| `AGENT_REQUIRE_MANIFEST_SIGNING_KEY_ID` | `false` | Requires update manifests to carry a signing key ID. Not fleet-wide: older agent builds ignore the pushed value. Only enable once the missing-ID count has been zero for 7 consecutive days. |
| `AUTH_BROWSER_TERMINAL_PREPARATION_ENABLED` | `false` | Enables the terminal/native logout-preparation flow described in [Cloudflare Access trust](/deploy/cloudflare-access-trust/). Validated at boot: must be a boolean (`true`/`false`, `1`/`0`, `yes`/`no`, `on`/`off`) when set. It no longer depends on any other flag. |

**Removed in v0.112.0: `AUTH_BROWSER_TRANSITIONS_ENFORCED`:**
  Browser-session binding — tying an issued session to a browser-generated binding value so a stolen refresh token alone cannot move a session to another browser — is now **always enforced** on every sign-in path (password, SSO, Cloudflare Access, MFA, passkey, refresh, registration, invitation). The rollout switch is gone and is ignored if still present in `.env`; delete the line. There is no configuration that restores the unguarded issuance path. See the [v0.112.0 upgrade notes](/deploy/upgrades/#v01120--windows-msi-fix-security-remediations-bare-metal-recovery).

sections.heading: Feature Flags
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ENABLE_REGISTRATION` | `true` | Allow new user registration |
| `PENDING_ACCOUNT_MEETING_URL` | — | Optional absolute `http(s)` URL to a scheduling page. When set, a partner whose account is still **pending** sees it as a secondary link beside the billing call-to-action on the account-inactive screen, so a partner who cannot complete payment is not left at a dead end. Values that are not `http`/`https` are ignored. |
| `PENDING_ACCOUNT_MEETING_LABEL` | `Book a call with us` | Optional link text for the pending-account booking link above. |
| `ENABLE_2FA` | `true` | Enable two-factor authentication |
| `ENABLE_API_DOCS_UI` | on outside production, off in production | Serve the interactive Swagger UI and OpenAPI spec at `/api/v1/docs`. The UI loads its scripts and styles from unpkg, which is why it defaults off in production. (The former `ENABLE_API_DOCS` variable was never read and has been removed.) |
| `USE_AGENT_SDK` | — | Use Claude Agent SDK for AI chat |
| `PORTAL_STATE_BACKEND` | `memory` | Portal state backend: `memory` or `redis` (auto `redis` in production) |
| `PUBLIC_ENABLE_EDR_INTEGRATIONS` | `false` | Surface the EDR UI: the `/security/edr` fleet page, the device Security-tab EDR panel, and the Security dashboard summary cards. Set `true` at web image build time to enable. |
| `BREEZE_EDR_ACTIONS_ENABLED` | `true` | **v0.123.0+.** Server-wide off switch for EDR response actions (isolate, release, scan). Each EDR connection must also be opted in by a partner admin with MFA, and that is off by default. Empty means on; `false` (or any value that is not a recognised true value) stops new actions after a restart. |
| `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_ENABLED` | `false` | Turns on the Google Workspace identity connector. While off, its screens and AI actions are unavailable. Passed to the API by both Compose files from v0.123.0. |
| `M365_ENABLED` | `false` | Turns on the Microsoft 365 identity connector, as above. Passed to the API by both Compose files from v0.123.0. |
| `PUBLIC_ENABLE_ENDPOINT_MESSAGING` | `false` | Surface the **Send message** entry points (Devices bulk action, organization header, site header). Off by default because the server-side minimum-agent-version gates for endpoint messaging and live chat are held at a placeholder in v0.124.0, so every send returns "agent unsupported"; set `true` at web image build time to show the entry points anyway. The sidebar **Messages** page is visible regardless, to roles with `endpoint_messages:read`, and shows an empty history until the gates are lifted. |
| `PUBLIC_ENABLE_NETWORK_DEVICES_IN_LIST` | `true` | Surface network-discovered assets alongside agent endpoints in the Devices list view (on by default since v0.111). Set `false` at web image build time to return to the agent-only list. |
| `BREEZE_WORKSPACE_ENABLED` | `false` in the production compose files (`true` in the dev override) | Load the built-in **AI Workspace** extension. Off by default — leave it unset unless you want Workspace. **Requires a PostgreSQL image that provides the `pgvector` extension** (see the aside below). |
| `BREEZE_AI_AGENTS_ENABLED` | `false` | Surface **AI Agents** (Settings → AI Agents). Off by default — no agent exists, runs, or appears in the UI until this is `true`. Enabling the flag does not by itself let an agent change anything: every agent starts in **Off**, and moving one to **Act** is a separate, MFA-confirmed opt-in per agent. Must also be mapped in the `api` service's `environment:` block, not just set in `.env`. |
| `BREEZE_AI_AGENTS_POLICY_DECIDE_ENABLED` | `false` | Sub-flag of `BREEZE_AI_AGENTS_ENABLED` for the policy-decide capability, which is **not yet generally available** — leave it off. When enabled it lets an agent authorise a supervised-scope action on its own policy decision instead of sending it to a human approver, and it is what allows an operation to be **promoted** to that status from the Graduation panel. Automatic **demotion** is not gated by this flag and is always on. An operation only ever goes live on the organization's own agent — a partner-wide list is a ceiling, not a grant, so grant each organization explicitly before enabling this. See [AI Agents → Graduation](/features/ai-agents/#graduation-feedback-loop). An unrecognised value stops the API at boot rather than silently reading as off. |
| `BREEZE_AI_AGENTS_SWEEP_ACT_ENABLED` | `false` | Sub-flag of `BREEZE_AI_AGENTS_ENABLED` (also requires `BREEZE_AI_AGENTS_POLICY_DECIDE_ENABLED`) that lets a sweep schedule opt into Act mode, so intents an AI sweep raises can reach the same policy-decide path as other agent actions. Off by default. |
| `TOOL_SOURCES_ENABLED` | `false` | Enables external tool sources for AI Agents. Off by default; even when enabled, any tier-3 (destructive) external tool call still goes through the normal action-intent approval flow — this flag does not bypass approval. |
| `FLOWS_ENABLED` | `false` | **v0.125.0+, preview.** Turns on [Flows](/features/flows/) in the Tool Catalog. With it off every flow route answers 404. The `FLOW_*` limits are listed on that page. |
| `TOOL_SOURCES_ALLOW_PRIVATE_EGRESS` | `false` | Self-hosted only — refused when `IS_HOSTED=true`. Allows a tool source URL to resolve to a private, link-local, or loopback address. Leave off unless you specifically need a tool source on your internal network. |
| `CALLER_VERIFICATION_ENABLED` | `true` | Caller verification (anti-vishing). On by default: the technician workflow, the SMS/email link tier and the public `/verify/<token>` page are available, and **protected Microsoft 365 actions (`m365_disable_user`, `m365_reset_password`) require a fresh, unused caller verification** before they can be created or released. Unset means `true` (the shipped Compose files also map an empty value to `true`). Must be the exact literal `true` or `false`; any other value (`1`, `yes`, `on`) is refused at boot. Setting it to `false` hides the workflow (every caller verification route, including the public page, answers `404`, and every web surface is hidden) **and refuses those protected M365 resets and disables** — it is not a bypass. Rejected-verification emails are best-effort: they stop after three consecutive failures, and a deployment with no email transport sends only the in-app notice. |
| `CALLER_VERIFICATION_WORKSTATION_ENABLED` | `false` | The workstation verification tier (through the agent and Breeze Assist). Off by default and **not available in this release**: it is reported as unavailable, cannot be started, and a workstation grant is never accepted by the gate while this is off. Must be the exact literal `true` or `false`; other values are refused at boot. |
| `PAM_OWNERSHIP_EPOCH_TRANSFER` | `false` | **v0.124.0+, groundwork.** Lets a device's PAM ownership move with it across an organization transfer instead of the move being refused. Off by default, and a transfer also needs a database-side switch that only the database owner can set, so leave it alone. Passed to the API by both Compose files. |
| `BREEZE_YARA_BUILTIN_PACK_DISABLED` | — | **v0.124.0+.** Kill switch for the built-in YARA rule set: when set, the API disables the set at boot and loads no rule pack. YARA ships dark in v0.124.0 (no rule UI),  so this normally stays unset. Passed to the API by both Compose files. |
| `DEVICE_COMMAND_QUEUE_TTL_HOURS` | `168` (7 days) | How long a queued **standard** action may wait for its device before it expires undelivered. Covers scripts, patch installs, patch scans, software installs, and automation actions. |
| `DEVICE_COMMAND_QUEUE_SHORT_TTL_HOURS` | `24` | Deadline for **self-superseding** queued work — inventory refreshes, log-level changes, agent auto-update and rollback, browser-policy application, and the audit, security, reliability, hardware and encryption-key collections. The next run of any of these replaces the last, so a week-old copy would be stale by the time it landed. |
| `DEVICE_COMMAND_QUEUE_POWER_STATE_TTL_HOURS` | `24` | Deadline for queued **power-state** work: reboot, shutdown, and scheduled restart. |

**Queue deadlines are per action type:**
  All three deadlines are read per queued action when it is created, in hours, and any value that is not a positive number falls back to the default. Each one is fleet-wide: it applies to every queued action in its class, for every organization, and there is no per-organization or per-action override. `DEVICE_COMMAND_QUEUE_TTL_HOURS` covers most queued work, so raising it keeps every queued script, patch and install waiting longer, not just one kind. Lowering one does not shorten rows that are already queued — the deadline is stamped at queue time. A row that reaches its deadline without the device coming back expires **undelivered**, and the action reports as expired rather than sitting pending forever. See [Devices → Queued actions](/features/devices/) for what a technician sees.

  Variables prefixed with `PUBLIC_` are **web build-time flags** — they are baked into the web bundle when the image is built and cannot be changed at runtime by editing `.env`. To toggle them, set the value in your build environment and rebuild the web image. The exceptions are `PUBLIC_ABUSE_CONTACT`, `PUBLIC_SECURITY_CONTACT` and `PUBLIC_SECURITY_POLICY_URL` (see [Server](#server)), which the web container reads at runtime.

**Enabling AI Workspace requires pgvector:**
  Workspace's migrations run `CREATE EXTENSION vector` when the API boots. On a stock `postgres:16-alpine` the API **refuses to start** with `extension "vector" is not available`, naming the flag and both remedies.

  Use a Postgres image that ships the extension — the `POSTGRES_IMAGE_REF` default (`pgvector/pgvector:pg16`) already does, and is the same Postgres major version as stock with the extension baked in. On a managed Postgres, confirm your provider offers `pgvector` before turning the flag on.

  If you do not want Workspace, leave `BREEZE_WORKSPACE_ENABLED` unset — no extension is needed and nothing else changes.

sections.heading: Durable event dispatch
sections.text:
Event dispatch settings select how a subscriber receives events. They do not enable or disable the feature behind that subscriber. For example, the ticket-helpdesk and anomaly agent lanes still run in-process with the default `off` mode. See [AI Agents](/features/ai-agents/) for lane requirements and durable trigger guidance.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `EVENT_DISPATCH_MODE` | `off` | Accepts `off`, `shadow`, or `enforce`. `off` uses in-process delivery only. `shadow` also mirrors routing plans into delivery receipts for observability but executes nothing through the queue. `enforce` sends each named subscriber through the BullMQ queue only, skips its in-process delivery, and leaves unnamed subscribers in-process. |
| `EVENT_DISPATCH_QUEUE_SUBSCRIBERS` | — | Comma-separated subscriber IDs used only when the mode is `enforce`: `ai-agent-alert-verdict`, `ai-agent-anomaly`, `ai-agent-ticket-helpdesk`, `automation-worker`, `dns-threat-alerts`, `notification-dispatcher`, `policy-alert-bridge`, `webhook-delivery`. An empty list is accepted but leaves everything in-process and produces a boot warning. The variable is ignored in other modes. |

Both variables are validated when the API starts. An invalid mode or an unknown subscriber ID stops the API from starting and identifies the invalid value. As with other API settings, map each variable in the `api` service's `environment:` block of your compose file as well as setting it in `.env`.

sections.heading: MCP Server
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `MCP_SSE_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE` | `30` | SSE connection rate limit per API key |
| `MCP_MESSAGE_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE` | `120` | Message rate limit per API key |
| `MCP_TOOLS_LIST_PAGE_SIZE` | `0` | 0/unset = single page; set to e.g. 50 once every connected client honours `nextCursor`. Cursor offsets are best-effort if the visible tool list changes or tenant-tool resolution fails. |
| `MCP_MAX_SSE_SESSIONS_PER_KEY` | `5` | Max concurrent SSE sessions per API key |
| `MCP_REQUIRE_EXECUTE_ADMIN` | `true` | In production, Tier 3+ tools require the `ai:execute_admin` scope. Set to `false` to fall back to `ai:execute`. No effect outside production. |
| `MCP_EXECUTE_TOOL_ALLOWLIST` | — | Comma-separated allowed Tier 3 tools (empty = deny all) |
| `MCP_INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE_HTTP_403` | `false` | When `true`, an OAuth bearer's `tools/call` refused only for a missing tier scope (`ai:write` or `ai:execute`) returns HTTP 403 with an `insufficient_scope` `WWW-Authenticate` challenge (current plus required `mcp:*` scopes) instead of HTTP 200. Never applies to API-key callers, tool-domain, approval, MFA or RBAC denials, or the legacy HTTP+SSE transport. See [MCP Server](/features/mcp-server/#authentication-challenges). |
| `MCP_STATELESS_ENABLED` | `false` | When `true`, `POST /api/v1/mcp/sse` also speaks the stateless `2026-07-28` MCP protocol alongside the legacy `initialize` + `Mcp-Session-Id` era. Off by default; a stateless request is then refused with HTTP 400 (`-32600`) and dual-era clients fall back to `initialize`. The API refuses to boot on a non-boolean value. See [MCP Server](/features/mcp-server/#protocol-2026-07-28-stateless). |
| `MCP_HEADER_MISMATCH_ALERT_THRESHOLD` | `50` | Stateless requests whose `MCP-Protocol-Version`, `Mcp-Method` or `Mcp-Name` header is missing or disagrees with the request body are refused with `-32020`. Per API process and per 60-second window: when this many true header/body mismatches occur within one window, one Sentry warning is raised for that window. Read at startup. |
| `OAUTH_CIMD_ENABLED` | `false` | Accept Client ID Metadata Documents: an OAuth client may use an https URL as its `client_id` and the authorization server fetches its metadata document. Works next to Dynamic Client Registration. Needs `MCP_OAUTH_ENABLED=true`. The API refuses to boot on a non-boolean value. See [MCP Server](/features/mcp-server/#client-id-metadata-documents-cimd). |
| `OAUTH_CIMD_ALLOWED_HOSTS` | (empty) | Optional comma-separated hostnames, or `.suffix` entries meaning any subdomain of the suffix (for example `client.example.com,.example.org`), allowed to publish CIMD documents. Unset means any public https host. The API refuses to boot on a malformed entry (scheme, path, port, wildcard or empty item). A change takes effect when the API restarts. |
| `MCP_UNATTENDED_TIER3_PRINCIPALS` | — | Operator opt-in, empty = nobody. By default every Tier 3 tool/action (and `collect_evidence`) is denied over MCP with `MCP_APPROVAL_REQUIRED` because MCP has no interactive approval step. Comma-separated `api_key:<api key id>` / `oauth_client_user:<client_id>/<user id>` / `partner_sp:<partner service principal id>` entries (OAuth binds client AND user; a shared client_id alone never qualifies; a `partner_sp` entry names the principal, so key rotation keeps it, and like an OAuth entry it applies in every org the principal reaches) lift only that deny, only for those principals (trusted unattended agents). `ai:execute`, `ai:execute_admin` (production), `MCP_EXECUTE_TOOL_ALLOWLIST` (production), RBAC, rate limits, the Tier 3 execution ledger and the audit log still apply, and `collect_evidence` is gated as Tier 3. Tier 4, tenant (BYO MCP) tools and the onboarding bootstrap tools stay approval-only. At startup the API logs a WARN listing the configured principals, and a separate WARN for any entry that is not well formed (it can never match). Each bypassed call's audit row carries `approvalBypass: "unattended_principal"` and `approvalBypassPrincipal` (the matched entry). |

**v0.125.0+, all off or inert by default.** These are mapped in both shipped Compose files and described on the MCP Server page: `MCP_TIER3_INTENTS_ENABLED` (`false`), `MCP_INTENT_MAX_LIVE_PER_PRINCIPAL` (`20`), `MCP_INTENT_CREATES_PER_HOUR` (`60`), `MCP_INTENT_CREATES_PER_USER_PER_HOUR` (`60`), `MCP_APPROVAL_WAIT_MS` (`20000`) and `MCP_APPROVAL_WAITS_PER_PRINCIPAL` (`2`) under [Approvals over MCP](/features/mcp-server/#approvals-over-mcp); `MCP_APPS_ENABLED` (`false`); and `MCP_TASKS_ENABLED` (`false`, needs `MCP_STATELESS_ENABLED`), `MCP_TASK_PENDING_POLL_INTERVAL_MS` (`30000`), `MCP_TASK_POLL_INTERVAL_MS` (`5000`) and `MCP_TASK_TTL_GRACE_MS` (`3600000`). A non-boolean value for any of the `*_ENABLED` flags stops the API from booting.

sections.heading: Backup (Enterprise Agent Backup)
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `AGENT_BACKUP_SERVER_URL` | — | Instance-level backup control-plane URL, pushed to every agent through its config, enrollment response, and heartbeat reply. Lets you point the [enterprise backup](/deploy/binaries/#backup-binary) subsystem (Hyper-V, MSSQL, system image) at a separate backup control plane instead of the main API. Must be `https://` in production; `http://` is accepted only for `localhost`/`127.0.0.1`. Leave unset to keep backups pointed at the main API. |
| `RECOVERY_MEDIA_WORK_DIR` | `/data/recovery-work` (Compose) | Scratch directory for building [bare-metal recovery](/backup/bare-metal-recovery/) bundles and ISOs (a 45–65 MB helper binary plus a tarball or ISO per build). The `api` and `worker` containers mount `/tmp` as a 64 MB tmpfs, so building under the OS temp directory fails with `ENOSPC`; the shipped Compose files default this to a directory on the persistent `api_data` volume. Override only to move it elsewhere on durable storage, and map it in the `api` service `environment:` block. |
| `RECOVERY_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY` | — | minisign secret key (the key file contents; create it without a password, `minisign -G -W`) used to sign recovery bundles and their helper binary. **From v0.118.0 a bundle built without signing configured refuses to run**, because its launch script has no key to verify the helper with. Set it together with `RECOVERY_SIGNING_PUBLIC_KEY`. See [Recovery bundle signing](/backup/bare-metal-recovery/#recovery-bundle-signing). |
| `RECOVERY_SIGNING_PUBLIC_KEY` | — | The matching minisign public key. It is written into each bundle when the bundle is built. |
| `RECOVERY_SIGNING_KEY_ID` | derived from the public key | Optional identifier for the signing key. |
| `RECOVERY_SIGNING_KEYS_JSON` | — | Optional JSON array of additional published verification keys (`keyId`, `publicKey`), for rotating keys. |
| `RECOVERY_MINISIGN_BIN` | `minisign` | Path to the `minisign` binary the API runs to sign bundles. It must be available to the API process. |
| `DEV_PUSH_WORK_DIR` | `/data/dev-push` (derived from `PATCH_REPORT_STORAGE_PATH`) | Staging directory for dev-push agent binary uploads (non-production, or when `DEV_PUSH_ENABLED=true`). Never the container's small `/tmp` tmpfs. Uploads larger than the free space here are rejected with HTTP 507 naming this directory. |
| `BACKUP_GC_GRACE_MS` | `172800000` (48 h) | How long an expired snapshot's storage objects are kept before the retention sweep deletes them. **Lab/test knob only.** In production the API enforces a floor of one hour and logs when a lower value is ignored. Leave unset. |
| `BACKUP_GC_ORPHAN_MANIFEST_MAX_AGE_MS` | `777600000` (9 d) | **v0.113.0+, lab/test only.** How long an upload that never finished, or whose record could not be reconciled, sits idle before the storage sweep reclaims its prefix. Production floor: 7 days. Re-read on every sweep, no restart needed. |
| `BACKUP_GC_MANIFESTLESS_PREFIX_MAX_AGE_MS` | `777600000` (9 d) | **v0.113.0+, lab/test only.** How long the data of an upload that never published a restore point sits idle before the storage sweep reclaims it. The window covers the seven days an interrupted backup can still resume. Production floor: 7 days. |
| `BACKUP_BASE_LEASE_MS` | `604800000` (7 d) | **v0.113.0+, lab/test only.** How long a base restore point another backup is building on stays protected from reclamation, and the deadline by which that backup must publish. The backup helper stops publishing one hour before the deadline, so a value of one hour or less fails every backup. Production floor: 2 hours. |
| `BACKUP_RESTORE_PIN_LINGER_MS` | `604800000` (7 d) | **v0.113.0+, lab/test only.** How long a restore point stays pinned after a restore or verification referenced it. Production floor: 1 hour. |
| `BACKUP_PUBLISH_MARGIN_MS` | `3600000` (1 h) | **v0.113.0+, lab/test only.** Safety margin around a restore point's publish time before its objects are considered for reclamation. Production floor: 5 minutes. |

sections.heading: Cloud-to-Cloud Backup (M365)
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `C2C_M365_CLIENT_ID` | — | Azure AD app (client) ID for multi-tenant M365 backup. When set with the secret below, enables one-click admin consent flow for connecting Microsoft 365 backups. |
| `C2C_M365_CLIENT_SECRET` | — | Azure AD app client secret for multi-tenant M365 backup |

  These variables are optional. When unset, the C2C connection wizard falls back to manual credential entry (Client ID, Secret, Tenant ID). Setting both enables a streamlined "Grant Access" button that redirects to Microsoft's admin consent flow.

sections.heading: Inbound email-to-ticket (Mailgun)
sections.text:
These power the **native inbound address** — the `partner@yourdomain` address shown on the Inbound email card, which customers mail directly (or which you forward an existing support mailbox to). This is the self-hosted equivalent of what we configure once, centrally, on hosted Breeze. It is **independent** of the Microsoft 365 mailbox path below: you can run either, both, or neither.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `TICKETS_INBOUND_DOMAIN` | — | The domain inbound ticket addresses live on, e.g. `tickets.yourmsp.com`. Each partner's address is `<local part>@<this domain>`. **Until this is set, the Inbound email card reports that no platform inbound domain is configured** (naming this variable and linking back here on self-hosted instances) and no address can be generated. |
| `MAILGUN_INBOUND_SIGNING_KEY` | — | Mailgun's **HTTP webhook signing key**, used to HMAC-verify deliveries. The inbound webhook is unauthenticated by design — this signature is its only security — so when the key is unset every delivery is rejected with `401`. |
| `INBOUND_QUEUE_MAX_PER_SEC` | `20` | v0.116.0+. Global ceiling on how many inbound email-to-ticket jobs are **processed** per second across all senders and partners — flood backpressure for the inbound queue. Jobs over the ceiling are delayed, never dropped. Raise it for a high-volume tenant, lower it to slow down a burst; it bounds the rate of ticket creation, not the total. |

  `MAILGUN_DOMAIN` (in the [Email](#email) section above) and `TICKETS_INBOUND_DOMAIN` are different settings. The first is the domain Breeze **sends** from; this one is the domain it **receives** on. They may be the same domain, but setting one does not configure the other. Likewise, `MAILGUN_INBOUND_SIGNING_KEY` is the webhook **signing key** from Mailgun's webhook settings, not your `MAILGUN_API_KEY`.

sections.heading: Mailgun setup
sections.text:
Setting the variables is only half of it — mail has to reach Breeze:

1. Add `tickets.yourmsp.com` to Mailgun as a **receiving** domain and publish the MX records it gives you.
2. Create a Mailgun **Route** matching that domain (`catch_all()`, or `match_recipient(".*@tickets.yourmsp.com")`) with the action `forward("https://<PUBLIC_URL>/api/v1/webhooks/tickets/email-inbound")`.
3. Copy the domain's **HTTP webhook signing key** into `MAILGUN_INBOUND_SIGNING_KEY`.
4. Set `TICKETS_INBOUND_DOMAIN`, restart the API, then set the local part and enable email-to-ticket under **Settings → Ticketing → Inbound email**.

Two failure modes are silent from the sender's side, so check these first if mail vanishes:

- **Every delivery returns `401`** — `MAILGUN_INBOUND_SIGNING_KEY` is unset or wrong. Mailgun treats this as permanent and will not retry.
- **Deliveries return `429`** — the webhook's per-IP rate limiter fails closed, so this is also what you get when Redis is unreachable. Confirm `TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS` matches your reverse proxy, or the limiter keys every request to the proxy's own IP.

Breeze trusts the `Authentication-Results` header only when Mailgun itself stamped it, and requires **DMARC pass** to mark a sender verified — SPF and DKIM alone are not sufficient.

sections.heading: Ticket Mailbox (M365 email-to-ticket)
sections.text:
These enable partners to connect a Microsoft 365 shared support mailbox so customer email becomes tickets and replies are sent from that mailbox. This is a **separate** Azure app registration from the Cloud-to-Cloud Backup app above, and an alternative to the Mailgun inbound path above — it needs no MX records or DNS changes.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `TICKET_MAILBOX_M365_CLIENT_ID` | — | Azure AD app (client) ID for the **Breeze Ticketing** app. When set with the secret, the Microsoft 365 mailbox card appears under Settings → Ticketing → Inbound Email, and its Application Access Policy PowerShell snippet is filled in with this id at runtime (it is the app's public client id, not a secret). |
| `TICKET_MAILBOX_M365_CLIENT_SECRET` | — | Client secret for the Breeze Ticketing Azure app. |

  Optional and independent of C2C backup. Register a **multi-tenant** app with Microsoft Graph **application** permissions `Mail.ReadWrite` and `Mail.Send`, plus the **delegated** permission `Directory.Read.All`, and add the redirect URI `<PUBLIC_APP_URL>/api/v1/tickets/mailbox/callback`. The Microsoft 365 mailbox card shows the exact value to register. The API builds it from `PUBLIC_URL`, then `PUBLIC_APP_URL`, then `DASHBOARD_URL`; the stock `docker-compose.yml` passes only `PUBLIC_APP_URL` to the API, so on a standard install it comes from `PUBLIC_APP_URL`. Open Breeze at that same scheme and host when you connect: the consent flow is bound to a browser cookie, and a different host drops it. `Directory.Read.All` lets Breeze confirm that the person completing consent is a Global Administrator or Privileged Role Administrator by reading their directory roles from Microsoft Graph when the ID token carries no `wids` claim; without it, consent in those tenants fails with *insufficient role* (the API logs `[ticketMailbox] consent admin-role check failed` with the failing check). When unset, the Microsoft 365 mailbox card is hidden and the connect routes return `400` -- nothing else is affected. See [Email-to-Ticket → Microsoft 365 support mailbox](/features/ticketing/#connecting-a-microsoft-365-support-mailbox).

sections.heading: Ticket import migration windows
sections.text:
**v0.123.0+, groundwork for the coming ticket importers.** A migration window is the time box and write budget an admin gives one ticket import. Mapped in the v0.123.0 root `docker-compose.yml`. `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml` maps them from v0.124.0; on v0.123.0 with that file, add them to the `api` service's `environment:` block if you need to change them.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `MIGRATION_WINDOW_MAX_DAYS` | `14` | Longest window an admin can open. A longer migration opens a new window. |
| `MIGRATION_WINDOW_DEFAULT_WRITES_PER_HOUR` | `6000` | Import writes per hour a new window gets when the admin sets none. Kept between 600 and the maximum below. |
| `MIGRATION_WINDOW_MAX_WRITES_PER_HOUR` | `20000` | Most import writes per hour an admin can set. Kept between 600 and 100000. |

sections.heading: Customer Microsoft 365 Graph-read consent (optional)
sections.text:
This feature is **off by default and safe to leave unset** — every variable below stays empty in a normal deployment. The API only reads and validates them when you turn the feature on. Concretely, the API **refuses to boot when either `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_READ_ONBOARDING_ENABLED=true` or `M365_GRAPH_READ_TOOLS_ENABLED=true` *and* one of the required variables is missing or malformed**; while both flags are off (or absent) these variables are never parsed and any values you set are ignored.

Customer Graph-read lets a customer administrator grant read-only Microsoft Graph consent to Breeze's dedicated multi-tenant application without handing you a reusable secret. The Entra certificate and Key Vault access live entirely inside an isolated [executor sidecar](/deploy/production/) — the API holds only an opaque, version-pinned reference and a private key it uses to sign short-lived internal requests to that sidecar. See [Customer Graph Read](/features/identity-integrations/#customer-graph-read-recommended-for-read-only-inventory) for the admin-facing side.

| Variable | Required when enabled | Format / example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_READ_ONBOARDING_ENABLED` | — (the switch) | `true` / `false` (default `false`) | Master switch for **new** consent initiation only. Existing connection status, retest, and disconnect flows are independent of it. When `false` (and `M365_GRAPH_READ_TOOLS_ENABLED` is also off), none of the variables below are validated. |
| `M365_GRAPH_READ_TOOLS_ENABLED` | — (the switch) | `true` / `false` (default `false`) | Independent switch for the six read-only `m365_query_*` AI tools. Separate from onboarding: you can run the tools without allowing new consent. Turning it on forces full validation of every variable below at boot, including the executor settings. |
| `M365_GRAPH_READ_TOOLS_ORG_IDS` | Yes, when `M365_GRAPH_READ_TOOLS_ENABLED` is on | Literal `*` or comma-separated canonical org UUIDs | Which Breeze organizations get the `m365_query_*` tools. Boot fails if the tools flag is on and this is empty or malformed. Leave empty while the flag is off. |
| `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_READ_ONBOARDING_ORG_IDS` | Yes | Literal `*` or comma-separated canonical org UUIDs (e.g. `*` or `1111...,2222...`) | Which Breeze organizations may start consent. `*` = all organizations; otherwise an allowlist of canonical UUIDs. Boot fails if enabled and this is empty. |
| `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_READ_CLIENT_ID` | Yes | Canonical UUID | Entra application (client) ID of the shared multi-tenant Graph-read app. |
| `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_READ_CREDENTIAL_VERSION` | Yes | Exactly 32 lowercase hex characters | Pins which stored credential version the executor must use. Must equal the version segment of `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_READ_VAULT_REF`. |
| `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_READ_VAULT_REF` | Yes | `akv://<vault-host>/m365-customer-graph-read/<32-lowercase-hex-version>` | Opaque Key Vault reference to the app's certificate material. The trailing version segment **must match** `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_READ_CREDENTIAL_VERSION`, or boot fails. |
| `M365_GRAPH_READ_EXECUTOR_URL` | Yes | Origin-only HTTPS, e.g. `https://m365-executor.internal` (no path, query, fragment, or userinfo) | Private base URL of the executor sidecar. Anything other than a bare `https://host[:port]` origin is rejected at boot. |
| `M365_GRAPH_READ_EXECUTOR_AUDIENCE` | Yes | Literal `m365-graph-read-executor` | JWT audience for the API→executor internal auth token. Must equal that exact string. |
| `M365_GRAPH_READ_EXECUTOR_SIGNING_KID` | Yes | Non-empty string | Key ID of the API's signing JWK. If the JWK file carries a `kid`, it must match this value. |
| `M365_GRAPH_READ_EXECUTOR_SIGNING_PRIVATE_JWK_FILE` | Yes | Absolute path to a file, e.g. `/run/secrets/m365_graph_read_executor_signing_private_jwk` | The API's Ed25519 (`kty: OKP`, `crv: Ed25519`) **private** signing JWK. The file must be a regular file whose mode denies all group/other access (**`0600` or stricter**) and should be mounted **read-only**. Boot fails on a symlink, a relative path, over-broad permissions, or a JWK that isn't a valid 32-byte Ed25519 key. Do **not** put the private JWK inline in an env var. |

**How the consent callback URL is derived:**
  The API does **not** read a `..._CALLBACK_URL` variable.
