It builds the OAuth consent callback from `PUBLIC_URL` (falling back to `PUBLIC_APP_URL`, then `PUBLIC_API_URL`) and appends `/api/v1/m365/consent/callback`. In production at least one of those origin variables must be set. The `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_READ_CALLBACK_URL` line in `.env.example` is **not consumed by the API** — it is read only by the separate executor sidecar (where it must equal that exact `https://<origin>/api/v1/m365/consent/callback` URL). On an API-only host you can ignore it.

sections.heading: API-side tenant sync
sections.text:
These are read by the **API**. The master switch defaults off — see the
Microsoft 365 tenant sync release note on the release notes page for the
flag-on rollout order.

| Variable | Required | Format / example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `M365_TENANT_SYNC_ENABLED` | — (the switch) | `true` / `false` (default `false`) | Master switch for the scheduled tenant snapshot (users, sign-in activity, Intune devices, Conditional Access, licenses, Secure Score). Gates **every** entry point: the ticker, post-consent seeding, the on-demand sync route, and the disconnect hook. Off means no sync work of any kind runs. |
| `M365_SYNC_CONCURRENCY` | No | Positive integer (default `4`) | Sync jobs processed concurrently per API instance. The Graph fetch holds no database connection, so this bounds persist work, not fetch work. |
| `M365_SYNC_MAX_BACKLOG` | No | Positive integer (default `500`) | Queue depth (`waiting + prioritized + delayed + active`) above which the ticker skips a tick. Due rows keep their past due time and are picked up next tick. |
| `M365_SYNC_TICK_BATCH` | No | Positive integer (default `200`) | Rows claimed per 60-second tick. This is the capacity dial: target at most 50 % utilisation of `batch × 1440` runs per day. |

sections.heading: Executor-side tenant-sync tuning (v0.113.0+)
sections.text:
These are read by the **`m365-graph-read-executor` sidecar**, not the API. They tune the Microsoft 365 tenant-sync feature that ships in v0.113.0. All are optional; the executor refuses to start on a malformed value rather than guessing.

| Variable | Default | Format | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `M365_SYNC_CONTINUATION_KEY` | — (ephemeral per process) | Exactly 32 bytes, base64-encoded (44 characters) | Secret used to seal sync continuation tokens so a long sign-in-log sync can resume across executor restarts or replicas. When unset, the executor mints a key at boot: continuations then die with the process and the sync restarts that domain from page 1 — a self-healing default, so an existing executor keeps working without it. Set it when you run more than one executor replica. |
| `M365_SYNC_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` | `4` | Integer `1`–`64` | Maximum concurrent tenant-sync operations the executor will run. |
| `M365_MAX_IN_FLIGHT` | `32` | Integer `1`–`1024` | Overall in-flight Graph request ceiling for the executor. **Must be greater than or equal to `M365_SYNC_MAX_IN_FLIGHT`**, or the executor refuses to start. |
| `M365_SIGNIN_ACTIVITY_RPM` | `4` | Positive integer | Token bucket for sign-in-activity Graph requests. Microsoft's limit is **10 per minute per application across all tenants**, so divide this across every region and replica that shares one app registration. |
| `M365_SIGNIN_PAGES_PER_CALL` | `5` | Positive integer | Pages fetched per sign-in call before returning an opaque continuation. |
| `M365_SYNC_MAX_ITEMS_USERS` | `25000` | Positive integer | Per-pull user cap. A tenant over the cap syncs as `partial` and never has vanished rows marked stale; raising the cap is the remedy. |
| `M365_SYNC_MAX_ITEMS_DEVICES` | `25000` | Positive integer | Same, for Intune managed devices. |
| `M365_SYNC_MAX_ITEMS_CA` | `500` | Positive integer | Same, for Conditional Access policies. |
| `M365_SYNC_MAX_ITEMS_SKUS` | `200` | Positive integer | Same, for subscribed SKUs. |

  With Docker secrets, `M365_GRAPH_READ_EXECUTOR_SIGNING_PRIVATE_JWK_FILE` points at the in-container mount path (e.g. `/run/secrets/...`), while `M365_GRAPH_READ_EXECUTOR_SIGNING_PRIVATE_JWK_SOURCE_FILE` in `.env` is the **host path** of the source JWK that feeds that secret. Provision the source file with a numeric owner and mode `0400`; only the mounted `..._FILE` path is validated at boot.

**Map new variables into the api service:**
  Setting a value in `.env` is necessary but **not sufficient** on a custom Compose file. Every variable above must also be listed in the `api` service's `environment:` block — Compose only interpolates variables it maps explicitly. A value present in `.env` but not mapped through Compose reaches the container as empty, so an "enabled" deploy would fail to boot as if the variable were unset.

sections.heading: Customer Microsoft 365 Graph-actions (write) executor (optional)
sections.text:
Like Graph-read above, this feature is **off by default and safe to leave unset** — every variable below stays empty in a normal deployment. The API only reads and validates them when `M365_GRAPH_ACTIONS_TOOLS_ENABLED=true` or `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_ACTIONS_ONBOARDING_ENABLED=true`; while both flags are off (or absent) these variables are never parsed and any values you set are ignored.

Where Graph-read is read-only inventory, Graph-actions authorises **write** operations against a customer's Microsoft 365 tenant — the identity actions the AI can propose: reset a password, disable a user, revoke sessions, assign or remove a licence, add to or remove from a group, retire an Intune device, create a user, and set an auto-reply. Those tools are Tier 3, so they still require human approval before anything executes (see [AI Risk Engine → Approval workflow](/features/ai/#approval-workflow)); from v0.124.0, password resets and account disables also need a fresh [caller verification](/security/caller-verification/). The actions beyond reset and disable arrived in v0.124.0 with a new permission set, so a customer tenant consented earlier needs a one-time re-consent before they work; its existing consent keeps covering reset and disable. If you run the executor yourself, deploy the executor build that accepts object-id-only requests before upgrading the API to v0.124.0.

It uses the same isolation model as Graph-read: the Entra certificate and Key Vault access live entirely inside a **separately deployed** executor sidecar, and the API holds only an opaque version-pinned reference plus a private key it uses to sign short-lived internal requests.

| Variable | Required when enabled | Format / example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_ACTIONS_ONBOARDING_ENABLED` | — (the switch) | `true` / `false` (default `false`) | Master switch for **new** Graph-actions consent initiation (the **Step 2 · Admin actions** card). Independent of `M365_GRAPH_ACTIONS_TOOLS_ENABLED`; turning on either one forces full validation of the variables below at boot. In production, one of `PUBLIC_URL`, `PUBLIC_APP_URL`, or `PUBLIC_API_URL` must be set so the consent callback origin can be derived. |
| `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_ACTIONS_ONBOARDING_ORG_IDS` | Yes, when onboarding is on | Literal `*` or comma-separated canonical org UUIDs | Which Breeze organizations may start Graph-actions consent. Boot fails if onboarding is on and this is empty or malformed. |
| `M365_GRAPH_ACTIONS_TOOLS_ENABLED` | — (the switch) | `true` / `false`, `1` / `0`, `yes` / `no`, `on` / `off` (default `false`) | Master switch for the M365 write-action tools. When `false`, none of the variables below are validated and the write tools are unavailable. **From v0.106.0 a value outside the list above stops the API from starting** (it was previously read as "off", silently leaving the write tools dark), and turning it on additionally requires `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_ID`. |
| `M365_GRAPH_ACTIONS_TOOLS_ORG_IDS` | Yes | Literal `*` or comma-separated canonical org UUIDs | Which Breeze organizations may use M365 write actions. `*` = all organizations; otherwise an allowlist. Leave empty while the feature is off. |
| `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_ACTIONS_CLIENT_ID` | Yes | Canonical UUID | Entra application (client) ID of the multi-tenant Graph-actions app. |
| `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_ACTIONS_CREDENTIAL_VERSION` | Yes | Exactly 32 lowercase hex characters | Pins which stored credential version the executor must use. Must equal the version segment of `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_ACTIONS_VAULT_REF`. |
| `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_ACTIONS_VAULT_REF` | Yes | `akv://<vault-host>/m365-customer-graph-actions/<32-lowercase-hex-version>` | Opaque Key Vault reference to the app's certificate material. The trailing version segment **must match** `M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_ACTIONS_CREDENTIAL_VERSION`. |
| `M365_GRAPH_ACTIONS_EXECUTOR_URL` | Yes | Origin-only HTTPS, e.g. `https://m365-actions.internal` (no path, query, fragment, or userinfo) | Private base URL of the Graph-actions executor sidecar. Must be HTTPS; anything other than a bare origin is rejected at boot. |
| `M365_GRAPH_ACTIONS_EXECUTOR_AUDIENCE` | Yes | Literal `m365-graph-actions-executor` | JWT audience for the API→executor internal auth token. Must equal that exact string. |
| `M365_GRAPH_ACTIONS_EXECUTOR_SIGNING_KID` | Yes | Non-empty string | Key ID of the API's signing JWK. If the JWK file carries a `kid`, it must match this value. |
| `M365_GRAPH_ACTIONS_EXECUTOR_SIGNING_PRIVATE_JWK_FILE` | Yes | Absolute path, e.g. `/run/secrets/m365_graph_actions_executor_signing_private_jwk` | The API's Ed25519 **private** signing JWK. Same rules as the Graph-read key: a regular file, mode `0600` or stricter, mounted read-only. Never inline the private JWK in an env var. |

**The executor is not part of the bundled Compose stack:**
  The Graph-actions executor is **deliberately not deployed** by the generic Compose stack. Run its separately released, digest-pinned image (`ghcr.io/lanternops/breeze/m365-graph-actions-executor@sha256:<digest>`) in an environment that supplies a managed or workload identity, private authenticated ingress, and controlled HTTPS egress to Key Vault, Microsoft identity, and Graph. Never expose it through Caddy or a public tunnel, never publish its container port, and never configure a plaintext executor URL.

  As with Graph-read, `M365_GRAPH_ACTIONS_EXECUTOR_SIGNING_PRIVATE_JWK_FILE` is the in-container mount path, while `M365_GRAPH_ACTIONS_EXECUTOR_SIGNING_PRIVATE_JWK_SOURCE_FILE` in `.env` is the **host path** of the source JWK feeding that secret. Standalone Compose cannot apply secret uid/gid/mode, so provision the source file with numeric owner `1001:1001` and mode `0400`. The executor receives only the matching **public** JWK.

**Map new variables into the api service:**
  As with every optional block above, a value in `.env` is necessary but **not sufficient** on a custom Compose file — each variable must also appear in the `api` service's `environment:` block, or it reaches the container empty and an "enabled" deploy fails to boot.

sections.heading: Microsoft 365 communications (delegated, optional)
sections.text:
Off by default and safe to leave unset. This feature works per **user** rather than per organization, so its allowlists are lists of Breeze **user** UUIDs. The API reads and validates the variables below only when `M365_COMMS_ONBOARDING_ENABLED` or `M365_COMMS_TOOLS_ENABLED` is truthy; otherwise they are ignored.

| Variable | Required when enabled | Format / example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `M365_COMMS_ONBOARDING_ENABLED` | — (the switch) | `true` / `false` (default `false`) | Master switch for new delegated-communications consent initiation. |
| `M365_COMMS_ONBOARDING_USER_IDS` | Yes, when onboarding is on | Literal `*` or comma-separated canonical user UUIDs | Which Breeze users may start consent. A malformed entry fails boot rather than being dropped. |
| `M365_COMMS_TOOLS_ENABLED` | — (the switch) | `true` / `false` (default `false`) | Switch for the delegated communications AI tools. Independent of onboarding. |
| `M365_COMMS_TOOLS_USER_IDS` | Yes, when tools are on | Literal `*` or comma-separated canonical user UUIDs | Which Breeze users get the tools. |
| `M365_COMMS_CLIENT_ID` | Yes | Canonical UUID | Entra application (client) ID of the delegated communications app. |
| `M365_COMMS_EXECUTOR_URL` | Yes | Origin-only HTTPS, e.g. `https://comms-executor.internal` | Private base URL of the communications executor sidecar. |
| `M365_COMMS_EXECUTOR_AUDIENCE` | Yes | Literal `m365-communications-executor` | JWT audience for the API→executor token. Must equal that exact string. |
| `M365_COMMS_EXECUTOR_SIGNING_KID` | Yes | Non-empty string | Key ID of the API's signing JWK; must match the `kid` in the JWK file. |
| `M365_COMMS_EXECUTOR_SIGNING_PRIVATE_JWK_FILE` | Yes | Absolute path, e.g. `/run/secrets/m365_comms_executor_signing_private_jwk` | The API's Ed25519 **private** signing JWK. Same file rules as Graph-read: a regular file, mode `0600` or stricter, mounted read-only; never inline the key in an env var. |

With the stock Compose file, `M365_COMMS_EXECUTOR_SIGNING_PRIVATE_JWK_FILE` is the in-container mount path and is set for you; set `M365_COMMS_EXECUTOR_SIGNING_PRIVATE_JWK_SOURCE_FILE` in `.env` to the **host path** of the source JWK that feeds that secret (same ownership and mode rules as Graph-read). Leaving it unset mounts an empty placeholder and boot fails once the feature is enabled.

The consent callback origin comes from `PUBLIC_URL`, then `PUBLIC_APP_URL`, then `PUBLIC_API_URL`, with `/api/v1/m365/comms-consent/callback` appended. In production one of them must be set.

sections.heading: Docker Deployment
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `BREEZE_VERSION` | `latest` | Breeze release tag for Docker images (e.g. `0.50.0`). Also used by GitHub redirect mode for agent binary downloads. |
| `DOCKER_PLATFORM` | `linux/amd64` | Container platform. GHCR images are amd64 only. On Apple Silicon, use `docker-compose.override.yml.local-build` to build native arm64 images instead. |
| `REDIS_MAXMEMORY` | `256mb` | Maximum memory Redis is allowed to use. Redis runs with `noeviction` policy so BullMQ jobs are never silently dropped — which also means a Redis that reaches this ceiling starts rejecting writes and **stays full across a restart**, because the AOF replays the same over-cap dataset. Raise this value before you get there; see [Redis memory growing](/reference/troubleshooting/#redis-memory-growing-and-oom-errors-that-survive-a-restart). |

sections.heading: Billing
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `BILLING_SERVICE_URL` | — | URL of the billing service for AI credit checks and deductions. When unset, AI usage is unlimited. |
| `BILLING_SERVICE_API_KEY` | — | API key for authenticating to the billing service |
| `STRIPE_SESSION_REVOCATION_MODE` | `enforce` | **v0.113.0+.** How strictly Breeze cancels a customer's open Stripe Checkout payment link when the invoice it belongs to is reset, paid manually, voided, or the Stripe key is replaced. `enforce` (default) refuses the transition with `503 STRIPE_REVOCATION_PENDING` if it cannot prove every open Checkout session is dead; the revocation intent is kept and retried by a 60-second sweep, so the refusal is short-lived. `observe` still records the intent and calls Stripe, but a failure never blocks the transition — an incident de-escalation lever, not a normal setting. Any other value is treated as `enforce` with a warning. Roll back by flipping to `observe`, never by reverting the migration. |
| `STRIPE_ACCOUNT_CACHE_REFRESH_ENABLED` | `true` | Runs a job at start-up and daily that fills in each connected Stripe account's currency and country where Breeze has not recorded them. `false` stops scheduling it. |

  Billing integration is optional. When these variables are unset, AI chat sessions proceed without credit checks.

sections.heading: AI
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | — | The platform Anthropic API key (hosted: Breeze's key; self-hosted: yours). Partners can add their own key under AI Providers & Models. |
| `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | — | **Self-hosted only.** Point the AI Agent at an Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages` backend (vLLM 0.23+, LiteLLM). Must be an `http(s)` URL. Permitted only when `IS_HOSTED` is explicitly `false` (or `0`/`no`/`off`); refused at boot if `IS_HOSTED` is `true`, unset, or invalid. |
| `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` | — | Bearer token for the custom backend (use instead of `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` when `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` is set). |
| `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` | `claude-sonnet-5-5` | Override the default model id for a raw vLLM backend. Leave unset with a LiteLLM gateway that aliases `claude-sonnet-5-5` → your model (releases before the Sonnet 5.5 default used `claude-sonnet-4-6`; update the alias when you upgrade). On a self-hosted deployment it is also the default model new partners start with; if the registry does not list it, Breeze adds it once at the documented conservative rate (see below). |
| `AI_PLATFORM_INFERENCE_GEO` | — | Optional. Inference geography sent to Claude for platform-key traffic, where the model and transport support it. Allowed values: `us` or `global`. Unset = the provider default. `eu` is **not** accepted by the platform key: setting it (or any other value) makes every platform model unavailable (`residency_unavailable`) rather than sending traffic elsewhere, and the API logs a warning at startup. EU residency is not available on the platform key. |
| `AI_GATEWAY_HEADERS_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | — | Optional. How long the AI model gateway waits for a bring-your-own OpenAI-compatible endpoint to start responding, in seconds. Defaults to 120 on self-hosted and 30 on hosted; clamped to 5–600. Raise it for slow or CPU-only local model servers with long prompt prefill. |
| `AI_TOOL_SEARCH` | `auto` | AI chat tool loading. `auto`: on the Anthropic API, chat sends a small core tool set and loads the rest on demand through tool search; on any other `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` or BYO provider it sends every tool, because many gateways reject tool-search blocks. `on`: also use tool search on a custom base URL, only if that endpoint speaks the Anthropic Messages API end to end and forwards `tool_reference` blocks. A Breeze OpenAI-compatible connection never qualifies: its translator cannot carry `tool_reference` blocks, so `on` fails every tool round-trip with a 400 (see #9770). `off`: always send every tool. Helper, scripts and AI agents always use a fixed tool set. |
| `AI_TOOL_INDEX` | `lazy` | How the AI chat system prompt describes its tools. `lazy`: one line per tool domain (what it covers, in plain words) plus the domain notes; a chat opened on a device or alert page also gets that page's domains with every tool listed (and its actions, when it has seven or fewer). Every tool stays available either way: with tool search the model sees all tool names and loads the ones it needs; without it every tool is sent. `full`: the previous index that lists every tool in the prompt. A conversation picks up a change when its AI session is next started (a new conversation, or an existing one after an API restart or model switch). |
| `BREEZE_AI_SCRIPT_AUTHORING_ENABLED` | `true` | **v0.113.0+.** Lets the AI assistant and background agents write a script as a reviewed proposal ([AI Script Authoring](/features/ai-script-authoring/)). Set `false` to hide the `propose_script` / `get_script_proposal` tools and the `/api/v1/ai/script-proposals` routes entirely. Accepts `true`/`false`, `1`/`0`, `yes`/`no`, `on`/`off`; any other value stops the API from starting. The shipped Compose file defaults it to `true` as well. This flag does **not** control the unattended lane, which stays off until a partner raises its ceiling and an organization opts in. |
| `BREEZE_TRUST_CIS_FRAMEWORK_VIEW` | `false` | Shows the CIS Controls v8 framework view on public [Trust Center](/security/trust-center/) pages and makes it selectable in the page editor. Leave it off until CIS licensing is confirmed; while off, the default framework view is NIST CSF 2.0, and with it on, CIS Controls v8 becomes the default. Accepts `true`/`false`, `1`/`0`, `yes`/`no`, `on`/`off`. |
| `BREEZE_AI_ARTIFACT_CAPTURE_ENABLED` | `false` | **v0.117.0+.** Store oversized AI tool results (redacted) in your object storage so the assistant can page back through them with `read_artifact`, instead of receiving a truncated result. Off by default because it writes blobs your organizations can download. Setting it `true` requires an artifact bucket and keys: `ARTIFACT_S3_BUCKET_US` / `ARTIFACT_S3_BUCKET_EU` (matching your region) or `S3_BUCKET`, plus `ARTIFACT_S3_ACCESS_KEY` / `ARTIFACT_S3_SECRET_KEY` or `S3_ACCESS_KEY` / `S3_SECRET_KEY`. Without them, or with a value that is not a boolean, the API refuses to start. |
| `AI_TRANSCRIPT_SWEEPER_ENABLED` | on only when `NODE_ENV=production` | **v0.124.0+.** Nightly deletion of stale AI chat session transcripts from the container's disk, once their session has ended and the grace period has passed. Runs by default in production; set `true` to run it elsewhere, or `false` to turn it off. The sweeper runs only in containers that hold agent connections (`BREEZE_ROLE=api` or `all`), each sweeping its own disk, so a [worker split](/deploy/worker-split/) does not move it. |
| `AI_TRANSCRIPT_SWEEPER_CRON` | `38 4 * * *` | When the transcript sweeper runs (UTC), five minutes after the tool-output scrub. |
| `AI_TRANSCRIPT_SWEEPER_GRACE_HOURS` | `24` | Hours a transcript is kept after its session is no longer resumable. |
| `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` | `~/.claude` | Directory the AI chat transcripts are written to and swept from. Passed through by both Compose files from v0.124.0; an empty value means unset, so the default applies. |

sections.heading: AI Operator (preview, off by default)
sections.text:
[AI tasks](/features/ai-tasks/) hands a long-running task
to an agent that keeps working after the browser is closed. It is gated
separately from the rest of the AI-agent subsystem, and `BREEZE_AI_AGENTS_ENABLED`
still has to be on above it.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `AI_OPERATOR_TASKS_ENABLED` | `false` | Admit AI tasks and their continuation runs. With this off, the **Start an AI task** action does not appear and no task can be created. |
| `AI_OPERATOR_RECIPE_SERVICE_RECOVERY_ENABLED` | `false` | Allow the **service recovery** recipe. Task admission needs this as well as the flag above. |
| `AI_OPERATOR_RECIPE_IDENTITY_OFFBOARDING_ENABLED` | `false` | **v0.125.0+, preview.** Allow the **identity offboarding** recipe. Needs `AI_OPERATOR_TASKS_ENABLED` too. Leave off until the recipe is generally available. |
| `AI_OPERATOR_RECIPE_IDENTITY_ONBOARDING_ENABLED` | `false` | **v0.125.0+, preview.** Allow the **identity onboarding** recipe, which creates accounts. Needs `AI_OPERATOR_TASKS_ENABLED` too. Leave off until the recipe is generally available. |

With both flags off the whole subsystem is inert. Its two background workers —
the task coordinator (15-second tick) and the task-event publisher (5-second
tick) — are still registered so that a task already in flight when you turn the
feature off can finish cleanly, but with no tasks being admitted neither has
anything to do. No new queue is added.

sections.heading: Self-hosted: alternative Anthropic-compatible backends
sections.text:
A self-hosted operator can run the AI Agent against any backend that speaks the
Anthropic `/v1/messages` dialect — keeping full tool-use and the `aiGuardrails`
stack — by setting:

```bash
IS_HOSTED=false                            # required — ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is refused otherwise
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8000   # your vLLM / LiteLLM endpoint
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=<backend bearer token>
# Raw vLLM only — match the served model id (skip with a LiteLLM alias):
ANTHROPIC_MODEL=<served-model-id>
```

The recommended route is a **LiteLLM gateway** that aliases `claude-sonnet-5-5`
to your backend model, so no `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` override is needed. For a
recognised Claude model id, Breeze sends adaptive thinking and an effort level
(`medium`), so the gateway must accept or drop those parameters (LiteLLM:
`drop_params: true`). If it can do neither, set `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` to your
backend's own model id instead; Breeze then sends thinking `disabled`, as
before. For an
OpenAI-dialect-only endpoint, use `MCP_LLM_PROVIDER=openai-compatible` with the
`MCP_LLM_*` variables instead. At boot Breeze creates a read-only, env-managed
connection per partner with one priced, auto-verified model that supports tools
(see [Bring Your Own LLM Key](/features/bring-your-own-llm-key/#instance-wide-openai-compatible-endpoint)).
Hosted deployments refuse `MCP_LLM_PROVIDER=openai-compatible`.

`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` is **fail-closed**: it is honored only when self-host is
affirmatively declared (`IS_HOSTED` explicitly `false`/`0`/`no`/`off`). If
`IS_HOSTED` is `true`, unset, or set to an unrecognized value, the API refuses
to boot when `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` is present, and the value is also stripped
from the SDK subprocess environment — so a stray or unmapped `IS_HOSTED` can
never redirect platform AI traffic to a third-party endpoint.

Cost tracking uses the platform model registry, never the SDK's own cost
figure. When `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` names a model the registry doesn't list, Breeze
adds it once (when your partners move to the registry) and prices it at
conservative Opus-tier rates ($5/$25 per MTok) — likely an *over*-estimate for
a cheap local model, not `$0`. For accurate accounting, set that model's
prices on **Admin → AI models**, or use the openai-compatible path's
`MCP_LLM_PRICE_INPUT_PER_M_USD` / `MCP_LLM_PRICE_OUTPUT_PER_M_USD` variables.

sections.heading: Warranty lookups
sections.text:
The warranty worker looks each physical device's serial number up against its manufacturer so the device page and [warranty-expiry alerts](/features/warranty-tracking/) carry real coverage dates. Every vendor is off until configured; an unconfigured vendor leaves its devices at status `unknown`. Apple coverage is reported by the macOS agent and needs no configuration.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `DELL_CLIENT_ID` | — | OAuth client ID from Dell's [TechDirect](https://techdirect.dell.com) Warranty API |
| `DELL_CLIENT_SECRET` | — | Matching Dell OAuth client secret. Both are required for Dell lookups. |
| `LENOVO_API_KEY` | — | ClientID for Lenovo's official [Warranty API](https://supportapi.lenovo.com/Documentation/Warranty.html) (`supportapi.lenovo.com`), issued through a Lenovo partner manager |
| `LENOVO_WARRANTY_ENABLED` | — | `true` enables credential-free Lenovo lookups through the JSON endpoint behind Lenovo's public warranty-lookup page. It is not documented by Lenovo and may stop working without notice, so it is opt-in. |
| `HP_WARRANTY_ENABLED` | — | `true` or `1` enables HP lookups through HP's public support warranty endpoint, one serial at a time and rate limited. It is not an official API and may stop working without notice. |

  When both Lenovo settings are present the official API is authoritative: a definite "no warranty found" from it is final, and the public endpoint is only consulted when the official call itself fails (bad key, outage). HP's official Warranty API is not available to MSP or RMM vendors, so HP devices stay `unknown` unless you turn on `HP_WARRANTY_ENABLED`, which uses HP's public support endpoint instead.

sections.heading: Breeze AI for Office (add-ins, optional)
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `CLIENT_AI_ENTRA_CLIENT_ID` | — | Entra application (client) ID for the multi-tenant **Breeze AI for Office** add-in app registration. The entire `/api/v1/client-ai/admin/*` admin surface (tenant mapping, org policy, usage, templates) answers `404` ("Breeze AI for Office is not enabled") until this is set. Leave unset if you don't use the Office add-ins' AI features. |

sections.heading: Accounting (QuickBooks Online)
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `QBO_CLIENT_ID` | — | Intuit OAuth client ID for the QuickBooks Online integration |
| `QBO_CLIENT_SECRET` | — | Intuit OAuth client secret |
| `QBO_REDIRECT_URI` | — | OAuth callback URL registered with Intuit (e.g. `https://your-domain/api/v1/accounting/quickbooks/callback`) |
| `QBO_ENVIRONMENT` | — | `sandbox` or `production` |
| `QBO_WEBHOOK_VERIFIER_TOKEN` | — | Intuit app verifier token for `POST /api/v1/webhooks/quickbooks`. Optional. Without it the webhook endpoint answers `503` on every delivery (so Intuit keeps retrying) and payments arrive on the 15-minute reconcile sweep instead — the sweep is the guaranteed path either way, the webhook only makes it faster. Intuit allows one webhook endpoint per app, so a multi-region deployment can only point it at one region. |

  The first four are optional and validated lazily — the API boots fine without them. Until they're set, the in-app QuickBooks connect flow reports that QuickBooks isn't configured on this instance. Set all four to enable [Accounting integration](/features/integrations/#accounting-integrations). `QBO_WEBHOOK_VERIFIER_TOKEN` is independent of them and only affects how quickly recorded payments come back.

sections.heading: Accounting (Xero)
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `XERO_CLIENT_ID` | — | Client ID of your Xero Web app (developer.xero.com → My Apps). The Xero card only appears when this is set. |
| `XERO_CLIENT_SECRET` | — | That app's client secret |
| `XERO_REDIRECT_URI` | — | OAuth callback registered on the app, e.g. `https://your-domain/api/v1/accounting/xero/callback` |
| `XERO_WEBHOOK_KEY` | — | The app's webhook signing key. In the Xero app's Webhooks page, subscribe to Invoices with delivery URL `https://your-domain/api/v1/webhooks/xero`, then send "Intent to receive". Without it, payments recorded in Xero still reach Breeze through the 15-minute sweep, just more slowly. |
| `XERO_DAILY_CALL_LIMIT` | `1000` | Per-organisation daily API budget for your Xero tier (Starter 1000; Core, Plus and Advanced 5000). Background sweeps pause below 20% of it; invoice and payment pushes keep priority. |

  Xero has no sandbox: connections are always "production", and testing uses Xero's Demo Company. Breeze connects to exactly one Xero organisation per partner. Disconnecting removes only Breeze's own connection in Xero — it never revokes the rest of your Xero app authorisations.

sections.heading: Vulnerability Management
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `NVD_API_KEY` | — | Optional NIST NVD API key. Raises NVD request rate limits so vulnerability feed syncs run faster. Without it, syncs use the slower public rate; the feature works either way. |

sections.heading: Partner trust probation (hosted service only)
sections.text:
**Self-hosted installs can skip this section:**
  These variables drive the signup-abuse controls on the hosted Breeze service, where anyone can create a partner account. On a self-hosted install they do nothing: the mode resolves to `off` unless `IS_HOSTED=true`, whatever value you set, and with it off no trust code path touches the database, Redis, or the network. You do not need to set any of them.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `PARTNER_TRUST_MODE` | `off` when `IS_HOSTED` is not `true`; otherwise `shadow` | `off` disables the feature entirely. `shadow` classifies new self-serve partners and records what it *would* have done without denying anything. `enforce` places new partners in probation until a card payment settles and ages, or an admin approves them from the trust queue. |
| `IP_CLASSIFY_PROVIDER` | — | IP-reputation provider used to classify a signup's origin. Unset means signups classify as `unknown` and promotion out of probation is manual only. |
| `IP_CLASSIFY_API_KEY` | — | API key for that provider. Setting a provider without a key logs a warning and falls back to the offline classifier. |
| `TRUST_ACTION_TOKEN_SECRET` | falls back to `JWT_SECRET` | Signs the one-time action links in trust-review emails. |
| `PARTNER_MEETING_URL` | — | Booking link offered to a partner under review so they can talk to a human. Omitted from the notice when unset. |

title: Network Proxy Dedicated Origin
description: Serve Network Proxy device UIs from their own origin per tunnel (host mode) - second domain, wildcard DNS and certificate, Caddy and API settings, boot-time validation, Cloudflare rules, and the Public Suffix List caveat.
headings: Behind Cloudflare Tunnel (TLS at the edge)
Caddy terminates TLS (Origin CA or your own certificate)

sections.text:
[Network Proxy](/features/remote-access/#network-proxy) can serve a device's web UI in two ways. **Path mode** is the default and needs no setup. **Host mode** (the dedicated tunnel origin) gives every tunnel its own browser origin. This page covers what host mode needs, how to configure it, and what to do if you can't meet its requirements.

  Host mode is optional. If you leave the variables below unset, path mode keeps working exactly as before.

sections.heading: What host mode changes
sections.text:
In path mode the device UI is served under your Breeze hostname at `/api/v1/tunnel-http/<tunnel-id>/`. Breeze has to rewrite device content and confine it with a sandbox, so device UIs that build absolute URLs or depend on their own cookies or local storage can still break.

In host mode each tunnel is served from its own origin:

```text
https://<tunnel-id>.<region>.tunnel.example.net
```

The device owns that origin, so root-relative links, cookies, and local storage behave as they would on the device itself. The dashboard embeds it in a frame, and **Open In New Tab** opens it in its own tab.

This is only safe if the tunnel hostnames sit on a **different registrable domain** from Breeze (`tunnel.example.net` versus `breeze.example.com`). Browsers treat subdomains of one registrable domain as the same site, so device content on a sibling subdomain could read or overwrite dashboard cookies. The API checks this at boot (see [Validation errors](#validation-errors)).

sections.heading: Requirements
sections.text:
1. **A second registrable domain** (for example `tunnel.example.net`) that you control. A subdomain of your Breeze domain does not work.
2. **Wildcard DNS** for `*.<region>.tunnel.example.net`, pointing at the same place as your Breeze traffic. `<region>` is any label you choose, such as `us`.
3. **A wildcard certificate** for the tunnel hostnames, by one of:
   - **Let's Encrypt DNS-01** with a Caddy build that includes your DNS provider's module. Wildcards cannot use the HTTP challenge.
   - **A Cloudflare Origin CA certificate** for `*.<region>.tunnel.example.net`, mounted into the Caddy container, with the Cloudflare proxy in front.
   - **Cloudflare Tunnel with Advanced Certificate Manager (ACM)**, where Cloudflare terminates TLS at the edge and forwards plain HTTP to Caddy. Universal SSL does not cover names this deep, so you need ACM (or an equivalent) for `*.<region>.tunnel.example.net`.

sections.heading: Configuration
sections.text:
Set these in `.env`. The compose files already pass every one of them through.

```bash
# API: the origin template and who may frame it
TUNNEL_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE=https://{id}.us.tunnel.example.net
TUNNEL_FRAME_ANCESTOR=https://breeze.example.com

# Caddy: which hostnames the tunnel site block answers
TUNNEL_SITE_ADDRESS=*.us.tunnel.example.net, *.*.us.tunnel.example.net
TUNNEL_HOST_SUFFIX=us.tunnel.example.net
```

| Variable | Used by | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `TUNNEL_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE` | API | `https://{id}.<suffix>`, with `{id}` as the whole leftmost label. Unset means path mode. |
| `TUNNEL_FRAME_ANCESTOR` | API | The exact `https://` origin allowed to frame tunnel content. Defaults to the origin of `PUBLIC_APP_URL`, else `DASHBOARD_URL`. Set it explicitly if neither is set. |
| `TUNNEL_SITE_ADDRESS` | Caddy | Site address for the tunnel domain. List both wildcards: `*.<suffix>` matches the tunnel host, and `*.*.<suffix>` sends two-label names to the tunnel block (where the API refuses them) instead of the app. Unset, it matches nothing. |
| `TUNNEL_HOST_SUFFIX` | Caddy | The bare suffix (`<region>.tunnel.example.net`). Hosts at or under it that miss the wildcards get `421` from the app block instead of being served as the app. |
| `TUNNEL_TLS_DIRECTIVE` | Caddy | Empty by default. A full `tls <cert> <key>` line when Caddy terminates TLS for the tunnel domain with your own certificate. |

  Do not set `TUNNEL_SITE_ADDRESS`, `TUNNEL_HOST_SUFFIX` or `TUNNEL_TLS_DIRECTIVE` to an empty string. Leave them unset when host mode is off; compose supplies a harmless default. An empty site address stops Caddy from starting.

sections.heading: Behind Cloudflare Tunnel (TLS at the edge)
sections.text:
Cloudflare terminates TLS and sends plain HTTP to Caddy, so use `http://` site addresses and no certificate on Caddy:

```bash
TUNNEL_SITE_ADDRESS=http://*.us.tunnel.example.net, http://*.*.us.tunnel.example.net
```

Add a public hostname for `*.us.tunnel.example.net` to your tunnel, pointing at `http://caddy:80`. The API variables stay `https://`, because that is the origin the browser sees.

sections.heading: Caddy terminates TLS (Origin CA or your own certificate)
sections.text:
Put the certificate and key where Caddy can read them, then point the directive at them:

```bash
TUNNEL_SITE_ADDRESS=*.us.tunnel.example.net, *.*.us.tunnel.example.net
TUNNEL_TLS_DIRECTIVE=tls /etc/caddy/tunnel.pem /etc/caddy/tunnel.key
```

Compose does not mount the certificate for you. Add the mounts to the `caddy` service in a `docker-compose.override.yml`:

```yaml
services:
  caddy:
    volumes:
      - ./certs/tunnel.pem:/etc/caddy/tunnel.pem:ro
      - ./certs/tunnel.key:/etc/caddy/tunnel.key:ro
```

sections.heading: Trusted proxies and `FORCE_HTTPS`
sections.text: The API trusts `X-Forwarded-Proto` only from addresses in `TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`. If Caddy's address is not in that list, the API treats the request as plain HTTP. With `FORCE_HTTPS=true` it then answers every tunnel-host request with `400 FORCE_HTTPS_NON_CANONICAL_HOST`, because a tunnel host is never the canonical API host. (App hosts get a `308` redirect in the same situation.) This is deliberate. Fix the CIDR list rather than disabling `FORCE_HTTPS`.

sections.heading: Per-partner opt-in
sections.text: Setting the variables only makes host mode **available**. Each partner turns it on in **Settings → Partner → Remote Access → Serve Network Proxy from a dedicated origin**. The choice applies to all of the partner's organizations. A partner that has not chosen stays on path mode.

sections.heading: Validation errors
sections.text:
The API refuses to boot if `TUNNEL_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE` is malformed or unsafe, in every `NODE_ENV`. Each message starts with the variable name. The ones you are likely to see:

- Wrong template shape:

```text
  TUNNEL_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE must be exactly https://{id}.<suffix> — lowercase, {id} as the whole leftmost label, no userinfo, path, query, fragment or port
```

  An unusable suffix repeats that sentence followed by `(invalid suffix "<suffix>")`.
- Shares a registrable domain with an app origin:

```text
  TUNNEL_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE suffix "us.breeze.example.com" shares a registrable domain with PUBLIC_APP_URL origin https://app.breeze.example.com; tunnel content must live on a separate registrable domain
```

  The comparison covers `PUBLIC_APP_URL`, `DASHBOARD_URL`, `PUBLIC_API_URL`, `PUBLIC_PORTAL_URL`, `PUBLIC_WEB_URL`, `PUBLIC_URL`, `API_URL`, `TUNNEL_FRAME_ANCESTOR`, `WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN` and `CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`. The name in the message tells you which one collided.
- An app origin that can't be checked: `TUNNEL_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE cannot verify separation from <SOURCE> entry "<value>": not a parseable origin` (or `host has no registrable domain`). Fix or remove that entry. For example, a portal URL with no hostname fails here.
- Scheme and port:
  - `TUNNEL_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE must use https:// (http is accepted only for *.localhost outside production)`
  - `TUNNEL_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE must not contain a port (accepted only for *.localhost outside production)`
- Frame ancestor:
  - `TUNNEL_FRAME_ANCESTOR is required when TUNNEL_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE is set (no PUBLIC_APP_URL/DASHBOARD_URL to default from)`
  - `TUNNEL_FRAME_ANCESTOR must be an exact https origin such as https://app.example.com (got "<value>")`. Use `scheme://host` with no trailing slash or path.
- No registrable domain: `TUNNEL_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE suffix "<suffix>" has no registrable domain`

sections.heading: Cloudflare
sections.text:
If the tunnel domain is proxied through Cloudflare, configure the tunnel hostnames so Cloudflare does not alter device content:

- **Bypass the cache** for `*.<region>.tunnel.example.net`. Device pages are per-user and per-session.
- **Turn off challenges** (Bot Fight Mode, managed challenges, and "I'm Under Attack" rules) for those hostnames. A challenge page can't be completed inside the frame, and it breaks asset requests from the device UI.
- Leave **Rocket Loader**, **Auto Minify** and other content-rewriting features off for the same hostnames.

sections.heading: Without a second domain
sections.text: You don't need any of this to use Network Proxy. Leave `TUNNEL_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE`, `TUNNEL_FRAME_ANCESTOR`, `TUNNEL_SITE_ADDRESS`, `TUNNEL_HOST_SUFFIX` and `TUNNEL_TLS_DIRECTIVE` unset and path mode keeps working. Upgrading does not change existing deployments.

sections.heading: Public Suffix List
sections.text:
Even on a separate registrable domain, devices behind different tunnels share that domain: `a.us.tunnel.example.net` and `b.us.tunnel.example.net` are the same site to a browser. A device UI could set a cookie for the parent domain that every other tunnel on it then receives (cookie tossing).

The [Public Suffix List](https://publicsuffix.org/) closes that gap. Browsers treat a suffix on the list as a boundary no cookie can cross. Once `<region>.tunnel.example.net` is listed, each tunnel is its own site. Inclusion is a request to the list maintainers, and it takes time to reach shipped browsers.

Until your tunnel suffix is listed, treat host mode as **opt-in**. The per-partner switch is off by default, so enable it only for partners who need better compatibility with specific device UIs. If you operate the tunnel domain for others, submit your suffix to the list before relying on host mode.

  The boot-time check separates the tunnel domain from your app domains. It does not add your suffix to the Public Suffix List.

title: Production Deployment
description: Deploy Breeze RMM to production with Docker Compose. Covers Caddy automatic TLS, API, dashboard, customer portal, PostgreSQL, Redis, and monitoring.
headings: Signed, digest-pinned image references (v0.112.0 and later)

sections.text: Breeze ships as pre-built Docker images on GitHub Container Registry. A single `docker compose up -d` brings up a fully working production stack with automatic TLS.

sections.heading: What Gets Deployed
sections.text:
The core stack (`docker-compose.yml`) includes:

| Service | Image | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Binaries Init** | `ghcr.io/lanternops/breeze/binaries` | Copies agent/viewer binaries to a shared volume, then exits |
| **Caddy** | `caddy:2.8-alpine` | Reverse proxy, auto-TLS, security headers |
| **API** | `ghcr.io/lanternops/breeze/api` | Hono API server |
| **Web** | `ghcr.io/lanternops/breeze/web` | Astro SSR dashboard |
| **Portal** | `ghcr.io/lanternops/breeze/portal` | Astro SSR customer portal, served under `/portal` (see [Customer Portal](/features/portal/)) |
| **PostgreSQL** | `pgvector/pgvector:pg16` | Primary database |
| **Redis** | `redis:7-alpine` | Job queue, caching, rate limiting |
| **Coturn** | `coturn/coturn:4-alpine` | TURN relay server for WebRTC remote desktop (opt-in via `--profile turn`) |

The `pgvector` extension is required **only if you enable the Workspace built-in** (`BREEZE_WORKSPACE_ENABLED=true`), which uses it for content embeddings. Workspace ships inside the API image but is off by default: with the flag unset, no Workspace migrations run and any Postgres 16 image works. The bundled `POSTGRES_IMAGE_REF` default is pgvector-capable regardless, so enabling Workspace later needs no database swap — supply your own Postgres image and you must provide `pgvector` yourself before setting the flag, or the API will fail to start with `extension "vector" is not available`.

**Do not swap Postgres images over an existing data volume:**
`postgres:16-alpine` is built against **musl**; `pgvector/pgvector:pg16` is built against **glibc**. Starting one image over a data directory initialized by the other produces a **collation version mismatch**: Postgres warns at startup, and every text index (including unique constraints on text columns) is potentially inconsistent until rebuilt — which can return wrong rows rather than failing loudly.

If you are already running on a stock image and want Workspace, either:

- dump and restore into a freshly-initialized volume on the new image, or
- after the first start on the new image, run `REINDEX DATABASE <dbname>;` followed by `ALTER DATABASE <dbname> REFRESH COLLATION VERSION;`.

If you do not need Workspace, keep the Postgres image you are already running.

An optional monitoring stack (Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, Loki, Promtail, exporters) is available as a separate overlay — see [Monitoring](#adding-monitoring).

An optional **`m365-graph-read-executor`** sidecar (published as `ghcr.io/lanternops/breeze/m365-graph-read-executor`) isolates the Microsoft 365 customer Graph-read certificate and Key Vault access away from the API. It is only exercised when Customer Graph-read consent is enabled (`M365_CUSTOMER_GRAPH_READ_ONBOARDING_ENABLED=true`); otherwise it sits idle and can be left undeployed. It is not part of the bundled compose files by default — see [Customer Microsoft 365 Graph-read consent](/deploy/environment/#customer-microsoft-365-graph-read-consent-optional) for the full variable contract, including the private base URL and read-only signing-key mount it depends on.

**Customer portal lives at /portal:**
The customer portal is served under the `/portal` path on your main domain (for example `https://breeze.example.com/portal/login`) — no separate hostname or TLS certificate is required. It reaches the API on the same origin, so there is no extra CORS configuration. Set `PUBLIC_PORTAL_URL` (default `https://${BREEZE_DOMAIN}/portal`) so customer-facing links in emails resolve correctly. If you maintain a **custom Compose file**, a `BREEZE_VERSION` bump alone won't add the portal — make sure the `portal` service and the Caddy `/portal` route are present, then `docker compose up -d portal && docker compose restart caddy`.

sections.heading: Deploy Steps
sections.text:
1. **Prepare the server**

   You need Docker and Docker Compose on a Linux VPS. See [Prerequisites](/getting-started/prerequisites/).

2. **Clone and configure**

```bash
   git clone https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze.git
   cd breeze
   cp .env.example .env
```

     `git clone` fails with `destination path 'breeze' already exists and is not
     an empty directory` if you previously ran the
     [Quickstart](/getting-started/quickstart/) here, which creates its own
     `breeze/` directory. Stop and remove the old stack first — renaming the
     directory is **not** enough, because both installs share the container names
     and the `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=breeze` Docker volumes:

```bash
     cd breeze && docker compose down     # add -v to also discard the test database
     cd .. && rm -rf breeze               # or move it somewhere outside your working dir
```

3. **Set your domain and secrets**

   Edit `.env` and set these required values:

```bash
   BREEZE_DOMAIN=breeze.yourdomain.com
   ACME_EMAIL=admin@yourdomain.com
```

   Generate all secrets at once. These commands rewrite the placeholder values
   `.env.example` ships **in place** — do not append a second copy of a key to
   the end of the file:

```bash
   for key in JWT_SECRET APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY MFA_ENCRYPTION_KEY \
     ENROLLMENT_KEY_PEPPER MFA_RECOVERY_CODE_PEPPER \
     METRICS_SCRAPE_TOKEN SESSION_SECRET AGENT_ENROLLMENT_SECRET; do
     sed -i "s|^${key}=.*|${key}=$(openssl rand -hex 32)|" .env
   done

   # Canonical base64 decoding to >= 32 bytes; must not reuse JWT_SECRET.
   # The API refuses to boot in production without this one.
   sed -i "s|^PARTNER_API_CURSOR_SIGNING_KEY=.*|PARTNER_API_CURSOR_SIGNING_KEY=$(openssl rand -base64 32)|" .env

   POSTGRES_PASSWORD="$(openssl rand -base64 24 | tr -d '/+=')"
   REDIS_PASSWORD="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
   sed -i "s|^POSTGRES_PASSWORD=.*|POSTGRES_PASSWORD=${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}|" .env
   sed -i "s|^REDIS_PASSWORD=.*|REDIS_PASSWORD=${REDIS_PASSWORD}|" .env
   sed -i "s|^REDIS_URL=.*|REDIS_URL=redis://:${REDIS_PASSWORD}@redis:6379|" .env
```

   On macOS, use `sed -i ''` instead of `sed -i`.

   Confirm no required secret was left at its placeholder:

```bash
   grep -nE 'replace-with|generate-a-random|change-in-production|your-super-secret|changeme' .env \
     | grep -v '^[0-9]*:GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD='
```

   That should print nothing. `GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD` is filtered out because it
   belongs to the optional monitoring stack and is generated in that section
   below; `TURN_SECRET` is only needed if you enable the TURN profile in step 4.

   Then set these required deployment-mode flags. Without them the API refuses to boot in production:

```bash
   # Self-hosted by default. Set to "true" only if you're running the hosted SaaS edition.
   IS_HOSTED=false

   # Trust anchor (raw base64 Ed25519 public key) for the official Breeze GitHub
   # releases. This is a public key — also embedded in the agent and CI — so it is
   # safe to commit. Leave the default below unless you build and sign your own binaries.
   RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS=yzx8ftmcls6uBetFC5SYnZhBo+cbur3IX50TbBthTso=
```

   Then set the initial admin account. The API creates it automatically the
   first time it starts against an empty database — in production this is
   **required**: without both variables set, that first-boot seed throws and
   the API crash-loops instead of starting.

```bash
   BREEZE_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL=you@yourdomain.com
   BREEZE_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD="$(openssl rand -base64 24)"
```

     The password must be at least 16 characters and can't look like a
     placeholder (`changeme`, `password`, `change-in-production`, etc.) — the
     API rejects it and refuses to start otherwise. Rotate it after your first
     login.

   If Breeze is behind a reverse proxy, also set `TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true` and list the proxy's CIDRs in `TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`. See [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/) for details.

4. **Configure TURN server**

   The TURN server enables remote desktop connectivity across NATs and firewalls. Set the server's public IP address:

```bash
   # Set to this server's public IP address (required for remote desktop)
   TURN_HOST=203.0.113.10

   # Optional: TURN realm (defaults to breeze.local)
   TURN_REALM=breeze.local
```

   Generate the shared secret coturn uses to mint credentials:

```bash
   sed -i "s|^TURN_SECRET=.*|TURN_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32)|" .env
```

   Coturn is behind a Docker Compose profile and does not start by default. To enable it:

```bash
   docker compose --profile turn up -d
```

   Or add `COMPOSE_PROFILES=turn` to your `.env` file for persistent activation.

     Skipping remote desktop? Leave `TURN_HOST` and `TURN_SECRET` blank — the rest
     of the stack starts without them. If you *do* enable the profile, coturn
     refuses to start on an empty `TURN_SECRET` rather than running as an open
     relay, since an empty shared secret makes TURN credentials forgeable.

     If your server is behind **Cloudflare Tunnel** or another HTTP-only proxy, TURN cannot run on the same host because it requires UDP. Deploy TURN on a separate VPS instead — see [TURN Server](/deploy/turn-server/) for a step-by-step guide.

5. **Start the stack**

```bash
   docker compose up -d
```

   That's it. On first start, the API container automatically runs database migrations and seeds the initial admin user with the `BREEZE_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL`/`BREEZE_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD` you set in step 3. Caddy obtains a TLS certificate from Let's Encrypt.

6. **Verify the deployment**

```bash
   # Check health
   curl https://breeze.yourdomain.com/health

   # Check running containers
   docker compose ps

   # View API logs
   docker compose logs -f api
```

  The API auto-migrates the database on startup by default. To manage migrations manually, set `AUTO_MIGRATE=false` in `.env` and run migrations from the host or a one-off container.

sections.heading: Adding Monitoring
sections.text:
The monitoring stack lives in a separate compose overlay file (`docker-compose.monitoring.yml`) and includes Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, Loki, Promtail, and database exporters.

To deploy with monitoring:

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.monitoring.yml up -d
```

Add a Grafana password to `.env`:

```bash
GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -base64 16 | tr -d '/+=')
```

Grafana is available at `http://127.0.0.1:3000` (localhost only by default).

sections.heading: Pinning a Version
sections.text:
`.env.example` ships with an explicit `BREEZE_VERSION` pin, so a fresh deployment is already pinned. Change it deliberately when you upgrade. There is no `latest` fallback: every image reference in `docker-compose.yml` is digest/tag-pinned and required, so clearing `BREEZE_VERSION` (or any of the `*_IMAGE_REF` variables) makes `docker compose` refuse to run at all, with an error like `Set BREEZE_VERSION in .env`, rather than silently pulling a newer image. To pin to a specific release:

```bash
# In .env
BREEZE_VERSION=0.67.1
```

Then pull and restart:

```bash
docker compose pull && docker compose up -d
```

That applies to tag-form image refs only. On a digest-pinned install (below), changing `BREEZE_VERSION` alone does not change the images, and `docker compose pull` fetches the same digests again. Upgrade those installs with `guided-setup.sh --upgrade`. See the [Upgrade Guide](/deploy/upgrades/#docker-compose-upgrade).

sections.heading: Signed, digest-pinned image references (v0.112.0 and later)
sections.text:
Since v0.112.0 every release publishes a **signed image inventory** — `release-artifact-manifest.json` plus its `.ed25519` signature on the GitHub Release — listing the exact `repository@sha256:…` digest of the API, web, portal and binaries images. `.env.example` now ships the four `BREEZE_*_IMAGE_REF` variables as `@sha256:replace-with-signed-release-digest` placeholders rather than `:${BREEZE_VERSION}` tags, so a fresh install pins to verified digests and a GHCR tag or package page is never the authorization source.

- **Guided installer:** `guided-setup.sh` downloads the inventory for the release you pick, verifies its signature against `RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS`, and fills the four image refs itself. Verification is fail-closed: if it cannot download or verify the inventory, no image is pulled. The installer refuses a release older than 0.112.0, or a version that is not an exact release, because release signatures do not cover those images. To install one anyway, for example a locally built image tag, pass `--allow-unverified-release`. The installer then warns and uses its unverified image tags. To upgrade later, fetch the current script and run `bash guided-setup.sh --upgrade [VERSION]` (copies downloaded before `--upgrade` was added do not have it). It runs the same verification for the target release, backs up `.env`, rewrites `BREEZE_VERSION` and the four refs together, then pulls and restarts.
- **Manual setup:** resolve the digests yourself with the verifier script that ships with the release, then copy the four lines it emits into `.env`:

```bash
  TAG=v0.112.0   # the release you are pinning
  curl -fsSLO https://github.com/lanternops/breeze/releases/download/$TAG/release-artifact-manifest.json
  curl -fsSLO https://github.com/lanternops/breeze/releases/download/$TAG/release-artifact-manifest.json.ed25519
  curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lanternops/breeze/$TAG/scripts/release/verify-release-images.sh
  RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS="$(grep '^RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)" \
    bash verify-release-images.sh \
      --manifest release-artifact-manifest.json \
      --signature release-artifact-manifest.json.ed25519 \
      --expected-repository lanternops/breeze \
      --expected-release "$TAG" \
      --emit-env images.env
  cat images.env   # BREEZE_API_IMAGE_REF=…@sha256:…, and the web, portal and binaries refs
```

  Repeat this on every upgrade — a digest pin does not follow `BREEZE_VERSION`, so bumping the version alone changes nothing until the four refs are updated too. Keep `BREEZE_VERSION` in step with the pinned release: it still selects the agent release your fleet is offered. `guided-setup.sh --work-dir <dir> --env-file <file> --upgrade [VERSION]` automates these steps for a manual install as well. Since v0.119.0, once your Compose file no longer sets `APP_VERSION` (see [APP_VERSION comes from the image](/deploy/upgrades/#v01190--app_version-comes-from-the-image)), the API logs a `[version]` warning at startup when `BREEZE_VERSION` and the running image differ, and shows it under **Administration → System → Connections**.
- **Existing installs** whose `.env` still carries the older `ghcr.io/lanternops/breeze/api:${BREEZE_VERSION}` form keep working; the upgrade guide's `docker compose pull` line is unchanged for them. Switching to digest pins is recommended but not required.

**Rotating the manifest signing key is a fleet re-enrollment:**
  `RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS` is also the key every enrolled agent pins for its own update manifests, and there is no remote revocation yet — an agent enrolled under the old key keeps trusting it and never learns the new one. Treat a rotation as re-enrolling the fleet; see [Binary Distribution](/deploy/binaries/) and [Key rotation](/deploy/sign-your-own-packages/#key-rotation).

sections.heading: Resource Tuning
sections.text:
Override default resource limits via environment variables:

```bash
# Redis memory limit (default: 256mb)
REDIS_MAXMEMORY=512mb
```

sections.heading: Redis Authentication
sections.text:
Redis password authentication is **required in production**. The API will refuse to start if `REDIS_URL` doesn't carry a password. The secret-generation loop above already produces `REDIS_PASSWORD`; pair it with a `REDIS_URL` that uses it:

```bash
REDIS_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
REDIS_URL=redis://:${REDIS_PASSWORD}@redis:6379
```

The `docker-compose.yml` passes `REDIS_PASSWORD` to the Redis container automatically. See [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/) for details.

sections.heading: Updating
sections.text:
```bash
cd breeze
git pull origin main
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d
```

Pre-built images are pulled from GHCR. Database migrations run automatically on startup.

  For zero-downtime upgrades, see [Upgrade Guide](/deploy/upgrades/).

title: Rollout Modes & Compatibility Switches
description: Why Breeze asks you to set upgrade-mode variables explicitly, what each one does, and which ones you still need to close out after a release.
headings: What you still owe after an upgrade

sections.text:
Some Breeze releases add environment variables that the API **refuses to boot
without** in production, and a few compose files fail before the container even
starts. This page explains why they exist, so you can set them with confidence
rather than copying a value and hoping.

sections.heading: The problem they solve
sections.text:
A security fix usually cannot be switched on the moment its code is deployed.
While you are upgrading, two versions of Breeze are running at once — or a fleet
of agents is running a mix of old and new builds. For that window, the *only*
safe behaviour is the permissive one: keep accepting the old format, or the
upgrade itself breaks working sessions.

Once the upgrade finishes, the permissive behaviour becomes the liability. Now
the safe behaviour is the strict one.

So there are two correct values, and which one is correct depends on where you
are in the rollout — something Breeze cannot reliably detect from inside a single
process. Rather than guess, it asks.

That is the whole design rule: **when no default is safe in both states, Breeze
makes the operator state which state they are in.** Where a safe default *does*
exist, the variable is optional and defaults to the safe value. You will see both
kinds below.

sections.heading: Four kinds of switch
sections.text:
Not every mode variable behaves the same way, and the difference tells you what
follow-up you owe.

| Kind | What it means | Follow-up |
|---|---|---|
| **Transition** | Two values; you move from the compatible one to the strict one once a drain completes | **Yes** — you are not done until you flip it |
| **Operational** | A valve you open and close whenever operations require it | No — it has a normal steady state |
| **Attestation** | You are declaring a fact about your infrastructure | No — it only changes if your infrastructure changes |
| **Opt-in** | Off by default; turning it on is a deliberate security upgrade | Optional, but it is where the benefit lives |

sections.heading: Required in production
sections.text:
These are validated at boot when `NODE_ENV=production` (or `DEPLOYMENT_ENV=staging`).
In development they fall back to safe defaults, so local work is unaffected. The
compose files additionally use `${VAR:?}` for these, which stops the container
before it starts if the value is missing.

sections.heading: `EVENT_PERMISSION_EPOCH_MODE` — transition
sections.text:
`compat` | `enforce` · start at `compat`

Permission changes now take effect immediately rather than at the next token
refresh, by stamping a permissions epoch onto event-WebSocket tickets. Servers
that predate this release emit tickets with no epoch.

- `compat` accepts those older tickets — required while any old server is still writing.
- `enforce` rejects them.

Flip to `enforce` at least 60 seconds after the last old server stops. Set it to
`enforce` too early during a rolling deploy and you reject live tickets from
servers that have not been replaced yet.

If this value fails to parse, Breeze falls back to `enforce` — the closed mode.
A typo fails secure, not open.

sections.heading: `REMOTE_WS_AUTH_MODE` — transition
sections.text:
`post_upgrade` | `pre_upgrade` · start at `post_upgrade`

Controls whether remote-session tickets minted by pre-upgrade servers are still
accepted. `post_upgrade` accepts them; `pre_upgrade` rejects them and applies the
full authorization checks before the WebSocket upgrade.

Stay on `post_upgrade` until every legacy viewer token has expired — that is a
full viewer-token lifetime (2 hours) after the last old issuer stops, then one
further ticket lifetime (60 seconds). The waits are sequential and cannot be
inferred from "the deploy finished."

sections.heading: `REMOTE_ACCESS_ADMISSION_MODE` — operational
sections.text:
`open` | `closed` · steady state `open`

The remote-access barrier. `closed` makes every terminal, desktop, VNC and tunnel
endpoint return `503` at the proxy, before any request reaches the API.

This is not a migration setting — it is a valve you will use again. You close it
during the lease cutover described in the [Upgrade Guide](/deploy/upgrades/#remote-access-lease-cutover),
and any time you need remote traffic stopped for maintenance.

sections.heading: `REMOTE_WS_REDIS_TOPOLOGY` — attestation
sections.text:
`standalone-single-primary` · the only accepted value

Remote sessions coordinate ownership through an atomic Redis lease, so exactly one
server owns a session at a time. That guarantee only holds on a single primary.
Under asynchronous replication a failover can promote a replica that has not yet
seen the latest lease write, leaving two servers each convinced they own the same
session — which means two technicians could drive the same machine.

You are asserting that your Redis is a standalone single primary with AOF enabled,
`maxmemory-policy noeviction`, and cluster mode disabled. A runtime topology monitor
independently checks this and **freezes remote admission** if reality disagrees, so
the variable is your declaration and the monitor is the verification.

If you run Redis Sentinel, Redis Cluster, or a managed Redis with automatic
failover, remote access will refuse to admit sessions. This is deliberate, not a
bug. Everything else in Breeze continues to work normally. Move Redis to a single
primary before upgrading if you need remote access.

sections.heading: Opt-in, off by default
sections.text:
These ship disabled. Nothing changes on upgrade; each is a separate decision with
its own rollout procedure.

sections.heading: `AGENT_MTLS_BINDING_MODE`
sections.text:
`off` (default) | `audit` | `enforce`

Whether the edge certificate assertion is checked against the device's certificate
history. `audit` computes and counts the decision without ever denying; `enforce`
denies a mismatch. Requires a validating proxy in front of the API — leave `off` if
you do not have one. Never inferred from `NODE_ENV`, `IS_HOSTED`, or your Cloudflare
settings. See [mTLS](/security/mtls/).

sections.heading: `MANAGED_SOFTWARE_POLICY_MODE`
sections.text:
`compat` (default) | `enforce`

In `compat`, a private download destination still requires an upgraded agent and
fails closed, while an apparently-public destination is still permitted to an agent
that has not been upgraded yet — so deploy day does not break in-flight software
pushes. In `enforce`, every managed-software command requires an upgraded agent.

Check your count of not-yet-upgraded devices before flipping. In `enforce` they are
denied every managed-software command.

sections.heading: `AGENT_REQUIRE_MANIFEST_SIGNING_KEY_ID`
sections.text:
`false` (default) | `true`

Requires agent update manifests to carry a signing key ID. Only set `true` once
every update response includes one — watch the missing-ID count sit at zero for
seven consecutive days across every active server version first.

This is not a fleet-wide switch. An agent on a capable build applies the pushed
value at its next update check; older builds ignore it entirely and keep accepting
manifests without an ID.

sections.heading: `DEVICE_METRICS_RETENTION_DAYS`
sections.text:
`30` (default) · clamped to 1–365

`device_metrics` is the raw one-row-per-heartbeat series. It previously had no
retention and grew without bound. A retention worker now prunes it in batches.

Your history charts are unaffected — they are served from `metric_rollups`, which
has always had its own separate retention. What this bounds is raw per-heartbeat
detail.

On the first run after upgrading, everything older than the retention window is
pruned. If you need to keep more than 30 days of raw metrics, set this **before**
starting the new version.

sections.heading: What you still owe after an upgrade
sections.text:
Deploying the code is not the same as getting the protection. After a release that
introduces transition switches, two items stay on your list until closed:

1. `EVENT_PERMISSION_EPOCH_MODE` → `enforce`, once old writers have drained.
2. `REMOTE_WS_AUTH_MODE` → `pre_upgrade`, once the viewer-token and ticket waits have elapsed.

The opt-in switches above are where the remaining security benefit lives. Each has
its own gate, and none of them should be flipped on upgrade day.

title: Sign Your Own Agent Packages
description: Sign official Breeze agent releases with your own Windows and macOS certificates using the breeze-selfhost-signing template.
headings: What you'll have at the end
Part 1 — Azure Artifact Signing from zero
4. App registration + GitHub OIDC federated credential
Part 5 — Point your instance at your builds
Migration flow for an existing fleet

sections.text:
Self-hosted Breeze deployments sign the official agent packages with **their
own** code-signing certificates. LanternOps publishes every release's build
outputs *unsigned* alongside a cryptographically signed manifest; the
[`breeze-selfhost-signing`](https://github.com/lanternops/breeze-selfhost-signing)
template repository turns those into fully signed Windows and macOS packages
under your identity — no fork, no build environment, no Windows or Mac
hardware of your own. For how official releases are signed, see
[Code Signing](/deploy/code-signing/).

---

sections.heading: Why signing matters
sections.text:
An RMM agent installs silently, runs as SYSTEM/root, and captures screens —
exactly the profile operating systems and AV engines are paranoid about.
Unsigned agent packages mean SmartScreen interception on every Windows
install, Gatekeeper refusal on macOS, and elevated AV false-positive rates.
Signing *once per release* also matters: reputation systems score the
certificate **and the file hash**, so a stable signed artifact accrues trust
where per-download re-signing never could.

sections.heading: What you'll have at the end
sections.text:
- A private GitHub repo (from the template) that signs each Breeze release
  with one button press and publishes it as `v<version>` on that repo.
- Signed + timestamped Windows `breeze-agent.msi` and component exes; signed,
  notarized, stapled macOS pkgs and `Breeze Installer.app`.
- Your own Ed25519-signed release manifest that your Breeze API verifies
  end-to-end.
- Your instance pulling from your repo via `BINARY_GITHUB_REPOSITORY`,
  with agents updating through the existing per-deployment trust chain.

sections.heading: Cost and time expectations
sections.text:
| Item | Cost | Lead time |
|---|---|---|
| Azure Artifact Signing (formerly Trusted Signing), Basic tier | ~US$9.99/mo | Identity validation typically takes **1–7 business days**; available to organizations and, in the US and Canada, individuals |
| Apple Developer Program | US$99/yr | Enrollment usually 1–2 days (D-U-N-S lookup can add time for organizations) |
| GitHub Actions | Free minutes generally suffice (one run per Breeze release) | — |

sections.heading: Choosing a Windows signing path
sections.text:
Adapted from the maintainer decision matrix in
`docs/signing/WINDOWS_INSTALLER_SIGNING.md`:

| Option | Fit | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Azure Artifact Signing** (recommended) | Most self-hosters | No hardware token, HSM-backed keys, OIDC from GitHub Actions, cheap. The template's default mode. |
| **CA cloud-signing service** (DigiCert KeyLocker, SSL.com eSigner, …) | Orgs already invested in a CA | Works in principle (they expose `signtool`-compatible flows) but is **not wired into the template in v1** — you would adapt the PFX steps yourself. |
| **PFX file** | Legacy / internal PKI **only** | Since June 2023 the CA/B Forum requires publicly trusted code-signing keys to live in hardware modules, so newly issued OV certs are generally **not exportable** as PFX. Use only with an internal enterprise CA whose root your fleet already trusts. |

**SmartScreen is not instant:**
  A valid signature is necessary but not sufficient. SmartScreen reputation
  ramps per certificate and per file hash over days-to-weeks of installs.
  Expect "Windows protected your PC" on early installs of a brand-new
  certificate — see [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

---

sections.heading: Part 1 — Azure Artifact Signing from zero
sections.text:
You will create four things: an Artifact Signing account, a validated
identity, a certificate profile, and an Entra app registration with a GitHub
OIDC federated credential.

sections.heading: 1. Create the Artifact Signing account
sections.text:
1. In the [Azure portal](https://portal.azure.com), search for **Artifact
   Signing** (formerly *Trusted Signing*) and select **Create**.

2. Pick your subscription and a resource group, an **account name** (this
   becomes the `AZURE_SIGNING_ACCOUNT_NAME` secret), and a region. Note the
   region's endpoint URL, e.g. `https://eus.codesigning.azure.net` for East
   US — this becomes `AZURE_SIGNING_ENDPOINT`.

3. Select the **Basic** SKU and create the account.

sections.heading: 2. Complete identity validation
sections.text:
1. In your Artifact Signing account, open **Identity validations** →
   **New identity** → **Public**.

2. Enter your legal organization name, registration number, and address
   exactly as legally registered. For US/Canada individuals, choose the
   individual flow and complete the identity-verification session.

3. Submit and wait. Validation is performed by Microsoft's verification
   partner and typically completes in 1–7 business days; you'll get email
   updates. You cannot create a certificate profile until the identity shows
   **Completed**.

sections.heading: 3. Create a certificate profile
sections.text:
1. In the account, open **Certificate profiles** → **Create** →
   **Public Trust**.

2. Name the profile (this becomes `AZURE_CERT_PROFILE`) and bind it to your
   completed identity validation. The generated certificates are short-lived
   and rotated by Azure automatically — nothing to renew.

sections.heading: 4. App registration + GitHub OIDC federated credential
sections.text:
1. In **Microsoft Entra ID** → **App registrations** → **New registration**,
   create an app (e.g. `breeze-selfhost-signing`). Record the **Application
   (client) ID** (`AZURE_CLIENT_ID`) and **Directory (tenant) ID**
   (`AZURE_TENANT_ID`).

2. In the app: **Certificates & secrets** → **Federated credentials** →
   **Add credential** → scenario **GitHub Actions deploying Azure
   resources**. Enter your GitHub org, the signing repo name, and entity type
   **Environment** with value `signing` (the workflow's signing jobs run in
   the `signing` environment). No client secret is created — the workflow
   authenticates with short-lived OIDC tokens.

3. Back in the Artifact Signing account: **Access control (IAM)** → **Add
   role assignment** → role **Trusted Signing Certificate Profile Signer** →
   assign to the app registration's service principal.

---

sections.heading: 1. Enroll and create certificates
sections.text:
1. Enroll in the [Apple Developer Program](https://developer.apple.com/programs/enroll/)
   (US$99/yr). Organizations need a D-U-N-S number; the legal entity name
   becomes the publisher string users see.

2. In [Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles](https://developer.apple.com/account/resources/certificates/list),
   create **two** certificates: **Developer ID Application** (signs the
   binaries and the Installer.app) and **Developer ID Installer** (signs the
   `.pkg` files). Generate the CSRs in Keychain Access on any Mac
   (Certificate Assistant → Request a Certificate From a Certificate
   Authority), or via `openssl` if you have no Mac.

3. Install both certificates into the same Keychain Access keychain, select
   the two certificates **with their private keys**, and export as a single
   `.p12` with a strong password.

sections.heading: 2. App-specific password for notarization
sections.text:
1. Sign in at [account.apple.com](https://account.apple.com) with the Apple
   ID that belongs to (or is invited to) your developer team.

2. Under **Sign-In and Security** → **App-Specific Passwords**, generate one
   (label it e.g. `breeze-notarytool`). This is the `APPLE_PASSWORD` secret —
   notarization does not accept your account password, and the template does
   not support App Store Connect API keys in v1.

3. Find your 10-character **Team ID** under
   [Membership details](https://developer.apple.com/account#MembershipDetailsCard)
   (`APPLE_TEAM_ID`).

Compute the secret values:

```bash
base64 -i developer-id-export.p12 | pbcopy   # -> APPLE_CERTIFICATE
security find-identity -v -p codesigning     # copy the exact strings for
                                             # APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY, e.g.
                                             # "Developer ID Application: Example Org (ABCDE12345)"
```

`APPLE_INSTALLER_IDENTITY` is the matching
`Developer ID Installer: Example Org (ABCDE12345)` string (installer
identities don't appear under `-p codesigning`; use
`security find-identity -v` and pick the Installer entry).

---

sections.heading: Part 3 — Create your signing repo
sections.text:
1. Open [`lanternops/breeze-selfhost-signing`](https://github.com/lanternops/breeze-selfhost-signing)
   and click **Use this template** → **Create a new repository**. Private is
   fine — the workflow only reads public official releases.

2. Clone it and run `./scripts/generate-manifest-key.sh`. Store the printed
   PEM as the `RELEASE_MANIFEST_ED25519_PRIVATE_KEY` Actions secret and keep
   the printed `RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS` line for Part 5. Only
   the private key is ever stored; the workflow re-derives the public key on
   every run.

3. Create a GitHub **Environment** named `signing`
   (Settings → Environments) and add yourself as a **required reviewer**.
   The workflow's signing jobs run in this environment, so every run that
   can touch your certificates waits for your approval. Add the secrets to
   this environment (or as repository secrets if you skip the reviewer
   gate).

4. Add the platform secrets from Parts 1–2. The full tables live in the
   template's README: Azure mode needs `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`, `AZURE_TENANT_ID`,
   `AZURE_SIGNING_ENDPOINT`, `AZURE_SIGNING_ACCOUNT_NAME`,
   `AZURE_CERT_PROFILE`; macOS needs `APPLE_CERTIFICATE`,
   `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD`, `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY`,
   `APPLE_INSTALLER_IDENTITY`, `APPLE_ID`, `APPLE_PASSWORD`,
   `APPLE_TEAM_ID`.

5. Validate the plumbing with a **dry run**: Actions → *Sign Breeze
   Release* → Run workflow → set `dry-run: true` and a current Breeze
   version. A dry run downloads and verifies the official inputs and builds
   the MSI/pkgs/app with signing stubbed — it needs **no secrets and no
   certificates**, so you can do this before paying anyone. Your manifest
   key is never used on a dry run either: the manifest is signed with a
   throwaway key generated in-run, so the resulting bundle (uploaded as
   `dry-run-unsigned-assets`) is exactly what its name says and cannot be
   mistaken for a release. Note that dry runs still run in the `signing`
   environment, so if you configured required reviewers they must approve
   the run before it starts.

---

sections.heading: Part 4 — Run the workflow
sections.text:
Dispatch **Sign Breeze Release** with the version from the official release
you want (e.g. `0.106.0` — no leading `v`). What each job does:

| Job | What it does |
|---|---|
| `validate` | Checks the version and enum inputs, and refuses to overwrite an existing `v<version>` release on your repo (signing must happen once per release so reputation accrues on a stable hash). |
| `windows` | Verifies the official manifest against the committed official key, pins the tag to the manifest's `sourceCommit`, checks out the Breeze build scripts at that commit, downloads + hash-verifies the four unsigned exes, signs them (Azure Artifact Signing or PFX), builds the MSI with WiX, signs the MSI, then asserts every output carries a signer **and an RFC3161 timestamp** and records that result as a signing attestation. |
