| `macos` | Same verify preamble; imports your `.p12` into an ephemeral keychain (deleted even on failure), codesigns all eight darwin binaries with hardened runtime + the repo's entitlements, notarizes them, builds both pkgs, `productsign`s, notarizes + staples, builds `Breeze Installer.app` from source around **your** pkgs, signs/notarizes/staples it, then verifies with `codesign --verify --strict`, `pkgutil --check-signature`, and `spctl -a -t install`. The package check requires the exact configured Developer ID Installer leaf identity and Team ID and records both in the signing attestation. |
| `publish` | Mirrors the never-signed official assets (Linux agent/backup/watchdog, viewer, helper, `latest.json` — each hash-verified against the official manifest), generates **your** `release-artifact-manifest.json` (+ `.ed25519` signed with your manifest key), writes `checksums.txt`, and creates release `v<version>` on your repo. The run summary prints the exact env block for Part 5. |

**One run per version — a partial run consumes it:**
  A successful run publishes `v<version>` and every later run for that
  version is refused, so a signature never changes under a hash the world
  has already seen. The corollary: running with `platforms: windows` or
  `platforms: macos` **claims the version**. You cannot add the other
  platform afterwards without deleting the release in the GitHub UI first.
  Use `platforms: all` unless you specifically want a single-platform
  release.

**How `platformTrust` is decided:**
  The manifest never infers trust from a filename. Each asset's
  `platformTrust` comes either from the platform job's signing attestation
  (something ran `codesign` / `Get-AuthenticodeSignature` on those exact
  bytes) or, for mirrored assets, from the already-verified official
  manifest. `publish` refuses to build a manifest covering an asset that
  neither accounts for — so a component that slips past a signing step
  fails the run instead of being published as "signed". Package entries also
  carry `signingIdentity` and `signingTeamId`, copied only from the macOS
  runner's exact leaf-certificate check. Every generated entry also carries
  `edition: "self-host"`, including unsigned dry-run evidence manifests.

**Verifying outputs locally:**
  Windows: `Get-AuthenticodeSignature .\breeze-agent.msi` should report your
  organization as signer (Status `Valid`, or `UnknownError` on a machine that
  hasn't yet cached the Azure Artifact Signing root — that status still means
  "signed"). macOS: `pkgutil --check-signature breeze-agent-darwin-arm64.pkg`
  and `spctl -a -vv -t install breeze-agent-darwin-arm64.pkg` should show
  your Developer ID and `source=Notarized Developer ID`. Then install the MSI
  and pkg on clean test VMs before promoting to your fleet.

---

sections.heading: Part 5 — Point your instance at your builds
T1 (recommended): repointed GitHub mode
sections.text:
Add to your instance `.env`:

```bash
BINARY_SOURCE=github
BINARY_GITHUB_REPOSITORY=your-org/your-signing-repo
BINARY_VERSION=0.106.0        # the version you signed (or rely on BREEZE_VERSION)
RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS=<your raw base64 key from Part 3>
AGENT_AUTO_PROMOTE=false      # recommended during first adoption
```

**And map every one of them** in your compose file's `api` service — a value
in `.env` alone never reaches the container:

```yaml
  api:
    environment:
      BINARY_SOURCE: ${BINARY_SOURCE:-github}
      BINARY_GITHUB_REPOSITORY: ${BINARY_GITHUB_REPOSITORY:-}
      BINARY_VERSION: ${BINARY_VERSION:-}
      RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS: ${RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS}
      AGENT_AUTO_PROMOTE: ${AGENT_AUTO_PROMOTE:-true}
```

See the [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/) reference for the full
deployment configuration.

**The key must be YOURS:**
  In production, overriding `BINARY_GITHUB_REPOSITORY` requires
  `RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS` to be set explicitly — and it must
  be **your** manifest key, not the official Breeze key. The official key
  cannot verify your releases; leaving it in place fails closed at sync time.

On restart, the API fetches your release, verifies your manifest, registers
the binaries, and re-signs update manifests with its **per-deployment key** —
agents keep trusting the same deployment key they pinned at enrollment, so no
agent-side changes are needed.

sections.heading: T2: local mode
sections.text:
Download your signed release assets and drop them into the API's binary
directories (`AGENT_BINARY_DIR`, `VIEWER_BINARY_DIR`, `HELPER_BINARY_DIR`)
with `BINARY_SOURCE=local`. See [Binary Distribution](/deploy/binaries/) for
directory layout and S3 offload. Also stage your original signed
`release-artifact-manifest.json` and `.ed25519` signature at the parent of
`AGENT_BINARY_DIR`, configure your manifest public key, and set
`BINARY_GITHUB_REPOSITORY` to the repository named by that manifest. macOS
installer delivery fails closed if the pair is absent, invalid, or describes a
different edition. This mode costs manual downloads per release.

sections.heading: Migration flow for an existing fleet
sections.text:
1. Set `AGENT_AUTO_PROMOTE=false` **before** the switch, so registering your
   release does not instantly become the fleet upgrade target.

2. Apply the T1 env changes and restart the API. Watch the logs for the
   sync: every platform/arch your fleet uses must register successfully
   (a missing asset here means a skipped platform in your signing run).

3. Verify a manual download of each platform installer from your instance,
   install on a test device, confirm it enrolls and heartbeats.

4. Promote explicitly with `POST /agent-versions/promote`. This is an
   API-only action — there is no UI for it — and it requires a platform
   admin **with MFA**. See
   [Controlled agent fleet rollout](/deploy/upgrades/#controlled-agent-fleet-rollout)
   for the exact call. Existing agents upgrade to your signed build like any
   normal version promotion.

sections.heading: Optional hardening
sections.text:
`AGENT_REQUIRE_MANIFEST_SIGNING_KEY_ID=true` makes agents refuse update
manifests that don't name an explicit trusted key, removing the embedded
official key as a possible update signer.

Enable it only once the missing-ID count has sat at **zero for seven
consecutive days across every active server version** — the same gate as
any other instance. See
[`AGENT_REQUIRE_MANIFEST_SIGNING_KEY_ID`](/deploy/rollout-modes/#agent_require_manifest_signing_key_id).

**This is not a fleet-wide switch:**
  Agents on a capable build apply the pushed value at their next update
  check; **older builds ignore it entirely** and keep accepting manifests
  without a key ID. Turning it on does not harden the agents that have not
  yet upgraded through your instance, so do not read a successful flip as
  "the fleet is now hardened". The rollout runbook is
  `docs/operations/agent-network-and-manifest-rollout.md`.

sections.heading: Key rotation
sections.text:
**Rotation adds trust — it doesn't remove it:**
  Agents pin the manifest public key(s) they were installed or last enrolled
  under (`RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS`). Generating a new manifest
  key and updating your instance's env var adds trust in the new key, but
  agents that enrolled under the retired key keep trusting that key too —
  there is no remote mechanism today to revoke it from already-enrolled
  agents. Treat a rotation as a fleet re-enrollment: afterwards, reinstall or
  re-enroll your fleet so agents pin only the current key, and keep the
  retired private key protected as a long-lived secret (or destroy it)
  rather than assuming rotation alone retires it. A signed key-retirement
  mechanism is planned so a future rotation won't require a full
  re-enrollment — no timeline yet.

---

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**SmartScreen still warns after signing.**
Expected at first. Reputation accrues per certificate and per file hash;
a brand-new Azure Artifact Signing identity starts near zero. It clears
after enough real installs — typically days to a few weeks. Verify the
signature is actually present (`Get-AuthenticodeSignature`) and keep the
release stable (never re-sign an already-published version; the workflow
enforces this).

**`UnknownError` from `Get-AuthenticodeSignature`.**
The file *is* signed; the machine just hasn't chained to the Azure Artifact
Signing root yet. The workflow treats this status as success with a warning,
matching the official pipeline.

**Notarization rejected (`status: Invalid`).**
The workflow prints the full `notarytool log` on failure. The most common
causes: the `.p12` is missing the private key (re-export from Keychain
Access with the key selected), the Apple ID isn't a member of the team in
`APPLE_TEAM_ID`, or `APPLE_PASSWORD` is an account password instead of an
app-specific password.

**Manifest verification failed / `sourceCommit` mismatch.**
The template refuses to run when the official manifest signature doesn't
verify or the release tag no longer points at the manifest's recorded
commit. Both indicate the official release changed after publication —
do not work around this; check the official repository's security
announcements and open an issue.

**Trying to sign a release from before BYO-signing support.**
The run stops in the `verify-official-release` step with
`manifest has no valid sourceCommit — this Breeze release predates
BYO-signing support`. Unsigned signing inputs ship with Breeze releases
from the BYO-signing release onward; you cannot self-sign releases older
than that. (The related `asset <name> is not present in the signed
manifest` means the release *is* recent enough but is missing an asset the
workflow expects — check the official release page for a partial upload.)

**Your API refuses to sync your release.**
Check that `RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS` is your key (raw base64,
44 chars), that it's mapped in the compose `environment:` block, and that
`BINARY_VERSION`/`BREEZE_VERSION` matches a release that exists on your
signing repo.

**AV flags your signed agent.**
Some engines flag new publishers regardless of signature. Add the
recommended exclusions per platform — see
[Antivirus Exceptions](/deploy/antivirus-exceptions/) — and submit
false-positive reports with your signed binaries; a stable hash makes those
reports effective.

---

sections.heading: Viewer and Helper apps
sections.text:
The technician-side Viewer and Helper (Tauri) apps are mirrored from the
official release as-is. If you want to sign those under your identity too,
the relevant official jobs are `build-viewer`,
`sign-windows-tauri-sslcom` (`sign-windows-tauri` is the gate that asserts it
ran and succeeded),
`build-viewer-macos`, and `build-helper-macos` in
`.github/workflows/release.yml` — that path is closer to a fork than to this
template, and Gatekeeper's right-click-open flow is generally tolerable for
technician tooling.

sections.heading: PFX mode details
sections.text:
`signing-mode: pfx` signs with `signtool sign /fd SHA256 /tr <timestamp> /td
SHA256` using `WINDOWS_PFX_BASE64` + `WINDOWS_PFX_PASSWORD`, with the
timestamp server overridable via the `PFX_TIMESTAMP_URL` repository
variable. It exists for internal-PKI deployments (your enterprise CA root is
already in your fleet's trust store via GPO/MDM). It is **not** a path to
public trust: publicly trusted code-signing keys must live in HSMs, so a
file-based key either predates that rule or is internal-only. SmartScreen
reputation never accrues for internal CAs — pair PFX mode with the
[AV exclusions](/deploy/antivirus-exceptions/) and GPO trust configuration.

sections.heading: MSI product identity
sections.text:
The Windows MSI this template builds carries the **self-hosted edition**
identity: `ProductName` "Breeze Agent (Self-Hosted)" and its own permanent
`UpgradeCode`, distinct from the `ProductName` "Breeze Agent" that
hosted-distribution builds use. The two identities can never install over
each other — that's intentional. The self-hosted `UpgradeCode` is what your
fleet's upgrade lineage tracks, and it matches the public unsigned self-host
MSI Breeze publishes with each release, so signing your own copy here keeps
your fleet on the same upgrade lineage rather than forking it. Signing a
release from before this edition parameter existed builds the original
("Breeze Agent") identity, matching what that release actually shipped.

sections.heading: Relationship to the fork path
sections.text:
This template signs **official, unmodified** Breeze builds — your
organization appears as publisher on Breeze-branded software, which is
expected and documented. If you need your own branding (product name,
identifiers, icons), that is the fork path: see Model B in
`docs/signing/ARTIFACT_SIGNING_OPERATIONS.md` in the repository.

title: TLS & Reverse Proxy
description: Configure TLS and reverse proxying for Breeze RMM with Caddy or Nginx, including certificates, WebSocket proxying, and security headers.
headings: Internal CA for domains Let's Encrypt cannot reach
Trusting the internal CA on agents
Troubleshooting: remote tools time out / event socket returns 400 behind your own proxy

sections.heading: Caddy (Default)
sections.text: Breeze ships with Caddy as the default reverse proxy. It automatically provisions TLS certificates from Let's Encrypt.

sections.heading: Production Caddyfile
sections.text:
Caddy's configuration lives in one canonical file, `docker/Caddyfile.prod`, which every Breeze compose file mounts read-only into the container (`./docker/Caddyfile.prod:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile:ro`) — there is no separate config generated inline, and no other Caddyfile to keep in sync. Edit that file directly if you need to add a route.

Routing is more than a two-way split between `web` and `api`. In match order, the file routes:

| Path | Destination | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `/api/v1/mcp/sse`, `/api/v1/helper/chat/sessions/*/messages`, `/api/v1/ai/sessions/*/stream` | `api:3001` | SSE/streaming — no compression, no buffering |
| `/api/v1/auth/billing-init` | `billing:3002` | Billing auth init |
| `/activate/complete`, `/activate/*` (with a `status` query) | `web:4321` | Account-activation pages |
| `/oauth/consent`, `/oauth/consent/*` | `web:4321` | OAuth consent UI — matched before the API's `/oauth/*` block |
| `/oauth/*`, the OAuth `.well-known` endpoints | `api:3001` | OAuth provider (authorize, token, registration, discovery) |
| `/billing/invoices*`, `/billing/quotes*` | `web:4321` | MSP invoicing/quotes UI — matched before the billing sidecar |
| `/billing`, `/billing/*` | `billing:3002` | Hosted billing UI sidecar |
| `/portal`, `/portal/*` | `portal:4322` | Customer portal |
| `/api/*`, `/s/*`, `/health*`, `/ready`, `/metrics/*`, `/i/*` | `api:3001` | General API traffic. Also normalizes the client-certificate assertion headers used by agent mTLS — see [Certificate Pinning & mTLS](/security/mtls/) |
| everything else | `web:4321` | Dashboard (catch-all) |

The same security headers shown below are set globally on every response.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.text:
1. Set `BREEZE_DOMAIN` and `ACME_EMAIL` in your `.env.prod`
2. Ensure port 80 and 443 are open and DNS points to your server
3. Caddy requests a certificate from Let's Encrypt on first start
4. Certificates auto-renew 30 days before expiry

sections.heading: Internal CA for domains Let's Encrypt cannot reach
sections.text:
If your Breeze domain is an internal name that only resolves on your LAN or VPN, or a host whose ports 80 and 443 are not open to the internet, Let's Encrypt cannot validate it. Left alone, the failed certificate order aborts the TLS handshake and the browser reports `ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR` with nothing to click through — which reads like a broken deployment rather than a certificate problem.

Set `CADDY_LOCAL_CERTS` to the literal value `local_certs` and Caddy issues from its own internal certificate authority instead of trying Let's Encrypt:

```bash
# .env.prod
CADDY_LOCAL_CERTS=local_certs
```

Browsers will warn on the self-issued certificate until you trust the internal root on each client machine. Export it with:

```bash
docker compose exec caddy cat /data/caddy/pki/authorities/local/root.crt
```

Leave the variable empty for any internet-reachable deployment. You do not need it for `localhost` or a bare IP address, which Caddy already self-signs.

sections.heading: Trusting the internal CA on agents
sections.text:
Browsers are not the only clients that must trust a self-issued certificate. The Breeze agent, the Windows install one-liner and the MSI all verify the server certificate against the operating system's trust store, exactly like a browser. Until the endpoint trusts your internal root, every install fails before the agent enrolls:

| Install path | What you see |
|---|---|
| Windows MSI | *"There is a problem with this Windows Installer package. A program run as part of the setup did not finish as expected."* The agent's own message, which names the certificate problem, is in `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\logs\enroll-last-error.txt` and in the Windows Application event log (source `BreezeAgent`) |
| Windows PowerShell one-liner | `Breeze: this machine rejected the TLS certificate of … (… UntrustedRoot)`. The text in parentheses is the reason Windows gave: `UntrustedRoot` means the CA is not trusted, while `RemoteCertificateNameMismatch` means the server URL does not match a name on the certificate. Older copies of the one-liner show `Could not establish trust relationship for the SSL/TLS secure channel` instead |
| macOS / Linux one-liner | `curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: self-signed certificate` or `unable to get local issuer certificate` |
| `breeze-agent enroll` | `Enrollment failed: the TLS certificate presented by … is not trusted by this machine` |

The fix is to trust the CA on each endpoint, not to turn verification off. Breeze has no option to skip certificate verification, and none is planned. An agent that accepts any certificate would hand its enrollment secret and device token to anyone who can intercept the connection.

1. Export the root certificate from the server. Trust the root, not the site certificate: Caddy renews the site certificate and its intermediate often, but the root stays the same.

```bash
   docker compose exec caddy cat /data/caddy/pki/authorities/local/root.crt > breeze-root.crt
```

   The same file covers a bare IP address or `localhost`, which Caddy also signs from its internal CA. If you front Breeze with your own proxy and a certificate from your organization's CA, use that CA's root instead.

2. Install it into the **machine** trust store on every endpoint, before you run the installer. The agent runs as `SYSTEM` or `root`, so a per-user store does not work.

     **Windows:**
```powershell
       # Elevated PowerShell
       Import-Certificate -FilePath .\breeze-root.crt -CertStoreLocation Cert:\LocalMachine\Root
```
       To reach a whole fleet, deploy the certificate with Group Policy (**Computer Configuration → Policies → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Public Key Policies → Trusted Root Certification Authorities**) or an Intune trusted-certificate profile.

     **macOS:**
```bash
       sudo security add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot \
         -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain breeze-root.crt
```
       For managed Macs, push the certificate in an MDM configuration profile.

     **Linux:**
```bash
       # Debian / Ubuntu
       sudo cp breeze-root.crt /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/breeze-root.crt
       sudo update-ca-certificates

       # RHEL / Fedora / Rocky / Alma
       sudo cp breeze-root.crt /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/breeze-root.crt
       sudo update-ca-trust
```

3. Run the installer again.

**Keep the Caddy data volume:**
  Caddy generates its internal root once and stores it in its data volume. If that volume is deleted, Caddy creates a new root on the next start, and every enrolled agent loses its connection until you distribute the new root. Back up the volume with the rest of the deployment. A publicly trusted certificate (Let's Encrypt, or a commercial CA with a DNS challenge for internal names) avoids this step completely.

sections.heading: WebSocket Proxying
sections.text:
Caddy automatically handles WebSocket upgrade for:
- Agent connections at `/api/v1/agent-ws/:id/ws`
- Remote desktop / terminal sessions at `/api/v1/remote/sessions/:id/ws`, `/api/v1/desktop-ws/*`, and `/api/v1/tunnel-ws/*`
- The one-time-ticket event stream at `/api/v1/events/ws`

It also disables buffering (but does not upgrade the connection) for the SSE endpoints used by MCP and streaming AI chat: `/api/v1/mcp/sse`, `/api/v1/helper/chat/sessions/*/messages`, and `/api/v1/ai/sessions/*/stream`.

No additional configuration needed.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting: remote tools time out / event socket returns 400 behind your own proxy
Nginx (Alternative)
Security Headers
sections.text:
Both configurations include these security headers:

| Header | Value | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `Strict-Transport-Security` | `max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload` | Force HTTPS for 1 year |
| `X-Content-Type-Options` | `nosniff` | Prevent MIME sniffing |
| `Referrer-Policy` | `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` | Control referrer information. From v0.124.0 the bundled `Caddyfile.prod` sets it as a default only (`?Referrer-Policy`), so the stricter `no-referrer` the application sends on capability URLs (verification pages, public invoices, unsubscribe links) is kept rather than overwritten. If you front Breeze with your own proxy, do not add a `Referrer-Policy` header on those paths. |
| `Permissions-Policy` | `camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=()` | Turn off browser features Breeze never uses. Since v0.125.0 the bundled `Caddyfile.prod` sets it as a default (`?Permissions-Policy`), so static assets that the web application does not handle get it too. |
| `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy` | `same-site` | Stop other sites from loading Breeze pages and assets (v0.125.0+, Caddy only). Set as a default on every path **except** `/api/*`, `/s/*`, `/i/*`, `/activate/*`, `/health*`, `/ready`, `/metrics/*`, `/oauth/*` and `/.well-known/*`, so the public Trust Center badge and branding images stay embeddable on customers' own sites. |

Since v0.125.0 the bundled `Caddyfile.prod` sets `Strict-Transport-Security` and `X-Content-Type-Options` with Caddy's `>` (replace) form, so a response that already carries one from the application is not sent with the header twice. If you maintain your own copy of `Caddyfile.prod`, carry over the `>` form, the `?Permissions-Policy` default and the `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy` block with its path exclusions.

The web application adds its own headers on top of the proxy's. From v0.125.0 HTML pages are sent with `Cache-Control: no-store`, and the `Content-Security-Policy` `connect-src` list is built per request from your configured API and WebSocket hosts, with no plaintext `ws:` in production. If a page needs to reach another origin, add it with `CSP_CONNECT_HOSTS` on the `web` service. See [HTTP Security Headers](/security/overview/#http-security-headers).

title: TURN Server
description: Deploy a dedicated coturn TURN relay for WebRTC remote desktop: server provisioning, firewall rules, relay port sizing, and credential handling.
headings: Configure Breeze to Use External TURN

sections.text:
WebRTC remote desktop and terminal sessions need a TURN relay when a direct peer-to-peer connection is not possible — symmetric NAT, restrictive corporate firewalls, or carrier-grade NAT all prevent direct connections. Without TURN, these sessions will fail for affected users.

The Breeze `docker-compose.yml` includes a bundled coturn container that works when the server has a public IP. However, if your Breeze stack runs behind Cloudflare Tunnel (or any other tunnel/proxy that only handles HTTP), **TURN must run on a separate host** because TURN uses UDP, which tunnels cannot carry.

sections.heading: Architecture Options
sections.text:
| Setup | TURN Location | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| **Bundled** | Same host as Breeze | Server has a public IP with UDP ports open |
| **External** | Dedicated VPS | Breeze is behind Cloudflare Tunnel, NAT, or a load balancer that doesn't pass UDP |

  A dedicated TURN server costs as little as $4/month (512 MB RAM is more than enough). coturn is very lightweight — it just relays UDP packets.

---

sections.heading: External TURN Server Setup
sections.text: This guide uses a DigitalOcean droplet, but any VPS provider (Hetzner, Vultr, Linode, AWS Lightsail) works identically.

sections.heading: Requirements
sections.text:
- A VPS with a **public IPv4 address**
- Ubuntu 22.04+ or Debian 12+
- TCP+UDP ports open: **3478** and **49152–49252** (relay range)
- SSH access

sections.heading: Provision the server
sections.text:
**DigitalOcean CLI:**

```bash
# Generate a TURN shared secret
TURN_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
echo "TURN_SECRET=${TURN_SECRET}"

# Create the droplet
doctl compute droplet create breeze-coturn \
  --region sfo3 \
  --size s-1vcpu-512mb-10gb \
  --image ubuntu-24-04-x64 \
  --ssh-keys YOUR_SSH_KEY_ID \
  --tag-names breeze,coturn \
  --wait
```

**Manual:**

1. Create a 512 MB+ VPS with Ubuntu 24.04
2. Note the public IP address
3. Generate a shared secret: `openssl rand -hex 32`

sections.heading: Install and configure coturn
sections.text:
SSH into the server and run:

```bash
# Install coturn
apt-get update && apt-get install -y coturn

# Enable the service
sed -i 's/^#TURNSERVER_ENABLED=1/TURNSERVER_ENABLED=1/' /etc/default/coturn
```

Write the configuration file:

```bash
cat > /etc/turnserver.conf <<'EOF'
listening-port=3478
tls-listening-port=5349
fingerprint
use-auth-secret
static-auth-secret=YOUR_TURN_SECRET_HERE
realm=breeze.local
relay-threads=2
user-quota=4
total-quota=1000
max-bps=5000000
no-tcp-relay
no-multicast-peers
# Relay only to public peers. Refused: loopback, private/VPC, CGNAT
# (100.64/10, also used by tailnets), link-local (including the cloud metadata
# address 169.254.169.254), documentation/benchmark, 6to4/Teredo, multicast and
# reserved ranges, for IPv4 and IPv6. coturn refuses the unspecified address
# itself. Never list `::` or `0.0.0.0` on its own, or start an IPv6 range at
# `::`: coturn reads an all-zero bound as "no bound", so such an entry refuses
# every peer and no relayed session can connect.
# Never add this relay's own public IP (the external-ip) to this list: when
# both peers are relayed through this server, relay-to-relay traffic targets
# that address and would be refused.
denied-peer-ip=0.0.0.0-0.255.255.255
denied-peer-ip=10.0.0.0-10.255.255.255
denied-peer-ip=100.64.0.0-100.127.255.255
denied-peer-ip=127.0.0.0-127.255.255.255
denied-peer-ip=169.254.0.0-169.254.255.255
denied-peer-ip=172.16.0.0-172.31.255.255
denied-peer-ip=192.0.0.0-192.0.0.255
denied-peer-ip=192.0.2.0-192.0.2.255
denied-peer-ip=192.88.99.0-192.88.99.255
denied-peer-ip=192.168.0.0-192.168.255.255
denied-peer-ip=198.18.0.0-198.19.255.255
denied-peer-ip=198.51.100.0-198.51.100.255
denied-peer-ip=203.0.113.0-203.0.113.255
denied-peer-ip=224.0.0.0-239.255.255.255
denied-peer-ip=240.0.0.0-255.255.255.255
denied-peer-ip=::1
denied-peer-ip=64:ff9b:1::-64:ff9b:1:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff
denied-peer-ip=2001::-2001:1ff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff
denied-peer-ip=2002::-2002:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff
denied-peer-ip=fc00::-fdff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff
denied-peer-ip=fe80::-febf:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff
denied-peer-ip=ff00::-ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff
# IPv4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:0:0/96) and the NAT64 well-known prefix
# (64:ff9b::/96) are IPv6 spellings of IPv4 addresses. No legitimate peer uses
# them, and relay-to-relay is unaffected (it targets the relay's own address).
denied-peer-ip=::ffff:0:0-::ffff:ffff:ffff
denied-peer-ip=64:ff9b::-64:ff9b::ffff:ffff
min-port=49152
max-port=49252
no-cli
log-file=stdout
external-ip=YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_HERE
EOF
```

Replace `YOUR_TURN_SECRET_HERE` and `YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_HERE` with your actual values.

The `denied-peer-ip` lines keep the relay from reaching anything but public
peers: loopback, private/VPC networks, CGNAT and tailnet addresses, link-local
(including the cloud metadata address `169.254.169.254`), multicast and
reserved ranges. `no-tcp-relay` is safe to keep: Breeze's WebRTC sessions only
use UDP relay allocations. Two rules to follow when you adjust the list:

- **Never deny the relay's own public IP** (your `external-ip`). When both
  peers are relayed through this server, relay-to-relay traffic targets that
  address, and denying it breaks those sessions.
- Keep the IPv4-mapped (`::ffff:0:0/96`) and NAT64 (`64:ff9b::/96`) lines.
  They refuse IPv6 spellings of IPv4 addresses, which no legitimate peer uses,
  and they do not affect relay-to-relay traffic.

`tls-listening-port=5349` above does nothing on its own: coturn skips the TLS
listener without complaint unless you also add `cert=` and `pkey=` pointing at
a certificate readable by the user coturn runs as, open TCP 5349 in the
firewall, and set `TURN_TLS_HOST` (the hostname on that certificate) in
Breeze's `.env` so the API advertises `turns:`. Remember that coturn does not
reload the certificate — restart it on every renewal.

Start the service:

```bash
systemctl enable coturn
systemctl restart coturn
systemctl status coturn
```

sections.heading: Configure the firewall
sections.text:
**DigitalOcean Cloud Firewall:**

```bash
doctl compute firewall create \
  --name breeze-coturn-fw \
  --droplet-ids YOUR_DROPLET_ID \
  --inbound-rules "protocol:tcp,ports:22,address:0.0.0.0/0 \
    protocol:tcp,ports:3478,address:0.0.0.0/0 \
    protocol:udp,ports:3478,address:0.0.0.0/0 \
    protocol:tcp,ports:49152-49252,address:0.0.0.0/0 \
    protocol:udp,ports:49152-49252,address:0.0.0.0/0" \
  --outbound-rules "protocol:tcp,ports:all,address:0.0.0.0/0 \
    protocol:udp,ports:all,address:0.0.0.0/0 \
    protocol:icmp,address:0.0.0.0/0"
```

**UFW:**

```bash
ufw allow 22/tcp
ufw allow 3478/tcp
ufw allow 3478/udp
ufw allow 49152:49252/tcp
ufw allow 49152:49252/udp
ufw enable
```

sections.heading: Verify connectivity
sections.text:
From your local machine:

```bash
# Check TCP port is reachable
nc -z -w 3 YOUR_TURN_IP 3478

# Check UDP port is reachable
nc -u -z -w 3 YOUR_TURN_IP 3478

# Check the service is running
ssh root@YOUR_TURN_IP systemctl status coturn
```

---

sections.heading: Configure Breeze to Use External TURN
1. Update `.env`
sections.text:
Add or update these variables in your Breeze `.env` file:

```bash
TURN_HOST=YOUR_TURN_IP
TURN_PORT=3478
TURN_SECRET=YOUR_TURN_SECRET_HERE
TURN_CREDENTIAL_TTL_SECONDS=600
```

`TURN_REALM` only configures the **bundled** coturn container's `--realm` flag in `docker-compose.yml` — the API never reads it when generating credentials, so it has no effect here. Set the realm directly in your external coturn's own config instead.

  The `TURN_SECRET` is a shared HMAC key used to generate temporary credentials. Never share it publicly. Treat it like a database password — it should only exist in your `.env` and in the coturn config.

sections.heading: 2. Restart the stack
sections.text:
The bundled coturn container is behind a Docker Compose profile and does not start by default. If you previously enabled it via `COMPOSE_PROFILES=turn` in your `.env`, remove that line so only your external TURN server is used.

```bash
docker compose pull api web
docker compose up -d
```

The API will now generate TURN credentials pointing to your external TURN server.

---

sections.heading: Using the Bundled TURN Server
sections.text:
If your Breeze server has a public IP (not behind a tunnel), the bundled coturn container works out of the box. Set these in `.env`:

```bash
TURN_HOST=YOUR_SERVER_PUBLIC_IP
TURN_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
```

Then start Breeze with the `turn` profile enabled:

```bash
docker compose --profile turn up -d
```

:::tip
You can also set `COMPOSE_PROFILES=turn` in your `.env` file so `docker compose up -d` automatically starts coturn.
:::

The bundled coturn runs with `network_mode: host`, so it needs direct access to the network — no port mapping is required, but the host firewall must allow:

- **TCP+UDP 3478** — TURN listening port (TCP is required for clients behind restrictive firewalls)
- **TCP 5349** — TURN over TLS (`turns:`), only once you have configured a certificate (see below)
- **TCP+UDP 49152–65535** — relay port range (default, can be tightened in `docker/turnserver.conf`)

:::caution
The coturn image runs as `nobody` (uid `65534`). If you bind-mount your own `turnserver.conf`, make it world-readable or owned by uid `65534`. When coturn cannot read the file it logs `WARNING: Cannot find config file` and runs on defaults (no auth, empty realm, every interface), so check the startup log for that line.
:::

sections.heading: TURN over TLS (`turns:`)
sections.text:
The bundled coturn is started with `--tls-listening-port=5349`, but coturn
**silently skips the TLS listener when it has no certificate** — so out of the
box only 3478 listens. TURNS matters for reachability, not confidentiality
(WebRTC media is already end-to-end encrypted with DTLS-SRTP): `turns:` over
TCP/5349 is what gets through customer networks that block UDP or allow only a
short list of TCP ports.

To enable it, set in `.env`:

```bash
# Directory on the host containing cert.pem and privkey.pem
TURN_TLS_DIR=/opt/breeze/coturn-tls
# The hostname ON that certificate (not the bare IP in TURN_HOST)
TURN_TLS_HOST=turn.your-domain.example.com
# TURN_TLS_PORT=5349
```

`TURN_TLS_DIR` is bind-mounted read-only at `/etc/coturn/tls`, and coturn is
given `--cert`/`--pkey` only when both files are readable. Leave `TURN_TLS_DIR`
unset and nothing changes — except that the container now logs *why* 5349 is
not listening instead of saying nothing. An expired or unparseable certificate
still enables the listener (coturn binds it either way) but logs a loud
`WARNING` at startup, since every handshake against it will fail.

The API also warns at startup when only one half is configured — a
`TURN_TLS_HOST` with no `TURN_TLS_DIR` advertises a `turns:` URL that nothing
is listening for, and a `TURN_TLS_DIR` with no `TURN_TLS_HOST` brings up a
listener no client is ever told about.

The API advertises `turns:` only when `TURN_TLS_HOST` is set, because a
certificate cannot validate against the bare public IP that `TURN_HOST` holds.
Point that hostname's DNS at the TURN server.

  **Two things that are easy to get wrong.**

  1. **Ownership.** coturn drops to uid `65534` (`nobody`), while Caddy writes
     its certificate and key as `0600 root`. Bind-mounting Caddy's certificate
     directory therefore does not work, and loosening the mode at the source
     does not survive renewal — Caddy rewrites both files. Copy the pair to a
     staging directory instead, at mode `0640` with a group `nobody` can read.
  2. **Renewal.** coturn reads the certificate once at startup and never
     reloads it. Without a restart or `SIGHUP` when the certificate is renewed,
     TURNS breaks silently roughly 60 days after deployment, and nothing
     surfaces it until a customer cannot connect. Drive the copy and the
     restart from the same hook or timer that watches the certificate:

```bash
  install -o root -g nogroup -m 0640 /path/to/cert.pem /opt/breeze/coturn-tls/cert.pem
  install -o root -g nogroup -m 0640 /path/to/privkey.pem /opt/breeze/coturn-tls/privkey.pem
  docker compose restart coturn
```

---

sections.heading: Relay Port Range Sizing
sections.text:
Each active WebRTC session uses one relay allocation (one UDP port). The default range in the bundled config is `49152–65535` (16,383 ports). For an external dedicated server, a tighter range reduces firewall surface:

| Expected concurrent sessions | Recommended range | Ports |
|---|---|---|
| Up to 50 | 49152–49202 | 50 |
| Up to 100 | 49152–49252 | 100 |
| Up to 500 | 49152–49652 | 500 |

Edit `min-port` and `max-port` in the coturn config and match the firewall rule.

---

sections.heading: How Credentials Work
sections.text:
Breeze uses the TURN **time-limited credential** mechanism (RFC 5766 long-term credentials with a shared secret):

1. The API receives a request for ICE servers from a desktop-session or viewer-token endpoint.
2. It verifies the caller is bound to an active desktop session, then generates a temporary username containing the Unix expiry, user/session/device scope, and random nonce.
3. The credential pair (username + HMAC password) is returned to both the viewer and agent.
4. Credentials expire after a configurable TTL (default: 10 minutes, clamped to 1–15 minutes).
5. coturn validates incoming TURN allocations against the same shared secret via `use-auth-secret`.

Clients never see `TURN_SECRET` — they only receive short-lived derived credentials.

From v0.118.0, credentials are not issued for sessions that have ended, and each user may request 30 credentials per 10 minutes (`429` above that). Tune the limit with `TURN_CREDENTIAL_MINT_LIMIT_PER_WINDOW` and `TURN_CREDENTIAL_MINT_WINDOW_SECONDS`; `0` turns it off. See [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/#agent-traffic-and-ingest-budgets).

---

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**Remote desktop fails with "ICE failed"**
- Verify the TURN server is reachable: `nc -z -w 3 TURN_IP 3478` (TCP) and `nc -u -z -w 3 TURN_IP 3478` (UDP)
- Check coturn logs: `ssh root@TURN_IP journalctl -u coturn -f`
- Confirm `TURN_HOST` in `.env` matches the TURN server's public IP exactly
- Ensure the firewall allows **both TCP and UDP** on port 3478 and the relay port range — Breeze advertises `transport=tcp` and `transport=udp` TURN URLs

**Coturn starts but clients can't allocate**
- Check `external-ip` in `/etc/turnserver.conf` — it must be the server's actual public IP
- Verify `static-auth-secret` matches `TURN_SECRET` in Breeze's `.env`
- Check the `realm` value in your external coturn's own config — Breeze's `TURN_REALM` only configures the bundled coturn container and has no effect on an external one

**Sessions end with only host and srflx candidates (no relay), but `TURN_SECRET` matches**
- The coturn image runs as `nobody` (uid `65534`). A bind-mounted `turnserver.conf` must be world-readable or owned by uid `65534`; a `0600` file owned by another user cannot be read.
- If coturn cannot read its config, it logs `WARNING: Cannot find config file` and **starts on built-in defaults**: no authentication, an empty realm, and every interface. Treat that line as "not running your configuration".
- A server on defaults answers every Allocate with `Allocate Success` and never sends the `401` challenge. Breeze clients only authenticate in response to that challenge, so they never get a relay candidate. This looks the same as a wrong `TURN_SECRET`.
- At startup the Breeze API sends one unauthenticated Allocate to `TURN_HOST:TURN_PORT` and logs a `[turn-preflight]` warning when it receives success instead of `401`. Platform admins can read the last result at `GET /api/v1/admin/system/connections/turn` and re-run it with `POST /api/v1/admin/system/connections/turn/probe`. A timeout is reported as informational only, because the relay may simply be filtered from the API host.

**High bandwidth usage on the TURN server**
- TURN relays all media when direct P2P fails. Each desktop session at 5 Mbps = ~2.25 GB/hour
- Monitor with `vnstat` or DigitalOcean's bandwidth graphs
- Keep `max-bps`, `user-quota`, `total-quota`, and a narrow relay port range enabled. Raise them only after adding bandwidth alerts and provider-level egress budgets.

**WebSocket fallback is active instead of WebRTC**
- The viewer falls back to WebSocket when WebRTC negotiation fails entirely
- Check browser console for ICE errors
- Ensure both STUN and TURN candidates are being generated from a session-scoped ICE endpoint response

sections.heading: Docker Compose Upgrade
sections.text:
1. **Back up the database**

```bash
   ./scripts/backup.sh --db
```

   Database migrations are forward-only. Rolling the container tag back does not roll the schema back. See [Backup & Restore](/security/backup/).

2. **Diff your Compose files against the tagged release** and merge the required changes before pulling images; follow [Compose file changes](#compose-file-changes), preserving your local configuration. Back up `.env`, the active Compose files, and overrides alongside the database backup.

3. **Check how your images are pinned**

```bash
   grep '^BREEZE_API_IMAGE_REF=' .env
```

   - **Digest-pinned** — the value ends in `@sha256:…`. Every install made with `guided-setup.sh` for v0.112.0 or later looks like this. Follow step 4a.
   - **Tag-form** — the value ends in `:${BREEZE_VERSION}` (older installs, and manual installs that never switched). Follow step 4b.

   **On a digest-pinned install, `docker compose pull` does not upgrade:**
     The image refs name exact digests, so `docker compose pull` fetches the release you already run, and editing `BREEZE_VERSION` alone leaves the old images running. `BREEZE_VERSION` also selects the agent release your fleet is offered, so a hand-edited value can move agents ahead of the server.

4. **Move to the new release**

   **4a. Digest-pinned: run `guided-setup.sh --upgrade`**

```bash
   # Fetch the current installer. --upgrade is new; an older copy does not have it.
   curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lanternops/breeze/main/scripts/guided-setup.sh

   # Run from the directory that holds docker-compose.yml and .env, or pass --work-dir.
   bash guided-setup.sh --upgrade 0.118.2   # omit the version to use the latest release
```

   The script:
   - downloads the target release's signed image inventory and verifies it against `RELEASE_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEYS`, the same fail-closed check as a fresh install;
   - backs up `.env`, then rewrites `BREEZE_VERSION` and the four `BREEZE_*_IMAGE_REF` digests together. If verification fails, `.env` is left unchanged and nothing is pulled;
   - prints links to the target release's `docker-compose.yml` and `.env.example`. It never edits your Compose file, so complete step 2 for the target release;
   - pulls the verified images, runs `docker compose up -d`, and waits for the API to report healthy.

   Add `-y` to run it without prompts, for example from a script. Add `--no-up` to update `.env` only and restart later. The script refuses a target older than your current `BREEZE_VERSION`. Migrations are forward-only, so restore the matching database backup before you pass `--allow-downgrade`. Targets older than 0.112.0 are always refused, because release signatures do not cover those images; `--allow-unverified-release` does not apply to `--upgrade`. It also re-pins the digests when `BREEZE_VERSION` already names the target, which repairs an install where only `BREEZE_VERSION` was edited.

   If you run the manual verifier instead, follow [Signed, digest-pinned image references](/deploy/production/#signed-digest-pinned-image-references-v01120-and-later) and update `BREEZE_VERSION` and all four refs together.

   **4b. Tag-form: set the version, then pull and restart**

```bash
   # In .env: set to the version you want (e.g. 0.118.2)
   BREEZE_VERSION=0.118.2
```

```bash
   docker compose pull
   docker compose up -d
```

   `BREEZE_VERSION` also selects the agent release your fleet is offered, so set it to a version that is **published** on GitHub, not one that has only been tagged. See [Binary Distribution](/deploy/binaries/#github-mode-default).

   Either path pulls the new API, web, and binaries images and restarts all services.
   Database migrations run automatically on API startup when `AUTO_MIGRATE=true` (the default).

   **Expected downtime**: Typically **5--15 seconds** while containers restart. If the new version includes database migrations, the API container will take additional time to apply them before accepting traffic -- usually under 60 seconds for routine schema changes, but potentially several minutes for large data migrations. Agents continue running independently during this window and reconnect automatically. From agent 0.125.0, agents spread that reconnect over up to 30 seconds (was 1–5 seconds), so a device can show offline up to about 30 seconds longer after an API restart. An API that is shedding load answers with `503` and a `Retry-After` delay, which agents honour; see [Agent reconnect settings](#agent-reconnect-settings).

5. **Verify**

```bash
   # Check API health
   curl -s https://breeze.yourdomain.com/health | jq .version

   # Check all running image versions
   docker compose images

   # Check agent version (on the device)
   breeze-agent version
```

   `/health` reports the version baked into the running API image. If it does not match `BREEZE_VERSION` in `.env`, the image was not upgraded. The API logs `[version] BREEZE_VERSION=… but this API image is …` at startup, and **Administration → System → Connections** shows the same warning. This requires the Compose change described in [APP_VERSION comes from the image](#v01190--app_version-comes-from-the-image).

   Also sign in through your public URL and confirm agents resume checking in. `/health` bypasses the HTTPS redirect and can stay healthy while a stale proxy address sends other requests into a redirect loop.

  The `binaries-init` container uses `pull_policy: always`, so `docker compose up -d` automatically pulls the latest binaries image and refreshes the volume — no manual steps needed.

sections.heading: Agent reconnect settings
sections.text:
From agent 0.125.0, agents pace their own traffic after an API restart or overload:

- **Spread reconnect.** After a stable connection drops, an agent waits a random 1–30 seconds before it redials, instead of 1–5 seconds. The first connection after the agent process starts waits a random 0–10 seconds, also after a self-update.
- **Drain hint.** An API instance that is shutting down can tell its agents `{"type":"drain","reconnectWithinMs":N}` before it closes their sockets. Agents then spread their reconnect over that window, at least 5 seconds. No Breeze API sends this yet; it is ready for rolling deploys.
- **Server delays honoured across cycles.** When the API answers a periodic upload (inventory, monitoring results, process samples, logs, UniFi telemetry) with `503` or `429` and a `Retry-After`, the agent skips that upload until the delay has passed, up to 300 seconds, instead of retrying on its next cycle. Heartbeats and command results are never delayed.
- **Spread startup uploads.** The full inventory, hardware and patch uploads after an agent starts each wait a random 0–120 seconds, and the first service-monitoring pass waits up to one check interval (at most 60 seconds).

Two `agent.yaml` keys restore the earlier behaviour on a device:

| Key | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `ws_first_reconnect_window_seconds` | `30` | Upper bound of the reconnect spread after a stable connection, 0–300 seconds. `0`–`5` restores the 1–5 second spread of earlier agents. |
| `loop_retry_after` | `true` | `false` restores per-request handling: the agent waits out a `Retry-After` only inside the request it was given, and retries on its next cycle. |

The agent reads both at start; restart the agent service after changing them.

sections.heading: Check what an upgrade retires
sections.text:
Every API image carries a list of the API fields and endpoints Breeze has retired, with the version each one was deprecated and removed in and what replaces it. The list is cumulative, so an image knows every retirement you cross even when you skip versions. The API also records each version your deployment boots, so it can tell which retirements are new to you.

**At every boot**, before migrations run, the API logs a report headed `[upgrade-preflight]`. It lists each retirement the upgrade crosses, the endpoints and fields affected, and the replacement. Read it after upgrading:

```bash
docker compose logs api | grep upgrade-preflight
```

**Before upgrading**, you can run the same check with the new image against your current database, after `docker compose pull` and before `docker compose up -d`:

```bash
docker compose run --rm --no-deps api node dist/scripts/upgrade-preflight.cjs
```

This only reads. It does not run migrations or record a version. It exits 0. Add `--strict` (or set `BREEZE_UPGRADE_PREFLIGHT_STRICT=true`) to exit 1 when a removal is crossed, for use in an upgrade script.

The report never blocks the API from starting. If the deployment has no recorded version history (the first upgrade to a version with this check, or a database the check could not read), the report lists every retirement in effect for the new image and marks it as possibly crossed. It does not report "no issues" in that case.

sections.heading: In the web UI
sections.text: Platform administrators can see the same information at **Administration → System** (`/admin/system`, v0.117.0+). The **Deprecations** tab lists every retirement the running image knows about with its status for this deployment (crossed, possibly crossed, in effect, or upcoming), along with the running version, the last version recorded, the applied and pending migration counts, and the deployment's version history. The **Connections** tab shows each integration the API container is configured for, grouped by area, as enabled, disabled, misconfigured, or required but missing. It reads the API container's environment only, never shows secret values, and does not contact the services themselves, so "enabled" means configured, not reachable. Both tabs are read-only.

sections.heading: Compose file changes
sections.text:
`docker compose pull` updates images; it does **not** download a new `docker-compose.yml`, override file, or `.env.example`. Current images can therefore run with old network settings or missing environment mappings. Review the configuration shipped with **every target release**, including when skipping versions; the entries below highlight changes that need operator action, not a complete Compose changelog.

Fetch a separate copy of the target release's Compose file and compare it with the one you actually deploy. Replace the placeholder with the published release tag matching your intended `BREEZE_VERSION`:

```bash
release_tag="v<target-version>"
release_compose=$(mktemp)
curl --fail --show-error --location \
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LanternOps/breeze/${release_tag}/docker-compose.yml" \
  --output "$release_compose" && diff -u docker-compose.yml "$release_compose"
```

`diff` exits with status 1 when differences exist; a failed download must be resolved before continuing. If you deploy `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml` or additional override files, compare those same paths at the same tag too. Review the tagged `.env.example` and any configuration files referenced by changed services.

Merge the required changes into your backed-up local files, preserving custom services, domains, mounts, secrets, and proxy topology. Do not overwrite `.env` with `.env.example`. Add required variables to both `.env` and the appropriate service's `environment:` mapping; setting `.env` alone does not pass a variable to the container. For digest-pinned deployments, update the image references to the target release as well as `BREEZE_VERSION`. `guided-setup.sh --upgrade` does this for you (step 4a).

Validate the merged configuration before the pull/restart step:

```bash
docker compose config --quiet
```

Use the same `-f` options and profiles you normally deploy for validation, pull, and restart so your overrides are included. Validation checks the Compose configuration; it does not prove that a trusted proxy address matches the running proxy.

sections.heading: v0.125.0 — DNS Security retention, Flows and MCP preview switches, Caddy header defaults
sections.text:
The [v0.125.0 Compose files](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/blob/v0.125.0/docker-compose.yml) change the `api` environment and `docker/Caddyfile.prod`. Both Compose files gain the same lines.

| Change | Required action |
|---|---|
| New `api` mappings, each as `${VAR:-}` so unset keeps the built-in default: `AI_TOOL_INDEX`, `BREEZE_ADMISSION_RISE_TICKS`, `BREEZE_ADMISSION_LEVEL1_HOLD_MS`, `DNS_SECURITY_RETENTION_DAYS_DEFAULT` / `_BATCH_SIZE` / `_MAX_BATCHES`, `OAUTH_CIMD_ENABLED`, `OAUTH_CIMD_ALLOWED_HOSTS`, `MCP_STATELESS_ENABLED`, `MCP_HEADER_MISMATCH_ALERT_THRESHOLD`, `MCP_TIER3_INTENTS_ENABLED`, the three `MCP_INTENT_*` limits, `MCP_APPROVAL_WAIT_MS`, `MCP_APPROVAL_WAITS_PER_PRINCIPAL`, `MCP_APPS_ENABLED`, `MCP_TASKS_ENABLED` and the three `MCP_TASK_*` timers. | Copy the lines into your own Compose file if you want to set any of them. See [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/). |
| New `api` mappings with an explicit default: `FLOWS_ENABLED` (`false`) and the six `FLOW_*` limits, `AI_OPERATOR_RECIPE_IDENTITY_OFFBOARDING_ENABLED` and `AI_OPERATOR_RECIPE_IDENTITY_ONBOARDING_ENABLED` (`false`), `BREEZE_WISP_ENABLED` (`false`) and `BREEZE_WISP_CONNECTOR_ENABLED` (`false`). | Nothing for the defaults. `BREEZE_WISP_ENABLED` is for Breeze Cloud only; leave it unset on a self-hosted server. `BREEZE_WISP_CONNECTOR_ENABLED` is another name for `BREEZE_WORKSPACE_ENABLED`, not the Wisp switch. |
| `PROMPT_HOST_ENABLED_KINDS` is mapped as `${PROMPT_HOST_ENABLED_KINDS-default}` (no colon), so leaving it out of `.env` passes the built-in list, and an explicitly empty value is the kill switch. | Nothing. Nothing uses it in this release. |
| `PAM_OWNERSHIP_EPOCH_TRANSFER` and `BREEZE_YARA_BUILTIN_PACK_DISABLED` (from v0.124.0) are now mapped as `${VAR:-}`. | Nothing, unless you added your own mapping on v0.124.0; keep one. |
| `docker/Caddyfile.prod` sends `Strict-Transport-Security` and `X-Content-Type-Options` with the `>` (replace) form so they are no longer sent twice, adds a default `Permissions-Policy`, and adds a default `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-site` on every path except the API, OAuth, health and public-badge paths. | If you maintain your own copy of `Caddyfile.prod`, carry all three over. See [Security headers](/deploy/tls/#security-headers). |
| `.env.example` documents the Microsoft 365 Graph-read, Graph-actions and comms executor variables in one place, and shows the comms signing key as `M365_COMMS_EXECUTOR_SIGNING_PRIVATE_JWK_SOURCE_FILE` (a host path mounted into the container). | Nothing. Existing values keep working. |

Not mapped in Compose (add them to the `api` service yourself if you need to change one): the IOC sweep limits `SECURITY_SWEEP_*` and `IOC_HUNT_FOUR_EYES_DEVICE_THRESHOLD`. See [IOC sweeps](/features/security/#ioc-sweeps).

sections.heading: v0.124.0 — caller verification on by default, AI retention and sweeper settings, web security contacts, Caddy tunnel host
sections.text:
The [v0.124.0 Compose files](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/blob/v0.124.0/docker-compose.yml) change the `api`, `web` and `caddy` environments:

| Change | Required action |
|---|---|
| `CALLER_VERIFICATION_ENABLED` is mapped in both files as `${CALLER_VERIFICATION_ENABLED:-true}`; it defaulted to `false` before. Microsoft 365 password resets and account disables now need a fresh caller verification, and an explicit `false` refuses them instead of leaving the feature dark. | **Check `.env` before upgrading.** Earlier `.env.example` files shipped `CALLER_VERIFICATION_ENABLED=false`; remove the line, or set it to `true`. See [the v0.124.0 notes](#v01240--trust-center-connection-health-security-agents-from-policy-verified-m365-actions). |
| New `api` mappings in both files: `AI_TOOL_OUTPUT_RETENTION_CRON` / `_BATCH_SIZE` / `_MAX_BATCHES`, `AI_TRANSCRIPT_SWEEPER_ENABLED` / `_CRON` / `_GRACE_HOURS`, `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, `PAM_EVIDENCE_RETENTION_ENABLED` / `_DAYS`, `MCP_INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE_HTTP_403`, `WEBHOOK_DELIVERY_RETENTION_DAYS` / `_BATCH_SIZE` / `_MAX_BATCHES` and `RESTORE_POINT_ATTEMPT_RETENTION_DAYS` / `_BATCH_SIZE` / `_MAX_BATCHES`, each as `${VAR:-}` so unset keeps the built-in default; plus `CALLER_VERIFICATION_WORKSTATION_ENABLED` and `BREEZE_TRUST_CIS_FRAMEWORK_VIEW` as `${VAR:-false}`. | Copy the lines into your own Compose file if you want to set any of them. See [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/). |
| `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml` now maps `MIGRATION_WINDOW_MAX_DAYS`, `MIGRATION_WINDOW_DEFAULT_WRITES_PER_HOUR` and `MIGRATION_WINDOW_MAX_WRITES_PER_HOUR`, which the root file has mapped since v0.123.0. | Nothing, unless you added your own mapping on v0.123.0; keep one. |
| New `web` mappings `PUBLIC_ABUSE_CONTACT`, `PUBLIC_SECURITY_CONTACT` and `PUBLIC_SECURITY_POLICY_URL`, all empty by default. Unlike the other `PUBLIC_*` flags, the web container reads these at **runtime**, so they work with the published image. | Set them to publish a "Report abuse" / "Security" footer on the sign-in pages and `/.well-known/security.txt`; unset publishes nothing. On your own Compose file, add the three lines to the `web` service's `environment:` block. |
| New `caddy` mappings `TUNNEL_SITE_ADDRESS`, `TUNNEL_TLS_DIRECTIVE` and `TUNNEL_HOST_SUFFIX`. Their defaults match nothing, so Network Proxy host mode stays off. | Nothing for the defaults. Leave them unset rather than empty: an empty `TUNNEL_SITE_ADDRESS` stops Caddy from starting. See [Dedicated tunnel origin](/deploy/network-proxy-tunnel-origin/). |
| `docker/Caddyfile.prod` sets `Referrer-Policy` only when the application did not set one (`?Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"`), and gains a site block that serves the Network Proxy tunnel host from the `TUNNEL_*` variables. | If you maintain your own copy of `Caddyfile.prod`, carry both over. Without the `?` form, the proxy overwrites the `no-referrer` the application sends on verification pages, public invoices and unsubscribe links. |

sections.heading: v0.123.0 — ECH and retain-state switches, admission control, 25 newly passed API settings
sections.text:
The [v0.123.0 Compose files](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/blob/v0.123.0/docker-compose.yml) change the `api` environment:

| Change | Required action |
|---|---|
| `AGENT_ECH_ENABLED` and `HEARTBEAT_RETAIN_STATE_ENABLED` are mapped in both files as `${VAR:-true}`. Both accept only `true` or `false`; any other value stops the API from booting. | Nothing for the defaults. Never set `AGENT_ECH_ENABLED=false` casually; see [Agent connection switches](/deploy/environment/#agent-connection-switches). |
| `BREEZE_ADMISSION_MODE` and its seven `BREEZE_ADMISSION_*` tuning knobs, `AGENT_BODY_RECEIVE_TIMEOUT_MS`, `AGENT_BODY_RECEIVE_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_MS`, `BREEZE_EDR_ACTIONS_ENABLED`, `TUNNEL_ORIGIN_TEMPLATE`, `TUNNEL_FRAME_ANCESTOR` and the three `LLM_EGRESS_EVENTS_RETENTION_*` settings are mapped in both files as `${VAR:-}`, so unset keeps the built-in default. | Copy the lines into your own Compose file if you want to set any of them. See [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/). |
| Both files pass 22 existing variables that Compose used to ignore (25 in the root file): `CF_ACCESS_TRUST_ENABLED`, `CF_ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN`, `CF_ACCESS_AUD`, `CF_ACCESS_TRUSTS_MFA`, `CSP_REPORT_URI`, `EMAIL_SUPPORT_ADDRESS`, `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_ENABLED`, `M365_ENABLED`, `HP_WARRANTY_ENABLED`, `IP_CLASSIFY_PROVIDER`, `IP_CLASSIFY_API_KEY`, the six `MCP_LLM_*` settings, `NVD_API_KEY`, `PARTNER_MEETING_URL`, `PARTNER_TRUST_MODE`, `SENTRY_PROFILES_SAMPLE_RATE` and `STRIPE_ACCOUNT_CACHE_REFRESH_ENABLED`. The root `docker-compose.yml` also gains `APPLE_APP_ATTEST_APP_ID`, `APPLE_APP_ATTEST_ENVIRONMENT` and `PARTNER_HOOKS_URL`. | **A value already in your `.env` now takes effect.** Check `.env` for stale entries before upgrading: a leftover `CF_ACCESS_TRUST_ENABLED=true` without its team domain and AUD, or a malformed `MCP_LLM_*` value, stops the API from booting. `PARTNER_TRUST_MODE` has no effect unless `IS_HOSTED=true`. |
| `METRIC_ANOMALY_EPISODE_MIN_BUCKETS` is mapped in both files, and `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml` gains the four `PARTNER_API_*` ticket and idempotency settings from v0.122.1. | Nothing, unless you added your own mapping for them on v0.122.1; keep one. |
| `MIGRATION_WINDOW_MAX_DAYS`, `MIGRATION_WINDOW_DEFAULT_WRITES_PER_HOUR` and `MIGRATION_WINDOW_MAX_WRITES_PER_HOUR` are mapped in the root `docker-compose.yml` only in v0.123.0; `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml` maps them from v0.124.0. | On v0.123.0 with `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml`, add them to the `api` service's `environment:` block if you need them. The defaults apply without them. |
| `PUBLIC_ENABLE_ENDPOINT_MESSAGING` is a web **build-time** flag, default off. | Only takes effect in a web image you build yourself. The published web image is built with it off. |
| `docker/Caddyfile.prod` gains a global `log default { format filter { … } }` block that redacts credential headers and credential query parameters in every Caddy log. | If you maintain your own copy of `Caddyfile.prod`, carry the block over. |

sections.heading: v0.122.1 — installer token default, 63 newly passed API settings, Partner API ticket settings
sections.text:

| Change | Required action |
|---|---|
| `INSTALLER_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN_TTL_MINUTES` defaults to `10080` (7 days) in both files; it was `1440` (1 day). | Nothing if you want the new default. To keep 1 day, set `INSTALLER_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN_TTL_MINUTES=1440` in `.env`. Values above `43200` (30 days) are clamped. See [the v0.122.1 notes](#v01221--remote-desktop-clipboard-v2-diagnostic-file-access-partner-api-tickets-restore-integrity). |
| Both files pass 63 more variables to the API: retention windows, agent ingest quotas and rate limits, screenshot and log-forwarding caps, `DB_POOL_MAX`, the offboarding drain window, the public download key TTL and login lockout. Each is passed as `${VAR:-}`, so an unset value keeps the built-in default. | A value already in your `.env` that Compose used to ignore now takes effect. Check `.env` for stale entries before upgrading. |
| New optional settings are mapped in both files: `PATCH_REPORT_RETENTION_DAYS`, `PATCH_REPORT_ORPHAN_MIN_AGE_MS`, `DB_POOL_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT_MS` and `DB_TIMER_LAG_GRACE_MS`. | Copy the lines into your own Compose file if you want to set any of them. See [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/). |
| `PARTNER_API_TICKET_WRITE_RATE_LIMIT_PER_HOUR`, `PARTNER_API_TICKET_WRITE_PARTNER_RATE_LIMIT_PER_HOUR`, `PARTNER_API_IDEMPOTENCY_RETENTION_ENABLED` and `PARTNER_API_IDEMPOTENCY_RETENTION_DAYS` are mapped in the root `docker-compose.yml` only in v0.122.1; `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml` maps them from the next release. | On v0.122.1 with `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml`, add them to the `api` service's `environment:` block if you need to change them. The defaults apply without them. |
| `METRIC_ANOMALY_EPISODE_MIN_BUCKETS` is not passed to the api container by either v0.122.1 Compose file; both map it from the next release. | On v0.122.1, add it to the `api` service's `environment:` block if you want to change the default of `3`. |
| The `BREEZE_AI_SCRIPT_REVIEWER_MODEL` mapping is removed; the API no longer reads it. | Delete it from your own Compose file and `.env`. |
| `docker/Caddyfile.prod` gains a `@webBillingAutopay` matcher that sends `/billing/autopay*` to the web app, ahead of the `/billing/*` route. | If you maintain your own copy of `Caddyfile.prod`, carry the matcher over, or the automatic-payment pages are routed to the wrong service. |

sections.heading: v0.121.0 — new optional AI and enrollment settings; production Compose catches up
sections.text:

All are optional; empty keeps the defaults. | Copy the lines into your own Compose file if you want to set any of them. See [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/). |

Check `.env` for stale entries before upgrading. Installs on the root `docker-compose.yml` (including `guided-setup.sh`) are unaffected. |
| The stock Compose file does not pass `MCP_LLM_*` to the API. | If you use `MCP_LLM_PROVIDER=openai-compatible`, keep your own mapping and read [the v0.121.0 notes](#v01210--ai-model-registry-byo-openai-compatible-models-encrypted-backup-credentials) first. |

Before this release Compose installs ignored them even when they were set in `.env`. | Copy the entries into your own Compose file if you set any of them. sections.heading: v0.119.0 — `APP_VERSION` comes from the image
sections.text:
Earlier Compose files set `APP_VERSION: ${BREEZE_VERSION...}` in the API environment. That value replaced the version baked into the image, so `/health`, the upgrade preflight, and the recorded version history reported whatever `.env` said, even when the running image was older. The shipped `docker-compose.yml` and `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml` no longer set it.

| Change | Required action |
|---|---|
| The `APP_VERSION:` line is removed from the shared API environment block (`x-api-env` in `docker-compose.yml`, the API environment in `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml`). | Delete the `APP_VERSION:` line from your own Compose file. Keep `BREEZE_VERSION:`, which still selects the agent release. Until you remove the line, `/health` keeps reporting `BREEZE_VERSION` and the version-mismatch warning cannot fire. |

sections.heading: v0.119.0 — coturn relays again
sections.text:
| Change | Required action |
|---|---|
| The v0.118.0 coturn configuration listed `denied-peer-ip=::`. coturn reads an all-zero address as "no bound", so that one entry refused every peer and relayed (TURN) connections could not be set up. The entry is removed from `docker/turnserver.conf`, `docker-compose.yml` and `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml`; coturn already refuses the unspecified address on its own. | Delete the `denied-peer-ip=::` line (`'--denied-peer-ip=::'` in a Compose file) from your coturn configuration and restart coturn, even if you skip this release. Do not replace it with `0.0.0.0` or a range starting at `::`. |

sections.heading: v0.119.0 — coturn refuses IPv4-mapped and NAT64 peers
sections.text:
| Change | Required action |
|---|---|
| The two `denied-peer-ip` lines that v0.118.0 shipped commented out are now active in `docker/turnserver.conf`, `docker-compose.yml` and `deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml`: `::ffff:0:0-::ffff:ffff:ffff` (IPv4-mapped IPv6) and `64:ff9b::-64:ff9b::ffff:ffff` (NAT64 well-known prefix). Relay-to-relay sessions are unaffected. | Nothing if you use the bundled coturn with the shipped files. If you run your own coturn, add both lines from [TURN Server](/deploy/turn-server/#install-and-configure-coturn) and restart it. **Never deny the relay's own public IP.** |

sections.heading: v0.118.0 — coturn peer restrictions and API stop grace
sections.text:
The [v0.118.0 Compose files](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/blob/v0.118.0/docker-compose.yml) and `docker/turnserver.conf` change two things:

| Change | Required action |
|---|---|
| coturn relays only to public addresses: `denied-peer-ip` rules for loopback, private, CGNAT, link-local, documentation and reserved ranges (IPv4 and IPv6), plus `no-tcp-relay`. `verbose` is turned off. | Nothing if you use the bundled coturn with the shipped files. If you run your own coturn, apply the same rules from [TURN Server](/deploy/turn-server/#install-and-configure-coturn). **Never deny the relay's own public IP**: relay-to-relay traffic targets it. The IPv4-mapped and NAT64 lines ship commented out; enable them only after checking relay-to-relay on your deployment. |
| The `api` service (and `worker`) has `stop_grace_period: 90s`, so background work in the process can finish during a restart. | Copy it into your own Compose file if you maintain one. |

sections.heading: v0.95.0 — stable Caddy address and proxy trust
sections.text:
The [v0.95.0 Compose file](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/blob/v0.95.0/docker-compose.yml) introduced these coupled settings. If your deployed file predates them, apply all three even if your images are already newer:

| Compose setting | Required action |
|---|---|
| `networks.breeze.ipam.config.subnet` uses `BREEZE_DOCKER_SUBNET` | Merge the IPAM configuration. If the shipped subnet overlaps another Docker network, host route, or VPN, choose a non-overlapping subnet in `.env`. |
| `services.caddy.networks.breeze.ipv4_address` uses `BREEZE_CADDY_IP` | Merge the static address pin. If you customize the subnet, choose an unused Caddy address inside it and set `BREEZE_CADDY_IP` alongside `BREEZE_DOCKER_SUBNET`. |
| `services.api.environment.TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS` defaults to `BREEZE_CADDY_IP` with a `/32` mask | Merge the derived default. An explicit `TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS` in `.env` or an override takes precedence: remove a stale override when using bundled Caddy, or set it to the actual immediate proxy's stable address for a custom topology. |

Keep `TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true` when using the bundled proxy. Do not widen trust to an entire private network to work around an address mismatch. A proxy's dynamically assigned address can move after a container recreation or host reboot.

Changing an existing network's IPAM/subnet requires recreating that network during a maintenance window; `docker compose restart` cannot apply it. For a standalone stack whose network is used only by that stack, stop/remove its containers and network with `docker compose down`, then recreate them with `docker compose up -d` after pulling the target images. **Do not use `down -v`**, which deletes named data volumes. If other containers share the network, coordinate their migration before recreating it. This network migration takes longer than the routine image-only restart described above.

Before upgrading a proxy-fronted deployment to **v0.103.0 or later**, verify that `TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS` matches the proxy that directly connects to the API. That release's TRANSPORT-001 enforcement only honors forwarded HTTPS headers from trusted peers; a stale address can cause repeated `308` redirects for the UI and agents while `/health` still returns `200`. After restarting, check public sign-in and agent check-ins as well as API logs for `[proxy-trust]` or `[force-https]` warnings (available from v0.104.0).

sections.heading: v0.125.0 — agreements sent for signature, ticket merge and business-hours SLAs, ring-controlled Windows feature updates
sections.text:
**Two defaults change data or devices on the first run:**
  - **DNS Security history older than 90 days is deleted** by the first nightly retention run (22:18 UTC). Before this release, an integration with no retention setting kept everything. To keep more, set **retention days** on each integration **before you upgrade**, or set `DNS_SECURITY_RETENTION_DAYS_DEFAULT` (1–365). See [Data retention](/features/dns-security/#data-retention).
  - **The agent no longer hides Windows feature releases by itself.** On agent 0.125.0 each update ring decides, and every ring starts on **Block**, which matches the old behaviour. Nothing new is offered until you set a ring to **Allow** or **Pin**. See [Windows Feature Updates](/features/update-rings/#windows-feature-updates).

**Upgrade order.**

1. Back up the database, or note a point-in-time recovery point. **Rolling back below v0.124.0 needs a database restore** (see Migrations below).
2. If you need more than 90 days of DNS Security history, raise each integration's retention days now (see the aside above).
3. Check `.env` for `AGENT_ENROLL_RATE_WINDOW_SECONDS`. A value above `230` now stops the API from booting (see Stricter than before).
4. Upgrade the server. Check how your install pins its images with `grep '^BREEZE_API_IMAGE_REF=' .env`:
   - **Digest-pinned** (the value ends in `@sha256:…`; every `guided-setup.sh` install since v0.112.0): fetch the current `guided-setup.sh` from `main`, then run `bash guided-setup.sh --upgrade 0.125.0`. Don't edit only `BREEZE_VERSION` on a digest-pinned install; that re-pulls the images you already run.
   - **Tag-form** (the value ends in `:${BREEZE_VERSION}`): set `BREEZE_VERSION=0.125.0`, then run `docker compose pull api web portal && docker compose up -d`. If you run the optional `worker` container, pull and restart it too.

   **Replace every API and worker instance in the same deploy**, and do not run an instance older than v0.124.0 next to this release. Once this release writes a backup snapshot under a path prefix, an older instance cannot read it.
5. `--upgrade` does not change your `docker-compose.yml`. To set any of this release's new optional variables, add them to the `api` service's `environment:` block, or take the v0.125.0 Compose files, which already map most of them. A value only in `.env` does not reach the container. If you maintain your own `docker/Caddyfile.prod`, carry over the new header defaults (see [Compose file changes](#v01250--dns-security-retention-flows-and-mcp-preview-switches-caddy-header-defaults)).
6. Watch the API start log for `[auto-migrate] Applied 64 migration(s)` (from v0.124.0) and `[startup] pinned built-in package refresh: refreshed N, failed M`.
7. Let agents, Breeze Assist and Breeze Viewer update to 0.125.0. Ring-controlled feature updates, install scripts and zip packages, the Breeze Assist availability checks, **Force reboot now**, reconnect pacing and derived Windows update severities all need this release's agent.

#### Stricter than before

No change breaks an install on default settings. Check these before you upgrade a customised install:

- **`AGENT_ENROLL_RATE_WINDOW_SECONDS` above 230 refuses to boot.** The default is 60. The limit keeps every `Retry-After` an agent is told under the agent's 300-second ceiling.
- **Uploading, copying and moving files with System Tools needs `scripts:execute`** as well as `devices:execute`, the same as running a script. The AI assistant's file write and rename follow the same rule. See [System Tools](/features/system-tools/).
- **Approving a UAC elevation request needs `devices:execute`** as well as `pam:approve`, and approvals from the approvals inbox and the mobile app need an MFA-verified session. A custom role that relied on `pam:approve` alone gets a 403. See [PAM](/features/pam/).
- **Backup destinations with an invalid stored Path Prefix stop backing up.** That means an empty segment, `.` or `..`, characters outside `A–Z a–z 0–9 ! _ . * ' ( ) -`, a `snapshots` segment, or more than 256 characters. Those backups fail with `invalid_destination_prefix`, and **Test connection** fails too. Fix the prefix in the destination form. See [Key prefix](/backup/storage/#key-prefix).
- **MCP clients calling `manage_catalog`** should switch to `manage_billing_catalog`. The old name works for this release only.
- **Direct-SQL reports on `software_compliance_status`** see no rows without a tenant context: row-level security is now forced on that table on databases created from the baseline.

#### Behaviour changes and feature flags

- **Windows feature updates are decided by the update ring.** The agent's `patch_exclude_feature_updates` now defaults to `false` and acts only as a kill switch; the ring's **Windows feature updates** setting (Block, Allow or Pin) decides. **Pin** writes the Windows Update for Business target-release policy on each device, and switching back removes only the values Breeze wrote; a target-release policy set by your own GPO is left as found. Unless the patch policy's exclusive Windows Update setting is on, Windows may install an allowed or pinned release on its own schedule. A blocked release shows as **Excluded by policy** on the device's Patches tab. Agents older than 0.125.0 keep excluding feature releases locally. Agent log lines: `applied Windows feature-update policy`, `ignoring feature_update_settings`. See [Update Rings](/features/update-rings/#windows-feature-updates).
- **DNS Security retention.** A nightly job (22:18 UTC) deletes events and daily statistics older than each integration's retention days, else `DNS_SECURITY_RETENTION_DAYS_DEFAULT` (90). Retention days can now be edited on an existing integration. Deleting an integration now runs in the background: `DELETE /dns-security/integrations/:id` returns **202**, and the row shows **Deleting…** until it finishes. See [DNS Security](/features/dns-security/#data-retention).
- **Agent reconnect pacing (agent 0.125.0).** After an API restart a device can show offline up to about 30 seconds longer, because agents spread their reconnect over 1–30 seconds instead of 1–5. Startup uploads are spread over up to 2 minutes, and a `503`/`429` with `Retry-After` defers that periodic upload for up to 300 seconds. Heartbeats and command results are never deferred. See [Agent reconnect settings](#agent-reconnect-settings).
- **Admission control** rises only under sustained pressure: level 1 now needs event-loop lag of 200 ms or database wait of 150 ms (was 100 / 75) for three consecutive checks, and holds for 5 seconds (was 15). The emergency threshold is unchanged. The commented defaults in `.env.example` changed to match. See [Agent admission control](/deploy/environment/#agent-admission-control).
- **Breeze Assist.** New Breeze Assist policies start with **Deploy Breeze Assist to devices** on; existing policies, and devices with no Assist policy, are unchanged. The agent now removes only an Assist it installed itself; a copy installed by Intune or by hand is reported as not installed by Breeze and left alone, and with deploy on the first heartbeat after the upgrade adopts an Assist it finds. On Windows the agent does not start Assist on a WebView2 Runtime older than 92.0.902.49 and reports **Assist unavailable** with the reason. See [Breeze Assist](/agents/helper/#enabling--disabling-helper-chat).
- **The native remote-support consent dialog defaults to Deny.** Pressing Enter, or letting the dialog time out, declines the session. See [Session Consent](/features/remote-access/#session-consent--end-user-notification).
- **Patch compliance** on the dashboard is now the share of fully patched devices, matching the Patches page. It was the share of individual patches installed, so the number may change. `GET /patches/compliance` adds fields and changes none.
- **Derived Windows update severities (agent 0.125.0).** A Windows update with no MSRC rating can now be rated **important** from its classification and title, labelled **Derived rating**. A ring that auto-approves **important** will therefore approve Windows cumulative and security updates that used to be unrated. See [Severity Levels](/features/patch-management/#severity-levels).
- **Breeze AI.** The chat is called Breeze AI everywhere, and the full-page chat moves to `/ai/chat`; `/workspace` and `/wisp/chat` redirect, and `#session=<id>` links still open. A conversation moves between the side panel and the full-page chat with its history. `GET /api/v1/ai/sessions` and `/search` now return only chat conversations and add `orgId`, `type` and `deviceId`. The chat system prompt lists tools by domain (about 4.4 KB smaller), and every tool stays available; if tool choice gets worse for you, set `AI_TOOL_INDEX=full`. See [Breeze AI](/features/breeze-ai/).
- **Agreements.** The new `agreements:send` permission (send, copy link, void, Record signed agreement) is granted by migration to every role with `agreements:write`, `*:write` or `*:*`; remove it afterwards from roles that should edit templates but not send. Automatic reminders are **off** by default and links expire after 30 days by default. Customer mail uses the partner's sending identity.
