title: AI Impact
description: Report what your AI agents handled, what the model time cost, and an estimate of the human time it stood in for.

sections.text:
The **AI Impact** page answers the question a partner gets asked at every renewal: what did the AI actually do, and was it worth what it cost? It counts outcomes your [AI agents](/features/ai-agents/) produced, shows the actual model spend behind them, and prices the outcomes into an *estimate* of the human time they stood in for.

Open **AI → AI Impact** in the sidebar. It needs the `ai_agents:read` permission — the same one that lets you see agents and their runs.

sections.heading: Choosing a window
sections.text:
Pick **Last 7 days**, **Last 30 days** (the default), or **Last 90 days**. The window and the organization filter both live in the page's URL, so a view you are looking at is a view you can send someone.

With a single organization selected in the organization switcher you get that organization's figures. With several, you get the total across the organizations you can see, plus a **By organization** table ranked by estimated time saved.

sections.heading: What each counter means
sections.text:
| Counter | What it counts |
|---|---|
| **Alerts judged** | Every alert verdict an agent recorded that day. |
| **Flagged as noise** | The subset of those verdicts judged self-healed, a recurring pattern, or a duplicate of an already-grouped condition. |
| **Suppressions applied** | Alert suppressions an agent proposed that were approved and actually executed. |
| **Tickets triaged** | Ticket-triggered runs that finished with a triage proposal — either completed, or stopped to wait on an approval. |
| **Drafts sent** | AI-drafted replies and resolution notes that a technician actually sent. A draft that was discarded, superseded or left sitting counts for nothing. |
| **Fixes proposed** | Remediation actions an agent put forward, whether they went to the Approvals inbox or were only surfaced on the run. |
| **Fixes executed** | Remediation actions that actually ran and succeeded — approved-and-executed ones, plus Act mode's own executions where the follow-up verification did not fail. |
| **Fix watches held** | Follow-up checks after a remediation run that confirmed the fix held. |
| **Fix watches recurred** | Follow-up checks where the condition came back. |
| **Weekly reports delivered** | Weekly-report schedule runs that produced a report. A run that found no schedule, or failed to write the report, earns nothing. |
| **LLM spend** | Actual model spend for every agent run queued that day, whatever its kind or outcome. |

  A fix watch is **one remediation run**, not one action. A single run that restarted three services and then held is one held watch, not three.

The page shows the headline tiles, an **Outcomes per day** chart, and the by-organization table. The [PDF export](#exporting-a-pdf) carries all ten counters plus the spend, whether or not each has its own tile.

sections.heading: Estimated time saved
sections.text:
**Estimated time saved is an estimate, and Breeze never presents it as anything else.** It is not measured. Breeze credits each outcome with a fixed allowance of human time and adds them up. The tile is labelled *Estimated time saved*, its tooltip lists the allowance behind every line, and it sits beside the LLM spend tile — which is the actual figure, not an estimate — on purpose.

Six of the counters are priced. The rest are quality and funnel signals and contribute nothing to the estimate.

| Priced outcome | Default allowance |
|---|---|
| Alert judged | 90 seconds |
| Flagged as noise | 240 seconds |
| Ticket triaged | 360 seconds |
| Draft sent | 300 seconds |
| Fix executed | 900 seconds |
| Weekly report delivered | 1800 seconds |

sections.heading: Changing the weights
sections.text:
Click **Edit weights** to set your own allowances. The drawer says what they do: *"These weights only change the estimate — they never change what your AI agents do."* Each weight is a number of seconds, capped at 86,400 (one day). **Reset to defaults** clears your overrides.

Weights belong to the partner, not to an individual agent or organization — one MSP, one estimate model. Editing them requires the `ai_agents:write` permission **and** partner-wide policy authority, so a partner administrator with access to all organizations can change them; an organization-scoped user or a partner user limited to selected organizations cannot, and does not see the button.

Changing a weight re-prices **all** history the next time the page loads. Figures you exported before the change will not match figures you export after it.

sections.heading: Positive feedback rate
sections.text:
The **Positive feedback rate** is the share of thumbs-up among the alert verdicts that were rated in the window, with the raw counts beside it ("*n* helpful, *n* not helpful"). Only current verdicts count — a verdict that has since been superseded drops out. If nobody rated anything in the window, no rate is shown.

  This is a *feedback* rate, not accuracy and not precision. A thumbs-up records that a technician found the verdict useful; it is not evidence that the verdict was correct.

sections.heading: Promotion-eligible operations
sections.text: When an agent has operations with enough clean evidence to be pre-authorized, a **Promotion-eligible operations** tile appears. It is a pointer, not a list — click it to open **Settings → AI Agents**, where the Graduation panel shows the evidence and the Promote action. See [Graduation](/features/ai-agents/#graduation-feedback-loop).

sections.heading: How current the figures are
sections.text:
Breeze rebuilds the report nightly rather than computing it on every page load, so the page reports what it has and tells you how old that is.

- Every day is a **complete UTC day**. The line under the header reads *"Data through <date> (UTC) · rebuilt <time>"*.
- **Today is never included.** The most recent day you can see is yesterday, in UTC. That is deliberate — a partial day would make every trend line dip at the right-hand edge.
- The nightly pass rebuilds the **last 7 complete days** for each organization, which is what picks up late-arriving facts. The first time it runs for an organization it rebuilds the full **90 days**, so the 30- and 90-day windows are complete from the start rather than filling in over three months.
- **Refresh** rebuilds the last 90 complete days on demand. The button shows **Rebuilding…** while it waits and tells you when the new figures are in. A rebuild covering more than 200 organizations is refused — narrow to a single organization in the switcher and try again. Pressing it twice is harmless.

  Rebuilds are queued as background work. If a rebuild is still running after a couple of minutes the page says so and asks you to reload later rather than spinning indefinitely.

sections.heading: Exporting a PDF
sections.text: **Export PDF** produces a report of the current window containing all ten counters, the estimated time saved, the actual LLM spend, the window and its through-date, when the figures were last rebuilt, and the six weights the estimate was priced with. Dates in the export are UTC. Recording the weights alongside the numbers is what makes an exported report reproducible after somebody re-tunes the estimate model.

sections.heading: If everything reads zero
sections.text: The nightly rollup only runs while AI agents are enabled for the deployment (`BREEZE_AI_AGENTS_ENABLED`). With agents off, no outcomes are produced and none are counted, so the page truthfully reports zero rather than hiding. The page itself stays reachable either way. See [Enabling agents](/features/ai-agents/#enabling-agents).

title: AI Script Authoring & Review
description: How the AI assistant and background agents can write, get reviewed, and run scripts on your devices — and the controls that keep a human in the loop.

sections.text:
When no existing script in your library fits, the Breeze AI assistant (in chat) and background AI agents can **write one**, get it independently reviewed, and — after a human approves it, or your organization has explicitly opted in to unattended runs — execute it on the devices you're working on.

Nothing the AI writes ever runs unless a human reads a plain-language summary of it and approves, or your partner and your organization have both opted in to the unattended lane described below and the script cleared every safety check.

---

sections.heading: The three review layers
sections.text:
Every AI-written script goes through three checks, in order, before it can run:

1. **Automated scan.** The script is scanned for known-dangerous patterns (disabling security tools, deleting system files, exfiltrating credentials, and similar) before anyone — human or AI — sees it. A match on the most dangerous pattern list stops the process immediately; nothing is shown to a reviewer or an approver.

2. **Independent AI review.** A second AI model — one that never sees your conversation with the assistant, only the script itself and the devices it targets — reads the script and produces a plain-language summary, a risk tier (Low, Medium, High, or Critical), a list of findings, and a recommendation to approve, request changes, or reject.

3. **Human approval.** You see a readable approval card: what the script is for, what it does, the reviewer's summary and risk tier, and the code itself — never raw JSON. Low- and Medium-risk scripts can be approved by one qualified technician; High- and Critical-risk scripts require a second, independent approver ("four eyes").

sections.heading: The approval card
sections.text:
When the assistant or an agent proposes a script, you're shown:

- **Goal and expected effect**, in the AI's own words
- **Risk tier** and the reviewer's summary
- **Findings** the reviewer flagged, with severity
- **The script itself**, exactly as it will run
- **Rollback notes**, if the AI provided any

Approving runs the exact script you read — there is no "edit and approve" option. If you want changes, choose **Request changes** with a note; the AI gets your feedback and the reviewer's findings, and proposes a revised script that goes through all three review layers again.

Some scripts also require an extra acknowledgement before you can approve: any script that matched a "strict" pattern (for example, a registry change under `HKLM`) needs the approver to hold the Scripts permission and complete a fresh multi-factor authentication check — the same requirement as approving a strict pattern on a script from your library.

sections.heading: Provenance
sections.text:
Every script version and every execution that comes from this feature carries its origin:

- The **script library** shows an **Origin** column (Human, AI proposal, Imported, or System) and a "Reviewed" / "Edited since review" badge — editing an AI-authored script by hand clears the review badge, because what was reviewed is no longer exactly what would run.
- **Script detail** has a **Provenance panel**: who authored it, the reviewer's summary and risk tier, who approved it and how, and links to every execution.
- **Device Activity** on a device's page lists AI-authored script runs with an AI badge and a link to the originating proposal — opening that link shows the goal, status, risk tier, and the reviewer's summary.

If the organization that produced a proposal is later merged into another organization, or its data retention period ends, the proposal's own record may be erased. The script version and execution it produced remain visible; the provenance panel and the device-activity link both show "evidence erased" instead of a broken page.

sections.heading: Promotion to the library
sections.text: An AI-authored script is not added to your library automatically. After it has run and its author-specified verification claim has been independently confirmed (not just "the command exited 0" — an actual check, like confirming a service is running), **Save to library** becomes available on the proposal. Saving requires the Scripts permission and a fresh MFA check, exactly like creating a script by hand. From then on it's an ordinary library script, usable anywhere a library script is — including in an AI agent's autonomous "Act mode" toolkit.

sections.heading: The unattended lane
sections.text:
For narrow, low-risk, high-confidence cases, Breeze can run an AI-authored script **without waiting for a human** — but only when every one of the following is true:

- Your **partner** (MSP) has raised the ceiling that allows the unattended lane for its organizations at all.
- **Your organization** has separately and explicitly turned the lane on. A partner-level ceiling never turns it on by itself.
- The independent reviewer rated the script **Low or Medium risk** (never higher), found it matched the stated goal, is reversible, and has an adequate verification plan.
- The script touches only a small, configurable allow-list of resource classes (for example: services, temporary files, DNS cache, printing) — never credentials, security tooling, disk, boot configuration, user/group accounts, firewall rules, shell evaluation, or anything the scanner can't confidently classify.
- It targets exactly **one device**, has a timeout of 5 minutes or less, and — on Windows, for the resource classes that warrant it — a System Restore point is captured immediately before the run.
- Your organization hasn't had two unattended runs in a row fail their independent verification — if it has, the lane pauses itself for that organization until an administrator resets it.
- An hourly cap on unattended runs, set by your organization within your partner's ceiling, hasn't been reached.

Any script that doesn't clear every one of these goes to a human instead — there is no partial credit. On Linux and macOS, the resource classes that would need a restore point (registry, services, filesystem changes) are not eligible for the unattended lane at all in this release, because only Windows can take one.

Helper coverage for the checks behind this lane is partial today — treat the unattended lane as an MSP-managed capability you opt individual organizations into deliberately, not a default you enable fleet-wide without reviewing which devices and script classes it will actually touch.

sections.heading: Admin setup
sections.text:
The unattended lane is off for every organization by default. Turning it on requires two separate actions.

1. Your **partner** administrator raises the partner-wide ceiling (maximum risk tier, allowed resource classes, hourly cap) under partner-level AI settings.
2. An **organization** administrator with the Approvals permission and a fresh MFA check turns the lane on for that organization, optionally tightening any of the partner's limits further (but never loosening them).
3. The **AI Risk Dashboard**'s Script Proposals panel shows unattended-run counts and the lane's current state (open/closed) so you can monitor it.

sections.heading: FAQ
sections.text:
**Can the AI run any script it writes?**
No. Every AI-authored script is reviewed by an independent model and then either approved by a human or, only if your partner and your organization have both opted in, cleared through the unattended lane's fixed safety checks.

**What if I disagree with the reviewer?**
You decide. The reviewer's risk tier and recommendation are advisory to you (though they set the deterministic floor for the unattended lane) — you can approve a script the reviewer flagged as Medium risk, or reject one it recommended approving, and the AI Risk Dashboard tracks how often that happens.

**Does this replace the Script Builder AI in the editor?**
No — [Script Builder AI](/features/script-ai/) is a separate, in-editor assistant that helps you write scripts by hand and only runs a script with your explicit click. This feature is about the chat assistant and background agents authoring and running a script mid-conversation or mid-task, with independent review in between.

**Can I turn this off entirely?**
Yes — script proposing can be disabled per organization independently of the unattended lane.

title: AI tasks
description: Hand a long-running job to the workers with Start an AI task - recipes from the Library, the task page, approvals, and the flags that turn it on.

sections.text:
An [agent run](/features/ai-agents/#runs) is a single pass: it fires on a trigger, does what it can, and finishes. An **AI task** is the other shape: a long-running job you hand off and walk away from. Start an AI task for a service-recovery incident and it keeps working through investigation, action and verification after you close the browser, waiting for your approval at the step that needs it.

An AI task is not a separate actor. It is **handled by** an [agent](/features/ai-agents/), and when [Wisp](/features/wisp/#specialists) hands a job to a specialist, the result shows up as a run or an AI task that says who it was done for.

**Off by default, and a thin first slice:**
  AI tasks ship **disabled**, behind two flags of their own *and* the main
  `BREEZE_AI_AGENTS_ENABLED` kill switch. Exactly one recipe, **service
  recovery**, is shipped in this release. Nothing appears in the UI and no task
  can be created until an operator turns it on. See
  [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/#ai).

sections.heading: Recipes and the Library
sections.text: A **recipe** is a task template. The **Library** is where recipes live. Each recipe is an ordered list of steps and states which of them change anything. Starting an AI task means choosing a recipe and filling in what it needs.

sections.heading: Starting an AI task
sections.text: With the feature on, a **Start an AI task** button appears on the device page and on alert detail. Choose it, name the service that needs recovering, confirm, and Breeze opens the task's own page and starts work. Starting one needs **`ai_agents:write`** and a multi-factor confirmation, the same bar as moving an agent to Act mode.

sections.heading: What the task page shows
sections.text:
The task page is the record of the whole hand-off: the task's current state and phase, what it is waiting on if it is waiting, each operation it has performed, its final outcome, **Handled by** (the agent doing the work), and links to the underlying agent runs so you can read the detail of any single step. The device page also carries an **AI Tasks** feed so you can see task activity in the device's own timeline.

Reading tasks needs **`ai_agents:read`**. A task belonging to an organization or site you cannot see is reported as not found rather than as forbidden, so the route never confirms that someone else's task exists.

sections.heading: The service-recovery recipe
sections.text:
The one shipped recipe walks five ordered steps: **investigate, execute, observe, verify, document**. Only the `execute` step changes anything, and it is **always supervised**: the AI task raises a service-restart request into your existing [Approvals](/features/ai-agents/#approving-what-an-agent-proposes) page and waits there. There is no path in this recipe where an AI task restarts a service without a human approving it.

A service you have listed as a protected resource is refused **at start time**, before any request reaches Approvals, so a domain controller's critical services can never become a pending approval someone might wave through.

sections.heading: What runs in the background
sections.text: Two background workers ship with the feature: a task coordinator that ticks every 15 seconds, and a publisher that drains task events every 5 seconds. Both are registered whether or not the flags are on, deliberately, so that a task already in flight when you turn the feature off still finishes cleanly rather than stranding an approval. With the flags off no new task is ever admitted, so neither worker has anything to do. No new queue is added.

title: AI tools reference
description: AI tool workflows, configuration policy inlineSettings shapes, patch approval, backup profiles, billing examples, and troubleshooting by domain.
headings: Read documents and keep currencies separate
Quote lines and recurring device sets

sections.text: Tool descriptions summarize purpose and inputs. This reference carries the longer workflows and examples. Tools available to a caller depend on their permissions and surface. Resolve the organization and target before writing, preview changes, and follow each tool's approval requirements. Replace example UUIDs with IDs returned by read tools.

sections.heading: Core
sections.text:
Use `list_organizations` to resolve organization and site IDs before creating quotes, contracts, or invoices. Partner callers see accessible organizations; organization callers see their own. Use `query_devices` or `get_fleet_health` for fleet counts and status.

For `analyze_fleet_metrics`, per-device average, peak p95, and maximum come from rollups. The fleet field `p95ApproxAvgOfDevicePeaks` averages each device's peak per-bucket p95; it is not a recomputed fleet-wide percentile.

sections.heading: Devices
sections.text:
Read the target before sending `execute_command`. These are command **payloads**, not complete tool requests:

| Command | Payload shape and limits |
| --- | --- |
| `list_processes` | `{"page":1,"limit":50,"search":"","sortBy":"name","sortDesc":false}`; maximum limit 500, larger values reset to 50. |
| `event_logs_query` | `{"page":1,"limit":100,"logName":"System","level":"error","source":"Service Control Manager","eventId":7031}`; Windows only, page maximum 20, limit maximum 500. |
| `file_list` | `{"path":"C:\\Logs","limit":100}`; maximum 5000, no paging. Narrow the path to see more. |
| `start_service`, `stop_service`, `restart_service` | `{"serviceName":"wuauserv"}`; `name` is an alias. The agent receives `name`. |
| `kill_process` | `{"processName":"notepad.exe","pid":1234}`. |
| `file_read` | `{"path":"C:\\Logs\\app.log"}`. |

If a response includes `stdoutTruncation` or `_chat`, page or narrow the filters instead of repeating the same call. Include the process name from a prior read when requesting a kill through `manage_processes`: PIDs can be reused. The name helps the reviewer verify intent but is not rechecked against the live process list at dispatch.

Read-only command types `list_processes`, `file_list`, and `event_logs_list` skip durable approval in auto-execute modes but remain audited; per-step mode still confirms them. `list_services`, `event_logs_query`, mutations, and `file_read` require full approval.

sections.heading: Scripts & automation
sections.text:
For `run_script`, supply exactly one of a saved `scriptId` or a reviewed `proposalId` from `propose_script`. A maintenance-suppressed result is deferred, not failed; do not retry it during the window.

`run_script` also takes `groupId` (one saved device group UUID) in place of `deviceIds`; supply exactly one of the two. The group is resolved to concrete devices when the approval is requested. The approval shows the device list, the member count, and a short hash of the resolved device ids, and that list is what runs; later membership changes do not alter it. A group that resolves to more than 10 devices is refused with the resolved count (never truncated), and a group outside the conversation's organization is refused with the same message as a missing group. For larger groups use the Run Script modal or the API; see [Running on device groups](/features/scripts/#running-on-device-groups). The assistant cannot create, update or delete automations (with or without group targets); manage them in the UI or through configuration policies.

A `proposalId` call refused with `proposal_not_found` means no such proposal exists in this organization — do not retry it. `proposal_review_pending` means the review hasn't finished yet — poll `get_script_proposal` until its status is no longer pending, then retry `run_script`. `proposal_review_failed` means the review ended negatively (static-scan rejection or a technical failure) — submit a new proposal instead of retrying the same id.

A `timeout` means the 60-second wait expired while execution may continue. Read the returned `executionId` with `get_script_execution` before deciding the script failed or changing it. Also use execution lookup for external runs, such as editor Test Run or IDs from `get_script_execution_history`. Other `run_script` outcomes are final and do not need another lookup.

Run context `system` uses LocalSystem/root privileges. Context `user` uses the logged-in desktop session for profiles, mapped drives, and interactive desktop work. Omitting context uses the script's saved default. The context is shown to the approver and does not bypass approval.

sections.heading: Scan, approve, install
sections.text:
1. Resolve the exact devices and organization, then scan with `manage_patches`.
2. Read the patch inventory and per-device installation status. Present the selected patches and targets for confirmation.
3. Approve selected patches in the intended ring or explicitly confirmed partner-wide scope.
4. Install only the approved selection on the confirmed devices. Approval changes eligibility; it does not itself install patches.

| `manage_patches` action | Required fields |
| --- | --- |
| `list`, `compliance` | None; use `deviceId` on list for per-device status. |
| `scan` | `deviceIds` |
| `approve`, `decline`, `defer` | `patchId` or `patchName` |
| `bulk_approve` | `patchIds` |
| `install` | Both `patchIds` and `deviceIds` |
| `rollback` | Both `patchId` and `deviceIds` |

`patchName` matches a title, KB, or external ID present in the organization's fleet. Ambiguous matches return candidates instead of guessing. `ringId` scopes approval, decline, or deferral to one ring; omission uses the partner-wide blanket. For decline only, `allRings` revokes approval in every ring and cannot be combined with `ringId`.

sections.heading: Configure auto-approval
sections.text:
Create an update ring with `manage_update_rings`, then link its ID using `manage_policy_feature_link`, `featureType: "patch"`, and `featurePolicyId`. Put schedule and reboot settings on the configuration-policy feature. Example `autoApprove` value for an update ring:

```json
{
  "enabled": true,
  "severities": ["critical", "important"],
  "deferralDays": 0,
  "thirdPartyApps": false,
  "thirdPartyDeferralDays": null
}
```

OS severities are `critical`, `important`, `moderate`, and `low`. An enabled rule needs at least one severity or `thirdPartyApps: true`. Third-party approval also requires third-party sources on the linked configuration policy. On update, omitting `thirdPartyApps` or `thirdPartyDeferralDays` preserves the existing values; send explicit values to change them.

sections.heading: CVE findings and software policies
sections.text:
Use `get_vulnerability_report` for fleet CVEs and `get_device_vulnerabilities` for one device. Posture scores describe controls; patch inventory describes KBs and approval state. Neither answers a CVE question. An empty report means no findings are currently correlated; coverage is incomplete, so never claim there are no vulnerabilities.

`remediate_vulnerability` takes finding IDs from those reports and requires approval. Only partner-approved patches install; unavailable, unapproved, or out-of-site findings appear in `skipped`. Supplying `deviceId` pins the batch and rejects findings on other devices.

Software policies default to organization ownership. Partner-owned templates require full partner organization access. Example `remediationOptions`:

```json
{"autoUninstall":false,"notifyUser":true,"gracePeriod":7,"cooldownMinutes":30,"maintenanceWindowOnly":false}
```

`autoInstall` cannot be armed through these AI tools; a human operator needs `devices.execute` and MFA.

sections.heading: Monitoring & alerts
sections.text:
Create monitor definitions through `manage_monitor_definitions` before attaching their IDs to a configuration policy's `monitors` feature. A definition compiles into managed alert templates, rules, and automations; do not edit those compiled rows directly.

On create, the full definition requires `name`, `kind`, a matching `condition`, `severity`, `enabled`, `cooldownMinutes`, `autoResolve`, `responses`, `deliveryMode`, `deliveryChannelIds`, `escalationPolicyId`, `recurrenceThreshold`, `recurrenceWindowHours`, `recurrenceActions`, `pauseResponsesOnEscalation`, and `aiAgentId`. Consult the tool schema for the supported kinds and matching conditions. `ownerScope` and `orgId` are optional; organization ownership is the default and partner ownership requires full partner access. Updates accept a subset; ownership cannot change after creation.

Use `manage_delivery` to resolve delivery and manage routing/escalation. Set ownership with `orgId`/`ownerScope`, write fields in `data`, and identify update/delete targets with `id`. Its `set_default` action edits the “Everything else” fallback; empty `channelIds` means inbox only. Use `manage_notification_channels` for channel management. Use monitor definitions for both agent service/process checks and server-evaluated conditions, then attach them on the policy **Monitors** tab. The retired `alert_rule` and `monitoring` feature links are rejected; use `manage_monitor_definitions` and the `monitors` feature instead.

sections.heading: Network
sections.text: For discovered printers, switches, access points, cameras, and NAS devices, use `get_network_asset_reachability`. Always state evidence source and age: “responding via SNMP two minutes ago.” An `unverified` state means no recent check, not that the device is down.

sections.heading: Configuration policy workflow
sections.text:
1. Call `manage_policy_feature_link` with `action: "describe"` and `featureType`. This read-only reference lookup needs no existing policy ID.
2. Create the configuration policy with `manage_configuration_policy`. Organization ownership is the default. A partner-owned policy is a reusable library item and applies to no organizations until assigned.
3. Create any standalone prerequisite: update ring, backup profile, software policy, peripheral policy, or monitor definition. Link the returned ID as described below; link-only types do not accept inline settings.
4. Add the feature with the configuration policy ID and the returned `inlineSettings` shape.
5. Preview and confirm assignment scope, then use `apply_configuration_policy` with optional role/OS filters.

Only partner-owned policies support partner-level assignment. Omit `targetId` at that level; the server derives the policy's partner. Organization, site, device-group, and device assignments require `targetId`. Partner ownership requires full partner organization access. Maintenance authoring suppresses monitoring and requires an interactive user session; API-key and OAuth-grant callers cannot author it.

```json
{"action":"describe","featureType":"backup"}
```

sections.heading: Full inline settings reference
sections.text:
Each row is a shape reference, not literal JSON: `?` marks optional fields, alternatives are separated by a vertical bar, and explanatory text describes validation and behavior. The model receives the same reference on demand through `describe`.

| Feature type | Full shape and behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `patch` | `{ sources: ["os","third_party"], scheduleFrequency: "daily"\|"weekly"\|"monthly", scheduleTime: "02:00", scheduleDayOfWeek?: "tue", scheduleDayOfMonth?: 1, rebootPolicy: "never"\|"if_required"\|"always"\|"maintenance_window" } for schedule/reboot only; set featurePolicyId → existing update ring UUID to attach approval behaviour. Approval (auto-approve severities, deferral) and per-app block/pin rules live on the linked Update Ring (manage_update_rings), not on the policy.` |
| `maintenance` | `{ recurrence: "once"\|"daily"\|"weekly"\|"monthly", windowStart?: "naive ISO-8601 local datetime for once (e.g. 2026-03-15T02:00) \| HH:MM local time of day for daily/weekly/monthly (omit or null = 00:00). Never pass a Z-suffixed or offset-bearing instant for a recurring cadence — it is rejected and the window falls back to midnight.", durationHours: 1-72, timezone: "America/New_York", suppressAlerts: true, suppressPatching: true, suppressAutomations: false, suppressScripts: false, notifyBeforeMinutes?: 15, notifyOnStart: true, notifyOnEnd: true }` |
| `automation` | `{ items: [{ name, enabled: true, triggerType: "schedule"\|"event"\|"manual", cronExpression?: "0 2 * * *", timezone?: "America/New_York", eventType?: "device.offline"\|"alert.triggered"\|"compliance.failed"\|"patch.available", actions: [{ type: "run_script"\|"send_notification"\|"create_alert"\|"execute_command", scriptId?\|channelId?\|severity?\|message?\|command? }], onFailure: "stop"\|"continue"\|"notify" }] }` |
| `event_log` | `{ retentionDays: 30, maxEventsPerCycle: 100, collectCategories: ["security","hardware","application","system"], minimumLevel: "info"\|"warning"\|"error"\|"critical", collectionIntervalMinutes: 15, rateLimitPerHour: 12000 }` |
| `compliance` | `{ items: [{ name, enforcementLevel?: "monitor"\|"warn"\|"enforce" (default "monitor"; enforce also runs the rule's remediation), checkIntervalMinutes?: 60, rules: 1-50 of [ { type: "required_software", softwareName: "Contoso Agent" (case-insensitive name match against installed software), softwareVersion?: "7.0", versionOperator?: "any"\|"eq"\|"gte"\|"gt"\|"lte" (omit or "any" = presence only; any other operator REQUIRES softwareVersion; "gt" is evaluated as >=) } \| { type: "prohibited_software", prohibitedName } \| { type: "disk_space_minimum", minGb: number (minimum FREE space in GB), diskPath?: "C:" (default: every disk) } \| { type: "os_version", osType?: "windows"\|"macos"\|"linux"\|"any" (default "any"), minOsVersion?: "10.0.19045" } \| { type: "registry_check", registryPath, registryValueName, registryExpectedValue? (omit = the value only has to exist) } \| { type: "config_check", configFilePath, configKey, configExpectedValue? } ] }] }. Each rule may also carry description? and remediation?. A failing rule marks the device non-compliant (see configuration_policy_compliance). enforcementLevel "warn" and "enforce" also raise an alert per device (medium / high) that auto-resolves once the device is compliant again; "monitor" only reports. To be alerted when an app is missing or removed, use a required_software rule with enforcementLevel "warn", or a software_presence monitor (manage_monitor_definitions, condition { name, presence: "not_installed" }).` |
| `security` | `{ realTimeProtection: true, behavioralMonitoring: true, cloudLookup: true, scheduledScans: true, scanHour: "2", scanMinute: "0", scanDayOfWeek: "*", scanDayOfMonth: "*", autoQuarantine: true, notifyUser: true, blockUntrustedUsb: false, exclusions: [] }` |
| `backup` | `{ schedule: { frequency: "daily"\|"weekly"\|"monthly", time: "02:00", dayOfWeek?: 2 (0=Sunday..6=Saturday), dayOfMonth?: 1 (1..28), timezone?: "UTC" }, retention: { preset: "standard"\|"extended"\|"compliance"\|"custom", retentionDays?: 30, maxVersions?: 5 }, paths: [], targets: { paths: [], excludes: [] }, backupMode: "file"\|"hyperv"\|"mssql"\|"system_image", destinationConfigId?: "UUID" }. featurePolicyId → backup PROFILE UUID (manage_backup_profiles — "what to protect"), combined with inlineSettings { schedule, retention, destinationConfigId? } (destination omitted = the device org's default destination). Legacy links with featurePolicyId → backup config UUID still work. Partner-wide policies may link partner-wide profiles; their destination always resolves per device org. Compression, encryption and notification flags are not persisted by configuration-policy backup settings.` |
| `sensitive_data` | `{ detectionClasses: ["credential","pci","phi","pii","financial"], includePaths: [], excludePaths: [], fileTypes: [], maxFileSizeBytes: 104857600, workers: 4, timeoutSeconds: 300, scheduleType: "manual"\|"interval"\|"cron", intervalMinutes?: 60, cron?: "...", timezone: "UTC" }` |
| `warranty` | `{ enabled: true, warnDays: 90, criticalDays: 30 }` |
| `helper` | `{ enabled: true, showOpenPortal: true, showDeviceInfo: true, showRequestSupport: true, portalUrl?: "" } — the show* flags pick which tray-menu items appear; the tray icon itself is always shown.` |
| `pam` | `inlineSettings {uacInterceptionEnabled: boolean} — Windows UAC elevation prompt capture (default false / opt-in: capture is OFF when no policy assigns this feature). PAM rules/approvals are managed separately in the /pam console, not via config policies.` |
| `vulnerability` | `inlineSettings {enabled: boolean} — per-device CVE correlation / vulnerability scanning (default false / opt-in: devices with no policy are NOT scanned). Findings appear in the /vulnerabilities console; correlation runs daily.` |
| `device_lifecycle` | `inlineSettings {purgeRemovedAfterDays: number\|null} — permanently delete removed devices N days after removal (1..3650); null/absent = keep forever. Purge is IRREVERSIBLE: it destroys the device record and all of its history. A daily job applies it; devices whose agent uninstall is still queued are skipped until it completes. Closest level wins, so an org-level link with null opts that org out of a partner-wide window.` |
| `remote_access` | `{ webrtcDesktop: true, vncRelay: false, remoteTools: true, clipboardHostToViewer: true, clipboardViewerToHost: true, enableProxy: false, defaultAllowedPorts: [80,443], autoEnableProxy: false, maxConcurrentTunnels: 5, idleTimeoutMinutes: 5, maxSessionDurationHours: 8 (whole hours, 1..12 — remote desktop sessions are hard-capped at 12h and "unlimited"/0 is rejected), sessionPromptMode?: "off"\|"notify"\|"consent", consentUnavailableBehavior?: "proceed"\|"block", notifyOnSessionEnd?: true, showActiveIndicator?: true, technicianIdentityLevel?: "name_email"\|"name"\|"generic", allowUserEndSession?: true (the person at the device may end the session from the on-screen indicator, after a confirmation; default true) } — all fields optional; updates MERGE over the currently stored settings, so send only the fields to change. Unknown keys are stripped, never applied — use exactly these key names.` |
| `onedrive_helper` | `{ silentAccountConfig?, filesOnDemand?, kfmSilentOptIn?, kfmFolders? (Desktop/Documents/Pictures), kfmBlockOptOut?, tenantAssociationId?, restartOnChange?, libraries?: [{ libraryId, displayName, targetingMode (everyone\|graph_group\|local_ad_group), groupId?, groupName?, siteUrl? }] }` |
| `software_policy` | `Link-only: featurePolicyId → existing software policy UUID; no inlineSettings.` |
| `peripheral_control` | `Link-only: featurePolicyId → existing peripheral policy UUID; no inlineSettings.` |
| `monitors` | `{ items: [{ monitorId: "existing monitor definition UUID", enabled: true, overrides?: {}, sortOrder?: 0 }], inheritance: "cumulative"\|"replace" (default "cumulative"), checkIntervalSeconds: 60 }. Check interval accepts 10–3600 seconds and controls agent service/process checks. Up to 200 attachments; create monitor definitions with manage_monitor_definitions before linking.` |
| `hardware_monitoring` | `{ enabled: true, pollIntervalMinutes: 10, diskHealthIntervalMinutes: 60 } — inline-only RAID and disk-health collection settings. All fields are optional; these are the defaults. enabled is boolean; pollIntervalMinutes is an integer in 5..60; diskHealthIntervalMinutes is an integer in 15..1440. Collection is enabled without a policy link. Attach hardware monitors separately for alerts.` |
| `time_sync` | `{ enforceNtp: false, ntpServers: [], pollIntervalMinutes: 60, timezone: { expected: 'site', pinnedTimezone: null, autoFix: false } } — inline-only domain-aware Windows time settings. Up to 5 NTP hosts, no flags or ports; at least one host when enforceNtp is true. pollIntervalMinutes is an integer in 15..1440. A pinned IANA timezone must have a Windows mapping and overrides the site timezone. Workgroup, Entra-only and forest-root PDC devices use manual peers; members, DCs and other PDCs use the domain hierarchy. Unknown roles are skipped. GPO wins. autoFix defaults to false.` |
| `workload_inventory` | `{ enabled: false, dockerEnabled: true, podmanEnabled: true, hypervEnabled: true, proxmoxEnabled: true, intervalMinutes: 60 } — inline-only workload inventory settings. enabled defaults to false (opt-in): runtimes are always detected, but containers and VMs are listed only when enabled is true and the runtime's own flag is true. Turning a runtime off deletes its listed workloads. intervalMinutes is an integer in 15..1440. Collection is read-only.` |
| `system_protection` | `{ beforePatching: true, beforeScripts: false, beforeSoftwareInstall: false, labelPrefix: 'Breeze' } — inline-only Windows System Restore checkpoint toggles. Strict: unknown keys are rejected, so there is no onFailure/abort setting. beforePatching defaults to true (matches existing agent behaviour); the other two default to false (opt-in). labelPrefix is 1..64 characters with no control characters. A checkpoint is best-effort and not a backup: Windows may throttle or later remove it.` |
| `security_agents` | `{ version: 1, agents: [{ vendor: "huntress"\|"sentinelone"\|"controld"\|"nextdns", enabled: boolean, platforms?: ["windows"\|"macos"\|"linux"] }] } — inline-only third-party security agent selection. Strict: no keys, tokens or other fields (per-customer keys come from the vendor integration). Each vendor at most once; agents: [] opts the assigned devices out. No featurePolicyId. This tool cannot enable a vendor (enabling installs software, which needs a person with devices.execute); it can only list vendors as disabled.` |

sections.heading: Backup & recovery
sections.text:
Create storage with `manage_backup_configs` and a reusable “what to protect” profile with `manage_backup_profiles`. Link the profile to a configuration policy using `featureType: "backup"` and `featurePolicyId` equal to the **profile** ID. Put the destination configuration ID in `inlineSettings.destinationConfigId`, never in the new link's `featurePolicyId`.

Example profile `selections` (at least one source must be enabled; file selection requires paths):

```json
{
  "file": {"enabled":true,"paths":["C:\\Data"],"excludes":["*.tmp"]},
  "system_image": {"enabled":false,"includeSystemState":true},
  "mssql": {"enabled":false,"backupType":"full","excludeDatabases":[]},
  "hyperv": {"enabled":false,"consistencyType":"application","excludeVms":[]}
}
```

SQL backup types are `full`, `differential`, or `log`; Hyper-V consistency is `application` or `crash`. Profiles can be organization-owned or partner-wide. Example link request after the policy, profile, and destination have been created:

```json
{
  "action":"add",
  "configPolicyId":"11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111",
  "featureType":"backup",
  "featurePolicyId":"22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222",
  "inlineSettings":{
    "schedule":{"frequency":"daily","time":"02:00","timezone":"UTC"},
    "retention":{"preset":"custom","retentionDays":30,"maxVersions":5},
    "destinationConfigId":"33333333-3333-4333-8333-333333333333"
  }
}
```

Omitting the destination uses each device organization's default. Partner-wide policies can link partner-wide profiles, but destinations resolve per device organization. Schedule and retention must be nested objects. Compression, encryption, and notification flags are not persisted in configuration-policy backup settings.

Use `query_backups` for existing jobs and `trigger_backup` for an approved on-demand backup. For `restore_as_vm`, `engine: "hyperv"` (default) creates a VM on a Windows target. `engine: "rebuild"` rebuilds a Linux whole-machine snapshot with a disk-layout manifest into a VHDX on a Linux rebuild host. It gives the image a new machine identity; attach the VHDX to a Hyper-V VM manually.

sections.heading: Tickets & time
sections.text:
With `manage_tickets`, use `list` to search, `get` for details, `create` to open, `comment` for a reply/internal note, and `assign` to set ownership. `update_status` requires a `resolutionNote` when resolving. Send either a core `status` or a partner-configured `statusName` such as “Waiting on vendor,” never both. Use `draft` to store a proposed reply or resolution note for human review. `link_device` accepts an exact hostname or serial number.

For completed work, `log_time_entry` requires both `startedAt` and `endedAt`. `start_timer` automatically stops any current timer; `stop_timer` stops the running one. `list_work_types` returns active names and IDs. A work type can be supplied by name or ID at log/start time; omission uses the ticket-category default. It cannot be changed at stop time: edit the time entry instead. Hourly rate overrides are in the ticket organization's currency and require `time_entries:manage_billing`.

sections.heading: Service deliverables
sections.text:
Use `list_deliverables` to see cadence, due date, last delivery, and status (`on_track`, `due_soon`, `late`, `missed`, `inactive`). Set `occurrencesFor` to include one deliverable's recent occurrences. Example create `input` for `manage_deliverables`:

```json
{"name":"Monthly sign-in review","cadence":"monthly","anchorDueDate":"2026-10-01","effectiveFrom":"2026-10-01","leadDays":7,"graceDays":3,"artifactRequired":true,"portalVisible":false}
```

Cadences include `monthly`, `quarterly`, `semiannual`, `annual`, and `one_time`. Optional fields also include `contractId`, `completionMode`, `ownerUserId`, `ticketCategoryId`, and `autoEvidenceReportId`.

Link a report run with `link_evidence` before delivering an occurrence that requires an artifact; otherwise delivery returns `EVIDENCE_REQUIRED`. Occurrences can be delivered, waived, reopened, or rescheduled. `apply_template` copies all template items into the organization, optionally tied to a contract, and arms future unattended ticket creation, so approval is required. Name collisions abort the whole operation and return the colliding names.

A template's `autoEvidenceReportType` resolves to the organization's managed report definition, created on demand. Evidence runs are generated on the due day and become customer-visible only when the occurrence is delivered. `list_deliverable_templates` includes cadence, lead/grace days, artifact requirements, internal `instructions`, and `checklistTemplateId` for occurrence tickets. Never repeat those internal runbooks/checklists to customers.

sections.heading: Read documents and keep currencies separate
sections.text:
Use `list_invoices`, `list_contracts`, or `list_quotes` to find accessible documents, newest first, optionally filtered by organization or status. The corresponding `get_invoice`, `get_contract`, and `get_quote` tools return full details: invoice headers and lines; contract headers, lines, and billing-period history; or quote headers, derived totals, deposits, category breakdowns, blocks, and lines. Invoice reads include `depositDue` and, when a deposit is configured, derived `depositPaid`.

Every document carries a three-letter `currencyCode`. Subtotals, tax, totals, balances, line prices, payments, contract per-period totals, and generated invoices use their document's currency. Never sum documents with different currencies: group by `currencyCode` and report separate totals. Catalog prices are selected from that currency's price book, never converted.

For a large quote, first request `includeBlockContent: false` to inspect block types and order without their content. Then page with `blocksOffset` and `blocksLimit`; `blocksPagination` reports `total`, `returned`, and `hasMore`.

```json
{
  "quoteId": "11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111",
  "blocksOffset": 0,
  "blocksLimit": 10,
  "includeBlockContent": false
}
```

sections.heading: Assemble and issue invoices
sections.text:
`manage_invoices` supports `create_draft`, `add_manual_line`, `add_catalog_line`, `add_bundle_line`, `add_contract_line`, `update_line`, `remove_line`, `update_header`, `delete_draft`, `assemble_from_org`, `assemble_from_ticket`, `issue`, `void`, `record_payment`, `void_payment`, and `create_pay_link`. Build and inspect a draft before issuing it. Issue, void, and payment actions finalize financial state and require approval.

Assembly defaults to the organization's currency. A `blockedByCurrency` response lists unbilled work in other currencies; assemble a separate draft with the appropriate `currencyCode` for each. Line `unitPrice` and payment `amount` are in the invoice currency.

Catalog lines fail with `NO_PRICE_FOR_CURRENCY` (409) when the selected item lacks an invoice-currency price. Bundle lines return that error for a missing headline price, or `PRICE_BOOK_INCOMPLETE` (409) for a missing component price. Fill the price book or use `add_manual_line` with an explicit price. `add_contract_line` requires `invoiceId`, `contractId`, and `contractLineId`; it returns `line`, `pricedFrom`, and `overages`. A catalog line priced from `contract_snapshot` used the contract's stamped price because the price book had a gap. `overages` describes bill/flag allowance excesses and the sibling `invoiceLineId` when excess units were billed.

Relay a `create_pay_link` warning with code `CURRENCY_DIFFERS_FROM_STRIPE_ACCOUNT` to the user. It means the invoice and partner Stripe-account currencies differ; it does not block the link.

sections.heading: Contract lines and allowances
sections.text:
For `manage_contracts`, use `line` with `add_line`, header `patch` with `update`, and line `patch` with `update_line`. A new line requires `description` and `lineType`. Without `catalogItemId`, supply both `unitPrice` and `taxable`. Contract money and quantity inputs are decimal strings. With `catalogItemId`, the server resolves price and taxable status in the contract currency, ignoring supplied overrides. Missing prices cause `NO_PRICE_FOR_CURRENCY` (409); use a non-catalog line with an explicit price instead.

| `lineType` | Counting and required fields |
| --- | --- |
| `flat` | Flat recurring charge. |
| `per_device` | Organization's billable devices; optional `siteId`. |
| `per_device_role` | Nonempty `deviceRoles`; optional `siteId`. Allowed roles: `workstation`, `server`, `printer`, `router`, `switch`, `firewall`, `access_point`, `phone`, `iot`, `camera`, `nas`. `unknown` devices are reported as uncovered, never billed as a role. |
| `per_device_group` | `deviceGroupId` in the contract organization. Static groups use current members; dynamic groups evaluate their filter live at estimate/invoice time, except a filter's `groupId` condition reads the referenced group's cached membership. Do not supply `siteId`; the group's own site narrows membership. |
| `per_seat` | Seat-based recurring charge. |
| `manual` | Requires `manualQuantity`. |

`per_device`, `per_device_role`, `per_device_group`, and `per_seat` may include an allowance: positive whole-number `includedQuantity` together with `overageMode`. The included quantity is billed every period even when the live count is lower. `bill` adds a second invoice line for excess units at the required `overageUnitPrice`, in the contract currency. `flag` charges no excess; the estimate, generation result, and billing log report it for human review. Supply `overageUnitPrice` only with `bill`.

Example `manage_contracts` call, using an existing contract ID:

```json
{
  "action": "add_line",
  "contractId": "11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111",
  "line": {
    "lineType": "per_device_role",
    "description": "Managed workstations",
    "deviceRoles": ["workstation"],
    "unitPrice": "25.00",
    "taxable": false,
    "includedQuantity": "20",
    "overageMode": "bill",
    "overageUnitPrice": "30.00"
  }
}
```

`update_line` retains the line ID and invoice lineage. Lines are editable only on draft or active contracts; changes affect future periods, not generated invoices. `lineType` cannot change: remove and re-add the line to change it. A `siteId` of `null` widens an eligible site-scoped line to the organization.

For a catalog link, omitting `catalogItemId` retains both the current link and stamped price. A different item ID relinks and resolves price/taxable in the contract currency, ignoring supplied overrides. The same ID changes nothing; use `refreshCatalogPrice: true` to reprice the unchanged link. Sending `catalogItemId: null` unlinks it and requires both `unitPrice` and `taxable` in that patch.

Patch validation applies to the merged line: omitted allowance fields remain unchanged, and `null` clears them. `includedQuantity` and `overageMode` must remain paired, with `overageUnitPrice` only for `bill`. To remove an allowance, clear all three:

```json
{
  "action": "update_line",
  "contractId": "11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111",
  "lineId": "22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222",
  "patch": {
    "includedQuantity": null,
    "overageMode": null,
    "overageUnitPrice": null
  }
}
```

sections.heading: Build a quote
sections.text:
Use `manage_quotes` to create a draft, edit its header, add blocks and lines, inspect it with `get_quote`, then send it with approval. Accepted quotes support pay links. Required arguments are:

| Action | Required arguments |
| --- | --- |
| `create_draft` | `input` |
| `update` | `quoteId`, `patch` |
| `delete_draft`, `send`, `decline`, `create_pay_link` | `quoteId` |
| `add_block` | `quoteId`, `block` |
| `update_block` | `quoteId`, `blockId`, `block` |
| `delete_block` | `quoteId`, `blockId` |
| `reorder_blocks` | `quoteId`, `blockIds` |
| `add_manual_line` | `quoteId`, `line` |
| `add_catalog_line` | `quoteId`, `catalogItemId`, positive `quantity`; optional `blockId` |
| `update_line` | `quoteId`, `lineId`, `patch` |
| `remove_line` | `quoteId`, `lineId` |
| `move_line` | `quoteId`, `lineId`, target `line_items` `blockId` |
| `reorder_lines` | `quoteId`, `blockId`, `lineIds` |

The create `input` requires organization UUID `orgId`. Optional fields are `siteId`, `title`, three-letter `currencyCode` (defaults to organization currency), `expiryDate` (`YYYY-MM-DD`), `introNotes`, `terms`, and `termsAndConditions`. Resolve IDs from actual accessible records before using examples.

```json
{
  "action": "create_draft",
  "input": {
    "orgId": "11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111",
    "title": "Managed endpoint services",
    "currencyCode": "USD"
  }
}
```

Header `patch` supports `depositType` (`none`, `percent`, `selected_lines`), and `depositPercent` strictly between 0 and 100 with two decimal places, used only for `percent`. Omit to preserve values; `depositPercent: null` clears it. `coverPage` is an object with required boolean `enabled` and optional `title`, `coverImageId`, `preparedForName`, and `showPreparedBy` (default true). Its image UUID must belong to this same quote; `coverImageId: null` clears the image. `coverPage: null` clears the cover, while omission preserves it. For line updates, `depositEligible` controls inclusion in a `selected_lines` deposit.

sections.heading: Quote blocks
sections.text:
Both `add_block` and `update_block` take a `blockType` and matching `content` object. Updates must restate the existing type and cannot change it. Optional fields are marked with `?` below.

| `blockType` | `content` shape |
| --- | --- |
| `heading` | `text`, optional `level` (1–3). |
| `rich_text` | `html`. |
| `image` | Quote-image UUID `imageId`, `caption?`, `width?`. |
| `line_items` | `label?`. |
| `contract` | `templateId`, `templateVersionId`, `variableValues?` (manual fill-ins keyed by variable name), `label?`. Version must be published, belong to that template, and be visible to the quote's organization/partner; otherwise `INVALID_CONTRACT_TEMPLATE`. |
| `table` | `columns` (1–8 objects containing `label`, `align?`, `weight?`), `rows` (1–100 objects with string-array `cells` matching the column count), `caption?`, `zebra?`, `headerStyle?` (`accent` or `plain`). |
| `callout` | `variant` (`info`, `accent`, `warn`), `title?`, `html`. |

```json
{
  "action": "add_block",
  "quoteId": "11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111",
  "block": {
    "blockType": "table",
    "content": {
      "columns": [{ "label": "Service" }, { "label": "Schedule" }],
      "rows": [{ "cells": ["Endpoint review", "Monthly"] }],
      "zebra": true,
      "headerStyle": "plain"
    }
  }
}
```

sections.heading: Quote lines and recurring device sets
sections.text:
For `add_manual_line`, supply `sourceType` (`manual`, `catalog`, or `bundle`; use `manual` for hand-entered lines), numeric `unitPrice` in quote currency, boolean `taxable`, and at least one of `name` or `description`. Ordinary lines require positive numeric `quantity`. Optional fields are `name`, `description`, `customerVisible` (default true), `recurrence` (`one_time`, `monthly`, `annual`; default `one_time`), `termMonths`, `billingFrequency` (`monthly` or `annual`), `unitCost`, `sku`, `partNumber`, `depositEligible` (default false), `blockId`, and `catalogItemId`.

`add_catalog_line` looks up an item UUID, not a part number, and resolves the price in quote currency. A missing price causes `NO_PRICE_FOR_CURRENCY` (409); add a manual line instead.

A recurring manual line may set `contractLineType` to `per_device`, `per_device_role`, `per_device_group`, or `per_seat` and omit `quantity`. The server counts devices/seats, then recounts every billing period after acceptance. `per_device_role` requires `deviceRoles`; `per_device_group` requires `deviceGroupId`; `per_device` and `per_device_role` may include `siteId`. Each of the four supports positive whole-number `includedQuantity` plus `overageMode`; `bill` requires `overageUnitPrice` in quote currency. The included quantity is charged each period even when the live count is lower. Quote quantities are labeled estimates on the customer document; the resulting contract bills actual counts subject to any allowance.

```json
{
  "action": "add_manual_line",
  "quoteId": "11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111",
  "line": {
    "sourceType": "manual",
    "name": "Managed workstations",
    "unitPrice": 25,
    "taxable": false,
    "recurrence": "monthly",
    "contractLineType": "per_device_role",
    "deviceRoles": ["workstation"],
    "includedQuantity": 20,
    "overageMode": "bill",
    "overageUnitPrice": 30
  }
}
```

Device sets cannot be attached to one-time lines or bundle components. On existing recurring device-set lines, `deviceRoles`, `deviceGroupId`, `siteId`, `includedQuantity`, `overageMode`, and `overageUnitPrice` may be patched. `quantity` stays server-derived, and `contractLineType` cannot change; remove and re-add to change the type.

sections.heading: Catalog and distributor lookup
sections.text:
`search_catalog` searches the partner catalog by item name, SKU, manufacturer part number, or SYNNEX SKU, with optional item-type, bundle, and currency filters. Results include per-currency `prices`; an item missing the document currency needs a manual line.

For a product not yet in the catalog, use `lookup_distributor_product` before pricing a quote. It makes a partner-scoped, read-only outbound TD SYNNEX EC Express lookup for one distributor SKU or manufacturer part number, returning reseller cost, MSRP, currency, total stock, and per-warehouse availability. Use `search_catalog` for existing catalog items.

When `manage_billing_catalog` uses `set_bundle_components`, `allocationCurrency` is the ISO-4217 currency for component `revenueAllocation` amounts and is required if any component specifies an allocation. Allocations apply only in that currency and are never converted.

sections.heading: Accounts
sections.text:
Use `manage_organizations` for intake. Partner-only `create_org` requires a name and creates a default “Main Office” site. `create_site` takes `orgId`, name, and optional address. `add_contact` requires `orgId` and at least one of name, email, phone, or mobile; optional fields include title, roles, siteId, and isPrimary.

Organization/site/contact writes require approval. Suspending or churning an organization severs its agents. A status change (suspend, churn, reactivate) requires a second approver; a name edit or contact creation can be self-approved by the requester.

Example `input` for `manage_key_dates` create:

```json
{"label":"Insurance renewal","date":"2026-12-01","kind":"insurance_renewal","recursAnnually":true,"remindDaysBefore":30,"portalVisible":false}
```

Kinds also include `vendor_contract_end`, `compliance_deadline`, `audit`, and `other`. Optional fields include `ownerUserId` and `notes`. Reminders open a ticket before the date; annual recurrence rolls the date forward.

`manage_org_documents` works on files already in the organization's library. `update_metadata` changes title (1–200 characters), description (string or null), category from the advertised enum, or `portalVisible`. `set_portal_visibility` shows/hides the file on the portal. `supersede` marks `documentId` as the newer version of `supersedesDocumentId`; both must be current versions. Only a technician in the web app can upload or replace file content.

sections.heading: Integrations
sections.text:
Use `manage_notification_channels` to manage channels and test connectivity before routing alerts to them. Channel-specific `config` examples:

| Type | Config |
| --- | --- |
| `email` | `{"recipients":["operator@example.com"]}` |
| `slack` | `{"webhookUrl":"https://your-domain.example.com/slack-webhook"}` |
| `teams` | `{"webhookUrl":"https://your-domain.example.com/teams-webhook"}` |
| `webhook` | `{"url":"https://your-domain.example.com/events","headers":{}}` |
| `pagerduty` | `{"routingKey":"your-routing-key"}` |
| `sms` | `{"phoneNumbers":["+12025550123"]}` |

Replace the placeholders with the provider's actual configuration. Store secrets in channel configuration, not in ticket notes or customer-facing documents.

sections.heading: Microsoft 365 identity actions
sections.text:
With a customer's Microsoft 365 tenant connected for Admin actions (see [Cloud Tenant Integrations](/features/identity-integrations/)), the assistant can run these account actions. Each needs a reason and a human approval.

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `m365_reset_password` | Reset a user's password to a temporary one the user must change at first sign-in |
| `m365_disable_user` | Block a user's sign-in |
| `m365_revoke_sessions` | Revoke all of a user's Microsoft 365 sign-in sessions and refresh tokens |
| `m365_assign_license` / `m365_remove_license` | Assign or remove licences (SKUs); assigning fails closed when no seat is free |
| `m365_add_to_group` / `m365_remove_from_group` | Add a user to, or remove a user from, a group |
| `m365_retire_intune_device` | Retire an Intune-managed device — removes company data and unenrols it; not a full wipe |
| `m365_create_user` | Create a user with a temporary password the user must change at first sign-in |
| `m365_set_auto_reply` | Set, schedule or disable a mailbox automatic reply (out of office) |

The eight actions beyond reset and disable are new in v0.124.0 and are **four-eyes** actions: a second approver decides them every time, never the requester. They need a **one-time re-consent** of the Admin actions permission set in the customer tenant. Until it is granted, they are refused with a "consent upgrade required" error, while reset and disable keep running on the consent the tenant already holds.

`m365_reset_password` and `m365_disable_user` are pinned to one Entra account and need a fresh [caller verification](/security/caller-verification/) of that account. Without one the request is refused with "caller verification required" — in chat, over MCP, and again when an approved action is released — until a verification exists.

sections.heading: Administration
sections.text:
`capture_agent_pprof` requires approval and captures heap/goroutine profiles to diagnose agent memory growth or goroutine leaks. The tool returns metadata (sizes, capture time, and runtime gauges such as goroutine count). Download raw profiles from the device command API and analyze them with `go tool pprof`.

`trigger_agent_restart` targets the watchdog to recover an “Agent silent · watchdog OK” device even when the main agent is unresponsive. The watchdog acts while supervising/failing over the agent; a healthy agent is left untouched.

`get_invite_funnel` measures deployment invites sent, clicked, enrolled, and currently online, with up to ten recent enrollments including device ID, hostname, OS, invited email, and enrollment time. Devices enrolled without invites can produce zero counts here. Use fleet tools for device counts; a zero invite funnel does not mean an empty fleet.

`export_dataset` pages a dataset to completion without the ordinary 8,000-character response compaction. Use the returned artifact handle with `workspace_stage`. Supported datasets are `event_logs`, `agent_logs`, `device_inventory`, `software_inventory`, `metrics`, `vulnerabilities`, and `custom_fields`.

`delete_tenant` only affects the tenant owning the API key. Its `confirmation_phrase` must exactly equal `delete <tenant_name> permanently` (lowercase and trimmed). Soft deletion retains devices, users, and data for 30 days; contact support to restore during that window. Data is permanently removed afterward.

sections.heading: AI agents
sections.text:
`manage_ai_agents` action `authorize_supervised_key` grants a pre-authorized `opKey`, such as `manage_services:restart`, to the current organization's agent of the specified kind. The key must already fit the partner baseline ceiling and be earned through recent evidence. It requires a second approver and is unavailable to an AI agent itself.

`orgId` must equal the authenticated current organization, not a different target. The approval pins that organization's authorized-key list; scope and state are checked again before release. Future runs may use the authorized key without raising another approval.

title: AI usage chargeback
description: Bill your clients for the AI usage Breeze meters, using a price set on a billing profile.

sections.text: Breeze records every AI request your technicians and agents make for a client. You can rebill that usage on the client's invoice.

sections.heading: Turn it on
sections.text:
1. Go to **Settings → Billing → Rates** and open a billing profile.
2. In the **AI usage** section, set **AI usage billing**:
   - **Billable**: usage is billed to the client.
   - **Included**: usage is covered by the client's agreement. It appears in reports and never on invoices.
   - **Not billed**: the default for every profile.
3. Set the price:
   - **Markup on cost (%)**: a percentage over Breeze's metered cost. It applies only on a USD profile, because Breeze's cost is in USD and is never converted.
   - **Price list**: a price per million tokens for specific models, in the profile's currency. Each row has an input, output, cache read and cache write price. A model on the price list uses its price. Any other model uses the markup.

The organization's billing profile decides the price: the one assigned to it, otherwise your default profile in its currency. To give one client a different AI price, clone a profile, change its AI section, and assign it to that client.

sections.heading: What is billed
sections.text:
- Only usage on client-work features: chat, the Helper, the script builder and script reviewer, the Office add-ins, and AI agents. Catalog enrichment, extension content and patch tests are never billed.
- Only usage after you turn billing on. The price is fixed when the request is recorded. Changing the profile later never re-prices past usage.
- A billable profile with no price for a model, for example a EUR profile with no price-list row, records that usage as **unpriced**. It appears in the report and is never billed at zero.

sections.heading: When it is billed
sections.text:
- Usage is grouped by UTC calendar month. A request belongs to the month in which Breeze recorded it. A request made just before midnight UTC on the last day of a month, but recorded after midnight, belongs to the next month. This includes a request that Breeze had to replay later: it bills in the month of the replay.
- Shortly after each month ends, Breeze closes it once per client. Each model becomes one charge, rounded once to the currency's smallest unit. A charge that rounds to zero is not billed.
- Usage recorded for a month that was already closed, for example after merging two clients, is billed with the next month and labelled "usage from" and the month.
- A month's charge exists only after that month closes, which happens shortly after 00:00 UTC on the 1st (by about 05:30 UTC). This month's usage therefore appears on the next invoice, not on one you create today.
- Charges that round to zero, and usage older than 92 days, are never invoiced. They show in the report's unbilled column.

sections.heading: Putting it on an invoice
sections.text:
AI usage reaches an invoice through **Create invoice from unbilled work**. When you create an invoice from unbilled work, Breeze adds every unbilled AI usage charge for a month that has already closed and started on or before the invoice's end date. A month closes shortly after it ends (UTC), so this month's usage appears on the next invoice. Each charge becomes a line: "AI usage — (model) — (month) · (n) requests · (n) tokens".

- Issuing the invoice marks the charges billed.
- Voiding it releases them to be invoiced again.
- Charges in another currency are listed as blocked, never converted.
- AI usage lines are **non-taxable** by default. You can edit a draft line to change that.

Invoices that a [recurring contract](/features/contracts/) generates do not include AI usage.

sections.heading: The report
sections.text: **Reports → AI usage by client** shows each client's requests, tokens, Breeze cost, billable amount (billed and unbilled) and unpriced usage for a period. Report periods use your timezone, while billing uses UTC months, so a report period's edges can differ slightly from the invoice.

sections.heading: Rounding
sections.text: Each request's price is computed exactly and rounded to 6 decimal places. Each monthly charge is summed exactly, then rounded once (half up) to the currency's smallest unit. Because each model's charge is rounded separately, the invoice total can differ from the unrounded monthly total by at most half a cent per charge.

sections.heading: Related
sections.text:
- [Rates](/features/rates/) -- billing profiles and how an organization picks one
- [Invoices](/features/invoices/) -- assembling, issuing and voiding
- [Reports & Analytics](/features/reports/#business-reports) -- the AI usage by client report

title: AI in Breeze
description: How AI fits together in Breeze - operators, the workers, Wisp, and governance - plus the AI risk engine, approvals, rate limits, cost tracking and privacy.
headings: AI attribution on the device page
The model an AI agent uses

sections.text:
**Operators run Breeze. The workers do the work. Wisp runs your day.**

```
Operators run Breeze.            → people, roles, permissions, Approvals (you hold them)
The workers do the work.         → the built-in AI everyone has:
                                    Breeze AI (the chat door) · Agents (the roster) ·
                                    Runs · AI tasks (long-running jobs) · Library (recipes)
Wisp runs your day.              → one per person, hosted: home · thread · brief ·
                                    nudges · memory · grant · spend meter
Governance                       → Risk engine · Approvals · Budgets & usage ·
                                    Providers & models · Tool sources · Kill switch · Audit
Doors for other people           → Breeze Helper / Breeze Assist (end users on the device)
                                    Breeze AI for Office (end users in Office)
                                    MCP server (AI clients) · Mobile
```

sections.heading: Operators
sections.text: You and your technicians are the operators. Roles and permissions decide who can use AI at all (`ai_sessions:use`), who can manage agents (`ai_agents:*`) and who can approve what the AI proposes. There is one approval object and one place for it: **Approvals**. See [Approvals](#approval-workflow) below and [Approval security](/features/approval-security/).

sections.heading: The workers
sections.text:
The workers are the built-in AI every Breeze deployment has.

- **[Breeze AI](/features/breeze-ai/)** is the chat door: the side panel and the full chat page, suggested fixes and per-device memory.
- **[Agents](/features/ai-agents/)** are named, permission-scoped workers that wake on a trigger and write up what they found. Each pass is a **run**; see also [Analysis runs](/features/ai-analysis-runs/) and [AI impact](/features/ai-impact/).
- **[AI tasks](/features/ai-tasks/)** are long-running, multi-step jobs you hand off and walk away from, started from a recipe in the Library.

sections.heading: Wisp
sections.text: **[Wisp](/features/wisp/)** is one per person and sits above the workers. It keeps an eye on the estate that person can see, nudges them when something needs a human, and hands focused jobs to the workers. What it hands off shows up as a run or an AI task. Wisp runs on Breeze Cloud only: on a self-hosted server its sidebar entry and page show a lock, and there is nothing to configure.

sections.heading: Governance
sections.text:
AI settings have one home, **Settings → AI** (`/settings/ai`, v0.125.0+). It gathers the AI cards you are allowed to open, including AI Usage, Script authoring and Tool Sources; their pages keep their addresses.

The same controls apply to every worker: the [AI risk engine](#ai-risk-engine) and its tiers, [Approvals](#approval-workflow), [rate limits](#rate-limits), [cost tracking](#ai-cost-tracking), [bring your own LLM key](/features/bring-your-own-llm-key/), [tool sources](/features/tool-sources/) and the audit trail.

sections.heading: Doors for other people
sections.text:
- **[Breeze Helper](/agents/helper/)** gives end users an AI chat on their own device (see [Helper AI Chat](#helper-ai-chat)).
- **[Breeze AI for Office](/features/ai-for-office/)** brings it to your clients in Office.
- **[MCP server](/features/mcp-server/)** connects Claude Desktop, Cursor and other AI clients.
- **[Mobile](/features/mobile/)** carries approvals and Wisp nudges in your pocket.

---

sections.heading: AI Risk Engine
sections.text: The AI Risk Engine categorises every AI tool into one of four tiers that control how it executes. Navigate to it via **Security → AI Risk** in the sidebar.

sections.heading: AI-authored scripts
sections.text:
You can also extend the assistant with your own tools: point Breeze at an MCP server you run and its tools appear alongside these, with the same tiers and approvals — see [Tool Sources](/features/tool-sources/).

The assistant and background agents can author a script mid-conversation, have it independently reviewed, and run it once you approve — see [AI Script Authoring & Review](/features/ai-script-authoring/) for the full walkthrough. The AI Risk Dashboard's **Script Proposals** panel tracks proposals per day, unattended runs, and how often a human's decision disagrees with the independent reviewer's recommendation.

sections.heading: Tool tiers
sections.text:
| Tier | Execution | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Tier 1** | Auto-execute (read-only, no approval) | `query_devices`, `analyze_metrics`, `get_security_posture`, `ioc_hunt` (list_rule_sets/preview_sweep/list_sweeps/sweep_status), `get_active_users`, `disk_cleanup` (preview), `system_cleanup` (status), `propose_action_plan`, `list_configuration_policies`, `get_effective_configuration`, `preview_configuration_change`, `get_configuration_policy`, `configuration_policy_compliance`, `get_service_monitoring_status`, `query_monitors`, `manage_monitors` (get/create/update/delete), `query_backups`, `get_backup_status`, `browse_snapshots`, `get_incident_timeline`, `generate_incident_report`, `manage_software_policy` (list/get), `manage_browser_policy` (list), `list_playbooks`, `get_playbook_history`, `get_vulnerability_report`, `find_proven_fixes`, `get_device_vulnerabilities`, `search_documentation`, `propose_script`, `get_script_proposal` |
| **Tier 2** | Auto-execute + audit logged | `manage_alerts` (acknowledge/resolve), `manage_services` (list), `ioc_hunt` (cancel_sweep), `manage_processes` (list), `manage_scheduled_tasks` (list), `system_cleanup` (list), `analyze_disk_usage` (refresh), `analyze_boot_performance` (triggerCollection), `set_device_context`, `resolve_device_context`, `apply_configuration_policy`, `remove_configuration_policy_assignment`, `manage_configuration_policy` (activate/deactivate), `create_incident`, `revoke_elevation`, `assign_security_training`, `acknowledge_network_device`, `registry_operations` (read_key/get_value), `file_operations` (list), `execute_command` (list_processes/file_list/event_logs_list) |
| **Tier 3** | Requires human approval before execution | `execute_command` (kill_process/start_service/stop_service/restart_service/file_read/list_services/event_logs_query), `run_script`, `disk_cleanup` (execute), `system_cleanup` (run), `network_discovery`, `security_scan` (quarantine/remove/restore), `ioc_hunt` (sweep/import_iocs), `file_operations` (read/write/delete/mkdir/rename), `manage_configuration_policy` (create/update/delete), `manage_processes` (kill), `manage_scheduled_tasks` (run/disable/enable), `registry_operations` (set_value/create_key/delete_key), `create_remote_session`, `request_elevation`, `trigger_agent_restart`, `trigger_agent_upgrade`, `configure_network_baseline`, `trigger_backup`, `restore_snapshot`, `execute_containment`, `collect_evidence`, `execute_playbook`, `remediate_vulnerability`, `manage_ai_agents` (authorize_supervised_key) |
| **Tier 4** | Blocked — never executed | Cross-org operations |

`manage_monitors` supports `get` only. Its retired `create`, `update`, and `delete` actions return guidance without approval or write permission. Author network checks with `manage_monitor_definitions` using kind `network_check`; retire unconverted checks through the conversion ledger to preserve history.

  Tier classification is action-level, not tool-level. For example, `disk_cleanup` is Tier 1 when previewing and Tier 3 when executing. `system_cleanup` follows the same split — reading a run's status is Tier 1, listing the OS-native cleaners a device offers asks the device live and is Tier 2, running them is Tier 3; `analyze_disk_usage` and `analyze_boot_performance` read stored data at Tier 1, and only a fresh scan (`refresh`) or collection (`triggerCollection`) from the device is Tier 2; `manage_alerts` is Tier 1 for list/get and Tier 2 for acknowledge/resolve. `execute_command` resolves per `commandType`: `list_processes`, `file_list`, and `event_logs_list` are Tier 2; `list_services` and `event_logs_query` stay Tier 3 despite being reads, because they can return unredacted credential- or PII-bearing content (service binary paths, raw event-log messages); mutating types and `file_read` are Tier 3 too. `collect_evidence` is Tier 2 when it collects logs, processes or connections, and Tier 3 as soon as the request includes a screenshot (it is listed under Tier 3 because the unqualified call is checked at the stricter level). The AI resolves the tier for each specific action at runtime.
