Some security-service clients do not create a network adapter of their own. **Zscaler Client Connector on Windows** steers traffic through a filter driver bound to the existing Ethernet and Wi-Fi adapters, so there is normally no tunnel interface for the agent to see. Breeze can confirm the client is running, but not whether its tunnel is up, so on Windows Zscaler is usually shown as **Disconnected** (client running). Treat that state as "installed and running", not as proof the tunnel is down. Netskope may behave the same way.

For Cisco Secure Client and FortiClient, only the VPN component counts: the Cisco VPN agent and the FortiClient SSL-VPN daemon. Their other modules (Cisco Umbrella, FortiClient antivirus and web filtering) are not reported as a VPN. Cisco's VPN agent is part of the core install, so a device running Cisco Secure Client only for Umbrella can still show **Cisco Secure Client — Disconnected**.

On macOS, Zscaler's tunnel is a plain `utun` with no network-extension owner, so it is named by the single-running-client rule described below.

sections.heading: Naming tunnels on macOS
sections.text:
macOS tunnels are all named `utunN`, which carries no provider information. The agent resolves the owner per interface from the network extension that created it, so a Mac running several VPN clients at once still names each tunnel correctly.

Clients that create a plain `utun` from a background daemon rather than a network extension — NetBird and OpenVPN among them — expose no owner. Those tunnels are named only when exactly one known VPN client is running on the device; otherwise they show as the generic **VPN** provider rather than risk naming the wrong one. When a tunnel cannot be attributed this way, no VPN on that device is reported as disconnected either, since the unattributed tunnel may well belong to one of the running clients.

  VPN data is the latest snapshot from the agent's periodic network inventory report (roughly every 15 minutes), not a live view. A blank value means either no VPN was detected or the agent is too old to report VPN presence.

sections.heading: On the device list
sections.text:
Enable the **VPN** column via the column picker (it is hidden by default). It shows a badge per provider — connected VPNs first in the provider's color, then any disconnected clients in a muted badge — is sortable, and adds a filter dropdown with:

- **All VPN** — no VPN filtering
- **Any active VPN** — only devices with at least one active VPN
- One entry per provider seen in the current list (e.g. **Tailscale**), to show only devices running that provider

Hovering a VPN badge shows the full detail — interface, addresses, and DNS name, or `disconnected` for a client with no tunnel up. The filter matches **connected** VPNs only, so a device whose VPN client is running but disconnected does not count as having a VPN.

sections.heading: On the device Info tab
sections.text:
When a device has reported at least one VPN, its **Info** tab shows a **VPN** section with a card per VPN — connected tunnels first, then any disconnected clients:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **State** | Connected, or Disconnected when the client is running with no tunnel up. |
| **Interface** | The tunnel interface name on the device. Omitted when disconnected. |
| **VPN IPv4 / VPN IPv6** | The device's overlay-network addresses. |
| **VPN DNS Name** | The device's name on the overlay network (Tailscale). |
| **Detection Source** | How the VPN was identified (interface, adapter, service, or process). |
| **Last Reported** | When the agent last reported this VPN. |

The section is hidden entirely when the device has reported no VPNs at all.

---

sections.heading: Battery and Power Status
sections.text:
For devices with a battery (laptops and other portables), the agent reports power status with every heartbeat:

- **Battery charge** (percent)
- **Charging state** (charging, discharging, full, or not charging)
- **Power source** (plugged into AC or running on battery)
- **Estimated time remaining** while on battery, or **time to full** while charging (where the platform reports it)

This surfaces in two places:

- **Device list** — an optional **Power** column (enable it via the column picker) showing the charge percent with a charging/plugged-in icon, sortable by charge level. Devices without a battery show a dash.
- **Device Info tab** — a **Power** section with the battery charge, charging state, power source, time estimates, and when the status was last reported. The section only appears for devices that actually have a battery.

---

sections.heading: Memory Modules
sections.text:
The device **Hardware** tab lists installed memory per physical slot, so you can plan an upgrade without opening the case or running a script.

The **Memory** card shows total installed RAM, how many slots are in use (for example, **2 of 4 slots used**), and the memory speed. The speed is a single value when every module runs at the same speed and a range when they differ, labelled **configured** (the speed the modules actually run at) or **rated** (the module's rated speed, shown when the configured speed is not reported). On-package memory that has no slots, such as on Apple Silicon Macs, shows **On-package memory** instead of a slot count.

Below the summary cards, the **Memory Modules** table lists one row per slot:

| Column | Contents |
|--------|----------|
| **Slot** | The slot label (for example `DIMM_A1`) and bank label, when reported. |
| **Capacity** | Module size. |
| **Type** | Memory type and form factor (for example DDR4 · DIMM or DDR5 · SODIMM). |
| **Speed** | Configured speed in MT/s, with the rated speed alongside when it differs. |
| **Manufacturer**, **Part Number**, **Serial** | As reported by the module. |

Empty slots are listed by label and marked **Empty**. Fields the firmware leaves blank or fills with a placeholder (such as "To Be Filled By O.E.M.") show a dash.

**Collection.** The agent reads memory inventory from the SMBIOS tables on Windows and Linux and from `system_profiler` on macOS. It collects when the agent starts, every 24 hours, and on a manual hardware refresh, alongside the rest of the hardware inventory. If memory collection fails on a device, the rest of the hardware inventory still updates and the last good memory inventory is kept. Virtual machines report the virtual memory devices their hypervisor presents, which may not match physical hardware.

**Agent requirement.** Memory module inventory needs an agent release that collects it. Until a device runs one, the table shows **Not reported yet — needs agent update**.

The same data is available outside the UI:

- **REST API** — `GET /devices/{id}/hardware` returns `memoryModules` (ordered by slot) next to `hardware`, which carries `memorySlotsTotal`, `memoryMaxCapacityMb`, `memorySoldered` and `memoryObservedAt`.
- **Partner API** — the `device-inventory` export includes a `memoryModules` array and the slot summary under `hardware.memory`.
- **AI assistant** — `get_device_details` includes the module list and a used/free slot summary, so you can ask "how many free RAM slots does this server have?".

---

sections.heading: The Device Info Tab
sections.text:
The device page header (v0.124.0) shows the display name once, with the hostname in the sub-line, and an **Offline · last seen …** pill when the device is not checking in; CPU and RAM read **—** while the device is offline or its last sample is stale. When the device belongs to an organization other than your working organization, the header says **Viewing a *Org* device** with a **Switch to *Org*** action that changes your working organization and keeps you on the record.

Opening a device and selecting **Info** shows the device's identity and inventory at a glance:

| Section | Contents |
|---------|----------|
| **System** | Hostname, display name (editable), serial number, manufacturer, model. |
| **Device Role** | The device's assigned role and how it was determined. |
| **Function** | What the device is *for* (domain controller, kiosk, finance workstation, …), assessed by the AI Fleet designer or set by hand — see [Device function](#device-function) below. |
| **Operating System** | OS type, version, build, and architecture. |
| **Hardware Summary** | CPU model, cores/threads, RAM, disk, GPU, motherboard, BIOS version. |
| **Power** | Battery and power status (portable devices only — see above). |
| **VPN** | Active VPN/overlay clients (only when at least one is active — see above). |
| **Agent** | Agent, watchdog and helper (Breeze Assist) versions, status, last seen, enrollment date, system uptime, logged-in user. A warning appears here when agent updates are withheld from the device. A **Breeze Assist** row (v0.125.0+) reads **Installed**, **Not deployed**, or **Unavailable** with the reason; see [Breeze Assist availability](/agents/helper/#enabling--disabling-helper-chat). |
| **Desktop Access** | macOS remote-desktop readiness (macOS devices only). |
| **Tags** and **Custom Fields** | Organizational metadata, when present. |

The device's **Overview** tab also has a **Responsible contacts** card: who to contact about this device for each role (billing, technical, escalation and so on), resolved from its device group, site or organization. See [Responsible contacts](/reference/organizations-and-sites/#responsible-contacts).

The device **Overview** tab also has a **Physical placement** card (v0.125.0+) for the room, rack, rack unit and height (rack unit and height are whole numbers from 1 to 100). **Add** or **Edit** needs `devices:write` and an MFA check; clearing every field removes the placement. Discovered network assets have the same card on their detail page; an asset that is linked to a managed device shows the device's placement read-only, with a link to the device. The API is `GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE /devices/:id/placement` and `/discovery/assets/:id/placement`.

sections.heading: System Restore tab
sections.text: Separately from the Info tab, Windows devices have a **System Restore** tab (`#system-restore`) that lists each time Breeze asked for a System Restore checkpoint: when it was requested, what triggered it (patch install, script run or software install) and the outcome. From **agent 0.124.0** the device takes one restore point per command, just before its first change, and reports the outcome here; a device on an older agent keeps reading **Awaiting the device**. The list records requests and what the device reported; it does not mean a restore point still exists. See [System Protection](/features/configuration-policies/#system-protection). Entries are kept for 90 days from the request (set `RESTORE_POINT_ATTEMPT_RETENTION_DAYS`, up to 365). An entry still awaiting the device is removed only once it is past that window and its command can no longer report back.

sections.heading: Device function
sections.text:
**Function** (v0.113.0+) records what a device is *for*, as distinct from the billable **Device Role**. The built-in functions are Domain controller, File server, Print server, Hypervisor, Database server, Line-of-business workstation, Finance workstation, Executive workstation, Shared workstation, Conference room, Kiosk, Core switch, Edge firewall, Backup target and Unknown; **Custom…** lets you enter your own short label.

A function is either assessed by the [Fleet designer](/features/ai-agents/#fleet-designer) AI agent — badged **AI**, with a confidence percentage and a **Why the designer thinks so** explanation — or set by a technician with **Change function**, badged **Manual**. A manual assessment supersedes the AI one and the designer never overwrites it; **Clear** removes the assessment and the field reads **Not assessed**. Changing or clearing a function needs `devices:write` and a fresh MFA check.

Function is also available as the **Device Function** field in the device catalog filters and saved filters.

---

sections.heading: Queued Actions
sections.text:
A laptop that is asleep, a workstation someone shut down for the weekend, a
server on a maintenance reboot — Breeze no longer throws away work aimed at a
device that happens to be offline. Instead the action is **queued** with a
delivery deadline and handed to the device the moment it checks in again.

The device page shows a **Queued actions** section listing everything currently
waiting for that device: what the action is, who asked for it, when it was
queued, and when it expires. Anything in the list can be **cancelled** from
there if you no longer want it to run.

Elsewhere in the product a waiting step reads **"Queued — device offline"**
rather than Failed, so a nightly automation over a fleet of sleeping laptops no
longer shows a wall of red. A script run reads **"Queued — waiting for the
device to pick it up"** instead when the device itself still reports online but
no agent session has taken the command yet; it is delivered on the agent's next
check-in. The trade-off is worth knowing: **work that used to
fail fast now sits pending for up to a week.** If a step is only meaningful
against a live device, set it to skip instead — see the offline behaviour control
in [Automations](/features/automations/) and the patch-policy equivalent in
[Patch Management](/features/patch-management/).

Deadlines depend on the kind of work:

| Kind of work | Waits for |
|---|---|
| Scripts, patch installs, patch scans, software installs, automation actions | **7 days** |
| Inventory refreshes and other self-superseding config syncs | **24 hours** |
| Reboot, shutdown, and scheduled restart | **24 hours** |

A queued action that reaches its deadline without the device coming back expires
undelivered and is reported as expired — it never sits pending forever, and it
never runs late enough to surprise someone. Self-hosters can tune all three
deadlines; see [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/#feature-flags).

  Interactive work is deliberately **not** queued. Anything where you are waiting
  on a live answer — a terminal session, a remote-desktop connection, browsing
  files, listing or controlling processes and services — still reports the device
  as offline immediately rather than promising an answer later.

---

sections.heading: The Change History Tab
sections.text:
Opening a device and selecting **Change History** shows a newest-first timeline of what has physically and logically changed on that endpoint over time — a swapped disk, added memory, a new CPU, a BIOS update, or an operating-system upgrade. Use it to answer questions like "when did this machine's RAM change?" or "did the OS get upgraded before that issue started?" without cross-referencing screenshots or asking the user.

Breeze detects these changes automatically: the agent takes periodic inventory snapshots and compares each one against the previous snapshot. Any difference is recorded as a change entry and surfaced here. A device that has just been upgraded to a newer agent records nothing on its first snapshot, so upgrading never produces a spurious burst of "added" entries.

sections.heading: What's Recorded
sections.text:
Alongside the system-level changes covered in [Change Tracking](/features/change-tracking/) (software, services, startup items, network, scheduled tasks, and user accounts), the Change History tab records:

| Category | Examples |
|----------|----------|
| **Hardware** | Memory capacity (for example, "4 GB → 8 GB"), CPU model or core count, total fixed-disk capacity, BIOS, and serial / motherboard changes. |
| **OS Version** | Operating-system version upgrades. |

  Disk changes are tracked by **total fixed-disk capacity**, so an upgrade that increases capacity is recorded. Swapping a disk for one of the same size is not distinguished as a separate change.

sections.heading: Reading the Timeline
sections.text:
Each entry shows:

| Column | Contents |
|--------|----------|
| **When** | Timestamp of the detected change. |
| **Type** | The change category (Hardware, OS Version, Software, Service, and so on). |
| **Action** | Added, Removed, Modified, or Updated. |
| **Subject** | What changed. |
| **Change** | The before-and-after values — rendered as `old → new`, with additions shown as a new value and removals struck through. |

Two filters narrow the list: a **Type** filter (including dedicated **Hardware** and **OS Version** options) and an **Action** filter (Added / Removed / Modified / Updated). The tab loads in pages of 100 entries with a **Load more** control, and is deep-linkable via the `#change-history` anchor.

---

Related pages: [Device Groups](/features/device-groups/) for organizing devices into collections, [Tags](/features/tags/) and [Custom Fields](/features/custom-fields/) for metadata, [Change Tracking](/features/change-tracking/) for software and configuration change auditing, [IP History](/features/ip-history/) for the timeline of a device's network addresses, and [Workload Inventory](/features/workload-inventory/) for the containers and VMs on a host (the **Workloads** tab).

title: Diagnostic File Access
description: Let the Breeze AI assistant read specific log folders on one device, read-only, after an administrator approves it — and what can never be granted.

sections.text:
By default the AI assistant cannot read files in locations such as a user's `AppData` folder, `/etc`, or other profile and system paths. **Diagnostic file access** lets it ask for **read-only** access to specific folders on one device, for a limited time, after an administrator approves the request. It is meant for application and crash logs that live in those locations.

A grant never allows writes, deletes, renames, scripts or registry changes. It covers listing folders and reading files, and nothing else.

sections.heading: How a request works
sections.text:
1. **The assistant asks.** In AI chat or over MCP, the assistant calls `request_diagnostic_access` with the device, one to twenty absolute paths (each either *recursive* — the whole subtree — or *this folder only*), the operations it needs (list, read or both), a purpose, and a duration. Nothing is readable yet.

2. **Administrators are notified.** The request appears in **Approvals** and on the Breeze mobile app for every eligible approver. The card shows the organization, device, every path with its recursion, the operations, the duration, who asked and the stated purpose.

3. **An administrator decides.** Approving activates the grant for the requested duration, counted from approval. Denying closes it. The first decision wins; the other approvers' cards close.

4. **The assistant reads.** While the grant is active, `diagnostic_list_directory` and `diagnostic_read_file` work on paths inside the approved locations, for the person or key that asked — nobody else's session can use it. Each command is authorized again when it is delivered, so revoking a grant stops every command the device has not yet received.

The requester or an administrator can end a grant early with `revoke_diagnostic_access`. A grant also ends when it expires, when the device moves to another organization, or when its organization is merged.

Diagnostic reads need the v0.122.1 or later Breeze agent on the device. An older agent answers with `agent_update_required`; update the agent, then ask again.

sections.heading: Who can request and approve
sections.text:
| Role | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Requester** | `devices:execute` on the device. A user session, an API key or an MCP OAuth connection can hold a grant; AI agent runs and partner service keys cannot. |
| **Approver** | `devices:execute` **and** `approvals:decide` for the device's organization, plus access to the device's site. Eligibility is checked again at the moment of the decision. |

sections.heading: Request limits
sections.text:
| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Paths per request | 1 to 20 |
| Path depth | At least two levels below the drive or filesystem root (`C:\ProgramData\Vendor`, `/var/log`); `C:\`, `C:\Users` and `/home` are too broad |
| Grant duration | 5 to 1,440 minutes (default 240), from approval |
| Waiting for a decision | A request lapses after 1 hour |
| Pending requests | At most 5 per device for the same requester |
| Read size | Up to 992 KiB per read, paged with `offset` / `nextOffset` |
| Listing size | Up to 5,000 entries per page |

sections.heading: What can never be granted
sections.text:
Some locations are refused whatever the request says and whoever approves it. Requests that name them are rejected, a grant never covers them, and the Breeze agent on the device refuses them on its own as well — so a server-side mistake cannot reach them.

- **The Breeze agent's own configuration and state** (for example `C:\ProgramData\Breeze`, `/etc/breeze`, `/Library/Application Support/Breeze`).
- **Virtual and device filesystems**: `/proc`, `/sys` and `/dev`.
- **Credential material**, wherever it sits inside an approved folder:
  - **Browser secrets** — saved passwords, cookies and their encryption keys (Chrome/Edge `Login Data`, `Cookies`, `Local State`; Firefox `key4.db`, `logins.json`; Safari cookies).
  - **Credential stores** — registry hives under `System32\config`, DPAPI master keys, Credential Manager and Vault, Windows Hello containers, macOS keychains, GNOME keyring and KWallet, `/etc/shadow` and `sudoers`, Kerberos keytabs, setup answer files (`unattend.xml`) and Group Policy preference files.
  - **Private keys** — SSH user and host keys, GnuPG, TLS key files (`.pem`, `.key`, `.pfx`, `.p12`, `.ppk`) and Windows key containers.
  - **Stored tokens** — `.aws`, `.kube`, `.azure`, gcloud and Docker credentials, `.env` files, git credentials, Kerberos ticket caches, browser web storage, and shell and PowerShell command history.

When the assistant lists an approved folder, entries in these classes are left out entirely; the listing reports how many were withheld (`hiddenSensitive`). Reading one directly returns a `credential_material` refusal.

The agent also refuses any path that reaches its target through a symbolic link, junction, mount redirection, 8.3 short name or extra hard link. Ask for the real location instead.

  These lists name **known** locations. Anything else inside an approved folder is readable, so approve only the folders the stated purpose needs.

sections.heading: Content redaction
sections.text:
Every file read under a grant is passed through secret redaction **before the AI assistant sees it**. Breeze reads 16 KiB of extra context on each side of the requested range and redacts over that whole window, so a read that starts inside a value or a key still returns no part of it; UTF-16 text is covered too. Because of that context, one read returns at most 992 KiB. Password and token assignments (`password=…`, `api_key: …`), bearer tokens, JWTs, cloud access key IDs, connection strings and PEM private-key blocks are replaced with a redaction marker. When anything was replaced, the result carries `contentRedacted: true`, so the assistant knows part of the file was withheld. Binary files read as base64 are redacted the same way and re-encoded; a file with nothing to redact is returned unchanged.

Redaction is a second layer and recognizes known secret shapes only. It does not make credential stores readable — those stay refused as described above.

sections.heading: Self-approval by a sole operator
sections.text:
The person who asked can never approve their own request while anyone else is eligible to. They get no approval card, and the decision path re-checks this live when anyone approves.

When the requester is the **only** eligible approver — a one-person MSP, for example — they receive the single card, and approving it requires:

- **A fresh second factor for this decision.** The approval must be signed with a hardware-backed factor at assurance level L3 or higher: a passkey on this device or the Breeze Authenticator on a registered phone. A plain session tap, a TOTP code or a step-up reused from an earlier approval does not count, and the request is shown at **critical** risk. See [Approval Security](/features/approval-security/) for the assurance levels.
- **An audit record.** Breeze writes a `diagnostic_access.self_approval` record before the grant can become active. If that record cannot be written, the approval is refused (`503`, `audit_unavailable`) and can be retried; a self-approved grant never becomes active without it. The `diagnostic_access.approved` record that follows confirms the activation; a self-approval record with no matching approval marks one that did not complete (for example, the request lapsed at that moment).

A requester can always **deny** their own request.

sections.heading: Audit trail
sections.text:
Every step is recorded in the audit log. File contents are never logged.

| Event | When |
|---|---|
| `diagnostic_access.requested` | A request is created |
| `diagnostic_access.self_approval` | A sole operator approves their own request (written before activation) |
| `diagnostic_access.approved` / `diagnostic_access.denied` | A decision is made (the approved record says whether it was a self-approval) |
| `diagnostic_access.revoked` | A grant is revoked or a pending request withdrawn |
| `diagnostic_access.file_read_authorized` / `diagnostic_access.directory_list_authorized` | A signed authorization is handed to the device, before it reads anything |
| `diagnostic_access.file_read` / `diagnostic_access.directory_listed` | Each read or listing, with the path, the location the device actually opened, the outcome and whether content was redacted |

title: Network Discovery
description: Scan subnets with ARP, ICMP ping, TCP port scans, and SNMP to discover devices, classify asset types, map open services, and build network topology.
headings: Connecting to a discovered device's web UI

sections.text:
Network Discovery lets you scan subnets across your managed sites to find devices, identify their type and manufacturer, map open services, and build a topology of how hosts connect through routers and switches. Scans are executed by the Breeze agent running on a device within the target network. The agent performs ARP resolution, ICMP ping sweeps, TCP port scans, and SNMP queries, then reports results back to the API via WebSocket. Discovered assets are stored per-organization and automatically linked to enrolled devices when a MAC or IP address match is found.

Discovery profiles define what to scan and how. A profile is scoped to a single site and contains target subnets, scan methods, port ranges, SNMP communities, and a schedule. When a scan is triggered, a discovery job is created and dispatched through a background queue to an online agent at the profile's site. Results are processed asynchronously — assets are created or updated, topology edges are enriched, and the job record is updated with summary statistics.

---

sections.heading: Scan Types
sections.text:
| Method | Description | Privilege Required |
|--------|-------------|--------------------|
| `arp` | Sends ARP requests on the local subnet to resolve IP-to-MAC mappings using raw packet capture (pcap) | Root / Administrator |
| `ping` | ICMP echo request sweep to identify live hosts and measure round-trip time | Root / Administrator |
| `port_scan` | TCP connect scan against configured port ranges to identify open services | None |
| `snmp` | Queries SNMP system OIDs (sysDescr, sysObjectID, sysName) to identify device type and manufacturer | None |

sections.heading: Discovery Profiles
sections.text: A profile defines the complete configuration for a scan: which subnets to target, which methods to use, port ranges, SNMP credentials, and when scans should run. Profiles are scoped to an organization and site. Multiple profiles can exist per site to cover different network segments or scan strategies.

sections.heading: Discovered Assets
sections.text:
Each unique IP address found during a scan is stored as a discovered asset within the organization. Assets are classified by type (workstation, server, printer, router, switch, etc.) and tracked along two independent axes: an approval status you set, and a liveness indicator the system sets.

| Approval Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `pending` | Recently discovered, not yet reviewed |
| `approved` | Reviewed and accepted — shows up in dashboards and reports |
| `dismissed` | Explicitly excluded from dashboards and reports |

Separately, every asset carries an **online/offline** indicator based on whether it was seen in the most recent scan — this is independent of approval status, so a `pending` or `approved` asset can be online or offline at any time. Linking an asset to an enrolled device (see [Asset-to-Device Linking](#asset-to-device-linking) below) is a separate concept from approval status: a linked asset can be `pending`, `approved`, or `dismissed` just like any other.

sections.heading: Asset Types
sections.text:
| Type | Classification Criteria |
|------|------------------------|
| `printer` | SNMP sysDescr contains "printer", or ports 9100/631 are open |
| `router` | SNMP indicates router, or gateway IP (.1/.254) with HTTP but no SSH/RDP |
| `switch` | SNMP sysDescr or sysObjectID contains "switch" |
| `firewall` | SNMP sysDescr or sysObjectID contains "firewall" |
| `nas` | SNMP indicates NAS/Synology/QNAP, or ports 5000+5001 open |
| `access_point` | SNMP indicates wireless or access point |
| `server` | SSH open with database or service ports (3306, 5432, 1433, 6379, etc.) |
| `workstation` | RDP (3389), SMB (445), SSH (22), or VNC (5900) open |
| `camera` | MAC vendor (OUI) matches a known camera manufacturer (Hikvision, Dahua, Axis, Vivotek, Hanwha, Avigilon, Reolink) |
| `phone` | MAC vendor (OUI) matches a known VoIP phone manufacturer (Polycom, Yealink, Grandstream) |
| `iot` | MAC vendor (OUI) matches a known single-purpose IoT/smart-home manufacturer (Espressif, Tuya, Shelly, Sonoff, Raspberry Pi) |
| `unknown` | Insufficient data to classify |

`camera`, `phone`, and `iot` are only ever assigned by the MAC vendor (OUI) lookup -- there's no port or SNMP signature for them. This is the weakest classifier in the precedence order below, so a stronger signal (an agent scan or UniFi controller record) can still override one of these three if it disagrees.

When several detection sources disagree about a device's type, the better-informed source wins: a UniFi controller record outranks an agent network scan, which outranks a MAC/OUI vendor guess — so a lower-confidence source can no longer flip a device's type back and forth between scans (e.g. a UniFi switch flapping to `access_point`). A manual **Asset Type** override always beats all three, and **Reset to auto-detected** restores the best available machine classification, not simply the last one written.

sections.heading: Network Topology
sections.text:
Discovery builds an interactive map of how your network actually fits together -- a measured backbone of switches and routers with the hosts attached to them -- and lets you hand-map anything discovery can't see. Connections carry their provenance (how Breeze knows about them) so you can tell measured links from ones you drew yourself. See [Network Topology (classic view)](#network-topology-classic-view) below. Where it's enabled, agents assemble a live logical **[Site Map](#site-map)** from passive network evidence instead, with shared configuration templates and on-demand diagnostics.

---

sections.heading: ARP Scan
sections.text:
ARP scanning sends broadcast ARP requests on each matching network interface to resolve IP-to-MAC address mappings for all targets in the subnet. This is the most reliable method for discovering devices on the local L2 network segment.

  ARP scanning requires root (Linux/macOS) or Administrator (Windows) privileges because it uses raw packet capture via libpcap. When the agent is built without CGO or lacks permissions, ARP scan falls back to reading the OS ARP cache, which only contains entries for hosts the agent has recently communicated with.

The agent iterates over local network interfaces, matches them against the requested subnets, and sends ARP requests for each target IP. Replies are collected within the configured timeout window.

sections.heading: ICMP Ping Sweep
sections.text:
The ping sweep sends ICMP Echo Request packets to every target IP in parallel using a configurable worker pool (default: 128 concurrent workers). Each responding host is recorded with its round-trip time.

  ICMP ping requires root or elevated privileges to open raw sockets. The agent performs a pre-flight check before spawning workers — if the ICMP socket cannot be opened, the entire ping sweep is skipped gracefully with a warning log.

When both ping and port scan are enabled, the port scanner targets only the hosts that responded to ping, reducing scan time on large subnets.

sections.heading: TCP Port Scan
sections.text:
Port scanning uses TCP connect probes to check whether specific ports are open on each target. The scanner identifies well-known services by port number:

| Port | Service | Port | Service |
|------|---------|------|---------|
| 22 | SSH | 445 | SMB |
| 23 | Telnet | 1433 | MSSQL |
| 25 | SMTP | 3306 | MySQL |
| 53 | DNS | 3389 | RDP |
| 80 | HTTP | 5432 | PostgreSQL |
| 135 | RPC | 5672 | AMQP |
| 139 | NetBIOS | 5985/5986 | WinRM |
| 161 | SNMP | 6379 | Redis |
| 443 | HTTPS | 9100 | Printer |

Port scanning does not require elevated privileges and works on all platforms.

**Default ports** (when no `portRanges` are specified): `22, 80, 443, 445, 3389, 161, 139, 135, 5985, 5986, 9100`

sections.heading: SNMP Discovery
sections.text:
SNMP discovery queries each target on UDP port 161 (or the port set in the profile's SNMP settings) using the profile's SNMP credentials. It fetches three system OIDs:

| OID | Field | Usage |
|-----|-------|-------|
| `1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0` | sysDescr | OS and device identification, manufacturer detection |
| `1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0` | sysObjectID | Device model and type classification |
| `1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0` | sysName | Hostname / device name |

SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3 (noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv and authPriv) are supported. The profile's `snmpCredentials` object carries the version and, for v3, the user name, authentication protocol (MD5, SHA, SHA224, SHA256, SHA384, SHA512) and privacy protocol (DES, AES, AES192, AES256) with their passphrases; passphrases are stored encrypted and masked on read. For v2c the community string goes in `snmpCommunities`:

```json
{
  "snmpCommunities": [],
  "snmpCredentials": {
    "version": "v3",
    "username": "ro-monitor",
    "authProtocol": "sha",
    "authPassphrase": "…",
    "privacyProtocol": "aes",
    "privacyPassphrase": "…",
    "port": 161,
    "timeout": 2000,
    "retries": 1
  }
}
```

The agent tries the structured credential first, then each `snmpCommunities` entry (the legacy `v3:<user>` prefix for a noAuthNoPriv v3 user is still honoured). The built-in `public` community is used **only** when the profile configures no SNMP credential at all — a profile set to v3 is never probed with v2c/`public`. When a target rejects the configured v3 credentials (unknown user, wrong digest, decryption error) the agent logs a warning with the credential summary (user name and protocols, never passphrases) and the count of rejecting targets, so "no SNMP data" can be told apart from "device does not speak SNMP".

SNMP data is used by the asset classifier to determine manufacturer (Cisco, HP, Dell, Juniper, MikroTik, Synology, QNAP, Ubiquiti, Fortinet) and device type.

---

sections.heading: Discovery Profiles
sections.text: Creating, editing, or deleting a profile; triggering or cancelling a scan; and approving, dismissing, linking, unlinking, or deleting a discovered asset all require an MFA-verified session. If your account has MFA enrolled, you may be prompted to step up before the action completes. (Network Topology edits are not affected.)

sections.heading: Creating a Profile
sections.text:
Profiles define the full scan configuration and are scoped to an organization and site.

```bash
POST /discovery/profiles
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "orgId": "uuid",
  "siteId": "uuid",
  "name": "Office LAN Scan",
  "description": "Weekly scan of main office subnet",
  "subnets": ["192.168.1.0/24", "192.168.2.0/24"],
  "excludeIps": ["192.168.1.1"],
  "methods": ["arp", "ping", "port_scan", "snmp"],
  "portRanges": ["22,80,443,445,3389"],
  "snmpCommunities": ["public"],
  "schedule": {
    "type": "cron",
    "cron": "0 2 * * 0"
  },
  "deepScan": false,
  "identifyOS": true,
  "resolveHostnames": true,
  "timeout": 3,
  "concurrency": 128
}
```

sections.heading: Profile Fields
sections.text:
| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| `orgId` | UUID | Yes* | Organization ID. Auto-resolved for org-scoped tokens |
| `siteId` | UUID | Yes | Site the profile belongs to |
| `name` | string | Yes | Human-readable name (max 255 chars) |
| `description` | string | No | Optional description |
| `subnets` | string[] | Yes | CIDR subnets or individual IPs to scan |
| `excludeIps` | string[] | No | IPs to skip during scanning |
| `methods` | string[] | Yes | Scan methods: `arp`, `ping`, `port_scan`, `snmp` |
| `portRanges` | any | No | Port ranges for port scan (e.g., `["22,80,443", "1000-2000"]`) |
| `snmpCommunities` | string[] | No | SNMPv1/v2c community strings (legacy `v3:<user>` prefix = noAuthNoPriv v3 user) |
| `snmpCredentials` | object | No | Structured SNMP settings: `version` (`v1`/`v2c`/`v3`), `username`, `authProtocol`, `authPassphrase`, `privacyProtocol`, `privacyPassphrase`, `port`, `timeout` (ms), `retries` |
| `schedule` | object | Yes | Schedule configuration (see below) |
| `deepScan` | boolean | No | Allow subnets larger than /16 (65,536+ hosts). Without it, a profile with such a subnet is refused on save. Default `false` |
| `identifyOS` | boolean | No | Attempt OS fingerprinting from SNMP and port data. Default `false` |
| `resolveHostnames` | boolean | No | Perform reverse DNS lookups. Default `false` |
| `timeout` | integer | No | Per-probe timeout in seconds. Default `2` |
| `concurrency` | integer | No | Number of concurrent workers. Default `128` |

sections.heading: Schedule Types
sections.text:
| Type | Required Fields | Description |
|------|-----------------|-------------|
| `manual` | None | Only runs when triggered via `POST /discovery/scan` |
| `cron` | `cron` | Standard cron expression for recurring scans. Accepts an optional `timezone` (IANA identifier, e.g. `America/New_York`; defaults to `UTC`) so the expression evaluates in that zone rather than UTC |
| `interval` | `intervalMinutes` | Run every N minutes |

In the profile form, the **Schedule** cadence dropdown offers **Manual**, **Hourly**, **Custom interval**, **Daily**, **Weekly**, and **Monthly**. Daily, Weekly, and Monthly (which compile to a `cron` schedule) show a **Timezone** field alongside the time picker; Hourly and Custom interval don't need one since they aren't clock-aligned. A new profile's **Custom interval** cadence defaults to running every 60 minutes until you change it.

  A profile with a subnet larger than a /16 (65,536 hosts) is refused on save with `400` (*Subnet "…" is too large: the agent skips subnets over 65,536 addresses (larger than a /16). Split it into smaller ranges.*) unless `deepScan` is `true`. The check runs when a profile is created and whenever an update changes its subnets or `deepScan`. This prevents accidental full-class-B scans that could take a long time and generate significant network traffic. `deepScan` is set through the API.

sections.heading: Updating a Profile
sections.text:
```bash
PATCH /discovery/profiles/:id
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "subnets": ["10.0.0.0/24"],
  "enabled": false
}
```

Only the fields you include are updated. Omitted fields retain their current values.

sections.heading: Deleting a Profile
sections.text:
```bash
DELETE /discovery/profiles/:id
```

Deleting a profile also removes all associated discovery jobs in a single transaction.

---

sections.heading: Triggering a Scan
sections.text:
To run a scan immediately, POST to the scan endpoint with the profile ID and an optional agent ID:

```bash
POST /discovery/scan
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "profileId": "uuid",
  "agentId": "optional-agent-id"
}
```

If `agentId` is omitted, the system automatically selects an online agent from the profile's site. The scan is dispatched through a background queue to the discovery worker, which sends a `network_discovery` command to the agent via WebSocket.

  The response returns a discovery job object with status `scheduled`. The scan transitions to `running` once the agent receives the command, and to `completed` when results have been processed.

sections.heading: Scan Execution Flow
sections.text:
1. **API creates a discovery job** with status `scheduled` and enqueues a dispatch-scan task in the background queue.

2. **Discovery worker picks up the task**, loads the profile, finds an online agent at the site, and sends a `network_discovery` command via WebSocket.

3. **Agent receives the command** and runs the configured scan methods (ARP, ping, port scan, SNMP) against the target subnets.

4. **Agent returns results** via WebSocket as a `command_result` message containing the list of discovered hosts.

5. **API enqueues a process-results task** in the background queue. The worker creates or updates discovered assets, auto-links matches to enrolled devices by MAC/IP, enriches the network topology, and marks the job as `completed`.

sections.heading: Monitoring Job Status
sections.text:
**List all jobs:**

```
GET /discovery/jobs?orgId=uuid
```

**Get job detail with discovered assets:**

```
GET /discovery/jobs/:id
```

The detail endpoint returns the job record plus all discovered assets associated with the job.

sections.heading: Cancelling a Job
sections.text:
Jobs with status `scheduled` or `running` can be cancelled:

```bash
POST /discovery/jobs/:id/cancel
```

The job status is set to `cancelled` and the system attempts to remove it from the background queue. If the scan is already in progress on the agent, cancellation takes effect when results arrive — cancelled jobs skip result processing.

sections.heading: Job Statuses
sections.text:
| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `scheduled` | Job created, waiting to be dispatched to an agent |
| `running` | Command sent to agent, scan in progress |
| `completed` | Results processed, assets upserted |
| `failed` | No online agent available, profile not found, or dispatch error |
| `cancelled` | Cancelled by an administrator before completion |

---

sections.heading: Viewing Assets
sections.text:
List all discovered assets with optional filters:

```
GET /discovery/assets?orgId=uuid&approvalStatus=pending&assetType=router
```

**Filter parameters:**

| Parameter | Values |
|-----------|--------|
| `orgId` | UUID of the organization |
| `approvalStatus` | `pending`, `approved`, `dismissed` |
| `assetType` | `workstation`, `server`, `printer`, `router`, `switch`, `firewall`, `access_point`, `phone`, `iot`, `camera`, `nas`, `unknown` |

**Quick Filters:** The discovered assets tab includes chip-style quick filter buttons at the top of the list. Filter by scan profile or subnet to quickly narrow down results. When filters are active, bulk actions (approve, dismiss) apply only to the currently filtered view -- unfiltered assets are not affected.

Each asset in the response includes monitoring status flags:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `snmpMonitoringEnabled` | Whether an active SNMP monitor is attached to this asset |
| `networkMonitoringEnabled` | Whether an active network monitor (ping, TCP, HTTP, DNS) is attached |
| `monitoringEnabled` | `true` if either SNMP or network monitoring is active |
| `linkedDeviceName` | Display name or hostname of the linked enrolled device, if any |

sections.heading: Adding a Network Asset Manually
sections.text:
Not every network asset can be discovered by a scan — a hosted website, a SaaS endpoint, or a device on a segment the agent can't reach still needs to show up alongside everything else in the unified **Devices** list. Use the **Add network asset** option from the Devices page's add-asset menu to hand-enter one.

A manually-added asset is a real discovered-asset row (`source: manual`) — it gets the same list presentation, monitors, alerts, and topology treatment as a scan-discovered one, it's just born without a first sighting (`status: unknown` until something actually reaches it).

**Identity.** Every asset needs at least one of: IP address, hostname, or URL. A `website` or `service` asset specifically requires a **URL** — those types have no stable IP (a hosted site's A record can change), so the URL is the identity, not a derived attribute.

**Manual vs. hand-added assets.** This is for assets with a *network identity* (IP, hostname, or URL) — printers, routers, websites, SaaS endpoints, anything reachable on the network or the internet. Equipment with no network identity (a UPS, a physical lock, a piece of furniture you just want tracked in inventory) is tracked separately as inventory, not a network asset. The two never overlap: if it has an IP, hostname, or URL, it's a network asset.

**A later scan updates it in place.** If a scan or the UniFi controller later finds the same IP, the existing row is updated — not duplicated — rather than creating a second, conflicting asset. A network scan never overwrites the hostname, manufacturer, or model you typed in on a manually-added row; MAC address and liveness fields (last-seen time, online status) always update from what the scan finds. A UniFi-adopted device that matches by MAC or IP is enriched the normal UniFi way and can update those same fields, since UniFi sync doesn't distinguish a manually-added row. A `website`/`service` asset, having no IP, is never touched by either path.

**Monitoring hand-off.** After creating a `website` or `service` asset, the form offers to add an HTTP check right away, pre-targeted at the URL you entered — see [Network Monitors](#network-monitors) below for what HTTP checks report. You can always add monitoring later from the asset's detail page instead.

sections.heading: Network Device Detail Page
sections.text:
Clicking a network-discovered device in the unified **Devices** list opens a dedicated detail page (`/devices/network/:id`) instead of a popup. The page has breadcrumbs back to **Devices** and a working back button, so you can navigate in and out without losing your place.

The page has two tabs — **Overview** (identity, IP/MAC, manufacturer/model, SNMP data, ping, open ports) and **Monitoring** (poll configuration, OIDs, and history). The selected tab is reflected in the URL hash (e.g. `#monitoring`), so you can bookmark or share a link directly to a specific tab.

From the **Overview** tab you can override the auto-detected device type using the **Asset Type** dropdown. If a device's type was set manually, a **Reset to auto-detected** link appears so you can revert to the type the scan originally detected.

**Reachability header.** The header always shows a reachability badge, never a bare "Online" — it names both the state and where that state came from: **Responding**, **Not responding**, or **Unverified**, followed by the source (**Network check**, **Probe**, **Scan**, **UniFi**, or **SNMP**) and how long ago, e.g. "Responding · Network check 2m ago." If nothing has ever reported on the device, it shows **"Nothing has reported on this device."** A **Check now** button triggers an on-demand probe.

**Health and Reachability cards.** The **Reachability** card breaks the headline status down by source, with its own detail line per check type. A stat strip below it shows **Reachability**, **Last poll**, and a device-type-specific slot (for example **Lowest supply** for a printer, or **Ports up** for a switch). A **Device health** or **Printer health** card (depending on the detected device type) surfaces the metrics most relevant to that device type, with a **View all N OIDs** link into the full collection and a **Choose a template** prompt if no SNMP template is assigned yet.

**Monitoring tab.** The Monitoring tab shows a poll configuration summary, an OID table, and metric history charts. Each row in the OID table reports its own state: **Collecting**, **Unsupported**, **Stale**, or **Never polled**. A failed poll always says why — for example, an OID the device doesn't support reports the exact code it returned; a table value that needs a newer agent says so explicitly ("update the agent on the bridging device"); a walk that hit its row limit is marked **Partial**. The poll configuration summary itself reports overall collection status as **Polling**, **Failing**, **No template**, **No agent in site**, **Asset moved**, **Never polled**, or **Paused**.

**Template suggestion.** When Breeze recognizes a device's identity (from its SNMP `sysObjectID`), the Overview and Monitoring tabs show a suggested SNMP template with the reason it was suggested (e.g. "Suggested: Xerox Printer — matched by device identity"). Click **Use suggestion** to apply it. If no template is assigned at all, a warning explains that nothing is being polled until one is set.

All asset-level settings — identity, monitoring configuration, and the manual link to an enrolled Breeze device — are consolidated in a single **Settings** modal, opened from the button in the page header.

  SNMPv1 devices are polled using SNMP version 1 rather than being treated as v2c.

From the Settings modal's **Link** section you can see the asset's link state and **Unlink** it from its enrolled Breeze device. Unlinking is **durable** regardless of how the link was made: future scans will not silently re-link the asset — auto-linking is suppressed for it until you deliberately re-link. The network device detail page is also where you link (or re-link) an asset to an enrolled device manually.

sections.heading: Asset-to-Device Linking
sections.text:
Linking records which enrolled Breeze device corresponds to a discovered asset — it also sets the asset's approval status to `approved` as a side effect, and is used for **identity and asset tracking only**. Linking alone does not open remote access; see [Connecting to a discovered device's web UI](#connecting-to-a-discovered-devices-web-ui) below for proxy access.

Linking is **automatic and hidden**: during scan result processing, the worker matches assets to enrolled devices by MAC address or IP address within the same organization, with no action needed from you. The only manual acts are **overriding** a link (pointing the asset at a different enrolled device from its network device detail page) and **unlinking**. A manual unlink is permanent until you re-link — the next scan will not undo it.

The API equivalent:

```bash
POST /discovery/assets/:id/link
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "deviceId": "uuid"
}
```

The discovery asset list also supports filtering by linked device (`linkedDeviceId`).

sections.heading: Connecting to a discovered device's web UI
sections.text: Opening a LAN device's built-in web interface (router admin page, NAS panel, printer UI, switch management port, etc.) is done from the network device detail page: find the open web port and click **Open Web UI**. The proxied request rides an online agent on the same network — no VPN, firewall rules, or port forwarding required. See [Network Proxy](/features/remote-access/#network-proxy) in the Remote Access docs for the full workflow, allowlist configuration, session lifetime, and security model.

sections.heading: Approving and Dismissing Assets
sections.text:
Every discovered asset starts out `pending`. Approving it marks it reviewed and keeps it visible in dashboards and reports; dismissing it excludes it from dashboards and reports without deleting the underlying record.

```bash
PATCH /discovery/assets/:id/approve
```

```bash
PATCH /discovery/assets/:id/dismiss
```

Both record who made the change and when. Selecting multiple rows in the discovered assets list enables bulk **Approve** and **Dismiss** buttons, backed by:

```bash
POST /discovery/assets/bulk-approve
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "assetIds": ["uuid", "uuid"]
}
```

```bash
POST /discovery/assets/bulk-dismiss
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "assetIds": ["uuid", "uuid"]
}
```

Each bulk request accepts up to 200 asset IDs.

sections.heading: Deleting an Asset
sections.text:
```bash
DELETE /discovery/assets/:id
```

Deleting an asset also removes all associated SNMP devices (and their metrics and alert thresholds) and network monitors in a single transaction.

---

sections.heading: Network Change Alerts
sections.text: A discovery profile can alert you when a scan finds a network change since the last scan: a device shows up for the first time, a previously-seen device stops responding, or a known device's MAC address changes.

sections.heading: Enabling alerts on a profile
sections.text:
Network alerting is off by default. In the profile's create/edit form, open the **Network Alerting** section and turn on **Enable network alerting**, then choose which changes should raise an alert:

| Setting | Fires when |
|---|---|
| New devices | A device this profile hasn't seen before shows up in a scan |
| Disappeared devices | A device this profile previously saw no longer responds |
| Changed devices | A known device's MAC address changes |

**Retain change log (days)** sets how long detected-change records are kept before they're pruned (1-365, default 90).

  A newly-discovered device that matches a known guest entry is auto-approved and never triggers a "new device" alert, and a dismissed asset never alerts on any setting.

sections.heading: Viewing detected changes
sections.text:
Open **Network Discovery** in the sidebar and switch to the **Changes** tab to see detected changes across your organization. Each row shows the event type, the device's identity (IP/hostname/MAC), and when it was detected. Filter by site, discovery profile, event type, or acknowledgment status.

Click a row to see its detail, where you can link the change to an enrolled device. Use **Acknowledge** -- on a single row, or in bulk after selecting several with the row checkboxes -- to mark changes as reviewed; acknowledged changes stay in the list but drop out of the default unacknowledged view.

---

sections.heading: Network Topology (classic view)
sections.text:
The **Topology** tab on the Discovery page renders your network as an interactive map: subnets group their hosts, and lines show how infrastructure and endpoints connect. Every connection is labeled with how Breeze learned it, so you can trust what you're looking at.

  Breeze is rolling out a next-generation **Site Map** (per-site logical maps, shared configuration templates, and on-demand diagnostics) on this same **Topology** tab. Where it's enabled for your organization it replaces the view below automatically; otherwise this classic scan-and-SNMP map is what you'll see. See [Site Map](#site-map) below.

sections.heading: How connections are measured
sections.text:
Instead of guessing relationships from IP subnets, Breeze measures the backbone from the network devices themselves during SNMP-enabled scans:

| Connection | How it's measured | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Infrastructure links** (switch-to-switch, switch-to-router) | LLDP / CDP neighbor advertisements read from network devices. | High |
| **Host attachment** (which switch port a host hangs off) | The switch's MAC forwarding (bridge) table. | Medium |
| **Manual links** | Connections you draw yourself. | Asserted |

Uplink ports carrying many MAC addresses are filtered out of host-attachment so a trunk port doesn't appear to host hundreds of devices.

sections.heading: Exploring and editing the map
sections.text:
1. **Explore.** Pan and zoom the map, click a node to inspect its type, status, addresses, and the provenance of its connections, and use the full-screen view for large networks.

2. **Switch on Edit.** With the `topology:write` permission you get an **Edit** toggle. In edit mode, dragging a node saves its position so your layout persists across reloads.

3. **Add what discovery can't see.** Drop a manual placeholder node for unmanaged gear -- a patch panel, an unmanaged switch, a wiring closet -- choosing a role (switch, router, access point, firewall, patch panel, or other).

4. **Connect nodes.** Tap one node, then another, to draw a manual link between them. Manual links and nodes are never altered by future scans; remove them with the delete control when they no longer apply.

5. **Tidy up.** Use auto-arrange to lay out unplaced nodes (pinned nodes stay put) and fit-to-content to reset the view.

  A useful topology depends on the agent being able to reach your network gear over SNMP. Configure an SNMP community (v2c) or SNMPv3 credentials on the discovery profile and enable SNMP scanning, and make sure the scanning agent shares a routable path with the switches and routers you want mapped. Manual mapping works with no prerequisites.

---

sections.heading: Site Map
sections.text:
Where it's enabled, the **Topology** tab shows a per-site **Site Map** instead of the classic view above: a logical map of a site built automatically from what your agents passively observe on the network -- interfaces, routes, and neighbor tables -- refreshed on an interval without you having to run a scan. It adds shared configuration templates you can apply across many sites at once, automatic layout, and on-demand diagnostics you can launch straight from the map.

The physical view, per-connection evidence and coverage, link health and port history, recurring monitoring policies, the routed path trace, impact analysis and the **Explain this** AI investigation are covered in [Network Topology Explorer](/features/network-topology/).

  Site Map needs agents running **v0.115.0 or later** to collect the passive network evidence it's built from. Sites with older agents keep showing the classic Topology view (or an emptier map) until their agents are updated.

sections.heading: Turning it on
sections.text:
Network Topology (Beta) is off for every partner by default. A partner admin enables it from **Settings → Partner → Modules**: the main toggle turns on topology materialization and the UI together, and four sub-toggles underneath control physical topology, interface health, diagnostics, and AI insights independently (see [what each toggle unlocks](/features/network-topology/#turn-the-feature-on)). Until it's turned on, a device's Topology tab shows an empty state explaining that Network Topology is off -- with a link straight to Modules settings for a partner admin, or "Ask your MSP to enable it" for an organization user.

  Network Topology shipped in v0.115.0 but had no way to enable it until this Modules toggle landed in v0.116.0 -- every device's Topology tab showed a raw `materialization_disabled` code in the meantime. If you're on v0.115.0, there is no supported way to turn it on; upgrade to v0.116.0 or later.

sections.heading: Exploring a site's map
sections.text:
Pick a site from the site selector at the top of the tab (it's skipped if you only manage one site). The map opens on the **Overview** view; switch to **Logical** for the addressing-and-routing picture, or **Physical** where interface-level detail has been observed. A **List** toggle swaps the diagram for a searchable table of the same nodes -- useful on a large site or for keyboard-only navigation.

Click any node or connection to open its **Inspector**, which shows what it is, its health, how confidently Breeze knows about it (measured evidence vs. an inferred placeholder), and how recently it was last observed. A node that resolves to an enrolled device or discovered asset links straight to its inventory page. Large or partially-scoped sites show a frontier control you can expand to pull in more of the map on demand.

sections.heading: Automatic layout
sections.text: The map lays itself out automatically -- **Arrange** nudges new nodes into place, and **Reflow** rebuilds the whole layout from scratch. If you have edit access, drag a node to reposition it, use **Pin** to hold a node in place through future auto-layouts, and **Save layout** to persist your arrangement; **Fit** resets the view to frame everything. If someone else saves a layout change while you're mid-edit, you're prompted to reload rather than silently overwriting their work.

sections.heading: On-demand diagnostics
sections.text: Select a node or connection and click **Diagnose** to run an on-demand, ping/traceroute-style check without leaving the map. Choose what to test against -- the device's reported gateway, its configured DNS server, general internet reachability, a target you've configured explicitly, or a bounded routed path trace -- pick an agent to run it from, and start the check. Results stream back step by step (each hop's method, outcome, and round-trip detail), and you can cancel a run that's still in progress. Diagnostics require the **Diagnostics** module toggle, the `topology:execute` and `devices:execute` permissions, and an eligible agent at the site. See [Diagnostics and routed path trace](/features/network-topology/#diagnostics-and-routed-path-trace) for each check and the trace limits.

sections.heading: Shared configuration templates
sections.text:
Instead of configuring passive collection and diagnostic targets one site at a time, build a **configuration template** once -- at the partner level (applies across all your managed organizations) or the organization level -- and pin sites to a version of it. From the map's **Configuration** panel you can:

- See which template version (partner and/or organization) a site is currently pinned to, and where each effective setting is coming from.
- **Preview changes** before committing: the preview shows exactly what will change on every selected site, flags any site with a conflicting revision, and expires a few minutes after it's generated so you're never applying a stale preview.
- **Apply** the previewed change across up to 500 sites at once, then watch each site's apply status resolve individually.
- Add per-site overrides on top of the pinned template -- for example, an explicit HTTPS or DNS diagnostic target -- without forking the whole template.

  Recurring (scheduled) template application isn't available yet -- **Apply** runs once, immediately, against the sites you select.

---

Discovered assets can be attached to network monitors for ongoing health checking. Monitors are managed from **Fleet Management → Network Monitor** (`/monitoring`) and support four check types:

| Monitor Type | Description |
|--------------|-------------|
| `icmp_ping` | Periodic ICMP ping to check availability and measure latency |
| `tcp_port` | TCP connect check against a specific port |
| `http_check` | HTTP/HTTPS request with status code and response time validation |
| `dns_check` | DNS resolution check for a target hostname |

Each monitor tracks its current status (`online`, `offline`, `degraded`, `unknown`), last response time, consecutive failure count, and stores a history of check results. Alert rules can be configured per monitor to trigger notifications on failure thresholds.

The asset list endpoint (`GET /discovery/assets`) includes `snmpMonitoringEnabled` and `networkMonitoringEnabled` flags so you can see at a glance which assets have active monitoring.

---

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**ARP and ping scans return no results.**
ARP scanning requires root/Administrator privileges and the libpcap library. ICMP ping also requires raw socket access. If the agent runs as a non-privileged user, both methods are skipped. Check agent logs for messages like "ARP scan unavailable (built without CGO/pcap)" or "ICMP ping unavailable (requires root/elevated privileges)". Port scanning works without elevated privileges and can be used as an alternative.

**Scan job stays in `scheduled` status.**
The discovery worker requires Redis and the background queue to dispatch scan commands. Verify Redis is running and accessible. If Redis is unavailable, the job is immediately marked as `failed` with the message "Background job service unavailable." Also confirm at least one agent at the profile's site is online — the worker selects an online agent from the same site to execute the scan.

**A profile with a large subnet won't save.**
Subnets larger than /16 (65,536+ hosts) are refused on save (the error names the subnet) to prevent excessive scan times and network traffic. Split the range into /16 or smaller subnets, or set `deepScan: true` on the profile through the API to allow it. Profiles saved with an oversized subnet before v0.122.1 still have it skipped by the agent until `deepScan` is set. Monitor the agent's resource usage when scanning large address ranges.

**Discovered assets are not auto-linking to enrolled devices.**
Auto-linking matches assets to enrolled devices by MAC address or IP address within the same organization using the `device_network` table. If the enrolled device has a different IP than what discovery sees (e.g., the device is behind NAT or uses a VPN), auto-linking will not find a match. Use `POST /discovery/assets/:id/link` (or the network device detail page) to manually link the asset to the correct device. Also note that if an asset was manually unlinked, auto-linking is suppressed for it by design until you re-link it.

title: Distributor Integrations — Pax8 & TD SYNNEX
description: Connect Pax8 and TD SYNNEX from the Distributors tab to sync license subscriptions and pull live distributor pricing into your Product Catalog.
headings: Build and submit a direct order
Complete an order staged from a quote

sections.text:
Distributor integrations live on the **Distributors** tab of the Integrations page (**Integrations → Distributors**, `/integrations#distributors`). They let you bring vendor licenses and live product pricing into Breeze: **Pax8** syncs client companies and license subscriptions you can map to organizations and link to recurring contract lines, and **TD SYNNEX Pricing** (EC Express) looks up real-time cost, MSRP, and stock availability you can import straight into your [Product Catalog](/features/product-catalog/).

The tab has two sub-tabs:

- **Pax8** — `/integrations#pax8`
- **TD SYNNEX Pricing** — `/integrations#tdsynnex-ec`

  Distributor integrations are **partner-account only**. They are configured once for your MSP and shared across all of your customers. If you sign in with an organization-scoped account, both sub-tabs show a message that the integration is available to partner accounts only — there is nothing to configure at the organization level.

  Legacy note: an older TD SYNNEX **Digital Bridge** connector is intentionally hidden. Its catalog endpoint isn't entitled for live pricing data, so **TD SYNNEX Pricing** (EC Express) is the working connector documented here. Existing Digital Bridge / price-file import workflows store the feed's currency as the catalog item's **Cost currency**. If you're looking for live TD SYNNEX product pricing, use the **TD SYNNEX Pricing** sub-tab.

---

sections.heading: Connecting a distributor
sections.text:
**Pax8:**

Pax8 connects with your Pax8 **OAuth client credentials**. Once connected, Breeze pulls your Pax8 companies and their license subscriptions so you can map them to Breeze organizations and link them to recurring contract lines.

1. Open **Integrations → Distributors → Pax8** (`/integrations#pax8`).

2. In the **Connection** card, fill in:
   - **Display name** — a label for this connection (defaults to `Pax8`).
   - **Client ID** — your Pax8 OAuth client ID.
   - **Client secret** — your Pax8 OAuth client secret.
   - **Webhook secret** *(optional)* — stored with the integration, but not required by the ordering or scheduled-sync workflow.

3. Click **Connect Pax8**. Secrets are stored encrypted; once saved, each field shows a **Configured** badge. When updating an existing connection you can leave a secret field blank to keep the stored value.

4. Click **Test connection** to verify the credentials reach Pax8.

5. Click **Sync now** to pull companies and subscriptions. The sync runs in the background — the **Sync status** card shows the last sync time, status, and any last error once it finishes.

  Pax8 write actions (connecting, syncing, mapping companies, linking subscriptions, and authoring or submitting orders) are **MFA-gated** on the server. If you see an "MFA required" message, enable multi-factor authentication on your Breeze account and retry.

**What syncs from Pax8**

- **Companies** — your Pax8 client companies, with status, shown in the **Company mapping** table. Map each Pax8 company to a Breeze organization (or leave it unmapped).
- **License subscriptions** — pulled per company, including product name, vendor, quantity, unit cost, unit price, currency, billing term, and status.
- **Catalog import** — products imported from the Pax8 catalog (see [Product Catalog → Pax8](/features/product-catalog/#pax8)) store the feed's currency as the item's **Cost currency**; margin is computed only against a sell price in that same currency.
- **Contract-line linkage** — once a company is mapped to an organization, each subscription can be linked to a manual contract line. Breeze keeps the billing quantity on that contract line and records the Pax8 quantity separately as an observation.

**Behavior change: Pax8 no longer overwrites billing quantities:**
  Existing links with `sync_enabled` will **stop automatically updating contract-line quantities from Pax8**. This is intentional: the quantity reported by the Pax8 subscription API does not reliably match the quantity Pax8 invoices. The Breeze order ledger and its linked manual contract-line quantity are now the billing source of truth. Scheduled sync records Pax8's reported quantity for comparison and surfaces drift instead of silently changing customer billing.

**Subscription links on the Integrations page**

A subscription only becomes linkable after its company is mapped to a Breeze organization. On **Integrations → Distributors → Pax8**, each subscription row offers:

| Action | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Link for observation** | Connect the subscription to a contract line (or create a new manual line) |
| **Change link** | Re-point the subscription to a different contract line |
| **Pause observations** | Stop recording Pax8 quantity observations for this link while keeping the link intact |
| **Resume observations** | Resume recording observations and drift detection for this link |
| **Unlink** | Remove the connection between the subscription and the contract line |

These Integrations-page actions manage the contract-line link and whether scheduled sync records observations; that table's **Pax8 reported** column is not a Breeze billing quantity. To compare quantities or stage an order action, open the mapped organization's **Pax8** tab. The organization tab shows **Breeze quantity** (the authoritative manual contract-line billing quantity), **Pax8 reported** (the latest known observation), and a **Drift** badge when both values are known and disagree. A missing or unknown Pax8 quantity is not treated as zero and does not produce a drift warning.

sections.heading: Prepare an organization for ordering
sections.text:
Ordering is managed from the organization's **Pax8** settings tab, but remains a partner-account operation:

1. Sync the integration so the Pax8 company, subscriptions, and product mappings are current.
2. Open **Settings → Organizations → _organization_ → Pax8**, or go directly to `/settings/organizations/<org-id>#pax8`.
3. Map exactly one Pax8 company to the organization.
4. Confirm the mapped company is **Active** in Pax8 and has primary **Admin**, **Billing**, and **Technical** contacts. The organization tab shows the Pax8 company status. When the mapping is not order-ready, it shows one combined warning; it does not show contact details or separate indicators for the three contact roles.
5. Link recurring subscriptions to the corresponding manual contract lines. A linked line is required before the organization tab can stage a quantity change or cancellation.

The **New order** action stays unavailable until the company mapping is order-ready and at least one active Product Catalog item is mapped to a Pax8 product.

sections.heading: Build and submit a direct order
sections.text:
The organization tab keeps one mutable direct order per organization. Returning to **New order** reopens that draft until it is submitted.

1. Click **New order** and choose an active, Pax8-mapped catalog product.

2. Set its billing term and quantity. If Pax8 reports commitment choices, select one. Complete any product-specific provisioning fields that you know; Breeze leaves all of these fields optional because Pax8 does not identify required fields in its metadata.

3. Add the product to the order. You can edit its commitment and provisioning details or remove the line while the order is still mutable.

4. To change an existing subscription, enter the target **Breeze quantity** and click **Stage change**. To cancel, click **Cancel** and confirm the warning. Breeze checks the subscription's active commitment dependencies before staging either action and blocks increases, decreases, or early cancellation that Pax8 says are not allowed. If the active commitment cannot be determined unambiguously, refresh the Pax8 data and resolve that ambiguity before ordering.

5. Click **Review & submit**. Breeze first sends a mock Pax8 order for new-subscription lines. If Pax8 returns validation details, Breeze shows the raw message beside the affected line so you can add or correct provisioning values. Quantity changes and cancellations are dependency-checked when staged; Pax8's mock-order preflight applies only to new subscriptions.

6. After preflight passes, Breeze submits each action and records the result on every line. Successful quantity changes and cancellations update the linked manual contract-line quantity (`0` for a completed cancellation); successful new subscriptions update their linked line when one exists.

**Do not blindly retry an uncertain submission:**
  Pax8 does not accept an idempotency key for these writes. If Breeze cannot determine whether a request completed, the line is marked **Needs reconcile** instead of being sent again. Click **Reconcile**: Breeze reads Pax8 orders and subscriptions and reclassifies the existing attempt without issuing another write. If the result remains unknown, investigate before taking any manual action in Pax8 or Breeze.

The order history shows direct and quote-originated orders with their current status. Selecting an order changes the URL hash to `#pax8/<order-id>`, so the same order can be bookmarked and browser Back/Forward navigation works.

sections.heading: Complete an order staged from a quote
sections.text:
Accepting a quote that contains Pax8-backed catalog items creates the invoice and contracts as usual, then stages a Pax8 order in the **same database transaction**. Acceptance does **not** submit anything to Pax8 and a missing company mapping never blocks the customer from accepting.

On a converted quote, technicians see **“This quote staged a Pax8 order (N items) awaiting provisioning details”**. Follow **Open Pax8 order** to the organization's deep link, map an order-ready company if needed, then review each new-subscription line. The catalog item, quote source, and linked recurring contract line are preserved; you only complete the commitment and provisioning details. Run preflight and submit it using the same flow as a direct order. One-time quote lines can be ordered, but are not linked to a recurring contract line.

  **TD SYNNEX Pricing:**

**TD SYNNEX Pricing** connects to TD SYNNEX **EC Express** to look up real-time cost, MSRP, and stock availability, and import products straight into your [Product Catalog](/features/product-catalog/). It authenticates with your EC Express account credentials.

1. Open **Integrations → Distributors → TD SYNNEX Pricing** (`/integrations#tdsynnex-ec`).

2. Fill in your EC Express connection details:
   - **Customer No** — your TD SYNNEX customer number.
   - **Region** — your account region (defaults to `US`).
   - **Email** — your EC Express account email.
   - **Password** — your EC Express account password (stored masked).

3. Tick **Enabled**, then click **Save settings**. The password is stored securely and shown masked afterward.

4. Click **Test connection** to verify the credentials against EC Express. The status label shows whether the last test succeeded or failed (with the error message on failure). *Test connection requires the integration to be enabled.*

**What you can pull from TD SYNNEX**

TD SYNNEX Pricing is a **live lookup + import** flow rather than a background sync:

- **Product lookup** — search by SYNNEX SKU or manufacturer part number. Each result shows the product name, status, description, your **cost**, **MSRP**, **total available** quantity, and a per-warehouse stock breakdown (available, on order, ETA).
- **Import to catalog** — import a result into your Product Catalog. Breeze stores the EC Express feed currency as the item's **Cost currency**. The sell price in that currency is pre-filled from your partner default markup over cost (falling back to MSRP, then cost) and is editable.
- On import, Breeze records the product name, SKU (SYNNEX SKU or manufacturer part), description, your entered sell price, the cost basis and currency, and whether the item is taxable (following your partner's hardware-tax policy). Margin and markup-derived pricing are available only when the cost and sell currencies match; otherwise the UI shows **“Cost in CAD — margin unavailable”** (for example).

The same cost-currency rule applies to TD SYNNEX Digital Bridge / price-file imports: Breeze takes the **Cost currency** from the feed and does not convert it when you add sell prices in other currencies.

This same live lookup is also reachable through the AI/MCP surface via the `lookup_distributor_product` tool, with reseller cost hidden for organization-scoped callers — see the [MCP Server documentation](/features/mcp-server/#billing-tools).

  Lookups require the integration to be **enabled** and connected. For the full catalog-import workflow, see [Product Catalog → Importing from distributor catalogs](/features/product-catalog/#importing-from-distributor-catalogs).

---
