---

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: The SentinelOne integration provides deeper operational capabilities beyond data sync. In addition to importing agent and threat data, you can isolate devices and take threat actions (kill, quarantine, rollback) directly from the Breeze dashboard -- commands are dispatched to the SentinelOne management console via API.

sections.heading: Setting Up SentinelOne
sections.text:
1. Set your scope selector to **All orgs**, then navigate to **Integrations**, open the **Security** tab, and select **SentinelOne**. SentinelOne is configured once for the whole partner.
2. Provide a **name** for the integration.
3. Enter your **SentinelOne management console URL** (e.g., `https://usea1.sentinelone.net`).
4. Enter your **SentinelOne API token**. This is encrypted at rest before being stored.
5. Click **Save & Connect**. An initial sync is automatically scheduled.

  The SentinelOne integration is configured at the **partner** level — one SentinelOne tenant serves all of your customer organizations. The connection and credential fields are only available with your scope selector set to **All orgs**. You then map each SentinelOne site to a Breeze organization (see [Site Mappings](#site-mappings) below). Organization users can view the threats and agents for their mapped org but cannot change the connection or mappings.

  Creating or updating a SentinelOne integration requires the `orgs:write` permission and MFA verification. Only one active SentinelOne integration is allowed per partner.

#### MFA Requirements by Operation

The following SentinelOne operations require MFA verification before they can be executed:

| Operation | MFA Required |
|-----------|-------------|
| Create or update integration | Yes |
| Isolate / unisolate devices | Yes |
| Execute threat actions (kill, quarantine, rollback) | Yes |
| Trigger manual sync | No |
| View status, threats, or sites | No |

sections.heading: Data Model (For Integrators)
sections.text:
#### SentinelOne Agents

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `s1AgentId` | String | Unique agent identifier from SentinelOne |
| `deviceId` | UUID | Mapped Breeze device (nullable if unmapped) |
| `status` | String | Agent connection status |
| `infected` | Boolean | Whether the agent has active threats |
| `threatCount` | Integer | Number of threats detected on this agent |
| `policyName` | String | Applied SentinelOne policy name |
| `lastSeenAt` | Timestamp | Last check-in time |
| `metadata` | JSON | Additional agent metadata including site name |

#### SentinelOne Threats

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `s1ThreatId` | String | Unique threat identifier from SentinelOne |
| `deviceId` | UUID | Affected Breeze device (nullable if unmapped) |
| `classification` | String | Threat classification (e.g., Malware, PUP) |
| `severity` | String | Severity level (low, medium, high, critical) |
| `threatName` | String | Name of the detected threat |
| `processName` | String | Process that triggered the detection |
| `filePath` | String | File path of the threat |
| `mitreTactics` | JSON | MITRE ATT&CK tactic mappings |
| `status` | String | Current threat status (active, in_progress, resolved, etc.) |
| `detectedAt` | Timestamp | When the threat was first detected |
| `resolvedAt` | Timestamp | When the threat was resolved (nullable) |
| `details` | JSON | Full threat details from SentinelOne |

#### SentinelOne Actions

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `action` | String | Action type (isolate, unisolate, kill, quarantine, rollback) |
| `status` | String | Action status: `queued`, `in_progress`, `completed`, `failed` |
| `providerActionId` | String | Action ID from SentinelOne API |
| `requestedBy` | UUID | User who initiated the action |
| `requestedAt` | Timestamp | When the action was requested |
| `completedAt` | Timestamp | When the action finished (nullable) |
| `error` | Text | Error message if the action failed |

sections.heading: Site Mappings
sections.text:
SentinelOne organizes agents into "Sites." Breeze lets you map SentinelOne sites to Breeze organizations, enabling multi-tenant EDR management from a single SentinelOne console.

1. With your scope selector set to **All orgs**, open **Integrations > Security > SentinelOne** and find the **Site mapping** section.
2. Review the list of discovered SentinelOne sites, each shown with its agent count.
3. For each SentinelOne site, select the Breeze organization it should map to. Unmapped sites stay quarantined — their agents and threats are not attributed to any customer — until assigned.
4. The mapping saves immediately.

To remove a mapping, clear the selected Breeze organization.

sections.heading: Device Isolation
sections.text:
You can isolate compromised devices directly from Breeze. The isolation command is sent to SentinelOne, which enforces network isolation at the endpoint level.

1. Select one or more devices in the Breeze dashboard.
2. Click **Isolate** (or **Unisolate** to restore connectivity).
3. Breeze identifies the corresponding SentinelOne agents and dispatches the isolation command.
4. The action status is tracked and reported back.

  Device isolation requires the `devices:execute` permission and MFA verification. You can isolate up to 200 devices in a single request.

sections.heading: Threat Actions
sections.text:
Take direct action on detected threats without leaving Breeze:

| Action | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `kill` | Terminate the malicious process |
| `quarantine` | Move the threat file to quarantine |
| `rollback` | Roll back changes made by the threat (Windows only) |

1. Navigate to the **Threats** view and find the threat(s) to act on.
2. Select the threat action (kill, quarantine, or rollback).
3. Confirm the action. Up to 200 threats can be acted on in a single request.
4. The action is dispatched to SentinelOne and the status is tracked.

  Threat actions require the `devices:execute` permission and MFA verification.

sections.heading: Status Dashboard
sections.text:
The SentinelOne status endpoint provides a comprehensive summary:

| Metric | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `totalAgents` | Total SentinelOne agents synced |
| `mappedDevices` | Agents matched to Breeze devices |
| `infectedAgents` | Agents with active infections |
| `activeThreats` | Threats with `active` or `in_progress` status |
| `highOrCriticalThreats` | Threats with `high` or `critical` severity |
| `pendingActions` | Actions with `queued` or `in_progress` status |
| `reportedThreatCount` | Sum of threat counts across all agents |

sections.heading: Listing Threats
sections.text:
Threats can be filtered by multiple criteria:

| Filter | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `orgId` | UUID | Filter by organization |
| `integrationId` | UUID | Filter by specific integration |
| `deviceId` | UUID | Filter by affected Breeze device |
| `status` | String | Filter by threat status |
| `severity` | String | Filter by severity level |
| `search` | String | Search by threat name, process name, or file path |
| `start` | ISO datetime | Threats detected on or after this time |
| `end` | ISO datetime | Threats detected on or before this time |
| `limit` | Number | Results per page (1-500, default 100) |
| `offset` | Number | Pagination offset |

---

sections.heading: Bitdefender GravityZone
sections.text:
**API only in v0.122.1:**
  GravityZone is the first provider on Breeze's new EDR provider framework. In v0.122.1 it is read-only and **API only**: there is no dashboard UI for it yet, and its detections do not appear on the `/security/edr` page or the device Security tab. Use the `/api/v1/edr` endpoints below.

A partner-wide admin (all-organization access, `orgs:write`, MFA) connects a GravityZone API key once for the partner:

1. In GravityZone, create an API key with access to the companies and endpoints you manage, and note your console's Access URL (a `*.gravityzone.bitdefender.com` address ending in `/api`).

2. Create the connection: `POST /api/v1/edr/connections` with `provider: "bitdefender"`, a `name`, the Access URL as `baseUrl`, and `credentials: { "apiKey": "..." }`. The key is checked against GravityZone, stored encrypted and never returned.

3. List the GravityZone companies the key can see with `GET /api/v1/edr/connections/:id/tenants`, and map each one to a Breeze organization with `PUT /api/v1/edr/tenants/:id/mapping` (`{ "orgId": "..." }`). Remapping a company keeps its earlier detections under the previous organization as history.

Once a company is mapped, Breeze syncs in the background: endpoint inventory hourly and detections every 10 minutes by default, lengthened automatically if needed to stay inside GravityZone's API request budget. `POST /api/v1/edr/connections/:id/sync` queues a sync now. Endpoints are linked to Breeze devices by **hostname** (GravityZone's fully qualified names are compared by their first label); an endpoint that matches no device, or more than one, is listed as unlinked or ambiguous and can be linked by hand with `PUT /api/v1/edr/endpoints/:id/link`.

---

sections.heading: Promote to Incident
sections.text:
From the `/security/edr` fleet page or from a device's **Security** tab, you can escalate a Huntress incident or a SentinelOne threat directly into a tracked Breeze incident. Click **Promote to incident** on the item, confirm the pre-filled title and severity (mapped from the EDR severity level), and Breeze creates the incident and navigates you to it. The promotion records the source (Huntress or SentinelOne), the original title, any affected device, and the detection time as the incident's detected-at timestamp.

Promotion uses the standard `POST /incidents` endpoint and follows normal incident-creation permissions.

---

sections.heading: Deploying EDR Agents
sections.text: Once a Huntress or SentinelOne integration is connected, both vendors appear as built-in deployment packages under **Software → Deployment**. You can push the EDR agent to any managed device — or group of devices — with a single click, without leaving Breeze.

sections.heading: Huntress
sections.text: Huntress deployment is fully built in: no binary upload is required. Breeze uses the **Deployment Account Key** you entered during integration setup to generate and deliver the Huntress installer to the target device. Simply navigate to **Software → Deployment**, select **Huntress** from the catalog, choose your target devices, and click **Deploy**.

sections.heading: SentinelOne
sections.text:
SentinelOne deployment requires a one-time setup step: upload the SentinelOne MSI to the deployment catalog before pushing it to devices.

1. Download the SentinelOne Windows MSI from your SentinelOne management console.
2. Navigate to **Software → Deployment** in Breeze and open the **SentinelOne** catalog entry.
3. Upload the MSI using the **Upload package** option.
4. Select your target devices and click **Deploy**.

Once the MSI is uploaded, subsequent deployments to new devices re-use the same package — you only need to re-upload when SentinelOne releases a new installer version.

**Install arguments must carry the site token placeholder:**
  From v0.124.0 a SentinelOne deployment is refused at dispatch when the package version's install arguments do not include `SITE_TOKEN={s1_site_token}` — blank arguments, a generic `msiexec` line, or a hard-coded literal token all fail with `SentinelOne install arguments must include SITE_TOKEN={s1_site_token} — edit the installer version`. Breeze substitutes the placeholder with the site token of the device's mapped organization at install time; before this check, such a package installed unregistered or enrolled every organization into one site. Fix the arguments on the package's **Versions** tab.

Package uploads are **chunked and resumable** with a live progress bar, so large installers (200 MB+) upload reliably — an interrupted upload resumes where it left off rather than starting over, and long uploads are no longer cut short by session-token expiry.

sections.heading: Automating EDR deployment
sections.text: Both Huntress and SentinelOne deployment packages can also be driven through [Automations](/features/automations/) using the **Deploy Software** action type. This lets you automatically push an EDR agent to newly enrolled devices by pairing a **Device Enrolled** event trigger with a **Deploy Software** action targeting the relevant catalog item.

sections.heading: Deploy from a configuration policy
sections.text:
From v0.124.0 you can keep the agent installed across a whole scope instead of pushing it device by device. Open a configuration policy, switch **Deploy Huntress** or **Deploy SentinelOne** on in its **Security Agents** tab, and assign the policy — it can be partner-wide. Every in-scope Windows device whose organization is mapped in that vendor's integration gets the agent with that organization's own keys (Huntress organization keys, SentinelOne site tokens); unmapped organizations are skipped and read **Not applicable**, with no failed deployments. Breeze generates a read-only managed software policy for the rollout and evaluates coverage per device — **Covered**, **Gap**, **Vendor only**, **Vendor offline**, **Mismatched org**, **Not applicable** or **Pending** — on the **Software → Policies** compliance view. A device that falls into **Gap** raises a medium alert.

SentinelOne needs the built-in SentinelOne package to have a Windows MSI as its latest version, with install arguments that include `SITE_TOKEN={s1_site_token}`; otherwise the policy save is refused with a link to the package's **Versions** tab. An organization with no SentinelOne site mapping reads **Organization not mapped to the vendor**. Endpoints the SentinelOne console stops returning are marked absent at the next sync and drop out of coverage. Turning a vendor off stops enforcement but never uninstalls the agent. Control D and NextDNS are DNS-filtering vendors configured through the same Security Agents policy (coming soon; see [DNS filtering vendors](/features/configuration-policies/#dns-filtering-vendors)). See [Security Agents](/features/configuration-policies/#security-agents) and [Managed security agent policies](/features/software-policies/#managed-security-agent-policies).

---

sections.heading: Syncing
sections.text: Both integrations support manual and automatic syncing.

sections.heading: Manual Sync
sections.text:
Trigger a sync from the Breeze dashboard or API. The sync job is queued via the background queue and processes in the background.

| Vendor | Requirements |
|--------|-------------|
| Huntress | `orgs:write` permission, MFA, active integration |
| SentinelOne | `orgs:write` permission, active integration |

sections.heading: Sync Status
sections.text:
Each integration tracks its last sync result:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `lastSyncAt` | Timestamp of the most recent sync |
| `lastSyncStatus` | Result: success or failure indicator |
| `lastSyncError` | Error message from the last failed sync (nullable) |

After you click **Sync Now** for Huntress, Breeze polls the integration and shows the live status (Syncing → Connected/Error). On success it reports the result counts (for example, agents, incidents, and organizations synced); on failure it shows the actual error from the last run rather than a generic "triggered" message.

sections.heading: Sync Error Handling and Retries
sections.text:
Sync jobs are processed through a background queue. If a sync fails (for example, due to a network timeout or an API rate limit from the EDR vendor), the following happens:

- **SentinelOne syncs** automatically retry up to **3 times** with exponential backoff (starting at 2 seconds, then 4 seconds, then 8 seconds).
- **Huntress syncs** automatically retry up to **3 times** with exponential backoff, so a transient failure (network timeout, rate limit, or a temporary database connection drop) recovers without operator intervention. The integration's live status and the last run's result counts are surfaced in the dashboard so you can see whether the most recent sync succeeded.
- The `lastSyncError` field on the integration record is updated with the error message from the most recent failure. Check this field in the dashboard or API to diagnose sync issues.
- If the initial sync scheduled on integration creation fails, a warning is returned in the API response: *"Initial sync could not be scheduled. Data will sync on the next scheduled cycle."*

---

sections.heading: Huntress
sections.text:
All authenticated endpoints require `organization`, `partner`, or `system` scope. Mounted at `/api/v1/huntress`.

| Method | Path | Auth | Description |
|--------|------|------|-------------|
| `POST` | `/webhook` | No (signature verified) | Receive Huntress webhook events |
| `GET` | `/integration` | Yes | Get the Huntress integration for the current org |
| `POST` | `/integration` | Yes + MFA | Create or update a Huntress integration |
| `POST` | `/sync` | Yes + MFA | Trigger a manual Huntress sync |
| `GET` | `/status` | Yes | Get integration status and coverage summary |
| `GET` | `/incidents` | Yes | List Huntress incidents with filters |

sections.heading: SentinelOne
sections.text:
All endpoints require authentication. Credentials and mappings are managed at **partner** scope; organization-scoped users get read-only access to their mapped data and a `403` on credential or mapping changes. The partner is resolved from the caller's token; system-scope callers pass an optional `partnerId` query parameter. Mounted at `/api/v1/s1`.

| Method | Path | Auth | Description |
|--------|------|------|-------------|
| `GET` | `/integration` | Yes | Get the partner's SentinelOne integration |
| `POST` | `/integration` | Yes + MFA (partner) | Create or update the SentinelOne integration |
| `GET` | `/status` | Yes | Get integration status and threat summary |
| `GET` | `/threats` | Yes | List threats with filters |
| `POST` | `/isolate` | Yes + MFA | Isolate or unisolate devices |
| `POST` | `/threat-action` | Yes + MFA | Execute a threat action (kill, quarantine, rollback) |
| `POST` | `/sync` | Yes | Trigger a manual SentinelOne sync |
| `GET` | `/sites` | Yes | List SentinelOne sites with agent counts and org mappings |
| `POST` | `/organizations/map` | Yes (partner) | Map or unmap a SentinelOne site to a Breeze organization (`{ integrationId, s1SiteId, orgId }`) |

sections.heading: EDR provider framework (Bitdefender GravityZone)
sections.text:
Mounted at `/api/v1/edr`. Connection, test, sync and mapping changes need partner scope, all-organization access, `orgs:write` and MFA; endpoint reads work at organization scope too and are narrowed to what the caller can see.

| Method | Path | Auth | Description |
|--------|------|------|-------------|
| `GET` | `/providers` | Yes (partner) | List available EDR providers and their credential fields |
| `GET` | `/connections` | Yes (partner) | List the partner's EDR connections (credentials are never returned) |
| `POST` | `/connections` | Yes + MFA (partner) | Create a connection (`provider`, `name`, `baseUrl`, `credentials`, optional sync intervals) |
| `PATCH` | `/connections/:id` | Yes + MFA (partner) | Rename, pause, rotate credentials or change intervals |
| `POST` | `/connections/:id/test` | Yes + MFA (partner) | Test the stored credentials against the vendor |
| `POST` | `/connections/:id/sync` | Yes + MFA (partner) | Queue an inventory and detection sync now |
| `DELETE` | `/connections/:id` | Yes + MFA (partner) | Permanently delete the connection and its synced data. The first call returns `409 CONFIRM_COUNTS` with the open detection, endpoint and company counts; repeat it with `?confirm=<detections>:<endpoints>` to proceed |
| `GET` | `/connections/:id/tenants` | Yes (partner) | List the vendor companies the connection can see, with their mapping |
| `PUT` | `/tenants/:id/mapping` | Yes + MFA (partner) | Map a vendor company to a Breeze organization |
| `GET` | `/endpoints` | Yes | List synced endpoints with their device link and open detection count; filter by `connectionId`, `orgId`, `state` (`unlinked`, `ambiguous`, `linked`, `all`) |
| `PUT` | `/endpoints/:id/link` | Yes + MFA (`devices:write`) | Link an endpoint to a device, or `null` to unlink |

---

sections.heading: Automation Events
sections.text:
Both integrations emit platform events that can trigger [automations](/features/automations/) and outbound webhooks. Select these event types in the automation builder (**Automations > Create > Event** trigger) to react to security activity — for example, creating a ticket when a critical incident is reported, or notifying the on-call channel when an endpoint is isolated.

| Event type | Fires when |
|------------|------------|
| `huntress.incident_created` | A new Huntress incident is synced or received via webhook |
| `huntress.incident_updated` | An existing incident changes severity, status, or resolution |
| `huntress.agent_offline` | A Huntress agent transitions from online to offline |
| `s1.threat_detected` | A new SentinelOne threat is detected |
| `s1.device_isolated` | A device isolation initiated from Breeze completes in SentinelOne |
| `s1.threat_action_completed` | A threat action initiated from Breeze (kill, quarantine, rollback) completes |

---

sections.heading: Credential Storage
sections.text: API keys and tokens for both Huntress and SentinelOne are encrypted at rest using AES encryption before being stored in the database. The `apiKeyEncrypted` and `apiTokenEncrypted` fields are never returned in API responses -- only a boolean `hasApiKey` or similar flag is exposed.

sections.heading: Webhook Verification
sections.text: Huntress webhooks use HMAC signature verification. The webhook secret is encrypted at rest and decrypted only at verification time. Webhooks without a configured secret or with an invalid signature are rejected.

sections.heading: Permission Requirements
sections.text:
| Operation | Required Permission | MFA Required |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------|
| View integration status | `organization`, `partner`, or `system` scope | No |
| Create/update integration | `orgs:write` | Yes |
| Trigger manual sync | `orgs:write` | Huntress: Yes, SentinelOne: No |
| Isolate devices | `devices:execute` | Yes |
| Execute threat actions | `devices:execute` | Yes |

---

sections.heading: Sync shows "Integration is inactive"
sections.text: Activate the integration by updating it with `isActive: true` before triggering a sync.

sections.heading: Huntress webhook returns 403 "Webhook secret not configured"
sections.text: You must configure a webhook secret on the integration before Breeze will accept webhook payloads. Update the integration with a `webhookSecret` value that matches what you configured in your Huntress dashboard.

sections.heading: Huntress webhook returns 409 "Multiple active integrations match"
sections.text: When multiple Huntress integrations share the same account ID, Breeze cannot determine which one to route the webhook to. Include the `integrationId` as a query parameter on your webhook URL or in the `x-huntress-integration-id` header.

sections.heading: SentinelOne isolation returns 502
sections.text: A 502 response means the isolation command was sent to SentinelOne but the provider returned an error. Check the `warning` field in the response for details and verify the target devices have active SentinelOne agents.

sections.heading: Unmapped agents
sections.text: After syncing, some EDR agents may not be matched to Breeze devices. This happens when the hostname or identifier in the EDR system does not correspond to any enrolled Breeze device. Enroll the missing devices in Breeze or verify the hostname matches.

sections.heading: "API token is required for new integrations"
sections.text: When creating a new SentinelOne integration, the API token is mandatory. For updates to existing integrations, the token is optional (the existing encrypted token is preserved).

title: EDR Provider Framework
description: Connect additional EDR products to Breeze through a common framework, map vendor tenants to organizations, link endpoints to devices, and review detections alongside your other security data.

sections.text:
The EDR provider framework is a common way for Breeze to connect to Endpoint Detection and Response products. A provider supplies the vendor-specific parts (credentials, tenant and endpoint discovery, detections); Breeze supplies the shared parts: tenant-to-organization mapping, endpoint-to-device linking, the incidents feed, the device page section, alerts, and the customer portal summary.

Currently one provider is available:

| Provider | Key |
|----------|-----|
| Bitdefender GravityZone | `bitdefender` |

Huntress and SentinelOne keep their own dedicated integrations; see [EDR Integrations](/features/edr-integrations/).

  Response actions arrived in v0.124.0 and are off until you turn them on. Each connection card has an **Allow response actions** switch; while it is off, the device page shows the provider's data read-only. Changing it, like any connection setting, needs a partner user with full organization access and MFA. The switch, the actions and their history are only visible when the web image is built with `PUBLIC_ENABLE_EDR_INTEGRATIONS=true`, which the published image does not set — see the flag note in [EDR Integrations](/features/edr-integrations/).

sections.heading: Connecting a provider
sections.text:
1. Set your scope selector to **All orgs**. Connections are partner-level and require a partner admin with all-organization access.
2. Go to **Integrations**, open the **Security** tab, and select **EDR providers**.
3. Choose the provider and give the connection a name.
4. Fill in the credential fields. The fields come from the provider, so they differ per product. Secret values are encrypted at rest and are never shown again after saving.
5. Enter the **Access URL** if the provider asks for one.
6. Save, then use **Test connection** to confirm Breeze can reach the vendor. An initial sync is scheduled automatically.

A connection reports its own health: connected, needs re-authentication, or error, along with the last inventory and detection sync times. You can pause a connection, trigger a manual sync, or delete it. Deleting is permanent and asks you to confirm the number of detections and endpoints that will be removed.

The connection card also carries two switches (v0.124.0), both off by default:

- **Allow response actions** — lets technicians who hold device execute permission isolate and release devices and run scans on endpoints managed through this connection. Turning it on asks you to confirm.
- **Push events** — the provider notifies Breeze about new events, which triggers a sync sooner than the regular schedule; scheduled syncs keep running. It needs the server's public URL set and HTTPS, and the connection active. If the provider already pushes to another destination (for example a SIEM), Breeze asks before replacing that feed. A **Send test event** button checks the path; the card shows when the last push event arrived.

sections.heading: Mapping vendor tenants to organizations
sections.text:
Providers expose their own customer or company structure, called tenants. Each tenant must be mapped to a Breeze organization before its data is attributed to that customer.

- Breeze may show a **suggested match** when a tenant name matches an organization name. Suggestions are never applied automatically; you confirm each one.
- You can leave a tenant deliberately unmapped.
- Unmapping a tenant detaches its data from the organization again.
- A tenant that disappears from the vendor is flagged **missing since** with the date it was last seen, rather than being silently removed.

Until a tenant is mapped, its endpoints and detections are not visible to any organization.

sections.heading: Linking endpoints to devices
sections.text: During each sync Breeze tries to match vendor endpoints to enrolled devices. Endpoints that cannot be matched are listed as **unlinked**, and endpoints that match more than one device are listed as **ambiguous**. From the connection's endpoint list you can link an endpoint to the correct device, or unlink one that was matched wrongly.

sections.heading: Where the data appears
sections.text:
| Location | What you see |
|----------|--------------|
| **Security → EDR → Other EDR** tab | Detections from framework providers. The tab carries the provider name when only one provider is connected. |
| **Incidents** | An incidents feed of framework detections, with **Promote to incident** to open a Breeze incident from a detection. |
| **Device page → EDR section** | Endpoint health, isolation state and detections for the linked device. With **Allow response actions** on for the connection, **Isolate device**, **Release isolation** and **Run scan** buttons (isolating and releasing confirm first, with an optional reason; running any response action asks you to verify with MFA), plus a **Recent response actions** history showing each request as Queued, In progress, Succeeded or Failed. One response action runs at a time per device. |
| **Alerts** | Alerts raised from framework detections. |
| **Customer portal** | An optional generic status and threat count; see below. |

sections.heading: Reading coverage correctly
sections.text: Every detection list reports coverage. An empty list with incomplete coverage (a tenant not yet mapped, a sync that failed, or a sync that has not run) does not mean there are no threats, and Breeze says so instead of showing an all-clear. Sync health is visible to partner users only; organization-scoped users see a note saying so rather than the sync details.

sections.heading: Customer portal
sections.text:
The portal flag `enableEdrVisibility` controls whether an organization's portal users see EDR information. It is off by default and is included when you use **Enable all visibility**.

When on, customers see a generic **Managed endpoint protection** status and threat counts from connected providers. Vendor and product names are never shown in the portal.

To change it, open **Settings → Organizations**, choose the organization, open the **Customer Portal** tab, and toggle **Endpoint protection (EDR)**. See [Customer Portal](/features/portal/) for the full visibility list.

title: Event Log Forwarding
description: Forward managed-device event logs to any Elasticsearch- or OpenSearch-compatible store, configured per organization or partner-wide.

sections.text:
Event Log Forwarding ships the event logs collected from your managed devices -- Windows Event Log entries, syslog, and application logs -- to an external log store that the customer owns and controls. Breeze's agents already gather these device logs; this feature additionally streams them outbound to the customer's own SIEM or search cluster for long-term storage, search, and analysis. The destination can be any Elasticsearch- or OpenSearch-compatible store that accepts the standard bulk-ingest protocol, and forwarding can be configured per organization or applied partner-wide across every customer at once.

**Not the same as Log Shipping:**
  Event Log Forwarding is **distinct from the agent diagnostic "Log Shipping" feature**. Log Shipping sends the agent's *own internal diagnostic logs* back **to Breeze** so you can troubleshoot the agent itself. Event Log Forwarding sends the *customer's managed-device event logs* **out to the customer's own SIEM** -- never to Breeze. One answers "is the agent working?"; the other answers "what is happening on the customer's machines?".

---

sections.heading: Supported Destinations
sections.text:
Forwarding works with any log store that speaks the standard Elasticsearch/OpenSearch bulk-ingest wire protocol. The destinations named in the product are:

| Destination | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Elasticsearch** | Official Elasticsearch clusters |
| **OpenSearch** | Self-managed OpenSearch |
| **Wazuh indexer** | The Wazuh SIEM indexer |
| **AWS OpenSearch Service** | Amazon-managed OpenSearch |

  Any store that accepts the same bulk protocol will work. Generic HTTP/JSON, Splunk HEC, Datadog, and syslog targets are **not** supported today -- those are planned for a future phase.

---

sections.heading: What You Configure
sections.text:
For a destination you set:

| Setting | Description |
|---|---|
| **Enable / disable** | Forwarding only runs when turned on. When enabled, logs are forwarded on a recurring schedule (not real-time per event) |
| **Log endpoint URL** | The base URL of the compatible log store, e.g. `https://logs.example.com:9200`. Must use HTTPS -- Breeze appends the bulk path itself |
| **Index prefix** | Defaults to `breeze-logs`. Logs land in date-stamped indices named `<prefix>-YYYY.MM.DD` (one per day) |
| **Authentication** | Either an **API key** or a **username / password** (basic auth) |

Stored credentials are encrypted at rest and masked when the settings screen reloads. Outbound requests are also protected against being pointed at internal or private addresses.

  Which categories of event logs are collected (and therefore forwarded) is governed separately under **Configuration Policies**, where you choose the categories -- security, application, system, and hardware -- along with a minimum severity, collection interval, and retention. The forwarding screen links you to Configuration Policies for those collection-side controls.

---

sections.heading: Per-Organization Configuration
sections.text:
An organization administrator configures forwarding in **Settings**, in the Event Logs section (under Security & Access) for the currently selected organization. There you set the enable toggle, the endpoint URL, the index prefix, and authentication (API key or username and password). This points a single customer's device logs at their own cluster.

1. Open **Settings** and select the **Event Logs** section (under Security & Access) for the organization.

2. Toggle forwarding on.

3. Enter the **endpoint URL** (HTTPS) and an **index prefix** (or keep the `breeze-logs` default).

4. Choose an authentication method and enter the **API key** or **username and password**.

5. Save. Confirm the categories you want collected are enabled in Configuration Policies.

---

sections.heading: Partner-Wide Configuration
sections.text:
At the partner level, a dedicated **Event Logs** tab lets the MSP configure forwarding once and apply it across all child organizations. The toggle is labeled **Enable centralized event log shipping**. When the partner enables it and fills in the endpoint URL, index prefix, and credentials, every child organization ships its event logs to that single configured destination.

How the two levels interact:

| Partner setting | Effect on organizations |
|---|---|
| **Disabled** | Each organization configures its own destination individually. Partner fields show a "Not set -- orgs configure individually" placeholder |
| **Enabled and set** | Becomes a managed, locked setting. The matching fields in the org-level screen are read-only with a **"Managed by partner"** label, and the system rejects org-level attempts to change locked fields |

  Partner configuration is a true override, not just a default. When the partner locks a field, organizations cannot edit it. When the partner leaves forwarding disabled, organizations are free to self-serve their own destinations.

---

sections.heading: What Gets Shipped
sections.text:
Logs are sent in **batches** using the standard bulk-ingest format. Each forwarded event document contains:

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| **timestamp** | When the event occurred |
| **hostname** | The source device's host name |
| **device & organization identifiers** | Which device and customer the event came from |
| **category** | security, application, system, or hardware |
| **level** | Severity: info, warning, error, or critical |
| **source** | The originating log source or provider |
| **message** | The event text |
| **raw data** | The original underlying event payload, when available |

Each document is given a deterministic ID derived from its content, so re-sending a batch overwrites rather than duplicates -- retries are safe and will not create duplicate entries in the destination. Batches hitting transient errors (rate limiting, server errors) are retried with backoff; permanent rejections (bad credentials, a malformed mapping) are dropped and reported rather than retried forever.

---

sections.heading: Fleet-Wide Log Search
sections.text:
Independently of forwarding to an external SIEM, Breeze also keeps managed-device event logs centrally and lets you search across multiple devices and organizations at once:

```bash
curl -X POST /api/v1/logs/search \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "query": "patch installation failed",
    "timeRange": {
      "start": "2026-02-01T00:00:00Z",
      "end": "2026-02-28T23:59:59Z"
    },
    "level": ["error", "critical"],
    "category": ["system"],
    "deviceIds": ["UUID1", "UUID2"],
    "limit": 100,
    "sortBy": "timestamp",
    "sortOrder": "desc"
  }'
```

`level` accepts `info`, `warning`, `error`, `critical`; `category` accepts `security`, `application`, `system`, `hardware` -- the same values as the event log fields above.

sections.heading: Additional Fleet Log Features
sections.text:
| Feature | Endpoint | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Aggregation | `GET /api/v1/logs/aggregation` | Time-bucketed counts grouped by level, category, source, or device |
| Trends | `GET /api/v1/logs/trends` | Top error patterns and trending log sources |
| Correlation detection | `POST /api/v1/logs/correlation/detect` | Find patterns appearing across multiple devices |
| Correlation list | `GET /api/v1/logs/correlation` | List detected correlations with status |
| Saved queries | `GET/POST/DELETE /api/v1/logs/queries` | Save and reuse common search filters |

  This searches Breeze's own stored copy of the event logs, not the external SIEM destination -- it works whether or not forwarding is enabled. For per-device diagnostic logs from the agent itself (not managed-device event logs), see [Querying Diagnostic Logs](/features/log-shipping/#querying-diagnostic-logs) in the Log Shipping docs.

---

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**No "test connection" button.**
There is no pre-save connection test. Save the configuration, then confirm logs are arriving by searching for the day's index (`<prefix>-YYYY.MM.DD`) in your log store. Delivery failures are reported to operations through error tracking rather than shown at save time.

**Logs are not arriving in the destination.**
Confirm forwarding is enabled, the endpoint URL is correct and uses HTTPS, and the credentials are valid. Confirm the relevant log categories are enabled in Configuration Policies -- if nothing is being collected, nothing will be forwarded. Check that the endpoint is publicly reachable and is not an internal or private address, which is blocked.

**An organization cannot change its forwarding settings.**
The partner has enabled centralized event log shipping and locked those fields. The org-level screen will show a **"Managed by partner"** label. Change the configuration at the partner level instead.

**Logs are delayed.**
Forwarding runs on a recurring schedule, not in real time per event. A short delay between an event occurring on a device and it appearing in the destination is expected.

**Am I sending agent diagnostics to my SIEM?**
No. Event Log Forwarding sends managed-device event logs only. The agent's own diagnostic logs are handled separately by the Log Shipping feature and are sent to Breeze, not to your SIEM.

title: Extensions
description: First-party extension modules compiled into the API image, off by default and enabled per deployment via flags, currently the Workspace extension.

sections.text:
Extensions are **first-party modules compiled into the API image**. They are
not downloaded, installed, or provisioned — the code is already in the image
you run. Breeze currently ships one: **Workspace**.

Compiled in is not the same as loaded. Every built-in is **off by default** and
loads at boot only when its deployment enable flag is set. A built-in that is
switched off costs nothing: no migrations run, no tables are created, and none
of its infrastructure requirements apply.

| Extension | Enable flag | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workspace (file/email indexing and content search) | `BREEZE_WORKSPACE_ENABLED` | Requires a Postgres image with `pgvector` available |

The flag is strict: only the exact string `true` enables the extension.

  This page covers **built-in extensions** (`installed_extensions`, the
  manifest-declared modules under `ee/`). It is unrelated to the separate,
  older [Plugins](/features/plugins/) catalog (`plugin_catalog` /
  `plugin_installations`).

---

sections.heading: What an enabled extension contributes
sections.text:
When its flag is set, the extension's migrations are applied at API startup and
its manifest-declared contributions become active:

- **HTTP routes**, mounted at `/api/v1/ext/<name>/…` with an alias at
  `/api/v1/<routeNamespace>/…`. They run in-process against the same
  request-scoped, RLS-bounded database handle core routes use.
- **Web surfaces** — pages, navigation entries, and slot elements — discovered
  by the web app through `GET /api/v1/extensions/registry`.
- **Background jobs and AI tools**, where the manifest declares them.

A built-in is required code shipped inside the image, so any failure while
loading one (migration, staging, validation, activation) **aborts API startup**
rather than degrading silently.

sections.heading: What Breeze does not have
sections.text:
- **No third-party extension mechanism.** There is no way to add an extension
  to a running deployment; the set of extensions is whatever the image was
  built with.
- **No signed runtime bundles.** There is no artifact format, no packing or
  signing tool, no `extensions.yaml`, and no extensions directory to mount.
- **No per-organization activation.** An enabled extension serves every
  organization on the server. There are no per-org install or activation
  endpoints.

sections.heading: Enabling Workspace
sections.text:
Set the flag on the API service and restart:

```bash
BREEZE_WORKSPACE_ENABLED=true
```

Workspace's migrations run `CREATE EXTENSION vector` on boot, so the database
must be a `pgvector`-capable Postgres. The `POSTGRES_IMAGE_REF` that Breeze
ships by default (`pgvector/pgvector:pg16`) already includes it; if you supply
your own Postgres image, provide `pgvector` before setting the flag or the API
will fail to start with `extension "vector" is not available`. See
[Production deployment](/deploy/production/) for the database details,
including the upgrade caveat about swapping images over an existing data
volume.

sections.heading: Who can use Workspace
sections.text: Since v0.112.0, Workspace administration is gated by four dedicated permissions rather than the general device permissions: **`workspace:read`** (view sources and processing status), **`workspace:write`** (configure sources and settings), **`workspace:credentials`** (manage source credentials) and **`workspace:execute`** (run crawling and content processing). Partner Admin holds all four through its full-access grant and the built-in Org Admin is granted them on upgrade; **any other role, including custom roles, must be granted the keys in Settings → Roles** before its users can open or operate Workspace. Workspace is administered from a partner-scope session.

title: Filesystem Analysis & Disk Cleanup
description: Per-volume filesystem scanning, a preview-then-execute file cleanup pinned to what was previewed, and a closed catalog of OS-native cleaners (Windows Disk Cleanup, DISM, Time Machine snapshots, Homebrew, package caches, the journal).
headings: Preview expiry and the pinned run
"No filesystem snapshot available. Run a scan first." (404 on cleanup-preview)
Scan command returns 502 or times out
"No valid cleanup paths selected from latest previewable candidates" (400)
Execute returns `run_not_previewed`, `preview_expired` or "Cleanup run not found"
Cleanup reported success but no space was freed
Scan shows "partial: true" in the snapshot
Permission denied errors in scan results

sections.text:
Filesystem Analysis & Disk Cleanup shows what is consuming disk space on a device and gives you safe, auditable ways to reclaim it. Three things work together: a **scan** that builds a per-volume snapshot, a **file cleanup** that previews candidates and then deletes exactly the paths you approved, and a set of **OS-native cleaners** that reclaim the space a file scanner structurally cannot see -- the Windows component store, `Windows.old`, APFS local snapshots, the systemd journal.

  Viewing snapshots, volumes and run history requires `devices.read`. Starting a scan, previewing or executing a file cleanup, and listing or running the OS-native cleaners require `devices.execute` **and** an MFA-verified session. Every mutation is audit-logged with the volume, the paths or action ids, per-item status and byte counts.

---

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
Disk exhaustion is one of the most common and disruptive problems in a managed fleet: application crashes, failed updates, corrupted databases. Breeze answers it in three layers, each feeding the next:

1. **Analysis** -- a parallel, resumable scan of one volume produces a snapshot: largest files and directories, temp accumulation, old downloads, unrotated logs, trash usage, duplicate candidates and the list of *cleanup candidates*.
2. **File cleanup** -- a preview turns the snapshot's candidates into a pinned plan; execute deletes only paths from that plan, permanently, and reports what actually happened to each one.
3. **OS-native cleaners** -- a closed catalog of vetted maintenance tools (Windows Disk Cleanup handlers, DISM, `tmutil`, `brew`, `apt-get`/`dnf`, `journalctl`) that is listed with estimates, then run with explicit confirmation.

**One concept, one home.** All three live in the device's **Disk Cleanup** tab (`/devices/:id#filesystem`). The File Manager no longer carries its own inline cleanup section; its **Disk Cleanup** button navigates to this tab. Everything is also available through the REST API and the AI assistant.

---

sections.heading: Volumes
sections.text:
A scan targets one **volume** at a time. `GET /devices/:id/filesystem/volumes` lists the volumes a device can scan and clean, derived from the disk inventory the agent already reports:

```json
{
  "success": true,
  "data": [
    {
      "mountPoint": "C:\\",
      "scanPath": "C:\\",
      "fsType": "NTFS",
      "totalGb": 476.9,
      "usedGb": 401.2,
      "freeGb": 75.7,
      "usedPercent": 84.1,
      "isOsRoot": true,
      "scanState": {
        "lastRunMode": "incremental",
        "lastBaselineCompletedAt": "2026-10-18T02:14:00.000Z",
        "hasCheckpoint": false
      },
      "latestSnapshot": {
        "id": "8f2b...",
        "capturedAt": "2026-10-20T09:31:00.000Z",
        "partial": false,
        "cleanupEstimateBytes": 12884901888
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `mountPoint` | Exactly what the agent reported, so the UI can show the operator's own string. |
| `scanPath` | The normalised key (see below). This is what `scan_path` stores and what `POST /scan` sends. |
| `fsType`, `totalGb`, `usedGb`, `freeGb`, `usedPercent` | From the disk inventory. `null` (never `0`) when no disk row backs the volume. |
| `isOsRoot` | `true` for the OS volume (`C:\` on Windows, `/` elsewhere). |
| `scanState` | The volume's own last run mode, last baseline time and whether a resumable checkpoint exists; `null` if it has never been scanned. |
| `latestSnapshot` | The newest snapshot **for this volume**, with its cleanup estimate; `null` if none. |

Only **fixed local volumes** are offered. The following filesystem types are never listed (`NON_SCANNABLE_FS_TYPES`): read-only media `cdfs`, `udf`, `iso9660`, `squashfs`; memory filesystems `tmpfs`, `devtmpfs`; kernel filesystems `proc`, `sysfs`; container and network mounts `overlay`, `nfs`, `nfs4`, `cifs`, `smbfs`, `9p`, `autofs` and every `fuse*` variant. Windows UNC paths (`\\server\share`) are excluded as well. Deleting through a network mount frees space on a machine that is not the one being cleaned, which is the cross-volume mistake this design exists to stop. A volume whose `fsType` is blank is still offered, because the agent reported a real mount point. At most 24 volumes are listed per device.

The device's OS volume is always listed, even on a device that has not yet reported a disk inventory, so a fresh endpoint can still be scanned.

In the tab, the volumes appear as **chips** at the top (used/free bar, last-scan age, an **OS** badge). Selecting a chip re-keys every panel below it -- scan controls, snapshot panels and the file-cleanup panel all show that volume's state. The chip selection is component state, not part of the URL.

  **Every volume keeps its own state.** Scan checkpoints, the incremental baseline, the hot-directory list and the "latest snapshot" a cleanup preview reads are all keyed on `(device, scan path)`. A scan of `D:\` neither resets nor is read by anything belonging to `C:\`.

sections.heading: Scan paths are normalised
sections.text:
The volume key is a normalised path (`normalizeScanPath` in `@breeze/shared`). It is what `scan_path` stores, what `?path=` expects, and what the agent receives in the `filesystem_analysis` command:

- **Windows** -- separators become `\`, repeats collapse, the drive letter is upper-cased, and a trailing `\` survives only on a volume root. `c:/Users//Todd/` and `C:\Users\Todd` are the same path; `c:\`, `C:/` and `C:` are all `C:\`. A UNC path keeps its two leading separators so the volumes filter can recognise and refuse it.
- **macOS and Linux** -- repeats collapse, `.` and `..` resolve, and a trailing `/` survives only on `/` itself. Case below the root is preserved: `/Users` and `/users` are different directories on a case-sensitive volume, and folding them would silently merge two scans.

Requests may send any of these forms; the API normalises before reading or writing. This is why `c:\` and `C:\` are the same volume and resume the same checkpoint, and why every response that concerns one volume echoes the normalised `scanPath` it used.

---

sections.heading: Deep Filesystem Scan
sections.text: A scan is started with a `POST` to the scan endpoint naming a volume (or a directory inside one). The API queues a `filesystem_analysis` command to the agent over WebSocket (preferred) or the command queue. The agent walks the tree with a **worker pool** -- several goroutines each process a subtree and report to a coordinator -- so a volume with millions of entries completes in minutes rather than hours.

sections.heading: Scan strategies
sections.text:
| Strategy | Behavior | When to use |
|----------|----------|-------------|
| `baseline` | Full recursive scan from the path, up to `maxDepth`. | First scan of a volume, or after a large change in usage. |
| `incremental` | Scans only the "hot directories" that changed significantly since the last baseline. | Routine follow-ups to detect new accumulation. |
| `auto` | The API picks `baseline` or `incremental` from the volume's scan state. | Default. |

With `auto`, the API decides in this order:

1. If the normalised path is **not** one of the device's volume scan paths (a subdirectory), a `baseline` scan is always used.

2. If a previous scan of this volume was interrupted and checkpoint data exists, a `baseline` scan resumes from the checkpoint.

3. If no baseline has ever completed for this volume, a `baseline` scan is started.

4. If the volume's disk usage has changed by more than 3% since its last baseline, a `baseline` scan is triggered.

5. Otherwise, if hot directories exist from the previous scan, an `incremental` scan targets only those.

Scan state is keyed by **(device, scan path)**. Scanning `D:\` no longer resets the `C:\` baseline, pollutes its hot-directory list, or becomes the snapshot a `C:\` preview would delete from.

sections.heading: Resumable state
sections.text:
Long baseline scans checkpoint into `device_filesystem_scan_state`: which directories are done and which are pending. If the scan is interrupted (agent restart, network drop, timeout), the next `auto` or `baseline` scan of the **same volume** resumes from the checkpoint rather than starting over.

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `deviceId` | UUID | First half of the primary key. |
| `scanPath` | text | Normalised volume path. Second half of the primary key -- one state record per volume. |
| `scanGeneration` | UUID | The command that owns the current scan; results from a superseded command are rejected. |
| `lastRunMode` | string | `baseline` or `incremental`. |
| `lastBaselineCompletedAt` | timestamp | When the last full baseline finished. |
| `lastDiskUsedPercent` | real | Usage at the last baseline, used for the 3% rescan rule. |
| `checkpoint` | JSONB | Pending directories and depth information for resume. |
| `aggregate` | JSONB | Accumulated results from completed subtrees. |
| `hotDirectories` | JSONB | High-churn directories for incremental scans (up to 24). |

sections.heading: Scan configuration
sections.text:
```bash
POST /api/v1/devices/:deviceId/filesystem/scan
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "path": "D:\\",
  "strategy": "auto",
  "maxDepth": 32,
  "topFiles": 50,
  "topDirs": 30,
  "maxEntries": 5000000,
  "workers": 8,
  "timeoutSeconds": 300,
  "followSymlinks": false
}
```

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `path` | string | OS volume | Volume or directory to scan. Normalised server-side. Max 2048 characters. |
| `strategy` | enum | `auto` | `auto`, `baseline`, or `incremental`. |
| `maxDepth` | number | -- | Maximum directory depth (1-64). |
| `topFiles` | number | -- | Largest files to keep (1-500). |
| `topDirs` | number | -- | Largest directories to keep (1-200). |
| `maxEntries` | number | -- | Hard traversal cap (1,000 to 25,000,000). |
| `workers` | number | -- | Parallel scan workers (1-32). |
| `timeoutSeconds` | number | 300 (baseline) / 120 (incremental) | Scan timeout (5-900). |
| `followSymlinks` | boolean | -- | Follow symbolic links during traversal. |

"Root-scoped" means *the normalised path equals one of the device's volume scan paths* -- not a string compare against `C:\`. A scan of `D:\` on a two-drive machine is root-scoped for `D:\`.

The response is `202 Accepted` with the command id and the chosen mode:

```json
{
  "success": true,
  "data": {
    "commandId": "a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890",
    "status": "queued",
    "createdAt": "2026-02-20T14:30:00.000Z",
    "scanMode": "baseline",
    "strategy": "auto",
    "scanPath": "D:\\"
  }
}
```

---

sections.heading: Filesystem Snapshots
sections.text:
When a scan completes, the result is saved as an immutable **snapshot** in `device_filesystem_snapshots`.

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `id` | UUID | Snapshot identifier. |
| `deviceId` | UUID | The device that was scanned. |
| `scanPath` | text | The normalised volume or path this snapshot covers. |
| `capturedAt` | timestamp | When the snapshot was created. |
| `trigger` | enum | `on_demand` (user-initiated) or `threshold` (automatic). |
| `partial` | boolean | `true` if the scan was interrupted or incomplete. |
| `summary` | JSONB | Files, directories and bytes scanned, max depth, permission-denied count. |
| `largestFiles` | JSONB | Largest files by size (up to 50). |
| `largestDirs` | JSONB | Largest directories (up to 30). |
| `tempAccumulation` | JSONB | Temp accumulation by category (bytes per category). |
| `oldDownloads` | JSONB | Download-directory files not accessed recently (up to 200). |
| `unrotatedLogs` | JSONB | Large log files that have not rotated (up to 200). |
| `trashUsage` | JSONB | Trash / recycle bin contents (up to 16). |
| `duplicateCandidates` | JSONB | Likely duplicates by size and name (up to 200). |
| `cleanupCandidates` | JSONB | Everything eligible for safe cleanup (up to 1,000). |
| `errors` | JSONB | Scan errors, permission denied and the like (up to 200). |

"Latest snapshot" is always **per scan path**. `GET /devices/:id/filesystem?path=` returns the newest snapshot for that volume (default: the OS volume) and echoes the `scanPath` it resolved; a scan of another volume never changes the answer.

```bash
GET /api/v1/devices/:deviceId/filesystem?path=D:\
```

```json
{
  "success": true,
  "data": {
    "id": "snapshot-uuid",
    "deviceId": "device-uuid",
    "scanPath": "D:\\",
    "capturedAt": "2026-02-20T14:35:00.000Z",
    "trigger": "on_demand",
    "partial": false,
    "scanMode": "baseline",
    "path": "D:\\",
    "summary": { "filesScanned": 1250000, "dirsScanned": 85000, "bytesScanned": 450000000000, "maxDepthReached": 24, "permissionDeniedCount": 12 },
    "topLargestFiles": [],
    "topLargestDirectories": [],
    "tempAccumulation": [ { "category": "browser_cache", "bytes": 2500000000 } ],
    "oldDownloads": [],
    "unrotatedLogs": [],
    "trashUsage": [],
    "duplicateCandidates": [],
    "cleanupCandidates": [],
    "errors": []
  }
}
```

sections.heading: Snapshot merging
sections.text:
An incremental scan is merged into the volume's existing snapshot: summary counts accumulate, max depth takes the maximum, largest files and directories deduplicate by path keeping the larger size, temp accumulation sums per category, cleanup candidates, old downloads, unrotated logs and trash entries deduplicate by path, and error lists concatenate up to 200.

---

sections.heading: Disk Cleanup
sections.text:
File cleanup is **select → confirm → execute → result**, inside the tab:

1. The **Cleanup panel** shows category cards with byte totals and a candidate table sorted by size, with per-row checkboxes and "select all in category". The panel reads the selected volume's latest snapshot.
2. **Execute** opens a destructive confirmation naming the volume, the count and bytes, and the first paths. Recycle-bin and trash rows carry a note that their *contents* are deleted, not the folder.
3. The request is pinned to the preview's `cleanupRunId`. The result panel reports reclaimed bytes and the `completed / skipped_locked / rejected / skipped_budget` counts; failures are listed in an amber list, never a green box.

  Starting a scan, previewing and executing all require an MFA-verified session. If your account has MFA enrolled you may be prompted to step up.

sections.heading: What gets cleaned
sections.text:
Candidates are classified by a **rooted rule table** shared byte-for-byte by the agent, the API and the web app (`packages/shared/src/utils/cleanupRules.json`, embedded into the agent binary). Rules match **path components from the volume root**, never substrings: a directory that merely happens to be *named* `tmp` or `Caches` -- `/opt/myapp/tmp`, `/System/Library/Caches` -- is not in scope. Patterns are lower-cased, `/`-separated, and start at `<vol>` (the scanned volume root) on Windows or `/` on POSIX; `*` matches exactly one component and `**` the subtree.

| Category | OS | Matches | Excludes | Min age |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `temp_files` | Windows | `<vol>/windows/temp/**`, `<vol>/users/*/appdata/local/temp/**` | -- | 24 h |
| `temp_files` | macOS | `/tmp/**`, `/private/tmp/**`, `/private/var/tmp/**`, `/private/var/folders/*/*/t/**` | -- | 24 h |
| `temp_files` | Linux | `/tmp/**`, `/var/tmp/**` | `/tmp/.X11-unix/**`, `/tmp/.ICE-unix/**`, `/tmp/systemd-private-*/**` | 24 h |
| `browser_cache` | Windows | Chrome, Edge, Brave and Chromium `User Data/*/{Cache, Code Cache, GPUCache, DawnCache, GraphiteDawnCache, ShaderCache}` and `Service Worker/{CacheStorage, ScriptCache}`; Firefox `profiles/*/{cache2, startupCache, shader-cache}` | -- | -- |
| `browser_cache` | macOS | `/users/*/library/caches/**`, `/library/caches/**` | Homebrew (goes to `package_cache`), `com.apple.bird`, `CloudKit`, `com.apple.icloud*` | -- |
| `browser_cache` | Linux | `/home/*/.cache/**`, `/root/.cache/**` | `pip` (goes to `package_cache`) | -- |
| `package_cache` | Linux | apt archives, `dnf`, `yum`, pip and npm caches | `apt/archives/lock`, `apt/archives/partial/**` | -- |
| `package_cache` | macOS | Homebrew cache, npm `_cacache`, pip, NuGet `*.nupkg` | -- | -- |
| `package_cache` | Windows | pip, `npm-cache/_cacache`, Chocolatey cache, NuGet `*.nupkg`, UWP `AC/INetCache`, `AC/Temp`, `TempState` | -- | -- |
| `trash` | Windows | `<vol>/$recycle.bin/*` (each SID directory; only when the scan root is the volume root) | -- | -- |
| `trash` | macOS | `/users/*/.trash` | -- | -- |
| `trash` | Linux | `/home/*/.local/share/Trash`, `/root/.local/share/Trash` | -- | -- |

Temp files younger than 24 hours are never candidates. Trash rules have **contents** granularity: the candidate is the bin directory, and execute deletes its children while the directory itself (and `desktop.ini`, which Explorer needs) survives.

**Never candidates**, whatever the snapshot says: Chrome, Edge and Firefox `Bookmarks`, `History`, `Cookies`, `Login Data` and `places.sqlite` (they are not under a cache pattern), and anything under a **cleanup-denied root**, which is rejected even when a rule matched: `<vol>/windows/system32`, `<vol>/windows/winsxs`, `<vol>/program files`, `<vol>/program files (x86)` on Windows; `/system`, `/usr`, `/bin`, `/sbin`, `/etc`, `/private/var/db`, `/library/apple` on macOS; `/usr`, `/bin`, `/sbin`, `/etc` on Linux.

Rules are enforced **twice**: at execute the API re-filters the pinned candidates through the shared table (so a snapshot captured by an older agent cannot be executed against), and the agent re-checks each path under `cleanupGuard` before deleting.

The scanner also reports **old downloads**, **unrotated logs**, **duplicate candidates** and the **largest files**. These are informational and are never auto-cleaned.

sections.heading: Preview
sections.text:
The preview builds a plan from the volume's latest snapshot without touching the device.

```bash
POST /api/v1/devices/:deviceId/filesystem/cleanup-preview
Content-Type: application/json

{ "path": "D:\\", "categories": ["temp_files", "browser_cache"] }
```

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| `path` | string | No | Volume to preview. Defaults to the OS volume. Normalised server-side. |
| `categories` | array | No | Restrict to specific categories. Default: all four. Max 10 entries. |

The response creates a cleanup run with status `previewed` and pins **both** the `snapshotId` and the `scanPath` into the run's plan; the `cleanupRunId` is what execute must present:

```json
{
  "success": true,
  "data": {
    "cleanupRunId": "run-uuid",
    "scanPath": "D:\\",
    "snapshotId": "snapshot-uuid",
    "estimatedBytes": 4300000000,
    "candidateCount": 156,
    "categories": [ { "category": "temp_files", "count": 89, "estimatedBytes": 1800000000 } ],
    "candidates": [
      { "path": "D:\\Temp\\old_installer.exe", "category": "temp_files", "sizeBytes": 450000000, "safe": true, "reason": "Temporary file older than 24 hours", "modifiedAt": "2026-01-15T10:00:00.000Z" }
    ]
  }
}
```

sections.heading: Execute
sections.text:
```bash
POST /api/v1/devices/:deviceId/filesystem/cleanup-execute
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "cleanupRunId": "run-uuid",
  "paths": ["D:\\Temp\\old_installer.exe", "D:\\$Recycle.Bin\\S-1-5-21-..."]
}
```

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| `cleanupRunId` | UUID | **Yes** | The `previewed` run to execute. There is no "latest snapshot" fallback. |
| `paths` | array | Yes | Paths to delete. Min 1, max 200, max 4096 characters each. |

What execute guarantees:

- **Nothing is deleted that was not previewed.** A path outside the pinned plan is reported in `rejectedPaths` (and as an action with `status: "rejected"`) and is never dispatched. If *every* path is screened out, the request fails with `400 No valid cleanup paths selected from latest previewable candidates` and the body still carries `rejectedPaths` so you can see why.
- **Deletion is permanent.** The agent is sent `permanent: true` and `cleanupGuard: true`. There is no trash move -- that is what makes the bytes actually free (a trash move on the same volume frees nothing, and across volumes it copied files onto the OS drive).
- **Symlinks and reparse points are refused**, at the target and among the children of a contents-granularity delete. The agent uses `Lstat` throughout and never follows a link.
- **Locked files are never forced.** A Windows sharing violation reports `skipped_locked`.
- **Bins are deleted by contents.** A recycle-bin or trash candidate deletes its current children; the directory and `desktop.ini` survive.
- **A 4-minute budget** bounds the request. Deletes are sequential with a 30-second command timeout each; paths not reached are `skipped_budget`, the run is recorded `executed` with `partial: true`, and you re-run for the rest.
- **Run state is claimed.** The run flips `previewed → running` for the duration and lands as `executed` or `failed`; a second execute against the same run answers `409 run_not_previewed` with its current status.

Per-path `status` is one of `completed`, `partial` (something was removed but the target is not clear -- some children failed, or were held back as links or as changed since the preview), `failed`, `skipped_locked`, `rejected`, `skipped_budget`. "Emptied most of the bin, three children failed" is `partial`, never `completed`. The response:

```json
{
  "success": true,
  "data": {
    "cleanupRunId": "run-uuid",
    "scanPath": "D:\\",
    "status": "executed",
    "bytesReclaimed": 4100000000,
    "selectedCount": 2,
    "failedCount": 0,
    "counts": { "completed": 2, "partial": 0, "failed": 0, "skipped_locked": 0, "rejected": 1, "skipped_budget": 0 },
    "rejectedPaths": ["D:\\Projects\\notes.txt"],
    "partial": false,
    "budgetMs": 240000,
    "actions": [
      { "path": "D:\\Temp\\old_installer.exe", "category": "temp_files", "sizeBytes": 450000000, "status": "completed", "bytesFreed": 450000000 }
    ]
  }
}
```

`bytesFreed` on an action is the agent's sum of `Lstat` sizes actually removed -- *logical* bytes. If every dispatched path fails the run is `failed` (HTTP 500 with the same body); if at least one completes it is `executed`.

sections.heading: Run history
sections.text:
- `GET /devices/:id/filesystem/cleanup-runs?limit=&cursor=` -- paginated (default 20, max 100), newest first, **both kinds** (`files` and `system`). An invalid cursor is `400 invalid_cursor` rather than silently page 1.
- `GET /devices/:id/filesystem/cleanup-runs/:runId` -- one run with its plan, executed actions and error.

The tab's **Run history** panel reads these. Retention is a background job: `previewed` runs are deleted after **7 days** (an abandoned preview has no value), and the pinned `plan.candidates` list is trimmed from finished runs after **90 days** while the summary, status, byte count and executed actions stay. Both windows are configurable (`FILESYSTEM_CLEANUP_PREVIEW_RETENTION_DAYS`, `FILESYSTEM_CLEANUP_PLAN_RETENTION_DAYS`).

---

sections.heading: OS-Native Cleaners
sections.text:
The file scanner can only reclaim what it can enumerate. A component store, `Windows.old`, an APFS local snapshot and a systemd journal are invisible to it -- the operating system manages them through its own tools. Breeze runs those tools as a **second cleanup engine** on the same tab, in the **System cleanup** panel below the file cleanup.

The native engine has no itemised preview to check a selection against, so instead it is constrained by a **closed catalog**: a fixed list of vetted actions, every command line built from constants inside the agent, binaries by absolute path, no shell, timeouts and output caps on every process. The only client input is a list of action ids and one bounded integer.

The flow is two steps:

1. **List** -- `POST /devices/:id/filesystem/system-cleanup/list` queues a `system_cleanup_list` command (`202` with a `commandId`); poll `GET .../system-cleanup/list/:commandId` until `status: "completed"` returns the device's `catalog`: each action with its label, description, availability (and `unavailableReason`), an **"up to"** estimate or *size unknown*, its risk flags and the volumes it affects, plus `volumesBefore` free-space readings. Estimation runs with a 3-minute cap; an estimate that times out reports `estimateKnown: false`.
2. **Run** -- `POST /devices/:id/filesystem/system-cleanup/run` with `{ actionIds, params? }` records a `kind: "system"` cleanup run and queues `system_cleanup_run` (`202` with `cleanupRunId` and `commandId`); poll `GET .../system-cleanup/run/:cleanupRunId`. Actions run **sequentially** in catalog order (cleanmgr and DISM must not overlap); one failing does not stop the next. Each action reports `completed | failed | timed_out | unavailable | busy | not_started`, its exit code, duration and output tail.

On an agent older than the minimum version both POSTs answer `409 agent_update_required` with `minAgentVersion`; the panel shows an update banner and disables **Run**. A device runs **one** OS cleanup at a time -- a second run while one is in flight is `409 run_in_progress` with the running `cleanupRunId`, because Windows Disk Cleanup is driven by a shared on-disk selection profile and two overlapping runs would each execute whatever the other wrote last. Each run's deadline is the sum of its selected actions' timeouts plus 10 minutes of slack, capped at 3 hours; a run past its deadline is failed as `run_expired` and its command cancelled.

`freedBytes` on the result is **measured**: the agent samples free space per volume before and after the whole run and reports the delta (`volumes[].freeBefore` / `freeAfter`). That figure, not the estimate, is what the run achieved. Note that component-store cleanup (`win_dism_component_cleanup`) releases some of its space only after the next reboot, so those bytes are not in `freedBytes`.

sections.heading: Catalog
sections.text:
| Action id | Platform | What it runs | Timeout |
|---|---|---|---|
| `win_cleanmgr` (or `win_cleanmgr:<handler>`) | Windows | Sets `StateFlags5555` on the selected built-in Disk Cleanup handlers and runs `cleanmgr.exe /sagerun:5555`. The bare id means "every allowlisted handler present on this device"; a `:<slug>` sub-id selects one. Allowlisted handlers: `delivery_optimization_files`, `device_driver_packages`, `previous_installations`, `upgrade_discarded_files`, `windows_upgrade_log_files`, `setup_log_files`, `temporary_setup_files`, `service_pack_cleanup`, `system_error_memory_dump_files`, `system_error_minidump_files`, `windows_error_reporting_files`, `windows_error_reporting_system_archive_files`, `windows_error_reporting_system_queue_files`, `temporary_files`, `windows_defender`, `old_chkdsk_files`, `diagnostic_data_viewer_database_files`, `branchcache`, `content_indexer_cleaner`. Handlers absent on the device's Windows build are simply not offered. `update_cleanup` is **no longer offered**: cleanmgr's Windows Update cleanup handler deadlocks under the SYSTEM service before it frees anything -- use `win_dism_component_cleanup`, which performs the same component-store cleanup. Disk Cleanup itself never exits in session 0 (it waits on a progress window that cannot be shown), so the agent ends the run once the process tree has used no CPU for 5 minutes and reports it as `completed`; the 60-minute cap remains as a backstop. | 60 min |
| `win_dism_component_cleanup` | Windows | `dism.exe /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup` -- removes superseded components from WinSxS. Never `/ResetBase`, so installed updates stay removable. | 90 min |
| `mac_tm_local_snapshots` | macOS | `tmutil listlocalsnapshots /`, then `tmutil deletelocalsnapshots <date>` for each listed snapshot. Backups on the Time Machine destination are untouched. | 10 min |
| `mac_brew_cleanup` | macOS | `brew cleanup --prune=all`. Installed software stays at its current version. | 10 min |
| `linux_pkg_cache_clean` | Linux | `apt-get clean` / `dnf clean all` / `yum clean all` (first present). Removed archives are re-downloadable. | 5 min |
| `linux_pkg_autoremove` | Linux | `apt-get -y autoremove` / `dnf -y autoremove`. **Uninstalls packages.** | 15 min |
| `linux_journal_vacuum` | Linux | `journalctl --vacuum-size=<bytes>`. `params.journalVacuumBytes` sets the target: 64 MiB - 4 GiB, default 256 MiB. Archived journals only; the active journal is preserved. | 5 min |

sections.heading: Risk flags
sections.text:
Every action declares zero or more risk flags. The panel renders them as badges, and the confirmation dialog names the specific loss rather than asking a generic "are you sure":

| Flag | Carried by | What it means for the customer |
|---|---|---|
| `long_running` | `win_cleanmgr`, `win_dism_component_cleanup` | Can hold the device for up to 60 or 90 minutes. |
| `may_require_reboot_free_state` | `win_dism_component_cleanup` | Some of the space is released after the next restart. |
| `removes_driver_rollback` | `win_cleanmgr:device_driver_packages` | Older driver packages are deleted; you can no longer roll a driver back to a previous version. |
| `removes_packages` | `linux_pkg_autoremove` | Software is **uninstalled** (whatever the package manager considers orphaned). |
| `removes_os_rollback` | `win_cleanmgr:previous_installations`, `win_cleanmgr:upgrade_discarded_files` | Deletes `Windows.old` / `$WINDOWS.~BT` / `$WINDOWS.~WS` -- the path back to the previous Windows build. **Irreversible.** |
| `removes_recovery_points` | `mac_tm_local_snapshots` | Deletes the only on-disk restore points a Mac has when its Time Machine destination is not attached. No in-place rollback remains. |

Selecting any action that carries `removes_packages`, `removes_driver_rollback`, `removes_os_rollback` or `removes_recovery_points` arms the destructive dialog's **second checkbox**; the run button stays disabled until it is ticked.

sections.heading: What is deliberately excluded
sections.text:
These are excluded **in code, not configuration** -- the catalog is an `as const` list pinned by tests on both sides of the Go/TypeScript boundary, and an id outside it is rejected before anything is queued:

- DISM `/ResetBase` (makes every installed update permanent).
- The `DownloadsFolder` handler (user data).
- `Windows ESD installation files` (breaks *Reset this PC*).
- `Language Pack` (uninstalls installed languages).
- Every per-user cleanmgr handler (`Recycle Bin`, `Thumbnail Cache`, `Temporary Internet Files` and the rest): under the SYSTEM service account they operate on the SYSTEM profile, and the file engine already covers user bins.
- Docker prune, Storage Sense and `snap` revision pruning.

---

sections.heading: AI Integration
sections.text:
The AI assistant has three tools. Tiers and rate limits are the ones enforced by the guardrails (see [AI in Breeze](/features/ai/)).

| Tool | Tier | What changed |
|---|---|---|
| `analyze_disk_usage` | 1 / 2 with `refresh: true` | Gains `path` (normalised server-side; default OS root). Without `refresh` it reads the latest stored snapshot **for that path** (`devices.read`) and never scans; with no stored snapshot it says so. `refresh: true` scans that path on the device, which needs `devices.execute`, like `POST /devices/:id/filesystem/scan`. |
| `disk_cleanup` | 1 for `preview` / 3 for `execute` | Gains `path`. `preview` returns a `cleanupRunId`, which the tool remembers; `execute` runs against that run, or against an explicit `cleanupRunId` -- without either it answers `cleanup_run_required`. Same pinning, expiry, `rejectedPaths` and permanent-delete semantics as the route. |
| `system_cleanup` | 2 for `list` / 1 for `status` / 3 for `run` | New. Three actions, used in order. `list` asks the device for its catalog, so it needs `devices.execute` like the route, and is a read-only Tier 2 action (no prompt, audit-logged). It queues a catalog request and waits up to 60 seconds for the device; if the device has not answered by then it returns `status: "pending"` with a `commandId`, and calling `list` again with that `commandId` re-checks the same request instead of starting a new one. `run` requires `actionIds` from the shared allowlist (plus optional `params.journalVacuumBytes`), starts the run and returns **immediately** with a `cleanupRunId`, the `commandId` and the run's stored `deadlineAt` -- it never waits, because a run can take hours (DISM alone is capped at 90 minutes). `status` takes that `cleanupRunId` and returns the persisted state of the run -- `running`, `executed` or `failed` -- with `freedBytes`, per-action status and volume deltas once the agent has reported; it is the same code path as the web panel's poll, including the lazy deadline timeout that finalises a run the device never answered. A run whose every action failed reports `failed`. `run` is supervised Tier 3: it always takes human approval. The per-tool rate limit is **30 calls per hour** across all three actions; the single-run-per-device claim, not the rate limit, is what stops a second run starting while one is in flight. |

All three refuse an agent below the minimum version with `agent_update_required` and the required version.

**Over MCP**, a Tier 3 action is refused outright -- there is no interactive approval surface on that transport -- so an MCP client can diagnose with `analyze_disk_usage`, `disk_cleanup preview`, `system_cleanup list` and `system_cleanup status`, and a technician executes in the Breeze web app. A key with only `ai:read` reads stored results; a fresh scan (`refresh: true`) and `system_cleanup list` reach the device and need `ai:write`. See [MCP Server](/features/mcp-server/).

---
