sections.heading: Preview expiry and the pinned run
sections.text:
Two properties of a pinned run a technician has to know before approving:

- **A preview expires after 24 hours.** An execute against an older run is refused with `409 preview_expired` (the body carries `requestedAt` and `ttlHours`), and the technician previews again. A day-old plan is a guess about a machine nobody has looked at since.
- **A bin is live.** Pinning a recycle-bin or trash path pins the *path*, not its contents: execute deletes whatever is in the bin **at the moment it runs**, not the files the preview enumerated. The same is true of a temp file replaced between preview and execute. The confirmation dialog says so on those rows.

A run is single-use: once it has left `previewed` it cannot be executed again (`409 run_not_previewed`).

sections.heading: Agent version requirements
sections.text:
- **Permanent file cleanup** requires an agent at **`0.115.0`** (`MIN_AGENT_VERSION_CLEANUP_GUARD`) or newer. Execute sends `permanent: true` with `cleanupGuard: true`; an older agent has no guard and would perform an unguarded recursive permanent delete, so both the route and the AI tool **refuse** an older agent with `409 agent_update_required` before anything is dispatched. The body carries `minAgentVersion` and the device's current `agentVersion`; the panel renders the required version in its error.
- **OS-native cleaners** require **`0.116.0`** (`MIN_AGENT_VERSION_SYSTEM_CLEANUP`) or newer and answer `409 agent_update_required` below it. They first shipped in `0.115.0`, but that agent's Disk Cleanup (`cleanmgr`) run hangs until the 60-minute cap kills it, so `0.115.x` agents are refused until they update. The gate compares the core version only, so a release candidate of the gate release counts. As a defence in depth, an agent that reports a new-enough version but answers `unknown command type:` resolves to the same 409 on poll.

Both gates fail **closed**: an empty or unparseable `agent_version` is treated as too old.

sections.heading: How to read an estimate
sections.text:
Every reclaim figure shown before a run is **heuristic and an upper bound**:

- The file engine's candidate totals are the snapshot's sizes at scan time; a locked file, a link, a changed bin or the 4-minute budget can all leave part of it in place.
- Native-cleaner estimates are labelled **"up to X"**, **heuristic**, or **size unknown**. "Up to" is a genuine ceiling such as a cache directory's current size. Heuristic figures are reliable only to an order of magnitude: DISM's `/AnalyzeComponentStore` fields are component-store *overhead*, and `StartComponentCleanup` frees an amount related to but not equal to them; `journalctl --vacuum-size` only removes *archived* journals, so the estimate is usage minus target, floored at zero; `autoremove`'s figure is the packages' installed size, which over-counts shared files. Time Machine local snapshots report a **count** only -- their byte size is unknown. *Unknown* is never rendered as *0*, because a confident zero reads as "nothing to reclaim", which is a different and possibly wrong claim.

Contrast `freedBytes`, which is **measured** from the free-space delta either side of the run. When the two disagree, the measured figure is the truth.

---

sections.heading: API Reference
sections.text:
All endpoints are prefixed with `/api/v1/devices/:deviceId`.

| Method | Path | Description | Permission |
|--------|------|-------------|------------|
| `GET` | `/devices/:id/filesystem/volumes` | List the volumes this device can scan and clean | `devices.read` |
| `GET` | `/devices/:id/filesystem?path=` | Latest snapshot for a volume (default: OS volume) | `devices.read` |
| `POST` | `/devices/:id/filesystem/scan` | Trigger a scan of a volume or directory | `devices.execute` + MFA |
| `POST` | `/devices/:id/filesystem/cleanup-preview` | Preview safe candidates for a volume; returns `cleanupRunId` | `devices.execute` + MFA |
| `POST` | `/devices/:id/filesystem/cleanup-execute` | Execute the pinned run on the selected paths | `devices.execute` + MFA |
| `GET` | `/devices/:id/filesystem/cleanup-runs` | Paginated run history, both kinds | `devices.read` |
| `GET` | `/devices/:id/filesystem/cleanup-runs/:runId` | One cleanup run | `devices.read` |
| `POST` | `/devices/:id/filesystem/system-cleanup/list` | Queue a catalog request; returns a `commandId` | `devices.execute` + MFA |
| `GET` | `/devices/:id/filesystem/system-cleanup/list/:commandId` | Poll the catalog request | `devices.read` |
| `POST` | `/devices/:id/filesystem/system-cleanup/run` | Run selected actions; returns a `cleanupRunId`, or `409 run_in_progress` | `devices.execute` + MFA |
| `GET` | `/devices/:id/filesystem/system-cleanup/run/:cleanupRunId` | Poll the run | `devices.read` |

Audit actions: `device.filesystem.cleanup.preview`, `device.filesystem.cleanup.execute`, `device.filesystem.system_cleanup.list`, `device.filesystem.system_cleanup.queue`, `device.filesystem.system_cleanup.run`.

---

sections.heading: "No filesystem analysis available yet" (404)
sections.text: No snapshot exists for **this volume**. Run `POST /devices/:id/filesystem/scan` with the volume's `path` and wait for it to complete. Scanning another volume does not help -- snapshots are per scan path.

sections.heading: "No filesystem snapshot available. Run a scan first." (404 on cleanup-preview)
sections.text: The preview needs a snapshot of the requested volume to build candidates from. Scan that volume first.

sections.heading: Scan command returns 502 or times out
sections.text: Large scans can exceed the command timeout. Increase `timeoutSeconds` (up to 900), reduce `maxEntries` or `maxDepth`, or scan a subdirectory. A timed-out baseline resumes from its checkpoint on the next attempt of the same volume.

sections.heading: Cleanup preview returns zero candidates
sections.text: Only candidates that matched a rule in the shared table (`safe: true`) in one of the four categories are previewed. If the snapshot lists candidates but the preview is empty, they are informational items (old downloads, unrotated logs, duplicates), temp files younger than 24 hours, or under a cleanup-denied root. Also check that your `categories` filter matches what the snapshot contains.

sections.heading: "No valid cleanup paths selected from latest previewable candidates" (400)
sections.text: Every path in the request was screened out before dispatch. The body's `rejectedPaths` and `actions` say which and why: `not_in_plan` (the path is not in the pinned run -- copied from a different preview, hand-typed, or the wrong volume), `rule_rejected` (it no longer matches a cleanup rule) or `denied_root`. Preview again and submit paths from that response.

sections.heading: Execute returns `run_not_previewed`, `preview_expired` or "Cleanup run not found"
sections.text: The pinned run was already consumed (it is single-use), is older than 24 hours, or belongs to another device. Preview again -- the plan is cheap, the mistake is not.

sections.heading: Execute returns `agent_update_required` (409)
sections.text: The device's agent is older than `0.115.0` and lacks `cleanupGuard`; cleanup is refused rather than degraded, because an unguarded permanent delete is worse than no delete. The body carries `minAgentVersion` and the device's `agentVersion`. Update the agent and retry.

sections.heading: Cleanup reported success but no space was freed
sections.text: Check the run's per-path results: `skipped_locked` and `partial` entries kept their bytes, and `bytesReclaimed` counts only what was removed. On a device whose agent predates the `cleanupGuard` gate, earlier releases moved files to the agent's own trash directory instead of deleting them; current releases refuse such agents with `409 agent_update_required`, so a "success" that freed nothing on a current API means the bytes are still held by locked or skipped paths. For OS-native cleaners, `Windows Update cleanup` and DISM release their space after a reboot, and `freedBytes` is measured at the moment the run ends.

sections.heading: A native cleaner reports `unavailable`
sections.text: The catalog row's `unavailableReason` says why: the binary is absent (`cleanmgr.exe` is not present on Server Core), or the agent's sandbox denies writes to the cache path (`/var/cache/apt`, `/var/log/journal`) on a hardened systemd unit. `busy` means another maintenance operation (a concurrent run, a patch job's Homebrew cleanup, DISM) held the agent's process-wide lock -- nothing was attempted and a retry is right; `not_started` means the run's overall budget expired before that action's turn, as opposed to `timed_out`, where the action itself ran and overran its own cap.

sections.heading: System cleanup returns `run_in_progress` (409)
sections.text: One OS cleanup runs per device at a time. Wait for the running `cleanupRunId` to finish (poll it), or for it to pass its deadline, then retry.

sections.heading: Cleanup actions partially failed
sections.text: Per-path status explains it: the file was already gone, it is locked by a running process (`skipped_locked`), it is a link (`rejected`), or the 4-minute budget ran out (`skipped_budget`). The run is `executed` if at least one path completed and `failed` if every dispatched path failed; `bytesReclaimed` reflects only removed paths.

sections.heading: Incremental scan returns minimal results
sections.text: Incremental scans traverse only the hot directories the previous baseline identified for that volume. If the disk is stable there is little to scan. Run a `baseline` scan for a full view.

sections.heading: Scan shows "partial: true" in the snapshot
sections.text: The scan was interrupted (agent restart, disconnect, timeout). The partial snapshot is valid for what was scanned; the next scan of the same volume resumes from the checkpoint and merges.

sections.heading: Permission denied errors in scan results
sections.text: Directories the agent cannot read are recorded in the snapshot's `errors` array with the path and error type. Running the agent as root/SYSTEM reduces these but is not always necessary.

title: Fleet Hygiene Findings
description: Surface cross-device patterns as single fleet findings and remediate every affected device from one run, with per-device outcomes.

sections.text:
Fleet Hygiene turns per-device noise into fleet-wide signal. Instead of raising one alert per device, Breeze groups related device signals into a single **finding** — "CPU spike pattern on 7 devices", "Low reliability: 12 devices below 50" — and lets you fix the whole population with **one remediation run**, tracking the outcome on every device individually.

The findings feed lives on the **Fleet** page (`/fleet`), under the fleet stat cards: *"Cross-device patterns worth one action instead of many."*

---

sections.heading: Finding Types
sections.text:
Breeze currently detects three kinds of systemic defect. The fleet is re-scanned roughly every 10 minutes.

| Finding type | What it detects | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| **Metric anomaly** | Open metric anomalies grouped by metric and anomaly type. A single device spiking is not a fleet pattern — a finding opens only when **2 or more devices** show the same anomaly. | Critical when the strongest anomaly is severe; Warning otherwise |
| **Log correlation** | An active log correlation rule matching across devices; the finding lists the devices the rule flagged. | Inherited from the correlation rule |
| **Reliability offenders** | One org-wide finding listing every device whose [reliability score](/features/reliability/) has dropped below 50. | Error if any device is below 25; Warning otherwise |

Quick Support (ephemeral) devices and decommissioned devices are never counted — they aren't hygiene offenders, and nothing can be remediated on them.

sections.heading: Finding Lifecycle
sections.text:
A finding is **Open** when first detected. From there:

- **Acknowledge** — mark it as seen; it stays in the default feed view.
- **Dismiss** — suppress it (a dismissal note is required). Dismissed findings stop updating but remain visible under the *Dismissed* filter.
- **Reopen** — return an acknowledged or dismissed finding to Open.
- **Resolved** — automatic only. When the underlying signal clears (anomalies close, the correlation deactivates, reliability recovers), the finding resolves itself on the next scan. You cannot resolve a finding by hand, and a resolved finding never reopens — if the pattern recurs, a **new** finding is created so each episode keeps its own history.

While a finding is open, each scan keeps it current: devices join and leave the affected list, and the severity, title, and device count refresh as the pattern evolves. A dismissed finding still auto-resolves when its source clears — dismissal suppresses a finding, it doesn't pin it open.

sections.heading: Remediating a Finding
sections.text:
Remediation requires the device-execute permission and a fresh **MFA check** — it is the one action in this feature that re-prompts for MFA.

1. **Open the finding** from the Fleet Findings feed. The drawer shows the summary, evidence, the affected-devices table, and the finding's remediation history.

2. **Click "Remediate across N devices"** and pick one of three fixes:
   - **Run a script** — choose a script from your library and fill its parameters. Devices whose OS can't run the script are automatically excluded.
   - **Restart a service** — restart one named service on every selected device.
   - **Reboot devices** — restarts happen immediately on dispatch; active sessions end and unsaved work is lost.

3. **Choose the targets.** Every affected device is pre-selected; deselect any you want to leave alone.

4. **Confirm.** The run is created and dispatched in the background; the result step lists how many devices were targeted and which were skipped (with reasons), and links to live progress.

5. **Watch the run.** The progress panel refreshes every few seconds, showing each device as Pending → Queued → Succeeded / Failed / Skipped, and the run itself as Queued / Running / Partial / Succeeded / Failed.

sections.heading: How targets are validated
sections.text:
Targets are re-validated **at dispatch time**, not when you click — so a device that was decommissioned, left the finding, or moved out of your site access between click and dispatch is skipped rather than acted on. Offline devices are skipped, not queued indefinitely. A run times out after 30 minutes; still-pending devices are marked failed with a timeout reason.

Skip reasons you may see per device: *Site not accessible to you*, *No longer affected by this finding*, *Device is decommissioned*, *Timed out after 30 minutes*, *Never dispatched — queueing failed*, or `unreachable` (the device was not online at dispatch time).

Every remediation run — and every acknowledge/dismiss/reopen — is recorded in the [audit log](/reference/audit-logs/).

sections.heading: Scope and Access
sections.text:
- **Findings are per-organization.** Partner-scope users see findings across all their organizations in one feed (each row shows its organization); filtering by organization narrows the view. There is no cross-org merging — the "all orgs" view is a union.
- **Site-restricted technicians** see only findings with at least one device in their sites, with device counts computed from their in-scope devices; findings entirely outside their scope are hidden.
- Viewing findings requires device-read permission; acknowledging/dismissing requires device-write; remediation requires device-execute plus MFA.

Fleet findings can be disabled per organization via the organization's fleet settings (they are enabled by default). The AI assistant can also read the findings feed through its `get_fleet_findings` tool.

title: Flows
description: Build multi-step workflows that run on a schedule, on a platform event, or on demand, with approvals for sensitive steps and clear limits on what they can do.
headings: Enabling a flow and what it delegates

sections.text:
A flow is a saved, multi-step workflow. Each step runs one Breeze tool (for example, running a script on a device), and steps can wait, set values, or repeat over a list of items. A flow runs under its own automation identity rather than a person's login, so enabling a flow is a delegation decision.

Flows are off by default. An administrator of your Breeze deployment turns them on with `FLOWS_ENABLED=true`. Everything on this page, including webhook triggers, built-in steps, flow tools and monthly limits, is behind that one setting.

sections.heading: Enabling a flow and what it delegates
sections.text:
A flow is a draft until someone enables it. Enabling publishes an immutable version of the flow and makes you its **delegator**: the flow acts with authority you are lending it.

To enable a flow you must:

- Hold the permission for **every step** in the flow. If any step needs a permission you lack, enabling is refused.
- Have unrestricted access in the flow's scope. A user limited to specific sites cannot enable a flow, because a flow acts across the whole organization. For a partner-wide flow you need access to all organizations of the partner, with no site restriction.

A flow that is enabled cannot be edited. Edit it while it is a draft, paused, or disabled, then enable it again to publish a new version.

**The delegator must stay valid.** If the delegator is deactivated, deleted, removed from the flow's scope, or loses access below the requirements above, the flow pauses. This also applies to runs that are already waiting for an approval. An administrator can re-enable the flow under a new delegator.

sections.heading: Pre-approving a step
sections.text:
By default, any step that Breeze classifies as sensitive (Tier 3) stops the run and waits in the Approvals inbox. At enable time you can pre-approve certain steps so scheduled and event-driven runs do not wait for a person.

A step can be pre-approved only when it is a **Run script** step and all of these hold:

- The script is chosen directly (not looked up from a variable) and its parameters are fixed values.
- It targets exactly one device.
- The script's approval scope is supervised (not four-eyes).
- The script uses no tenant variables.
- The step is not inside a for-each loop.

The pre-approval is **bound to the script's content**. If the script is edited after you enable the flow, the next run detects the change, the flow pauses with the reason `binding_drift`, and you must review and enable it again.

**Runs started by an AI never use pre-approvals.** When someone starts a flow from Breeze AI with `run_flow`, or a run is started with an API key, every sensitive step waits for a human approval. A manual run started from the web interface honors pre-approvals only when the person starting it could run every step themselves (and, for a partner-wide flow, has access to all of the partner's organizations).

**Who can start a run.** Starting a run uses the flow's delegation, which is organization-wide, so Breeze refuses to start a run for anyone limited to specific sites. This includes a person whose membership is site-limited, a token with a site ceiling, and an API key whose creator is site-limited. The start is rejected with `delegation_scope_restricted`; it does not start without pre-approvals. A run started with an API key is also clamped to the key's scopes: the key must be allowed to do everything the flow's steps do.

Enabling, disabling, starting and cancelling a flow all require a session that has completed multi-factor authentication. Without it the request is refused with `MFA_REQUIRED`.

Event flows react to platform events whatever caused them. An alert resolved by an AI action, for example, can trigger an event flow that has a pre-approved script. The script and its parameters are fixed, so the event can only choose which single device in the organization it runs on. Enable event flows with that in mind.

sections.heading: Approvals
sections.text:
Sensitive steps that are not pre-approved park the run in **awaiting approval** and appear in the Approvals inbox. The card shows the flow name and the step, for example "Flow Disk cleanup" and "Step cleanup: run_script".

- Supervised steps can be approved by an eligible approver, including the flow's delegator.
- Four-eyes steps exclude the delegator and, for manual runs, the person who started the run. If the only eligible approver is one of those people, the run fails with `no_eligible_approvers` instead of approving itself.
- Approvals expire after `FLOW_APPROVAL_TTL_HOURS` (default 24 hours).

sections.heading: Triggers
sections.text:
| Trigger | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Manual | Start from the flow page, or from Breeze AI with `run_flow`. |
| Schedule | Runs at each scheduled time. If runs were missed (for example during an outage), only the latest occurrence runs; there is no backfill. |
| Event | Runs when a matching platform event occurs. |
| Webhook | Runs when an external system sends a signed `POST` to the flow's webhook URL. See [Webhook trigger](#webhook-trigger). |

sections.heading: Event trigger prerequisites
sections.text:
Event flows need durable event delivery. Your deployment must set:

- `EVENT_DISPATCH_MODE=enforce`
- `EVENT_DISPATCH_QUEUE_SUBSCRIBERS` including `flow-event-trigger`

Without both, enabling an event flow is refused, and event flows that are already enabled are paused when the deployment stops delivering events durably. Event delivery is at-least-once after publication, but an event that fails to be queued at the moment it is published is dropped before any flow sees it.

Flows that are triggered by other flows are limited to a chain depth of 3 to prevent loops.

sections.heading: Webhook trigger
sections.text:
A webhook flow starts when an outside system sends an HTTP request to the flow's URL. The URL is shown on the flow's **Webhook** tab:

```
POST /api/v1/webhooks/flows/<flowId>
```

The body must be a JSON object of at most 256 KB (262,144 bytes). The content type must be `application/json`. Other content types get `415`. A larger body gets `413`.

sections.heading: Authentication
sections.text:
You choose one of two modes in the trigger.

| Mode | How the sender proves it knows the secret |
|---|---|
| `hmac` (default) | Sends `X-Breeze-Timestamp` (unix seconds or milliseconds) and `X-Breeze-Signature: sha256=<hex>`. The signature is HMAC-SHA256 over `<timestamp>.<raw body>`. The timestamp must be within 300 seconds of the server's clock. |
| `token` | Sends the secret itself in `X-Breeze-Webhook-Token`. |

`token` mode is weaker than `hmac`. The secret travels with every request, so anyone who sees one request can send more. Without a delivery id there is no replay protection. Use `token` only for senders that cannot compute a signature.

Query-string tokens (`?token=`) are not supported, because query strings end up in logs.

```bash
SECRET="bwh_replace_with_your_secret"
BODY='{"customer":"acme","event":"disk_low"}'
TS=$(date +%s)
SIG=$(printf '%s.%s' "$TS" "$BODY" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$SECRET" | sed 's/^.* //')

curl -X POST "https://api.example.com/api/v1/webhooks/flows/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Breeze-Timestamp: $TS" \
  -H "X-Breeze-Signature: sha256=$SIG" \
  -H "X-Breeze-Delivery-Id: ticket-1042-attempt-1" \
  --data "$BODY"
```

sections.heading: Retries and replays
sections.text:
Send an optional `X-Breeze-Delivery-Id` (letters, digits and `. _ : -`, 1 to 128 characters) so that retries of the same delivery run once.

- In `hmac` mode, a replayed signature runs once. The repeat gets `200` with `{ "status": "duplicate", "runId": "..." }`.
- In `token` mode, only the delivery id dedupes.

sections.heading: The secret
sections.text:
Create or rotate the secret on the flow's **Webhook** tab. This needs `automations.write` and a session with multi-factor authentication. For a partner-wide flow you also need access to all organizations of the partner.

- The secret is shown once. It starts with `bwh_`.
- Rotating cuts the old secret off immediately. There is no grace period.
- A webhook flow cannot be enabled without a secret.
- If you enable a new version whose draft changed since the secret was created, the secret is cleared and the interface tells you so. Create a new secret and give it to the sender.

sections.heading: Partner-wide webhook flows
sections.text:
A partner-wide webhook flow must say which organization each delivery is for. Add an org resolver to the trigger:

```json
{ "orgResolver": { "path": "body.customer", "system": "psa" } }
```

`path` points at a field in the JSON body. With `system`, the value is matched against organization external IDs of that external system. Alternatively use `{ "path": "body.org", "kind": "breeze_org_id" }` for a Breeze organization ID. Only live organizations of the flow's partner can match. If the value matches nothing, Breeze records an `org_unresolved` delivery, starts no run and answers `422`.

sections.heading: Approvals
sections.text: Webhook runs never use pre-approvals. Every step that requires approval waits for a person.

sections.heading: Delivery log
sections.text:
The Webhook tab lists deliveries with one of these statuses: `accepted`, `org_unresolved`, `refused`, `invalid_body`.

Requests that fail authentication are never logged as deliveries. The tab shows the reason for the last refused request instead. Users limited to some sites or devices see deliveries without the delivery id and the resolver value.

Non-accepted deliveries are deleted after `FLOW_WEBHOOK_DELIVERY_RETENTION_DAYS`. The per-flow rate limit is `FLOW_WEBHOOK_RATE_PER_MINUTE`. See [Settings for administrators](#settings-for-administrators).

sections.heading: Built-in steps
sections.text: Besides running a Breeze tool, a step can be one of three built-in kinds.

sections.heading: `http_request`
sections.text:
Calls a URL without credentials. Authenticated calls to a vendor go through Tool Sources (MCP or OpenAPI), not through this step.

- The method and the URL origin (scheme, host and port) must be written out literally. The path, query and body can use templates.
- HTTPS only. Plain `http` is allowed only for private targets, and only on self-hosted deployments with `TOOL_SOURCES_ALLOW_PRIVATE_EGRESS=true`.
- Breeze's own API origin is refused.
- Redirects are never followed. A `3xx` answer is an `http_status` failure.
- Timeout up to 30 seconds. Response up to 1 MB (at most 256 KB is stored). Request body up to 256 KB. Up to 100 calls per run.
- These headers cannot be set: `host`, `content-length`, `transfer-encoding`, `connection`, `upgrade`, `te`, `trailer`, `cookie`, `authorization`, `proxy-*`, `x-forwarded-*`, `forwarded` and `x-breeze-*`.
- Literal headers or query values that look like credentials are refused when you save.
- `GET` and `HEAD` are Tier 2. `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` are Tier 3 and wait for approval on every run.
- Enabling a flow with an `http_request` step needs `external_tools.write`.
- Failures are `egress_blocked` and `http_status`.

sections.heading: `notify`
sections.text:
Sends a message to a notification channel: `{ channelId, title, message, severity? }`.

- Tier 2. Needs `alerts.write`.
- Supported channel types: email, Slack, Teams, SMS and Pushover. Webhook and PagerDuty channels are refused. Use `http_request` for those.
- Up to 20 per run.
- The channel must be visible to the flow's owner. A partner-wide flow can use only partner-wide channels.

sections.heading: `ai`
sections.text:
Asks Breeze AI a question and gets structured data back: `{ prompt, tools?, output, maxTurns?, maxOutputTokens? }`.

- `tools` may list only Tier 1 (read) tools, up to 20.
- `output` is a JSON Schema of at most 16 KB. The answer must match it.
- `maxTurns` is 1 to 8 (default 4). `maxOutputTokens` is 256 to 4096 (default 1024).
- Usage is billed to the run organization's AI budget, and each run has an AI token limit (see [Monthly limits](#monthly-limits)).
- Failures are `ai_budget_exhausted`, `ai_output_invalid` and `ai_token_cap_reached`.
- An organization flow with an `ai` step cannot be enabled when the organization has no AI budget to spend.
- Calls to a partner's own catalog endpoint are recorded in the LLM egress audit.

sections.heading: For-each concurrency
sections.text:
A for-each normally processes items one at a time. Set `forEach.concurrency` above 1 to run items in parallel. This works only for steps of Tier 2 or lower that are not `wait` steps.

- Effective parallelism is the smaller of `concurrency` and `FLOW_FOREACH_MAX_PARALLEL`.
- Outputs stay in item order.
- With `onFailure: stop`, Breeze stops launching new items after a failure.

sections.heading: Run statuses
sections.text:
| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Queued | Waiting for a free slot. |
| Running | Executing steps. |
| Waiting | Parked on a wait step; it resumes by itself. |
| Awaiting approval | Parked on a sensitive step until someone decides. |
| Completed / Failed / Cancelled | Finished. |
| Expired | An approval the run was waiting on expired before anyone decided. |

A step can also end **unknown outcome**: a step that changes things timed out or lost its executor, so Breeze cannot tell whether it took effect. The run fails; check the target before re-running.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.text:
| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Steps per flow | 50 |
| For-each items | 500, one at a time unless the step sets `forEach.concurrency` |
| Active time per run | 1 hour (time spent waiting or awaiting approval does not count) |
| Active runs per owner | 1,000 |
| Running runs per owner | 20 by default (`FLOW_MAX_RUNNING_PER_OWNER`) |
| Running runs per flow per organization | 1 |
| Flow-triggers-flow chain depth | 3 |
| Run detail retention | Inputs, outputs and payloads are cleared after 90 days by default (`FLOW_RUN_RETENTION_DAYS`); the run record and step history remain |

sections.heading: Monthly limits
sections.text:
Each owner, flow and AI step has a cap. Defaults and platform ceilings:

| Limit | Default | Ceiling |
|---|---|---|
| Runs per flow per month | 10,000 | 100,000 |
| Runs per owner per month | 100,000 | 1,000,000 |
| AI tokens per run | 100,000 | 1,000,000 |

The owner is the organization (all its flows) or, for partner-wide flows, the partner. Months are UTC calendar months. A flow's document can set `limits.monthlyRuns` lower still.

Set limits on **Settings > Flow limits** (`/settings/flow-limits`):

- A **partner default** needs `automations.write`, multi-factor authentication and access to all organizations of the partner.
- An **organization override** can only lower the partner value. The server refuses a raise.

When a cap is reached, new runs are refused with `flow_monthly_cap_reached` or `owner_monthly_cap_reached`. Webhook and manual runs get HTTP `429`. Schedule and event triggers drop the refused run and do not retry. The flow is **not** paused. Its page shows a banner and the flow list shows a "Runs refused" badge. One notice per flow, month and reason goes to the person the flow runs for, and to the flow's notice channel if it has one.

The same limits are available over the API:

- `GET /api/v1/flows/limits` (optionally `?orgId=`) returns the effective values.
- `PUT /api/v1/flows/limits` with `{ "orgId"?, "limits": { "monthlyRunsPerOwner"?, "monthlyRunsPerFlow"?, "aiTokensPerRun"? } }` sets them. A `null` value clears a limit so it inherits again.

sections.heading: Using flows from Breeze AI
sections.text:
Four AI tools work with flows:

- `run_flow` starts a flow. It always requires a human approval tap, and it is not available to MCP clients.
- `list_flow_runs` and `get_flow_run` read run history and the step ledger.
- `cancel_flow_run` cancels an active run. People using Breeze AI can call it directly; autonomous AI agents cannot use it.

There is no AI tool for enabling a flow. Enabling is the delegation decision and stays a person's action in the web interface.

sections.heading: Flows as tools
sections.text:
An enabled flow with a manual trigger is also a tool named `flow__<slug>`. It appears in Breeze AI chat, in Breeze's MCP server and to AI agents. Its tier is the flow's live tier: the higher of the recorded tier and the tier recomputed now.

- **Chat:** Tier 1 runs directly, Tier 2 asks for confirmation, Tier 3 goes through approval.
- **MCP:** Tier 3 flows are never listed or callable. Tier 2 flows need an `ai:write` key.
- **Agents:** only flows named in the agent's tool allowlist, only Tier 1 flows, and only in agent runs that are not limited to a device or site.

A session can use at most 20 flow tools. A flow is never a step of another flow. To chain flows, use the `flow.run.completed` event.

sections.heading: Settings for administrators
sections.text:
| Setting | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `FLOWS_ENABLED` | off | Turns the Flows feature on. |
| `FLOW_APPROVAL_TTL_HOURS` | 24 | How long a parked step waits for approval. |
| `FLOW_MAX_RUNNING_PER_OWNER` | 20 | Concurrent running runs per owner. |
| `FLOW_RUN_RETENTION_DAYS` | 90 | Age at which run bodies are cleared. |
| `FLOW_WEBHOOK_RATE_PER_MINUTE` | 120 | Inbound webhook deliveries accepted per flow per minute (1-6000); over it the request gets a 429. |
| `FLOW_WEBHOOK_DELIVERY_RETENTION_DAYS` | 30 | Days a webhook delivery that was not accepted (refused, org unresolved, invalid body) is kept (1-365); accepted deliveries live as long as their run. |
| `FLOW_FOREACH_MAX_PARALLEL` | 5 | Most for-each items one flow step runs at once (1-10); a step's own `forEach.concurrency` is capped by this. |
| `EVENT_DISPATCH_MODE` / `EVENT_DISPATCH_QUEUE_SUBSCRIBERS` | see above | Required for event triggers. |

title: Hardware & RAID Monitoring
description: See controller, array, physical disk and cache-battery health, and attach hardware monitors to configuration policies.

sections.heading: What Breeze monitors
sections.text:
Open a device's **Hardware** tab and find **Storage & RAID**. It shows controller identity, virtual disks and RAID level, physical disk model and serial, slot, size, temperature, error counters and rebuild progress when the source reports them. The **OS-visible disks** group separates operating-system observations; disks backed by a RAID virtual disk are collapsed beneath that note and do not create duplicate alerts.

**Requires agent 0.117.0:**
  Hardware collection ships in Breeze v0.117.0 and needs the matching agent. A device on an older agent shows no hardware data until its agent is updated.

Breeze detects installed tools and reads their output. It never downloads or bundles vendor utilities, changes controller configuration, starts a rebuild or clears a foreign configuration. Collection works on supported Windows and Linux hosts with an agent; it is capability-detected rather than restricted to devices classified as servers. macOS and agentless hypervisors are outside this feature.

The device list has an optional **Hardware** column. Enable it in the column picker for the rollup pill and component-count tooltip. To filter on it, use **Add filter → Hardware Health** in the device filter bar (values `ok`, `warning`, `critical`, `unknown`); the same field works in saved filters and dynamic groups, and group membership re-evaluates when a device's rollup changes. A dash means no rollup has been received; it is distinct from an observed Unknown rollup, and such devices match no Hardware Health value.

sections.heading: Supported tools
sections.text:
| Source | OS | Detection / read commands | Data | Cadence / timeout | Validation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `storcli` | Windows, Linux | `storcli64` or `storcli`; `/call show all J`, `/call/vall show all J`, `/call/eall/sall show all J`, `/call/cv show all J`, `/call/bbu show all J` | Controllers, virtual and physical disks, cache/battery, enclosures, progress | RAID; 30 seconds per command | fixture-only |
| `perccli` | Windows, Linux | `perccli64` or `perccli`; same read syntax as storcli | Same controller family data | RAID; 30 seconds | fixture-only |
| `megacli` | Windows, Linux | `MegaCli64`, `MegaCli` or `megacli`; `-AdpAllInfo -aALL`, `-LDInfo -Lall -aALL`, `-PDList -aALL`, `-AdpBbuCmd -GetBbuStatus -aALL`, `-LDPDInfo -aALL` | Controllers, virtual/physical disks, BBU and membership | RAID; 30 seconds | fixture-only |
| `ssacli` | Windows, Linux | `ssacli`, `hpssacli` or `hpacucli`; `ctrl all show status`, `ctrl all show config detail` | HPE controllers, cache/battery, logical and physical drives | RAID; 60 seconds | fixture-only |
| `arcconf` | Windows, Linux | `GETVERSION`, then `GETCONFIG` with controller number and `AL` | Controllers, logical/physical devices, battery/ZMM | RAID; 30 seconds | fixture-only |
| `omreport` | Windows, Linux | `storage controller -fmt ssv`, `storage vdisk -fmt ssv`, `storage pdisk controller=` with controller ID and `-fmt ssv`, `storage battery -fmt ssv` | Dell controllers, disks, predictive flags and batteries | RAID; 60 seconds | fixture-only |
| `mdadm` | Linux | Arrays listed in `/proc/mdstat`; `mdadm --detail` for each array | Arrays, members, recovery/resync/check progress | RAID; 15 seconds | Live lab: mirror fault, rebuild and recovery |
| `zfs` | Linux | `zpool list` nonempty; `zpool list -H -o name,health,size,alloc,free`, `zpool status -pP`; JSON when supported | Pools, members, scrub/resilver progress and error counters | RAID; 30 seconds | fixture-only |
| `storage_spaces` | Windows | Non-primordial pool; `Get-StoragePool`, `Get-VirtualDisk`, pooled `Get-PhysicalDisk` | Pools, virtual disks and member disks | RAID; 60 seconds | Live lab: mirror fault and recovery (see note) |
| `windows_physical_disk` | Windows | `Get-PhysicalDisk`, `Get-StorageReliabilityCounter` | OS-visible health, temperature, wear and counters | Disk health; 60 seconds | Live lab: disk inventory |
| `smartctl` | Windows, Linux | `--scan-open -j`, then `-a -j` per device with its detected type | SMART overall status, ATA attributes and NVMe log; enriches an unambiguous vendor disk serial | Disk health; 15 seconds per disk, 3 minutes total, at most 64 devices | Live lab: standalone disk inventory (emulated NVMe) |
| `ipmi` | Windows, Linux | `ipmitool lan print 1`; `ipmitool mc info` | In-band management-controller address, MAC, firmware and vendor | RAID tier, at most daily; 20 seconds per command | fixture-only |
| `racadm` | Windows, Linux | `racadm getniccfg`; `racadm getversion` | In-band management-controller address, MAC, firmware and vendor | RAID tier, at most daily; 20 seconds per command | fixture-only |
| `hponcfg` | Windows, Linux | `hponcfg -w` with a temporary output file (RIBCL export) | In-band management-controller address, MAC, firmware and vendor | RAID tier, at most daily; 20 seconds | fixture-only |

  “Live lab” means the source was exercised end to end on a lab machine running a real agent: collection, the Hardware tab and, where stated, fault injection with per-component alerts and recovery. The Storage Spaces and mdadm lab runs used file-backed and loop-backed virtual disks, not physical drives or a hardware controller. On Storage Spaces, a disconnected member used to leave its physical-disk alert open after the member returned; this is fixed in v0.117.0.

  “fixture-only” means parser behavior has been checked against samples, without a verified capture from a live deployment of that vendor source. A supported parser is not a claim of hardware lab validation. These markers change only when a real capture and its validation are recorded.

The Broadcom-family preference is **storcli → perccli → MegaCli**. Dell OMSA storage is used only when none of those is installed. HPE ssacli and Microchip arcconf run independently when present. The footer identifies superseded tools so installed-but-unused does not look like a failure.

Management-controller address/firmware collection is available through installed `ipmitool`, `racadm` or `hponcfg` tools. The Hardware tab’s **Management controller** card shows the in-band address, MAC, vendor and firmware, collected at most daily, and links to the matching discovered asset when there is one. Chassis sensors, SEL ingestion and out-of-band Redfish/SNMP monitoring remain outside this feature.

sections.heading: Install the tools
sections.text:
Use the controller or server vendor's supported package for the machine's model and operating system:

- **Lenovo/Broadcom:** obtain StorCLI from the [Lenovo server guidance](https://datacentersupport.lenovo.com/us/en/products/servers/thinksystem/da240-enclosure/solutions/ht512617-how-to-collect-log-files-for-lenovo-servers-using-storcli) or the controller's [Broadcom support downloads](https://www.broadcom.com/products/storage/raid-controllers/megaraid-9580-8i8e). Use the legacy MegaCli package only for hardware requiring it.
- **Dell:** use [PERCCLI](https://www.dell.com/support/home/en-us/drivers/driversdetails?driverid=1p7r9) matched to your PERC and OS, or install OpenManage Server Administrator for `omreport`. Dell provides [OpenManage Linux installation guidance](https://linux.dell.com/repo/community/openmanage/). Breeze does not install either package.
- **HPE:** install the **SSA CLI** package containing `ssacli`, not only the graphical SSA application. Consult [HPE's SSA CLI guidance](https://www.hpe.com/jp/ja/collaterals/collateral.a50013828jpn.html) and select the appropriate OS package for your server.
- **Adaptec/Microchip:** use the [maxView / ARCCONF installation instructions](https://onlinedocs.microchip.com/oxy/GUID-A735A5E3-4456-4763-9EA6-B7AE0E5FE7E8-en-US-19/GUID-486273E7-5D76-4507-9B57-6E71242D83D8.html) for the controller family.
- **SMART:** install `smartmontools` from the OS package repository or the [upstream releases](https://github.com/smartmontools/smartmontools/releases). The executable Breeze detects is `smartctl`.
- **Linux software RAID:** install the distribution's `mdadm` package for existing md arrays; see the [Linux md documentation](https://kernel.org/doc/html/v6.7/admin-guide/md.html). For ZFS, follow [OpenZFS's distribution-specific setup](https://openzfs.github.io/openzfs-docs/Getting%20Started/index.html). Do not create an array merely to enable monitoring.
- **Windows built-ins:** Storage Spaces and physical disk collection use the existing Windows storage PowerShell cmdlets and require no vendor CLI.

Breeze searches `PATH`, known vendor installation directories and your agent-local additions. Detection is cached for one hour, so an installation may not appear immediately. The source footer links here when a tool is not installed.

sections.heading: Configure collection
sections.text:
The configuration-policy feature **Hardware Monitoring** (`hardware_monitoring`) controls collection independently of alert attachments. It supports partner-wide policies and normal policy inheritance.

1. Open the configuration policy that applies to the device and select **Hardware Monitoring**.
2. Keep collection enabled, or disable it to stop probing the applicable devices.
3. Set the RAID interval: **10 minutes** by default, allowed **5–60 minutes**. Set disk health: **60 minutes** by default, allowed **15–1440 minutes**.
4. Save, then check the device's **Effective Config** and **Hardware** tabs. Without a policy setting, collection uses the enabled defaults. A policy change reaches the agent after the configuration cache and heartbeat refresh, then takes effect at the next collection gate.

A disabled collector preserves its previous evidence; it does not mean the disk recovered. No detected tooling produces an explicit report, normally once daily. Failed tools retain their last observations. After three failed collection cycles a tool backs off for six hours; the footer shows its error and retry time.

sections.heading: Attach the four built-in monitors
sections.text:
These defaults are provisioned but **not attached** to policies. Collection alone does not opt devices into alerts.

| Built-in name / key | Components | Threshold | Consecutive snapshots | Predictive flag | Severity / cooldown |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RAID array degraded or failed (`raid_array_degraded`) | Virtual disk, controller | Critical | 2 | Excluded | Critical / 60 minutes |
| Physical disk failed or predicted to fail (`physical_disk_failed`) | Physical disk | Critical | 2 | Included | High / 60 minutes |
| Controller cache battery problem (`cache_battery_problem`) | Cache battery | Warning | 3 | Excluded | Medium / 240 minutes |
| Hardware monitoring tool failing (`hardware_collector_failing`) | Collector | Warning | 3 | Excluded | Low / 1440 minutes |

1. Open **Alerts → Monitors** and locate the four hardware defaults.
2. Open the configuration policy assigned to the intended devices, select its **Monitors** tab, and attach the desired defaults.
3. Save the policy and confirm its assignment covers the organization, site, group or device you intend.
4. Inspect the device after its next collection. An array failure normally needs two RAID snapshots plus sweep time, approximately 25 minutes at the default interval. A disk-health-only signal follows the longer disk interval.

The editor also offers the `hardware_health` kind for custom monitors. A rebuilding-only notification can use virtual disks with Warning; it is deliberately not a built-in default.

sections.heading: Understand the evidence and alerts
sections.text:
Alerts are **per component**: two failing disk slots produce two alerts and notifications. Recovery resolves each subject independently when auto-resolve is enabled and enough recovery snapshots have arrived. Device automation responses run at most once for the shared monitor/device incident.

A degraded virtual disk is critical; **rebuilding is warning**. A critical array alert may therefore recover after enough rebuilding observations rather than waiting for optimal. Unknown, stale, disabled or unavailable evidence is not recovery: **unknown does not resolve** an existing alert. Brief one-poll failures or recoveries do not satisfy the consecutive-snapshot threshold.

Rows absent from a complete successful source report turn stale. Rows older than three times their source tier's interval also show “not seen since”, even when the source never produced a complete report proving removal. Both are greyed in the Hardware tab. Stale component rows remain for seven days; event history is retained for 180 days, with the latest 50 shown on the tab.

SMART counters are observations, not a prediction model. Alerts use the controller's predictive-failure flag or the drive's own failed self-assessment. Breeze does not calculate “days until failure”.

sections.heading: Agent-local tool directories
sections.text:
For tools unpacked outside standard directories, add directories to the agent configuration file. This setting is local to the agent and has no web policy control:

```yaml
hardware:
  tool_dirs:
    - 'D:\tools'
```

On Linux, a directory such as `/opt/vendor-tools` can be listed instead. Provide directories, not executable command strings. Keep the vendor package maintained using your normal software-management process.

sections.text:

- [Configuration policies](/features/configuration-policies/)
