sections.text:
- [Devices](/features/devices/)
- [Device Groups](/features/device-groups/)

title: Log Shipping
description: Collect structured agent diagnostic logs, ship them in gzip-compressed batches, and query them centrally by level, component, and full text.

sections.text:
Log Shipping collects diagnostic logs from the Breeze agent and stores them centrally for querying, correlation, and troubleshooting. Every agent component -- heartbeat, commands, patching, enrollment, discovery, terminal, and more -- writes structured log entries through Go's `slog` package. The logging subsystem intercepts these entries, buffers them in memory, compresses them with gzip, and ships them to the API in batches every 60 seconds. On the server side, logs are stored in PostgreSQL with indexes on device, timestamp, level, and component, making it fast to search across thousands of devices.

This is distinct from the fleet event log system (which collects Windows Event Log, syslog, and application logs from managed devices). Log Shipping specifically handles the Breeze agent's own diagnostic output -- the internal telemetry that helps you understand what the agent is doing, debug enrollment failures, diagnose command execution issues, and monitor agent health across your fleet.

---

sections.heading: Log Levels
sections.text:
| Level | Description | Numeric Priority |
|---|---|---|
| `debug` | Verbose diagnostic output for development and deep troubleshooting | Lowest |
| `info` | Normal operational messages (startup, enrollment, heartbeat success) | Default |
| `warn` | Non-fatal issues that may indicate a problem (retry, degraded state) | Medium |
| `error` | Failures that require attention (command execution failed, connection lost) | Highest |

sections.heading: Log Entry Fields
sections.text:
| Field | Type | Max Length | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `timestamp` | ISO 8601 datetime | -- | When the log entry was created on the agent |
| `level` | enum | -- | One of: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` |
| `component` | string | 100 chars | Which agent subsystem produced the entry (e.g., `heartbeat`, `commands`, `patching`) |
| `message` | string | 10,000 chars | Human-readable log message |
| `fields` | JSON | 32 KB | Structured key-value data (command IDs, durations, error details, etc.) |
| `agentVersion` | string | 50 chars | Version of the agent that produced the entry |

sections.heading: Common Components
sections.text:
| Component | What It Logs |
|---|---|
| `heartbeat` | Heartbeat send/receive, metric collection, cert renewal |
| `executor` | Script/command execution, timeouts, cancellation, result reporting |
| `patching` | Patch scan, download, install, reboot handling |
| `enroll` | Enrollment attempts, token exchange, config persistence |
| `websocket` | Command channel connect, reconnect, message parsing |
| `terminal` | PTY allocation, resize, data relay |
| `desktop.proxy` | Remote desktop capture proxy lifecycle |
| `updater` | Self-update checks, downloads, binary replacement |
| `mtls` | Certificate loading, renewal, TLS configuration |
| `monitoring` | Monitor config apply, check intervals, auto-restart of watched services |

---

sections.heading: Agent-Side Architecture
sections.text: The agent's logging subsystem has three layers:

sections.heading: 1. Local Logging
sections.text:
The agent writes logs to stdout (or a file via `RotatingWriter`) using Go's `slog` package. The format is configurable as `text` (default) or `json`.

```go
// Create a component logger
logger := logging.L("heartbeat")
logger.Info("heartbeat sent", "statusCode", 200, "durationMs", 45)
```

sections.heading: 2. Log File Rotation
sections.text:
When file logging is enabled, the `RotatingWriter` handles size-based rotation:

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Max file size | 50 MB | Rotates when the log file exceeds this size |
| Max backups | 3 | Keeps up to 3 rotated files (`.1`, `.2`, `.3`) |
| File permissions | `0600` | Owner read/write only |
| Directory permissions | `0700` | Owner read/write/execute only |

Rotation works by shifting existing backups (`.3` is deleted, `.2` becomes `.3`, etc.) and renaming the current file to `.1`.

sections.heading: 3. Remote Shipping
sections.text:
The `Shipper` intercepts all log entries via a custom `slog.Handler` wrapper (`shippingHandler`) and forwards them to the API:

1. **Every slog call** passes through the `shippingHandler`, which writes to the local handler (stdout/file) and also enqueues the entry for remote shipping if it meets the minimum level threshold.

2. **Entries are buffered** in a channel with capacity for 500 entries. If the buffer is full, entries are dropped and a counter is incremented. The dropped count is reported in the next heartbeat.

3. **Every 60 seconds** (or when 500 entries accumulate), the shipper flushes the buffer. Entries are serialized as JSON and gzip-compressed.

4. **The compressed batch is POSTed** to `POST /api/v1/agents/:agentId/logs` with `Content-Encoding: gzip` and `Authorization: Bearer` headers.

5. **On failure**, the shipper retries up to 2 additional times with 1-second backoff plus random jitter. Server errors (5xx) and network errors trigger retries. Client errors (4xx) do not.

6. **On graceful shutdown**, the shipper drains remaining buffered entries and ships them before exiting.

  The minimum shipping level is configurable at runtime via `SetShipperLevel()`. By default, it ships entries at `warn` level and above. You can dynamically lower it to `debug` or `info` for a specific device to capture verbose diagnostics without restarting the agent.

---

sections.heading: API Ingest Endpoint
sections.text:
Agents ship logs to:

```
POST /api/v1/agents/:agentId/logs
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Encoding: gzip
Authorization: Bearer AGENT_TOKEN
```

sections.heading: Request Body
Constraints
sections.text:
| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Max entries per request | 200 |
| Max request body size | 256 KB |
| Max decompressed payload | 10 MB |
| Max message length | 10,000 characters |
| Max component length | 100 characters |
| Max fields JSON size | 32 KB |
| Batch insert size | 100 rows per database insert |

If the API returns `429` (per-agent or per-org rate limit) or `503`, the agent honors the server's `Retry-After` header and waits the requested duration before retrying — capped at 300 seconds so a misconfigured server can't park agents indefinitely. When the header is absent, the agent falls back to its normal exponential backoff schedule.

sections.heading: Response Codes
sections.text:
| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `201` | All logs accepted and stored |
| `200` | Empty batch (0 logs) -- no-op |
| `207` | Partial success -- some logs stored, some failed |
| `400` | Invalid request body, decompression failure, or validation error |
| `404` | Agent/device not found |
| `500` | All logs failed to insert |

---

sections.heading: Querying Diagnostic Logs
sections.text:
Diagnostic logs are queried per-device through the devices API:

```bash
curl "/api/v1/devices/:deviceId/diagnostic-logs?level=warn,error&component=patching&since=2026-02-01T00:00:00Z&search=failed" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

sections.heading: Query Parameters
sections.text:
| Parameter | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `level` | string | Comma-separated levels to include (e.g., `warn,error`) |
| `component` | string | Exact component name to filter by |
| `since` | ISO 8601 datetime | Only logs at or after this time |
| `until` | ISO 8601 datetime | Only logs at or before this time |
| `search` | string | Case-insensitive text search across message and fields |
| `page` | integer | Page number (default 1) |
| `limit` | integer | Results per page (default 1000) |

sections.heading: Response Format
sections.text:
```json
{
  "logs": [
    {
      "id": "uuid",
      "deviceId": "uuid",
      "orgId": "uuid",
      "timestamp": "2026-02-15T14:30:00.000Z",
      "level": "error",
      "component": "patching",
      "message": "patch installation failed",
      "fields": {
        "patchId": "KB5034441",
        "exitCode": 1603,
        "error": "HRESULT 0x80070005: Access denied"
      },
      "agentVersion": "1.2.0",
      "createdAt": "2026-02-15T14:30:05.000Z"
    }
  ],
  "total": 47,
  "limit": 1000,
  "offset": 0
}
```

  The `search` parameter performs a case-insensitive `ILIKE` search across both the `message` field and the `fields` JSON column. This lets you search for specific error codes, command IDs, or any structured data embedded in the log entry.

---

sections.heading: Log-Shipping Health
sections.text:
From v0.123.0 the agent reports in each heartbeat whether its log uploads are working, so a device that has quietly stopped shipping logs is visible without opening its logs. Agents older than v0.123.0 report nothing, and no health line is shown for them.

**Device detail.** The device **Info** tab shows a **Log shipping** line:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Healthy** | The agent is uploading its logs normally. |
| **Quiet** | The agent has no recent upload attempt to report (an attempt's result is reported for 15 minutes). This is not a fault. |
| **Failing** | The last upload failed, logs were dropped since the last good report, or the agent's upload queue is nearly full. The tooltip gives the time it started and the reason, for example *The server returned HTTP 503*, *The request timed out*, *The secure connection failed* or *The server rejected the agent credentials*. |

**After raising the log level.** If you raised a device's log level to `debug` or `info` more than five minutes ago and no logs have arrived since, the Info tab adds *No logs received since the log level was raised (…)*. It is shown only while the device is online and the raised level is still in effect.

**Fleet view.** On the Devices page, the **Log Shipping Failing** quick-filter chip (or the `logShippingFailing` filter field) lists online devices whose uploads have been failing for at least 30 minutes. The same count is returned as `logShippingFailingCount` by `GET /devices/stats`. Because the field comes from the agent's own report, it cannot be used to target scripts, automations, policies or dynamic groups. See [Filters and Search](/reference/filters-and-search/).

---

sections.heading: Dropped Log Monitoring
sections.text:
When the agent's buffer is full (500 entries), new log entries are dropped. The agent tracks dropped entries and reports the count in each heartbeat. After a successful heartbeat, the counter resets to zero.

You can monitor this by checking the heartbeat data for a device. A non-zero dropped log count indicates the agent is producing logs faster than it can ship them. Common causes:

- **Network latency** to the API server is high
- **Debug-level logging** is enabled, producing high volume
- **Agent is under heavy load** (e.g., running many concurrent commands)

To mitigate, increase the shipping level to `warn` or `error`, or investigate the root cause of the high log volume.

---

sections.heading: Agent Ingest
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `/api/v1/agents/:id/logs` | Ship a batch of diagnostic log entries |

sections.heading: Device Diagnostic Logs
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/api/v1/devices/:id/diagnostic-logs` | Query diagnostic logs for a specific device |

  Searching across multiple devices and organizations at once uses a separate fleet-wide search over managed-device **event logs** (Windows Event Log, syslog, application logs), not agent diagnostic logs. See [Fleet-Wide Log Search](/features/event-log-forwarding/#fleet-wide-log-search) in the Event Log Forwarding docs.

---

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**Logs not appearing for a device**
Verify the agent is enrolled and the log shipper is initialized. The shipper starts after enrollment when the agent has a valid server URL, agent ID, and auth token. Check the agent's local stdout for `[log-shipper]` messages indicating shipping errors.

**Only seeing warn-level and above**
The default minimum shipping level is `warn`. To capture `info` or `debug` entries, dynamically adjust the shipping level via the agent's configuration or use `SetShipperLevel("debug")`. Note that debug-level logging significantly increases volume and may cause buffer drops.

**Logs delayed by up to 60 seconds**
This is expected. The shipper flushes every 60 seconds or when the buffer reaches 500 entries, whichever comes first. For time-critical debugging, lower the minimum level to produce more entries and trigger faster flushes.

**"Device not found" when agent ships logs**
The ingest endpoint looks up the device by `agentId` (the `:id` path parameter). If the agent was recently re-enrolled with a new agent ID, the old ID will return 404. Verify the agent's configuration file has the correct agent ID.

**Search returns no results despite logs existing**
The `search` parameter on the diagnostic logs endpoint uses PostgreSQL `ILIKE` against the `message` column and the `fields` JSON cast to text. Ensure your search term does not contain special SQL characters. Also verify the `since`/`until` time range includes the logs you are looking for.

**High dropped log count in heartbeat**
The agent's buffer holds 500 entries. If the shipper cannot deliver batches fast enough (network issues, API downtime), entries are dropped. The dropped count resets after each successful heartbeat. Investigate network connectivity between the agent and API, or raise the minimum shipping level to reduce volume.

title: Maintenance Windows
description: Schedule maintenance windows that suppress alerts, patching, automations, and scripts for targeted devices via policies or standalone windows.
headings: Rebooting Devices with a Pending Reboot
Device shows as not in maintenance despite an active window
Alerts still firing during a maintenance window
Device with a pending reboot isn't rebooting during the window

sections.text:
Maintenance Windows let you define scheduled time periods during which alerts, patching, automations, and script execution are selectively suppressed for targeted devices. This prevents false-positive alerts and unwanted automated actions during planned work such as server reboots, firmware upgrades, or infrastructure migrations.

The system supports two sources for maintenance settings. **Configuration Policies** are the primary mechanism, resolved through the multi-tenant hierarchy (partner, organization, site, device group, device). **Standalone maintenance windows** are the legacy approach that targets devices by explicit ID lists, site IDs, or group IDs. When both exist, configuration policy settings are checked first; standalone windows serve as a backward-compatible fallback.

All maintenance window operations are audit-logged, and every create, update, cancel, and delete action records the actor, resource, and change details.

A standalone maintenance window can also be created **partner-wide** so it applies to devices across every organization the partner manages -- see [Partner-wide Windows](#partner-wide-windows-all-organizations) below.

---

sections.heading: Window Statuses
sections.text:
| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **`scheduled`** | The window is defined but its start time has not yet been reached |
| **`active`** | The window is currently in effect; suppression rules are being enforced |
| **`completed`** | The window's end time has passed and normal operations have resumed |
| **`cancelled`** | The window was manually cancelled before or during execution |

sections.heading: Recurrence Types
sections.text:
| Recurrence | Behavior |
|------------|----------|
| **`once`** | Runs a single time between the specified start and end times |
| **`daily`** | Repeats every N days (default interval: 1) |
| **`weekly`** | Repeats every N weeks, optionally on specific days of the week |
| **`monthly`** | Repeats every N months, optionally pinned to a specific day of the month |
| **`custom`** | Uses a custom interval; defaults to weekly cadence if no specific rule is provided |

sections.heading: Suppression Flags
sections.text:
Each maintenance window controls four independent suppression toggles:

| Flag | Default | Effect |
|------|---------|--------|
| **`suppressAlerts`** | `true` | Skips server-evaluated monitor alerts during an active configuration policy window. See [Alert Suppression Behavior](#alert-suppression-behavior). |
| **`suppressPatching`** | `true` (standalone) / `false` (config policy) | Prevents patch jobs from being created or dispatched to affected devices. |
| **`suppressAutomations`** | `false` | Blocks both scheduled and event-triggered automations from running on affected devices. |
| **`suppressScripts`** | `false` | Prevents ad-hoc script execution on affected devices. |

You can enable alert suppression while leaving patching active, or any other combination. Each flag operates independently, so you can tailor the window to exactly the type of work being performed.

sections.heading: Target Types
sections.text:
Standalone maintenance windows use a `targetType` field to determine which devices are affected:

| Target Type | Scope |
|-------------|-------|
| **`all`** | Every device in the organization |
| **`site`** | Devices belonging to one or more specified sites (via `siteIds`) |
| **`group`** | Devices belonging to one or more specified device groups (via `groupIds`) |
| **`device`** | Specific devices by ID (via `deviceIds`) |

---

sections.heading: Manual Maintenance Mode
sections.text: Distinct from the scheduled windows the rest of this page describes, a technician can put a **single device** into maintenance mode by hand -- from the device page, or several devices at once from the device list. This is a per-device action with its own gate and its own record. It is not a maintenance window, it is not resolved through the configuration policy hierarchy, and it does not appear in `GET /maintenance/active`.

sections.heading: What entering requires
sections.text:
1. **A signed-in technician.** API keys, MCP tools, and other machine principals cannot enter, extend, or exit maintenance mode on a device. The route requires an interactive user session, and that requirement holds whether or not two-factor authentication is enabled for the deployment.

2. **A fresh second factor, on entry *and* on extension.** An assured session is not enough on its own -- the technician re-verifies at the moment of the action. The console verifies with an authenticator app code or a passkey, so a technician whose only second factor is SMS must add an authenticator app or a passkey before they can use maintenance mode. Exiting needs no factor.

3. **A reason and a duration.** Both are required. The reason is 3--500 characters; the duration is a whole number of hours from 1 to 168 (one week). Both are stored on the device record alongside who started the window and when, and both are written to the audit trail.

sections.heading: Extending means "N hours from now"
sections.text:
Submitting maintenance for a device that is already in a manual window **replaces** the window rather than adding to it. Choosing 4 hours always means "until four hours from now," whether the device had three hours left or three minutes. Submitting repeatedly cannot compound a window into a longer one.

The original start time and the technician who started it are preserved across extensions; only the end time and the reason change. An extension is audited as `device.maintenance.extend` rather than `device.maintenance.enable`.

sections.heading: Exiting
sections.text:
Exit is not gated by a second factor. If the device still has a `maintenance` status, exit recomputes it from when its agent was last seen, so a device that dropped off the network returns as `offline`. Other statuses remain unchanged.

Exiting a device that was not in a manual window succeeds, changes nothing, and writes no audit event.

sections.heading: Which devices can enter
sections.text: A device must be `online`, `offline`, or already in `maintenance`. A device that is `quarantined`, `pending`, or `updating` is refused with a `409` (`MAINTENANCE_STATE_CONFLICT`) until it settles, and a `decommissioned` device is refused with a `400`.

sections.heading: Several devices at once
sections.text:
`POST /devices/bulk/maintenance` takes a list of device IDs with one reason and one duration, and costs a **single** second-factor prompt for the whole batch. It covers entry and extension only -- exiting stays per-device. The response reports `succeeded` and `failed` separately, so a call in which every selected device was ineligible still returns `200` with an empty `succeeded` list.

**What manual maintenance mode does not do yet.** Entering manual maintenance mode records and audits a window on the device. It does not by itself change which alerts fire, which patches install, or which automations and scripts run. Suppression is still governed by the configuration policy maintenance feature and by the scheduled windows documented above.

---

sections.heading: Via Configuration Policy (Recommended)
sections.text:
Configuration policies attach maintenance settings through the standard policy hierarchy. A `maintenance` feature link on a configuration policy carries a single settings row that defines the recurrence, duration, timezone, and suppression flags.

The configuration policy approach inherits from the hierarchy resolution system: a maintenance setting assigned at the device level overrides one at the device group level, which overrides site, organization, and partner levels. The closest (most specific) assignment wins.

The `config_policy_maintenance_settings` table stores:

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `recurrence` | `varchar(20)` | One of `once`, `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly` |
| `durationHours` | `integer` | How long the window lasts from its computed start time |
| `timezone` | `varchar(100)` | IANA timezone identifier (e.g., `America/New_York`). Defaults to `UTC`. |
| `windowStart` | `varchar(30)` | For `once` recurrence, the ISO-8601 datetime the window runs at (e.g., `2026-03-15T02:00:00`). For `daily`, `weekly` and `monthly`, its time-of-day sets when each window opens; when empty, the window opens at midnight. |
| `suppressAlerts` | `boolean` | Default: `true` |
| `suppressPatching` | `boolean` | Default: `false` |
| `suppressAutomations` | `boolean` | Default: `false` |
| `suppressScripts` | `boolean` | Default: `false` |
| `rebootIfPending` | `boolean` | Reboot devices that already have a reboot outstanding once the window opens. Default: `false`. See [Rebooting Devices with a Pending Reboot](#rebooting-devices-with-a-pending-reboot) below. |
| `notifyBeforeMinutes` | `integer` | Minutes before the window opens to send a notification. Default: `15`. |
| `notifyOnStart` | `boolean` | Send a notification when the window becomes active. Default: `true`. |
| `notifyOnEnd` | `boolean` | Send a notification when the window closes. Default: `true`. |

sections.heading: Via Standalone API (Legacy)
sections.text:
The standalone maintenance window routes (`POST /maintenance/windows`, `PATCH /maintenance/windows/:id`, etc.) are deprecated. New deployments should use configuration policies. These routes remain available for backward compatibility.

1. **Choose your targets.** Decide whether the window applies to `all` devices, specific `site` IDs, `group` IDs, or individual `device` IDs.

2. **Define the schedule.** Set the `startTime` and `endTime` as ISO-8601 datetimes. The `endTime` must be after `startTime` (enforced by validation). Specify a `timezone` string and a `recurrence` type.

3. **Configure suppression.** Set `suppressAlerts`, `suppressPatches`, and `suppressAutomations` to control which actions are paused.

4. **Submit the request.** POST to `/maintenance/windows`. The system creates the window and auto-generates up to 10 upcoming occurrences based on the recurrence rule.

```bash
POST /maintenance/windows
{
  "orgId": "uuid",
  "name": "Weekend Server Maintenance",
  "description": "Routine weekend patching window",
  "startTime": "2026-03-01T02:00:00Z",
  "endTime": "2026-03-01T06:00:00Z",
  "timezone": "America/Chicago",
  "recurrence": "weekly",
  "recurrenceRule": {
    "interval": 1,
    "daysOfWeek": [0, 6]
  },
  "targetType": "site",
  "siteIds": ["site-uuid-1", "site-uuid-2"],
  "suppressAlerts": true,
  "suppressPatches": true,
  "suppressAutomations": false
}
```

The response returns the created window object with a `201` status code.

The standalone routes previously accepted `notifyBefore`, `notifyOnStart`, and `notifyOnEnd`. Nothing ever consumed them -- no notification was sent -- so they were removed from the request schema. Sending them is harmless (they are ignored), but they no longer appear in the documented surface. End-user notification for maintenance windows is tracked separately.

sections.heading: Partner-wide Windows (All organizations)
sections.text:
A standalone maintenance window is normally owned by a single organization (`orgId`). A partner-scoped user with access to every organization can instead create it as **partner-wide**, so the same window suppresses alerts, patching, automations, and scripts for devices in *every* organization under the partner -- useful for MSP-wide work like a shared patch-management provider outage window.

To create a partner-wide window, submit `"ownerScope": "partner"` instead of `orgId` in the create request. Ownership is set at creation time only -- it cannot be changed on update. Creating, updating, cancelling, or deleting a partner-wide window (and modifying its occurrences) requires partner-wide management access.

Partner-wide windows are also recognized by the primary Configuration Policy path: create the config policy itself as partner-wide and attach a `maintenance` feature link, and the resulting maintenance settings apply hierarchy-wide across every org the partner manages. See [Configuration Policies](/features/configuration-policies/).

---

sections.heading: One-Time Windows
sections.text:
Set `recurrence` to `once`. The window runs exactly once between `startTime` and `endTime`. A single occurrence record is generated.

For configuration policy maintenance settings, set the `windowStart` field to the desired ISO-8601 datetime. The window lasts for `durationHours` from that point.

sections.heading: Recurring Windows
sections.text:
For recurring windows, the system generates occurrence records automatically. Standalone windows pre-generate up to 10 upcoming occurrences at creation time, bounded by the optional `maxOccurrences` and `endDate` fields in the recurrence rule.

**Recurrence rule fields (standalone windows):**

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `interval` | `integer` | Number of periods between occurrences. Default: `1`. |
| `daysOfWeek` | `integer[]` | For `weekly` recurrence: array of day numbers (0=Sunday through 6=Saturday). |
| `dayOfMonth` | `integer` | For `monthly` recurrence: day of the month (1-31). Clamped to the last day if the month is shorter. |
| `endDate` | `ISO-8601 string` | Stop generating occurrences after this date. |
| `maxOccurrences` | `integer` | Maximum number of occurrences to generate. |

**Configuration policy recurrence** works differently. The recurrence type determines when the window starts relative to the current time in the configured timezone:

| Recurrence | Window Start |
|------------|--------------|
| `daily` | The configured start time, in the configured timezone, every day |
| `weekly` | The configured start time on the most recent Sunday in the configured timezone |
| `monthly` | The configured start time on the 1st of the current month in the configured timezone |

Set **Start time** on the policy's Maintenance tab to choose the time of day each window opens, in the selected timezone. A policy that has no start time stored — including every recurring policy saved before this was configurable — falls back to **midnight (00:00)**, which is how those windows have always behaved.

The window remains active for `durationHours` from its computed start time.

---

sections.heading: Timezone Handling
sections.text:
Both standalone windows and configuration policy settings store a `timezone` field as an IANA timezone identifier (e.g., `America/New_York`, `Europe/London`, `Asia/Tokyo`). The default is `UTC`.

For configuration policy maintenance, the system converts the current UTC time to the configured timezone using `Intl.DateTimeFormat` before computing whether the window is active. This means a `daily` window with timezone `America/Chicago`, `durationHours: 4` and no start time set is active from midnight to 04:00 Central time, regardless of the server's timezone. Give it a start time of `02:00` and the same window runs from 02:00 to 06:00 Central instead.

If an invalid timezone string is provided, the system logs a warning and falls back to UTC. This prevents a misconfigured timezone from permanently disabling maintenance windows.

For standalone windows, `startTime` and `endTime` are stored as UTC timestamps. The `timezone` field is stored for display and informational purposes; the actual window boundaries are determined by the UTC timestamps.

---

sections.heading: Alert Suppression Behavior
sections.text:
Server-evaluated monitors check the device's effective **configuration policy maintenance settings** before evaluating conditions. During an active window with `suppressAlerts: true`, new alerts are suppressed for every monitor kind, including network checks and component-level hardware alerts. Ordinary monitor evaluation is skipped; component-level hardware checks continue only to recover already-open alerts. No new monitor alerts or recurrence escalations are created by those checks.

Skipped evaluations are not queued. If the condition persists after the window closes, the next evaluation can create an alert. An active window with `suppressAlerts: false` allows evaluation as usual.

Already-open alerts remain visible, and their normal auto-resolution checks continue during maintenance. Entering a window does not itself resolve or suppress them.

This monitor check uses configuration policy settings; standalone windows and their `allowedAlertSeverities` setting do not override it. Feature-engine alerts, such as patch, compliance, and automation alerts, retain their own handling.

---

sections.heading: Automations
sections.text:
The automation worker checks maintenance status before executing any automation on a device. This check applies to both scheduled (cron-based) and event-triggered automations:

- For **scheduled automations**, the worker resolves maintenance config for each target device. Devices with an active window where `suppressAutomations` is `true` are excluded from the run. If all target devices are in maintenance, the job returns `{ skipped: 'all_devices_in_maintenance' }`.

- For **event-triggered automations**, each device is checked individually before queuing the automation. If the device is in an active maintenance window with automation suppression, the event-triggered automation is silently skipped for that device.

The maintenance check follows a **fail-closed** policy: if the maintenance status lookup fails for a device (e.g., due to a database error), the device is excluded from the automation run rather than risk executing during an unverifiable maintenance window.

sections.heading: Patching
sections.text:
The patch job service checks `checkDeviceMaintenanceWindow()` before creating a patch job for a device. If the device is in an active maintenance window with `suppressPatching: true`, the function returns `null` and no patch job is created.

---

sections.heading: Rebooting Devices with a Pending Reboot
sections.text:
Some changes -- a patch install, an application update, an OS feature update -- leave a device with a reboot outstanding until someone (or something) restarts it. Maintenance windows can close that gap automatically: enable **Reboot if a reboot is pending** on a configuration policy's Maintenance settings (under **Actions During Window**), and Breeze reboots any qualifying device that's sitting with a pending reboot once its window opens.

This is a **configuration policy** feature only -- the underlying `rebootIfPending` setting lives on `config_policy_maintenance_settings`. It has no equivalent on legacy standalone maintenance windows.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
A periodic check runs every 10 minutes, independent of any individual window's start time. On each pass it looks for devices that are:

- Reporting a **pending reboot** -- the device already needs a restart, regardless of what caused it (a patch, an app install, a policy change, etc.), and
- Currently **online**, and
- Inside a maintenance window whose configuration policy has **Reboot if a reboot is pending** enabled

Matching devices are rebooted right away -- Breeze doesn't wait for the window to close first.

sections.heading: Platform behavior
sections.text:
**Windows:**
Breeze issues a scheduled reboot with a grace period pulled from the device's effective patch Configuration Policy — the same [`rebootDelayMinutes`](/features/patch-management/#patch-settings-fields) setting used after a patch job installs updates (default 15 minutes; 15 is also the fallback if the policy can't be resolved). The signed-in user is warned as soon as the reboot is scheduled, with a reminder ladder counting down to the reboot.

**Linux:**
Same as Windows: Breeze schedules the reboot with the effective-policy grace period, and the signed-in user is warned as soon as it's scheduled, with a reminder ladder counting down to the reboot. With [end-user restart prompts](/features/patch-management/#end-user-restart-prompts) enabled, a user at a Linux desktop can postpone it (never past the end of the window), and your custom restart-prompt text is used. A headless box with no graphical session gets the same warnings broadcast with `wall` to logged-in terminal sessions.

**macOS:**
Not supported. Breeze cannot detect a pending-reboot state on macOS, so macOS devices are never rebooted by this feature -- reboot them manually or through a script instead.

sections.heading: Avoiding repeat reboots
sections.text:
Once a reboot has been issued to a device, that device is skipped for **60 minutes**, even if it still shows a pending reboot on a later check. This keeps a single outstanding reboot from being re-triggered several times in a row while the device works through it or while the window remains open.

**Don't confuse this with the `rebootPolicy` patch setting.** [`rebootPolicy`](/features/patch-management/#patch-settings-fields) (under patch management) controls whether a device reboots *immediately after a patch job installs updates* -- `never`, `if_required`, `always`, or `maintenance_window`. **Reboot if a reboot is pending** is a separate, ongoing check that isn't tied to patch jobs at all: it periodically looks for devices that already have a reboot outstanding, from any source, and clears it during the window. The two settings are independent and can be used on their own or together -- for example, set `rebootPolicy: never` so patching never reboots a device on its own, and rely on **Reboot if a reboot is pending** to clear any outstanding reboots the next time a maintenance window opens.

---

sections.heading: Per-Device Status Check
sections.text:
Query the resolved maintenance status for a specific device:

```bash
GET /maintenance/device/:deviceId/status
```

This endpoint resolves maintenance status using the unified `isDeviceInMaintenance` function, which checks in order:

1. **Configuration Policy path**: Resolves the device's maintenance settings through the hierarchy (device > device group > site > organization > partner). If an active configuration policy maintenance window is found, its suppression flags are returned with `source: "config_policy"`.

2. **Standalone window fallback**: Queries the `maintenance_windows` table for any window that is `scheduled` or `active`, whose time range includes the current moment, and whose target (by `targetType`, `deviceIds`, `siteIds`, or `groupIds`) includes the device. This match includes both windows owned by the device's own organization and any partner-wide window owned by that organization's partner. Returns with `source: "standalone"`.

3. **No active window**: Returns `active: false` with `source: "none"` and all suppression flags set to `false`.

Partner-wide standalone windows are matched by checks that consult standalone maintenance status across the partner's organizations. Server-evaluated monitor alerts instead use the device's effective configuration policy maintenance settings, as described in [Alert Suppression Behavior](#alert-suppression-behavior).

**Response:**

```json
{
  "data": {
    "deviceId": "uuid",
    "active": true,
    "source": "config_policy",
    "suppressAlerts": true,
    "suppressPatching": false,
    "suppressAutomations": false,
    "suppressScripts": false
  }
}
```

sections.heading: Active Windows Query
sections.text:
List all currently active maintenance windows for an organization, optionally filtered by a specific device, site, or group:

```bash
GET /maintenance/active?orgId=uuid&deviceId=uuid
```

Query parameters are all optional (except `orgId` for partner/system scope):

| Parameter | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `orgId` | Organization to query (required for partner and system scopes) |
| `deviceId` | Filter to windows affecting this specific device |
| `siteId` | Filter to windows affecting this specific site |
| `groupId` | Filter to windows affecting this specific device group |

The endpoint finds occurrences that are either explicitly `active` or `scheduled` with their time range encompassing the current moment. Results include the parent window's suppression flags.

---

sections.heading: Occurrences
sections.text: Standalone maintenance windows generate **occurrence** records that represent individual instances of the window. Each occurrence tracks its own status, actual start/end times, and optional overrides or notes.

sections.heading: Listing Occurrences
sections.text:
**For a specific window:**

```bash
GET /maintenance/windows/:id/occurrences
```

Returns all occurrences for the window, ordered by start time ascending.

**Across all windows (calendar view):**

```bash
GET /maintenance/occurrences?orgId=uuid&from=2026-03-01T00:00:00Z&to=2026-03-31T23:59:59Z
```

| Parameter | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `orgId` | Organization to query |
| `status` | Filter by occurrence status (`scheduled`, `active`, `completed`, `cancelled`) |
| `from` | Return occurrences starting at or after this time |
| `to` | Return occurrences ending at or before this time |

Each occurrence in the response includes its parent window's `id`, `name`, and `targetType`.

sections.heading: Modifying an Occurrence
sections.text:
Individual occurrences can be adjusted without changing the parent window:

```bash
PATCH /maintenance/occurrences/:id
{
  "startTime": "2026-03-01T03:00:00Z",
  "endTime": "2026-03-01T07:00:00Z",
  "notes": "Delayed by 1 hour due to vendor schedule"
}
```

Time changes are stored as `overrides` on the occurrence record, preserving the original schedule from the parent window.

sections.heading: Manual Start and End
sections.text:
Start an occurrence early or end one before its scheduled time:

```bash
POST /maintenance/occurrences/:id/start
```

Sets the occurrence status to `active` and records the `actualStartTime`. The occurrence must be in `scheduled` status.

```bash
POST /maintenance/occurrences/:id/end
```

Sets the occurrence status to `completed` and records the `actualEndTime`. The occurrence must be in `active` status.

---

sections.heading: API Reference
sections.text: All routes are mounted under `/maintenance` and require authentication. Scope requirements are `organization`, `partner`, or `system`.

sections.heading: Maintenance Windows
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `GET` | `/maintenance/windows` | List windows for an organization. Supports `status` and `targetType` query filters. |
| `POST` | `/maintenance/windows` | Create a new maintenance window with occurrences. Set `ownerScope: "partner"` (instead of `orgId`) for a partner-wide window. *(Deprecated -- use configuration policies.)* |
| `GET` | `/maintenance/windows/:id` | Get window details including the next 10 upcoming occurrences. |
| `PATCH` | `/maintenance/windows/:id` | Update window properties. *(Deprecated.)* |
| `DELETE` | `/maintenance/windows/:id` | Delete a window. Future occurrences are removed; past occurrences are preserved for audit. *(Deprecated.)* |
| `POST` | `/maintenance/windows/:id/cancel` | Cancel a window and all its future occurrences. Already-cancelled windows return a `400` error. *(Deprecated.)* |

sections.heading: Occurrences
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `GET` | `/maintenance/windows/:id/occurrences` | List all occurrences for a specific window. |
| `GET` | `/maintenance/occurrences` | List occurrences across all windows with date range and status filters. |
| `PATCH` | `/maintenance/occurrences/:id` | Update an occurrence's start time, end time, or notes. *(Deprecated.)* |
| `POST` | `/maintenance/occurrences/:id/start` | Manually start a scheduled occurrence early. *(Deprecated.)* |
| `POST` | `/maintenance/occurrences/:id/end` | Manually end an active occurrence early. *(Deprecated.)* |

sections.heading: Device Status
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `GET` | `/maintenance/device/:deviceId/status` | Resolve the current maintenance status for a device (checks config policy first, then standalone windows). |
| `GET` | `/maintenance/active` | List currently active maintenance windows, optionally filtered by device, site, or group. |
| `POST` | `/devices/:id/maintenance` | Enter, extend, or exit [manual maintenance mode](#manual-maintenance-mode) on one device. Entry and extension require an interactive session and a fresh second factor. |
| `POST` | `/devices/bulk/maintenance` | Enter or extend manual maintenance mode on many devices, with one second-factor prompt for the batch. |

---

sections.heading: Device shows as not in maintenance despite an active window
sections.text:
1. **Check the source.** Call `GET /maintenance/device/:deviceId/status` to see which source is being evaluated. If `source` is `"none"`, neither configuration policy nor standalone windows matched.

2. **Verify the target.** For standalone windows, confirm the device's ID is in the window's `deviceIds` array, or its site ID is in `siteIds`, or one of its group memberships is in `groupIds`. Windows with `targetType: "all"` affect every device in the organization.

3. **Check the timezone.** For configuration policy maintenance settings, the active window is computed in the configured timezone. A window set to `America/New_York` with `daily` recurrence and `durationHours: 4` is active from midnight to 04:00 ET, not UTC.

4. **Check hierarchy resolution.** Configuration policy settings follow the standard hierarchy. A device-level assignment overrides site-level settings. Use the device status endpoint to see which policy won.

sections.heading: Alerts still firing during a maintenance window
sections.text:
- Confirm `suppressAlerts` is set to `true` on the maintenance window or configuration policy maintenance settings.
- Server-evaluated monitors use configuration policy maintenance settings. Standalone windows and `allowedAlertSeverities` do not control this check.
- Alert suppression only applies to new alerts evaluated during the window. Alerts that were already open before the window started are not retroactively suppressed or resolved.

sections.heading: Automations running during maintenance
sections.text:
- Verify `suppressAutomations` is `true`. This flag defaults to `false`, so it must be explicitly enabled.
- The automation worker uses a fail-closed policy: if the maintenance check itself fails (database error, etc.), the device is excluded from the run. Check logs for `Maintenance check failed for device` warnings.

sections.heading: Patches deploying during maintenance
sections.text:
- Verify `suppressPatching` is `true` on the effective maintenance settings.
- In configuration policies, `suppressPatching` defaults to `false`. It must be explicitly set.
- In standalone windows, the field is named `suppressPatches` in the API request body and maps to `suppressPatching` in the database.

sections.heading: Invalid timezone fallback
sections.text: If the `timezone` field contains an invalid IANA timezone string, the system logs a warning (`Invalid timezone "...", falling back to UTC`) and evaluates the window in UTC. Correct the timezone in the maintenance settings to restore intended behavior.

sections.heading: Device with a pending reboot isn't rebooting during the window
sections.text:
- Confirm **Reboot if a reboot is pending** is enabled on the configuration policy's Maintenance settings -- it defaults to off.
- This feature only applies to configuration-policy maintenance windows. Legacy standalone maintenance windows don't support it.
- The device must be **online** and reporting a pending reboot at the time of a check. Checks run roughly every 10 minutes, so allow a few minutes after the window opens.
- macOS devices are never rebooted by this feature -- see [Rebooting Devices with a Pending Reboot](#rebooting-devices-with-a-pending-reboot).
- If a reboot was already issued to the device in the last 60 minutes, it's skipped to avoid re-triggering -- check the device's command history for a recent reboot command before assuming the feature isn't working.
- This is unrelated to the patch management `rebootPolicy` setting -- see the callout above for how the two differ.

title: Management Posture Detection
description: Visibility into what tools are actively managing each endpoint — MDM, RMM, endpoint security, backup agents, identity providers, and more.

sections.text:
Management Posture Detection gives visibility into what tools are actively managing an endpoint — MDM, RMM, endpoint security, backup agents, identity providers, and more. The Breeze agent scans each device on a regular schedule and reports back a structured snapshot of every detected management tool along with its operational status.

This feature is useful for auditing management overlap, identifying unmanaged devices, confirming security tooling is active, and conducting onboarding assessments.

---

sections.heading: Tool categories
sections.text:
Breeze detects tools across 11 categories:

| Category | Example tools |
|---|---|
| **MDM** | Microsoft Intune, JAMF Pro, Mosyle, Kandji |
| **RMM** | ConnectWise Automate, NinjaOne, Datto RMM, ScreenConnect, OpenFrame |
| **Endpoint Security** | CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne, Sophos Endpoint, Bitdefender |
| **Remote Access** | TeamViewer, AnyDesk, Splashtop, LogMeIn, SimpleHelp, MeshCentral, TightVNC, RealVNC, UltraVNC |
| **Policy Engine** | SCCM/MECM, Group Policy, Chef, Puppet, Salt |
| **Backup** | Veeam Agent, Acronis Cyber Protect, Datto BCDR |
| **Identity/MFA** | Okta Verify, Duo Desktop, JumpCloud |
| **Zero Trust/VPN** | Zscaler, Cloudflare WARP, Tailscale |
| **SIEM** | Splunk Universal Forwarder, Elastic Agent, Wazuh |
| **DNS Filtering** | Cisco Umbrella, DNSFilter, Netskope |
| **Patch Management** | Automox, Windows Update |

sections.heading: Detection status
sections.text:
Each detected tool is reported with one of three statuses:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `active` | The tool's service or process was found running at scan time |
| `installed` | Supporting files or registry keys are present but the service or process is not currently running |
| `unknown` | The tool was detected but its operational state could not be determined |

  A tool that is neither installed nor running produces no entry — it is simply absent from the results. In practice, only `active` and `installed` are currently emitted by the agent; `unknown` is reserved for future use.

sections.heading: Identity and directory detection
sections.text:
In addition to management tool detection, Breeze reports the device's directory join status. This data is collected in the same scan and displayed alongside tool results.

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| **Join type** | `hybrid_azure_ad`, `azure_ad`, `on_prem_ad`, `workplace`, or `none` |
| **Azure AD joined** | Boolean — whether the device is Azure AD / Entra ID joined |
| **Domain joined** | Boolean — whether the device is joined to an on-premises Active Directory domain |
| **Workplace joined** | Boolean — whether the device has a workplace (BYOD) registration |
| **Domain name** | The Active Directory or Entra ID domain the device is joined to |
| **Azure tenant ID** | The Azure AD / Entra ID tenant identifier (where applicable) |
| **MDM enrollment URL** | The MDM enrollment endpoint reported by the device |
| **Source** | Detection method used (e.g., `dsregcmd`, `dsconfigad`, `unsupported`) |

On Windows, directory join status is gathered using `dsregcmd`. On macOS, it is gathered using `dsconfigad` for Active Directory binding and `profiles status -type enrollment` for MDM enrollment state.

On platforms with no join-detection implementation (Linux and other Unix variants), the agent reports a **Source** of `unsupported`. The identity card then shows **Join Detection Not Supported** and marks the three join flags as *Unknown* — it does **not** report the device as "Not Joined", because no check was performed. A Linux device that is in fact Entra ID or Intune enrolled will show this unknown state until Linux join detection is implemented.

---

sections.heading: Platform support
sections.text:
| Platform | Detection methods |
|---|---|
| **Windows** | Service queries (SCM), registry keys, file existence, `dsregcmd` (Azure AD / Entra ID and on-premises AD join status), GPO enumeration |
| **macOS** | Process checks, launch daemon plist file detection, `profiles status -type enrollment` (MDM enrollment state), `dsconfigad` (Active Directory binding) |
| **Linux** | Process and file existence checks are supported, but no tool signatures currently target Linux. Linux detection coverage is planned for a future release. |

Detection on Windows and macOS is signature-based: the agent evaluates each known tool's service name, process name, installation paths, and registry keys in order.

---

sections.heading: Viewing posture in the UI
sections.text:
1. Navigate to a device's detail page.

2. Click the **Management** tab.

3. Detected tools are grouped by category. Each tool shows its name, optional version, and a status badge (`active` or `installed`).

4. Identity and directory information appears in a separate **Identity & Directory Status** card at the top of the tab.

5. The collection timestamp and scan duration are shown in the footer.

If posture data has not yet been collected for a device, the Management tab displays a placeholder message. Data is collected automatically during the agent's heartbeat cycle — no manual trigger is required.

---

sections.heading: Fleet Posture report
sections.text:
Beyond the per-device tab, the **Fleet Posture** page (sidebar → Reporting → Fleet Posture, or `/devices/posture`) aggregates posture across the whole fleet — the primary surface for RMM migrations and decommissions:

- **Counts by detected product and status** for a chosen category (RMM by default), with the device list behind each count one click away.
- **Coverage denominators next to every count**: total devices, never scanned, stale scans, and scanned-with-nothing-detected. A device that has never reported posture is shown as **unknown** — never as clean. "0 devices still run the old RMM" only means "safe to uninstall" when the scans backing it are fresh.
- **Per-organization migration progress**: enrolled in Breeze, running both agents (the healthy mid-migration state), Breeze-only (verified clean), and unknown.
- **Orphaned remote-access agents flagged as a security finding.** ScreenConnect survives a ConnectWise Automate uninstall; Splashtop survives Atera and Syncro uninstalls. These are called out separately as a standing exposure, not migration housekeeping.
- **CSV export**, so the report can go to the customer as evidence of a completed migration.

The fleet report is served by two aggregate endpoints (see the API reference below) — one request for the whole fleet instead of one call per device.

---

sections.heading: Data freshness
sections.text:
- Posture is collected every **15 minutes** as part of the agent heartbeat cycle.
- The exact collection timestamp and scan duration (in milliseconds) are shown in the UI.
- If a device goes offline, the Management tab continues to show the last known posture. The timestamp makes the age of the data visible.

---

sections.heading: API reference
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/api/v1/devices/:id/management-posture` | Get the management posture snapshot for a device |
| GET | `/api/v1/devices/management-posture/summary` | Fleet-wide counts by product/status plus coverage denominators. Query: `orgId?`, `category?` (default `rmm`), `stalenessDays?` (default 7) |
| GET | `/api/v1/devices/management-posture/devices` | Devices carrying a given product — the drill-down behind a summary count. Query: `product`, `category?`, `status?`, `orgId?`, `page?`, `limit?` |
| PUT | `/api/v1/agents/:id/management/posture` | (Agent only) Submit a posture scan result |

The summary response reports, per organization: `totalDevices`, `neverScanned`, `stale`, `scannedNoneDetected`, `detectedDevices`, `freshDetectedDevices`, and a `products` array of `{ product, status, deviceCount, freshDeviceCount }`. Devices that have never reported posture are counted in `neverScanned` — they are **unknown**, not clean.

sections.heading: Response fields — `GET /api/v1/devices/:id/management-posture`
sections.text:
| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `deviceId` | string | Device UUID |
| `hostname` | string | Device hostname |
| `collected` | boolean | Whether posture data has been collected at least once |
| `posture` | object \| null | Posture snapshot, or `null` if not yet collected |
| `posture.collectedAt` | string (ISO 8601) | Timestamp when the scan ran |
| `posture.scanDurationMs` | number | How long the scan took, in milliseconds |
| `posture.categories` | object | Map of category key to array of detections |
| `posture.identity` | object | Directory and identity join status |
| `posture.errors` | string[] | Any non-fatal errors encountered during the scan |

  The agent-facing `PUT` endpoint requires Bearer token authentication using the device's enrollment token. It is called automatically during each heartbeat cycle and is not intended for direct use.

---

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**Some tools not detected**

Detection is signature-based. A tool may not appear if it was installed in a non-standard location or if its executable or service name differs from the expected value. Verify that the agent version is current, as new tool signatures are added in each release.

**Most or all tools absent from results**

The agent may lack the permissions needed to query services or registry keys. On Windows, the agent service account requires read access to the Service Control Manager (SCM). If the agent is running under a restricted account, elevate its privileges or run it as Local System.

**macOS MDM not detected**

MDM enrollment detection uses `profiles status -type enrollment`. This command may require elevated permissions on some macOS versions. If the Breeze agent is not running with administrator privileges, the enrollment state may not be readable and the MDM category may be absent or incomplete.

**Posture not updating**

Check that the device is online and that the agent service is running. Posture updates every 15 minutes; missed heartbeats delay the update by one cycle. If the device has been offline for an extended period, the Management tab timestamp will reflect the age of the last known state.

**Linux shows no results**

No tool signatures currently target Linux. While the agent supports process and file checks on Linux, no detection signatures have been defined for the platform yet. Linux detection coverage is planned for a future release.

title: MCP Server
description: Connect Claude Desktop, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible AI clients to your Breeze fleet via the Model Context Protocol.
headings: Limit a connection to tool areas
Tools not appearing in Claude Desktop

sections.text:
Breeze exposes a built-in **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** server that lets external AI clients -- Claude Desktop, Cursor, and any other MCP-compatible application -- interact directly with your fleet. Instead of copying data between dashboards and chat windows, you can ask an AI assistant to query devices, triage alerts, run scripts, and manage patches, all within the client you already use.

The MCP server reuses the same tools, guardrails, and audit infrastructure as the built-in Breeze AI assistant, so every operation is scoped to your organization and governed by the same tiered permission model.

---

sections.heading: How MCP works
sections.text:
The [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) is an open standard that defines how AI applications discover and invoke tools and resources hosted by external servers. A single MCP connection gives the AI client a live catalogue of everything it can do inside Breeze -- no custom plugin code required.

Breeze implements the **2024-11-05** protocol version with three capabilities:

| Capability | Description |
|---|---|
| **Tools** | 100+ callable operations across device management, monitoring, alerting, compliance, backups, configuration policies, ticketing, billing, analytics, and more |
| **Resources** | Read-only data endpoints (`breeze://devices`, `breeze://alerts`, etc.) |
| **Prompts** | Five guided MSP workflows the AI client can launch as ready-made starting points (see [Guided prompts](#guided-prompts)) |

On connection the server also returns an **`instructions`** string describing the Partner → Organization → Site → Device Group → Device hierarchy and a read-before-write approach, so the AI client orients itself to your tenant before it acts.

---

sections.heading: Transport
sections.text:
Breeze speaks both remote MCP transports on the **same path**, `/api/v1/mcp/sse`:

| Transport | How | Protocol revisions | Use it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Streamable HTTP** (recommended) | `POST /api/v1/mcp/sse` with a JSON-RPC body; the server answers inline JSON and issues an `Mcp-Session-Id` on `initialize`. Echo it on every later request, together with the negotiated `MCP-Protocol-Version` header. | 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25, and 2024-11-05 (negotiated on `initialize`) | Clients that support Streamable HTTP. |
| HTTP + SSE (legacy) | `GET /api/v1/mcp/sse` opens the event stream; the `endpoint` event names `/api/v1/mcp/message` for `POST`s. | 2024-11-05 | Older clients that only offer an "SSE" transport option. |

`initialize` reports the negotiated `protocolVersion`, `serverInfo.version` (the Breeze API release), and `instructions`. Every tool in `tools/list` carries a `title`, MCP `annotations` (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint`, `openWorldHint`) derived from Breeze's guardrail classifications, and `_meta["app.breeze/domain"]`. Annotations are hints for clients; they do not bypass permissions or approval checks.

Successful object results from `tools/call` include `structuredContent` matching the redacted JSON in the `text` block. Pure error objects, non-object results (arrays, scalars, and plain text), and summarized results omit `structuredContent`. The `_chat.outputCompacted` marker identifies a shortened list; natively shaped results retain `structuredContent`.

sections.heading: Protocol 2026-07-28 (stateless)
sections.text:
When the operator sets `MCP_STATELESS_ENABLED=true` (default off), `POST /api/v1/mcp/sse` also speaks protocol `2026-07-28` statelessly. There is no `initialize` and no session: every request is self-describing. Legacy clients (2024-11-05 through 2025-11-25, via `initialize` and `Mcp-Session-Id`) are unchanged.

A stateless request carries, on every call:

- `params._meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion"] = "2026-07-28"`
- `params._meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities"]`, an object
- Headers `MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28` and `Mcp-Method: <method>`
- For `tools/call`, `prompts/get` and `resources/read`, an `Mcp-Name` header equal to the tool name, prompt name or resource URI. A non-ASCII value may be sent as `=?base64?<b64>?=`.

Headers must agree with the body. An `Mcp-Session-Id` is ignored if sent and never returned.

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "server/discover",
  "params": {
    "_meta": {
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28",
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {}
    }
  }
}
```

`server/discover` (stateless only) replaces `initialize`. It returns `supportedVersions`, capabilities, `instructions` and `serverInfo`.

| Era | Methods |
|---|---|
| Stateless | `server/discover`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`, `resources/list`, `resources/templates/list`, `resources/read`, `prompts/list`, `prompts/get` |
| Legacy only | `initialize`, `notifications/initialized` |

`ping`, `logging/setLevel`, `resources/subscribe` and `subscriptions/listen` are not implemented in either era. In the stateless era they, and the legacy-only methods, return HTTP 404 with JSON-RPC `-32601` (the legacy era answers `-32601` with HTTP 200). `resources/templates/list` exists in both eras and lists `breeze://devices/{id}` when the devices tool area is granted.

Every stateless success result carries `resultType: "complete"` and `_meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo"]`. List, discover and read results also carry cache hints, always with `cacheScope: "private"`:

| Method | `ttlMs` |
|---|---|
| `server/discover`, `prompts/list` | 300000 |
| `tools/list`, `resources/list`, `resources/templates/list` | 60000 |
| `resources/read` | 0 |

The hints are for the client's cache. Breeze keeps no server-side result cache.

| Condition | HTTP | JSON-RPC code |
|---|---|---|
| A routing header is missing or disagrees with the body | 400 | `-32020` |
| Unknown `_meta` protocol version (`data.supported` and `data.requested` are returned) | 400 | `-32022` |
| `clientCapabilities` missing or not an object | 400 | `-32602` |
| Stateless envelope while the flag is off, a legacy version inside a stateless envelope, or `initialize` carrying a stateless `_meta` | 400 | `-32600` |
| Unknown or legacy-only method in the stateless era | 404 | `-32601` |

A client that supports both eras should try a stateless request first and fall back to `initialize` on the `-32600` response.

Authorization is identical to the legacy path: scope tiers, tool areas, approval, MFA, RBAC, rate limits and the IP allowlist all apply, with the same errors.

**Origin.** If a stateless request carries an `Origin` header that the app's CORS policy rejects, the server answers HTTP 403. For legacy-era requests a rejected `Origin` is only logged and counted for now; enforcement is a planned follow-up. CORS allows the request headers `MCP-Protocol-Version`, `Mcp-Session-Id`, `Mcp-Method` and `Mcp-Name`, and exposes `Mcp-Session-Id` and `WWW-Authenticate`.

**HTTP+SSE is deprecated:**
  The legacy HTTP+SSE transport (`GET /api/v1/mcp/sse` stream and `POST /api/v1/mcp/message`) is deprecated. Its responses carry `Deprecation: @1742947200` and `Sunset: Sun, 31 Jan 2027 23:59:59 GMT`. The sunset date is provisional and may move later, never earlier. Each new stream is recorded in the audit log as `mcp.transport.http_sse.open`. Move clients to Streamable HTTP (`POST /sse`), which is not deprecated.

Batch requests are not supported for any negotiated protocol version. Send one JSON-RPC request per POST. `DELETE /api/v1/mcp/sse` currently returns 204 as a no-op; it does not end a session.

`tools/list` returns a single page by default. Pagination is experimental and enabled only when the operator sets `MCP_TOOLS_LIST_PAGE_SIZE` to a positive value. Every connected client must follow `nextCursor` until it is absent. Cursors are offsets, so a catalog change mid-enumeration can skip tools; tenant-tool discovery failures can also change the list between pages.

---

sections.heading: Finding your MCP URL
sections.text:
Your tenant's MCP SSE endpoint is surfaced in two places in the dashboard so you can copy it without having to construct it by hand:

- **Login page** — a compact "Connecting an AI agent?" card sits below the sign-in form, so you can grab the URL before you authenticate.
- **Settings → Connected Apps** — a full card above the apps list with a one-click copy button, ready to paste into Claude.ai, ChatGPT, Cursor, or any other MCP-compatible client.

Both cards resolve the URL from the tenant you're connecting to, so what's shown is what the AI client should use.

**Who can see and disconnect connected apps:**
  Since v0.112.0 the **Settings → Connected Apps** list needs the `connected_apps:read` permission, and disconnecting an app needs `connected_apps:manage` plus a multi-factor step-up. Both are held by Partner Admin and (after the upgrade) the built-in Org Admin only; grant them to any other role that manages OAuth/MCP clients in **Settings → Roles**. Managing connected apps also requires a partner-scope session with access to every organization.

---

sections.heading: Authentication
sections.text: All MCP endpoints require an API key with `ai:*` scopes. Authentication is performed via the `X-API-Key` header.

sections.heading: Creating an API key
sections.text:
1. Navigate to **Settings > API Keys** in the Breeze dashboard.

2. Click **Create API Key**.

3. Enter a descriptive name (e.g., "Claude Desktop MCP").

4. Select the scopes you need (see [Scope-based access control](#scope-based-access-control) below).

5. Copy the generated key (it starts with `brz_`). You will not be able to see it again.

  Store your API key securely. It grants programmatic access to your organization's fleet data and, depending on scopes, the ability to execute commands on devices. Never commit API keys to version control.

sections.heading: Key format
sections.text: API keys follow the format `brz_<random>`. The server stores only a SHA-256 hash of the key; the plaintext is never persisted.

sections.heading: OAuth 2.1
sections.text:
For AI clients that implement OAuth 2.1 with Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) or Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) and PKCE — including **Claude.ai** and **ChatGPT** — Breeze can authorize MCP connections through a real OAuth handshake instead of pasted API keys. The user pastes the tenant's `/mcp/sse` URL into the client, signs in to Breeze, grants the AI client a scoped session, and the assistant receives a refreshable access token bound to that user and organization. No API key is created or copied.

OAuth is enabled with the `MCP_OAUTH_ENABLED=true` server setting. Once enabled, Breeze acts as a standards-compliant authorization server and advertises the following endpoints (all discoverable automatically by the client — there is nothing to configure by hand):

| Endpoint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` | Authorization server metadata (RFC 8414) — issuer, endpoints, supported scopes and grant types |
| `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` | Protected-resource metadata (RFC 9728) — tells the client which authorization server protects the MCP endpoint |
| `/.well-known/jwks.json` | Public signing keys for validating access tokens |
| `/oauth/auth` | Authorization endpoint — user sign-in and consent (PKCE `S256` required) |
| `/oauth/token` | Token endpoint — `authorization_code` and `refresh_token` grants |
| `/oauth/reg` | Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) — clients self-register |
| `/oauth/token/revocation` | Token revocation (RFC 7009) |
| `/oauth/token/introspection` | Token introspection (RFC 7662) |

Registered redirect URIs must be **HTTPS**, with one exception: native/CLI clients that bind a local callback server may register plain-HTTP **loopback** redirect URIs — `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`, `http://[::1]:<port>`, or `http://localhost:<port>` (any port, any path). This is what lets **Claude Code** (the CLI) complete its OAuth handshake; hostname matching is exact, so lookalike hosts such as `localhost.example.com` are still rejected.

OAuth sessions use the `mcp:read`, `mcp:write`, and `mcp:execute` scopes (plus `openid` and `offline_access`), which map to the same Tier 1 / 2 / 3 model as the `ai:*` API-key scopes. Access tokens are short-lived (30 minutes) and signed with EdDSA; refresh tokens last 14 days and **rotate on every use**. Revoking a grant invalidates all of its sibling access and refresh tokens immediately.

When OAuth is enabled, the MCP endpoints accept an `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` header and return a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge pointing OAuth-capable clients at the protected-resource metadata.

  OAuth is opt-in. It is off by default, and the `/oauth/*` and `/.well-known/oauth-*` routes only mount when `MCP_OAUTH_ENABLED=true`. In production, enabling it also requires `OAUTH_JWKS_PRIVATE_JWK` (token-signing key) and `OAUTH_COOKIE_SECRET` (session cookie secret) — the API refuses to boot without them. See [Environment variables](#environment-variables).

API key authentication via the `X-API-Key` header continues to work for every client, and remains the only option for self-hosted MCP clients (Claude Desktop, Cursor) that don't implement OAuth.

sections.heading: Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD)
sections.text:
A client has two ways to identify itself. A client that supports **Client ID Metadata Documents** can use an https URL it hosts as its `client_id`, and Breeze fetches the JSON metadata document from that URL. Clients that do not support CIMD keep using Dynamic Client Registration; `registration_endpoint` is still advertised, so both work side by side. Clients should prefer CIMD when the server advertises `client_id_metadata_document_supported: true`.

CIMD is off by default. Set `OAUTH_CIMD_ENABLED=true` to turn it on, and optionally `OAUTH_CIMD_ALLOWED_HOSTS` to restrict which hosts may publish documents (comma-separated hostnames, or `.suffix` entries meaning any subdomain, such as `client.example.com,.example.org`). With the allowlist unset, any public https host is accepted. See [Environment variables](#environment-variables).

| `client_id` rule | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Scheme | `https` only |
| Host | A hostname, never an IP literal |
| Path | A real path, not `/` |
| Forbidden | Userinfo, query string, fragment, dot segments |

| Document field | Requirement |
|---|---|
| `client_id` | Equal to the URL the document was fetched from |
| `client_name` | Required, 1–128 characters |
| `token_endpoint_auth_method` | Absent or `none` (public clients only) |
| `redirect_uris` | Same policy as DCR: https, or http only for `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]` or `localhost` |
| `grant_types` | Subset of `authorization_code`, `refresh_token` |
| `response_types` | Subset of `code` |
| `scope` | Subset of `openid offline_access mcp:read mcp:write mcp:execute` |
| Rejected fields | `jwks`, `jwks_uri`, `request_uris`, `sector_identifier_uri`, `software_statement`, `software_id` |

Fetching is hardened: requests are DNS-pinned and SSRF-guarded (private, loopback and metadata address ranges are refused), redirects are not followed, the body is capped at 5 KiB, and each fetch has a hard 5 second deadline. Breeze never fetches any other URL a document names.

| Budget | Limit |
|---|---|
| Document fetches per host | 10 per minute |
| Document fetches for client ids Breeze has not admitted yet, all hosts | 120 per minute |
| Refetches for already-admitted clients, all hosts | 1200 per minute (separate, so a flood of new ids cannot starve connected clients) |
| New CIMD clients | 200 per hour |

Fetch budgets are charged only when a document is not in the cache. They fail closed: in production a missing Redis, and anywhere a Redis error, refuses the fetch.

Documents are cached in-process for between 5 minutes and 24 hours. The lifetime comes from `Cache-Control: max-age`, or failing that `Expires`, clamped to that range; shorter values, including `no-store` and `no-cache`, are raised to 5 minutes on purpose to bound fetch traffic. The cache never bypasses policy: every use of a CIMD client, cache hits included, re-checks the flag, the host allowlist, the document and whether the client is disabled. Disabling a client takes effect on its next use; a change to `OAUTH_CIMD_ENABLED` or `OAUTH_CIMD_ALLOWED_HOSTS` takes effect when the API restarts. Access tokens already issued stay valid until they expire (at most 30 minutes) unless the client is disabled, which revokes them.

Each admitted CIMD client gets an `oauth_clients` row whose id is the URL, so grants, tokens, organization blocks and approvals work as they do for DCR clients. Disabling a client (global client-family revocation, which revokes its grants and tokens and sets `disabled_at`) refuses it from then on. Disabled, organization-blocked and approval-referenced clients are never removed by the stale-client cleanup. There is no operator UI for disabling a client yet.

On the consent screen a metadata-document client shows `App details published by <host>` and the callback destination. It is still labelled **Unverified integration**: the host proves who publishes the metadata, not who the app is. If the callback is a loopback address, the screen also warns: "This app will receive access on this computer. Continue only if you started this connection yourself."

sections.heading: Issuer identification (`iss`)
sections.text: Authorization server metadata always includes `authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported: true` (RFC 9207). Every redirect back to the client, success or error, carries an `iss` parameter, and clients should check that it equals the issuer. (An error that cannot be redirected, such as an unregistered `redirect_uri`, is shown by the server instead.) `client_id_metadata_document_supported: true` is included only when `OAUTH_CIMD_ENABLED=true`.

sections.heading: Partner service principal keys (partner-wide automation)
sections.text:
An organization API key reaches one organization, and an OAuth grant is tied to a signed-in user and expires. For an unattended automation that must work across every organization of the partner, use a **partner service principal** (the **Service principals** settings page, `/settings/partner-service-principals`) and send its `brz_sp_…` key in the same `X-API-Key` header.

- The principal must be granted the opt-in MCP scope `ai:read`, plus `ai:write`, `ai:execute` or `ai:execute_admin` as needed (each of those requires `ai:read`; a principal holding one without it is rejected when saved and refused by the MCP endpoint). They are never selected by default, they grant nothing on the Partner API, and a principal without one is refused by the MCP endpoint with 403.
- The key runs at **partner scope**: every organization of the partner, plus partner-wide rows, the same reach a partner admin's own partner-scope OAuth session has.
- Per-tool permission checks use the live partner role of the principal's **owner** (the admin who created it), exactly as they do for an organization service principal key. Only the owner can issue or rotate the principal's keys, re-enable it or widen it (another partner-wide admin can still revoke a key, disable the principal or narrow it), and the MCP endpoint accepts only keys the owner issued. See [Who can manage a partner service principal](/reference/api-keys/#who-can-manage-a-partner-service-principal).
- The key is bound to the owner's sign-in credential, like the owner's own API keys: the owner's password change or reset, an administrator changing the owner's account status, or a change to the owner's MFA factors ends every key issued before it. Signing out does not. Removing the owner from the partner, narrowing them below all-organization access, or reducing their role below the principal's MCP scopes also denies the next request (the reach is never silently narrowed). The key never acts as the owner in the database: it cannot read the owner's own sessions or other user-private rows, and its per-tool rate limits are its own.
- A partner service principal cannot create approval intents or queue cloud-to-cloud restores (those need a re-authorizable principal); such calls are refused.
- Revoking the key, disabling the principal, letting either expire, or a source-CIDR mismatch denies the next request. Nothing is cached.
- Tier 3 stays approval-only unless the operator names the principal in `MCP_UNATTENDED_TIER3_PRINCIPALS` as `partner_sp:<principal id>`. The entry names the principal, not a key, so rotating keys keeps it. It applies in every organization the principal reaches.
- The list of ticket actions the Partner API's `tickets:write` scope withholds (among them moving a ticket between organizations and editing or deleting comments) applies to the Partner API only. Over MCP the same key reaches the `manage_tickets` tool under its owner's live role and the usual tiers: internal notes are Tier 2 (`ai:write`), while a customer-visible reply, resolving a ticket or setting a custom status, changing the requester, editing or deleting a comment, and moving a ticket between organizations are Tier 3 and stay approval-gated unless the principal is listed in `MCP_UNATTENDED_TIER3_PRINCIPALS`.
- Every JSON-RPC request (initialize, tools/list, tools/call and so on) and every tool call is audited with the key id as actor (requests refused at authentication, and the SSE stream open/close transport requests, are not) and `principalType: "partner_service_principal"` plus the principal id in the details.
- It is an API-key-class machine caller everywhere else too: actions that require an interactive user session (for example authoring maintenance links) are refused, and its Tier 3 execution ledger names the principal and opens no user-owned session.

---

sections.heading: Connecting Claude Code
sections.text:
```bash
claude mcp add --transport http breeze-rmm https://your-breeze-instance.example.com/api/v1/mcp/sse \
  --header "X-API-Key: brz_your_api_key_here"
```

This URL is the Streamable HTTP endpoint; the client negotiates the protocol version automatically.
