sections.heading: Connecting Claude Desktop
Connecting Cursor
Available tools
sections.text:
Tools are the primary way AI clients interact with Breeze. Each tool maps to one or more fleet operations and is classified into a tier that determines how it executes. The MCP server filters the tool list based on the scopes attached to your API key -- you only see tools you are authorized to use.

List tools return `hasMore` and `nextCursor` in their result; when `hasMore` is `true`, call the same tool again with `cursor` set to the previous `nextCursor` and the same filters to get the next page. A result whose payload was too large to return in full is stored as an artifact and comes back with an `artifact.handle` instead -- `read_artifact` pages through that stored copy by byte offset. `read_artifact` only reads an artifact captured by your own chat session or agent run, and capture itself only happens on hosted deployments with the AI workspace enabled or, since v0.117.0, on a self-hosted deployment that opts in with `BREEZE_AI_ARTIFACT_CAPTURE_ENABLED` (see [Environment → AI](/deploy/environment/#ai)); otherwise an oversized result is truncated; an MCP `tools/call` has no session to anchor a capture to, so `read_artifact` over MCP usually returns `no_capture_anchor` today. It is listed for forward compatibility while MCP-side capture anchoring is designed.

sections.text:
| Tool | Tier | Description |

| `execute_command` | 3 | Execute system commands (list processes, manage services, file operations, event log queries) on a device. |

Since v0.117.0 an organization-scoped API key can also see and run its partner's **partner-wide** scripts (those created for "All organizations") through `list_scripts`, `get_script_details` and `run_script`. This is read access only; the key gains no new write access, and it never sees another partner's scripts.

To make sure `run_script` executes exactly the content you reviewed, take `contentSha256` from `get_script_details` and pass it to `run_script` as `expectedContentSha256`. If the script was edited in between, `run_script` refuses with `script_content_mismatch` before anything is dispatched. Omit the field to keep the previous behavior.

sections.heading: File and disk tools
sections.text:
| Tool | Tier | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `file_operations` | 2/3 | List directory contents (Tier 2, auto-execute + audit). Read, write, delete, mkdir, rename (Tier 3 — reading file contents requires approval because the agent reads as root/LocalSystem). |
| `analyze_disk_usage` | 1/2 | Filesystem analysis with cleanup candidate detection, for any fixed volume on the device (`path`), from the latest stored scan (Tier 1). `refresh: true` runs a fresh scan on an online device (Tier 2: needs `ai:write` and the `devices:execute` permission). |
| `disk_cleanup` | 1/3 | Preview cleanup candidates for a volume (Tier 1). Execute cleanup by deleting selected paths from a previewed run (Tier 3). |
| `system_cleanup` | 1/2/3 | List the OS-native maintenance cleaners a device offers — Windows Disk Cleanup handlers and DISM component cleanup, macOS local snapshots and Homebrew, Linux package caches and journal — with an "up to" reclaim estimate (Tier 2: `list` asks the device live, so it needs `ai:write` and `devices:execute`). Run the selected actions (Tier 3); `run` returns a `cleanupRunId` immediately and `status` (Tier 1) reads the run's progress and result. |

  **By default, Tier 3 actions cannot be executed over MCP.** (With `MCP_TIER3_INTENTS_ENABLED=true` they are filed for human approval instead; see [Approvals over MCP](#approvals-over-mcp).) This transport has no interactive approval surface, so `tools/call` answers a Tier 3 action with a structured `MCP_APPROVAL_REQUIRED` error *before* it checks scopes, RBAC, rate limits or the production allowlist — holding `ai:execute` does not change the outcome. `disk_cleanup` and `system_cleanup` stay listed because their read-only actions still work; `tools/list` appends a note to each one's description:

  `(Actions "run" require interactive approval and are not available over MCP — use the Breeze web app AI assistant for those.)`

  A tool whose *every* action is Tier 3 is not listed at all, because advertising a tool that can only ever answer with a refusal is worse than omitting it. The practical contract for an MCP client is therefore: `analyze_disk_usage`, `disk_cleanup` preview and `system_cleanup` list/status give you a complete read-only diagnosis, and you hand the destructive step to a technician in the Breeze web app AI assistant, where it goes through the approval workflow. A key with only `ai:read` gets the stored results; a fresh scan (`analyze_disk_usage` with `refresh: true`) and `system_cleanup` list ask the device live and need `ai:write`.

  **One operator-controlled exception:** principals named in `MCP_UNATTENDED_TIER3_PRINCIPALS` (`api_key:<id>`, `oauth_client_user:<client_id>/<user id>` or `partner_sp:<partner service principal id>`) are exempt from this deny for core-registry Tier 3 tools, so the tools are listed and callable for them without the approval step. Everything else still applies to them: `ai:execute`, `ai:execute_admin` in production, the production allowlist, RBAC, rate limits, the Tier 3 execution ledger and the audit log. Tier 4, tenant (BYO MCP) and onboarding bootstrap tools stay approval-only for everyone. Every call that skipped approval this way is marked in its audit row (`approvalBypass: "unattended_principal"` plus the matched `approvalBypassPrincipal`), and the API logs the configured principals at startup. See [Environment variables](/deploy/environment/).

  **Configuration policy changes also need MFA.** Applying or removing a configuration policy assignment, every `manage_configuration_policy` action, and `manage_policy_feature_link` `add`/`update`/`remove` require a signed-in session that has completed multi-factor authentication, matching the web app's step-up. API keys and OAuth MCP connections never carry that claim, so while `ENABLE_2FA` is on (the default) `tools/list` omits the wholly gated tools and notes the gated actions on the rest — `(Actions "add", "update" require a multi-factor-authenticated session and are not available over MCP …)` — and a call to one returns `{"error": "MFA required: …", "code": "MFA_REQUIRED"}` with `isError: true`. `MCP_UNATTENDED_TIER3_PRINCIPALS` does not lift this gate. The read actions (`list_configuration_policies`, `get_configuration_policy`, `manage_policy_feature_link` `list`/`describe`) stay available.

sections.heading: Ticketing tools
sections.text:
| Tool | Tier | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `manage_tickets` | 1/2/3 | Full ticket lifecycle. List/get are Tier 1. Create, internal notes, assign, status changes to a base status other than `resolved`, field updates (subject, description, category, priority, due date, tags, device), link/unlink alerts, create a ticket from an alert, time tracking (log or update a time entry, start/stop timer), and `bulk_update` (assign, a status other than `resolved`, or priority over up to 50 tickets of one organization) are Tier 2. A public comment (`isPublic: true`), resolving a ticket or setting any custom `statusName`, changing the requester (`submittedBy`, `submitterName`, `submitterEmail`), editing or deleting a comment, and moving a ticket to a different organization are Tier 3, so they are not callable over MCP unless the principal is listed in `MCP_UNATTENDED_TIER3_PRINCIPALS`. |
| `manage_ticket_checklist` | 1/2 | Ticket checklist steps and checklist templates. Listing steps and listing or reading templates are Tier 1. Adding, editing (label and detail), deleting and reordering steps, and applying a template, are Tier 2. Requires partner or system scope. Ticking a step done is not available to tools, and a step that is already ticked cannot be edited or deleted through the tool. |
| `manage_ticket_config` | 1/3 | Ticket statuses, priorities, SLA overrides, categories and customer email domains. The four reads (`get_config`, `get_org_settings`, `list_categories`, `list_domains`) are Tier 1; every write is Tier 3 (not callable over MCP unless the principal is listed in `MCP_UNATTENDED_TIER3_PRINCIPALS`), and `delete_domain` is four-eyes. Requires `tickets:read`/`tickets:write` (`organizations:read`/`organizations:write` for `get_org_settings`/`update_org_settings`), full partner access, and an admin role for statuses, priorities and domains. |
| `manage_ticket_checklist_templates` | 1/2/3 | Checklist template and step authoring. `list`/`get` are Tier 1; `create` of an organization template is Tier 2 and of a partner-wide template Tier 3; `update` and the step actions are Tier 3; `delete` is four-eyes. Requires partner or system scope. |
| `manage_ticket_inbox` | 2/3 | The inbound-email review queue. `list` is Tier 2 (sender text is untrusted); `convert` and `dismiss` are Tier 3. Requires partner or system scope and an admin role. |
| `manage_ticket_attachments` | 1/2/3 | `list` is Tier 1; `read_content` (text files only, never binary) and `attach_from_artifact` are Tier 2; `delete` is Tier 3. The attachment is staged until a person posts a comment with it. |
| `manage_ticket_forms` | 1/3 | Customer-visible intake forms. `list`/`available` are Tier 1; `create` and `update` are Tier 3; `delete` is four-eyes. |
| `manage_ticket_response_templates` | 1/3 | Partner-wide canned replies. `list` is Tier 1; `create` and `update` are Tier 3; `delete` is four-eyes. Requires full partner access. |

sections.heading: Billing tools
sections.text:
| Tool | Tier | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `list_invoices` | 2 | List invoices across the organizations you can access, newest first, with optional organization and status filters. |
| `get_invoice` | 2 | Full accounting view of one invoice — header plus all line items. |
| `manage_invoices` | 2/3 | Invoice lifecycle. Draft create/update/delete, line management (manual, catalog, bundle, and contract lines), assembling a draft from an organization's billable period or from a ticket's billable time and parts, and creating a Stripe payment link are Tier 2. Financial finalization — issue, void, record payment, void payment — is Tier 3. |
| `search_catalog` | 2 | Search the partner product catalog (hardware, software, services, bundles) by name or type. Returns `prices` as `{currencyCode, unitPrice}` entries; optional `currencyCode` filters to items with a price in that currency. |
| `get_catalog_item` | 2 | Full detail for one catalog item, including bundle components and `prices` per currency. |
| `lookup_distributor_product` | 2 | Live TD SYNNEX (EC Express) price & availability lookup for a single distributor SKU or manufacturer part number that isn't in your catalog yet — returns reseller cost, MSRP, currency, total stock, and per-warehouse availability. Partner-scoped: organization-scoped callers get availability but reseller cost is redacted, and a caller with no partner in context receives an error with no outbound call made. |
| `manage_billing_catalog` | 2/3 | Billing price book (renamed from `manage_catalog`; the old name is still accepted over MCP for one release, as a deprecated alias that `tools/list` does not advertise). Creating an item is Tier 2. Updating or archiving items, managing bundle components, setting or removing currency-specific organization overrides, and `set_price`/`remove_price` (price-book rows with `catalogId` and `currencyCode`; `set_price` also takes `price: { unitPrice }`) are Tier 3, because contract renewals bill the live catalog price, so they are not callable over MCP unless the principal is listed in `MCP_UNATTENDED_TIER3_PRINCIPALS`. |
| `list_contracts` | 2 | List recurring contracts across accessible organizations, newest first, with optional filters. |
| `get_contract` | 2 | Full contract view — header, lines, and billing-period history. |
| `manage_contracts` | 2/3 | Contract lifecycle. Draft create/update/delete and line management are Tier 2. Lifecycle state changes — activate, pause, resume, cancel — are Tier 3. |
| `manage_quotes` | 2/3 | Quote/proposal lifecycle. Draft, content-block, and line management are Tier 2. Recording a customer's decline, creating a payment link, and sending a quote to the customer are Tier 3, so they are not callable over MCP unless the principal is listed in `MCP_UNATTENDED_TIER3_PRINCIPALS`. |

  The billing read tools (`list_invoices`, `get_invoice`, `search_catalog`, `get_catalog_item`, `list_contracts`, `get_contract`) are deliberately classified Tier 2 even though they are read-only — financial data requires the `ai:write` scope, not just `ai:read`. In earlier releases these six tools appeared in the catalogue but every call failed; they work as of v0.89.0. `lookup_distributor_product` is Tier 2 for a different reason — it is read-only, but each call makes a billed outbound request to the TD SYNNEX distributor API, so it is gated on `ai:write` rather than plain `ai:read`. All ticketing and billing tools additionally require the matching role permission on the API key's creator (for example, issuing an invoice requires the invoices *send* grant, and contract lifecycle changes require the contracts *manage* grant).

  **Why is drafting a quote Tier 2 even for a large deal, while creating an organization is Tier 3?** The tier boundary for money-authoring tools tracks reversibility and external commitment, not the dollar amount involved. `create_draft`, `add_manual_line`, `add_catalog_line`, and other draft/line edits on invoices, contracts, and quotes only mutate an internal, editable record nobody outside Breeze has seen — that's Tier 2 regardless of the draft's total. The step that actually commits externally — issuing or voiding an invoice, recording or voiding a payment, **sending** a quote to the customer, or transitioning a contract's lifecycle (activate/pause/resume/cancel) — is what exposes the change beyond Breeze, so that step is Tier 3 no matter how small the amount. `manage_organizations: create_org` being Tier 3 is unrelated: it's gated on tenant-structure mutation, a separate axis from financial size, not a stricter version of the same rule. This is a deliberate design decision (not an oversight) — a partner-configurable dollar-amount escalation threshold for drafting was proposed and explicitly deferred; see [issue #2551](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/issues/2551) for the analysis and decision record.

  Tier classification is **action-level**, not tool-level. For example, `manage_alerts` is Tier 1 for list/get, but Tier 2 for acknowledge/resolve. The MCP server resolves the effective tier at runtime for each specific action.

sections.heading: Backup and disaster recovery tools
sections.text:
These write tools follow the same per-action tiers as in-product chat. Every Tier 3 action below is refused with `MCP_APPROVAL_REQUIRED` unless `MCP_TIER3_INTENTS_ENABLED=true` (the call is then filed for approval) or the principal is listed in `MCP_UNATTENDED_TIER3_PRINCIPALS`. A tool whose every action is Tier 3 (every row below except `manage_backup_profiles`, `configure_backup_sla` and `manage_dr_plan`) is also left out of `tools/list` unless one of those two paths applies.

| Tool | Tier | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `manage_backup_profiles` | 1/2/3 | List and get are Tier 1, and creating an organization profile is Tier 2. Creating a partner-wide profile (`ownerScope: partner`), updating a profile and deleting a profile are Tier 3: a profile may be partner-wide, and narrowing one stops protecting data in every organization. |
| `configure_backup_sla` | 2 | Create or update a backup SLA. |
| `manage_dr_plan` | 2/3 | Plan and group create/update are Tier 2, and refused while one of the plan's executions is pending or running. Deleting a group is Tier 3. |
| `configure_vault` | 3 | Create or update a device's local vault (path, type, retention); the device is reconfigured. |
| `trigger_vault_sync`, `trigger_c2c_sync`, `verify_mssql_backup` | 3 | Queue a vault sync, start a cloud-to-cloud sync, or verify a SQL Server backup on the device that took it. |
| `trigger_backup`, `trigger_hyperv_backup`, `trigger_mssql_backup` | 3 | On-demand backups. |
| `manage_hyperv_vm`, `manage_hyperv_checkpoints` | 3 | Hyper-V power actions and checkpoints. When filed for approval, deleting or applying a checkpoint needs a second approver. |
| `restore_snapshot`, `restore_as_vm`, `instant_boot_vm`, `restore_hyperv_vm`, `restore_mssql_database`, `restore_c2c_items`, `execute_dr_plan` | 3 | Restores and DR execution. When filed for approval, each needs a second approver. |

  **Changed in this release.** `trigger_vault_sync`, `trigger_c2c_sync` and `verify_mssql_backup` were Tier 2, and `configure_vault`, `manage_hyperv_checkpoints` `create`, and `manage_backup_profiles` `update`/`delete` and partner-wide `create` were Tier 2 actions. They are now Tier 3, so an MCP client that called them directly needs the approval flow above.

---

sections.heading: Available resources
sections.text:
Resources provide read-only access to fleet data via the `resources/read` JSON-RPC method. The AI client can read these to get context before invoking tools.

| URI | Name | Description | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `breeze://devices` | Device Inventory | All managed devices with hostname, status, OS, agent version, and last seen time. | 500 |
| `breeze://alerts` | Active Alerts | Currently active alerts with title, severity, status, and device ID. | 200 |
| `breeze://scripts` | Script Library | Available scripts with name, description, language, and category. | 200 |
| `breeze://automations` | Automation Rules | Configured automation rules with name, description, enabled state, and trigger. | 200 |
| `breeze://devices/{id}` | Device Detail | Full detail for a specific device by UUID. | 1 |

All resource reads are org-scoped -- the API key's organization determines which records are visible.

---

sections.heading: MCP Apps (preview)
sections.text:
Some MCP hosts can render a small interactive view next to a tool result instead of raw JSON. These hosts support the [MCP Apps](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps) extension (`io.modelcontextprotocol/ui`). Breeze ships one such view as a pilot: a **fleet reliability card** for the `get_fleet_health` tool. It is off by default. An operator turns it on with `MCP_APPS_ENABLED=true`.

**What an Apps-capable host sees.** The host declares the extension when it connects:

```json
{ "capabilities": { "extensions": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/ui": { "mimeTypes": ["text/html;profile=mcp-app"] } } } }
```

Legacy clients send this in `initialize`. Clients on protocol `2026-07-28` send it in every request's client capabilities. When the flag is on, the `get_fleet_health` entry in `tools/list` gains `_meta.ui.resourceUri = "ui://breeze/fleet-health/v1"`. The host then fetches that view with `resources/read` and shows the result of each `get_fleet_health` call in it:

- the score bands (critical 0–50, poor 51–70, fair 71–85, good 86–100), the degrading count and the average score, for **all matching devices**;
- a table of **the returned page** (worst first on the first page), with uptime, crash, hang, service-failure and hardware-error counts;
- a "N more — ask for the next page" hint when there are more devices. Paging stays with the assistant; the view has no buttons.

**Every other client gets exactly what it gets today.** The `get_fleet_health` result is the same text and the same `structuredContent` for every client, whether or not it declared the extension and whether or not the flag is on. A client that does not declare the extension sees no `_meta.ui` and cannot read the view. The legacy HTTP+SSE transport (`/api/v1/mcp/message`) never offers it.

**Who can see it.** The view is offered only to a connection that can already list `get_fleet_health`. That means the connection's [tool areas](#limit-a-connection-to-tool-areas) include `devices`, and the key's role holds `devices.read`. Anyone else gets the ordinary "Unknown resource URI" error for the view's address.

**What the view does not do.** The view makes no network requests and loads nothing from any server. It contains no data until the tool runs: it renders only the tool result the host hands it, and shows device names and other values as plain text. If the result is a summary or an error rather than the usual device list, the view shows the tool's text instead.

The view is English only. For the pilot evaluation, the audit log marks requests from Apps-capable clients with `details.uiExtension`. For a protocol `2026-07-28` client, every request is marked. For a legacy client, `initialize`, `tools/list`, `resources/read` and `tools/call` are marked. While the flag is on, each successful view fetch and each `get_fleet_health` call is also marked with `details.mcpApp = "fleet-health/v1"`, whether or not the client declared the extension.

---

sections.heading: Guided prompts
sections.text:
Beyond individual tools, the server advertises five **guided prompts** -- ready-made workflows for the tasks MSPs run most often. An AI client lists them with `prompts/list` and expands one with `prompts/get`; the prompt returns a structured starting message (with any argument you supply filled in) that steers the assistant through the right sequence of tools. They're a fast on-ramp: rather than describing a whole procedure, you pick the workflow and let it drive.

| Prompt | What it does | Arguments |
|---|---|---|
| **`breeze-fleet-triage`** | A read-only health sweep of the fleet -- surfaces what needs attention right now. | `scope` (optional org or site) |
| **`breeze-device-investigate`** | Deep-dives a single device and summarizes the likely root cause (read-only). | `device` (name, hostname, or ID) |
| **`breeze-patch-remediate`** | Safely patches a target -- scan, confirm, then apply. Touches higher-risk execute tools, so it stays approval-gated. | `target` (device, site, or org) |
| **`breeze-incident-kickoff`** | Opens and structures an incident with a timeline, evidence collection, and a report. | `summary` (required), `scope` (optional) |
| **`breeze-turnkey-setup`** | An opinionated baseline-configuration wizard -- partner-wide by default so a policy applies across every organization. | `scope` (optional; defaults to partner-wide) |

Prompts don't bypass permissions or approvals: every tool a prompt drives is still subject to your API key's [scopes](#scope-based-access-control), the [step-up approval](#step-up-approval-out-of-band) flow, and the [production allowlist](#production-allowlist-for-destructive-tools).

---

sections.heading: Approvals over MCP
sections.text: By default a Tier 3 `tools/call` is refused with `MCP_APPROVAL_REQUIRED` (see [Available tools](#available-tools)). Set `MCP_TIER3_INTENTS_ENABLED=true` and the same call instead **files an approval request** for a person to decide in the Breeze mobile or web app. With the flag off (the default), nothing here changes: Tier 3 calls are refused exactly as before.

sections.heading: What a Tier 3 call does
sections.text:
The call returns a normal result (not an error) whose `structuredContent` says the action is waiting:

```json
{
  "status": "pending_approval",
  "actionId": "5b0c1c7e-2f4a-4c1e-9a55-0d3f8e6b7a21",
  "toolName": "manage_services",
  "approvalScope": "four_eyes",
  "expiresAt": "2026-10-23T14:05:00.000Z",
  "approvalUrl": "https://app.example.com/approvals#intent-5b0c1c7e-2f4a-4c1e-9a55-0d3f8e6b7a21",
  "next": "Call get_action_status with this actionId; do not re-issue the call."
}
```

- **Nothing runs until a person approves** in the Breeze mobile or web app. Requests expire after 24 hours.
- **The release runs under the live credential that asked.** If you revoke the API key or OAuth grant, remove `ai:execute` from it, or narrow its tool areas before the approved action is released, the action fails instead of running.
- **Repeating an identical call** while the request is live returns the same `actionId` rather than filing a second request.

sections.heading: Checking and cancelling a request
sections.text:
Two tools are listed for API keys and OAuth grants (not service principals; `cancel_action` also needs `ai:write`). They stay available with the flag off so requests queued earlier can still be read or cancelled.

| Tool | Input | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `get_action_status` | `actionId` | Current status of a request. Poll this instead of re-issuing the original call. |
| `cancel_action` | `actionId` | Cancels a request that is waiting for approval or approved but not yet running. Returns `cancelled`, or `not_cancellable` with the current status. |

`get_action_status` reports one of `pending_approval`, `in_progress` (approved, running or about to run), `completed`, `failed`, `rejected`, `expired` or `cancelled`. Only `completed` means the action happened.

- A `failed` result with `outcomeUncertain: true` means the action may have had effects before it failed; verify the target before retrying.
- A result that carries a secret (for example a temporary password) is not returned over MCP. The status shows `resultWithheld: "secret_bearing"` and the value is revealed only in the Breeze web app.
- Only the credential that filed a request can read or cancel it. Any other key, grant or user gets `not_found`.

sections.heading: What is still refused
sections.text: These stay `MCP_APPROVAL_REQUIRED` even with the flag on: Tier 4 actions, `collect_evidence`, tenant (BYO MCP) tools, onboarding bootstrap tools, actions that need a multi-factor-authenticated session, and calls from service principals. With the flag on, the refusal JSON gains a `reason` field saying why the call could not be filed; with it off the JSON is unchanged. Principals named in `MCP_UNATTENDED_TIER3_PRINCIPALS` still skip approval as described above.

sections.heading: OAuth in production
sections.text: Filing a request needs exactly what a direct Tier 3 call needs: `ai:execute`, plus `ai:execute_admin` when `MCP_REQUIRE_EXECUTE_ADMIN` is on (the production default), plus the tool in `MCP_EXECUTE_TOOL_ALLOWLIST` in production. OAuth clients never receive `ai:execute_admin`, so in production an OAuth client (for example a hosted assistant) cannot file Tier 3 requests. Use an API key.

sections.heading: Reporting a request as suspicious
sections.text: When an approver reports a request that came from MCP as suspicious in the Breeze app, the request is rejected. If the reporter owns the MCP credential that filed it, that API key or OAuth grant is revoked. Otherwise nothing is revoked, and the credential's owner and the request's approvers are notified.

sections.heading: URL elicitation (2026-07-28 clients)
Tasks (2026-07-28 clients)
sections.text:
A client on the stateless `2026-07-28` protocol can declare the MCP Tasks extension on a request: `_meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities"].extensions["io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks"] = {}`. When the server has Tasks on, `server/discover` lists the extension under `capabilities.extensions`, and a Tier 3 call from that request that files (or repeats) a request still waiting or running returns a **task handle** instead of `pending_approval`. The client's host then polls `tasks/get` until the task ends, and can stop it with `tasks/cancel`.

```json
{
  "resultType": "task",
  "taskId": "5b0c1c7e-…",
  "status": "working",
  "statusMessage": "Waiting for approval in the Breeze mobile or web app: https://app.example.com/approvals#intent-5b0c1c7e-…",
  "createdAt": "2026-10-24T10:00:00.000Z",
  "lastUpdatedAt": "2026-10-24T10:00:00.000Z",
  "ttlMs": 90000000,
  "pollIntervalMs": 30000
}
```

Only Tier 3 calls that become approval requests become tasks. Tier 1 and 2 tools stay synchronous; a call refused outright, a repeat of a request that already finished, and principals listed in `MCP_UNATTENDED_TIER3_PRINCIPALS` never get a task. A client that also declares URL elicitation still gets the approval prompt first (above); a task follows when the request is still waiting after that exchange.

The task id **is** the request id, so `get_action_status` and `cancel_action` keep working on it. It is a name, not a capability: every `tasks/*` call needs the same scopes as those tools (`ai:read`; `tasks/cancel` needs `ai:write` or `ai:execute`) and only the credential that filed the request can see it. An unknown id, another credential's id (even your own other API key) and a malformed id all answer `-32602 Task not found`. A `tasks/*` request that does not declare the extension answers `-32021` with `data.requiredCapabilities`. On Streamable HTTP, `Mcp-Name` must equal `params.taskId`.

| Request | Task `status` | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Waiting for approval | `working` | `statusMessage` carries the approval link; polled every 30 s or slower |
| Approved or running | `working` | Polled every 5 s or slower |
| Completed | `completed` | `result` is the tool result. For `execute_dr_plan`, `trigger_backup`, `manage_patches` and a timed-out `run_script`, the work may still be running on the device; `statusMessage` names the tool to check it with |
| Failed, rejected or expired | `completed` | `result` is an error result (`isError: true`) with the status, `errorCode` and `outcomeUncertain` |
| Cancelled | `cancelled` | |

Breeze never reports Tasks `failed` or `input_required`. `tasks/cancel` is cooperative: it acknowledges with `{}`, and a request that is already running finishes and reports its real outcome. `tasks/update` acknowledges with `{}` (no input is ever requested). `lastUpdatedAt` is the time of the request's last status change, whoever made it (including a cancel in the Breeze app). Tasks are polled, never pushed: `pollIntervalMs` grows with the number of live requests on the credential so that polling uses at most half of `MCP_MESSAGE_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE`. `ttlMs` is the approval window plus `MCP_TASK_TTL_GRACE_MS`; `tasks/get` keeps answering after that for as long as the request exists. Earlier protocol versions do not get tasks.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `MCP_TASKS_ENABLED` | `false` | Turns Tasks on. Has effect only with `MCP_STATELESS_ENABLED=true`; creating a task also needs `MCP_TIER3_INTENTS_ENABLED=true` (existing tasks stay readable and cancellable without it). |
| `MCP_TASK_PENDING_POLL_INTERVAL_MS` | `30000` | Base poll interval while waiting for approval (1000–600000). |
| `MCP_TASK_POLL_INTERVAL_MS` | `5000` | Base poll interval while approved or running (1000–60000). |
| `MCP_TASK_TTL_GRACE_MS` | `3600000` | Added to the approval window to form `ttlMs` (60000–86400000). |

sections.heading: Limits and rollout
sections.text:
Three limits apply, set in [Environment variables](#environment-variables): live requests per credential (20), new requests per credential per hour (60), and new requests per requesting user per hour across all their credentials (60).

The flag is off by default in the release that ships it. Enable it per deployment once your approvers use the Breeze mobile or web app.

---

sections.heading: Scope-based access control
sections.text:
The tools visible and callable through MCP are determined by the scopes on your API key. Breeze uses a four-scope model for AI operations:

| Scope | Access level | Tools exposed |
|---|---|---|
| `ai:read` | Read-only fleet data | All Tier 1 tools (query devices, analyze metrics, list alerts, etc.) and all resources. Required for SSE connection. Reads that send a live command to a device (listing its processes, services, scheduled tasks or files, a fresh disk scan) are Tier 2 and need `ai:write`. |
| `ai:write` | Low-risk mutations | All Tier 1 + Tier 2 tools (acknowledge alerts, set device context, apply configuration policies, etc.) |
| `ai:execute` | Destructive operations | All Tier 1 + 2 + 3 tools (execute commands, run scripts, security scans, etc.) |
| `ai:execute_admin` | Production-hardened execute | Same as `ai:execute`, but required when the `MCP_REQUIRE_EXECUTE_ADMIN` flag is enabled in production. |

A wildcard scope (`*`) grants access to all tools.

sections.heading: How scope filtering works
sections.text:
When a client calls `tools/list`, the server filters the full tool catalogue:

1. **Tier 1** tools (read-only) are always included if the key has `ai:read`.
2. **Tier 2** tools are included if the key has `ai:write` (or `ai:execute`, which implies write).
3. **Tier 3+** tools are included only when *some* action of them is below Tier 3 and the key has `ai:execute`; a wholly Tier 3 tool is never listed — except for a principal named in `MCP_UNATTENDED_TIER3_PRINCIPALS` that also passes the `ai:execute` / `ai:execute_admin` / production-allowlist gates for that tool.
4. Unless [`MCP_TIER3_INTENTS_ENABLED`](#approvals-over-mcp) is on, a Tier 3 **action** is refused over MCP regardless of scope — see the caution above — unless the caller is a principal named in `MCP_UNATTENDED_TIER3_PRINCIPALS`. For every other principal, `MCP_REQUIRE_EXECUTE_ADMIN` and `MCP_EXECUTE_TOOL_ALLOWLIST` only affect which *tools* a key may see and reach, never whether a Tier 3 action executes; for a named principal they gate its Tier 3 calls as well.

When a client calls `tools/call`, the server re-checks scopes before execution. Attempting to call a tool your key lacks permission for returns a JSON-RPC error:

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "error": {
    "code": -32603,
    "message": "Tool \"execute_command\" requires ai:execute scope"
  }
}
```

sections.heading: RBAC permission checks
sections.text:
In addition to API key scopes, every tool call passes through the Breeze RBAC system. The user who created the API key must have the appropriate role-based permissions for the resource and action. For example, calling `run_script` requires the `scripts.execute` permission on the creator's role.

---

sections.heading: Limit a connection to tool areas
sections.text:
By default a connection can use every tool its scopes allow. You can instead limit an API key or an OAuth connection to specific **tool areas** (domains). This narrows what the connection can see and call over MCP, which is useful when you want an assistant to work with tickets and nothing else.

The default is **All tools (including areas added later)**. A connection set to all tools also gets any area Breeze adds in a future release. **Core** tools are always included and cannot be turned off. A restricted connection must name at least one area. The setting is stored as `mcpDomains`; `null` means all tools.

| Area (as shown in the UI) | `mcpDomains` value |
|---|---|
| Devices | `devices` |
| Scripts & automation | `scripts` |
| Patching & software | `patching` |
| Monitoring & alerts | `monitoring` |
| Network | `network` |
| Security & compliance | `security` |
| Backup & recovery | `backup` |
| Tickets & time | `tickets` |
| Billing | `billing` |
| Accounts | `accounts` |
| Integrations | `integrations` |
| Administration | `admin` |
| AI agents | `ai` |

sections.heading: What the limit covers
sections.text:
- It applies only to the MCP server (`/api/v1/mcp`): `tools/list`, `tools/call`, `resources/list` and `resources/read`. A tool outside the granted areas is not listed and cannot be called.
- REST API behavior of an API key is unchanged. The in-app AI assistant is not affected.
- It only narrows access. Scopes, roles (RBAC), approvals and MFA requirements still apply to every call in a granted area.
- Tenant (bring-your-own MCP) tools count as **Integrations**. Extension tools are available only to connections set to all tools.
- Resources map to areas as follows: the device list is core, device detail is Devices, alerts are Monitoring & alerts, and scripts and automations are Scripts & automation.
- Partner service principal (`brz_sp_`) keys are always unrestricted in this release.

sections.heading: When a call is refused
OAuth connections
sections.text: The areas are chosen on the consent screen, under **Tool access**, for each connection. Pick **All tools (including areas added later)** or **Only these areas**; **Core (always included)** is shown for reference. You cannot change the areas of an existing connection. To narrow one, revoke it under **Connected apps**, then reconnect.

sections.heading: API keys
sections.text:
When you check an `ai:*` scope in **Settings > API Keys > Create API Key**, a **Tool access** picker appears with the same choices. The picker is hidden when no `ai:*` scope is selected, and the key is stored with `mcpDomains: null`.

To change the areas later, call `PATCH /api/v1/api-keys/:id` with `{ "mcpDomains": ["tickets", "devices"] }`, or `{ "mcpDomains": null }` for all tools. Widening a key needs the same delegation rights as granting the key's scopes. Rotating a key keeps its setting. See [API keys](/reference/api-keys/#mcp-tool-areas-mcpdomains).

sections.heading: The `whoami` tool
sections.text:
`whoami` is always listed, even for a connection limited to core tools. It takes no arguments and returns:

- who the connection acts as (API key, OAuth connection or partner service principal), with its id and name
- the tenant scope (organization or partner)
- the effective `ai:*` scopes and the resulting capability (`read`, `write` or `execute`)
- `domains.granted`, the areas the connection can use, and `domains.available`, the areas you can ask for
- `notes`, short plain-language hints, such as which actions need the Breeze web app

`domains.available` lists areas that exist, not permissions you hold. `whoami` never returns secrets: no key, token or hash.

sections.heading: Authentication challenges
sections.text:
Every 401 from the MCP endpoint carries a `WWW-Authenticate` header:

```
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="breeze", resource_metadata="<issuer>/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource", scope="mcp:read mcp:write mcp:execute"
```

A 401 on the bearer-token path also includes `error="invalid_token"`. A bearer token without `mcp:read` gets a 403 with `error="insufficient_scope", scope="mcp:read"`.

By default a `tools/call` that is refused for a missing `ai:write` or `ai:execute` scope returns HTTP 200 with the JSON-RPC error in the body. If you set `MCP_INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE_HTTP_403=true` (default `false`), an OAuth bearer's `tools/call` refused **only** for a missing tier scope returns HTTP 403 with an `insufficient_scope` challenge that names the connection's current MCP scopes plus the required one, so the client can ask the user to re-authorize. The JSON-RPC error stays in the body. The 403 is never used for `X-API-Key` callers, domain denials, approval, MFA or RBAC denials, or the legacy HTTP+SSE transport, because re-authorizing cannot fix those.

---

sections.heading: Rate limiting
sections.text: Rate limiting is enforced at multiple levels to protect your fleet and the Breeze API.

sections.heading: Transport-level limits
sections.text:
These apply in production (`NODE_ENV=production`) and are backed by Redis sliding-window counters:

| Endpoint | Default limit | Window | Env override |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GET /api/v1/mcp/sse` | 30 connections | 60 seconds | `MCP_SSE_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE` |
| `POST /api/v1/mcp/message` | 120 requests | 60 seconds | `MCP_MESSAGE_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE` |

When a rate limit is exceeded, the server returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header.

sections.heading: Per-tool rate limits
sections.text:
Each tool has its own sliding-window rate limit, enforced per user:

| Tool | Limit | Window |
|---|---|---|
| `execute_command` | 10 | 5 min |
| `run_script` | 5 | 5 min |
| `security_scan` | 3 | 10 min |
| `ioc_hunt` | 30 | 10 min |
| `network_discovery` | 2 | 10 min |
| `file_operations` | 20 | 5 min |
| `manage_services` | 10 | 5 min |
| `analyze_disk_usage` | 10 | 5 min |
| `disk_cleanup` | 3 | 10 min |
| `system_cleanup` | 30 | 60 min |
| `manage_configuration_policy` | 20 | 5 min |
| `configuration_policy_compliance` | 30 | 5 min |
| `manage_deployments` | 10 | 10 min |
| `manage_patches` | 15 | 5 min |
| `manage_groups` | 20 | 5 min |
| `manage_maintenance_windows` | 15 | 5 min |
| `manage_automations` | 10 | 10 min |
| `manage_alert_rules` | 15 | 5 min |
| `generate_report` | 10 | 5 min |
| `set_device_context` | 20 | 5 min |
| `resolve_device_context` | 20 | 5 min |

Tools without an entry in this table (e.g., `query_devices`, `get_device_details`) have no per-tool rate limit.

These are the defaults. An organisation can raise all of them together with the **Per-tool rate limit multiplier** AI budget setting (a whole number from 1 to 10). Each limit becomes `ceil(limit × multiplier)`, and the multiplier can never lower or remove a limit. Over MCP, the API key's organisation selects the multiplier. A partner-scoped caller with no organisation uses the partner's value. The counter stays per user and per tool. See [AI → Raising the per-tool limits](/features/ai/#raising-the-per-tool-limits).

---

sections.heading: Session management
sections.text:
The MCP server supports concurrent SSE sessions with the following constraints:

| Parameter | Default | Env override |
|---|---|---|
| Max total SSE sessions (server-wide) | 100 | -- |
| Max SSE sessions per API key | 5 | `MCP_MAX_SSE_SESSIONS_PER_KEY` |
| Session TTL | 30 minutes | -- |

Stale sessions are cleaned up automatically when they exceed the 30-minute TTL. Each SSE session is owned by the API key that created it; the server verifies ownership before delivering responses to prevent cross-key session hijacking.

When the session limit is reached, the server returns HTTP 503 ("Too many active MCP sessions") for server-wide limits, or HTTP 429 ("Too many active MCP sessions for this API key") for per-key limits.

---

sections.heading: Organization isolation
sections.text: API keys are always scoped to a single organization. The MCP server constructs an `AuthContext` from the API key that enforces org-level data isolation on every query and mutation. There is no way to access data from another organization through MCP, even with a wildcard scope.

sections.heading: Guardrails
sections.text:
Every `tools/call` request passes through the guardrail system before execution:

1. **Scope check** -- verifies the API key has the required scope for the tool's effective tier.
2. **Guardrail check** -- evaluates action-level tier escalation (e.g., `file_operations` with `action: "delete"` escalates from Tier 1 to Tier 3).
3. **RBAC permission check** -- verifies the API key creator has the required role-based permission.
4. **Per-tool rate limit** -- enforces the sliding-window rate limit for the specific tool.
5. **Production allowlist** -- for Tier 3+ tools in production, the tool must appear in the `MCP_EXECUTE_TOOL_ALLOWLIST` environment variable.

If any check fails, the request is rejected with an appropriate error before the tool handler executes.

sections.heading: Step-up approval (out-of-band)
sections.text:
Beyond scope and RBAC checks, a sensitive tool call can require an explicit **out-of-band approval** before it executes. When step-up is required, Breeze creates an approval request, pushes it to the user's trusted mobile device, and blocks the action until the user decides on their phone:

- **Approved** — the tool call proceeds.
- **Denied** or **expired** — the tool call fails with the recorded reason.
- **Reported** — the user flagged the request as unrecognised; the requesting OAuth client's access is revoked immediately.

This makes the mobile app a second factor for high-risk automation: even a valid API key cannot complete a step-up-gated action without a live approval from a trusted device. See [Approval Mode](/features/mobile/#approval-mode) for the full request lifecycle, risk tiers, and trusted-device management.

sections.heading: Production allowlist for destructive tools
sections.text:
In production, Tier 3+ (destructive) tools are blocked by default unless explicitly listed in the `MCP_EXECUTE_TOOL_ALLOWLIST` environment variable. This is a comma-separated list of tool names:

```bash
# Allow specific tools
MCP_EXECUTE_TOOL_ALLOWLIST=execute_command,run_script,manage_services

# Allow all (not recommended)
MCP_EXECUTE_TOOL_ALLOWLIST=*
```

If the environment variable is unset or empty, all Tier 3+ tools are blocked in production.

sections.heading: Audit logging
sections.text:
Every JSON-RPC request is recorded in the Breeze audit log with:

- The API key ID as the actor
- The JSON-RPC method (e.g., `mcp.tools.call`)
- Whether a verified legacy session was active (`details.hasSession`; always `false` for stateless requests)
- Success or failure result
- Error message (if any)
- A server-minted per-request UUID as the resource id. Request and tool-call audit rows use it; the client never supplies it.
- `details.correlation`: the era (legacy or stateless), protocol version, transport, principal, OAuth token `jti`, the verified legacy session id (if any), and the client's `clientInfo`. `clientInfo` is self-reported and flagged `clientInfoTrust: "self_reported"`, so do not treat it as an identity.

Each new legacy HTTP+SSE stream is also recorded as the audit event `mcp.transport.http_sse.open`.

You can query MCP audit events using the `query_audit_log` tool or the Audit Log page in the dashboard.

sections.heading: Input validation
sections.text:
All tool inputs are validated against Zod schemas before execution. Invalid inputs are rejected with a descriptive error before reaching the tool handler.

---

sections.heading: MCP server
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `MCP_EXECUTE_TOOL_ALLOWLIST` | (empty) | Comma-separated list of Tier 3+ tool names allowed in production. Set to `*` to allow all. |
| `MCP_REQUIRE_EXECUTE_ADMIN` | `true` | In production, Tier 3+ tools require the `ai:execute_admin` scope. Set to `false` to fall back to `ai:execute`. (No effect outside production.) |
| `MCP_TIER3_INTENTS_ENABLED` | `false` | When `true`, a Tier 3 `tools/call` files an approval request (`pending_approval`) instead of being refused with `MCP_APPROVAL_REQUIRED`. See [Approvals over MCP](#approvals-over-mcp). |
| `MCP_INTENT_MAX_LIVE_PER_PRINCIPAL` | `20` | Maximum live (not yet finished) approval requests per MCP credential. |
| `MCP_INTENT_CREATES_PER_HOUR` | `60` | Maximum new approval requests per MCP credential per hour. |
| `MCP_INTENT_CREATES_PER_USER_PER_HOUR` | `60` | Maximum new approval requests per requesting user per hour, across all their credentials. |
| `MCP_APPROVAL_WAIT_MS` | `20000` | How long an `accept` retry of a URL-elicitation approval waits for the decision before returning `pending_approval`. |
| `MCP_APPROVAL_WAITS_PER_PRINCIPAL` | `2` | Concurrent `accept` waits per MCP credential; further ones return the current status without waiting. |
| `MCP_APPS_ENABLED` | `false` | When `true`, MCP hosts that declare the MCP Apps extension get the `get_fleet_health` fleet reliability view (`ui://breeze/fleet-health/v1`). Every other client's responses are unchanged. The API refuses to boot on a non-boolean value. See [MCP Apps (preview)](#mcp-apps-preview). |
| `MCP_MAX_SSE_SESSIONS_PER_KEY` | `5` | Maximum concurrent SSE sessions per API key. |
| `MCP_SSE_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE` | `30` | Maximum SSE connections per API key per minute. |
| `MCP_MESSAGE_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE` | `120` | Maximum JSON-RPC messages per API key per minute. |
| `MCP_MESSAGE_MAX_BODY_BYTES` | `65536` | Maximum accepted JSON-RPC request body size, in bytes (64 KB). Larger requests are rejected. |
| `MCP_TOOLS_LIST_PAGE_SIZE` | `0` (unset) | Experimental pagination: 0/unset returns a single page. Set to e.g. `50` only when every connected client follows `nextCursor`. Cursors are offsets; a catalog change mid-enumeration can skip tools. |
| `MCP_SESSION_TTL_SECONDS` | `660` | Idle lifetime, in seconds, of a minted streamable-HTTP session principal in Redis (11 minutes). |
| `MCP_INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE_HTTP_403` | `false` | When `true`, an OAuth bearer's `tools/call` refused only for a missing tier scope (`ai:write` or `ai:execute`) returns HTTP 403 with an `insufficient_scope` `WWW-Authenticate` challenge instead of HTTP 200. Never applies to API-key callers, domain, approval, MFA or RBAC denials, or the legacy HTTP+SSE transport. See [Authentication challenges](#authentication-challenges). |
| `MCP_STATELESS_ENABLED` | `false` | When `true`, `POST /api/v1/mcp/sse` also speaks the stateless `2026-07-28` protocol alongside the legacy `initialize` + `Mcp-Session-Id` era. Off by default; a stateless request is then refused with HTTP 400 (`-32600`) and dual-era clients fall back to `initialize`. The API refuses to boot on a non-boolean value. See [Protocol 2026-07-28 (stateless)](#protocol-2026-07-28-stateless). |
| `MCP_HEADER_MISMATCH_ALERT_THRESHOLD` | `50` | Stateless requests whose `MCP-Protocol-Version`, `Mcp-Method` or `Mcp-Name` header is missing or disagrees with the request body are refused with `-32020`. Per API process and per 60-second window: when this many true header/body mismatches occur within one window, one Sentry warning is raised for that window. Read at startup. |

sections.heading: OAuth 2.1
sections.text:
These apply only when OAuth is enabled. When `MCP_OAUTH_ENABLED=true` in production, `OAUTH_JWKS_PRIVATE_JWK` and `OAUTH_COOKIE_SECRET` are required — the API refuses to boot without them.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `MCP_OAUTH_ENABLED` | `false` | Master switch for OAuth 2.1. When `true`, the `/oauth/*` and `/.well-known/oauth-*` routes mount and MCP endpoints accept `Authorization: Bearer` tokens. |
| `OAUTH_ISSUER` | (empty) | Public issuer base URL (e.g. `https://api.example.com`). Used to build every advertised OAuth endpoint URL. |
| `OAUTH_RESOURCE_URL` | (empty) | Protected-resource identifier advertised in `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` (RFC 9728). |
| `OAUTH_JWKS_PRIVATE_JWK` | (empty) | EdDSA private signing key (JWK JSON) for access tokens. Required in production when OAuth is enabled. |
| `OAUTH_JWKS_PUBLIC_JWK` | (empty) | Matching public key, advertised at `/.well-known/jwks.json`. Derived from the private key if unset. |
| `OAUTH_COOKIE_SECRET` | (empty) | Secret used to sign sign-in / consent session cookies. Required in production when OAuth is enabled. |
| `OAUTH_DCR_ENABLED` | `false` | Allow Dynamic Client Registration at `POST /oauth/reg`. Off by default. When `true` in production you must also set **one** of the two posture flags below, or the API refuses to boot. |
| `OAUTH_DCR_REQUIRE_IAT` | `false` | Gate DCR behind an initial access token issued out-of-band. Closes the public-spam vector, but is **incompatible with public MCP clients** (Claude.ai / ChatGPT) — they register anonymously and cannot supply an IAT. Use `OAUTH_DCR_ALLOW_ANONYMOUS` instead for a public server. |
| `OAUTH_DCR_ALLOW_ANONYMOUS` | `false` | Deliberately permit anonymous DCR. **This is the required posture for connecting Claude.ai / ChatGPT** (see above). Spam risk is bounded by the controls on `/oauth/reg`: per-IP rate limit, forced public clients, mandatory PKCE S256, `software_id` rejection, and a daily stale-client GC. |
| `OAUTH_CIMD_ENABLED` | `false` | Accept Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD): a client may use an https URL as its `client_id`. Off by default. The API refuses to boot on a non-boolean value. See [Client ID Metadata Documents](#client-id-metadata-documents-cimd). |
| `OAUTH_CIMD_ALLOWED_HOSTS` | (empty) | Optional comma-separated hostnames, or `.suffix` entries meaning any subdomain of the suffix (for example `client.example.com,.example.org`). Unset means any public https host. The API refuses to boot on a malformed entry (scheme, path, port, wildcard or empty item). |
| `OAUTH_CONSENT_URL_BASE` | (empty) | Optional origin for the consent UI redirect (e.g. `http://localhost:4321` for split API/web dev). Defaults to a relative path, which works when the API and web app share an origin behind a reverse proxy. |

---

sections.heading: API reference
sections.text: The MCP server implements the following JSON-RPC 2.0 methods:

sections.heading: `initialize`
`prompts/list`
`prompts/get`
`tools/list`
`tools/call`
`resources/list`
`resources/read`
"Missing X-API-Key header" (401)
sections.text: The request does not include an `X-API-Key` header. Ensure your MCP client configuration includes the header. In Claude Desktop and Cursor, this goes in the `headers` block of the server config.

sections.heading: "Invalid API key format" (401)
sections.text: The key does not start with `brz_`. Verify you copied the full key from the API Keys page.

sections.heading: "Rate limit exceeded" (429)
sections.text: You have exceeded the per-minute transport rate limit. The response includes a `Retry-After` header with the number of seconds to wait. If this happens frequently, increase the limit via `MCP_SSE_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE` or `MCP_MESSAGE_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE`.

sections.heading: "Too many active MCP sessions" (503 or 429)
sections.text: Either the server-wide limit (100 sessions) or the per-key limit (default 5) has been reached. Close unused MCP clients, or increase the per-key limit via `MCP_MAX_SSE_SESSIONS_PER_KEY`.

sections.heading: "Service temporarily unavailable" (503)
sections.text: Redis is not available. The MCP server requires Redis for rate limiting in production. Check that your Redis instance is running and the `REDIS_URL` environment variable is set.

sections.heading: Tool returns "requires ai:execute scope"
sections.text: The API key does not have the `ai:execute` scope. Regenerate the key with the required scope, or use a key that already has it.

sections.heading: Tool returns "not in MCP_EXECUTE_TOOL_ALLOWLIST"
sections.text: In production, Tier 3+ tools must be explicitly allowlisted. Add the tool name to the `MCP_EXECUTE_TOOL_ALLOWLIST` environment variable.

sections.heading: Tools not appearing in Claude Desktop
sections.text:
1. Verify the SSE endpoint URL is correct and reachable from your machine.
2. Check that the API key has at least the `ai:read` scope.
3. Restart Claude Desktop after editing the config file.
4. Open the Claude Desktop developer console to check for connection errors.

sections.heading: "Unknown tool" errors
sections.text: The tool name in `tools/call` does not match any registered tool. Use `tools/list` to see the current catalogue. Tool names are case-sensitive.

sections.heading: Stale SSE session
sections.text: SSE sessions expire after 30 minutes. If you see errors about missing sessions, the client should reconnect to `/api/v1/mcp/sse` to obtain a new session.

title: AI Insights
description: Machine-learning features that surface metric anomalies, group correlated alerts into incidents, explain root causes, and forecast capacity.
headings: Enabling a feature for an organization
Alert Correlation and Root Cause Analysis

sections.text:
Breeze includes a suite of machine-learning features that turn raw fleet telemetry into actionable insight: it spots unusual metric behavior before it becomes an outage, groups noisy related alerts into a single incident, explains the likely root cause, suggests fixes, and projects when you'll run out of capacity.

These features are designed to be **turned on gradually**. Each one is governed independently so you can enable a capability, watch its output, judge its quality, and roll it back instantly if it isn't useful for your environment yet. Several start **off by default** — if a panel shows a "disabled" message, the feature simply hasn't been enabled for that organization yet (see [Availability and enabling](#availability-and-enabling) below).

The AI Insights suite covers:

- **Anomaly Detection** — flags unusual device metric behavior (CPU spikes, runaway memory/disk growth, etc.)
- **Alert Correlation** — groups related alerts into a single incident to cut inbox noise
- **Root Cause Analysis (RCA)** — gathers evidence on demand and proposes the likely cause of an incident
- **Remediation Suggestions** — recommends fixes (scripts, playbooks, diagnostics) for an anomaly or incident
- **Capacity Forecasting** — projects future resource utilization from recent usage

Two closely related capabilities have their own dedicated pages: [User Risk Scoring](/features/user-risk/) and [Device Reliability](/features/reliability/).

---

sections.heading: Availability and enabling
sections.text:
Every AI Insights capability is controlled by an independent feature flag. Flags resolve in a fixed order of precedence, so you can set a sensible organization-wide default and still flip a single capability on or off without redeploying:

1. **Global kill switches** (environment variables) — highest priority; can only *disable*
2. **Organization settings** — per-organization override
3. **Partner settings** — applies to every organization under a partner
4. **Built-in defaults** — used when nothing above applies

sections.heading: Default state
sections.text:
| Feature | Default |
|---------|---------|
| Device Reliability | **On** |
| User Risk scoring | **On** |
| Metric rollups (prepares the data anomalies are detected from) | **On** |
| Alert Correlation | **On** outside production; **off** in production unless enabled |
| Anomaly Detection | **Off** |
| Root Cause Analysis | **Off** |
| Remediation Suggestions | **Off** |
| Ticket Triage | **Off** |

  Anomaly Detection depends on metric rollups, which are on by default — so once you enable Anomaly Detection there is already recent data for it to analyze. Root Cause Analysis and Remediation Suggestions add the most value once Alert Correlation is also on.

sections.heading: Enabling a feature for an organization
sections.text:
ML feature flags live in the organization's settings under an `mlFeatureFlags` object, keyed by flag name. To enable Anomaly Detection, Root Cause Analysis, and Remediation Suggestions for an organization, set:

```json
{
  "mlFeatureFlags": {
    "ml.anomalies.enabled": true,
    "ml.rca.enabled": true,
    "ml.remediation_suggestions.enabled": true
  }
}
```

The available flags are:

| Flag | Controls |
|------|----------|
| `ml.anomalies.enabled` | Anomaly Detection panels |
| `ml.anomalies.create_alerts` | Whether anomalies can be promoted into alerts automatically |
| `ml.alert_correlation.enabled` | Alert Correlation / incident grouping |
| `ml.rca.enabled` | Root Cause Analysis ("Explain incident") |
| `ml.remediation_suggestions.enabled` | Remediation Suggestions ("Suggested Fixes") |
| `ml.device_reliability.enabled` | Device Reliability scoring |
| `ml.user_risk_v0.enabled` | User Risk scoring |
| `ml.metric_rollups.enabled` | Metric rollups (anomaly input data) |

A partner-level override using the same `mlFeatureFlags` shape applies to all of that partner's organizations unless an individual organization overrides it.

sections.heading: Global kill switches
sections.text:
For self-hosted operators, environment variables provide an emergency off-switch that overrides all per-organization settings. These only ever **disable** — they cannot turn a feature on.

| Variable | Effect |
|----------|--------|
| `ML_FEATURES_DISABLED` / `ML_OUTPUTS_DISABLED` / `ML_GLOBAL_KILL_SWITCH` | Disable **all** AI Insights features instantly |
| `ML_DISABLED_FLAGS` | Comma-separated list of flags to disable (supports wildcards, e.g. `ml.anomalies.*`) |
| `ML_<FLAG>_DISABLED` | Disable a single flag (e.g. `ML_RCA_DISABLED=true`) |

  Setting a kill switch to `false` does **not** enable a feature — it just leaves the switch disengaged so the per-organization setting and defaults apply. Use organization settings to turn features on; use kill switches only to force them off.

  Self-hosters running Breeze from source: the repository ships a full operations runbook at `docs/runbooks/ml-operations.md` covering every flag, kill switch, feedback signal, evaluation endpoint, background worker, and data-retention setting. Consult it for production rollout, quality measurement, and troubleshooting.

---

sections.heading: Anomaly Detection
sections.text:
Anomaly Detection watches each device's metric history and flags behavior that deviates from the device's own recent baseline — a CPU spike, a sudden drop, a steady upward trend, runaway memory or disk growth, or unusual network egress. It catches developing problems that a fixed alert threshold would miss.

To keep routine work out of the list, a run of unusual readings has to last at least 15 minutes (three consecutive 5-minute readings) before it shows up. Self-hosters can change the count with `METRIC_ANOMALY_EPISODE_MIN_BUCKETS` (default `3`; it was `2` before v0.122.1). On v0.122.1 the stock Compose files don't pass it to the api container, so add it to the `api` service's `environment:` block; later releases map it. A burst shorter than that, such as a Defender scan or an indexer run, closes on its own and is never shown. Memory growth also has to reach a new high for the device: a climb back to a level the device already reached in the past 7 days, such as a nightly job, is treated as normal for that device. Disk growth is always reported, because a disk filling back up after a cleanup still matters.

sections.heading: Where to find it
sections.text:
Open any device, then select the **Anomalies** tab. Each open anomaly is shown as a card with:

- The **anomaly type** (spike, drop, trend, process runaway, memory growth, disk growth, network egress)
- The **metric** involved (CPU, RAM, disk, network, processes)
- The **observed value** versus the device's **baseline**, and a **confidence** score

sections.heading: Acting on an anomaly
sections.text:
| Action | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| **Dismiss** | Marks the anomaly as not worth acting on |
| **Resolve** | Marks the underlying issue as handled |
| **Promote** | Turns the anomaly into a standard alert so it flows through your normal alert and notification process |

If Remediation Suggestions is enabled, each open anomaly also shows a **Suggested Fixes** panel (see [below](#remediation-suggestions)).

  When the **Anomalies** tab shows "Anomaly detection is disabled for this organization," the `ml.anomalies.enabled` flag is off for that organization. Enable it as described in [Availability and enabling](#availability-and-enabling).

A newly opened anomaly incident can also wake an AI triage agent. This is off unless that organization's triage agent is explicitly opted in. Anomaly-triggered runs are forced into Shadow mode, so they only observe and report. See [AI Agents](/features/ai-agents/#anomaly-lane) for the opt-in procedure and agent requirements.

sections.heading: Measuring anomaly detection quality
sections.text:
Before enabling Anomaly Detection more widely, you can check how it is performing with `GET /analytics/anomalies/evaluation` (requires analytics read access). It accepts `range` (`7d`, `30d` — the default — or `90d`) and optional `orgId` or `deviceId` filters, and returns:

- **Per-anomaly counts and rates** — how many anomalies are open, dismissed, promoted, or resolved, with dismiss, promote, and resolve rates. Anomalies that Breeze **cleared** automatically because the metric returned to normal are reported as their own `cleared` count and are left out of the total and every rate: an automatic close is not a technician's verdict, so it can't inflate or dilute the dismiss rate.
- **An `episodes` block** — Breeze groups a continuous run of anomalous readings on one device into a single episode, so a CPU spike that lasts an hour counts once here rather than once per reading. The block reports the number of episodes, a breakdown by status (`open`, `resolved`, `dismissed`) and by how each closed (`cleared`, `expired_offline`, `expired_no_data`, `detection_off`, `user`, `snoozed`), the median time to close, the share of episodes that are repeats of one that closed in the previous week, and the share of closed episodes a technician actually acted on (resolved, dismissed, or promoted to an alert).

A high share of episodes closing as `cleared` with a low hands-on share means most detections resolve on their own without anyone needing to look — the expected steady state, not a problem. A high repeat share on one device usually points at a scheduled task or a real unfixed issue re-triggering detection rather than detector noise.

---

sections.heading: Alert Correlation and Root Cause Analysis
sections.text: When many related alerts fire at once — a network outage taking devices offline, a failing service triggering a cascade — Alert Correlation groups them into a single **incident** so your inbox shows one item to triage instead of dozens.

sections.heading: The Correlations view
sections.text:
Open **Alerts → Correlations**. The page summarizes the impact of grouping across your fleet:

| Metric | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **Incidents** | Number of correlated groups |
| **Grouped alerts** | Total alerts pulled into those groups |
| **Inbox reduction** | How many individual alerts were suppressed into incidents |
| **Avg noise cut** | Average reduction in alert volume across groups |

Each incident shows its root-cause alert, severity, status, the number of related alerts, a correlation score, and the noise reduction it achieved. From an incident you can **Acknowledge**, **Resolve**, **Mark wrong group**, or **Dismiss grouping** — the last two feed back into the correlation quality (see [Feedback](#feedback-improves-the-models)).

sections.heading: Root Cause Analysis
sections.text:
With Root Cause Analysis enabled, an incident offers an on-demand **Explain incident** button. Breeze gathers evidence from around the incident's time window and produces:

- **Root cause candidates**, each with a confidence score and supporting evidence (the earliest alert, a recent device change, an aligned error log, and so on)
- **Suggested next steps**, each with a risk tier and links to the evidence behind it
- An **evidence timeline** stitched together from alerts, device changes (services, software, configuration), event logs, and agent logs
- **Evidence gaps** — what Breeze looked for but couldn't find

You can turn an RCA into a ticket with **Create ticket from RCA**, and rate it to improve future analyses.

  Evidence is gathered **on demand** when you click **Explain incident**, not continuously — so RCA has no ongoing cost until you ask for it.

---

sections.heading: Remediation Suggestions
sections.text: Remediation Suggestions (shown as **Suggested Fixes**) recommends concrete actions for an anomaly or incident — a script to run, a playbook to launch, or a diagnostic to collect — each with a rationale, an expected outcome, a confidence score, and a risk tier.

sections.heading: Acting on a suggestion
sections.text:
1. Review the suggestion's rationale and expected action.
2. **Accept**, **Edit**, or **Reject** it. Editing lets you adjust the title, risk, rationale, or expected action before acting.
3. For a script suggestion on a selected device, **Execute** runs it directly. High- and critical-risk actions route through [PAM approval](/features/pam/) first and show **Request approval** / **Approval pending** until an approver signs off.

  Remediation Suggestions never act on their own. Nothing runs until you accept and explicitly execute it, and elevated-risk actions still require approval.

---

sections.heading: Capacity Forecasting
sections.text:
Capacity Forecasting projects future resource utilization from recent usage so you can plan upgrades before you hit a wall.

Open **Analytics** and switch the dashboard to **Capacity Planning**. The **Capacity Forecast** panel charts current utilization alongside a projected trend line, with optional warning and critical threshold markers so you can see when usage is expected to cross them.

---

sections.heading: Feedback improves the models
sections.text:
Several AI Insights surfaces capture feedback, and that feedback is used to measure and improve quality over time:

- **User Risk** — mark a score as a **true positive** or **false positive**
- **Alert Correlation** — **Mark wrong group** or **Dismiss grouping** when a grouping is incorrect
- **Root Cause Analysis** — rate an explanation helpful or not, or mark it edited
- **Remediation Suggestions** — accept, edit, or reject a suggested fix

Providing this feedback during a gradual rollout is the fastest way to judge whether a feature is ready to enable more broadly.

---

sections.heading: Related features
sections.text:
- [User Risk Scoring](/features/user-risk/) — composite risk scores for users, with behavior analytics and access reviews
- [Device Reliability](/features/reliability/) — uptime, crash, hang, and BSOD tracking with a computed reliability score
- [Alerts](/features/alerts/) — the alerting system that correlation and RCA build on

title: Mobile App
description: Breeze mobile app for iOS and Android: device monitoring, alert inbox, remote actions, push notifications, approval mode, and biometric login.
headings: Fleet Hygiene Findings on the Systems Tab
Systems shows "Some data could not be refreshed."

sections.text:
The Breeze mobile app gives technicians and administrators on-the-go access to device monitoring, alert management, and remote actions from their iOS or Android device. Built with React Native and Expo, the app connects to the same Breeze API used by the web dashboard through a dedicated set of mobile-optimized endpoints mounted at `/api/v1/mobile`. Push notifications keep you informed of critical alerts in real time, and biometric authentication provides a secure, convenient login experience.

---

sections.heading: Installing the App
sections.text:
**iOS** -- install [Breeze RMM from the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/app/breeze-rmm/id6789370762). On first launch the app asks which server to sign in to: the hosted **US** region, the hosted **EU** region, or a **custom server** URL for a self-hosted deployment.

**Android** -- not published to Google Play yet. Build it from `apps/mobile` in the repo (`npx expo prebuild --platform android`, then a Gradle or EAS build). Push notifications require your own Firebase project's `google-services.json`, which is never committed.

Self-hosters can point the published iOS app at their own server, but password-manager autofill is limited to the hosted domains -- see the note below.

---

sections.heading: Supported Platforms
sections.text:
| Platform | Minimum Version | Bundle Identifier |
|----------|----------------|-------------------|
| iOS | iOS 13+ (with Expo SDK 57) | `com.breeze.rmm` |
| Android | Android 5.0+ (API 21, with Expo SDK 57) | `com.breeze.rmm` |

The app uses the Expo managed workflow and supports automatic light/dark theming based on the system color scheme. The interface orientation is locked to portrait mode.

  **Self-hosters building their own iOS app:** the published build is tied to the hosted regions' domains, so password managers only offer saved credentials (and their one-time codes) on those. Apple bakes associated domains into the signed entitlement at build time, so this cannot be a runtime setting -- set `BREEZE_ASSOCIATED_DOMAINS=breeze.example.com` before running the iOS prebuild. A bare hostname or a full URL both work; an invalid entry fails the build rather than quietly producing an app without your domain.

---

sections.heading: Dashboard Summary
sections.text:
The `GET /summary` endpoint returns an at-a-glance overview of your fleet and alert status, scoped to the authenticated user's organization or partner context. The response contains two sections:

- **Devices** -- total count plus breakdown by status (`online`, `offline`, `maintenance`).
- **Alerts** -- total count plus breakdown by status (`active`, `acknowledged`, `resolved`) and a count of unresolved critical alerts.

An optional `orgId` query parameter allows partner-scoped users to filter the summary to a specific organization.

sections.heading: Device Monitoring
sections.text:
Devices live under the **Systems** tab. Tap **View all devices** to open a browsable list of managed devices; each device card displays:

- Device name (display name or hostname)
- Operating system with platform-specific icon (Windows, macOS, Linux)
- Online/offline/warning status badge
- Last seen timestamp
- Live resource metrics (CPU, memory, disk usage) for online devices with progress bar indicators
- Organization and site context

The device list supports pull-to-refresh, a free-text filter over name, hostname, site, and operating system, and **All / Online / Offline** chips (a device in a warning state counts as offline). Offline machines are sorted first so problems surface at the top. Decommissioned devices are excluded by default unless explicitly filtered.

The list holds one page of devices at a time rather than the entire fleet, so a filter that finds nothing means nothing matched *on the loaded page* -- the screen says so explicitly instead of implying the fleet is empty.

Tapping a device opens a detail screen with the following rows (a field with no value renders as `—`, never blank):

| Field | Notes |
|-------|-------|
| **Hostname** | |
| **IP address** | LAN IP on the first line; the public/WAN IP is appended on a second line only when known |
| **Logged-in user** | |
| **Operating system** | OS label with its version appended (`Windows 11 · 23H2`); an unknown version falls back to the bare OS label rather than a dash |
| **Open alerts** | A real count, including `· 0` -- only a count that hasn't been reported yet shows a dash |
| **Open tickets** | Same convention as open alerts |
| **Agent version** | |
| **Last seen** | |
| **Organization** | |
| **Site** | |

Below the fields, live **CPU**, **memory**, and **disk** metrics are retrieved from `GET /devices/:id/metrics`.

sections.heading: Fleet Hygiene Findings on the Systems Tab
sections.text:
The Systems tab's **Active Issues** list is not alerts alone. It also rolls up your fleet's open [Fleet Hygiene findings](/features/fleet-hygiene/) -- the same VSS, Universal Print, Intel ME, and SCEP checks the AI assistant's fleet-findings tool reports -- as one summary row per organization, appended below the alert rows: **"N open findings"** with the org name underneath.

A findings row is display-only for now: there's no severity dot (a small "Finding" tag instead) and no swipe-to-acknowledge or tap-through to a findings detail screen -- act on a finding from the AI chat or the web dashboard's Fleet Hygiene page. Findings still count toward the top-of-screen issue total and the "N issues across M organizations" summary, so an org with open findings but no active alerts still shows up there.

  The findings counts endpoint (`GET /fleet/findings/counts`) doesn't exist on servers older than v0.111.0. Against an older server the findings row is silently omitted rather than shown as an error -- everything else on the Systems tab (alerts, devices, orgs) still loads normally.

sections.heading: Alert Inbox
sections.text:
The Alerts tab displays an inbox of alerts fetched from `GET /alerts/inbox`. Alerts are sorted by trigger time (newest first) and include:

- Severity badge (critical, high, medium, low)
- Alert title and message
- Associated device hostname and OS type
- Timestamps for triggered, acknowledged, and resolved events

The alert list supports pull-to-refresh, severity filtering (`all`, `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low`), and status filtering (`active`, `acknowledged`, `resolved`, `suppressed`) via query parameters.

From the alert detail screen, technicians can:

- **Acknowledge** an active alert with a single tap (`POST /alerts/:id/acknowledge`).
- **Resolve** an alert with an optional resolution note (`POST /alerts/:id/resolve`).

Both actions publish events (`alert.acknowledged`, `alert.resolved`) through the event bus and write audit log entries. Resolving a monitor alert applies its configured cooldown period. Historical alerts from retired policy rules can still be resolved; they no longer set a policy-rule cooldown.

sections.heading: Tickets
sections.text:
The **Tickets** tab puts the service desk queue in a technician's pocket. The list filters by **Open / Closed** and **Mine / All**, so you can jump straight to what is assigned to you.

Tapping a ticket opens the detail view, which shows the full activity stream -- comments alongside status changes, assignment changes, and logged time. From there a technician can:

- Post a **public** comment that the requester sees.
- Change status to **Open**, **Pending**, or **Resolved**. Only transitions the service desk allows from the ticket's current status are offered, and resolving prompts for a resolution note first.

- Attach files to a comment -- up to 5 per comment, 10 MB each, in JPEG, PNG, WebP or PDF. Files already on a ticket open in a full-screen viewer.
- Start and stop a timer against the ticket, or log time manually.

Time tracking keeps working without a signal: a timer started offline is held on the phone and submitted with its real start and end times once you reconnect, rather than being stamped with the time the phone came back.

The app can also suggest time entries from remote sessions you have just finished -- a partner setting that is off by default, and the one place that feature appears. See [Suggested time entries](/features/ticketing/#suggested-time-entries).

sections.heading: Arrival suggestions
sections.text:
When you open the app at a client site, Breeze can suggest starting a timer: *"Looks like you're at Acme Corp -- Main Office."* One tap starts an ordinary time entry for that organization and site. Nothing is started or stopped without your tap.

**Two opt-ins are required.** Neither one alone does anything:

1. **Your partner turns it on** under **Settings > Ticketing > Time Tracking** (off by default), and can set a default arrival radius.
2. **You turn it on** on your phone. The first time, the Time tab shows a short explanation and a **Turn on** button; only that tap raises the system location prompt. **Not now** hides the card for 30 days, and you can change your mind later in the app's **Settings > Location suggestions** row.

**What is and is not sent.** The app compares your position with the saved site locations *on the phone* and discards it. Your position is never sent to Breeze, and is never part of analytics or logs. The one exception is deliberate: when you tap **Save my current location as \<site\>** (below), that single reading becomes the site's saved location.

**When it prompts.** Only while the app is open -- when you return to it, open Home or Tickets, or pull to refresh on Tickets. It checks at most every 5 minutes (a pull to refresh checks right away). It stays quiet when:

- a timer is already running,
- the phone's location is not precise enough to tell sites apart (worse than about 500 m),
- you dismissed that site in the last 4 hours, or stopped a timer there in the last 30 minutes.

If more than one site is in range, you pick from a list sorted by distance -- Breeze never picks for you. With open tickets assigned to you at that organization you can start against one, or choose **Site visit -- no ticket**. A timer started offline still records the organization and site when it syncs.

**Still at the site?** For a timer that an arrival suggestion started, the app can later ask *"Still at Acme Corp? Timer has been running 2h 28m."* after two readings, at least 5 minutes apart, show you well away from the site. **Stop** stops the timer as of your tap; **Keep running** leaves it alone. This also only happens while the app is open.
