Software services reuse those same event IDs: Windows' Volume Shadow Copy service, for example, routinely logs its own event ID 13, which older versions miscounted as a memory error, unfairly dragging scores on healthy devices. Events whose message contains a hardware keyword ("machine check", "memory", "i/o error", etc.) are still classified as hardware regardless of source. Previously miscounted data self-heals automatically on the next score recompute — no reinstall or data migration needed.

Hardware errors are further classified by severity, and each severity carries a different relative weight when computing the hardware-error sub-score:

| Severity | Relative Weight |
|----------|-----------------|
| `critical` | 2 |
| `error` | 1 |
| `warning` | 0.34 |

These weights feed into the same rate-normalized, saturating curve described in [Score Calculation](#score-calculation) above -- they are not flat per-event point deductions. A single critical hardware error drops the hardware-error sub-score to roughly 51; two criticals to roughly 26.

---

sections.heading: Platform Support
sections.text:
**Windows:**
    The Windows collector reads from the Windows Event Log via the `EventLogCollector`. Detected signals include:

    - **BSOD/Bugcheck**: Event IDs 1001, 6008; messages containing "bugcheck", "blue screen", or "unexpected shutdown"
    - **Service failures**: Service Control Manager event IDs 7000, 7022, 7023, 7024, 7026, 7031, or 7034; messages with "service terminated" or "service failed"
    - **Application hangs**: Messages containing "hang" or "not responding"
    - **Hardware errors**: WHEA events, disk errors, memory errors
    - **System crashes**: Critical-level system events containing "crash"

    Windows provides the richest reliability telemetry due to the structured Event Log system.

  **macOS:**
    The macOS collector reads from system logs. Detected signals include:

    - **Kernel panics**: Messages containing "kernel panic" or "panic("
    - **Application crashes**: Messages containing "application crash" or "crashed"
    - **Application hangs**: Messages containing "hang" or "not responding"
    - **Service failures**: launchd messages containing "exited" or "failed"
    - **System crashes**: Critical-level system events containing "shutdown"
    - **Hardware errors**: Messages with "i/o error" or "memory" keywords

  **Linux:**
    The Linux collector reads from journald/syslog. Detected signals include:

    - **Kernel panics**: Messages containing "kernel panic", "oops", or "segfault"
    - **OOM kills**: Messages containing "oom" or "out of memory"
    - **Service failures**: systemd messages containing "failed" or "failure"
    - **Process hangs**: Messages containing "hang", "not responding", or "blocked for more than"
    - **Hardware errors**: Messages with "i/o error", "edac", or "mce" keywords

  On all platforms, if the event log collector fails (permissions, missing log source, etc.), the reliability collector falls back to returning base metrics only (uptime and boot time) without any event data. This ensures the uptime score remains accurate even when event collection is unavailable.

---

sections.heading: In the device list
sections.text: The **Devices** list includes a sortable **Reliability** column. Each device shows a colored score badge (0–100) with a trend arrow — improving, stable, or degrading — colored by band. Click the column header to sort the fleet worst-first or best-first. Devices that don't have a score yet (newly enrolled, or network devices) show a dash.

sections.heading: On the device detail page
sections.text:
Open a device and find the **Reliability** card. It is designed to explain the score, not just display it:

- **All five factors as rows.** Every factor (uptime, crashes, application hangs, service failures, hardware errors) is shown as a row with its points earned out of points available (e.g. "18 / 36 pts"), so you can see how the rows sum to the total score. Rows are sorted worst-first; hovering a row shows the exact figures. A weight-segmented score bar above the rows shows each factor's share of the score at a glance.
- **Humanized evidence per factor.** Problem factors show a plain-language evidence line (e.g. "24 in 30d · 11 in last 7d · 3 recovered"). Where per-event data exists (service failures, hardware errors, hangs), a **details** link expands a drill-down listing the top offending services, hardware components, and processes with event counts and last-occurrence dates. Service failures caused by Breeze's own agent/watchdog/helper services are annotated "from Breeze services, not scored."
- **Headline stat.** Servers and always-on infrastructure show 30-day uptime as the headline stat. Workstations — where uptime carries no weight — instead show **Biggest drag**: the factor costing the most points and its 30-day event count, so the headline is always meaningful.
- **Trend and MTBF** are shown alongside the score, and the "At risk" badge (score ≤ 70) names the biggest-drag factor in its tooltip.

Two actions are available: **Ask AI about reliability** hands the device's reliability snapshot to the Breeze AI assistant for a plain-language diagnosis and suggested next steps, and **Mark work done** places a baseline marker (below).

sections.heading: Baseline markers
sections.text:
After you fix a device, its old crashes and failures would otherwise keep dragging the score down for weeks. A baseline marker restarts scoring from the point the work finished, so only what happens afterwards counts.

1. On the device's **Reliability** card, click **Mark work done**.

2. Under **What was done**, choose **Reimaged**, **Remediated** or **Hardware replaced**. **Remediated** needs a note describing what was fixed; for the others the note is optional.

3. Set **When the work finished**. It can be up to 30 days in the past, but not in the future.

4. Click **Save marker**.

The card then shows a banner such as *Scoring since Reimaged on (date) by (technician)*. The score is marked **Provisional** until 14 days of data have been reported since the marker. A **Before → since** comparison sets the score and the 30-day crash, hang, service-failure and hardware-error counts from before the marker against now, and **Marker history** lists every marker on the device. **Clear** removes a marker from scoring: the score falls back to the previous marker, or to the device's full history, and the marker stays in the history marked **Cleared**. When a bare-metal recovery of the device completes, Breeze places a **Reimaged** marker automatically (shown as by *Breeze (automatic)*).

Placing or clearing a marker needs `devices:write` and is audit logged (`device.reliability.baseline_set`, `device.reliability.baseline_cleared`).

sections.heading: Fleet Overview
sections.text:
List reliability scores for all devices in your organization, sorted worst-first by default:

```bash
GET /reliability?orgId=uuid&scoreRange=critical&trendDirection=degrading&page=1&limit=25
```

sections.heading: List Query Parameters
sections.text:
| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `orgId` | UUID | Filter by organization |
| `siteId` | UUID | Filter by site |
| `scoreRange` | string | Filter by band: `critical`, `poor`, `fair`, `good` (also accepts legacy `0-50`, `51-70`, `71-85`, `86-100` format) |
| `trendDirection` | string | Filter by trend: `improving`, `stable`, `degrading` |
| `issueType` | string | Filter by issue type: `crashes`, `hangs`, `hardware`, `services`, `uptime` |
| `minScore` | integer | Minimum reliability score (0-100) |
| `maxScore` | integer | Maximum reliability score (0-100) |
| `page` | integer | Page number (default 1) |
| `limit` | integer | Results per page (1-100, default 25) |

The response includes a `summary` section with the average score, count of critical devices (score ≤ 50), and count of degrading devices:

```json
{
  "data": [...],
  "pagination": { "total": 150, "page": 1, "limit": 25, "totalPages": 6 },
  "summary": {
    "averageScore": 78,
    "criticalDevices": 5,
    "degradingDevices": 12
  }
}
```

sections.heading: Organization Summary
sections.text:
Get a high-level reliability overview for an organization, including the 10 worst devices:

```bash
GET /reliability/org/:orgId/summary
```

The response includes:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `devices` | Total device count with reliability data |
| `averageScore` | Organization-wide average reliability score |
| `criticalDevices` | Devices with score 0-50 |
| `poorDevices` | Devices with score 51-70 |
| `fairDevices` | Devices with score 71-85 |
| `goodDevices` | Devices with score 86-100 |
| `degradingDevices` | Devices with a degrading trend |
| `topIssues` | Ranked list of most common issue types across the org |
| `worstDevices` | The 10 lowest-scoring devices with full reliability details |

sections.heading: Single Device Detail
sections.text:
Get the full reliability snapshot and 30-day history for a specific device:

```bash
GET /reliability/:deviceId
```

The response contains two sections:

- **`snapshot`** -- The current computed reliability state: overall score, all sub-scores, uptime percentages (7d/30d/90d), event counts, MTBF, trend direction and confidence, and top issues.
- **`history`** -- An array of daily data points for the last 30 days, each containing sample count, max uptime seconds, crash/hang/service failure/hardware error counts, and a daily reliability estimate.

sections.heading: Device History
sections.text:
Retrieve daily reliability history for a configurable lookback window:

```bash
GET /reliability/:deviceId/history?days=90
```

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `days` | integer | Lookback window in days (1-365, default 90) |

Each data point in the response represents one day and includes:

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `date` | string | Day in `YYYY-MM-DD` format |
| `sampleCount` | integer | Number of telemetry submissions that day |
| `uptimeSecondsMax` | integer | Highest reported uptime that day |
| `crashCount` | integer | Total crash events |
| `hangCount` | integer | Total application hangs |
| `serviceFailureCount` | integer | Total service failures |
| `hardwareErrorCount` | integer | Total hardware errors |
| `reliabilityEstimate` | integer | Estimated reliability score for that day (0-100) |

---

sections.heading: AI Integration
sections.text:
The Breeze AI assistant can query device reliability data through its built-in tool system. The `query_device_reliability` tool allows natural language questions about fleet reliability to be answered with real data.

The AI tool supports the same filters as the list API: organization, score range, trend direction, issue type, and score bounds. When invoked, it returns the same paginated results with a summary section, allowing the AI to answer questions like:

- "Which devices have the worst reliability scores?"
- "How many devices are in a degrading trend?"
- "Show me all devices with hardware errors in the last 30 days"
- "What is the average reliability score for Contoso?"

  AI reliability queries are subject to the same organization-scoped data isolation as direct API access. The AI can only access reliability data for organizations the authenticated user has permission to view.

---

sections.heading: Fleet Reliability
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| GET | `/reliability` | List device reliability scores with filtering and pagination |
| GET | `/reliability/org/:orgId/summary` | Organization-level reliability summary with worst devices |
| GET | `/reliability/:deviceId` | Full reliability snapshot and 30-day history for a device |
| GET | `/reliability/:deviceId/history` | Daily reliability history with configurable lookback (`?days=`) |
| GET | `/reliability/:deviceId/baselines` | List the device's baseline markers, including cleared ones |
| POST | `/reliability/:deviceId/baselines` | Place a marker (body: `reason` = `reimaged`, `remediated` or `hardware_replaced`; optional `baselineAt`, at most 30 days back; `note`, required for `remediated`). Requires `devices:write` |
| DELETE | `/reliability/:deviceId/baselines/:baselineId` | Clear a marker. Requires `devices:write` |

sections.heading: Agent Ingestion
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| POST | `/agents/:id/reliability` | Submit reliability metrics from the agent (agent auth required) |

  All reliability query endpoints require authentication and one of these scopes: `organization`, `partner`, or `system`. Organization-scoped tokens are automatically restricted to their own organization's data. The agent ingestion endpoint uses agent bearer token authentication.

---

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**No reliability data for a device.**
Reliability data appears after the agent has submitted at least one telemetry payload via `POST /agents/:id/reliability`. Confirm the agent is online and the heartbeat cycle is running. The agent includes a 24-hour initial lookback on first collection, so the first submission should include recent events. If the device exists but has no reliability snapshot, the scoring computation may not have run yet -- check BullMQ worker status.

**Reliability score seems too low despite no visible issues.**
The score is a composite of five factors with different weights. A device can have a low score due to a single factor being severely penalized. Use `GET /reliability/:deviceId` to inspect the individual sub-scores (`uptimeScore`, `crashScore`, `hangScore`, `serviceFailureScore`, `hardwareErrorScore`) and identify which factor is dragging the score down. For example, a 90% uptime over 90 days produces an uptime sub-score of 0, which alone would reduce the overall score by up to 30 points.

**A laptop's reliability score looks fine even though it's powered off a lot.**
This is expected. Laptops and desktop workstations are not scored on uptime — they're expected to sleep and shut down — so normal power-off behavior does not lower their reliability score. Only servers and infrastructure are scored on uptime.

**Trend direction shows `stable` with low confidence.**
Trend computation requires at least 3 days of data and achieves full confidence at 14+ days. If the device was recently enrolled or has sparse telemetry, the trend will default to `stable` with `trendConfidence: 0`. Allow the device to accumulate more history before relying on trend data.

**Agent event collection failing on specific platform.**
On all platforms, if the event log collector encounters an error, the reliability collector gracefully falls back to base metrics (uptime and boot time only). Check agent logs for warnings like "reliability event log collection failed, returning base metrics only". Common causes include insufficient permissions to read system event logs, missing log sources, or the event log service being stopped.

**MTBF showing `null`.**
MTBF is only computed when there is at least one failure event (crash, hang, service failure, or hardware error) in the 90-day window AND the device has positive operating hours. A device with zero failures has no meaningful MTBF -- this is the ideal state. A device with zero uptime data also produces `null` MTBF.

**Score not updating after new events arrive.**
Score computation is enqueued via BullMQ after each telemetry submission. If the queue worker is down, the system falls back to inline computation, but this fallback may fail silently if the database is under load. Check BullMQ dashboard for failed or stalled `device-reliability-computation` jobs. The `computedAt` timestamp on the reliability snapshot indicates when the score was last calculated.

**Organization summary showing stale data.**
The org summary endpoint computes results in real time from the `device_reliability` table. If individual device scores have not been recomputed recently (check `computedAt`), the summary reflects outdated data. Trigger a fleet-wide recomputation by ensuring all agents are submitting telemetry and the reliability worker is processing jobs.

title: Remote Access
description: Remote Desktop and Remote Terminal for managed devices over WebRTC, with TURN relay support, WebSocket fallback, and MFA-gated session permissions.
headings: WebRTC needs webkit2gtk built with the GStreamer plugins
Viewer launches but no window appears
Gray window with no controls on NVIDIA

sections.text:
Breeze provides two real-time access capabilities for managed devices: **Remote Desktop** (interactive screen viewing and control) and **Remote Terminal** (browser-based interactive shell). Each is a separate session type created through the same `/remote/sessions` API. File movement between the technician and the device is handled by the device Files tab (the system-tools file browser), not by a remote session.

Remote desktop sessions use WebRTC as the primary transport. The Breeze server acts as a signaling relay during connection setup — it brokers the initial SDP offer/answer exchange and ICE candidate negotiation between the native viewer app and the device agent. Once the peer-to-peer connection is established, video, audio, and input data flow directly between the viewer and the agent and do not transit the Breeze server.

The Breeze stack includes a **coturn TURN server** that relays WebRTC traffic when a direct peer-to-peer connection is not possible (symmetric NAT, restrictive firewalls). The API generates short-lived TURN credentials via a shared secret and distributes them to both the viewer and agent during ICE negotiation. See [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/#webrtc--turn) for configuration.

If WebRTC negotiation fails even with TURN (e.g., TURN is misconfigured or unreachable), the viewer automatically falls back to a WebSocket transport that relays JPEG frames through the Breeze server. The WebSocket fallback has reduced capabilities compared to WebRTC — no audio, no clipboard sync, no multi-monitor switching, and no low-latency cursor streaming.

  Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is required for all remote access sessions. Your role must also include the `remote:access` permission — see **Settings → Roles** if session creation returns "Access denied."

---

sections.heading: Remote Desktop
sections.text: Remote Desktop streams the device's screen to your browser and forwards your mouse and keyboard input back to the device in real time, giving you full interactive control as if you were physically present at the machine.

sections.heading: Starting a desktop session
sections.text:
1. Navigate to **Devices**, locate the target device, and open its detail page.

2. Click **Connect** and select **Desktop**.

3. A fullscreen viewer opens once the WebRTC connection is active.

4. Mouse movement and clicks are captured and relayed to the device in real time.

5. Keyboard input is forwarded directly — use the **Release Input** button or press **Escape** (if configured) to return control to your browser.

sections.heading: Connection flow
sections.text:
The browser and device negotiate a WebRTC peer-to-peer connection through the Breeze server:

1. `POST /remote/sessions` with `type: "desktop"` — creates the session record.
2. `GET /remote/ice-servers` — retrieve STUN/TURN server configuration.
3. `POST /remote/sessions/:id/offer` — send the SDP offer from the browser.
4. The authenticated device agent returns its answer and any endpoint consent verdict over its command-result channel.
5. `POST /remote/sessions/:id/ice` — exchange ICE candidates.
6. `POST /remote/sessions/:id/ws-ticket` — mint a one-time WebSocket ticket.
7. Connect via WebSocket using the ticket.

Once the P2P connection is active, screen data flows directly between the browser and the agent.

sections.heading: Session lease and revocation
Session time limits
sections.text:
Every remote desktop session has a hard limit of **12 hours**, enforced both by the server and independently by the agent. A remote-access configuration policy can shorten it through **Max session duration**, but nothing can extend it past 12 hours.

  "Unlimited" is no longer a valid setting. A policy that stored `0` (formerly "no maximum") or a value above 12 hours now behaves as 12 hours, and saving a new value outside the 1–12 hour range is rejected. Existing policies keep working — they are simply capped.

The separate **Idle timeout** setting is unchanged, including `0` meaning "no idle timeout".

sections.heading: Windows Session 0 Support
sections.text:
When the Breeze agent runs as a Windows service, it operates in Session 0 — an isolated session with no interactive desktop. Standard screen capture APIs (DXGI, GDI) and input injection all fail in Session 0.

Breeze solves this with a **session broker** architecture:

1. The agent service detects it is running in Session 0 via `config.IsService`.

2. The session broker enumerates active user sessions using the Windows Terminal Services API (WTS).

3. When a remote desktop session is requested, the broker spawns a **SYSTEM-level helper process** into the target user's session using `CreateProcessAsUser` with session ID override.

4. The helper process owns the entire WebRTC pipeline — DXGI screen capture, H264 encoding via Media Foundation, and WebRTC for streaming. The service only relays signaling messages (SDP offer/answer) over IPC.

5. When the session ends, the helper process is torn down.

<details>
<summary>Windows implementation details</summary>

The helper uses a SYSTEM token (not `WTSQueryUserToken`) intentionally. SYSTEM can call `OpenInputDesktop(GENERIC_ALL)` which grants access to the UAC consent desktop and lock screen — something a user-level token cannot do.

The `list_sessions` command returns available user sessions by merging the WTS session detector output with the broker's helper state, showing which sessions have active remote desktop connections.

</details>

sections.heading: macOS and Linux Headless Support
sections.text:
The same session broker architecture extends to macOS and Linux. When the agent runs as a LaunchDaemon (macOS) or systemd service (Linux), it has no display access. The agent detects this via the `IsHeadless` flag (checked by `hasConsole()` on Unix).

In headless mode, all desktop and screenshot commands are routed through IPC to the Breeze Helper process running in the user's desktop session, rather than attempting direct screen capture which would silently fail. The Helper handles screen capture using platform-native APIs (Core Graphics on macOS, X11 on Linux).

**Wayland sessions are not supported yet:**
  Remote desktop and screenshots on Linux require an X11 session. Wayland-only sessions -- the default GNOME and KDE sessions on current Ubuntu and Fedora releases, and wlroots compositors such as Hyprland and Sway -- cannot be captured. When the device has no X11 display at all, the device page reports **Wayland Unsupported** and the **Connect Desktop** button is disabled. On compositors that run XWayland for legacy apps, the agent may attach to that XWayland display instead, so a session can connect but shows only X11 application windows rather than the desktop. Terminal, scripts, and monitoring are unaffected either way. Where the login screen offers an X11 session, selecting it restores remote desktop. See [Supported Linux Distributions](/agents/installation/#supported-linux-distributions).

  If no Helper process is connected when a remote desktop session is requested in headless mode, the agent returns an error immediately rather than streaming zero frames.

sections.heading: Multi-Display Support
sections.text:
Breeze supports multi-monitor remote desktop. The viewer can switch between displays on the target device. Each display is captured independently using DXGI Desktop Duplication.

  DXGI Desktop Duplication is delta-based — a static display with no visual changes produces zero frames. Breeze forces a desktop repaint using `InvalidateRect` and `RedrawWindow` after a monitor switch to ensure the first frame is captured immediately.

sections.heading: Adaptive Bitrate
sections.text:
The remote desktop pipeline uses adaptive bitrate control to maintain smooth streaming across varying network conditions. The encoder adjusts the H264 bitrate based on:

- Measured network throughput between viewer and agent
- Frame delivery latency
- Packet loss rate

The bitrate ramps up when conditions are good and drops when congestion is detected. Sessions start at a conservative bitrate and ramp up over the first seconds after connect (a brief slow-start), so expect image quality to sharpen shortly after the session opens. Each increase requires a short run of stable measurements to prevent oscillation — the first step after congestion is deliberately gentle, then consecutive clean steps accelerate, so recovery after a network dip completes in seconds rather than a minute.

sections.heading: Audio Streaming
sections.text: Remote desktop sessions can optionally stream system audio from the device to the viewer. Audio is captured from the device's default audio output and transmitted over a separate WebRTC audio track. Audio streaming is enabled by default on Windows.

sections.heading: Secure Desktop Capture
sections.text: Breeze can capture the Windows secure desktop (Ctrl+Alt+Del screen, UAC prompts, lock screen). This is possible because the helper process runs as SYSTEM with `GENERIC_ALL` access to the input desktop. Secure desktop capture is automatic — no additional configuration is required.

sections.heading: Session Consent & End-User Notification
sections.text:
By default, when a technician starts a remote desktop session the person sitting at the device is told about it. You can tune this per [Configuration Policy](/features/configuration-policies/) on the **Remote Access** feature, choosing one of three session-prompt modes:

| Mode | What the end user experiences |
|------|-------------------------------|
| **Off** | Nothing is shown. The session starts silently. |
| **Notify** *(default)* | A desktop notification appears — "*Jordan Lee connected to your computer*" — and the session begins immediately. No approval is required. |
| **Consent** | A dialog asks the user to **Allow** or **Deny** before the technician can see the screen. The technician's view does not start until the user allows it. |

When a session is active, a small indicator ("*Jordan Lee is connected*" with a live timer) is shown at the top of the user's screen for the duration of the session, and a "*Remote session ended*" notice appears when the technician disconnects. Both can be turned off per policy. The on-screen indicator is drawn on Windows, and by Breeze Assist on macOS and Linux; without Assist, macOS and Linux show the start and end notices only.

**What the end user sees in Consent mode**

The prompt asks the user to allow or deny the remote session, naming the technician (to the level set by *Technician identity shown*) and their organization. It is drawn by one of two renderers, and which one appears depends on whether Breeze Assist is running in the user's session:

| Renderer | When it is used | What it looks like |
|----------|-----------------|--------------------|
| **Breeze Assist card** | Breeze Assist is running in the signed-in user's session. | A branded card with **Allow** and **Deny** buttons. |
| **Native dialog** | Breeze Assist is not running, but the Breeze user helper in that session can draw a system dialog. | A **Remote Support Request** dialog: a system message box with **Yes** / **No** on Windows, an **Allow** / **Deny** dialog on macOS, a `zenity` dialog on Linux (requires `zenity` installed and a graphical display). |

Consent mode therefore works without Breeze Assist. Both renderers show a **30-second countdown** (the API ships the length with the session start). The countdown starts only once the prompt is confirmed on screen, and the technician's view does not start until the user answers.

**Deny is the default button on both renderers**, so a stray Enter keypress never grants access. (Native dialogs defaulted to Yes / Allow on agents released before this was changed in [#10187](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/issues/10187); update the agent to get the Deny default.) If the user doesn't answer in time, the dialog closes itself and Breeze applies the policy's fallback on Windows (see *When consent can't be asked* below); on macOS and Linux an unanswered prompt is refused, because they can't tell whether the screen was locked. A prompt that expired while the session was locked or disconnected counts as "could not be shown", not as unanswered.

A session is refused most commonly when someone is signed in and **neither** renderer can reach them: Breeze Assist is not running and the user helper cannot draw a native dialog (for example a Linux session with no display or without `zenity`).

**Settings (per Configuration Policy → Remote Access)**

| Setting | Options | Default | Effect |
|---------|---------|---------|--------|
| Session prompt mode | Off / Notify / Consent | **Notify** | Whether the user is notified and/or must consent. |
| When consent can't be asked | Proceed / Block | **Proceed** | What happens when **no one is signed in** to the session being viewed, or when the signed-in user doesn't respond in time. **Proceed** connects anyway; **Block** refuses the session. An explicit **Deny** always blocks regardless of this setting. With current agents, a session where someone **is** signed in but the prompt can't be shown to them (neither Breeze Assist nor the native dialog can reach them) is always refused, whatever this is set to. |
| Notify on session end | On / Off | **On** | Whether the "session ended" notice is shown. |
| Show active-session indicator | On / Off | **On** | Whether the top-of-screen indicator appears during the session. |
| Technician identity shown | Name & email / Name only / Generic | **Name & email** | How much of the technician's identity is revealed to the end user, in the prompt and the notices. **Name & email** shows both, **Name only** omits the address, and **Generic** shows "*A technician*" with no name or email. |

  These surfaces are drawn in the signed-in user's desktop session by Breeze Assist or, when Assist isn't running, by the Breeze user helper's native dialogs. On an unattended machine (no user signed in), there is no one to notify or ask — in **Consent** mode, Breeze then applies the *"When consent can't be asked"* fallback. With **Proceed** (the default), unattended and headless machines are never locked out. If a user is signed in but neither can show them the prompt, current agents refuse the session instead of connecting without asking. Only Windows reports whether the screen is locked, so on macOS and Linux a prompt that times out is refused.

  **Upgrade behavior:** Because the default prompt mode is **Notify**, devices with the Breeze Helper installed begin showing a start notice for remote sessions after upgrade. To restore silent behavior, set the **Remote Access** feature on a Configuration Policy to prompt mode **Off**.

Every consent outcome is audit logged — granted, denied, blocked, or bypassed — with the reason (for example `no_user_session` when nobody is signed in, or `helper_unreachable` when a signed-in user could not be asked) and, from current agents, whether the prompt was shown (`consentOutcome`) and whether anyone was signed in (`consentOccupancy`). Each consent audit entry also records `consentProtocol`: `2` for current agents, `1` for older agents that do not report these fields.

When a session is refused, the technician sees a message naming the specific cause: nobody is signed in, the prompt could not be shown, the user could not see it, or another consent request is already waiting on that device. If the device's answer to the session start cannot be read (typically an agent and server on mismatched releases), the session fails with a message saying so instead of waiting for a timeout.

The same prompt, notice and indicator apply when the viewer falls back to the WebSocket (JPEG) transport. The technician's view stays on *connecting* until the agent reports that the stream started, so in Consent mode nothing is shown or sent before the user allows it; a denial or an unanswered prompt ends the session with the reason, just as on WebRTC.

sections.heading: GPU-Accelerated Streaming
sections.text:
Remote desktop uses hardware GPU encoding when available for better performance. The agent supports NVIDIA (NVENC), AMD (AMF), and Intel (QuickSync) GPUs and auto-selects the best encoder based on the device's hardware.

As of v0.89.0, hardware encoding on Windows is significantly more reliable and faster: a bug that caused Intel systems to silently fall back to software encoding has been fixed, encode latency is dramatically lower, and streams show fewer artifacts and less smearing at high resolutions. No configuration is needed — devices pick up the improvement with the agent update.

If the hardware encoder stalls (for example, due to a driver issue), the agent automatically switches to a software encoder within approximately 600 milliseconds — previous builds took around 11 seconds to recover. Headless servers without a GPU use software rendering automatically with no configuration needed.

sections.heading: VNC Fallback and In-Window Switcher (macOS)
sections.text:
Some macOS devices and scenarios — older releases, certain hardware configurations, or sessions started at the login screen — cannot use WebRTC remote desktop. Breeze auto-detects these situations and falls back to VNC via the built-in macOS Screen Sharing service.

In the **Breeze Viewer** desktop app, you can switch between WebRTC and VNC transports inside the same session window. If WebRTC degrades or fails, the viewer hands off to VNC without closing the window or losing your place. When conditions improve, you can switch back. From the web app, the **Remote Desktop** button hands off to the viewer via a deep link when VNC is the right transport, so the experience is consistent whether you start from the browser or the app.

When the fallback activates, the system tunnels VNC through the agent connection. When you disconnect, the VNC password is cleared — no credentials persist on the device.

  The agent no longer disables Apple Remote Management on startup. If you use Screen Sharing alongside Breeze, it stays enabled. VNC fallback behavior is controlled by the `manageRemoteManagement` Configuration Policy flag (off by default). When VNC is needed and Screen Sharing is not already enabled, the agent returns an informative error asking you to enable the policy or enable Screen Sharing manually on the device.

sections.heading: Session Switcher
sections.text:
A dropdown in the remote desktop toolbar shows all active user sessions on the target device. Click a session to switch to it — there is no need to disconnect and reconnect.

This is particularly useful on multi-user Windows servers and macOS machines with multiple logged-in users. If the switch fails for any reason, the viewer automatically recovers the previous session.

sections.heading: OS Keyboard Shortcuts
sections.text:
The viewer toolbar includes a keyboard shortcut menu that adapts to the target device's operating system:

- **Windows**: Ctrl+Alt+Del, Win+L, Win+R, and other system shortcuts
- **macOS**: Cmd+Option+Esc, Cmd+Q, and other macOS shortcuts
- **Linux**: Ctrl+Alt+Backspace and other Linux shortcuts

Select a shortcut from the menu to inject it into the remote session. This avoids the problem of your local operating system intercepting the key combination before it reaches the viewer.

sections.heading: Viewer Shortcuts
sections.text:
The Breeze Viewer keeps its own shortcuts behind one prefix chord that remote applications do not use, so every other key combination reaches the remote:

| Action | Windows / Linux | macOS |
|--------|-----------------|-------|
| Fullscreen (toggle) | Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F | ⌃⌥⌘F |
| Paste as keystrokes (**Paste Text**) | Ctrl+Alt+Shift+V | ⌃⌥⌘V |
| **Release stuck keys** (in the toolbar's overflow menu) | Ctrl+Alt+Shift+R | ⌃⌥⌘R |

From v0.122.1, Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+V and Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+F are no longer viewer shortcuts: they go to the remote, so paste-as-plain-text and Find in Files work in remote applications.

sections.heading: Keyboard and Mouse Input
sections.text:
- **Nothing stays held down.** When the viewer window loses focus or the session drops, the viewer and agent release every key and mouse button they pressed on the remote. If a key still seems stuck, use **Release stuck keys**.
- **German and French keyboards** (QWERTZ and AZERTY) type the right letters on Windows and Linux remotes.

sections.heading: Keyboard Mode
sections.text:
The **Keyboard mode** control in the Breeze Viewer toolbar (v0.123.0+) sets how your keystrokes reach the remote:

- **Type what I see** (default). The remote resolves each key through its own keyboard layout, so the characters you see on your keys are what gets typed. IME composition (Chinese, Japanese, Korean input) and dead keys (for example ´ then E for É) are sent as finished text once you commit them. The remote sees nothing until the composition is committed.
- **Physical keys**. The viewer sends the physical key position, which keeps distinctions such as the numpad and the right-hand modifier keys. It needs a WebRTC session and an agent from v0.123.0 or later; on an older agent or a WebSocket session the option is disabled and its tooltip says why.

The mode is remembered for each device, and the last mode you chose becomes the default for devices that have no choice of their own. Keyboard mode does not apply to VNC sessions.

sections.heading: Viewer Options
sections.text:
The toolbar's **More options** menu (v0.123.0+) adds:

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| **View only** | Stops sending your keyboard and mouse to the remote, so you can watch without clicking anything by accident. Turning it on releases any held keys first, and an indicator shows while it is on. Nothing is sent to the device; it only affects your viewer. |
| **Block remote input** | Blocks the keyboard and mouse at the remote device while you work. WebRTC sessions only. The option is disabled when the device does not support it, and the toggle shows the device's confirmed state rather than assuming the request worked. |
| **Stats overlay** | Shows round-trip time, frame rate, bitrate, packet loss, codec and connection path. Off by default. |
| **Copy screenshot** / **Save screenshot** | Captures the current frame to your clipboard, or saves it as a PNG in your Pictures folder (Downloads if there is none). Screenshots stay on your machine and are never uploaded. |
| **Fit to window** / **100% (scroll)** | Scales the remote screen to the window, or shows it at one remote pixel per screen point with scrollbars. |

Scaling and audio are remembered per device, along with keyboard mode. These preferences are stored by the Breeze Viewer on your computer and are never sent to Breeze.

**Fullscreen keyboard lock.** In fullscreen, the viewer captures system shortcuts such as Alt+Tab, the Windows key and Esc, so they reach the remote instead of your computer. Exit fullscreen with the toolbar button or the fullscreen shortcut. Where the platform does not support keyboard lock, nothing changes and **Send Keys** remains the way to send those combinations.

**macOS viewer.** Cmd+H, Cmd+M and Cmd+W go to the remote; Hide, Minimize and Close Window are still in the menu bar. Cmd+Q asks before quitting while sessions are open.

sections.heading: Clipboard
sections.text:
On a WebRTC session the clipboard syncs in both directions: text up to 1 MiB and PNG or JPEG images up to 8 MiB. Each direction is a separate setting on the **Remote Access** feature of a configuration policy: **Clipboard: remote → viewer (copy from remote)** and **Clipboard: viewer → remote (paste to remote)**. Copying from the remote is the data-egress direction (whatever the end user copies reaches the technician) and is off by default on hosted Breeze.

The **Clipboard** chip in the viewer toolbar (it reads **Clipboard off** when both directions are disabled) shows what policy allows in each direction (*Remote → local* and *Local → remote*, each **On** or **Disabled by policy**) and the last transfer. Its menu has two actions:

- **Copy remote clipboard** brings the remote clipboard to your machine, for example when the viewer was in the background when something was copied on the remote.
- **Send clipboard to remote** pushes your clipboard to the remote, for applications where you paste from a menu rather than with a keyboard shortcut.

Pressing the remote's paste shortcut sends your clipboard first. If it can't be delivered (too large, disabled by policy, or the connection dropped), the paste is cancelled with a *Nothing pasted* message instead of pasting whatever was on the remote clipboard before. Connecting to a session no longer overwrites your local clipboard with the remote's.

Clipboard v2 needs agent and Breeze Viewer v0.122.1 or later. With an older agent the chip reports that the agent did not report clipboard status: text only, policy unknown. On a VNC session the clipboard is text only.

**Known gap: images copied on a Windows device:**
  An image copied on a Windows device does not reach the viewer yet. The desktop session runs as SYSTEM and cannot read the user's copied image formats. Text copies work in both directions, and images pasted *into* a Windows device are not affected. A fix is planned for a follow-up release.

sections.heading: Login Screen (macOS)
sections.text:
WebRTC remote desktop cannot control a Mac at the login window. macOS blocks remote keyboard and mouse input there for third-party agents, so a session would show the login screen while ignoring every click and keystroke. The agent therefore refuses to start a WebRTC session while the Mac is at the login window:

- If **VNC Relay** is enabled in the device's configuration policy, **Connect Desktop** opens VNC Relay instead. VNC Relay drives the login screen through macOS Screen Sharing, so you can sign in remotely.
- If VNC Relay is not enabled, Connect Desktop explains that the Mac is at the login window and how to enable VNC Relay. The Breeze Viewer shows the same reason if it was already open.
- If a user signs out during a session, the session ends with the same explanation instead of continuing as video only. Reconnect with VNC Relay, or connect again after a user signs in.

sections.heading: Network Proxy
sections.text:
Network Proxy lets you access web-based admin UIs on an agent's local network without a VPN — router web interfaces, NAS management panels, printer admin pages, switch management ports, and similar resources. There is no persistent tunnel: each request the browser makes to the target device is relayed as a separate command over the agent's existing connection, fetched locally by the agent, and returned. This keeps the network footprint minimal, but it does mean the target's own web UI runs through a per-request proxy rather than a raw socket — no WebSocket-based device UIs, and individual responses are capped at 16 MiB.

**Starting a proxy session:**

1. Go to **Devices → Network** and open the discovered device's detail page.

2. Find the open port for the service you want to reach (80, 443, 8080, and similar web ports are detected automatically) and click **Open Web UI** on that port.

3. In the **Proxy to `ip:port`** popover, pick the agent to proxy **through**. This defaults to the agent that discovered the device on its network — not any device you've linked to this asset for identity purposes, since bridging traffic through the identity-linked device would be a loopback. Choose a different online agent if needed, set the scheme, and check **Allow self-signed certificate** up front if you already know the target uses one (common for printers, iLO/IPMI, and switches).

4. Click **Connect**. The LAN device's web UI opens in a new tab.

  If the target device uses a self-signed certificate and you didn't check the box up front, the request fails with an untrusted-certificate error and the session shows a **Reconnect allowing self-signed certificate** button in place. Clicking it opens a fresh session to the same target with certificate verification skipped — it does not change any persistent trust settings, and it only applies to that session.

**Path mode and host mode:**

By default Network Proxy runs in **path mode**: the device's pages are served under your Breeze hostname, and Breeze rewrites links and sandboxes the frame. Some device UIs still misbehave, usually ones that build absolute URLs or depend on their own cookies or local storage.

If your administrator has set up a dedicated tunnel domain, a partner can turn on **Serve Network Proxy from a dedicated origin** in **Settings → Partner → Remote Access**. Each tunnel then gets its own origin, so the device UI behaves as it does on its own address. The setting applies to every organization under the partner. If your browser blocks cookies or storage for the embedded device page, a notice appears with an **Open In New Tab** button. Without a second domain, nothing changes and path mode keeps working. Administrators: see [Network Proxy Dedicated Origin](/deploy/network-proxy-tunnel-origin/).

**Session lifetime:**

A proxy session stays alive as long as it's actively used: each request slides the session's expiry forward, so there's no fixed cutoff while you're working — up to an absolute cap of 12 hours from when the session started. If the session sits idle for 10 minutes with no requests, it stops sliding and the page shows a **Session expired — Reconnect** state instead of silently failing behind the scenes. Clicking **Reconnect** reloads the embedded page from scratch, so any in-progress form state on the target device's own web UI (for example, a partially filled-out printer configuration page) is lost — save your work on the target's UI before stepping away for a while.

**Security model:**

- **Default-deny allowlists** control which destinations agents can proxy to. Configure allowlists per-site in **Settings → Remote Access**. Connecting through the popover automatically allowlists the single `ip:port` you connected to — it does not open the whole host.
- **Source IP restrictions** limit which users or networks can open proxy sessions.
- Idle timeout and an absolute 12-hour session cap apply to prevent long-lived, unattended sessions.
- A built-in SSRF-safe blocklist prevents proxying to internal metadata endpoints and loopback addresses.
- Each proxy session is associated with a specific user and fully audit logged.

sections.heading: Wake-on-LAN
sections.text:
Wake-on-LAN powers on an offline device from the Breeze dashboard without visiting it physically. Because the Breeze server cannot send packets on your local network, the wake is relayed through another online agent on the same network as the target.

**Requirements:**

- The target device must have Wake-on-LAN enabled in its BIOS/UEFI (often labelled "Power on by LAN" or "Wake on Magic Packet").
- The target must have checked in at least once so Breeze has its MAC address(es) and one or more recorded non-APIPA IPv4 subnets. APIPA addresses (`169.254.0.0/16`) are skipped — they're a sign of a broken DHCP lease and don't represent the real LAN.
- At least one other agent must be online at the same site and on a matching subnet to relay the magic packet. Breeze tries every plausible candidate subnet recorded for the target, in priority order, until one succeeds.

**Sending a wake:**

1. Go to **Devices** and open the offline device's detail page.

2. Click **Actions** and select **Wake**.

3. Breeze automatically chooses an online relay agent at the target's site and subnet, sends the magic packet, and reports the relay device and MAC addresses attempted.

If a wake cannot be sent, Breeze returns a specific reason rather than failing silently — the most common are: the target has no recorded MAC address, no known IPv4 subnet (only IPv6), or no online agent is available at its site and subnet to relay the packet. Every wake attempt — successful or not — is recorded in the audit log with the actor, target, relay device, MACs attempted, and result.

sections.heading: Pluggable Remote-Desktop Launcher
sections.text:
By default, **Connect → Desktop** opens the built-in Breeze WebRTC desktop session. MSPs that standardise on a third-party tool (RustDesk, ScreenConnect, TeamViewer, AnyDesk, and similar) can configure Breeze to hand off to that tool instead, per partner.

**Configuring a provider:**

1. Go to **Settings** and open **Remote Access** (under Security & Access; partner-level access required).

2. Keep the built-in WebRTC desktop session (the default, which cannot be deleted), or click **Add provider**.

3. Give the provider a name and a launch-URL template. The template supports placeholders that Breeze substitutes at click time:
   - `{id}` — the device's per-tool identifier, read from a device custom field
   - `{password}` — an optional preset password (URL-encoded automatically)
   - `{customFieldKey}` — the value of any device custom field by key

   Example: `rustdesk://{id}?password={password}` or `https://acme.screenconnect.com/Host#Access///{id}/Join`.

4. Specify the custom-field key that holds each device's identifier (for example `rustdesk_id`), and optionally a preset password. Mark the provider **Enabled**, and **Default** if it should replace the built-in launcher.

Each device then needs that custom field populated with its identifier for the tool. When a user clicks **Connect → Desktop**, Breeze substitutes the values and either opens the URL in a new browser tab (`http`/`https`) or hands it to the operating system's protocol handler (any other scheme, e.g. `rustdesk://`). If the launcher can't issue a URL — provider disabled, no provider configured, device is missing the required custom field, or the resolved URL fails the scheme check — the UI surfaces the specific reason instead of silently falling back to WebRTC, so you can fix the configuration rather than guess why a click did nothing.

**Security:**

- Launch URLs are validated against an allowed-scheme list both when the template is saved and again when the URL is issued. Dangerous schemes (`javascript:`, `data:`, `vbscript:`, `file:`, `about:`, `chrome:`, `jar:`, `blob:`, `view-source:`, `filesystem:`) are rejected.
- Preset passwords are stored server-side only and are never embedded in the web bundle or earlier API responses. The launch URL is issued one-shot in response to an explicit user click and each issuance is audit logged.

**Per-technician preference.** Each technician can pick their own remote tool from the tenant's enabled providers under **Settings → Profile → Preferred remote tool**. The preference only selects among providers the partner has already configured — it can never add one — and only affects that user's own **Connect → Desktop** clicks. If the chosen provider is later disabled or deleted, launches fall back to the tenant default. The chooser is hidden from users without remote-access permission.

---

sections.heading: Remote Terminal
sections.text:
Remote Terminal opens an interactive shell session rendered in the browser using xterm.js. It is a PTY session on the device — keystrokes are sent to the device's shell and output is streamed back in real time, with full terminal emulation including colour, cursor control, and resizing.

On Windows, terminal sessions use the modern **ConPTY** pseudo-console API, so colours, resizing, and interactive prompts behave the same as a local PowerShell window. macOS and Linux use a standard POSIX PTY.

sections.heading: Starting a terminal session
sections.text:
1. Navigate to **Devices**, locate the target device, and open its detail page.

2. Click **Connect** and select **Terminal**.

3. A browser terminal window opens. Wait for the **connected** indicator in the toolbar before typing — the terminal is ready only after the WebRTC P2P connection is fully established and the agent confirms the PTY is open.

4. Resizing the browser window (or the terminal pane) automatically adjusts the PTY dimensions on the device.

sections.heading: Connection flow
sections.text:
The connection flow is identical to Remote Desktop:

1. `POST /remote/sessions` with `type: "terminal"` — creates the session record.
2. `GET /remote/ice-servers` — retrieve STUN/TURN configuration.
3. `POST /remote/sessions/:id/offer` — send the SDP offer.
4. `POST /remote/sessions/:id/ws-ticket` — mint the WebSocket ticket.
5. Connect via WebSocket using the ticket.

---

sections.heading: Quick Support (ad-hoc sessions)
sections.text:
Quick Support connects you to a machine that runs **no permanently enrolled agent** — a customer's home PC, a prospect's laptop, a device not yet onboarded. Rather than enrolling the device for real, the end user runs a client that exists only for the duration of one session.

1. On **Remote Access → Quick Support**, create a session. Optionally attribute it to a customer organization and add a label (e.g. "Contoso — CFO laptop"). Attribution is for reporting only; it does not grant or change access to that customer's data.

2. Breeze returns a one-time code (`234-567-892`) and a link. Codes are digits only (2–9, with no 0 or 1) and displayed in groups of three so they read cleanly over the phone. **The code is shown once and cannot be retrieved again.** It expires in 15 minutes. Codes issued before v0.105.0 that contain letters remain redeemable.

3. Send the link or read the code out. The end user opens the link, downloads the client, and runs it. The code is embedded in the download's filename, so they normally never type it — the landing page also accepts manual code entry if they arrive without one.

4. When the client connects, the session becomes **Ready** and a Connect button appears. From there it is an ordinary remote desktop session.

5. **End session** revokes the client's credentials, tells it to remove itself, and drops its connection.

Clicking a row in the session history re-opens a live detail panel for that session — you can connect to (or end) a still-active session from history; only the one-time code stays create-time-only.

  Quick Support requires **partner scope**. An organization-scoped login cannot create these sessions. Sessions are visible to all technicians at your partner, not only their creator.

**What the end user's machine gets.** The client runs in the user's own session, is not installed as a service, and deletes itself when the session ends. It enrolls an *ephemeral* device that is deliberately invisible to the rest of Breeze: it never counts toward your device licence, never appears in device lists, reports or invoices, and is never patched, rebooted, backed up or alerted on. The reaper removes the device record six hours after the session ends.

**How a session ends.** Whichever comes first: you end it; the end user closes the client (detected when the device goes offline); or the eight-hour hard cap expires. If the self-destruct command is ever lost, the client's own ten-minute dead-man switch shuts it down.

**What the end user sees (v0.121.0+).** A standard (non-admin) Windows user can start Quick Support. The client keeps its configuration, state and logs in its own private session folder, never in an installed agent's folders. While a technician is viewing, the user sees an always-on-top "*Technician* is viewing your screen" pill with a session clock, and the support window names the technician and says how to stop sharing (close the window or press Ctrl+C). The indicator always shows during Quick Support, whatever the remote access policy's indicator setting says, because the user started the session themselves.

**AI screen tools are refused.** AI screenshots, screen analysis, computer control and **Diagnose** are refused for a Quick Support device with `409 SCREEN_ACCESS_UNAVAILABLE_IN_QUICK_SUPPORT`, because they would act outside the desktop session where the indicator is shown. Use the remote desktop session instead.

  Phase 1 ships a **Windows** client. macOS is planned. The elevated mode that allows control of UAC prompts is not yet available — the client currently runs with the end user's own privileges.

---

sections.heading: Who's Connected
sections.text:
When a colleague already has a live **Desktop**, **Terminal** or VNC session on a device, the device page shows a banner such as *Someone else has a session on this device* (or *N other people have sessions on this device*), with one row per person naming them, the session type and how long it has been open (or *connecting…*). Your own sessions are not listed. The banner is informational only: it never blocks or ends a session. It refreshes every 60 seconds while the tab is visible, and straight away when you return to the tab or the device's status changes. It needs `remote:access` and `devices:read`; an offline device shows no banner.

---

sections.heading: Session Lifecycle
sections.text:
All session types follow the same state machine:

```
pending → connecting → active → disconnected / failed / denied
```

| State | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `pending` | Session record created; device agent has not yet acknowledged the request |
| `connecting` | Device acknowledged; SDP offer/answer exchange and ICE negotiation in progress |
| `active` | WebRTC P2P connection established; data flowing between browser and device |
| `disconnected` | Session ended normally — user closed it or the agent reported a clean disconnect |
| `failed` | Connection could not be established, or an active connection dropped unexpectedly |
| `denied` | The end user declined the connection at the consent prompt (or the policy's *"When consent can't be asked"* fallback was set to **Block**). The technician sees that the user denied the remote connection. |

A session ended by the lease recheck (see [Session lease and revocation](#session-lease-and-revocation)) becomes `disconnected` with a recorded reason such as `revoked:membership_removed`, `revoked:permissions_changed`, `revoked:site_scope_lost` or `revoked:hard_deadline`, which appears in the session's history entry.

When a session ends (`disconnected` or `failed`), the platform records `durationSeconds` (calculated from start time). The `bytesTransferred` field is available but must be supplied by the caller when ending the session via `POST /remote/sessions/:id/end`.

---

sections.heading: Session Recording
sections.text:
Breeze does not record sessions itself. What it provides is a place to attach a link to a recording produced elsewhere — for example, a screen-recording pipeline your organization runs alongside remote sessions — and a way for technicians to open that link later from the session's history entry.

If the caller ending a session (`POST /remote/sessions/:id/end`) includes a `recordingUrl` in the request body, it is stored on the session. Only an absolute `http(s)` URL on an allow-listed origin (`RECORDING_URL_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`), or a same-origin path starting with `/`, is accepted — anything else is rejected.

1. Go to **Remote Access → Session History**.
2. Click a row to open its details panel.
3. If a recording link was attached when the session ended, a **Recording** section appears with a **View Recording** button that opens the link in a new tab. Sessions ended without a `recordingUrl` show no such section.

---

sections.heading: Rate Limits
sections.text:
Breeze enforces per-organisation and per-user limits on concurrent remote access resources. When a limit is reached, the creation request returns `429 Too Many Requests`.

| Resource | Per-org | Per-user |
|----------|---------|----------|
| Active sessions | 10 | 5 |

These defaults are configurable via environment variables on the API server:

| Variable | Default |
|----------|---------|
| `MAX_ACTIVE_REMOTE_SESSIONS_PER_ORG` | 10 |
| `MAX_ACTIVE_REMOTE_SESSIONS_PER_USER` | 5 |

sections.heading: Terminal input ceiling
sections.text:
Each terminal session has an abuse ceiling on keyboard/paste input, measured over a sliding 60-second window. It is deliberately far above normal use (every key press, arrow key and key repeat is one message). If a client exceeds it, the excess input is dropped and the terminal shows a one-time warning; the session stays open and input resumes once the burst leaves the window.

| Variable | Default |
|----------|---------|
| `TERMINAL_INPUT_MAX_MESSAGES_PER_MIN` | 6000 |
| `TERMINAL_INPUT_MAX_BYTES_PER_MIN` | 8388608 (8 MiB) |

To free session capacity, close active sessions from the Active Sessions list on the device detail page, or call `DELETE /remote/sessions/stale` — this marks `pending`, `connecting`, and `active` sessions as `disconnected`. Be aware this terminates any currently active sessions, not just stale ones.

---

sections.heading: Security
sections.text:
**MFA required for all remote access.** Every session creation request is gated by MFA verification at the route level. A valid MFA check must be present before a remote session can be created.

**Server is a signaling relay for WebRTC.** The Breeze server brokers WebRTC negotiation (SDP offer/answer and ICE candidates). Once the P2P connection is established, device data does not transit the server. If the WebSocket fallback is active, frame data is relayed through the server but is not persisted.

**All sessions are audit logged.** Every session creation, state transition, and termination is recorded with the actor identity, device identifier, start time, end time, duration in seconds, and bytes transferred. Audit records are immutable.

**Clipboard activity is summarised, never recorded.** Each desktop session writes one `session_clipboard_summary` audit entry describing its clipboard activity. Clipboard content is never logged.

**Consent is audit logged.** When session consent or notification is enabled by policy, each session records whether the end user granted, denied, or had consent bypassed (with the reason — for example, no user logged in), alongside the technician identity disclosed.

**Remote access requires the `remote:access` permission.** This permission is not granted by default on all roles. Navigate to **Settings → Roles** if a user receives "Access denied" when creating a session.

---

sections.heading: Sessions
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| POST | `/remote/sessions` | Create a session (body: `deviceId`, `type`) |
| GET | `/remote/sessions` | List sessions (`?deviceId=&status=&type=&includeEnded=`) |
| GET | `/remote/sessions/:id` | Get session details |
| GET | `/remote/sessions/history` | Session statistics (total sessions, total duration, average duration) |
| DELETE | `/remote/sessions/stale` | Terminate all pending, connecting, and active sessions |
| GET | `/remote/devices/:deviceId/active-sessions` | Live sessions on a device (all users), for the [Who's Connected](#whos-connected) banner |
| GET | `/remote/ice-servers` | Get ICE/TURN server configuration for WebRTC |
| POST | `/remote/sessions/:id/offer` | Send SDP offer from browser to device |
| POST | `/remote/sessions/:id/ice` | Exchange ICE candidates between browser and device |
| POST | `/remote/sessions/:id/ws-ticket` | Mint a one-time WebSocket ticket (required for terminal and desktop) |
| POST | `/remote/sessions/:id/end` | End a session (optional body: `bytesTransferred`, `recordingUrl` — see [Session Recording](#session-recording)) |

sections.heading: Network Proxy Tunnels
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| POST | `/remote/tunnels` | Create a tunnel session (body: `deviceId`, `targetHost`, `targetPort`) |
| GET | `/remote/tunnels` | List active tunnel sessions (`?deviceId=&status=`) |
| DELETE | `/remote/tunnels/:id` | Close a tunnel session |
| GET | `/remote/tunnels/allowlists` | List proxy allowlists for a site |
| POST | `/remote/tunnels/allowlists` | Create or update a proxy allowlist entry |
| DELETE | `/remote/tunnels/allowlists/:id` | Remove a proxy allowlist entry |

sections.heading: Wake-on-LAN & Remote-Desktop Launcher
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| POST | `/devices/:id/commands` | Body `{ "type": "wake" }` — dispatch a Wake-on-LAN magic packet to the device via an automatically selected relay agent. Returns the relay device and MACs attempted, or a specific failure reason. |
| POST | `/mobile/devices/:id/actions` | Body `{ "action": "wake" }` — equivalent quick-action wake used by the mobile app. |
| POST | `/devices/:id/remote-access-launch` | Issue a one-shot remote-desktop launch URL for the device's configured provider. Returns the resolved `launchUrl` and scheme, or `422` if no provider applies or the scheme is disallowed. |

Remote-access providers are configured per partner under **Settings → Remote**; see [Pluggable Remote-Desktop Launcher](#pluggable-remote-desktop-launcher).

sections.heading: Events
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| GET | `/events/ws` | Real-time event WebSocket — streams device status changes, alert triggers, and session lifecycle events |

---

sections.heading: Linux viewer (AppImage)
sections.text:
The Linux build of the Breeze Viewer ships as a single AppImage, `breeze-viewer-linux.AppImage`. Unlike the Windows MSI and the macOS DMG it is not installed — you download it, mark it executable, and run it once so it can register itself as the handler for `breeze://` links. Until that first run, choosing **Connect Desktop** in the console has nothing to hand the session to, and the download card reappears on every attempt.

1. Mark the download executable:

```bash
   chmod +x ~/Downloads/breeze-viewer-linux.AppImage
```

2. Run it once. A small "Breeze Viewer is ready" window confirms it launched and registered the `breeze://` scheme. You can close that window — the console reopens the viewer when a session starts.

```bash
   ~/Downloads/breeze-viewer-linux.AppImage
```

3. Confirm the scheme is claimed:

```bash
   xdg-mime query default x-scheme-handler/breeze
   # → breeze-viewer.desktop
```

Keep the AppImage at a stable path. The registration records the absolute path it was run from, so moving or deleting the file after the first run leaves `breeze://` pointing at a file that no longer exists — run it again from the new location to refresh the entry.

sections.heading: FUSE 2 is required
sections.text:
The AppImage runtime mounts itself with FUSE 2 at launch. On a distribution that no longer ships FUSE 2 by default, the AppImage exits immediately with a message about `libfuse.so.2`, `dlopen`, or `fusermount`, and no window ever appears.

The package that provides it was renamed as part of Debian's 64-bit `time_t` (`t64`) transition, which is why the familiar package name no longer resolves on current releases:

| Distribution | Package to install |
|---|---|
| Debian 13 (trixie) and newer, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and newer | `libfuse2t64` |
| Debian 12 and older, Ubuntu 22.04 and older | `libfuse2` |
| Fedora / RHEL | `fuse-libs` |
| Arch | `fuse2` |
| openSUSE | `libfuse2` (plus `fuse` for `fusermount`) |

```bash
# Debian 13 / Ubuntu 24.04+
sudo apt install libfuse2t64
```

`sudo apt install libfuse2` also works on those releases — apt reports `Note, selecting 'libfuse2t64' instead of 'libfuse2'` and installs the renamed package. That message is informational, not an error.

sections.heading: Running without FUSE
sections.text:
If you cannot install FUSE 2 — a hardened host, a container, or a policy that forbids the `fuse` kernel module — the AppImage can unpack itself to a temporary directory and run from there instead of mounting:

```bash
~/Downloads/breeze-viewer-linux.AppImage --appimage-extract-and-run
```

This works for a one-off session but is not a substitute for the first run above: the `Exec=` line written into the desktop entry does not carry the flag, so `breeze://` links launched from the console still take the FUSE path. To make the fallback permanent, set it in the environment the desktop session inherits:

```bash
# e.g. in ~/.profile
export APPIMAGE_EXTRACT_AND_RUN=1
```

Extract-and-run unpacks the whole bundle on every launch, so sessions start noticeably slower and each launch writes to `$TMPDIR`. Installing FUSE 2 is the better outcome where it is allowed.

sections.heading: WebRTC needs webkit2gtk built with the GStreamer plugins
sections.text:
The Linux viewer renders in webkit2gtk, the system WebView, rather than bundling its own browser engine. Whether WebRTC is available therefore depends on how your distribution compiled webkit2gtk and which GStreamer plugins are installed. This shows up two ways: on some builds `RTCPeerConnection` is not exposed at all, and on others it exists but fails the moment a connection is actually created.

The viewer handles both. The first is detected before connecting, so WebRTC is skipped outright; the second is discovered on the first attempt, after which the viewer stops retrying WebRTC for the rest of the session. Either way it falls back to the WebSocket (JPEG) transport, a notice in the session window explains the switch, and the toolbar badge reads **WS** rather than **WebRTC**. The session still works; you lose the WebRTC-only features:

| Available on WebSocket | Not available on WebSocket |
|---|---|
| Screen view, keyboard, mouse | Remote audio |
| Paste as keystrokes | Clipboard sync |
| Quality, scale and FPS limit | Multi-monitor switching |
| Reconnect, session end | Bitrate control |
| | Secure attention sequence (Ctrl+Alt+Del) |
| | Switching between user sessions |
| | Low-latency cursor streaming |

**Paste Text and keyboard layouts:**
  On a WebRTC session, **Paste Text** delivers the text literally, so accented
  characters and symbols arrive as typed regardless of the keyboard layout on
  either end. On the WebSocket fallback, paste is replayed as individual
  keystrokes and is still interpreted through the remote machine's layout —
  a non-US layout can turn `/` into `?` or drop characters. If pasted text
  arrives mangled, check whether the toolbar badge reads **WS**.

To get WebRTC, install the GStreamer plugin sets webkit2gtk uses for it, then relaunch the viewer:

```bash
# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt install gstreamer1.0-plugins-base gstreamer1.0-plugins-good \
  gstreamer1.0-plugins-bad gstreamer1.0-libav

# Fedora / RHEL
sudo dnf install gstreamer1-plugins-base gstreamer1-plugins-good \
  gstreamer1-plugins-bad-free gstreamer1-libav

# Arch
sudo pacman -S gst-plugins-base gst-plugins-good gst-plugins-bad gst-libav
```

  Some distributions ship a webkit2gtk built without WebRTC support regardless of which GStreamer plugins are present. If the viewer still reports no WebRTC after installing them, the WebSocket transport is the expected behavior on that host — remote desktop keeps working, at lower video quality.

sections.heading: Viewer launches but no window appears
sections.text: If the process shows up in `ps` but nothing is drawn, FUSE is working and the problem is the desktop stack, not packaging — typically a host GTK module or `gvfs` build that is incompatible with the bundled runtime. Run the AppImage from a terminal and read the messages: `Failed to load module` and `undefined symbol` lines name the offending host library. Starting with a clean environment (`env -i DISPLAY=$DISPLAY HOME=$HOME ~/Downloads/breeze-viewer-linux.AppImage`) confirms whether a host module is being injected.

sections.heading: Gray window with no controls on NVIDIA
sections.text:
On the NVIDIA driver, webkit2gtk's DMA-BUF renderer can fail to paint anything: the viewer window opens solid gray, with no toolbar, no transport badge and no buttons. The viewer now works around this itself. At startup on Linux it checks whether the NVIDIA kernel driver is loaded (`/proc/driver/nvidia/version` or `/sys/module/nvidia` exists) and, if so, sets `WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER=1` before its first window opens. webkit2gtk then falls back to its older compositing path. Run from a terminal, the viewer prints a line saying it did this.

The viewer never overrides a value you set yourself:

- **Gray window on a machine without the NVIDIA driver** (nouveau, some virtual machines): force the workaround on.

```bash
  WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER=1 ~/Downloads/breeze-viewer-linux.AppImage
```

- **NVIDIA machine where the DMA-BUF renderer works and you want to keep it**: set the variable to `0` and the viewer leaves it alone.

```bash
  WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER=0 ~/Downloads/breeze-viewer-linux.AppImage
```

To make either choice permanent, export the variable from your shell profile or put it in a small launcher script.

**Do not set LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE or GDK_BACKEND:**
  Workarounds posted for other webkit2gtk apps often also set `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1` and `GDK_BACKEND=x11`. Neither is needed for the gray window. `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1` moves all rendering onto the CPU, which makes remote video slow. `GDK_BACKEND=x11` forces XWayland on a Wayland desktop. If you added either to a launcher script for the viewer, remove it.

---

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**Linux viewer does nothing when run.**
The AppImage needs FUSE 2 to mount itself. On Debian 13 / Ubuntu 24.04+ the package is `libfuse2t64`, not `libfuse2`. See [Linux viewer (AppImage)](#linux-viewer-appimage) for the per-distribution package names and the `--appimage-extract-and-run` fallback.

**Linux viewer opens a gray window with no toolbar or buttons.**
This is webkit2gtk's DMA-BUF renderer failing, most often on the NVIDIA driver. The viewer disables that renderer automatically when it detects the NVIDIA driver; on other hosts, launch it with `WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER=1`. See [Gray window with no controls on NVIDIA](#gray-window-with-no-controls-on-nvidia).

**Linux viewer always connects on the WebSocket transport, never WebRTC.**
The host's webkit2gtk build does not expose `RTCPeerConnection`, so the viewer skips WebRTC and uses the WebSocket (JPEG) transport. The session window shows a notice saying so, and the browser console logs `WebRTC is unavailable in this WebView (no RTCPeerConnection global)`. Installing the GStreamer plugin sets usually restores it — see [WebRTC needs webkit2gtk built with the GStreamer plugins](#webrtc-needs-webkit2gtk-built-with-the-gstreamer-plugins). This is a property of the host, not of the device you are connecting to.

**Session stuck in `connecting`.**
WebRTC negotiation failed and the viewer has not yet fallen back to WebSocket. Confirm the device is online and the agent WebSocket connection is active (check the device detail page). Common causes:

- **TURN not configured** — Verify `TURN_HOST` and `TURN_SECRET` are set in `.env` and the coturn container is running (`docker compose logs coturn`). If using an external TURN server, check its status via SSH.
- **Firewall blocking TURN ports** — Coturn needs TCP and UDP port 3478, plus UDP ports in the relay range (default 49152–65535, or tightened to 49152–49252). Verify the ports are reachable with `nc -z -w 3 TURN_IP 3478` (TCP) and `nc -u -z -w 3 TURN_IP 3478` (UDP).
- **Wrong `TURN_HOST`** — Must be the TURN server's public IP, not a private address. If Breeze is behind Cloudflare Tunnel, TURN must run on a separate host with its own public IP — see [TURN Server](/deploy/turn-server/).
- **Shared secret mismatch** — `TURN_SECRET` in `.env` must exactly match `static-auth-secret` in the coturn config.

The viewer should automatically fall back to the WebSocket transport after a timeout.

**Poor video quality, high latency, or stalls — where are the WebRTC diagnostics?**
While a desktop session is live, the device emits two periodic diagnostic lines: `Viewer WebRTC stats` (RTT, jitter, packet loss, frame drops as reported by the viewer) and `Desktop WebRTC metrics` (`captureMs`, `convertMs`, `encodeMs`, frames captured/encoded/sent, bandwidth). Both are shipped to **Devices → Select Device → Agent Logs** for the duration of the session regardless of `log_shipping_level`, so you do not need to lower the level to see them. Read `captureMs` against `encodeMs`: a high `captureMs` with a low `encodeMs` means the screen capturer is the bottleneck, not the encoder.

On macOS with `isService=true` the desktop-helper writes the same lines locally to `/Library/Application Support/Breeze/logs/desktop-helper.log`; on Windows they are in `C:\ProgramData\Breeze\logs\user-helper.log`. The Windows user-role helper (toasts, chat, user-context scripts) runs as the logged-in user and writes `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Breeze\logs\user-helper.log` in that user's profile instead. Windows helpers have no log-shipping credentials of their own, so they relay their warning and error lines to the agent, which records them in Agent Logs under component `helper` with `helperRole` and `helperSessionId` (capped at about 20 lines a minute per helper). If the helper logs `Log shipping disabled: helper config is missing required keys` at startup, the listed `agent.yaml` keys are absent and nothing from that process reaches Agent Logs — re-enrol or repair the config, then restart the helper.

**Session limit hit (429).**
The organisation or user limit on concurrent sessions has been reached. Call `DELETE /remote/sessions/stale` to free capacity, or navigate to the Active Sessions list and close sessions that are no longer needed.

**Terminal garbled after resize.**
This was a race condition in older builds where the browser sent a PTY resize message before the server `connected` acknowledgement was received. Current builds wait for the `connected` message before sending any data, including resize events. Update the agent to a current release.

**"Access denied" when creating a session.**
The user account does not have the `remote:access` permission. Navigate to **Settings → Roles**, locate the role assigned to the user, and enable `remote:access`. Changes take effect immediately without requiring re-login.

title: Reports & Analytics
description: Generate, schedule, and export fleet reports covering inventory, compliance, performance, and executive summaries.
headings: Ownership: one organization, or all of them
What gets stored, and what gets capped
Creating a partner-wide report through the API
Data endpoint returns empty results despite existing devices

sections.text:
Breeze provides a full reporting and analytics subsystem for generating on-demand or scheduled fleet reports and querying real-time analytics data. Reports are scoped to organizations (the [business reports](#business-reports) can also run partner-wide) and enforce multi-tenant access at every layer -- organization-scoped users see only their own data, partner-scoped users can access reports for any organization they manage, and system-scoped users have unrestricted access.

The system is split into two complementary route groups:

- **`/reports`** -- Saved report definitions, ad-hoc generation, run history, and raw data endpoints for device inventory, software, alerts, compliance, and performance metrics.
