Accounts without an enrolled factor in a tenant that does not require MFA are admitted with a password alone.

sections.heading: Duplicating a script
sections.text:
Use **Duplicate** — in the row actions on the Scripts list, or in the script editor toolbar — to start a new script from an existing one. Breeze copies the content, execution settings, parameter definitions, and tags into a new, fully editable script named `<name> (copy)`. Execution history is not copied; the new script starts with a clean record.

This is the way to adapt a script from the system library without waiting for permission to edit the original, and the way to branch a working script for a customer who needs a variation. A partner-wide script duplicates as partner-wide by default; duplicating out of the system library requires you to say which organization the copy belongs to.

sections.heading: Version history and rollback
sections.text:
When you edit a script's content, the version number increments automatically. From the script editor, click **Execution History** to navigate to the script's execution page, or view the **Version History** panel to compare changes between versions using a side-by-side diff view. You can roll back to a previous version by clicking the **Rollback** button next to any earlier version.

Each script's detail page also shows a **Provenance panel**: whether it was written by a person, by the AI assistant (as a reviewed proposal), imported, or shipped as a system script, plus — for AI-authored scripts — the reviewer's summary, risk tier, and who approved it. The scripts list has a matching **Origin** column and filter, with a "Reviewed" / "Edited since review" badge; editing an AI-authored script by hand clears the review badge, since what was reviewed is no longer exactly what would run. See [AI Script Authoring & Review](/features/ai-script-authoring/).

---

sections.heading: Running a Script
sections.text:
1. **Select a script.** On the Scripts page, click the play button next to the script you want to run. The execution modal opens.

2. **Review script info.** The modal shows the script's language, category, target OS, and description.

3. **Choose the run-as context.** Under **Run as**, select **System** (runs as the agent service account) or **Logged-in user** (runs in the active user session).

   When you run a script from a single device — its **Scripts** tab, or the **Test Run** panel in the script editor — choosing **Logged-in user** on a device whose helper starts on demand also offers a **Target session** list: **Any active session**, or a specific signed-in user by name. Pick a session when a machine has more than one person signed in and it matters which desktop the script touches. Devices with an always-on helper own a single session, so there is nothing to choose and the list does not appear. Automation actions have a **Run as** setting but no session target — an automation fans out across a fleet, where a specific session has no meaning.

4. **Fill in parameters.** If the script defines parameters, fill in the values. Required parameters are marked with an asterisk. Boolean parameters show as checkboxes; select parameters show as dropdowns.

5. **Select target devices.** The device list shows only devices with a compatible OS. Filter by hostname search, site, or status (online/offline/maintenance). Click checkboxes to select individual devices, or click **Select all** to select every device listed. An **Advanced Filters** button opens the full filter builder for complex targeting. To run on saved device groups instead, switch **Run on** to **Device groups**; see [Running on device groups](#running-on-device-groups).

6. **Confirm and execute.** Click **Execute**. A confirmation banner appears showing the script name, device count, and run-as context. Click **Confirm Execute** to dispatch the script. A progress indicator shows submission status across all targeted devices.

  Devices in an active maintenance window with script suppression enabled are automatically excluded from execution.

---

sections.heading: System Restore checkpoints
sections.text: Scripts can be set up to request a Windows System Restore checkpoint before they run. This is **off by default** and is controlled by the **System Protection** policy setting, not by the script. From **agent 0.124.0** the device takes one restore point just before the script runs and reports the outcome as a badge in the execution details; a device on an older agent keeps reading **Awaiting the device**. A restore point that cannot be created is reported, and the script still runs. See [System Protection](/features/configuration-policies/#system-protection). System Restore is not a backup and does not protect personal files.

sections.heading: Viewing Execution History
sections.text:
Navigate to **Scripts** and click a script name to open the editor, then click **Execution History** in the top-right corner. The Execution History page shows all past runs for the script.

- **Search and filter.** Filter by status (Pending, Running, Completed, Failed, Timeout), time range (Last Hour, Last 24 Hours, Last 7 Days, Last 30 Days), or search by script name or device hostname.
- **Sort columns.** Click column headers (Script, Device, Status, Started, Duration, Exit Code) to sort ascending or descending.
- **View details.** Click any execution row to open the detail view with full stdout, stderr, exit code, error messages, and timing information.
- **Paginate.** Results are paginated with 10 per page by default.

sections.heading: Script Execution History on a device
sections.text:
Each device also has its own history. Open a device from **Devices** and select the **Scripts** tab, titled **Script Execution History**. It lists every script run reported for that device, regardless of who started it.

- **Scripts view.** A toggle switches between **Latest per script** (one row per script, showing its most recent run and a run count) and **All runs** (every execution, newest first).
- **Columns.** Script, Status, Started, Completed and Duration; the latest-per-script view also shows Last run and Last output.
- **Execution Details.** Click a row to see the run context, start and completion times, duration, exit code, and the full standard output and standard error, each with a copy-to-clipboard button. A run with no output shows **No output**.
- **Run again.** Open an execution and click **Run again** to rerun that script on this device (see below). After a single-device run, Breeze brings you back to this tab with the new execution highlighted.

sections.heading: Run again
sections.text:
Open any past execution and click **Run again**. The Run modal reopens with the same device and the same parameter values already filled in, so re-running a fix on a machine that regressed is one click and a confirmation rather than a re-entry exercise. Change anything you like before confirming — nothing is locked.

After the run is dispatched, a single-device re-run takes you to that device's **Scripts** tab with the new execution highlighted, so you can watch it finish in context. A multi-device run leaves you on the execution history.

---

sections.heading: Supported Languages
sections.text:
| Language | Extension | Windows Shell | macOS / Linux Shell |
|----------|-----------|---------------|---------------------|
| `powershell` | `.ps1` | `powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File` | `pwsh -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File` |
| `bash` | `.sh` | `bash.exe` (Git Bash / WSL) | `/bin/bash` |
| `python` | `.py` | `python` | `python3` |
| `cmd` | `.bat` | `cmd.exe /C` | Not available |

  `cmd` scripts are Windows-only. The agent rejects `cmd` execution on macOS and Linux. All other languages are available cross-platform provided the interpreter is installed.

sections.heading: Privilege Levels
sections.text:
| Run As | Behavior |
|--------|----------|
| `system` | Runs as the agent service account (default). No special configuration required. |
| `user` | Runs in the context of a connected user session. Requires an active user helper session on the device. |
| `elevated` | Runs with root/administrator privileges. On Unix, the agent uses `sudo -n`. On Windows, the agent service must already be running as administrator. |

sections.heading: Execution Status
sections.text:
| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `pending` | Execution record created, command not yet sent to the agent |
| `queued` | Command queued for delivery to the agent |
| `running` | Agent has acknowledged the command and execution is in progress |
| `completed` | Script finished with exit code 0 |
| `failed` | Script finished with a non-zero exit code |
| `timeout` | Script exceeded its `timeoutSeconds` limit and was killed |
| `cancelled` | Execution was cancelled by a user before completion |

sections.heading: Trigger Types
sections.text:
| Type | When it fires |
|------|---------------|
| `manual` | A user explicitly executes the script via the UI or API |
| `scheduled` | An automation with a schedule trigger runs the script |
| `alert` | An alert-triggered automation runs the script as a remediation action |
| `policy` | A configuration policy triggers the script as part of enforcement |

sections.heading: Severity by Exit Code
sections.text:
A script can raise an alert based on its exit code. This is **opt-in per script**: set the `exitCodeSeverityMapping` field (in the script form or via the API) to a JSON object mapping exit-code strings to severity levels. A script with no mapping, or an empty mapping `{}`, never raises an exit-code alert.

When a mapping is set, Breeze evaluates it each time the script completes on a device:

| Exit code | Result |
|---|---|
| `0` | No alert (cannot be overridden). |
| A mapped code (`1`, `2`, `3`, …) | An alert at the mapped severity: `low`, `medium`, `high`, or `critical`. |
| Negative values | `critical` (abnormal termination, e.g., killed by signal; cannot be overridden). |
| Unmapped non-zero | Falls back to the next-lower mapped entry, else `medium`. |

**Which runs raise alerts (v0.117.0+).** Only unattended runs create an alert: scheduled runs, automations, configuration policies, and alert-triggered remediations. A script you run by hand, or one run by a monitor, never creates one. Before v0.117.0 the mapping was saved but no alert was ever raised.

**One alert per script and device.** While an alert for a script on a device is open (active, acknowledged, or suppressed), later failures do not create another. The alert title names the script, the exit code and the device, and the message includes the first line of the script's error output. **Dismissing** the alert is a lasting opt-out: that script no longer raises exit-code alerts on that device.

**Automatic resolution.** The next run of the script on that device, including a manual re-run, that exits without an alert-worthy code resolves the open alert automatically.

Example mapping:

```json
{
  "exitCodeSeverityMapping": {
    "1": "low",
    "2": "medium",
    "3": "high",
    "4": "critical"
  }
}
```

Pass the field on both POST `/scripts` and PUT `/scripts/:id`.

---

sections.heading: Creating Scripts via API
sections.text:
Scripts can also be created and managed programmatically. A script belongs either to a single organization or to the partner as a whole (partner-wide — see [Partner-wide vs. organization scripts](#partner-wide-vs-organization-scripts)) and is scoped by the multi-tenant hierarchy. Partner-wide writes through the API are subject to the same full-partner-access requirement as the dashboard.

```bash
POST /scripts
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "orgId": "org-uuid",
  "name": "Clear temp files",
  "description": "Removes temporary files older than 7 days",
  "category": "Maintenance",
  "osTypes": ["windows", "linux"],
  "language": "bash",
  "content": "find /tmp -type f -mtime +{{days}} -delete",
  "parameters": {
    "days": {
      "type": "number",
      "default": 7,
      "description": "Delete files older than this many days"
    }
  },
  "timeoutSeconds": 120,
  "runAs": "system",
  "exitCodeSeverityMapping": { "1": "low", "2": "medium", "3": "high" }
}
```

The response includes the full script object with an auto-generated `id` and `version: 1`. The `exitCodeSeverityMapping` field is optional — see [Severity by Exit Code](#severity-by-exit-code) above.

---

sections.heading: Single device execution
sections.text:
To execute a script on one device via the API, pass a single-element `deviceIds` array:

```bash
POST /scripts/:scriptId/execute
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "deviceIds": ["device-uuid"],
  "parameters": { "days": "7" },
  "runAs": "system"
}
```

The API validates that the device is online, not decommissioned, matches one of the script's `osTypes`, and is not suppressed by an active maintenance window. If the device's agent is connected via WebSocket, the command is pushed immediately and the execution status transitions to `running`.

sections.heading: Batch execution
sections.text:
Pass multiple device UUIDs to execute across several devices at once:

```bash
POST /scripts/:scriptId/execute
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "deviceIds": [
    "device-uuid-1",
    "device-uuid-2",
    "device-uuid-3"
  ],
  "parameters": { "days": "7" },
  "triggerType": "manual"
}
```

When targeting more than one device, the API creates a **batch** (`scriptExecutionBatches`) that groups individual execution records together. The response includes a `batchId` along with per-device execution and command IDs:

```json
{
  "batchId": "batch-uuid",
  "scriptId": "script-uuid",
  "devicesTargeted": 3,
  "executions": [
    { "executionId": "exec-1", "deviceId": "device-1", "commandId": "cmd-1" },
    { "executionId": "exec-2", "deviceId": "device-2", "commandId": "cmd-2" },
    { "executionId": "exec-3", "deviceId": "device-3", "commandId": "cmd-3" }
  ],
  "status": "queued"
}
```

  Devices in an active maintenance window with script suppression enabled are automatically excluded from execution. The response includes a `maintenanceSuppressedDeviceIds` array listing any skipped devices.

sections.heading: Pre-execution checks
sections.text:
The execute endpoint validates the following before dispatching commands:

1. The script exists and the caller has org-level access to it.
2. Each device exists and belongs to an organization the caller can access.
3. Each device's `osType` matches one of the script's `osTypes`.
4. The device is not in `decommissioned` status.
5. The device is not in a maintenance window with script suppression enabled.

Devices that fail any check are silently excluded. If no devices remain after filtering, the API returns `400`.

sections.heading: Running on device groups
sections.text:
Instead of picking devices one by one, you can run a script on saved [device groups](/features/device-groups/). In the Run Script modal, set **Run on** to **Device groups**, then select up to 100 groups. The picker shows each group's device count, marks dynamic groups, and summarizes the unique devices across your selection, how many have a matching operating system, and how many are offline (offline devices run the script when they come online).

Through the API, send `target` instead of `deviceIds`:

```bash
POST /scripts/:scriptId/execute
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "target": { "type": "groups", "groupIds": ["group-uuid-1", "group-uuid-2"] },
  "parameters": { "days": "7" },
  "runAs": "system"
}
```

Provide exactly one of `deviceIds` or `target`. `targetSessionId` cannot be combined with `target`. The server resolves the groups to devices before dispatch, then applies the same per-device checks as any other run (see [Pre-execution checks](#pre-execution-checks)).

sections.heading: How groups are resolved
sections.text:
- Every requested group must exist, belong to an organization you can access and, if you are restricted to specific sites, sit at one of your sites. If any group fails these checks, the request returns `404` with code `GROUP_NOT_FOUND` and a `groupIds` array naming them. The message is the same whether a group does not exist or you cannot access it. The run is never silently reduced to the groups that did resolve.
- A device that belongs to several of the groups runs the script once.
- If you are restricted to specific sites, devices outside your allowlist are excluded and a warning says so.
- Static groups use their current members. Dynamic groups use the stored membership from the group's last evaluation. Breeze does not re-evaluate the filter when you run the script. Re-evaluation normally follows a device change within about 5 seconds, but that is not guaranteed: evaluation jobs can retry or back up. A device that just started matching a dynamic group may not be in the run yet.
- A dynamic group whose rules match on fields a device reports about itself is refused as an execution target and skipped, with a warning. These groups are marked unavailable in the picker.

sections.heading: Limits and errors
sections.text:
| Status | Code | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `404` | `GROUP_NOT_FOUND` | One or more groups do not exist or are not accessible. `groupIds` lists them. |
| `400` | `NO_TARGETS` | Every requested group was refused, or the groups have no members. Nothing was run. |
| `400` | `TOO_MANY_TARGETS` | The groups resolve to more than 500 unique devices. The response includes `count` and `perGroupCounts`. Nothing is dispatched and the list is not truncated; split the run across smaller groups. |

A successful group run returns `201` with the usual response plus a `warnings` array (refused groups, devices excluded by your site allowlist).

sections.heading: Audit
sections.text:
A group run writes the normal `script.execute` audit entry with two extra details, `target` and `resolvedGroups` (each group's id, organization, member count in this run, and whether it was refused). The resolved device ids are recorded in the entry's targets.

A separate `script.execute_group_target` entry is written for every group-target request, whether it was admitted, had no devices admitted, or was rejected. It records the devices the groups resolved to at that moment, so the record stays accurate after group membership changes.

sections.heading: AI assistant
sections.text:
The AI assistant's `run_script` tool accepts a `groupId` (one saved device group) in place of `deviceIds`; provide exactly one of the two. The group is resolved to a concrete device list when the approval is requested. The approval shows the device list, the member count, and a short hash of the resolved device ids, and that exact list is what runs once approved. Membership changes after the approval is requested do not change the run.

An AI run is limited to 10 devices. A group that resolves to more than 10 is refused with the resolved count; it is never truncated, and the 500-device limit above does not apply. Use the Run Script modal or the API for larger groups. A group outside the conversation's organization is refused with the same message as a group that does not exist. See [AI Tools](/features/ai-tools/#scripts--automation).

---

sections.heading: Script Parameters
sections.text: Parameters let you create reusable scripts with configurable values. Define parameters as a JSON object when creating the script, then pass runtime values at execution time.

sections.heading: Defining parameters
Parameter sources
sections.text:
Every parameter has a **source** that decides where its value comes from. By default the value is asked for at run time; the other sources resolve it automatically, per device, when the script is dispatched — nobody is prompted for them.

| Source | Resolves to |
|---|---|
| **Asked at run time** | A value supplied by whoever starts the run (or by the automation/schedule that triggers it). |
| **From a variable** | A non-secret [variable](#variables) for the target device's organization. |
| **From a secret variable (environment variable)** | A [secret variable](#secret-variables-in-scripts), delivered to the script only as an environment variable. |
| **From a device custom field** | A custom field value on the target device. |
| **From a device property** | A built-in device property, such as hostname or OS type. |

  This reads a custom field. To have a script **write** one back to the device — no API key required — see [Writing custom fields from a script](/features/custom-fields/#writing-custom-fields-from-a-script).

sections.heading: Using parameters in script content
sections.text:
Parameter values are delivered to your script as **data, never as script text**. Every parameter is exported into the script's environment as `BREEZE_PARAM_<KEY>` (the key upper-cased, `-` becomes `_`), and the agent rewrites each placeholder into a reference to that variable in the script's own language before the script runs. A value containing quotes, `$`, `&` or a newline is therefore just a value — it cannot become another command.

| Format | Example |
|--------|---------|
| `{{paramName}}` | `echo "Threshold is {{threshold}}"` |
| `${{paramName}}` | `echo "Threshold is ${{threshold}}"` |

Both formats work in every script type, inside or outside quotes, and both are equivalent to reading the environment variable yourself:

```bash
# These are equivalent inside a script:
echo "Threshold is {{threshold}}"
echo "Threshold is $BREEZE_PARAM_THRESHOLD"
```

```powershell
Write-Output "Threshold is {{threshold}}"
Write-Output "Threshold is $env:BREEZE_PARAM_THRESHOLD"
```

```python
print(f"Threshold is {{threshold}}")
print("Threshold is " + os.environ["BREEZE_PARAM_THRESHOLD"])
```

A placeholder whose name is not a parameter of the script is left in the script exactly as written.

#### Contexts a placeholder cannot be used in

A few places re-interpret the *contents* of a variable as code, so no reference can carry a value there safely. The agent fails the run before executing anything and names the parameter and the context. Reference the environment variable directly instead (`$BREEZE_PARAM_KEY`, `$env:BREEZE_PARAM_KEY`, `os.environ["BREEZE_PARAM_KEY"]`, `%BREEZE_PARAM_KEY%`), or assign it to your own variable first.

| Script type | Rejected context | Use instead |
|---|---|---|
| Bash | Arithmetic and subscripts — `$(( ))`, `(( ))`, `$[ ]`, `let`, `declare -i`, an assignment subscript (`arr[…]=`, `arr=( [.]=v )`), `${name:offset}`, `${name[…]}`, and `[[ … -eq … ]]` operands — unless the value is a plain integer. These apply inside an unquoted heredoc body too, which still expands them | A plain-integer parameter, or `$(( BREEZE_PARAM_N ))` after validating it yourself |
| Bash | A quoted heredoc (`<<'EOF'`), where nothing expands | An unquoted heredoc (`<<EOF`) with `$BREEZE_PARAM_KEY` in the body |
| Bash | `eval`, `trap` and `alias` command lines — however the word is spelled (`\eval`, `ev\al`, `"let"`, `command eval`, `builtin eval`) | Restructure so the value is an argument, not code |
| Bash | Variable-name positions (`read`, `unset`, `printf -v`, `for NAME in`, `declare -n`) unless the value is a valid identifier | A parameter restricted to identifiers |
| PowerShell | A literal here-string (`@' … '@`), where nothing expands | An expanding here-string (`@" … "@`) with `$env:BREEZE_PARAM_KEY` |
| PowerShell | `Invoke-Expression` / `iex` statements | Call the command directly with the value as an argument |
| Python | A raw string literal (`r"…"`) when the value contains a backslash or the literal's quote character | A normal literal, or `os.environ[...]` |
| Python | A bytes literal (`b"…"`) when the value is not ASCII | A text literal, or encode it yourself |
| Python | An f-string replacement field — the expression between `{` and `}`, e.g. `f"{ {{n}} }"` or a nested format spec `f"{x:{{w}}}"` | `f"{os.environ['BREEZE_PARAM_N']}"`, or put the placeholder in the literal's text instead |
| cmd | Values containing a line break; a `call` statement (only the statement the placeholder is in — `call foo & echo {{p}}` is fine); a `for /f … in ( )` clause | `%BREEZE_PARAM_KEY%` read into a variable first |

A single-quoted string is fine in both bash and PowerShell: the agent rewrites the quoting so the value still arrives as one literal datum.

#### A placeholder is always exactly one word

Because the value is passed by reference, a placeholder renders as a **single** quoted word. Four consequences are worth knowing:

- **A parameter holding several flags no longer splits.** `rsync {{flags}}` with `flags` set to `-a --delete` passes one argument `-a --delete`, not two. If you want the value split into words, read the variable unquoted — `rsync $BREEZE_PARAM_FLAGS` — and accept that the split is then driven by the technician's data, not by the script author. Cleaner still: take the options as an array in the script (`read -ra opts <<<"$BREEZE_PARAM_FLAGS"`) or as separate parameters.
- **Bash pattern matching is literal.** `[[ $x == {{pat}} ]]` and `[[ $x =~ {{re}} ]]` now compare against the value as a literal string. For glob or regex semantics, write the variable unquoted: `[[ $x == $BREEZE_PARAM_PAT ]]`, `[[ $x =~ $BREEZE_PARAM_RE ]]`.
- **A placeholder in command position selects the binary.** `{{tool}} --version` runs one program named by the whole value; it cannot carry its own arguments. Put arguments in their own parameters.
- **`runAs` via sudo needs `--preserve-env`.** The agent passes `sudo -n --preserve-env=BREEZE_PARAM_…` so the referenced variables survive. The sudoers rule must allow it (the `SETENV` tag, which an `ALL` command rule implies). On a host whose policy refuses `--preserve-env`, the run fails with sudo's own message instead of running with empty parameters — grant `SETENV` on the rule the agent uses.

  Because values are no longer part of the script text, the agent's security validator scans what the script *author* wrote. It is a guardrail against dangerous operations in the script itself, not an injection filter for parameter values — those can no longer be executed as code. Scripts with parameters are also syntax-checked (`bash -n`) after the rewrite, and cmd scripts run with delayed expansion (`/V:ON`) enabled, which consumes a literal `!` in the script's own text.

---

sections.heading: Variables
sections.text:
Variables solve the problem of the same script needing a different value for every customer — a vendor portal token, an internal repository URL, a site-specific path. Instead of keeping one copy of the script per customer, you define the value once and reference it by name.

Manage them under **Settings → Variables**.

sections.heading: Defining a variable
sections.text:
Each variable has:

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Applies to** | **All organizations** (partner-wide — available to every customer you manage) or **This organization** |
| **Key** | Lowercase letters, digits and underscores. This is the name scripts reference. |
| **Value** | The value substituted at run time |
| **Description** | Optional note for your team |
| **Secret** | Store the value write-once and masked. See [Secret variables](#secret-variables). |

An organization-scoped variable overrides a partner-wide one with the same key, so you can set a sensible default for everyone and special-case individual customers.

Switching the variables list to **All Organizations** lists partner-wide variables only, with a column naming the organization each row belongs to — org-scoped variables aren't shown there; open a specific organization to see or manage those.

sections.heading: Using variables in a script
sections.text:
Reference a variable as `{{var.key}}`:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer {{var.vendor_api_token}}" \
  "{{var.internal_repo_url}}/agent/latest"
```

Breeze resolves each reference **per device at dispatch**, using the variable that applies to that device's organization. One script, correct values everywhere.

sections.heading: Secret variables
sections.text:
Tick **Secret** and the value becomes write-once: it is never displayed again after saving — the list shows `••••••••` and the API returns no value at all. Secret values must be at least four characters long. Secrets are never pasted into a script body: a script binds one through a parameter and reads it as an environment variable. See [Secret variables in scripts](#secret-variables-in-scripts).

  A secret cannot be recovered through the UI or the API once saved. To change it, overwrite it with a new value.

sections.heading: Secret variables in scripts
sections.text:
A secret is never pasted into script text. `{{var.key}}` pointing at a secret is rejected when the script is saved. A script reaches a secret through a **parameter** instead:

1. In the script editor, add a parameter and set its **source** to **From a secret variable (environment variable)**.
2. Bind it to a secret variable key. Non-secret variables are not offered for this source.
3. Name the parameter using lowercase letters, digits and underscores — the name becomes the environment variable the script reads.

At dispatch, Breeze resolves the secret for each target device's organization and delivers it as the environment variable `BREEZE_VAR_<NAME>`, where `<NAME>` is the parameter name in uppercase. A parameter named `api_token` arrives as `BREEZE_VAR_API_TOKEN`:

  **PowerShell:**
```powershell
    Invoke-RestMethod -Uri $Url -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $env:BREEZE_VAR_API_TOKEN" }
```

  **Bash:**
```bash
    curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $BREEZE_VAR_API_TOKEN" "$URL"
```

The value is never substituted into the script body, never mirrored into `BREEZE_PARAM_*`, and never written to the execution record.

**Binding rules**

- Binding a secret through the plain **From a variable** source is rejected when the script is saved. So is binding a non-secret variable through the secret source.
- A script may bind a secret **at or below its own ownership tier, never above**.
  - A **partner-wide** script may bind a partner-wide secret — and may equally bind an *organization-owned* one, which resolves to each target device's own organization at run time. That per-organization resolution is the point: one partner-wide script, and every customer supplies their own value for the same key — a per-org site key, vendor token, or tenant identifier — without a copy of the script per customer.
  - An **organization-scoped** script may bind only that organization's own secrets. A partner-wide secret is refused when the script is saved, with a message naming the parameter, and refused again at dispatch. The second check is what makes the rule airtight: a script cannot be re-scoped or re-pointed into reaching a secret above its own tier.
- Where an organization defines a secret with the same key as a partner-wide one, the organization's value wins — the same org-over-partner precedence as ordinary variables. This is what makes the per-organization pattern work: set the partner-wide secret as the default, and override it only for the customers that need their own value.
- A script can declare at most **32** secret parameters.
- At run time, a target organization where the bound key resolves to a non-secret variable — or has no variable with that key — fails on that device with a message naming the parameter and the variable key. Devices whose organizations do resolve the secret still run.

**Requirements**

| Requirement | If it is not met |
|---|---|
| System-context execution | A script set to **Run as user**, or a run targeted at a specific user session, is refused: *"This script uses secret variables, which require system-context execution; ... was not executed."* |
| An agent that supports secure secret delivery — **agent v0.106.0 or later** | The device fails with *"Agent upgrade required: ... script not executed."* This is checked both when the run is queued and again when the agent picks the command up, so a script never runs with its secret environment variable unset. |

While the command waits for the device, the value is held in an encrypted envelope bound to that specific command, and it is erased from the command record once the run completes.

**Output redaction.** Exact occurrences of the secret value in stdout, stderr and error text are replaced with `[REDACTED]` — on the agent before the result is sent, and again on the server before the result is stored.

**Redaction is accidental-leak protection, not DLP:**
  Only the exact value is matched. A script that dumps its environment (`env`, `printenv`, `Get-ChildItem Env:`), traces itself (`bash -x`), or emits the value transformed in any way — base64, URL-encoded, split across lines — will disclose it. Treat permission to run a script as permission to use every secret that script binds — which is why a script can only bind secrets at or below its own ownership tier, and an organization-scoped script can never reach a partner-wide secret.

  [Software deployment](/features/software-inventory/#software-deployments) templates cannot use secret variables. A template that references a secret key fails the deployment with an explicit error rather than silently omitting the value.

  Fleet remediation cannot run a script that declares **any** server-resolved parameter — secret, variable, device field, or device property. That path resolves nothing per device, so such a script is rejected when the remediation run is created rather than executed with the values missing.

sections.heading: Variables and approvals
sections.text:
When a script run goes through approval, the approval digest pins the exact variable and parameter values it was approved with. If a value changes afterwards, the approval no longer matches and the run must be approved again — an approved run cannot be quietly re-pointed at different values.

---

sections.heading: Listing executions for a script
sections.text:
```
GET /scripts/:scriptId/executions?status=completed&page=1&limit=25
```

Returns paginated execution records with device hostname and OS type joined from the devices table. Filter by `status` and `deviceId`.

sections.heading: Execution detail with output
sections.text:
```
GET /scripts/executions/:executionId
```

Returns the full execution record including `stdout`, `stderr`, `exitCode`, `errorMessage`, and timing fields (`startedAt`, `completedAt`). Also includes the script name, language, device hostname, and device OS type.

  The agent captures up to 1 MB of stdout and 1 MB of stderr. Output exceeding this limit is truncated. The `truncatedFields` array in the agent result indicates which fields were truncated.

If the script printed a [custom-field write-back marker](/features/custom-fields/#writing-custom-fields-from-a-script), the response also includes `customFieldResult: { applied: string[], rejected: [{ key, reason }] } | null` — surfaced in the web UI's execution detail panel.

sections.heading: Cancelling an execution
sections.text:
Pending, queued, or running executions can be cancelled:

```bash
POST /scripts/executions/:executionId/cancel
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

The API sets the execution status to `cancelled` and cancels any device commands for that execution that have not yet been delivered.

  This stops an execution that has not reached the device yet. It does **not** reach into a device and kill a script that is already running — the process on the endpoint runs to completion or times out, and only the record in Breeze is marked cancelled.

---

sections.heading: Security
sections.text: The Go agent enforces security validation on all script content before execution. There is no global, partner, or organization-level setting that changes how strict this validation is — validation behaves identically everywhere, and every acknowledgement described below applies to one specific script, never to a partner, an organization, or the fleet.

sections.heading: Blocked patterns
sections.text:
The validator checks script content against two categories of dangerous pattern.

**Basic** -- clearly destructive operations, blocked unconditionally with no override of any kind, ever:
- Recursive deletion of root or system directories (`rm -rf /`, `rd /s /q C:\Windows`)
- Filesystem format commands (`mkfs`, `Format-Volume`, `Clear-Disk`)
- Direct writes to block devices (`dd of=/dev/sda`)
- Fork bomb patterns
- Dangerous permission changes on system paths

**Strict** -- risky-but-legitimate admin operations that can be acknowledged per script (see below):
- Remote code execution patterns (`curl | bash`, `Invoke-WebRequest | IEX`)
- Credential dumping tools and techniques
- Scheduled task / persistence creation
- Privilege escalation via setuid/setgid
- HKLM registry modifications
- Sudoers modifications

sections.heading: Acknowledging Strict patterns
sections.text:
Saving a script in the Scripts editor shows which Strict patterns its content currently matches, each with a plain-language explanation of the risk. Anyone who can write the script body — the same permission already required to save the script, no new permission is introduced — ticks the patterns they intend the script to trigger. The acknowledged descriptions are stored on the script record, audited (who, when, which patterns), and travel with every dispatch of that script. The agent then permits exactly those Strict patterns for that script and still blocks any other match.

**An acknowledgement names patterns, not the whole script:**
  The stored acknowledgement is the set of Strict pattern descriptions the content matched when it was approved — never a blanket "this script is trusted" flag. Editing the script later to introduce a *different* Strict pattern leaves that new pattern unacknowledged and still blocked, even though the original approval keeps working. Removing the risky line drops its acknowledgement automatically.

A script that matches a Strict pattern it has not been acknowledged for fails at execution time with an error naming the pattern and telling the operator to open the script in Breeze, acknowledge it under Security review, and run it again. For a one-off change on a single device, use Remote Tools (Registry or Terminal) instead of a script.

  The patterns are line-oriented regular expressions matched against the script body after parameter substitution. They are a guard rail against accidental destructive commands, not a containment boundary — anyone who can author or edit a script can already run arbitrary code on the device they dispatch it to.

sections.heading: Output sanitization
sections.text:
Script output is scanned for sensitive information before being stored. The agent redacts API keys, tokens, AWS credentials, private keys, connection strings, bearer tokens, and JWTs from stdout and stderr.

---

sections.heading: Script Approval (Breeze AI)
sections.text: When the Breeze AI assistant needs to run a script on a device, it goes through a tiered approval system. Script execution via the AI is classified as a **Tier 3** operation, meaning it always requires explicit user approval before it can proceed.

sections.heading: How approval works
sections.text:
1. **AI proposes a script action.** During an AI chat session, the assistant may determine that running a script is necessary (for example, executing a disk cleanup or restarting a service). Rather than running it immediately, the action is flagged for approval.

2. **Approval request appears.** A pending approval notification appears in the AI Risk Dashboard under the **Tier 3 Approval History** feed. The request shows the tool name, a description of the action, the target device, and the input parameters.

3. **Review and decide.** An administrator reviews the proposed action and either:
   - **Approves** -- the AI proceeds with execution. The action is logged to the audit trail.
   - **Rejects** -- the AI does not execute the action. The rejection is logged with the reason.

4. **Execution proceeds (if approved).** The approved script runs on the target device and the AI monitors the result, reporting back in the chat conversation.

sections.heading: Which actions require approval
sections.text:
The following script-related AI actions require Tier 3 approval:
- **Run Script** -- executing a script on up to 10 devices
- **Execute Command** -- running a system command on a device
- **Execute Playbook** -- running a self-healing playbook
- **Disk Cleanup (execute)** -- performing actual file deletion
- **Create Automation** -- creating a new automation rule

Read-only script operations (searching the library, viewing script details, checking execution history) run automatically at Tier 1 without approval.

sections.heading: MFA enforcement
sections.text: All script write and execute operations require an MFA-assured session, whether triggered by a user directly or approved through the AI workflow. A session is MFA-assured when it has completed MFA, or when the account has no factor enrolled and the effective MFA policy (organization or partner **Require MFA** setting, or a role that forces MFA) does not require one. If the session is not assured, the API returns a `403` error with code `MFA_REQUIRED`. To make MFA mandatory for script execution across a tenant, turn on **Require MFA** in the organization or partner security settings; users without a factor are then routed to enrollment before they can run scripts. The partner-wide **Require MFA** setting (Settings → Partner → Security) is on by default for partners created after 2026-09-18, so users without an enrolled factor are routed to enrolment at sign-in.

sections.heading: Viewing approval history
sections.text:
Navigate to the **AI Risk** section in the dashboard to see the full approval history. The **Tier 3 Approval History** feed shows all pending, approved, and rejected actions with timestamps, tool names, and who initiated the request. Use the status filter buttons (All, Pending, Approved, Rejected) to narrow the view.

---

sections.heading: API Reference
sections.text:
All script endpoints require authentication and the appropriate permission scope.

| Method | Path | Permission | Description |
|--------|------|------------|-------------|
| GET | `/scripts` | `scripts:read` | List scripts with filters (`?orgId=&category=&osType=&language=&search=&includeSystem=true&page=&limit=`) |
| GET | `/scripts/system-library` | `scripts:read` | List all system scripts available for import |
| POST | `/scripts/import/:id` | `scripts:write` | Clone a system script into the caller's organization |
| GET | `/scripts/:id` | `scripts:read` | Get a single script by ID |
| POST | `/scripts` | `scripts:write` | Create a new script |
| PUT | `/scripts/:id` | `scripts:write` | Update a script (increments version on content change) |
| DELETE | `/scripts/:id` | `scripts:delete` | Delete a script (blocked if active executions exist) |
| POST | `/scripts/:id/execute` | `scripts:execute` | Execute a script on one or more devices |
| GET | `/scripts/:id/executions` | `scripts:read` | List executions for a script (`?status=&deviceId=&page=&limit=`) |
| GET | `/scripts/executions/:id` | `scripts:read` | Get execution detail with stdout/stderr |
| POST | `/scripts/executions/:id/cancel` | `scripts:execute` | Cancel a pending, queued, or running execution |

  All write and execute endpoints require an MFA-assured session (see [MFA enforcement](#mfa-enforcement)). The API enforces multi-tenant access control -- organization-scope users see only their org's scripts, partner-scope users see scripts across their managed organizations, and system-scope users see everything.

---

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**Script fails with "unsupported script type".**
The agent only supports `powershell`, `bash`, `python`, and `cmd`. Verify the `language` field matches one of these values. If using `cmd`, confirm the target device is running Windows -- `cmd` is not available on macOS or Linux.

**Script times out unexpectedly.**
The default timeout is 300 seconds (5 minutes). The maximum allowed timeout is 3,600 seconds (1 hour) — the API rejects anything higher, matching the agent's own execution cap. Set `timeoutSeconds` when creating the script or override `runAs` at execution time. On timeout, the agent kills the entire process group to prevent orphaned children.

**Execution stuck in `pending` status.**
If the device is offline, this is expected: the command is queued and delivered automatically on the device's next successful heartbeat, up to a **7-day** delivery deadline, and it's visible and cancellable from the device's **Queued actions** list in the meantime. If the device is online but the execution is still `pending` after a few minutes, check the device's connection status and ensure the agent is running — the command is persisted in the `deviceCommands` table and transitions to `sent` only when the API successfully pushes it over the WebSocket.

**Script rejected by security validation.**
The agent's strict security validator blocks patterns that match known destructive or suspicious operations. Review the `errorMessage` field in the execution detail for the specific pattern that was detected. If the script is legitimate, consider restructuring the command to avoid matching the blocked pattern. Security validation runs after parameter substitution, so a parameter value could trigger a block.

title: Security
description: Monitor endpoint security posture, detect threats, enforce compliance, and get AI-powered security recommendations.
headings: Auto-quarantine runs under an approving user
Using rule sets in a policy
Posture score is 0 or not available

sections.text:
The Security module provides continuous visibility into the security posture of every managed device. The Breeze agent collects antivirus status, firewall state, disk encryption details, local administrator accounts, and password policy configuration from each endpoint. That data flows into the API where it is scored, trended, and surfaced through a unified dashboard. When the agent detects threats during a scan, those threats can be quarantined or removed directly from the console. A built-in recommendations engine analyzes posture data across the fleet and produces prioritized, actionable guidance to reduce risk.

---

sections.heading: Admin IP Allowlist
sections.text:
Partner admins can restrict dashboard access to specific source IP addresses or CIDR ranges from **Settings -> Security -> IP Allowlist**. The allowlist is partner-level: once configured, authenticated dashboard requests and password login attempts for that partner are checked before access continues. Agent endpoints use separate agent authentication and are not affected.

The allowlist requires working proxy trust. In production, set `TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true` and configure `TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS` so the API trusts only your reverse proxy hop, such as Caddy behind [Cloudflare Tunnel](/deploy/cloudflare-tunnel/). If Breeze cannot determine a trusted client IP, the allowlist fails open and reports inactive status instead of creating a false lockout guarantee. See [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/) for the proxy trust and `IP_ALLOWLIST_ENFORCEMENT_MODE` settings.

Platform administrators bypass the partner allowlist as a break-glass path, and each bypass is audited. Operators can also set `IP_ALLOWLIST_ENFORCEMENT_MODE=off` to globally disable enforcement during an emergency, then return it to `enforce` after correcting the partner settings.

---

sections.heading: Security Status
sections.text: The agent reports a `SecurityStatus` payload on each heartbeat. The payload includes the detected AV provider, real-time protection state, definition freshness, firewall status, disk encryption status, local admin accounts, and password policy configuration.

sections.heading: Collected Fields
sections.text:
| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **`provider`** | Normalized security provider identifier (e.g. `windows_defender`, `bitdefender`) |
| **`providerVersion`** | Version string of the installed AV product |
| **`definitionsVersion`** | Virus definition / signature version |
| **`definitionsDate`** | Timestamp of the most recent definitions update |
| **`realTimeProtection`** | Whether real-time scanning is active. `null` when the agent could not read it (collection failed or never reported); the UI shows **Unknown** and the device is not counted as protected or unprotected |
| **`lastScan`** | Timestamp of the most recent completed scan |
| **`lastScanType`** | Type of last scan: `quick`, `full`, or `custom` |
| **`threatCount`** | Number of active threats on the device |
| **`firewallEnabled`** | Whether the host firewall is active. `null` when the agent could not read it; shown as **Unknown** |
| **`encryptionStatus`** | Disk encryption state: `encrypted`, `partial`, or `unencrypted` |
| **`encryptionDetails`** | Per-volume encryption breakdown (method, mount point, protection status) |
| **`localAdminSummary`** | Local administrator account inventory with issue flags |
| **`passwordPolicySummary`** | Password policy settings (min length, complexity, lockout, history) |
| **`gatekeeperEnabled`** | macOS Gatekeeper status (macOS only) |

sections.heading: Detection Methods by Platform
sections.text:
**Windows:**
    - **AV detection**: Windows Security Center (`root/SecurityCenter2`) via CIM, with fallback to `Get-MpComputerStatus` for Windows Server
    - **Firewall**: `Get-NetFirewallProfile` queries all three profiles (Domain, Private, Public)
    - **Encryption**: `Get-BitLockerVolume` reads BitLocker protection status and encryption percentage per volume
    - **Local admins**: `Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators'` enumerates the local Administrators group
    - **Password policy**: `Win32_AccountPolicy` CIM class reads min length, max age, lockout threshold, and history count

  **macOS:**
    - **AV detection**: CylancePROTECT / Aurora Endpoint Defense via its app bundle (`/Applications/Cylance/CylanceUI.app`) and launch daemon (`com.cylance.agent_service`), then Microsoft Defender for Endpoint via `mdatp health --output json`, with app bundle fallback. Cylance is attributed first; Defender takes the provider only when nothing else was found or when it is the only product with real-time protection on
    - **Gatekeeper**: `spctl --status` checks Gatekeeper enforcement state
    - **Firewall**: `socketfilterfw --getglobalstate` or `defaults read com.apple.alf globalstate`
    - **Encryption**: `fdesetup status` detects FileVault state
    - **Local admins**: `dscl . -read /Groups/admin GroupMembership` lists admin group members
    - **Password policy**: `pwpolicy -getglobalpolicy` parses min chars, complexity, lockout, and history

  **Linux:**
    - **Firewall**: Checks `ufw status`, `firewall-cmd --state`, and `systemctl is-active firewalld` in order
    - **Encryption**: `lsblk -J` walks the block device tree looking for `crypt` type entries (LUKS)
    - **Local admins**: `getent group sudo` or `getent group wheel` enumerates privileged group members
    - **Password policy**: Parses `/etc/login.defs` for min length and max age, checks PAM modules for complexity, and reads `/etc/security/faillock.conf` for lockout threshold

---

sections.heading: Supported Providers
sections.text:
The agent normalizes detected AV products to one of the following provider identifiers. On Windows, multiple AV products may be registered simultaneously through the Security Center.

| Provider ID | Display Name | Vendor |
|-------------|-------------|--------|
| `windows_defender` | Microsoft Defender | Microsoft |
| `elastic_defend` | Elastic Defend | Elastic |
| `bitdefender` | Bitdefender | Bitdefender |
| `sophos` | Sophos | Sophos |
| `sentinelone` | SentinelOne Singularity | SentinelOne |
| `crowdstrike` | CrowdStrike Falcon | CrowdStrike |
| `malwarebytes` | Malwarebytes | Malwarebytes |
| `eset` | ESET | ESET |
| `kaspersky` | Kaspersky | Kaspersky |
| `emsisoft` | Emsisoft | Emsisoft |
| `webroot` | Webroot SecureAnywhere | OpenText |
| `withsecure` | WithSecure Elements | WithSecure |
| `cylance` | Aurora Endpoint Defense (CylancePROTECT) | Arctic Wolf |
| `other` | Other | Other |

ThreatDown (Malwarebytes' business brand) reports as `malwarebytes`. F-Secure products report as `withsecure`. Aurora Endpoint Defense still registers with Windows Security Center as CylancePROTECT and reports as `cylance`.

  On Windows workstations, the agent queries `root/SecurityCenter2` which returns all registered AV products. The product with active real-time protection is selected as the primary provider. On Windows Server (where Security Center is unavailable), the agent falls back to querying Microsoft Defender directly via `Get-MpComputerStatus`. Provider name matching is order-sensitive: Elastic Defend (registered as Elastic Agent / Elastic Endpoint Security) is matched before the generic Microsoft Defender pattern, since its registered product name can otherwise be misread as Microsoft Defender.

---

sections.heading: The IOC Scans Page
sections.text:
**Security → IOC Scans** (`/security/scans`) is the console for running on-demand scans and working detected threats without leaving the browser. It has three tabs:

- **Scans** — pick one or more devices (single- or multi-select), choose a scan type (Quick, Full, or Custom with an explicit path), and start the scan. Submission progress is shown per device as each request queues. Below that, **Active Scans** shows what's currently queued or running, and **Scan History** lists the most recent completed and failed runs with their result and duration.
- **Threats** — a filterable list of detected threats (by status, severity, device) across the fleet. Selecting a threat opens its detail view, where you can **Quarantine**, **Restore**, or permanently remove it; the bulk-action toolbar on the list lets you quarantine or remove several threats at once. Restoring a quarantined threat moves it back to allowed without re-scanning.
- **Sweeps** — run a detection rule set across many devices at once and follow the progress, cancel it, or open a group of sweeps by its link. See [IOC sweeps](#ioc-sweeps).

  Before v0.116.0, quarantine and restore were reachable only through the API (see [Threat Actions](#threat-actions) below) — a quarantined threat had no UI path to restore it. The Threats tab closes that gap.

Quarantine, Remove and Restore send a command to the device; they do not change the threat on their own. Since v0.117.0 the threat keeps its current status until the agent reports the result, and only then shows **quarantined**, **removed** or **allowed**. If the device is offline, the threat keeps its previous status until the device comes back and runs the command. Earlier versions changed the status as soon as the action was queued, so a threat on an offline device could show as quarantined when nothing had happened on the device.

sections.heading: Auto-quarantine runs under an approving user
sections.text:
IOC auto-quarantine (set on the **Security** feature of a configuration policy) moves files on every device the policy reaches with no one reviewing each scan, so it is treated as a device-execution grant. Saving Security settings with auto-quarantine on needs the `devices:execute` permission and MFA; with auto-quarantine off, `devices:write` is enough, and turning it off is never restricted. Because auto-quarantine is on by default, a technician with only `devices:write` must turn it off before the Security settings will save.

Scheduled scans quarantine only while the user who approved auto-quarantine is active and still holds `devices:execute`. Policies that had auto-quarantine on before v0.122.1 keep running under the user who created them on the same terms. Otherwise the policy shows *Auto-quarantine is paused* and its scans run detect-only until a user with `devices:execute` and MFA saves the Security settings again. A scan you start by hand runs under your own permissions; without a completed MFA check in your session it runs detect-only.

sections.heading: Detection rules
sections.text:
**Security → Detection Rules** (`/security/detection-rules`, v0.125.0+) is where you manage the YARA rule sets that IOC scans and sweeps use. Every change is checked on the server, with the same compiler devices use, before any device receives it. Scanning with rule sets needs agent 0.124.0 or later; older agents fall back to the built-in legacy signatures.

The list shows each set's owner (**Breeze (built-in)**, **All organizations** or **Organization**), how many rules it has and its published version, with badges such as **Has errors**, **Not published** and **Disabled**.

sections.heading: Rule sets
sections.text:
1. Click **New rule set** and give it a name, an optional description and an owner: **One organization**, or **All organizations (partner-wide)** if you work at partner level.
2. On the **Rules** tab, add a rule: a name (letters, digits and underscores), a severity (Low, Medium, High or Critical), optional tags, and the YARA source.
3. Save. Breeze checks the rule and, if every rule in the set compiles, publishes the set as a new numbered version ("Saved and published as version N").

There is no separate **Publish** button: adding, editing or deleting a rule republishes the set, and so does turning **Enabled** or **Auto-quarantine** on or off once the set has been published. If a rule does not compile, its row shows the error with the line number, a "Not published: fix the errors below" banner stays up, and devices keep the last good version.

The built-in **Breeze** set is read-only and updates with Breeze releases. A set holds up to 500 rules, each up to 64 KB of source.

sections.heading: Import IOCs
sections.text:
The **Import IOCs** tab turns a list of indicators into rules. Paste one indicator per line (`#` starts a comment) or a JSON array. Breeze recognises MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes, file names, file paths, domains, IP addresses and text strings; prefix a line (for example `sha256:`) to set the type yourself. Defanged values such as `example[.]com` are refanged, and duplicates are flagged.

Give the batch a label and a severity (High by default), review the preview, then click **Import N IOCs**. Each indicator type becomes one exact-match rule (split if it would grow too large), and the set is republished. Keep in mind:

- Domains and IP addresses match text **inside scanned files**, not network traffic.
- Hash indicators make full scans slower.
- One import takes up to 1,000 indicators and 256 KB of text. Importing the exact same batch again is refused.

sections.heading: Test a file
sections.text: The **Test a file** tab scans a file you upload (up to 10 MB) against the set's current rules, including changes that are not published yet, and lists the rules that matched. You can give the path the file would have on a device, since some rules match on it. The test runs in a sandbox on the Breeze server, not on a device. The file is not kept; the audit log records only its SHA-256, size and match count. Each user can run 10 tests every 10 minutes. If the server cannot isolate the scan, the tab says file tests are not available; editing, importing and device scans keep working.

sections.heading: Using rule sets in a policy
sections.text:
Choose which sets devices scan with on a configuration policy's **Security** tab, under **Detection rule sets** (up to 20 per policy). Both scheduled policy scans and manual scans send the selected sets to the device. A device can use only sets owned by its own organization, its partner's all-organizations sets, and the built-in set. A new Security policy starts with the built-in set selected; with no set selected, scans use the built-in legacy signatures only. A set that was deleted or is out of reach shows as **Unavailable rule set** and must be removed before the policy can be saved.

To run sets across many devices right now, use **Sweep now** in the rule-set editor; see [IOC sweeps](#ioc-sweeps).

sections.heading: Permissions
sections.text: Viewing rule sets needs `devices:read`. Creating, editing, deleting, importing and testing need `devices:write`, and turning on a set's **Auto-quarantine** also needs `devices:execute`. Site-restricted users cannot edit rule sets, and only partner-level users can edit all-organizations sets. The AI assistant can import indicators only with approval, and never into a set that has auto-quarantine on.

sections.heading: IOC sweeps
sections.text: A detection rule set lives under **Security → Detection Rules**; each time you publish it, it gets a numbered version. An IOC sweep runs one or more published rule sets against many devices at once and pins the exact versions it was approved with.

sections.heading: What a sweep is
sections.text: A sweep is one request that fans out into one ordinary IOC scan per eligible device, so every result shows up in the usual **Scan History** and **Threats** views. Start one from a rule set (**Sweep now** in the rule-set editor), from the API, or from the AI assistant. Follow it on the **Sweeps** tab of **Security → IOC Scans**: the list shows the rule sets and their versions, progress, how many scans ran with degraded coverage, threats found, who started it and when, and its state (**Active**, **Completed**, **Cancelled** or **Expired**). A sweep that spans several organizations is stored as one row per organization; they share a group, and `#sweeps&group=<groupId>` in the page address opens that group.

sections.heading: Sweeps only detect
sections.text: A sweep never quarantines or removes anything, whatever the rule set's auto-quarantine setting says. On Windows it also does not start a Microsoft Defender scan, unlike a single-device scan started from the Scans tab. A match is reported as a threat, and you decide what to do with it from the Threats tab.

sections.heading: Scope and eligibility
sections.text:
Choose the scope when you start the sweep:

- **All reachable devices** — every device your account can access.
- **Organizations**, **Sites**, **Device groups** or **Devices** — only those.

Scopes defined by device policies are not offered. A request is limited to 10,000 devices. Devices outside your access are never included, and asking for one explicitly is refused.

A device in scope can be skipped for one of three reasons, each shown with its count in the preview:

| Reason | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `agent_too_old` | The agent is older than 0.124.0 and cannot run YARA rule sets. Update it and sweep again. |
| `busy_same_sweep` | An identical sweep is still active on the device. |
| `rule_set_not_eligible` | The device's operating system or organization is outside the rule set's reach. |

Users limited to certain sites or devices do not see skip counts; the Sweeps tab shows a dash for them.

sections.heading: Preview and confirmation
sections.text: **Sweep now** opens a five-step dialog: scope, scan type (Quick, Full, or Custom with up to 20 paths of at most 1,024 characters), duration, preview and confirm. The preview shows how many devices in how many organizations will be scanned, the rule-set versions, and the skipped devices with the reason for each. Nothing is written until you confirm. Confirming sends a digest of what you previewed; if the devices or rule sets changed in the meantime, the dialog shows the new preview and asks again instead of running something you did not approve. If the same sweep is already running, the dialog links to it.

sections.heading: Multi-factor authentication above 50 devices
sections.text: A sweep of more than 50 devices needs an interactive sign-in with multi-factor authentication satisfied, as your organization's policy requires. When no second factor is enforced, a signed-in password session counts. If the check fails, the dialog says so and you can sign in again or narrow the scope. API keys and other machine credentials are refused above 50 devices whether or not multi-factor authentication is enforced; narrow the scope or run the sweep from the console.

sections.heading: Pinned rule versions
sections.text: When you confirm, the sweep pins each rule set's published version and content hash. Every scan of the sweep runs exactly those versions, and a threat found by a pinned scan shows **Version N** in its rule panel. If someone republishes a pinned rule set while the sweep is running, the scans that have not started yet fail with `rule_set_changed` rather than silently running different rules, and the Sweeps tab marks the row **Rules changed since this sweep started** with **Sweep again with the current rules**.

sections.heading: Duration and offline devices
sections.text: A sweep stays open for 24 hours by default; you can set 1 to 72 hours. An offline device keeps its queued scan and runs it when it returns within that time. When the time is up, scans that have not started become **Expired**, the sweep becomes **Expired**, and scans already running on a device are allowed a grace period before they are closed out.

sections.heading: Pacing
sections.text:
Each device runs one scan at a time. The server hands scans to devices in small batches on a timer, and also limits how many scans run at once per device, per organization and per partner, so a large sweep takes a while and does not flood a site. An organization can have 5 active sweeps at once, a partner at most 200 running scans, and a user can start 10 sweeps per hour. These limits and the operator settings behind them:

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `SECURITY_SWEEP_MAX_DEVICES` | 10000 | Devices per request |
| `SECURITY_SWEEP_MAX_ACTIVE_PER_ORG` | 5 | Active sweeps per organization |
| `SECURITY_SWEEP_PARTNER_RUNNING_CAP` | 200 | Running sweep scans per partner |
| `SECURITY_SWEEP_PUMP_INTERVAL_MS` | 30000 | How often queued scans are handed out |
| `SECURITY_SWEEP_PUMP_BATCH` | 100 | Scans admitted per sweep per organization per tick |
| `SECURITY_SWEEP_TTL_HOURS_DEFAULT` | 24 | Default duration |
| `SECURITY_SWEEP_MFA_DEVICE_THRESHOLD` | 50 | Devices above which multi-factor authentication is required |
| `SECURITY_SWEEP_RUNNING_GRACE_MINUTES` | 65 | Grace for scans already running at expiry |
| `IOC_HUNT_FOUR_EYES_DEVICE_THRESHOLD` | 25 | Devices above which an AI-started sweep needs a second approver |

sections.heading: Cancel
sections.text: **Cancel** stops a sweep; **Cancel all** stops every sweep of a group. Scans still queued stop at once. A scan already delivered to a device finishes there, because the agent cannot be recalled, and the confirmation says how many are still finishing. Cancelling an already finished sweep does nothing. You need permission to run commands on the devices, and a user limited to certain sites or devices can cancel only sweeps they started.

sections.heading: Running it again
sections.text: Sweeping again with the same rule sets, scope and scan type while one is active is refused with a link to the running sweep. Once it has finished, a new sweep starts fresh against the current published versions. A sweep does not remember its devices, so choosing **Sweep again with the current rules** reopens the dialog with the rule sets and scan type filled in and asks for the scope again.

sections.heading: Degraded coverage
sections.text: A scan counts as degraded when it completed or timed out on the legacy engine, or when some rules in the set could not be loaded on the device. The Sweeps tab shows the count, and the sweep's tone turns to a warning so a clean-looking result is not mistaken for full coverage. Failed, expired and cancelled scans are counted separately.

sections.heading: AI assistant and MCP
sections.text: The AI assistant and MCP clients use the `ioc_hunt` tool: listing rule sets, previewing, listing and checking sweeps are Tier 1 and need no approval; cancelling a sweep is Tier 2; starting a sweep and importing IOCs are Tier 3 and need an approved action (see [AI features](/features/ai/) and [MCP server](/features/mcp-server/)). A sweep started by the assistant is supervised up to 25 expected devices, and above 25 it needs a second approver. An assistant sweep covers one organization at a time. Importing IOCs adds them to a rule set and publishes it; importing into a set that has auto-quarantine turned on is refused. `ioc_hunt` is not part of any AI agent's tool catalog.

sections.heading: Audit events
sections.text:
Every sweep writes audit events for its organization row: `security.scan_sweep.create`, `security.scan_sweep.cancel`, `security.scan_sweep.expire` and `security.scan_sweep.complete`. They record the rule-set pins, scan type, scope kind, counts and origin (web, API, AI chat or MCP), never paths, device ids or IOC values.

---

sections.heading: Threat Types and Severity
sections.text:
The agent scans for known threat signatures using both filename pattern matching and file content analysis. Detected threats are classified by type and severity:

| Threat Type | Description |
|-------------|-------------|
| **`malware`** | General malicious software (e.g. Mimikatz, EICAR test file) |
| **`trojan`** | Trojan horse programs (e.g. Emotet, Trickbot) |
| **`ransomware`** | Ransomware indicators (e.g. ransom notes, decryption instructions) |
| **`spyware`** | Spyware and surveillance tools |
| **`pup`** | Potentially unwanted programs |

| Severity | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **`low`** | Minimal risk; informational detection |
| **`medium`** | Moderate risk; should be reviewed |
| **`high`** | Significant risk; prompt action recommended (e.g. Mimikatz, EICAR, ransomware notes) |
| **`critical`** | Severe risk; immediate action required (e.g. CobaltStrike beacons, Emotet) |

sections.heading: Which rule fired
sections.text: A threat found by a detection rule shows the rule, its rule set and the matched strings in the threat's rule panel. When the scan ran pinned rule-set versions (every IOC sweep does), the panel also shows **Version N**, the version of the rule set that was dispatched to the device. Threats found by the built-in signatures, and threats from scans that did not pin a version, show no version.

sections.heading: Threat Status Lifecycle
sections.text:
Each threat progresses through a status lifecycle:

| Status | DB Status | Description |
|--------|-----------|-------------|
| **Active** | `detected`, `failed` | Threat is present and unresolved |
| **Quarantined** | `quarantined` | Threat file moved to an isolated quarantine directory |
| **Removed** | `removed`, `allowed` | Threat file deleted or explicitly allowed |

sections.heading: Threat Actions
sections.text:
You can take action on detected threats directly from the API:

```bash
# Quarantine a threat (moves file to quarantine directory)
POST /security/threats/{threatId}/quarantine

# Permanently remove a threat
POST /security/threats/{threatId}/remove

# Restore a quarantined threat (mark as allowed)
POST /security/threats/{threatId}/restore
```

Each action queues a command to the agent and updates the threat status in the database. The quarantine directory defaults to:

| Platform | Path |
|----------|------|
| Windows | `%ProgramData%\Breeze\quarantine` |
| macOS | `/Library/Application Support/Breeze/quarantine` |
| Linux | `/var/lib/breeze/quarantine` |

  The agent's built-in threat scanner uses signature-based detection for known malware families. It is not a replacement for a full endpoint protection platform. Use it as a supplementary layer alongside your primary AV provider.

---

sections.heading: Triggering a Scan
sections.text:
Initiate an on-demand security scan on a specific device by posting to the scan endpoint:

```bash
POST /security/scan/{deviceId}
{
  "scanType": "quick",
  "paths": []
}
```

| Scan Type | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| **`quick`** | Scans high-risk locations: temp directories, Downloads folder, startup/launch directories |
| **`full`** | Comprehensive scan of all major system locations (entire drives on Windows, `/Applications`, `/Library`, `/Users` on macOS, `/` tree on Linux) |
| **`custom`** | Scans only the paths specified in the `paths` array |

The scan is queued as a `SECURITY_SCAN` command to the agent. The response returns a scan record with status `queued` and a `202 Accepted` status code.

sections.heading: Scan Lifecycle
sections.text:
| Status | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **`queued`** | Scan command sent to the agent, waiting for execution |
| **`running`** | Agent is actively scanning |
| **`completed`** | Scan finished; results include `threatsFound` count and `durationSeconds` |
| **`failed`** | Scan encountered an error |
| **`cancelled`** | The scan was stopped before it ran, for example when its sweep was cancelled |
| **`expired`** | The scan never ran because its sweep's time ran out |

sections.heading: Viewing Scan History
sections.text:
```bash
GET /security/scans/{deviceId}?scanType=quick&status=completed&startDate=2026-02-01
```

Returns paginated scan history for the device, filterable by `scanType`, `status`, and date range.

  On Windows, the scan also triggers a Microsoft Defender scan (`Start-MpScan`) alongside the Breeze agent's own signature scan, giving you dual-layer detection.

---

sections.heading: Security Posture Scoring
sections.text:
The security posture system computes a 0-100 score for each device based on eight weighted factors:

| Factor | Label | Weight | Description |
|--------|-------|--------|-------------|
| `patch_compliance` | Patch Compliance | 25% | Are critical and important patches up to date? |
| `encryption` | Disk Encryption | 15% | Is full-disk encryption active on all volumes? |
| `av_health` | AV Health | 15% | Is AV installed, real-time protection on, and definitions fresh? |
| `firewall` | Firewall Status | 10% | Is the host firewall enabled? |
| `open_ports` | Open Ports Exposure | 10% | Are unnecessary listening services exposed? |
| `password_policy` | Password Policy | 10% | Does the local password policy meet baseline requirements? |
| `os_currency` | OS Currency | 10% | Is the operating system version current and supported? |
| `admin_exposure` | Admin Exposure | 5% | Are local admin accounts minimized and hardened? |

The overall score is graded on a letter scale:

| Grade | Score Range |
|-------|-------------|
| **A** | 90 - 100 |
| **B** | 80 - 89 |
| **C** | 70 - 79 |
| **D** | 60 - 69 |
| **F** | 0 - 59 |

sections.heading: Risk Levels
sections.text:
Each device is assigned a risk level based on its posture:

| Risk Level | Meaning |
|------------|---------|
| **`low`** | Device is fully protected (score high, no active issues) |
| **`medium`** | Minor gaps detected (e.g. firewall off or encryption missing) |
| **`high`** | Multiple protection gaps or elevated threat count |
| **`critical`** | Severe exposure: unprotected with active threats |

sections.heading: Organization-Level Posture
sections.text:
The posture worker runs hourly via BullMQ, computing scores for every device across all organizations. Organization-level snapshots aggregate:

- **`devicesAudited`** -- total devices scored
- **`lowRiskDevices`**, **`mediumRiskDevices`**, **`highRiskDevices`**, **`criticalRiskDevices`** -- risk distribution
- Per-factor average scores
- **`topIssues`** -- most common compliance gaps

sections.heading: Password Policy Compliance
sections.text:
The API evaluates each device's local password policy against baseline requirements:

| Rule | Requirement |
|------|-------------|
| Minimum length | 12+ characters |
| Complexity required | Enabled |
| Maximum password age | 90 days or fewer |
| Account lockout threshold | 1-5 failed attempts |
| Password history | 5+ remembered passwords |

A device is **compliant** only if all five checks pass.

sections.heading: Admin Account Audit
sections.text:
The admin audit identifies three categories of risk in local administrator accounts:

| Issue Type | Description |
|------------|-------------|
| **`default_account`** | Built-in administrator accounts that are still enabled |
| **`weak_password`** | Admin accounts with passwords older than 180 days |
| **`stale_account`** | Admin accounts with no login activity in 90+ days |

sections.heading: Compliance Trend Tracking
sections.text:
```bash
GET /security/trends?period=30d
```

Returns time-series data points showing how the overall posture score has changed over the requested period (`7d`, `30d`, or `90d`). The response includes a summary with `current` score, `previous` score, absolute `change`, and directional `trend` (`improving`, `declining`, or `stable`).

---

sections.heading: Security Recommendations
sections.text: The recommendations engine analyzes posture data across the fleet and generates prioritized, actionable guidance. Recommendations are computed dynamically based on how many devices fall below threshold scores for each security factor.

sections.heading: How Recommendations Are Generated
sections.text:
1. The engine loads the latest posture snapshots for all devices in the organization.
2. For each security factor, it counts devices scoring below the target threshold (e.g. AV health below 80, firewall below 90).
3. If any devices are affected, a recommendation is generated with priority scaled to the percentage of the fleet impacted.
4. Recommendations are sorted by priority (critical first), then by affected device count.

sections.heading: Recommendation Categories
sections.text:
| Category | Trigger Threshold | Baseline Priority |
|----------|-------------------|-------------------|
| `antivirus` | AV health score below 80 | High |
| `vulnerability_management` | Active threats + open ports/OS currency below 70 | Critical |
| `firewall` | Firewall score below 90 | High |
| `encryption` | Encryption score below 90 | High |
| `password_policy` | Password policy score below 85 | Medium |
| `admin_accounts` | Admin exposure score below 85 | Medium |
| `patch_compliance` | Patch compliance score below 90 | High |

sections.heading: Priority Escalation
sections.text:
Priority is dynamically escalated based on what percentage of the fleet is affected:

| Fleet % Affected | Dynamic Priority |
|------------------|-----------------|
| 45%+ | Critical |
| 25-44% | High |
| 10-24% | Medium |
| Under 10% | Low |

The final priority is the higher of the baseline priority and the dynamic priority.

sections.heading: Recommendation Lifecycle
sections.text:
Each recommendation can be in one of three states:

| Status | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **`open`** | Active recommendation requiring attention |
| **`completed`** | Marked as resolved by an administrator |
| **`dismissed`** | Acknowledged but not acted upon |

Completing or dismissing a recommendation creates an audit log entry. To mark a recommendation:

```bash
# Mark as completed
POST /security/recommendations/{id}/complete

# Dismiss
POST /security/recommendations/{id}/dismiss
```

  Recommendations include a `steps` array with concrete remediation instructions. Each recommendation also carries `impact` (high/medium/low) and `effort` (low/medium/high) ratings to help you prioritize effectively.

---

sections.heading: Security Dashboard
sections.text:
The dashboard endpoint aggregates all security data into a single response for rendering the security overview UI.

```bash
GET /security/dashboard?orgId={orgId}
```

sections.heading: Dashboard Response Fields
sections.text:
| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
