sections.heading: Tag-related device endpoints
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `PATCH` | `/api/v1/devices/:id` | Set tags on a device (include `tags` in request body) |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/devices/:id` | Returns the device including its `tags` array |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/devices` | Lists devices; each includes its `tags` array |

sections.heading: Query parameters
sections.text:
**`GET /api/v1/tags`**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `search` | string | No | Case-insensitive substring filter on tag names |

**`GET /api/v1/tags/devices`**

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tag` | string | Yes | Exact tag to match (minimum 1 character) |

sections.heading: Device update body (tags)
Database schema
sections.text:
Tags are stored directly on the `devices` table:

| Column | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tags` | `text[]` | `[]` | Array of tag strings |

There is no separate tags table. Tag aggregation (listing unique tags and counts) is computed at query time by scanning the `tags` column across all accessible devices.

---

sections.heading: Tags disappeared from the listing
sections.text: The `GET /api/v1/tags` endpoint derives its list from the current state of devices. If no device carries a particular tag, that tag will not appear in the response. Tags are not stored independently -- they exist only as values in device records.

sections.heading: "No updates provided" when patching tags
sections.text: Ensure the request body includes the `tags` key. Sending an empty object `{}` returns a `400` error. To clear all tags, send `{"tags": []}`.

sections.heading: Tag search returns no results
sections.text: The `search` parameter on `GET /api/v1/tags` performs a case-insensitive substring match. Verify the search term is part of an existing tag. If you are an organisation-scoped user, you will only see tags from devices in your own organisation.

sections.heading: Tags not matching policy targets
sections.text: When a policy uses `targetType: "tags"`, the `targetIds` array must contain the exact tag strings (case-sensitive). A policy targeting `["Production"]` will not match devices tagged `"production"`. Use a consistent casing convention across your fleet to avoid mismatches.

sections.heading: Updating tags removes existing ones
sections.text: The `tags` field on device PATCH is a full replacement, not a merge. To add a new tag while preserving existing ones, first read the device to get its current tags, then send the combined array.

title: Customer Approval for Ticket Work
description: Ask the customer to approve over-budget and after-hours work before it is billed -- ticket budgets, after-hours work types, held time, the staff panel, the customer portal, emails and expiry.

sections.text:
Some customers want to know before a ticket costs more than planned, and some work types (an after-hours call-out, for example) carry a premium the customer has to agree to. Customer approval lets a technician keep working and recording time while the money question is settled in the open: time that crosses a budget or uses an after-hours work type is **held** until the customer approves, or until staff record the customer's consent.

This feature is **off until a partner turns it on**. Nothing about timers, time entries or invoices changes for a partner whose **Customer approval** setting is not enabled.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
1. A ticket has a **budget** (hours, an amount, or both) and/or a work type marked **after-hours**.
2. When a billable time entry would cross the budget, or uses an after-hours work type that has no consent covering it, Breeze records the entry and marks it **Awaiting approval**.
3. A **request** is created for the customer. Designated approvers decide it from the customer portal, or staff record the decision on the customer's behalf.
4. On approval, the held entries are re-checked against the new ceiling and released to normal billing. On denial, expiry or cancellation they stay held until staff resolve them.

Breeze never refuses to *record* work that already happened. The hold applies to billing, and the server enforces it: a held entry cannot be invoiced.

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
Customer approval resolves **partner default → organization override**, and the resolved values are copied onto each request when it is created, so a later settings change never rewrites a request in flight.

| Setting | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Enabled** | Master switch. Off means no gate, no requests, no holds. | Off |
| **Budget trigger** | Raise requests when work crosses a ticket budget. | On |
| **After-hours trigger** | Raise requests for after-hours work types. | On |
| **Enforcement** | **Soft** records and holds. **Hard** also refuses to *start* a billable timer that would need approval. | Soft |
| **Request lifetime** | Hours a request stays pending before it expires (1 to 720). | 72 |

Partner defaults live in the **Customer approval** section of the time tracking settings and need partner-wide rights to edit. Each organization can override any field in its ticketing settings; clearing an override returns that field to the partner default.

sections.heading: Ticket budgets
sections.text:
Open a ticket and use the **Budget** card to set a budget in hours, an amount, or both. The card shows consumed time against the ceiling, with held time shaded separately. The ceiling is the budget plus any approved extensions.

The amount is expressed in the organization's currency, and Breeze rejects amounts that currency cannot represent (for example fractional units in a currency with none). Organization-scoped users can view the budget but not change it.

sections.heading: After-hours work types
sections.text: In the **Work Types** card on the Billing **Rates** tab, tick **After-hours** on any work type that should need consent. Breeze does not read the clock: the flag belongs to the work type the technician (or the ticket category default) selects. An after-hours entry is covered when an approved after-hours request on the ticket has a coverage window that contains the entry's start, or when it was released by an approved request.

sections.heading: The gate and held time
sections.text:
| Situation | Soft | Hard |
|---|---|---|
| Entry fits the budget and is not uncovered after-hours | Recorded normally | Same |
| Finished entry (manual log, timer stop, edit) crosses the line | Recorded as **Awaiting approval**, linked to a pending request | Same -- past work is never refused |
| Billable timer **start** at or over the ceiling, or on an uncovered after-hours work type | Allowed; held at stop | Refused with an **Approval required** message |

When a hard-mode start is refused, the technician can retry the start as **non-billable** (this needs the same billing permission as any change to an entry's billable flag; without it they are told to ask someone who has it) or ask for approval. Held entries stay editable; editing one re-runs the check and may release it.

One entry can need both kinds of consent. After-hours is evaluated first, and a release re-runs the budget check.

sections.heading: The staff panel
sections.text:
On a ticket, the **Approvals** panel lists every request with its status, the ask, and the figures it was based on. From it, staff can:

- **Request approval** -- raise an ask yourself, optionally with an after-hours coverage window. A staff-raised amount is a floor: automatic recomputation never lowers it.
- **Cancel** a pending request. Linked entries re-run the check; those that fit are released and the rest stay held on a new request.
- **Ask again** -- after a denial or expiry, create a fresh request and move the held entries onto it.
- **Record on behalf** -- capture the customer's decision when it came by another route. Pick the **method** (verbal, email, signed document or other), enter a **reference** (required, for example an email subject or document id) and the signer's name. This needs the *record approval* ticket permission, which is separate from general ticket write access.
- **Write off** held time -- sets the entry to no charge, audited. This needs the billing management permission for time entries.

Held entries show an **Awaiting approval** chip in the ticket time list and the timesheet. If no approver is on file, the panel says so and suggests adding a billing contact or recording the decision on behalf.

Breeze has no "bill without consent" action: a held entry leaves the hold only by approval, by a write-off, or by being re-evaluated under a higher ceiling.

sections.heading: The customer portal
sections.text:
Customers see an **Approvals** page in the portal, with a pending count in the navigation and a banner on the ticket when a request is waiting.

- **Approvers** are active organization contacts with the **billing** role, frozen on the request when it is created. They can approve or deny.
- **Notify-only** recipients -- the ticket requester and any after-hours contacts, minus the approvers -- can see the request but cannot decide it.

The page shows the ticket number and subject, what is being asked, and the figures at request time, not the whole ticket. To decide, the approver types their **name** and chooses **Approve** or **Deny**, with an optional note. The decision records their address and browser details.

If staff change the request after the page was loaded (for example by adding more held time), the decision is refused with **"This request was updated, please review again"**, so a customer only ever approves the amount they saw. Deciding an already-decided request, or one that has expired, gets its own clear message too.

sections.heading: Emails
sections.text:
| Email | Goes to | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| **Approval request (approver)** | Approvers | The ask and a link to approve or deny in the portal |
| **Approval request (notify)** | Notify-only recipients | The same facts, with no decision link |
| **Decision** | Approvers and notify-only recipients | Confirmation that the request was approved or denied |

These send through the partner's normal email lane and can be overridden with partner email templates. Repeat sends for the same request are throttled. If ticketing is switched off for the customer, no request email is sent and staff get an in-app prompt to record the decision on behalf. Staff are also notified in-app when a request is decided.

sections.heading: Expiry
sections.text: A pending request expires after the configured lifetime. Its entries stay held. Staff then **Ask again** or write the time off.

sections.heading: What a pending request blocks
sections.text:
- **Invoicing.** An invoice cannot be issued while any of its source time is awaiting approval; the error names what is held.
- **Moving the ticket to another organization.** A pending request must be resolved first, because it belongs to the original customer's billing contacts.

sections.heading: Other places it appears
sections.text:
- **Outlook add-in.** Starting a timer that needs approval offers **Log as non-billable**. Entries recorded but held show a "held pending customer approval" notice.
- **Mobile app.** Held entries carry an **Awaiting approval** badge but stay editable. A refused start asks **"Approval required. Log as non-billable?"**. Time recorded offline is replayed as finished entries, which are held rather than refused; if a queued entry is ever rejected it is parked for the technician, never dropped.
- **AI assistant.** The assistant can read a ticket's budget and approval status and is told when time it logs is held. It cannot decide, record on behalf, write off or change a budget -- consent is a person's act.

sections.heading: Status
sections.text: Customer approval is complete across the API, the staff web interface, the customer portal, the Outlook add-in, the mobile app and the AI assistant's tool text. By design there is no AI tool to decide a request, record consent on behalf, write off held time or set a budget.

title: Ticketing
description: Built-in ticketing for MSP workflows -- a triage queue, public replies and internal notes, SLA chips, and tickets linked to alerts and devices.
headings: Moving a ticket to another organization
Connecting a Google Workspace support mailbox
Priority labels and partner-wide SLA defaults

sections.text:
Breeze includes a built-in ticketing system designed for MSP technician workflows. Tickets arrive from the customer portal, from alerts, from technicians creating them by hand, and through the API -- and they all land in one queue. Open **Tickets** from the left sidebar to start working.

Every ticket gets a number in the form `T-YYYY-NNNN` (for example `T-2026-0042`), which appears throughout the dashboard and is the easiest way to reference a ticket with your team or a customer.

sections.heading: The Queue
sections.text:
The Tickets page is a split-pane workspace: the ticket list on the left, and a workbench for the selected ticket on the right. Selecting a ticket in the list opens it instantly in the workbench -- no page reloads. On narrower screens, selecting a ticket opens its full page instead.

Across the top, view tabs slice the queue:

| Tab | Shows |
|---|---|
| **My tickets** | Open tickets assigned to you |
| **Unassigned** | Open tickets nobody owns yet |
| **All open** | Every open ticket you can see |
| **Breaching soon** | Open tickets whose SLA is at risk or already breached |
| **Closed** | Resolved and closed tickets, newest first |
| **Archived** | Deleted tickets, with a **Restore** action -- only visible to Partner Admins and Org Admins (see [Deleting and Restoring Tickets](#deleting-and-restoring-tickets)) |

Below the tabs, a filter bar narrows any view by **organization**, **priority**, **category**, and **assignee**, and a search box matches against ticket subjects. Each row shows the ticket number, subject, status, priority, and an SLA chip when the clock is running low.

sections.heading: Ticket types
sections.text:
Every ticket has a **type**: **Incident**, **Service request**, **Problem**, or **Change**. The type tells your team what kind of work a ticket is, separately from its category.

- **Defaults.** New tickets are Incidents, whether they come from an alert, the portal, email, the API, the AI assistant, or a technician. Planned work -- tickets created for a service deliverable occurrence or a project task -- starts as a Service request. The **Create ticket** form defaults to Incident and lets you pick another type.
- **In the queue.** Each row shows a type chip, and the filter bar has a **Filter by type** control. The Service Desk section of the sidebar has an entry per type -- **Incidents**, **Service Requests**, **Problems**, and **Changes** -- next to **Tickets**, which shows every type. The type filter is kept in the page URL, so a filtered view can be bookmarked.
- **On a ticket.** Users with ticket edit permission change the type from the **Ticket type** selector in the workbench; read-only users see the chip. Changing the type is recorded in the ticket's activity as an internal note. It does not recalculate the SLA or re-run category rules.
- **In the portal.** Customers see the type as a label next to the ticket number, but cannot choose it: tickets they submit get the default type.

The AI assistant's ticket tool can filter by type, set the type when it creates a ticket, and change it on an existing one.

sections.heading: Site-scoped technicians
sections.text: Organization users restricted to specific sites only see tickets whose device belongs to one of their sites. Tickets with no device attached (general, org-level requests) remain visible to every technician in the organization. Site-restricted users also can't create tickets against — or move tickets onto — devices outside their sites.

sections.heading: Working a Ticket
sections.text:
The workbench shows everything you need to resolve a ticket without leaving the queue:

- **Status** -- move the ticket between New, Open, Pending, On hold, Resolved, and Closed. Resolving always asks for a **resolution note**, which is visible to the requester, so the customer sees what was done.
- **Priority** -- change between Low, Normal, High, and Urgent.
- **Assignee** -- assign or unassign the ticket. Press `a` to grab the selected ticket for yourself.
- **Subject and description** -- click the subject to rename the ticket in place; the description has an **Edit** (or **Add description**) control. Changes save instantly and are recorded in the ticket's activity.
- **Category, due date, and tags** -- set the category from a dropdown (including **No category**), pick or clear a due date, and add or remove tags directly on the ticket. Every change is logged in the activity feed.
- **Requester** -- select or change who the ticket is for, so a ticket that came in under the wrong contact (or with none) can be corrected without recreating it.
- **Properties rail** -- requester, source, created date, due date, the reason a ticket is waiting, the resolution note, a **linked device** that links straight to the device's page (use **Link device** to attach one to an existing ticket, or **Change device** to swap it, v0.124.0+), and any **linked alerts** with one-click navigation to the alert itself.

Click the expand icon (or press `Enter`) to open the ticket as a full page when you need more room.

sections.heading: Related tickets
sections.text:
The **Related tickets** panel in the workbench links a ticket to other tickets in the same organization -- for example, several incidents to the problem behind them, or a change to the problem it resolves. Click **Link a ticket**, choose how this ticket relates to the other one, then search for it by number or subject:

| Link | Shown on this ticket | Shown on the other ticket |
|---|---|---|
| **is related to** | Related | Related |
| **was caused by** | Caused by | Causes |
| **resolves** | Resolves | Resolved by |
| **is a duplicate of** | Duplicate of | Duplicates |

Each linked ticket shows its number, subject, status, and type, and opens in its full-page view. A link to a ticket that was later deleted stays in the list with a **Deleted** marker so you can remove it.

Linking never changes either ticket's status, SLA, or assignee -- marking a ticket as a duplicate only records the relationship, so close the duplicate yourself. Adding or removing a link writes an internal note on both tickets and an entry in the audit log.

The panel refuses a link that breaks these rules, and says why:

- Both tickets must be in the **same organization**, and a ticket cannot link to itself.
- **Caused by** and **resolves** links cannot form a loop (A caused by B caused by A).
- Duplicates are one level deep: a ticket can be a duplicate of only one ticket, a ticket that already has duplicates cannot itself be marked as a duplicate, and you cannot mark a ticket as a duplicate of another duplicate -- link to the original instead.
- A ticket can have at most **50 links**. Links to tickets you cannot see (for example, at a site outside your access) still count toward the cap and these rules.

Viewing links needs ticket read permission; adding and removing them needs ticket edit permission. The AI assistant's ticket tool can list, add, and remove links under the same rules. Links are not shown in the customer portal, and moving a ticket to another organization removes its links.

sections.heading: Assignment notifications
sections.text:
When a ticket is assigned to someone, Breeze emails the new assignee. The email carries a short facts table (ticket number, customer, priority, status, requester and, when there is one, the linked device), the first 1,200 characters of the message, and an **Open ticket** link to the ticket in the dashboard. Assignees can also get a mobile push (see [Mobile app](/features/mobile/)) and, if they save their own key, a [Pushover push](/features/notifications/#ticket-assignments-over-pushover).

For a newly created ticket, the assignment notification is sent on the next notification pass after the ticket is saved, usually about 5 seconds later.

sections.heading: Moving a ticket to another organization
sections.text:
If a ticket landed under the wrong customer, use **Move to another org…** in the ticket header to reassign it to a different organization. Pick the target from the dropdown and click **Move**. The ticket — along with its time entries, parts, and linked alerts — follows to the new organization, and the move is recorded in the activity feed and the audit log.

Because the attached device belongs to the original organization, moving the ticket **detaches its device** (the ticket becomes device-less; you can link a device from the new org afterward). The assignee and category carry over unchanged. The ticket's business calendar is re-resolved for the target organization, and its response and resolution deadlines that haven't been met yet are recalculated on that calendar (see [Business hours](#business-hours)).

If the two organizations bill in different currencies and the ticket still has **unbilled** time entries or parts with amounts, the move is blocked: the dialog explains how many entries and parts are priced in the old currency and in which currency the target organization bills. The clean path is to invoice that work first (or assemble a draft in the old currency from the ticket), then move. If you need to move regardless, tick the acknowledgement and click **Move anyway** -- those items keep their amounts in the old currency, they are never converted, and they can only be invoiced later on a draft in that currency. "Move anyway" additionally requires invoice edit permission, and the acknowledgement is recorded in the activity feed and the audit log.

  Tickets can only be moved between organizations of the **same partner**. This is a high-privilege action: it requires ticket and organization edit permissions plus MFA confirmation, and isn't available to site-restricted technicians.

sections.heading: Merging duplicate tickets
sections.text:
When the same issue arrives twice (a customer emails and also calls, or two people report one outage), merge the duplicate into the ticket you want to keep.

1. Open the duplicate and choose **Merge into…** in the ticket header.
2. Pick the ticket to keep. The list shows the organization's open tickets, oldest first, and you can search it. Resolved and closed tickets cannot receive a merge.
3. Read the preview. It lists what moves to the kept ticket (comments, attachments, time entries, parts, checklist items, linked alerts and emails, tags), the links that are dropped, and whether the kept ticket keeps its own device or takes the duplicate's. When the ticket you picked is not the older one, the preview suggests the older one, which is usually the one to keep.
4. Decide whether to email the duplicate's requester. **Notify the requester** is ticked by default when the two tickets have different requesters.
5. Click **Merge** and confirm with MFA.

After the merge:

- The duplicate becomes a **closed, read-only record** with a banner linking to the kept ticket. Nothing can be added to it or changed on it. Comments that moved show "from T-…" next to the author.
- The kept ticket keeps its own SLA clock, priority and assignee. Time entries and parts move with their amounts and billing state unchanged.
- **Replies follow the merge.** Email sent to the duplicate's thread is added to the kept ticket.
- **In the customer portal**, the duplicate shows a "This request was merged into T-…" banner. Its requester can read and reply on the kept ticket.
- Merged tickets are hidden from the queue. Tick **Show merged** above the list to see them.

A merge cannot be undone. It is refused when the tickets belong to different organizations (move one first), when either ticket has a customer approval request or a budget, when either is tied to a service deliverable or an open migration import, when one is planned work and the other a support ticket, or when the duplicate has AI actions waiting for approval. The preview names the reason before you confirm.

Merging needs ticket edit permission and access to both tickets' sites and devices. The AI assistant can preview and perform a merge through its ticket tool, under the same rules and with approval.

sections.heading: Deleting and Restoring Tickets
sections.text:
Click **Delete**, next to **Move to another org…** in the ticket header, to remove a ticket. A confirm dialog explains that the ticket is hidden from every queue and can be restored by an admin, then deletes it. The same **Delete** action is available from the bulk action bar for a batch of selected tickets.

A deleted ticket disappears immediately from every list, from stats, from the customer portal, from AI tools, and from email threading -- a customer replying to an old email about a deleted ticket can't reopen it. No notification is sent to the requester when a ticket is deleted.

Deleting and restoring both require the **ticket management** permission, held by **Partner Admins** and **Org Admins** (technicians and viewers can't delete or restore). Find deleted tickets under the **Archived** tab and click **Restore** on any row to return it to the live queues. Both actions are recorded in the audit log.

sections.heading: Replies and Internal Notes
sections.text:
The composer at the bottom of every ticket has two modes:

- **Reply** (the default) -- a public response. If the ticket came from the customer portal, your reply appears in the requester's portal conversation. The requester also gets a laid-out email **notice** -- not the reply text. See [Public-reply email notice](#public-reply-email-notice).
- **Internal note** -- visible only to your team. The composer switches to a clearly marked highlighted style with an "Internal: not visible to requester" banner, so there is no ambiguity about who will see what you are typing. Internal notes do not email the requester.

Portal users only ever see public replies. Internal notes, status changes, and assignment history stay inside the dashboard.

Press `Cmd+Enter` (or `Ctrl+Enter`) to send without leaving the keyboard.

sections.heading: Public-reply email notice
sections.text:
A public technician reply emails the requester a laid-out transactional notice (subject, heading, and a **View ticket** button). **The reply text is never in the email.** The customer reads the reply in the [customer portal](/features/portal/). They respond by replying to the email. Email-only requesters (no portal login) never see the technician's words. Inbound comments (the customer writing in) also send no requester email, so they don't bounce in a loop.

Partners edit this notice, the ticket-received acknowledgement, and the resolved-ticket mail under **Settings → Partner → Email templates**. The same tab also holds quote, invoice, and portal-invite mail. The **View ticket** button always goes to `/portal/tickets/:id` on your portal origin; partners cannot point it somewhere else. Self-hosted: set [`PUBLIC_PORTAL_URL`](/deploy/environment/#server) (or `PUBLIC_APP_URL`) so that button is reachable.

Which path sends the mail is unchanged. A connected Microsoft 365 support mailbox still sends via Graph from that mailbox; otherwise the platform email service (EmailService) sends. `EMAIL_PROVIDER=auto` with no SMTP, Resend, or Mailgun host is a no-op on the EmailService path -- nothing is sent that way. Graph still sends if a mailbox is connected.

sections.heading: Attachments
sections.text:
You can attach files to a reply or an internal note — a screenshot of the error, a photo of a serial number, a signed PDF.

- Up to **5 files per comment**, each up to **10 MB**.
- **JPEG, PNG, WebP and PDF** only.

An attachment inherits the visibility of the comment it belongs to. Files on a public reply are visible to the requester in the customer portal; files on an internal note stay with your team. Deleting a comment removes access to its attachments too.

Technicians can add attachments from the ticket workbench and from the mobile app. Customers can open and download the files on a public reply from the portal, but cannot upload their own there.

sections.heading: Editing and deleting your replies
sections.text:
Each reply and internal note you wrote has **Edit** and **Delete** controls in its header. Editing opens the text inline with **Save** and **Cancel**; an edited entry is marked **edited** in the feed. Deleting asks you to confirm and leaves a small "deleted" placeholder in its place rather than removing the entry outright, so the conversation history stays intact.

You can edit or delete your **own** comments; technicians with ticket management permission can edit or delete anyone's. System entries — status changes, assignments, and time logs — can't be edited or deleted, and comments that came in from the customer portal aren't editable from the workbench. Editing or deleting a reply does **not** re-notify the customer.

sections.heading: Checklists
sections.text: A ticket can carry a **Checklist** of steps to tick off as the work is done. Steps are internal -- never shown to the customer -- and each can carry a note. Resolving a ticket with unticked steps asks you to confirm first. In the queue, a ticket with a checklist shows its progress as **n/m steps** (v0.124.0+).

sections.heading: Checklist templates
sections.text:
Reusable procedures live under **Settings → Ticketing → Templates**, in **Checklist templates**. A template is available to all organizations or to one, and has a name, a description, internal instructions and its steps; an inactive template stays linked where it is already used but stops appearing in pickers. On a ticket, **Apply template** either adds the template's steps to the existing checklist or replaces the unticked steps while keeping the completed ones.

Two shortcuts arrived in v0.124.0:

- **Save as template** turns the checklist on a ticket into a template. Give it a name and choose whether to make it available to all organizations. Steps created by an AI task and repeated steps are left out, and the confirmation says how many.
- **Duplicate** copies an existing template so you can adapt it without editing the original.

sections.heading: Canned Responses
sections.text: Partners can maintain a shared library of named reply templates that technicians insert directly into the ticket composer, removing repetitive typing for common answers, procedures, and closing messages.

sections.heading: Managing templates
sections.text:
Templates are managed under **Settings → Ticketing**. Each template has a **name**, a **body** (plain text, up to 5,000 characters), and an optional **category** for grouping (for example, "Billing", "Onboarding", "Closures"). Within a category, templates are sorted by the order you set. Creating, editing, and deleting templates requires **partner scope plus MFA confirmation**.

Templates are partner-wide and shared across all your customer organizations and technicians.

sections.heading: Inserting a canned response
sections.text:
While composing a reply or internal note, open the canned-response picker from the composer toolbar. Select a template to insert its body at the cursor position — the text is inserted, not sent. You can edit the inserted text before sending as normal.

  Inserting a canned response **never auto-sends** the message. The template text lands at the cursor so you can review and customize it before hitting send.

sections.heading: Keyboard Shortcuts
sections.text:
The queue is built to be worked without a mouse:

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `j` / `k` | Move down / up the list |
| `Enter` or `o` | Open the selected ticket as a full page |
| `a` | Assign the selected ticket to me |
| `r` | Focus the reply composer |
| `n` | Focus the internal note composer |
| `e` | Open the resolve form (resolution note) |
| `Esc` | Leave the composer / go back |

sections.heading: Bulk Actions
sections.text:
Select tickets with the checkboxes in the list and an action bar slides up from the bottom of the pane. From there you can:

- **Bulk assign** -- hand a batch of tickets to a technician, or unassign them.
- **Bulk status** -- move a batch to New, Open, Pending, On hold, or Closed.
- **Bulk delete** -- soft-delete every selected ticket at once (Partner Admins and Org Admins only; see [Deleting and Restoring Tickets](#deleting-and-restoring-tickets)). A confirm dialog shows the count before anything is deleted.

You can act on up to 100 tickets at once. Resolving is intentionally excluded from bulk actions: every resolution needs a per-ticket resolution note, so tickets are resolved individually from the workbench.

sections.heading: Creating Tickets
sections.text:
Tickets enter the queue from four directions:

- **By a technician.** Click **Create ticket** on the Tickets page, pick the organization, enter a subject and description, and optionally attach a device, category, and priority.
- **From an alert.** Open any alert and click its **Create ticket** button. The ticket is pre-filled from the alert and linked to it, so the alert shows up in the ticket's properties rail.
- **From the customer portal.** End-users submit tickets through their [Customer Portal](/features/portal/), and those tickets land directly in the queue for triage.
- **By email.** Customers email your inbound address and their message becomes a ticket -- see [Email-to-Ticket](#email-to-ticket) below.
- **Through the API**, for integrations and automation.

**Service Management has to be on:**
  Ticketing is part of the **Service Management** module, which is a partner-level
  switch (**Settings → Partner → Company → Modules**). With it turned **off**,
  Breeze runs as monitoring and management only: the Service Desk and Billing
  sections leave the sidebar and *every* path above refuses to create a new
  ticket — technician, portal, alert, inbound email, the AI assistant's ticket
  tool, and the API. Existing tickets stay readable, and turning the module back
  on restores everything with its history intact. See
  [Service Management mode](/reference/partner-management/#service-management-mode).

sections.heading: Routing rules
sections.text:
Routing rules set who a new ticket goes to, and how it starts, the moment it is created. Manage them in **Settings → Ticketing → Routing**.

A rule has **conditions** and **actions**:

- **Conditions:** where the ticket came from (portal, email, alert, technician, API, AI), its priority, its category, words in the subject, and the requester's email domain. A domain is either exact (`example.com`) or every subdomain (`*.example.com`, which matches `help.example.com` but not `example.com` itself). Within one condition any value can match; every condition you fill in must match. A rule with no conditions matches every ticket, and the editor warns you about it. A priority condition matches only a priority someone chose (the technician, the customer or an intake form); a ticket whose priority was left at the default doesn't match one, even though it is saved as Normal.
- **Actions:** assign a technician, set the priority, the category or the starting status, and add tags. A rule must have at least one action. The starting status can be a **New**, **Open**, **Pending** or **On hold** status; a ticket that starts Pending or On hold starts with its SLA clock paused.

How rules are applied:

- **Org rules first.** An organization's own rules are checked first, then the partner-wide rules (marked **All orgs**, or limited to the organizations you list). Within each group, the order on the page decides; drag a rule to reorder it. The **first** rule that matches wins.
- **A rule never overrides a choice.** It only fills in what the person or form creating the ticket left empty: a priority a technician picked, an assignee they chose, or an intake form's own category and priority always win. The rule's category and priority then decide the ticket's SLA targets.
- **If an action can't be applied**, it is skipped and the rest of the rule still applies. For example, if the technician a rule assigns can't be assigned that ticket (they were disabled, or they can't see that customer's organization), the ticket is created without that assignee. A rule whose only assignee has since been deleted becomes a rule with no action; the editor shows it so you can fix it.
- **Every routed ticket says why.** The ticket gets an internal note naming the rule and listing the actions it applied and any it skipped, and the ticket keeps that note even if the rule is later renamed or deleted.
- **Rules run once, at creation.** Editing a ticket later never re-routes it. Imported tickets, and tickets created as a continuation of a closed ticket (a reply to a closed email thread, an Office add-in follow-up), are not routed. Routing sends no notifications of its own; an assigned technician gets the usual [assignment notification](#assignment-notifications).

Use **Test a ticket** on the Routing tab to see which rule a ticket would match, and what it would set, without creating anything.

Partner-wide rules can be created and changed only by staff with access to all of your organizations. Staff with access to some organizations manage those organizations' own rules. Organization users can see the rules that apply to them but can't change them.

sections.heading: Email-to-Ticket
sections.text: Breeze can turn customer emails into tickets automatically, so your help desk works entirely over email like a full PSA. Configure it under **Settings → Ticketing → Inbound email**.

sections.heading: Turning it on and off
sections.text:
**Enable email-to-ticket** on the Inbound email card is the master switch for the whole feature. With it off, mail addressed to your partner is discarded — no ticket, no review-queue entry, no autoresponse — and each discarded message is still recorded in the inbound log for audit. It applies to both delivery paths: the native inbound address and a connected Microsoft 365 shared mailbox.

Two things to know:

- **New partners start with it off.** If you signed up from v0.109.0 onward, turn this on before publishing your support address — until you do, mail is discarded rather than queued.
- Existing partners are **on** by default. The switch had no effect before v0.106.0, so ingestion has always been running; leaving it alone keeps today's behavior.
- Switching it off **discards** mail rather than pausing it. Messages that arrive while it's off are not queued for replay when you switch it back on.

sections.heading: Your inbound address
sections.text:
Each partner gets an **inbound address** -- the email address customers send to. Copy it from the Inbound email card and share it with your customers (or forward your existing support mailbox to it). Mail sent to that address is converted into tickets.

**Self-hosted: this needs one-time operator setup:**
  On hosted Breeze the inbound domain is already configured, so the address is simply there. On a self-hosted instance it is not: until `TICKETS_INBOUND_DOMAIN` is set (and a Mailgun route points at Breeze), the card shows *"No platform inbound domain is configured…"* and names that variable instead of showing an address. See [Inbound email-to-ticket environment variables](/deploy/environment/#inbound-email-to-ticket-mailgun). If you'd rather not run inbound mail through Mailgun, [connecting a Microsoft 365 shared mailbox](#connecting-a-microsoft-365-support-mailbox) is an alternative that needs no DNS changes.

The address's local part (the bit before the `@`) is editable on the Inbound email card -- handy if your partner was bootstrapped with an awkward auto-generated value and you want something tidy like `support` or `tickets`. It must be lowercase, URL/email-safe (letters, numbers, and hyphens), and unique across partners. Changing it does **not** break your old address: the previous value keeps routing to you, so addresses you've already published to customers and any in-flight email threads continue to work. New outbound replies are sent from the new address.

sections.heading: How emails become tickets
sections.text:
- **New tickets.** An email from a recognized customer creates a new ticket, with the subject as the ticket subject and the body as the first message.
- **Threading.** Replies are matched back to their original ticket using the email's reply headers or the ticket number in the subject (for example `T-2026-0042`), so an ongoing conversation stays on one ticket. A reply to a resolved ticket reopens it.
- **Public replies thread back.** When a technician sends a public reply, the requester gets a laid-out email notice (the reply text is not in that mail), and their response threads back into the same ticket.

sections.heading: Autoresponder
sections.text:
An optional **autoresponder** sends customers a one-time acknowledgement when their email is received, so they know the ticket was created. It's rate-limited to avoid mail loops and is toggled per partner on the Inbound email card.

Edit the acknowledgement under **Settings → Partner → Email templates** (Ticket received acknowledgement) -- subject, heading, and HTML body. Merge variables: `{{ticket_number}}`, `{{ticket_subject}}`, `{{requester_name}}`, `{{requester_email}}`, `{{org_name}}`, and `{{partner_name}}`. Leave it on the default to keep the built-in wording. This mail has no portal button; the customer replies to the email. Plain-text subject and body previously saved on the Inbound email card still apply until you save a template here.

sections.heading: Review queue
sections.text:
Emails that Breeze can't automatically turn into a ticket land in a **review queue** instead -- so unsolicited or unprocessable mail doesn't flood the ticket queue. From there you can convert a message into a ticket (assigning it to the right organization) or dismiss it. Two kinds of mail land here:

- Any email that **failed to process** -- for example, one with no usable sender address.
- Emails from **unknown senders**, if your **Unknown senders** setting is left on its default. See [Unknown sender handling](#unknown-sender-handling) below to change that behavior.

  An email with no usable sender address can't become a ticket. Those appear in the review queue to be dismissed or followed up out-of-band.

sections.heading: Unknown sender handling
sections.text:
A sender is "unknown" when it isn't a portal user, a mapped customer domain, or a reply to an existing ticket. Choose what happens to that mail under **Settings → Ticketing → Inbound email**, in the **Unknown senders** section:

| Option | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Quarantine for review** (default) | Held in the Tickets **Review queue** for manual convert or dismiss. |
| **Route to the triage organization** | Auto-creates a ticket directly in a designated triage organization instead of quarantining it. This option requires a **Default triage organization** to already be selected above it -- it stays disabled until you pick one. |
| **Drop silently** | No ticket, no review-queue entry, no autoresponse. Breeze still keeps an internal record of the message. Use this to keep unmapped spam out of both triage and the review queue. |

Pick the **Default triage organization** from the dropdown above the Unknown senders options before you can select "Route to the triage organization."

#### Dropping mail that fails sender authentication

A separate checkbox on the same card, **Drop mail that fails sender authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC)**, controls mail that fails those checks -- independently of the Unknown senders setting above. When it's off (the default), unverified mail is quarantined for review. When it's on, unverified mail is dropped silently instead -- no ticket, no review-queue entry, no autoresponse. This applies to **all** unverified senders, including a message from an otherwise-recognized customer that individually fails the check, and takes priority over whatever you've chosen for unknown senders.

#### Filing staff forwards under the original sender's customer

Customers often email a technician directly, and the technician forwards that message to the support address. By default the new ticket is filed by the forwarder's address, which usually means your own organization. Turn on **File staff forwards under the original sender's customer** on the same card to file it under the customer instead. It's off by default.

When it's on, a new ticket is filed under the organization mapped to the **original** sender's domain when all of these hold:

- The forward arrives at a connected Gmail mailbox (see the caution below).
- The forward passes the sender-authentication check above.
- It comes from an **active partner-level** user of your account, not a customer-organization user, and that user has access to the customer's organization (all organizations, or a selected list that includes it).
- It doesn't reply to an existing ticket. Replies still thread onto their ticket as usual.
- The original sender's domain is mapped to a customer organization, and it isn't the forwarder's own domain.

Anything else is routed exactly as it would be with the setting off. The original sender is never emailed: there's no autoresponse and no contact is created. Breeze uses the original address only to pick the organization, never to verify who sent it.

**Connected Gmail mailboxes only:**
  Staff forwards are routed only for mail received by a **connected Gmail mailbox**. Mail sent to the native inbound address or a connected **Microsoft 365** mailbox always routes normally, because Breeze can't confirm it has the sender's own plain-text copy there. Breeze recognizes an inline forward by Gmail's `---------- Forwarded message ---------` line (or Outlook's older `-----Original Message-----` line) followed by a `From:` header block, read from the message's plain-text part. Modern Outlook marks a forward differently, and messages forwarded as attachments are never recognized. Because recognition is textual, a staff user who types the same marker and header block gets the same routing.

#### Default assignee for new inbound tickets

An unassigned ticket sends no assignee notification, so staff can miss it. Set a default assignee to give every ticket created from inbound email an owner. It's empty (off) by default. The setting lives at the bottom of **Settings → Ticketing → Routing**, under **If no rule assigns an email ticket** (it used to be on the Inbound email card).

- It is the **fallback** after [routing rules](#routing-rules): it applies only when no rule assigned the ticket, including when the matching rule set only a priority or category, or its assignee was skipped.
- Only **new** tickets are assigned. A reply that threads onto an existing ticket never changes who it's assigned to, and a ticket something else already assigned is left alone.
- You can pick an **active** member of your team whose organization access isn't set to none and whose role can view tickets. Breeze checks this every time the card saves, and rejects a user from another partner, a disabled user, or someone without ticket access. If the person you picked later stops qualifying, the card shows them as unavailable and won't save other changes until you pick someone else or clear the setting.
- Each ticket is checked again when it arrives. If the default assignee can no longer be assigned that ticket (for example, they were disabled, or their access doesn't include that customer's organization), the ticket is created **unassigned** and Breeze records why in its inbound email log. The email is never rejected because of this setting.
- The assignment is recorded like any other: it appears in the ticket's activity and the audit log, and the assignee gets the usual [assignment notification](#assignment-notifications) once the ticket has been saved.
- The setting applies to every inbound path: the native inbound address and connected Microsoft 365 and Gmail mailboxes.

sections.heading: Who the requester is
sections.text:
A ticket records **who asked** separately from **who signed in**. The requester is an organization [contact](/reference/organizations-and-sites/#contacts) — a person in the customer's business, whether or not they have ever logged into anything. The submitter is a portal login, and only exists when the ticket came in through the portal.

This matters when a ticket arrives by email. Breeze matches the sender to a contact on the customer's organization rather than inventing a login for them, so a customer who only ever emails you still has a clean history under their name.

It also decides what a customer sees in the portal. A portal user sees the tickets they submitted **and** the tickets raised by the contact their login is linked to — so someone who emails a request and later signs in to the portal finds it waiting for them, rather than an empty list.

Logins created through single sign-on or the Outlook add-in are linked to a matching contact automatically, provided the address is one the identity provider vouches for.

**Ambiguous invites are flagged, not guessed:**
  If several contacts on an organization share the email address you are inviting, Breeze creates the login without linking it to any of them and warns you at the time. That user will not see tickets raised by email under that address until you link them to the right contact. Merge or correct the duplicate contacts, then re-link.

sections.heading: Connecting a Microsoft 365 support mailbox
sections.text:
Instead of forwarding to your Breeze inbound address, you can connect a Microsoft 365 **shared support mailbox** (for example `support@yourmsp.com`) directly. Customer email to that mailbox becomes tickets, and your public replies are sent back **from that same mailbox** -- with no MX record or forwarding-rule changes. Breeze uses an app-only connection your Microsoft Global Administrator consents to once, so it survives staff turnover (there's no personal login tied to the mailbox). Set it up on the **Microsoft 365 support mailbox** card under **Settings → Ticketing → Inbound Email**.

1. Enter the shared mailbox address and an optional display name, then click **Connect**. Breeze redirects you to Microsoft, where a **Global Administrator** grants one-time admin consent.
2. Scope Breeze's access to **only** this mailbox. The card shows an exact **Application Access Policy** snippet (a `New-DistributionGroup` plus `New-ApplicationAccessPolicy` pair) to run in Exchange Online PowerShell as a tenant admin. Until you do this, the connection shows **Needs attention**, because the underlying mail permission is tenant-wide by default.
3. Click **Re-test**. Once Breeze can read the mailbox, the status flips to **Connected**.

Once connected, Breeze polls the mailbox every minute or two, turns new messages into tickets (threading and the review queue work exactly as above), and marks each handled message as read so your team can see what's been picked up. Only mail that arrives after you connect is ticketed -- existing inbox history is not imported. Public replies go out **from the support address** and thread natively in the customer's mailbox; internal notes and technician notifications are unaffected. You can connect more than one mailbox (for example `support@` and `billing@`). **Disconnect** stops polling immediately; to fully remove access, also revoke the app's consent in your Microsoft Entra admin center.

A temporary Microsoft Graph problem -- throttling, a Microsoft server error, a network failure or a request that times out -- does not stop the mailbox: it stays **Connected** and Breeze retries on the next poll. Only an authorization failure asks you to reconnect.

If a connection does not complete:

- **Consent not completed** means the Microsoft sign-in for that mailbox was not finished within its 10-minute window. Consent is two Microsoft sign-ins: the admin consent, then a second sign-in that confirms the consenting account is an administrator of that tenant. Closing the tab between them, or Microsoft never sending you back, leaves the mailbox here. Click **Retry consent**, or **Disconnect** it.
- A **cookie** error after Microsoft sends you back means the browser returned to a different address than the one you started from. The card shows the redirect URI Breeze sends to Microsoft; open Breeze at that same scheme and host (for example `https://`, not `http://`), allow cookies, and connect again.
- An **expired or already used** sign-in link means the consent took longer than 10 minutes or the page was reloaded. Connect again.
- To see why any attempt failed, check the API logs: `docker logs breeze-api 2>&1 | grep -i ticketmailbox`. Each failed or rejected callback logs one `[ticketMailbox] consent callback failed` or `[ticketMailbox] consent callback rejected` line naming the step that failed, and for a Microsoft error its error code and `AADSTS` number (for example `AADSTS65004`, consent declined). A redirect URI mismatch (`AADSTS50011`) is shown on the Microsoft page and never reaches Breeze, so it leaves no log line; compare the URI on the card with the one registered on the app. Tokens and Microsoft's full error text are never logged.

  Connecting or managing a mailbox requires **partner scope and MFA**. The Microsoft 365 mailbox card only appears once your operator has configured the Breeze Ticketing Azure app -- see [Ticket Mailbox environment variables](/deploy/environment/#ticket-mailbox-m365-email-to-ticket).

sections.heading: Connecting a Google Workspace support mailbox
sections.text:
A Google Workspace mailbox (for example `support@yourdomain.com` or an alias of it) can also feed tickets directly, with no MX or forwarding changes and no OAuth redirect. Breeze reads it through the **domain-wide delegation** service account of an organization's Google Workspace connection. Set it up on the **Google Workspace support mailbox** card under **Settings → Ticketing → Inbound Email**.

1. Pick the **organization** whose Google Workspace connection should read the mailbox, then enter the mailbox address and an optional display name, and click **Connect**. That organization holds the mailbox's credential, and the card shows it on each connected mailbox. For a mailbox your MSP owns (such as your own `help@`), pick the organization whose Workspace contains that mailbox. Because the mailbox belongs to that organization's credential, an export of that organization's data includes the mailbox's address and connection record, even for a mailbox your MSP owns.
2. In the Google Admin console, the service account's domain-wide delegation must include `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.readonly`, `openid` and `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.email`. By default Breeze only reads the mailbox; it never changes labels, read state or messages.
3. Optional: to label mail that became a ticket, click **Change mail handling** on the connected mailbox, enter a Gmail label name (for example `Breeze/Ticketed`) and choose whether to also archive that mail out of the inbox. This needs one more scope in the delegation grant, `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.modify`; the card shows it next to the field. Only mail that created a ticket or was added to one is labelled. Quarantined, ignored and failed mail stays in the inbox untouched. Gmail system labels such as `INBOX`, `TRASH` and `SPAM` cannot be used. Leave the label blank to turn it off.

How it behaves once connected:

- Only mail **received after you connect** becomes tickets. Older mail moved back into the inbox later is ignored, and existing inbox history is not imported.
- Only mail actually **delivered to the connected address** (per the `Delivered-To` header Google stamps) becomes a ticket. If the address is an alias on a person's account, that person's other mail is left alone.
- **Attachments are not imported yet.** The ticket gets a note naming each attachment that was left behind, so nothing disappears silently; open the original message in Gmail for the file.
- Public replies go out through the platform email service, not from the Gmail mailbox.
- If the service account loses access, the mailbox moves to **Re-auth required** and polling pauses until you reconnect it.
- Labelling is best effort and happens shortly after the ticket is created, separately from it. If Gmail is briefly unavailable or rate limited, Breeze tries the same message again for a few minutes.
- If labelling fails (for example because the grant lacks `gmail.modify`), the ticket is still created, the mail stays in the inbox, and the card shows why under the mailbox. The message clears after the next successful label or when you change the setting.
- In rare cases, such as a brief outage of Breeze's job queue right after the ticket is created, a message can be left unlabelled in the inbox. When Breeze can detect this, the card says so, and that notice stays until you save the setting or reconnect the mailbox.

sections.heading: Categories and SLAs
sections.text:
Go to **Settings > Ticketing** to manage ticket categories.

1. Enter a category name, pick a color, and click **Add**.

2. Use the categories to organize the queue -- they appear in the category filter and on the create-ticket form.

3. Deactivate a category to retire it without losing the tickets already filed under it.

Categories also carry SLA targets (response and resolution times) and can name a **default work type**, applied to a time entry logged against a ticket in that category when the technician didn't pick one -- pricing itself lives on the [Rates](/features/rates/) screen, not on the category. When a ticket's resolution target is running out, an **at-risk** chip appears in the queue, turning to **breached** once the target has passed -- and the **Breaching soon** tab collects all of them in one place.

  The automated SLA engine is live. Breeze tracks each ticket against its category's response and resolution targets, pauses the clock while a ticket is **On Hold**, monitors for breaches, and notifies the assignee (and escalates to the configured contacts) as a target approaches or is missed.

sections.heading: Business hours
sections.text:
SLA deadlines can be counted on business hours instead of the clock. Go to **Settings → Ticketing → Priorities & SLAs** and open the **Business hours** card to manage calendars. A calendar has a time zone, a weekly schedule (each weekday can have several open intervals, such as a split shift), and a list of holidays.

Which calendar a ticket uses is resolved when the ticket is created: the organization's own override if it has one, otherwise the partner's default calendar, otherwise round-the-clock (24×7). A partner-wide calendar is marked **All orgs**; the default is marked **Default**. The calendar and its current hours are then **snapshotted on the ticket**, so later edits don't silently shift deadlines on tickets that already exist.

- **Choosing a calendar for one organization.** In the organization's **Ticketing** settings, the **Business hours** field is blank by default and shows what it inherits (for example "Inherited: Support hours (partner default)"). Pick a calendar to override it for that organization.
- **Editing hours or the time zone affects new tickets only.** Open tickets keep the hours they were created with.
- **Holidays.** Adding or removing a holiday dated in the future recomputes the deadlines of open tickets. Holidays dated today or earlier don't change open tickets.
- **Apply to open tickets.** To move tickets that are already open onto a calendar's current hours, use **Apply to open tickets**. Breeze first shows a preview: how many tickets would be updated, how many of those would become breached immediately, and how many are skipped because they have been paused. Tickets that have ever been paused are never changed. If the hours change between the preview and your confirmation, the apply is rejected and the preview is reloaded so you can review the new counts.
- **Archiving and deleting.** An archived calendar can't be chosen for new work. A calendar that tickets or organizations still use, or that is the default, can't be deleted.
- **Customer portal.** The portal shows SLA status only; it doesn't show your calendars or hours.

sections.heading: Custom Statuses & SLA Configuration
sections.text: Go to **Settings → Ticketing** to configure statuses, priority labels, and SLA defaults. The page is tabbed: **Statuses**, **Priorities**, **Categories**, and **Export**.

sections.heading: Custom ticket statuses
sections.text:
Every ticket status maps to one of six core states: **New**, **Open**, **Pending**, **On Hold**, **Resolved**, and **Closed**. Within each core state you can create as many custom statuses as your workflow needs -- for example "Waiting on vendor" under Pending, or "Needs review" under Resolved. Custom statuses appear in the workbench status picker, grouped by their core state. Tickets that pre-date custom statuses show the core state label directly.

Statuses are partner-wide and apply across all your customer organizations. Built-in statuses cannot be deleted. Custom statuses can be deactivated (they disappear from the picker but existing tickets keep their status). Use the up/down arrows on any row to reorder statuses, which sets the order they appear in the picker.

sections.heading: Priority labels and partner-wide SLA defaults
sections.text: Under the **Priorities** tab you can rename each of the four priority levels (Low, Normal, High, Urgent) to match your team's language. For each priority you can also set partner-wide default **response** and **resolution** SLA targets (in minutes). These defaults apply to every ticket that doesn't have a more-specific override.

sections.heading: Per-organization SLA tiers
sections.text:
In an organization's settings, open the **Ticketing** tab to set per-priority SLA overrides for that customer. Labour pricing is no longer set here -- it lives on the organization's **Billing** tab as a billing profile (see [Rates](/features/rates/)).

  Saving organization-level ticketing settings requires MFA confirmation. SLA precedence: a category's SLA beats an organization override, which beats the partner-wide priority default.

sections.heading: Time Tracking & Parts
sections.text: Breeze lets technicians log time and record parts against any ticket. These records feed the billing summary on the ticket's properties rail and the weekly Timesheet view -- but are **never shown in the customer portal**.

sections.heading: Work types
sections.text:
A **work type** says *what* the work was -- Remote, On-site, Project, After hours. The technician picks it on the time entry; Breeze decides what the customer pays for it by looking the work type up on the organization's billing profile -- see [Rates](/features/rates/) for how profiles, coverage, minimums and rounding work, and how to manage the work-type list itself. Work types are partner-wide, so one list covers every customer organization you manage, and a ticket category can name a default one for entries logged without a pick.

The work-type picker appears everywhere technicians log time: the ticket's **Log time** quick-add, the **Start timer** form, the row editor on **/timesheet** (which also gains a **Work Type** column), the mobile app's timer, and the Outlook add-in's time widget. Choosing nothing is always allowed -- an entry with no work type is valid, and is priced from the profile's **All other work** row.

sections.heading: Rates
sections.text:
Time entries are priced automatically from the organization's assigned (or partner-default) billing profile -- see [Rates](/features/rates/) for the full picture of profiles, coverage, minimums and rounding. While logging time, the quick-add form, the timer stop popover, and the **/timesheet** row editor all show the resolved outcome next to the work-type picker -- for example *Included in Silver* or *$225/h · 1 h minimum*.

The rate field is **read-only** there unless you hold the **`time_entries:manage_billing`** permission (Partner Admins have it by default via `*:*`); with it, you can type a different rate, flip the billable flag, or hand-set a minimum for that one entry, which flags it **overridden** for the billing approval queue.

  **Upgrading from a release before Rates.** Your existing category rates and per-organization rates are converted into billing profiles automatically on upgrade: one *Standard rates* card per currency, one work type per priced category (set as that category's default work type), and a per-organization card for each organization that had its own rate or billable default. Existing time entries are not touched. Two things change for *new* entries: (1) an entry on an **uncategorised** ticket in an organization that had a rate but never set a billable default used to be silently non-billable and is now billable at that rate; (2) non-billable entries no longer carry a rate. Self-hosters should run `pnpm --filter @breeze/api dry-run:labour-pricing` **before** upgrading and read its *WILL START BILLING* section -- it names every organization affected by (1).

sections.heading: Timer widget
sections.text:
When you are working a ticket, click **Start timer** in the Time & Billing rail to begin tracking. A live clock appears in the top navigation bar, anchored to the ticket number, so the timer follows you across the queue. Only one timer can run per technician at a time -- starting a new timer automatically stops the previous one.

Click the stop icon in the header widget to open the stop popover, where you can add a description and mark the entry as billable before saving.

sections.heading: Manual time entry
sections.text: Click **Log time** in the ticket's Time & Billing rail to open the quick-add form. Enter the number of minutes, an optional description, and whether the entry is billable, then click **Save**. The entry is back-dated so the end time is now and the start time is now minus the minutes you entered.

sections.heading: Deleting a time entry
sections.text: Each entry in the ticket's Time & Billing rail and on the **/timesheet** row has a **Delete** action with a confirm dialog. Deleting is permanent. It is offered on any entry that has not been invoiced to users with time-entry write access; the server then decides per entry, so you can delete your own unapproved entries, while deleting someone else's entry or an approved one needs an administrator who manages all time entries. A refusal is explained in the dialog. Deleting the entry of a running timer also clears the timer in the header.

sections.heading: Time without a ticket
sections.text: A time entry does not have to belong to a ticket. Through the API, `POST /time-entries/start` and `POST /time-entries` accept an optional `orgId` and `siteId` (plus `source`, which only the mobile app's arrival prompt sets), so time spent at a customer site can be recorded against the organization and site directly. A `siteId` needs an `orgId` or a `ticketId`. When a ticket is also given, the ticket's organization always wins: a different `orgId` is refused with `422 ORG_MISMATCH`, and a site outside the organization with `422 SITE_ORG_MISMATCH`. `GET /time-entries` returns each entry's `siteId` and can filter by it.

sections.heading: Location suggestions
sections.text:
**Location suggestions** let the Breeze mobile app offer to start a timer when a technician arrives at a client site. Turn it on under **Settings → Ticketing → Time capture** with **Suggest a timer when a technician arrives at a client site**, and set a **Default arrival radius (m)** (default 150 m, 50--1000 m) for sites that have no radius of their own. The setting is partner-wide and **off by default**. Each technician must also allow location on their phone; location is checked on the phone and is never sent to Breeze. Only the site's own pinned coordinate is stored -- see [Site location](/reference/organizations-and-sites/#site-location) for how sites are pinned.

**Mobile prompt ships later:**
  v0.122.1 adds the setting, site pins and the API the mobile app reads (`GET /time-entries/location-sites`, which returns the setting, the default radius, whether the caller may pin sites, and the caller's sites, capped at 2,000 with a `truncated` flag). The arrival prompt itself ships in a later mobile app release, so turning the setting on changes nothing a technician sees yet.

sections.heading: Suggested time entries
sections.text:
When a remote session ends, Breeze can offer it as a one-tap time entry: *"You ran a 38-minute desktop session on ACME-DC01 and closed T-2026-1041 -- log it?"* Nothing is ever written until you tap it.

**Mobile app only:**
  The suggestion list, the one-tap confirm and the dismiss/restore control live in the **Breeze mobile app** and ship with it. In the web app this release adds only the partner setting described below and the provenance badge described at the end of this section -- there is no web suggestions panel. Turning the setting on changes nothing a technician sees on **/timesheet**.

**Turning it on.** Go to **Settings → Ticketing → Time capture** and enable **Suggest time entries from remote sessions**. The setting is off by default and applies partner-wide, to every technician in your organization. Two thresholds sit beside it:

- **Minimum session length** (default 120 seconds) -- sessions shorter than this are never suggested, so a mistyped connection does not become a billable line.
- **Merge gap** (default 10 minutes) -- back-to-back sessions on the same device within this gap are combined into a single suggestion rather than offered separately.

**Re-check this card if you saved it before v0.122.1:**
  Earlier versions always displayed **Suggest time entries from remote sessions** as off with default thresholds, and saving the card wrote those values back over your stored settings. From v0.122.1 the card loads and keeps the stored values. If you saved the Time Tracking card on an earlier version, open it and check the toggle and both thresholds.

**What gets suggested.** Ended remote sessions -- terminal, desktop and file transfer -- from the day you are looking at, attributed to the technician who ran them, with the session's recorded duration. Back-to-back sessions on one device inside the merge gap are combined into a single suggestion, and suggestions never overlap each other. Quick Support sessions appear with their attribution label and no organization until you attach a ticket.

**What does not.** Work you already logged (a session already covered by one of your own time entries is hidden), sessions you dismissed, sessions still running, and anything under the minimum length.

**Accuracy.** A session whose duration was recorded exactly shows that duration. One whose end time had to be reconstructed shows an estimate. One closed by the server's stale-session reaper is marked unreliable and asks you to enter the end time yourself before it will log anything.

**Ticket pairing.** A ticket you closed on that device around the same time is pre-selected. If two are equally likely, none is, and you pick. Changing the ticket can change the organization and therefore the currency the entry is priced in, so the picker shows the organization beside each ticket.

**Dismiss and restore.** Dismissing a suggestion hides it; **Show dismissed → Restore** puts it back. Deleting a time entry that came from a suggestion does *not* re-suggest the session -- restore it explicitly if you want it offered again.

**Where the provenance shows.** Entries created this way carry a small badge on the timesheet row and in the ticket's Time & Billing rail -- in the web app as well as on mobile -- so you can tell at a glance which entries were typed and which came from a session. That badge is the part of this feature the web app shows today.

sections.heading: Parts
sections.text: The Parts card on the ticket rail lets you record physical or consumable items used on a job. Each part has a **description**, **quantity**, **unit price**, and an optional **cost basis** for margin tracking. Parts default to billable; uncheck the box for internal-only consumables.

sections.heading: Timesheet
sections.text:
Open **/timesheet** from the sidebar to see a week-at-a-glance view of all your time entries, grouped by day with billable totals. Billable amounts -- here and in the ticket's Time & Billing rail -- are totalled **per currency**; if a technician's week spans organizations that bill in different currencies, you see one total per currency rather than a single combined figure. Use the week navigation buttons to move backwards and forwards. Technicians with a wildcard-permission admin role can switch to any other technician's timesheet via the dropdown.

Admins can select one or more completed entries and click **Approve selected** to mark them approved. Approved entries become immutable for non-admins.

Entries that were logged from a remote session carry a provenance badge on the row. The [suggested time entries](#suggested-time-entries) list itself -- the unlogged sessions waiting to be confirmed -- is a Breeze mobile app screen; the web timesheet does not show it.

sections.heading: Billables export
sections.text:
Under **Settings → Ticketing**, the Billables Export card lets you download a CSV of all time entries and parts for any date range up to 366 days. The export includes each entry's approval status, billable flag, computed amounts, and a `currency` column (the currency each amount is priced in), so totals can be grouped per currency when importing into external accounting tools. Amounts are never converted between currencies.

  Time entries and parts are technician-facing only. End-users accessing the customer portal never see time logs, cost data, or parts records.

sections.heading: Tickets on a Device
sections.text: Every device page has a **Tickets** tab listing the tickets attached to that device, with status, priority, and SLA chips. It is the fastest way to check whether the machine you are about to work on already has open issues.

title: Time synchronization
description: Inspect Windows time sources, synchronization health, timezone expectations, and recent time events.
headings: Expected timezone and the UTC default

sections.text:
The **Time** section in a device's Info tab shows the latest Windows time report. It appears after Operating System.

This visibility release accepts reports but requires an agent update that includes time sync before data appears. Until then, Windows devices show "No time data yet — this needs an agent update that includes time sync". Other operating systems show "Not supported on this OS yet".

sections.heading: What Breeze checks
sections.text:
A report includes the Windows Time service state and startup mode, synchronization type, configured NTP peers, whether Group Policy manages those settings, and whether a VM host time provider is enabled. It also includes the reported source, collection method, last successful synchronization, last error, stratum and poll interval.

Domain information identifies workgroup, Entra-only, member, domain-controller and PDC roles. Timezone information includes the current Windows timezone, bias, automatic timezone state and the expected timezone with its source. Unknown values remain Unknown; they are not guessed from translated command output.

Recent Time-Service events are display evidence. Breeze evaluates event IDs and structured values, not the translated message. A failure stays active for up to 24 hours unless a later successful synchronization clears it. A later recurrence becomes active again. These ages, and the `sync_stale` age, are measured on the device's own clock against the time the snapshot was collected, not on server time, so a device whose clock is far behind or ahead still shows its failures. If the device's clock is stepped back after an event (for example, when a clock that was ahead is corrected), events stamped more than 5 minutes after the collection time come from the old clock, so Breeze drops them instead of keeping the finding active into the future.

sections.heading: Freshness and health
sections.text:
Reports are expected every 30 minutes once a supporting agent is installed. A report received more than **90 minutes** ago is marked Stale. Its stored observations remain visible so you can inspect what was last reported; stale does not mean a new failure has been observed.

Critical findings take precedence over warnings. Information findings, including a timezone mismatch, do not make time synchronization unhealthy. If synchronization status is unavailable and there are no findings, health is Unknown.

sections.heading: Findings and fixes
sections.text:
| Finding | Meaning and suggested fix |
| --- | --- |
| `pdc_no_external_source` | A forest-root PDC is following the domain hierarchy or reports that it has no external source. Configure external NTP servers on that PDC; the domain follows it. |
| `source_local_clock` | Windows is using its local or free-running clock. Configure an NTP source, or check the domain controller if this is a domain member. |
| `dc_vm_host_sync` | A domain controller has a VM host time provider enabled or is using the host as its source. Disable VM host time synchronization on that DC. |
| `ntp_server_unresolvable` | Windows reported a name-resolution failure or an NTP peer name has invalid syntax. Correct the configured peer or DNS. W32Time flag suffixes such as `,0x9` are recognized and are not treated as part of the name. |
| `ntp_peer_unreachable` | A time peer did not respond. Check peer reachability and outbound UDP port 123. |
| `domain_source_unavailable` | Windows cannot locate a domain time source. Check domain-controller reachability. |
| `member_not_on_hierarchy` | A domain member or non-root DC is not using NT5DS or AllSync and the setting is not controlled by Group Policy. Restore domain-hierarchy synchronization. |
| `sync_disabled` | Synchronization type is NoSync or the Windows Time service is disabled. Enable Windows Time and select a suitable source. |
| `sync_stale` | The last successful synchronization exceeds the greater of three poll intervals or 24 hours, or Windows reports stale synchronization. Check the source and synchronize again. If no interval is reported, the fallback poll interval is seven days. |
| `correction_refused` | Windows refused a time correction. Correct the large clock difference manually or resynchronize using the appropriate Windows administration tools. |
| `timezone_mismatch` | The device's Windows timezone differs from its expected timezone and automatic timezone is not on. Review the site timezone and the device timezone. This is information, not a synchronization-health warning. |

A disabled service suppresses the separate stale-sync finding. Group Policy management suppresses the domain-hierarchy recommendation; this page does not change Group Policy or device configuration.

sections.heading: Expected timezone and the UTC default
sections.text:
By default, the expected timezone is derived from the device's site; a time policy can pin a different zone (see [Manage Windows time settings](#manage-windows-time-settings)). Site values **UTC** and **Etc/UTC** are treated as an unset default, so they do not produce a timezone mismatch—even when the device uses Pacific Standard Time.
