Open **Vulnerabilities** from the Security section of the left sidebar for the fleet-wide view, or open any device and select its **Vulnerabilities** tab for a single machine.

sections.heading: Enabling vulnerability scanning
sections.text:
Vulnerability scanning is **off by default**. A device only produces findings once it's covered by a configuration policy that turns scanning on, so you can roll the feature out organization by organization instead of flooding every customer at once.

1. Go to **Configuration → Policies** and open (or create) a policy.
2. On the **Vulnerability** feature tab, switch **Enable vulnerability scanning** on, and save.
3. Assign the policy to the scope you want covered -- a partner, organization, site, device group, or individual device.

Coverage follows the same closest-wins inheritance as every other policy feature: a device- or group-level setting of *off* overrides an organization-wide *on*, so you can enable scanning broadly and carve out exceptions. Once a scope is enabled, Breeze correlates its inventory against the CVE feeds **once a day** (around 13:00 UTC, after the feeds refresh) and populates the findings below. Platform administrators can also trigger a correlation pass on demand.

  Enabling is deliberate: if no device anywhere has scanning turned on, the daily job simply does nothing -- it never falls back to scanning your whole fleet. See [Configuration Policies → Vulnerability Scanning](/features/configuration-policies/#vulnerability-scanning) for the full feature.

sections.heading: What you can do
sections.text:
- Work a **fix-first queue** across your whole fleet, grouped by the fix that clears each finding.
- Triage at the fleet level -- deploy a patch, accept a risk, or mitigate across every affected device at once.
- Drill into one device to see its findings and act on them individually.
- Open a **ticket** from a finding so remediation lands on someone's work queue.
- Let the AI agent report on vulnerabilities and propose remediations for your approval.

sections.heading: The fleet dashboard
sections.text:
The **Vulnerabilities** page is a **fix-first queue**: instead of making you read a flat list of CVEs, it organizes open findings by the action that resolves them, and leads with the numbers that decide what to do first. It has two views, switched with a tab:

- **By software** (default) groups findings into one row per **remediation unit** -- the software product whose update clears them (for example, a browser or runtime), or "Windows / macOS / Linux OS updates" for operating-system findings. Each row shows how many devices and how many CVEs the one fix covers, so you remediate a whole class of exposure in a single action.
- **By CVE** is the classic one-row-per-vulnerability view, one row per CVE across every organization you can access.

The whole page follows the **organization selector**: with **All orgs** selected you see fleet-wide numbers, and selecting a single organization narrows the stat cards, both views, and their drill-down drawers to that customer. (The per-device Vulnerabilities tab always shows that device's findings, regardless of the selector.)

sections.heading: Priority stat cards
sections.text:
Four cards sit above the queue and double as filters -- click one to narrow the list to it:

| Card | What it counts |
|---|---|
| **Critical open** | Open findings at Critical severity. |
| **KEV exposure** | Open findings on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list -- the ones being used in the wild. |
| **Patch ready** | Open findings that have an available, approved patch you can deploy right now. |
| **Accepted, expiring soon** | Risk acceptances whose *Accepted until* date falls within the next 14 days, so nothing lapses back to open unnoticed. |

sections.heading: Columns and filters
sections.text:
The **By CVE** view shows, per row:

| Column | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **CVE** | The vulnerability identifier (e.g. `CVE-2024-1234`). |
| **Severity** | Critical / High / Medium / Low, color-coded. |
| **CVSS** | The standard 0–10 base severity score (shown as `—` until scored). |
| **Risk** | Breeze's prioritized 0–100 score (see [Risk scoring](#how-risk-is-scored)). |
| **Devices** | How many of your devices are affected by this CVE. |
| **Known exploited** | Flagged when the CVE is on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list. |

Narrow either view with the **Severity** and **Status** filters, a **KEV only** toggle, and a **Patch available** toggle.

sections.heading: Fleet-level triage
sections.text:
Open a software group or a CVE to see every device it affects, and act on all of them at once from that view.

A software group's drawer leads with **how many devices need updating**, then lists **one row per device** -- its installed version, how many of the group's CVEs are still open on it, and any accepted or mitigated waivers -- rather than one row per device per CVE. One outdated browser on 14 devices is 14 rows, however many CVEs the update clears. Expand a device to see its individual findings (and reopen a waiver); the drawer also breaks the group down by installed version and shows, for each CVE, how many devices still have it open. Select devices, not findings: an action applies to the open findings on the selected devices.

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Remediate** | Schedules the fixing patch across every affected device that has an available, approved patch. |
| **Accept risk** | Records a formal, time-boxed risk acceptance (with a reason and an *Accepted until* date) for the whole group. |
| **Mitigate** | Records a compensating control across the group. |
| **Create ticket** | Opens a [ticket](/features/ticketing/) for the finding and links it, so the work is tracked to closure. When a selection spans more than one customer, Breeze creates one ticket per organization. |

  Fleet-level triage acts on many devices in one step; the per-device tab below is still there when you need to act on a single machine.

**How Remediate finds the fix:**
  Breeze matches the fixing update even when a finding carries no CVE-tagged patch. For third-party applications it matches the pending update by product -- for example, the winget upgrade already waiting on the device -- and for Windows OS findings it targets the applicable cumulative update. Findings that previously reported *no available patch* for these cases now schedule the real fix.

**Retrying is safe:**
  Remediate never queues a second copy of an install that is still waiting for, or running on, a device. If you send the same selection again after an error, or two people remediate the same findings at once, the repeat attaches to the install already queued, and the confirmation says how many were **already queued**. An install that failed is queued again, which is what a retry is for.

sections.heading: The per-device tab
sections.text:
Each device's **Vulnerabilities** tab lists that machine's findings and is where you act on a single machine. A **status** filter switches between Open (default), Accepted, Mitigated, Patched, and All. Open findings show their CVE (with a **Patch available** badge when an installable fix exists), severity, status, CVSS, risk, known-exploited flag, and per-row actions.

| Action | What it does | When available |
|---|---|---|
| **Remediate** | Schedules the patch that fixes this CVE on this device. | Open findings with an available, approved patch. |
| **Accept risk** | Records a formal, time-boxed risk acceptance with a reason. | Any open finding. |
| **Mitigate** | Records that a compensating control reduces this risk. | Any open finding. |
| **Reopen** | Returns an accepted or mitigated finding to open. | Accepted / Mitigated findings. |

When patches are available for several findings, select them and use **Remediate selected** to schedule them together.

  A finding moves to **Patched** on its own: once the device reports a software or OS version that is no longer in the vulnerable range, Breeze closes the finding automatically. You don't mark something patched by hand.

sections.heading: Accept risk vs. mitigate
sections.text:
Both keep a finding off your open list, but they mean different things:

- **Accept risk** is a governance decision -- "we acknowledge this and choose to live with it until a date." It requires a reason and an *Accepted until* date. When that date passes, a nightly job automatically reopens the finding so it can't be quietly forgotten.
- **Mitigate** is a technical assertion -- "a control (a firewall rule, a disabled feature) reduces this risk." It requires a note and stays in effect until someone reopens it.

sections.heading: Where the data comes from
sections.text:
Breeze pulls vulnerability intelligence from several authoritative feeds and refreshes them on a schedule. The feeds themselves need no setup -- they are always kept current; you only choose which scopes to scan against them (see [Enabling vulnerability scanning](#enabling-vulnerability-scanning)). The sources:

| Source | Used for |
|---|---|
| **NIST NVD** | The core CVE catalog, CVSS scores, and affected-version ranges for third-party software. |
| **Microsoft MSRC** | CVEs and fixed builds for Windows and Microsoft products. |
| **Apple SOFA** | CVEs and fixed builds for macOS releases. |
| **CISA KEV** | Marks CVEs that are *known to be actively exploited*. |
| **FIRST EPSS** | A probability that a CVE will be exploited in the near term. |

  Self-hosted operators can set an optional `NVD_API_KEY` to raise NVD's request rate limits and speed up syncs. It's not required -- without it, syncs simply run at the slower public rate. See the [environment reference](/deploy/environment/).

sections.heading: How risk is scored
sections.text:
The **Risk** score (0–100) is designed to surface what attackers are most likely to use against you, not just what scores highest on paper. It builds on the CVSS base score and then adjusts for real-world signals:

- **CVSS severity** is the spine of the score.
- **Active exploitation (KEV)** lifts a finding into high-priority territory regardless of its base score -- a "medium" CVE that is being exploited in the wild should not sit at the bottom of your list.
- **Exploit likelihood (EPSS)** nudges the score up when a flaw is statistically likely to be weaponized soon.

The result is that a moderately-rated but actively-exploited vulnerability can outrank a higher-CVSS flaw that nobody is using. Scores refresh hourly, so newly-exploited CVEs re-prioritize themselves without any action from you.

sections.heading: Permissions
sections.text:
| Permission | Allows |
|---|---|
| `devices:read` | View the fleet dashboard and per-device tab. |
| `devices:execute` (plus MFA) | Schedule remediation (patch installs) from a finding. |
| `vulnerabilities:accept_risk` | Accept a risk, and reopen an accepted or mitigated finding. |
| `devices:write` | Mark a finding mitigated. |

Risk acceptance is deliberately gated by its own permission so that formally waiving a critical or actively-exploited finding is a higher-trust action than everyday device work.

sections.heading: With the AI agent
sections.text: Vulnerability data is available to the Breeze AI agent: it can summarize fleet-wide vulnerability posture, list a device's findings, and -- with your approval -- schedule remediations. Critical detections and remediation activity also appear on the device event timeline, so they can drive automations. See [AI Agent](/features/ai/).

title: Warranty Tracking
description: Configure warning and critical warranty expiry thresholds on configuration policies so Breeze raises alerts before device manufacturer warranties lapse.

sections.text:
The **Warranty** feature on a [configuration policy](/features/configuration-policies/) controls when Breeze raises an alert as a device's manufacturer warranty approaches expiry. You set two thresholds — a **warning** window and a **critical** window (both in days) — and Breeze evaluates each device's known warranty end date against them, opening an [alert](/features/alerts/) when the device falls inside a window.

Warranty alerting is **opt-in**. A device with no assigned, active warranty policy is never alerted, even if Breeze knows its warranty date. You turn it on by adding a Warranty feature to a policy and assigning that policy to the devices you care about.

sections.heading: Where warranty dates come from
sections.text:
Breeze stores one warranty record per device (`device_warranty`) with the manufacturer, serial number, coverage status, and start/end dates. A background worker runs every 6 hours and re-checks each device about once every 7 days (50 devices per run), looking the serial number up against the vendor providers your instance has configured — Dell (official API credentials) and Lenovo (official API ClientID and/or the credential-free opt-in); Apple/AppleCare coverage is reported by the macOS agent. HP has no lookup yet, so HP devices stay `unknown`. Vendor configuration is described under [Environment → Warranty lookups](/deploy/environment/#warranty-lookups). The Warranty **tab does not set warranty dates** — it only configures the alert thresholds evaluated against whatever dates the sync has discovered. Devices whose warranty status is still `unknown`, or that have no end date, are skipped.

Devices on an **active AppleCare subscription** are never alerted. The reported "end date" for a recurring subscription is the next renewal date, not a true expiry, so it perpetually rolls forward — Breeze treats it as covered and clears any stale expiry alert.

sections.heading: Configure in a policy
sections.text:
1. Open **Fleet Management → Config Policies** and select (or create) a policy, then open its **Warranty** tab.

2. Toggle **Enable warranty expiry alerts** on.

3. Set the **Warning threshold (days)** — Breeze raises a `high`-severity alert once a device's warranty is this many days or fewer from expiring. Default `90` (range 1–365).

4. Set the **Critical threshold (days)** — inside this closer window (and once expired) Breeze raises a `critical`-severity alert instead. Default `30` (range 1–365).

5. **Save**, then assign the policy to the scope you want covered (partner, organization, site, device group, or device).

The settings are stored **inline** on the policy's Warranty feature link. Resolution follows the standard closest-wins hierarchy — a device-level policy overrides group, site, organization, and partner. A policy created **partner-wide (all organizations)** applies these thresholds across every organization you manage, so you can define one warranty standard for your whole fleet. See [Configuration Policies](/features/configuration-policies/) for ownership and assignment details.

sections.heading: What alerts fire
sections.text:
Breeze picks a single severity per device based on days remaining until the warranty end date:

| Condition | Severity | Alert |
|---|---|---|
| Warranty already expired (0 days or past) | `critical` | "Warranty expired: *device*" |
| Within the **critical** threshold | `critical` | "Warranty expires in N days: *device*" |
| Within the **warning** threshold | `high` | "Warranty expires in N days: *device*" |
| Outside both thresholds | — | No alert (any existing one is auto-resolved) |

Each alert carries the manufacturer, serial number, end date, and days remaining. Only one open warranty alert exists per device at a time — Breeze won't create a duplicate while one is active, acknowledged, or suppressed. When a device moves back outside the thresholds (or becomes an AppleCare subscription), Breeze **auto-resolves** the open alert. A warranty alert a user has **dismissed** stays dismissed for that end date and won't be recreated; if the warranty is later renewed to a new end date and approaches expiry again, alerting resumes.

sections.heading: Related
sections.text:
- [Configuration Policies](/features/configuration-policies/) — how to create, own, and assign policies
- [Alerts](/features/alerts/) — reviewing, acknowledging, and resolving the alerts this feature raises
- [Devices](/features/devices/) — where a device's warranty status is shown

title: Agent Watchdog
description: A companion service that monitors the Breeze agent process, performs escalating recovery, and provides failover connectivity when the agent is down.
headings: Restarting the agent from the device page
Automatic repair of a missing watchdog
Troubleshooting a watchdog that is not installed

sections.text:
The **Breeze Watchdog** is a lightweight companion service that runs alongside the Breeze agent on every managed device. It continuously monitors the agent process, automatically recovers it when it becomes unhealthy, and maintains a fallback connection to the Breeze server when the agent is completely down.

The watchdog is installed automatically alongside the agent during normal installation — no separate setup is required.

  As of **v0.60.1**, the watchdog service is bundled in all platform installers — Windows MSI, macOS PKG, and Linux install scripts. New installs get automatic crash recovery out of the box with no separate installation step needed. Devices installed with earlier versions can upgrade their installer package to add the watchdog.

  As of **v0.62.25**, running `breeze-agent service install` from the CLI also auto-bootstraps the watchdog process, so unattended scripted installs are protected against agent crashes without an extra step. On macOS, agent auto-updates re-bootstrap the desktop helper and watchdog so remote control stays available across upgrades.

---

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.text:
The watchdog runs as a separate system service (`breeze-watchdog` on Linux, `BreezeWatchdog` on Windows) and monitors the agent through three independent health checks:

1. **Process liveness** — Is the agent process still running? Detects crashes and unexpected exits.
2. **IPC connectivity** — Can the watchdog reach the agent over its local IPC socket? Detects hangs and deadlocks.
3. **Heartbeat freshness** — Has the agent sent a heartbeat to the server recently? Detects networking failures and stuck loops.

When a check fails, the watchdog transitions through escalating states — from monitoring to recovery to failover — to bring the agent back to a healthy state.

:::note[Heartbeat freshness uses two independent sources]
The agent records its last successful heartbeat to a state file on disk, and also reports it to the watchdog over IPC. The freshness check uses **whichever of the two is more recent**.

This matters on endpoints where antivirus or endpoint-security software blocks writes to the agent's data directory. There, the state file is missing or frozen while the agent is demonstrably healthy and still checking in — a blocked *writer*, not a dead agent. Because the live IPC value outranks a stale file, the watchdog will not restart an agent that is still reporting in. Similarly, IPC connectivity counts **any** message received from the agent as evidence of life, not just a reply to the watchdog's own ping, so an agent busy with heavy collection work is not mistaken for a hung one.

From agent 0.124.0, a heartbeat the server answered with **429, 502, 503 or 504** (for example a 503 with `Retry-After` from admission control during an overload) also counts as evidence of life. The agent reached the server and was told to wait, so a restart would not help; the watchdog leaves it running instead of restarting a healthy agent against a busy server.
:::

---

sections.heading: States
sections.text:
The watchdog operates as a state machine with five states:

| State | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Connecting** | Starting up, attempting to establish IPC connection to the agent |
| **Monitoring** | Agent is healthy; running periodic health checks |
| **Recovering** | Agent is unhealthy; performing escalating restart attempts |
| **Standby** | Agent signaled a graceful shutdown (e.g., for an update); waiting a bounded window for it to come back |
| **Failover** | Recovery attempts exhausted; watchdog is communicating directly with the Breeze server on behalf of the device |

sections.heading: State transitions
sections.text:
```
CONNECTING ──ipc connected──→ MONITORING
CONNECTING ──agent not found─→ RECOVERING
CONNECTING ──agent unhealthy─→ RECOVERING

MONITORING ──agent unhealthy─→ RECOVERING
MONITORING ──shutdown intent─→ STANDBY

RECOVERING ──agent recovered─→ MONITORING
RECOVERING ──ipc connected───→ MONITORING
RECOVERING ──recovery exhausted──→ FAILOVER

STANDBY ────agent recovered──→ MONITORING
STANDBY ────ipc connected────→ MONITORING
STANDBY ────agent unhealthy──→ RECOVERING
STANDBY ────standby timeout──→ FAILOVER
STANDBY ────start agent──────→ RECOVERING

FAILOVER ───agent recovered──→ MONITORING
FAILOVER ───ipc connected────→ MONITORING
```

  The **Standby** state handles planned agent downtime — for example, when the agent shuts itself down to apply a self-update. Health signals are ignored for the duration of the announced window, so the watchdog does not fight the very restart the agent asked for.

  That window is bounded. Once it closes, the watchdog acts: if the agent is back and healthy it returns to **Monitoring**, and if the agent is still gone it escalates to **Recovering** and starts it. A shutdown reason the agent itself sends (a user stop, a self-update, a config reload) uses the short **standby grace** window; an unrecognised reason is held to the longer **standby timeout** ceiling and then parks in **Failover** — but only after a best-effort start, so a host is never left stopped indefinitely.

  Because the watchdog restarts an agent that stays down past its standby window, `breeze-agent service stop` is **temporary** while the watchdog is installed — the agent comes back after the standby grace period. To stop the agent durably, stop or uninstall the watchdog as well.

**Known wrinkle on Linux:**
  On Linux, `systemctl stop breeze-agent` currently runs its full 30-second stop
  timeout and ends in a kill rather than exiting promptly, so the graceful
  announced-shutdown path above does not complete in time and the agent is
  recovered through the ordinary unhealthy ladder instead — roughly 30 seconds
  either way. The practical effects are cosmetic: each `service install` takes
  about half a minute, and the unit is briefly reported as `failed` before it
  comes back up. Being restarted is still the outcome, so the durable-stop advice
  above is unchanged.

---

sections.heading: Recovery
sections.text:
When the agent is detected as unhealthy, the watchdog performs escalating recovery actions:

1. **Graceful restart** — asks the system service manager to restart the agent service cleanly.

2. **Force-kill + restart** — terminates the agent process, then starts the service. Used when the agent process is hung and not responding to service stop requests.

3. **Start only** — assumes the previous process is already gone and attempts a fresh service start.

Recovery attempts are tracked within a cooldown window. If the window elapses without exhausting all attempts, the counter resets. If all attempts are exhausted within the window, the watchdog transitions to **Failover**.

---

sections.heading: Failover
sections.text:
When recovery is exhausted, the watchdog enters **Failover** mode and takes over communication with the Breeze server. In this state the watchdog:

- Sends periodic heartbeats so the device remains visible in the dashboard
- Polls for commands from the server (restart agent, collect diagnostics, update agent, update watchdog)
- Ships watchdog health journal excerpts for remote diagnosis
- Accepts and applies agent or watchdog binary updates pushed from the server

Failover keeps the device manageable even when the agent process is completely down. Once the agent is successfully restarted (either via a server command or manual intervention), the watchdog transitions back to **Monitoring**.

  If a device shows `watchdog_status: failover` in the dashboard, it means the agent on that device has crashed and could not be automatically recovered. Use the **Restart Agent** action from the device detail page — the watchdog will receive and execute this command.

sections.heading: Restarting the agent from the device page
sections.text:
**Restart agent** is in the device page's action menu. It asks the watchdog, not the agent, to restart the agent, so it works when the agent itself has stopped responding.

1. Open the device and choose **Restart agent** from the actions menu.
2. The confirmation names the host and shows when the watchdog last reported. If the watchdog has not reported in the last 10 minutes, or never has, the dialog says the request will be refused.
3. Confirm with MFA. Breeze queues the request and says it was *requested*; the watchdog picks it up on its next poll, usually within about 30 seconds.

Only one restart can be waiting per device. The action needs the `devices:recover_agent` permission; the upgrade to v0.125.0 grants it to the built-in roles that hold `devices:execute` (Org Admin, Org Technician and Partner Technician; Partner Admin has every permission). Add it to custom roles that should use the action. Each request is recorded in the device's event log and the audit log. It is not offered for decommissioned devices.

The watchdog reports only while it is in **Failover**, so on a device whose agent is healthy the request is refused with "Watchdog is not reporting". That is expected: the action is for an agent that has stopped.

---

sections.heading: Agent-Silent Detection
sections.text:
The watchdog reports its own health to the server through its own connection. That means the watchdog can be perfectly healthy while the main agent has gone quiet — a "silent agent" condition that earlier versions of Breeze couldn't distinguish from a fully-offline device.

The server now watches for this asymmetry on every device. When the main agent stops checking in but the watchdog stays online, the device row shows an amber **Agent silent (watchdog OK)** badge in the dashboard. The badge tells you the device is still reachable through the watchdog and a remote **Restart Agent** action will work — versus a fully-offline device where neither component is responding.

The agent also supervises itself. If its main loop stops making forward progress for an extended period, the agent self-restarts before the watchdog needs to step in, keeping recovery fast for the common transient-stuck case.

---

sections.heading: Health Journal
sections.text:
The watchdog maintains a local rotating log file called the **health journal**. Each entry records a timestamped event (state transition, health check result, recovery action, IPC message) in structured JSON format.

Journal files rotate by size and count, keeping recent history available for diagnosis without consuming excessive disk space.

You can export the journal locally:

```bash
breeze-watchdog health-journal
```

The watchdog also ships journal entries to the Breeze server as diagnostic logs (component prefix `watchdog.*`), which you can query via the API — see [Watchdog Logs](#watchdog-logs-api) below.

---

sections.heading: Configuration
sections.text:
The watchdog reads its configuration from the same config directory as the agent. Default values are tuned for production use — most deployments do not need to change them.

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| Process check interval | 5 s | How often to check if the agent process is alive |
| IPC probe interval | 30 s | How often to ping the agent over IPC |
| Heartbeat stale threshold | 3 min | How long since the last heartbeat before the agent is considered stale |
| Max recovery attempts | 3 | Number of escalating recovery tries before entering failover |
| Recovery cooldown | 10 min | Window in which recovery attempts are counted; resets after expiry |
| Standby grace | 2 min | How long an announced shutdown the agent itself signalled is tolerated before the watchdog starts the agent again |
| Standby timeout | 30 min | Ceiling on any standby. Applies in full only to an unrecognised shutdown reason; the agent's own reasons use the standby grace above |
| Failover poll interval | 30 s | How often to poll the server for commands during failover |

---

sections.heading: Automatic repair of a missing watchdog
sections.text:
If the watchdog could not be installed during `breeze-agent service install` (for example because the download failed), an enrolled, running agent installs it later by itself. It does this only when the Breeze server offers a watchdog version for the device, which the server already does for devices with no watchdog and which honours any watchdog version pin. The agent downloads the watchdog through its normal authenticated update path (signed release manifest, SHA-256 checksum, and the same network policy as agent updates), runs that verified binary's own `service install`, and counts the install as successful only once the watchdog service is registered and running. On Linux the download is staged under `/var/lib/breeze/watchdog-stage` and the install runs through a `systemd-run` transient service.

Retries are bounded and persisted across agent restarts. After a failure the agent waits about 5 minutes, then 15 minutes, 45 minutes, 2 hours 15 minutes, and then 6 hours between attempts (with ±20% jitter), for 8 attempts in total. After that it checks once a day. Failures that retrying cannot fix (a signature, checksum, or network-policy refusal) stop immediately and are re-checked only once a week. Upgrading the agent to a new version allows one fresh round of attempts. The retry state is kept in `watchdog-install.state` in the agent's config directory. It is safe to delete, which resets the retry budget but never removes an opt-out. If the file is corrupt, the agent waits a day rather than retrying immediately.

The agent does nothing when its `auto_update` setting is off, when it is a development build, when the host is not yet enrolled (it waits for enrollment), when the host's init system is unsupported (Linux without systemd), or when the operator opted out with `service install --no-watchdog`. See [Installing the agent](/agents/installation#what-gets-installed) for how to opt out and re-enable.

sections.heading: Retry timeline
sections.text:
| Attempt | Waits before the next attempt after a failure |
|---|---|
| 1 | about 5 minutes |
| 2 | about 15 minutes |
| 3 | about 45 minutes |
| 4 | about 2 hours 15 minutes |
| 5–7 | about 6 hours |
| 8 | gives up; one probe attempt per day afterwards |
| Signature, checksum or network-policy failure (any attempt) | gives up at once; one probe attempt per week afterwards |

The first attempt happens on the first heartbeat after enrollment in which the server offers a watchdog version. All waits have ±20% jitter.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting a watchdog that is not installed
sections.text:
The device's **Info** tab shows a banner when the watchdog could not be installed:

- **Gave up**: the attempts above are used up, or a failure that retrying cannot fix occurred. The banner names the reason (for example a failed download, a signature or integrity check, or a failed install command) and the date it started.
- **Not supported**: the host cannot run the watchdog service, for example Linux without systemd.

A host that is still retrying, that opted out with `--no-watchdog`, or whose `auto_update` setting is off shows no banner. For those, check the agent log or the device's diagnostic logs.

To retry right away, run `service install --watchdog` on the host (`sudo breeze-agent service install --watchdog` on Linux and macOS, `breeze-agent.exe service install --watchdog` on Windows). It clears any opt-out, resets the retry state, and installs the watchdog now. Fix the cause first when the reason is a signature, integrity or network-policy failure, otherwise the next attempt fails the same way. Deleting `watchdog-install.state` from the agent's config directory also resets the retry budget without installing anything.

The banner clears when the agent stops reporting the failure. `service install --watchdog` restarts an enrolled agent, so the banner clears after its next heartbeat. If you install the watchdog another way (for example `breeze-watchdog service install`), restart the agent service afterwards to clear the banner.

---

sections.heading: Watchdog Logs API
sections.text:
Watchdog diagnostic logs are queryable through a dedicated API endpoint that filters specifically for watchdog-component logs.

```
GET /devices/:id/watchdog-logs
```

sections.heading: Query parameters
sections.text:
| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `level` | string | Comma-separated levels: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` |
| `component` | string | Filter to a specific watchdog sub-component (e.g., `watchdog.recovery`) |
| `since` | ISO 8601 | Include only logs at or after this datetime |
| `until` | ISO 8601 | Include only logs at or before this datetime |
| `search` | string | Full-text search across message and structured fields |
| `page` | number | Page number (1-based) |
| `limit` | number | Results per page (max 500) |

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
```bash
# Get recent watchdog error logs for a device
GET /api/v1/devices/DEVICE_ID/watchdog-logs?level=warn,error&limit=50
```

---

sections.heading: Dashboard Indicators
sections.text:
The devices table includes three watchdog-specific fields:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `watchdog_status` | Current watchdog state: `connected` (monitoring), `failover`, or `offline` |
| `watchdog_last_seen` | Timestamp of the last watchdog heartbeat or check-in |
| `watchdog_version` | Installed watchdog binary version |

These fields update as the watchdog reports its state through heartbeats and failover polling.

---

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**Watchdog status shows `failover`.**
The agent process crashed and could not be automatically recovered after the configured number of attempts. Use the **Restart Agent** action from the device detail page, or SSH into the device and manually restart the agent service. Check the watchdog logs for recovery failure details: `GET /devices/:id/watchdog-logs?level=error`.

**Watchdog status shows `offline`.**
The watchdog service itself is not running. Check the system service manager on the device (`systemctl status breeze-watchdog` on Linux, `launchctl list | grep breeze-watchdog` on macOS, `Get-Service BreezeWatchdog` on Windows).

**Agent keeps restarting in a loop.**
The watchdog recovers the agent, but it immediately crashes again. This is usually caused by a bad configuration file or a corrupted binary. Check the agent's own diagnostic logs for startup errors. The watchdog will eventually exhaust its recovery attempts and enter failover, preventing an infinite restart loop.

**No watchdog logs appearing.**
The watchdog ships logs through the same diagnostic log pipeline as the agent. Verify the watchdog service is running and the device is online. Watchdog logs use the `watchdog.*` component prefix — they do not appear in the standard agent logs filter unless you query the dedicated endpoint.

title: Webhooks
description: Push signed JSON event notifications to external HTTP endpoints with HMAC-SHA256 signatures, custom headers, retries, and delivery history.

sections.text:
Webhooks let you push real-time event notifications from Breeze to any external HTTP endpoint. When a device enrolls, an alert fires, a script completes, or any other tracked event occurs, Breeze sends a signed JSON payload to each webhook configured for that event type. Webhooks are scoped to an organization and support custom headers, HMAC-SHA256 signature verification, automatic retries with exponential backoff, and a full delivery history with per-delivery status tracking.

---

sections.heading: Creating a Webhook
sections.text:
1. Choose the events you want to subscribe to (see [Event Types](#event-types) below).

2. Send a POST request with the webhook name, destination URL, signing secret, and event list:

```bash
   POST /webhooks
   Content-Type: application/json

   {
     "name": "PagerDuty Alerts",
     "url": "https://events.pagerduty.com/integration/abc123/enqueue",
     "secret": "whsec_your_signing_secret",
     "events": ["alert.triggered", "alert.escalated", "device.offline"],
     "headers": [
       { "key": "X-Custom-Source", "value": "breeze-rmm" }
     ]
   }
```

3. The API validates the URL against the SSRF safety rules (see [URL Safety Validation](#url-safety-validation) — HTTPS to a publicly routable address on hosted Breeze; self-hosted deployments may also target private addresses), encrypts the secret, and returns the new webhook:

```json
   {
     "id": "d290f1ee-6c54-4b01-90e6-d701748f0851",
     "orgId": "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111",
     "name": "PagerDuty Alerts",
     "url": "https://events.pagerduty.com/integration/abc123/enqueue",
     "events": ["alert.triggered", "alert.escalated", "device.offline"],
     "headers": [{ "key": "X-Custom-Source", "value": "breeze-rmm" }],
     "status": "active",
     "hasSecret": true,
     "createdAt": "2026-02-18T12:00:00.000Z",
     "updatedAt": "2026-02-18T12:00:00.000Z",
     "lastDeliveryAt": null
   }
```

4. Send a test delivery to verify connectivity (see [Testing a Webhook](#testing-a-webhook)).

  Both the `secret` and the `url` are encrypted at rest using AES-256-GCM. The `secret` is never returned in API responses — only the `hasSecret` boolean indicates whether one is configured. The `url` is returned by GET responses, but any credentials embedded in it (HTTP basic-auth userinfo and signed query tokens) are stripped before the value is sent to the client.

sections.heading: Organization Scoping
sections.text:
Webhooks follow the standard multi-tenant access model:

| Auth Scope | Behavior |
|------------|----------|
| **Organization** | `orgId` is set automatically from the authenticated context. |
| **Partner** | `orgId` must be provided in the request body. The API verifies the partner has access to that organization. |
| **System** | `orgId` must be provided in the request body. |

---

sections.heading: Event Types
sections.text: Webhooks subscribe to events emitted by the Breeze event bus. Pass one or more event type strings in the `events` array when creating or updating a webhook. Use `*` to receive every event. The API rejects an event type that Breeze never publishes with a `400`, so a typo cannot save a webhook that silently never fires. The legacy name `alert.created` is accepted and stored as `alert.triggered`.

| `device.reinstalled` | A reinstalled machine was reattached to its existing device record: the record keeps its id, org, site and history, a new install takes it over, and the install incarnation advances. Payload: `deviceId`, `sourceDeviceId`, `orgId`, `sourceOrgId`, `siteId`, `installIncarnation`, `previousIncarnation`, `evidenceLevel`, `actorUserId`, `reattachmentId` |

sections.heading: Ticket Events
sections.text:
Ticket events are published from the ticketing transactional outbox with **id-only payloads**: identifiers, enum labels and field *names*, never a subject, description, resolution note or comment body. Read the full record through the API (staff JWT, or the Partner API `tickets:read` feed) when you need it. Rely only on the fields listed below: a payload can also carry other internal identifiers, which are not part of this contract.

| Event | Payload (besides `ticketId`) | Description |
|-------|------------------------------|-------------|
| `ticket.created` | `internalNumber`, `source`, `assigneeId`, `actorPrincipalId` | A ticket was opened (from the portal, email, an alert, the UI, the Partner API or AI). `actorPrincipalId` is the service principal that opened it (`null` otherwise) |
| `ticket.commented` | `commentId`, `isPublic`, `originPrincipalKind`, `originPrincipalId` | A comment, note or feed entry was added. `originPrincipalKind` and `originPrincipalId` are the comment's stored origin, the same values the Partner API feed returns for it: `service_principal` with the principal's id, `ai_agent` with the agent's id, `user` for people, and `system` for Breeze's own system notes, such as caller verification (`originPrincipalId` is `null` for the last two). A comment Breeze writes on a customer's behalf is `user` by design: a reply that arrives by email (or a public email linked from the Outlook add-in) and the reopen that reply triggers. A mirroring integration skips exactly the comments it wrote by matching `service_principal` and its own principal id |
| `ticket.status_changed` | `from`, `to`, `statusId` | The core status changed (`statusId` is the partner's custom status row, when one was used) |
| `ticket.updated` | `changed` (field names) | Fields were edited — subject, description, priority, category, due date, device, tags, requester |
| `ticket.assigned` | `assigneeId` (`null` when unassigned), `actorPrincipalId` | The assignee changed. `actorPrincipalId` is the service principal that made the change (`null` for people and the system), so a mirroring integration can skip its own assignments |
| `ticket.merged` | `sourceTicketId`, `targetTicketId`, `sourceInternalNumber`, `targetInternalNumber` | A ticket was merged into another. Sent once, on the surviving ticket (`ticketId` = `targetTicketId`). The source stays as a read-only record: a Partner API read of it returns `mergedIntoTicketId` and `mergedAt`. The source also gets a `ticket.status_changed` to `closed` when it was not already closed, and the survivor a `ticket.updated` with `changed: ["merge"]`. Comments moved by the merge are not re-sent as `ticket.commented` |
| `ticket.sla_breached` | `assigneeId` | A response or resolution SLA target was missed |

sections.heading: Migration Window Events
sections.text:
A ticket migration window lets a partner admin import ticket history from another system without notifying anyone or firing per-ticket events. Nothing the import writes produces a ticket event. When the window closes, each organization in it gets one summary event.

| Event | Payload | Description |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| `migration.window_closed` | `windowId`, `partnerId`, `sourceLabel`, `openedAt`, `endsAt`, `closedAt`, `closedReason`, `ticketsImported`, `commentsImported` | A migration window closed. Sent once per organization in the window, with that organization's counts. `closedReason` is `expired`, `closed_by_admin`, `principal_inactive` or `opener_inactive`. The event id is `<windowId>:<orgId>`, so a retried delivery is recognizable |

sections.heading: Integration Events
sections.text:
Integration events report the health of an organization's own connections: an integration, a sync or an OAuth grant. A health incident opens when a connection breaks and resolves when it recovers or is retired.

| Event | Payload | Description |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| `integration.health_opened` | `incidentId`, `orgId`, `sourceKind`, `sourceId`, `condition`, `severity`, `fixHref`, `openedAt`, `resolvedAt`, `resolution` | A connection health incident opened. `resolvedAt` and `resolution` are `null` |
| `integration.health_resolved` | `incidentId`, `orgId`, `sourceKind`, `sourceId`, `condition`, `severity`, `fixHref`, `openedAt`, `resolvedAt`, `resolution` | A connection health incident resolved |

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `incidentId` | string (uuid) | The incident. Both events for one incident carry the same value |
| `orgId` | string (uuid) | The organization that owns the connection |
| `sourceKind` | string | The kind of connection, for example `m365_connection`, `dns_filter` or `webhook` |
| `sourceId` | string or `null` | The connection's id. `null` for `oauth_grant`, because that id embeds a user id |
| `condition` | string | A fixed code for what is wrong, for example `sync_failed` or `reauth_required` |
| `severity` | string | `permanent` (needs someone to act) or `transient` (may clear on its own) |
| `fixHref` | string | A relative path in the Breeze web app where the connection can be repaired |
| `openedAt` | string (ISO timestamp) | When the incident opened |
| `resolvedAt` | string (ISO timestamp) or `null` | When the incident resolved. `null` while it is open |
| `resolution` | string or `null` | `recovered` or `retired`. `null` while the incident is open |

- **No free text.** The payload never contains provider error text or the connection's display name. Use `fixHref` and the API to look up more.
- **Organization connections only.** Only incidents about an organization's own connections emit events. Partner-wide connections do not.
- **Level-triggered.** Events follow the state seen at each health check, about every 15 minutes. A connection that breaks and recovers between two checks may emit nothing. A consumer can also receive an `integration.health_resolved` event for an incident it never saw open, for example an incident that existed before the feature shipped.
- **Stable event ids.** The event id is stable for a given incident and state, so retried deliveries are deduplicated.
- **No self-delivery.** An incident about a webhook is never delivered to that same webhook.

sections.heading: Delivery Mechanism
sections.text:
When an event is emitted on the Breeze event bus, the webhook delivery system routes it to all active webhooks in the same organization that are subscribed to that event type. Each delivery follows this sequence:

1. The event bus fires the event. The `initializeWebhookDelivery` subscriber matches the event type against all configured webhooks for the organization.

2. A delivery record is created in the `webhook_deliveries` table with status `pending` and `attempts` set to `0`.

3. The delivery job is queued onto the Redis list `breeze:webhooks:delivery`.

4. The `WebhookDeliveryWorker` picks up the job, validates the destination URL (including DNS resolution to block SSRF), and sends an HTTP POST with the signed payload.

5. If the response status is `2xx`, the delivery is marked `delivered`. Otherwise, the retry logic takes over.

sections.heading: Payload Format
sections.text:
Every webhook delivery sends a JSON POST body with the following structure:

```json
{
  "id": "event-uuid",
  "type": "device.offline",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-18T12:34:56.789Z",
  "orgId": "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111",
  "data": {
    "deviceId": "abc123",
    "hostname": "WORKSTATION-01",
    "lastSeen": "2026-02-18T12:30:00.000Z"
  }
}
```

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `id` | Unique event ID (UUID) |
| `type` | The event type string (e.g., `alert.triggered`) |
| `timestamp` | ISO 8601 timestamp of when the event was created |
| `orgId` | The organization the event belongs to |
| `data` | Event-specific payload; contents vary by event type |

sections.heading: Request Headers
sections.text:
Every delivery includes these headers:

| Header | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `Content-Type` | `application/json` |
| `User-Agent` | `Breeze-Webhooks/1.0` |
| `X-Breeze-Delivery-Id` | Unique ID for this delivery attempt |
| `X-Breeze-Event-Id` | The event ID from the payload |
| `X-Breeze-Event-Type` | The event type string |
| `X-Breeze-Timestamp` | Unix timestamp (milliseconds) of the delivery attempt |
| `X-Breeze-Signature` | HMAC-SHA256 signature (only if a secret is configured) |
| `X-Breeze-Signature-Timestamp` | Timestamp used in the signature computation |

Any custom headers configured on the webhook are merged into the request after the standard headers.

---

sections.heading: Retry Logic
sections.text:
Failed deliveries are retried automatically using exponential backoff. The default retry policy is:

| Parameter | Default Value |
|-----------|---------------|
| Maximum retries | 5 |
| Initial delay | 1,000 ms (1 second) |
| Backoff multiplier | 2x |
| Maximum delay | 300,000 ms (5 minutes) |
| Delivery timeout | 30,000 ms (30 seconds) |

The delay between retries follows the formula:

```
delay = min(initialDelay * (multiplier ^ attempt), maxDelay)
```

This produces the following schedule for the default policy:

| Attempt | Delay |
|---------|-------|
| 1st retry | 1 second |
| 2nd retry | 2 seconds |
| 3rd retry | 4 seconds |
| 4th retry | 8 seconds |
| 5th retry | 16 seconds |

sections.heading: Custom Retry Policy
sections.text:
You can override the default retry policy per webhook by setting the `retryPolicy` field in the database. There is no dashboard control or API field for this today -- creating and updating a webhook through the API or the dashboard does not accept a `retryPolicy` value, so this requires direct database access (self-hosted operators, or Breeze support on hosted accounts). The policy object accepts:

```json
{
  "maxRetries": 10,
  "initialDelayMs": 2000,
  "backoffMultiplier": 3,
  "maxDelayMs": 600000
}
```

sections.heading: Dead Letter Queue
sections.text:
After all retries are exhausted, the delivery job is moved to a dead letter queue (Redis key `breeze:webhooks:dlq`). Jobs in the DLQ can be inspected and retried through the worker API.

  Redirects are rejected (`redirect: "error"`). If your endpoint returns a 3xx redirect, the delivery will be treated as a failure and retried.

---

sections.heading: Bearer Token Authentication
Signature Verification
sections.text: When a webhook has a signing secret, every delivery includes an HMAC-SHA256 signature in the `X-Breeze-Signature` header. Use this to verify that the payload was sent by Breeze and has not been tampered with.

sections.heading: How the Signature Is Computed
sections.text:
The signature input is the concatenation of the timestamp and the raw JSON payload body, separated by a dot:

```
signature_input = timestamp + "." + payload_body
signature = HMAC-SHA256(secret, signature_input)
```

The `X-Breeze-Signature` header value is prefixed with `sha256=`:

```
X-Breeze-Signature: sha256=a1b2c3d4e5f6...
```

The `X-Breeze-Signature-Timestamp` header contains the same timestamp value used in the signature computation.

sections.heading: Verification Examples
Delivery History
sections.text:
Every webhook maintains a paginated delivery history. Each delivery record captures the event type, payload, response details, and retry state. The list returns status and timing only; the event payload and the receiver's response body are not included. Reading the history requires `webhooks:read`.

From v0.124.0, delivered and failed records are kept for **90 days** by default and then removed by a nightly job; records that are still pending or retrying are never removed. Self-hosters can change the window with the webhook delivery retention variables in [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/). A webhook whose retries are exhausted with no later success also opens a connection-health incident on **Integrations** -- see [Connection Health Checks](/features/notifications/#connection-health-checks).

sections.heading: Listing Deliveries
sections.text:
```bash
GET /webhooks/:id/deliveries?page=1&limit=50&status=failed
```

All query parameters are optional. Results are ordered by most recent first.

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `page` | integer | Page number (default: 1) |
| `limit` | integer | Results per page (default: 50, max: 100) |
| `status` | string | Filter by delivery status: `pending`, `delivered`, `failed`, `retrying` |

Response:

```json
{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "delivery-uuid",
      "webhookId": "webhook-uuid",
      "orgId": "org-uuid",
      "status": "delivered",
      "event": "alert.triggered",
      "eventId": "event-uuid",
      "responseStatus": 200,
      "attempt": 1,
      "nextAttemptAt": null,
      "createdAt": "2026-02-18T12:34:56.000Z",
      "deliveredAt": "2026-02-18T12:34:57.123Z"
    }
  ],
  "pagination": {
    "page": 1,
    "limit": 50,
    "total": 142
  }
}
```

sections.heading: Delivery Statistics
sections.text:
When you fetch a single webhook via `GET /webhooks/:id`, the response includes aggregated delivery statistics:

```json
{
  "id": "webhook-uuid",
  "name": "PagerDuty Alerts",
  "status": "active",
  "deliveryStats": {
    "total": 1284,
    "pending": 2,
    "delivered": 1250,
    "failed": 30,
    "retrying": 2,
    "lastDeliveredAt": "2026-02-18T12:34:57.123Z"
  }
}
```

sections.heading: Retrying a Failed Delivery
sections.text:
You can manually retry any delivery that has a `failed` status. The retry creates a new delivery record with the same event type and payload, and queues it for immediate processing.

```bash
POST /webhooks/:id/retry/:deliveryId
```

Response (202 Accepted):

```json
{
  "message": "Delivery retry queued",
  "delivery": {
    "id": "new-delivery-uuid",
    "status": "pending",
    "attempt": 0
  }
}
```

  Only deliveries with status `failed` can be retried. Attempting to retry a delivery with any other status returns a `400` error.

---

sections.heading: Testing a Webhook
sections.text:
Send a test delivery to verify that your endpoint is reachable and correctly processing payloads:

```bash
POST /webhooks/:id/test
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "event": "webhook.test",
  "payload": {
    "message": "Hello from Breeze RMM"
  }
}
```

Both `event` and `payload` are optional. If omitted, the test uses event type `webhook.test` and a default payload containing a message, timestamp, and webhook ID.

Response (202 Accepted):

```json
{
  "message": "Test delivery queued",
  "delivery": {
    "id": "delivery-uuid",
    "webhookId": "webhook-uuid",
    "status": "pending",
    "event": "webhook.test",
    "attempt": 0
  }
}
```

The test delivery is queued through the same delivery pipeline as real events, so it exercises the full path including HMAC signing, URL validation, and retry logic.

---

sections.heading: Updating a Webhook
sections.text:
Update any combination of name, URL, secret, events, headers, or status:

```bash
PATCH /webhooks/:id
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "events": ["device.enrolled", "device.offline", "alert.triggered"],
  "status": "paused"
}
```

| Status Value | Description |
|--------------|-------------|
| `active` | Webhook is enabled and will receive deliveries |
| `paused` | Webhook is temporarily disabled; no deliveries are sent |
| `failed` | Webhook has been marked as failed (can be set manually or by the system) |

  When you update the `url` field, the new URL goes through the same SSRF safety validation (see [URL Safety Validation](#url-safety-validation)) as during creation.

---

sections.heading: Deleting a Webhook
sections.text:
```bash
DELETE /webhooks/:id
```

  Deleting a webhook also removes all associated delivery records from the database. This action cannot be undone.

---

sections.heading: URL Safety Validation
sections.text:
Breeze validates webhook URLs at both creation time and delivery time to prevent SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) attacks.

**At creation and update time**, the API performs synchronous validation including DNS resolution. On hosted Breeze:

- URL must use HTTPS
- Hostname must not be `localhost`, `*.localhost`, or `*.local`
- IP addresses must not be private, loopback, or link-local (covers RFC 1918, RFC 6598, RFC 5737, and IPv6 equivalents)
- DNS resolution is performed to catch hostnames that resolve to blocked address ranges

**Self-hosted deployments** (`IS_HOSTED=false`) may point webhooks at private RFC 1918/ULA addresses on their own network — an on-prem SIEM or ticketing system, for example — and plain `http://` is permitted **only** when the target resolves to such a private address. Public destinations still require HTTPS, and cloud-metadata, loopback, and link-local addresses are blocked in every configuration.

**At delivery time**, the worker re-validates the URL before every delivery attempt. If the URL has become unsafe (e.g., DNS now resolves to a private IP), the delivery fails immediately without making an HTTP request.

---

sections.heading: API Reference
sections.text:
| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| **GET** | `/webhooks` | List webhooks for the organization (paginated, filterable by `status` and `orgId`) |
| **POST** | `/webhooks` | Create a new webhook |
| **GET** | `/webhooks/:id` | Get webhook details including delivery statistics |
| **PATCH** | `/webhooks/:id` | Update webhook name, URL, secret, events, headers, or status |
| **DELETE** | `/webhooks/:id` | Delete a webhook and all its delivery records |
| **GET** | `/webhooks/:id/deliveries` | List delivery history (paginated, filterable by `status`) |
| **POST** | `/webhooks/:id/test` | Send a test delivery |
| **POST** | `/webhooks/:id/retry/:deliveryId` | Retry a failed delivery |

All webhook routes require authentication and are scoped to `organization`, `partner`, or `system` roles. They also require a permission:

- **Reading** (`GET /webhooks`, `GET /webhooks/:id`, `GET /webhooks/:id/deliveries`) requires `webhooks:read`. The AI assistant's `query_webhooks` tool requires the same permission.
- **Managing** (create, update, delete, test, retry) requires `organizations:write`.

`webhooks:read` is granted by default to Org Admin, Org Technician and Partner Technician; Partner Admin holds it through `*:*`. In the dashboard, a user without `webhooks:read` does not see the Webhooks tab under Integrations, and a user without `organizations:write` sees webhooks and their delivery history without the create, edit, delete, test, pause/resume or retry controls. See [Users & Roles](/reference/users-and-roles/#permission-model) to grant either permission to a role.

**Upgrading to v0.122.1: some roles lose webhook visibility:**
  Before v0.122.1, `organizations:read` was enough to view webhooks. The upgrade grants `webhooks:read` to the built-in roles above and to every custom role that holds `organizations:write`, but not to viewer, billing or security-approver roles. **Partner Viewer** and **Partner Security Approver** no longer see webhooks, and a **custom role with `organizations:read` but not `organizations:write` loses access to webhooks and their delivery history until an administrator adds `webhooks:read` to it** under **Settings → Roles**. Self-hosters can find those roles in the upgrade log: the migration logs a `webhooks-read-permission:` warning with their count and up to 20 names.

---
