sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**"Invalid webhook URL" error when creating a webhook.**
On hosted Breeze, the URL must use HTTPS and must not resolve to a private, loopback, or link-local IP address (on self-hosted deployments, private RFC 1918/ULA targets are allowed — see [URL Safety Validation](#url-safety-validation)). Hostnames like `localhost`, `*.localhost`, and `*.local` are always blocked. If the hostname cannot be resolved via DNS, creation will fail.

**Webhook is not receiving events.**
Check the webhook status -- if it is `paused` or `failed`, deliveries are not processed. Verify that the `events` array includes the event types you expect. Use `POST /webhooks/:id/test` to confirm the endpoint is reachable.

**Deliveries are stuck in `retrying` status.**
The worker retries failed deliveries using exponential backoff. Check the `nextAttemptAt` field on the delivery to see when the next attempt is scheduled. If retries have been exhausted (default: 5 attempts), the delivery moves to `failed` and the job enters the dead letter queue.

**Signature verification fails on my endpoint.**
Ensure you are computing the HMAC over the correct input: the raw `X-Breeze-Signature-Timestamp` header value, followed by a dot (`.`), followed by the raw request body. Use the `X-Breeze-Signature-Timestamp` header (not `X-Breeze-Timestamp`) as the timestamp component. The signature uses SHA-256 and is hex-encoded.

**"Unsafe webhook URL" error during delivery.**
The worker re-validates the URL before each delivery attempt. On hosted Breeze, if your DNS records have changed and the hostname now resolves to a private IP range, deliveries will fail — update the webhook URL to point to a publicly routable address. On self-hosted deployments, private targets are deliverable; only metadata/loopback/link-local resolutions fail.

**"Only failed deliveries can be retried" error.**
The manual retry endpoint (`POST /webhooks/:id/retry/:deliveryId`) only accepts deliveries with status `failed`. Deliveries that are `pending`, `retrying`, or already `delivered` cannot be retried through this endpoint.

**"Organization context required" error.**
Webhook routes require an organization scope. If you are authenticated with a partner or system scope, pass the `orgId` query parameter (for list) or include it in the request body (for create) to specify which organization's webhooks you are managing.

**Response body is truncated.**
Webhook delivery response bodies are truncated to 1,000 characters to prevent excessive storage consumption. If you need the full response for debugging, check your endpoint's own logs.

title: Wisp
description: A continuous triage companion that watches what you may see, nudges you about it, and asks before it acts.
headings: What Wisp does alone vs asks first
Turning Wisp off for your company
Nudges, quiet hours and the morning brief

sections.text:
**Hosted Breeze only:**
  Wisp is available on hosted Breeze. On a self-hosted deployment Wisp is **off and cannot be turned on**: `/wisp` and the Wisp sidebar entry show a lock ("Wisp runs on Breeze Cloud. It is not available on this server."), no Wisp route, job or setting is active, there is no upgrade link, and there is nothing to enable. This page describes the hosted behavior.

sections.heading: What Wisp is
sections.text:
Wisp is a triage companion that works on behalf of one person. Once that person turns it on, Wisp keeps an eye on the estate they are allowed to see, notices things that need a human (a cluster of alerts, a stalled ticket, a failing patch ring), and tells them about it. It remembers preferences and decisions so it nags less over time, and it can hand focused jobs to specialists.

Wisp never has more authority than the person it works for. It acts inside a **grant** that snapshots that person's reach, and it cannot widen it. Anything that changes something in the world goes through the same approval cards you already use on web and mobile. Wisp adds no new approval tier and no bypass.

Wisp threads open at `/ai/wisp/thread/<id>`. Under an active grant the docked Breeze AI side panel speaks as Wisp (there is no toggle; see [Where you talk to Wisp](#where-you-talk-to-wisp)), and the **Wisp** entry in the AI section of the navigation opens the [Wisp home](#the-wisp-home).

sections.heading: Turning it on
sections.text:
Wisp is a paid-plan feature. It is enabled by default for **Pro, Enterprise and Unlimited** partners. On other plans the Wisp controls appear locked with an upgrade prompt; they are not hidden. Breeze operators control a deployment-level switch; if Wisp is off for the deployment, no partner can use it.

Creating a grant requires **step-up MFA**: you are asked to confirm your second factor, even if you signed in recently.

sections.heading: Switches that control Wisp
sections.text:
Wisp has three independent gates, and none of them overrides another:

- **The plan.** Wisp is a paid-plan feature (above). Without it the controls are locked with an upgrade prompt.
- **The deployment switch** (`BREEZE_WISP_ENABLED`). Turns the Wisp engine and the Wisp home on or off for a whole deployment.
- **The partner switch.** A partner administrator can turn Wisp off for their own company; see [Turning Wisp off for your company](#turning-wisp-off-for-your-company).

**For self-hosters and operators: the knowledge connector:**
  The built-in extension that indexes files and email for Wisp is labelled **Wisp knowledge connector** in the interface (its pages are **Knowledge sources** and **Knowledge dashboard**). It has its own flag, `BREEZE_WORKSPACE_ENABLED`, which also accepts the alias `BREEZE_WISP_CONNECTOR_ENABLED`; setting either one enables it. It needs the pgvector extension in Postgres. `BREEZE_WISP_ENABLED` is a separate flag and never loads the connector, and Wisp runs fine without the connector.

sections.heading: The Wisp home
sections.text:
The **Wisp** entry in the AI section of the navigation opens the Wisp home at `/wisp`. It is where you see, at a glance, what Wisp has been doing for you and what is waiting on you. The page is drawn from stored results; opening it never runs a model.

The home appears when Wisp is on for the deployment and you signed in at partner scope. If Wisp is off for the deployment (self-hosted), `/wisp` shows the page locked: "Wisp runs on Breeze Cloud. It is not available on this server." There is no upgrade link, and the Wisp sidebar entry shows the same lock. If you signed in at organization scope, `/wisp` sends you to Breeze AI at `/ai/chat`. If your plan does not include Wisp you see the same locked upgrade prompt as elsewhere. If you have no grant yet, a **Put Wisp to work** card starts one and opens the usual step-up confirmation.

The page is the conversation. One thread sits in the center at reading width with the composer at the bottom, and a rail on the right holds everything else. There is no page heading; the identity card in the rail carries the name.

The conversation column shows the whole thread, not just the current chat. Every earlier chat session with Wisp on this thread appears above the current one, in time order. Wisp's own output appears in the same flow as posts from Wisp, each with a small label and the time it was sent:

- **Morning brief** shows its sections.
- **Nudge** is a concern Wisp raised. The post has an **Open** link to the concern; snooze, dismiss and the other actions are in **Needs your attention** in the rail.
- **Digest** batches the items that waited for your digest cadence, such as a concern after two unanswered nudges.

An unread post, one whose notification you have not read yet, shows a small dot before its label.

How the thread reads:

- Wisp's replies run full width as prose, with **Wisp** shown above the first reply after each of your messages. Your messages are right-aligned bubbles.
- Tool activity folds into one line per run of checks, for example "Searched devices · Listed sites · 4s". Click the line to see each call. A failed check or a handoff that needs your approval opens the line by itself.
- When Wisp hands work to specialists, each one shows as a run card in the thread.
- Time dividers separate the conversation by day and after gaps of more than 20 minutes.
- Long threads load the newest page first. **Load earlier** at the top of the conversation brings in older messages and posts without moving what you are reading.
- New posts appear while the page is open. The home refreshes every 30 seconds, and the thread re-reads its newest messages when that refresh shows Wisp starting or finishing a check, a newer brief, or a change in the concerns that need you. If that read fails, the thread says so and offers **Retry**.
- An empty thread shows Wisp's welcome and four suggestions: **What needs me today?**, **Which devices are offline?**, **Run a health sweep** and **What happened overnight?**. Select one to send it. When a morning brief is already in the thread, only the suggestions show.

The composer says **Message Wisp**. Enter sends and Shift+Enter adds a line. The plus button links an item to the thread; see [Linked items](#linked-items). The thread resumes the last session instead of starting a new one on every visit. **New conversation** closes it, so its summary lands on the thread, and starts a fresh one on the grant. Nothing starts while the grant is paused or ended. While Wisp is paused, the conversation still shows its history, read-only, and the composer is replaced by the paused notice. When the grant has ended, the history is not shown.

The rail, from the top:

| Section | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Identity and grant controls | Wisp's name, its state ("Active" with the scope, or a live "Checking ..." line while an assessment runs), and the grant controls: refresh, settings, turn off, the spend meter, and pause and resume. |
| **Needs your attention** | Open and snoozed concerns for your grant, approvals first and then by severity, with a count of items waiting for your approval. Snooze, dismiss and give feedback exactly as on the thread page. Approvals open in the Approvals page. |
| **Workers** | Up to five recent specialist runs, with **All runs** linking to the full list. |
| **Linked items** | The tickets, devices and other items you pinned to Wisp; see [Linked items](#linked-items). |
| **Activity** | A timeline of what Wisp did. It starts collapsed; select **Show** to expand it. |

At the bottom of the rail are links to **All chats** (`/ai/chat`) and **Memory** (`/settings/wisp-memory`).

Below large screen widths the rail becomes a one-line strip under the page header: Wisp's state, how many items need you, and **Details**. **Details** opens the whole rail in a drawer. A link to a concern, such as `/wisp#concern=<id>`, opens the drawer by itself.

You can link straight to a section: `/wisp#needs-you`, `#activity`, `#thread` and `#links`. `#brief` scrolls to the thread, where the brief now lives. `/wisp#concern=<id>` opens **Needs your attention** on that concern. Below large screen widths, `#needs-you`, `#links`, `#activity` and `#concern=<id>` open the drawer instead of scrolling.

The thread page at `/ai/wisp/thread/<id>`, where nudges land, uses the same layout. The conversation is inline and is the same thread as the home, with the thread summary as its first post. The old **Open in chat** button is gone.

The side panel, when it speaks as Wisp, has an **Open in Wisp** link that goes to the home; concerns are listed on the home, not in the sidebar. On mobile, the Wisp thread screen shows the brief sections, the full activity timeline and the linked items (read-only, each opening its item).

sections.heading: Where you talk to Wisp
sections.text:
The multi-tab chat page is **Breeze AI**, at `/ai/chat`. It has the same tabs (up to five; open tabs survive a reload) and shortcuts, and it works with Wisp off. The old `/workspace` and `/wisp/chat` addresses redirect to it, and old `#session=<id>` links still open their tab. When you have an active grant for the organization selected in the header (or a grant for all organizations), a new tab on the page starts under that grant, the way the side panel does, and the tab header says **Wisp**. With no active grant, Wisp off, or an organization-scoped sign-in, the tab is an ordinary chat and its header says **Breeze AI**. A conversation you open from history keeps whatever grant it started under. The side panel speaks as Wisp only while you have an active grant; there is no toggle. Its **Open in Breeze AI** control moves a conversation to the page. See [Breeze AI](/features/breeze-ai/#where-you-talk-to-breeze-ai).

Breeze AI and the docked panel use the same message list as the Wisp home, so tool activity folds into one line there too, and the composer sends on Enter and adds a line on Shift+Enter.

sections.heading: Linked items
sections.text:
You can link items to your Wisp thread so Wisp keeps them in view. A thread holds up to 50 links. Link a ticket, quote, invoice, contract, device, organization, site, alert, agent run, operator task or user.

Add a link in either of two ways:

1. On the Wisp home, use **Link an item** in the Linked items section and pick a kind. The picker searches each kind's normal list, so you only see what you could already see.
2. On a ticket, quote, invoice, contract, device or organization page, click **Link to Wisp**. The button appears only when Wisp is on, you are signed in at partner scope, your partner's plan includes Wisp and you have an active grant. Once linked it reads **Linked in Wisp**.

Wisp can also link items during a conversation; those are marked **Added by Wisp**.

Links are re-checked against your current access and the grant's reach every time they are read:

- An item you can no longer see is hidden. The link is kept and reappears if your access returns.
- An item that was deleted disappears.
- The label is read from the item each time, so it follows renames.
- Removing a link never needs an active grant.

A link gives Wisp only a handle to the item (its kind, id and title), never the body of the record.

sections.heading: Grants
sections.text:
A grant is the standing permission you give Wisp.

- **Self-only.** You can grant Wisp to work for you, not for someone else. A grant is never shared.
- **Scope.** Either partner-wide or one organization. You can hold one live grant per scope.
- **Reach is a snapshot.** The grant records what you can reach at the time. If your access later shrinks, Wisp's does too; if it grows, you refresh the grant to widen it.
- **90-day expiry.** A grant lasts 90 days. Refreshing re-snapshots your current reach and renews the 90 days.
- **A conversation keeps the terms it started with.** Refreshing does not change a conversation that is already open; the header says so and offers **Start a new conversation**, which runs on the refreshed grant.
- **Revoke.** You, or a partner admin, can revoke a grant at any time.

A grant can be **paused** rather than ended. You can pause and resume it yourself, and Wisp stays quiet while you are paused. Breeze also pauses a grant by itself, and shows the reason:

| Reason | What it means |
|---|---|
| Access changed | You no longer have access to any of the organizations the grant covers, so Wisp stopped. (If your access only narrows, Wisp keeps going with the smaller reach.) Review and refresh the grant. |
| Account suspended | Your account is suspended. |
| Sign-in check expired | Your MFA confirmation lapsed. Confirm it and resume. |
| Plan no longer includes Wisp | The partner lost the entitlement. Grants pause rather than disappear. |
| Partner disabled | A partner administrator turned Wisp off for the company; see [Turning Wisp off for your company](#turning-wisp-off-for-your-company). |

sections.heading: What Wisp does alone vs asks first
sections.text:
| Wisp acts alone | Wisp asks first | Wisp never |
|---|---|---|
| Reads anything you may see. Drafts ticket replies. Nudges you. Opens a ticket from an alert that an existing rule already turns into a ticket. Re-runs a check. Schedules a sweep. Stages work in a sandbox. | Sends anything to a client contact. Closes or reassigns tickets. Applies or edits a configuration policy. Runs a script on a device. Changes alert thresholds. Anything billing. Anything that grants access. | Acts outside the authority of the person it works for. Lets a sub-agent exceed that authority. |

"Asks first" means an approval card in the Approvals inbox, on web and mobile. Approving is a decision by a person; Wisp cannot approve for itself.

sections.heading: Turning Wisp off for your company
sections.text:
A partner administrator can switch Wisp off for the whole company. Go to **Settings → AI Agents** and use the **Wisp enabled** switch on the Wisp card. It is set at partner level only (there is no per-organization override), is on by default, and changes autosave with a confirmation toast. Users who are not partner administrators see it read-only.

When the switch is off:

- New grants, resume and refresh are refused.
- Every active grant is paused (reason `partner_disabled`, shown as "Partner disabled" on the admin overview) at its next scheduled check. Saving the switch also triggers an immediate check. Nothing is deleted.
- On the Wisp home, someone with no grant is told that an administrator turned Wisp off, instead of being offered **Put Wisp to work**.

When you turn it back on, only grants that this switch paused resume. A grant you paused yourself, or one paused because the plan lost Wisp, stays paused.

This is a governance control. Your plan is the commercial gate and the deployment switch is the operator's kill switch; none of the three overrides another.

sections.heading: Nudges, quiet hours and the morning brief
sections.text:
Wisp tells you about a concern once, with one subject, one suggested next step and a link to the thread. If you ignore it, Wisp backs off rather than repeating itself, and after two unanswered nudges a concern moves to your in-app digest.

You control delivery in your nudge preferences:

- **Channels.** In-app and push, each on or off.
- **Quiet hours.** Wisp respects your quiet hours. You can let urgent items through (`urgent only`) or never.
- **Proactivity dial.** `quiet`, `normal` (the default) or `chatty`.
- **Digest cadence.** How often batched items arrive (default every four hours).
- **Morning brief.** A short summary at a time you choose (default 08:00) in your timezone.

Every nudge accepts feedback, and Wisp uses it to tune what it raises. The thread page also shows an activity feed of what Wisp did and a spend meter.

Every morning brief, concern nudge and digest is also kept on the Wisp thread as a post. Wisp records the post whatever your channel settings are, so it is kept even when both the in-app and push channels are off. Clearing notifications does not remove these posts. A retried delivery never creates a duplicate, because each delivery produces one post. The budget notice and other system notices are not posts; they stay notifications only. A paused thread still shows its history, and a revoked or expired delegation does not.

sections.heading: Memory
sections.text:
Wisp keeps short notes: your preferences, standing instructions, facts, and decisions ("leave that firewall alone until the renewal"). Notes belong to you, to an organization or to the partner.

Wisp writes notes; **people confirm, correct or retract them**. Open **Settings → Wisp memory** (`/settings/wisp-memory`) to review what Wisp has recorded and retract anything wrong. Each note is attributed to Wisp acting for you.

sections.heading: Budgets
sections.text:
Everything Wisp does under a grant (assessments, specialist runs, tasks) is metered against that grant's daily budget, in cents of AI spend.

| Plan | Default daily budget per grant |
|---|---|
| Pro | 200 ¢ |
| Enterprise | 500 ¢ |
| Unlimited | 1000 ¢ |

A partner admin can raise a grant's budget up to **5x the plan default**, never beyond the plan ceiling. The budget window is the UTC day. When a budget is exhausted, Wisp makes **no further model calls** under that grant until the window resets: assessments and specialist requests are skipped, while events are still recorded as concern updates by plain code and appear in your digest. The grant itself stays on (it is not paused), and the thread's spend meter shows the budget as used up.

sections.heading: Specialists
sections.text:
When a concern needs focused work, Wisp can ask a **specialist** to do it. A request names a kind and a reason. Specialists are limited to one level deep: a specialist cannot request another specialist.

| Kind | What it does | Starts |
|---|---|---|
| `sweep` | Collects evidence across the estate | On its own |
| `analysis` | Runs sandboxed analysis over staged data (see [AI Analysis Runs](/features/ai-analysis-runs/)) | On its own |
| `operator_recipe` | Runs an AI task recipe | After you approve |
| `patch_plan` | Drafts a patch plan | After you approve |
| `remediation_research` | Researches a fix for a problem | After you approve |
| `bulk_ticket_reply` | Sends one message to a list of tickets (for example, everyone hit by the same outage). The approval card shows the exact tickets and the exact message; no ticket is added after approval, and the batch stops at the first failure and reports | After you approve |

The kinds marked "after you approve" appear as an approval card; nothing starts until a person says yes. When you approve one, it runs with **your** authority at that moment, and every normal gate still applies. Anything the specialist then wants to change creates its own approval, as usual. Specialist requests count against the same daily budget.

`launch_specialist` itself runs only `sweep` and `analysis` on the call. `operator_recipe`, `patch_plan`, `remediation_research` and `bulk_ticket_reply` escalate to a supervised Tier-3 approval in chat.

Two refusals are user-visible. `bulk_reply_incomplete` means a bulk reply stopped part-way; what was sent and what was not is stored on the intent. `uncertain` means Wisp could not tell whether the work had taken effect, so it did not retry.

Work started this way is labeled **Wisp for** followed by the person's name on the agent run and the Operator task detail pages, so the audit trail shows who it was done for. Platform admins also have an `/admin/wisp` page with fleet-level health and counts.

title: Workload Inventory
description: See the containers, VMs and LXC guests running on a host, and turn collection on with a configuration policy.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text:
The Breeze agent detects container and virtual-machine runtimes on a device. When collection is enabled, it also lists the **workloads** running on that host: containers, VMs and LXC guests. Use it to answer "what is running on this server?" without logging in to it.

| Runtime | Detected | Workloads listed |
|---|---|---|
| Docker | Linux, Windows | Linux, Windows |
| Podman | Linux | Linux |
| Hyper-V | Windows | Arrives with a later agent release |
| Proxmox VE | Linux | Arrives with a later agent release |
| containerd | Linux | Never. containerd is detected only; its workloads are not listed. |

macOS devices report no runtimes, and Docker Desktop's per-user socket is not supported.

For each workload Breeze shows the name, state, image (repository, tag and digest) or guest OS, compose project and service, restart policy, CPU and memory where the runtime reports them, and start time.

**Detection runs; listing is opt-in:**
  Detection (is Docker installed, which version) always runs and reveals nothing about what is running. Workloads are **not** listed until a configuration policy enables the **Workload inventory** feature, because names and images can identify customer systems.

sections.heading: What the agent reads
sections.text:
Collection is read-only. The agent only issues GET requests to the engine API and never starts, stops or changes a container or VM. Environment variables, command lines, mounts and labels are never collected.

The agent only connects to a runtime that is already running. It does not start a stopped Docker daemon or a socket-activated Podman service; that host reports the runtime as unavailable. Podman hosts therefore need `podman system service` (or an enabled socket service that keeps it running) for workloads to appear.

sections.heading: Turn it on
sections.text:
1. Open **Fleet Management → Config Policies** and edit (or create) a policy. See [Configuration Policies](/features/configuration-policies/).
2. Add the **Workload inventory** feature.
3. Switch **Enabled** on and choose the runtimes to collect: **Docker**, **Podman**, **Hyper-V**, **Proxmox**.
4. Set the **collection interval** in minutes (15 to 1440, default 60).
5. Save and assign the policy as usual.

Partner-wide and organization policies both work, and the setting follows normal policy inheritance: the closest assignment wins. Devices pick up the change on their next policy refresh and collect on the interval you set.

sections.heading: The Workloads tab
sections.text:
Open a device and select the **Workloads** tab (URL hash `#workloads`). It shows, for each detected runtime, the version and a plain-language collection status, then counts and a table of workloads.

| Status you may see | What it means |
|---|---|
| Collection is off | Enable **Workload inventory** in a configuration policy that applies to the device. |
| Permission denied | The agent could not read the runtime's socket or service. |
| Unavailable | The runtime is installed but not running or not reachable. |
| Agent too old | The device's agent predates workload inventory. Update the agent. |

A **partial snapshot**, where some data could not be read, is shown with a note rather than as an error. Devices without any detected runtime show no Workloads section.

sections.heading: Fleet filters
sections.text:
Two fields are available in the device filter bar, saved filters and dynamic groups:

- **Hosts workloads**: yes or no.
- **Workload runtimes**: contains a runtime, for example Docker.

**Not usable for script targeting:**
  These values are reported by the agent, so they are not trusted for targeting. Filters and groups built on them are refused when selecting devices to run scripts or other commands on.

sections.heading: Ask the assistant
sections.text: The AI assistant can answer questions such as "what containers are running on this host?" using the read-only `query_device_workloads` tool. It returns up to 200 workloads per answer.

sections.heading: Image currency
sections.text:
Every 30 minutes Breeze compares each container's local image digest with the registry's current digest for the same repository and tag. The check runs on the server and needs no agent change. Only public images are checked.

| Image status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `current` | The local digest matches the registry. |
| `behind` | The registry has a newer digest for this tag. |
| `pending` | Not checked yet. |
| `pinned` | The image is referenced by digest, so there is nothing to compare. |
| `local` | Built locally; no registry digest exists. |
| `private` | The registry requires credentials. Private registries are not supported yet. |
| `unsupported_registry` | The registry is not on the supported list: Docker Hub, GHCR, Quay, MCR, registry.k8s.io, GCR and public ECR. |
| `not_found` | The tag no longer exists upstream. |
| `error` | A transient failure. Breeze retries. |

In the **Workloads** tab each container row shows an image status badge, and the tab has a status filter. `pending`, `private`, `unsupported_registry` and `error` display as **Not checked**, never as up to date.

**Local builds on Docker 29.0–29.2 with the containerd image store:**
  On Docker's containerd image store (the default for new Docker 29 installs), Docker lists a registry-style digest for every named image, local builds included. From Docker 29.3 (Engine API 1.54) the agent asks Docker where each image came from, so a local build shows **Local build** and its name is never sent to a registry. Docker 29.0 to 29.2 cannot answer that question: on those versions a locally built image is still looked up on the registry its name points to (Docker Hub for an unqualified name), usually shows **Not checked** ("Private registry — credentials required") instead of **Local build**, and counts in the "images not checked" figure. Upgrade Docker to 29.3 or later to get the correct status. Hosts on Docker's classic image store are not expected to be affected ([#8993](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/issues/8993)).

sections.heading: Patch compliance
sections.text:
Container images count toward patch compliance. Each distinct image (repository and tag) on a device counts once, however many containers or replicas run it.

- A `behind` image counts as one pending update.
- A `current` image counts as one installed update.
- Images that could not be checked (`pending`, `private`, `unsupported_registry`, `error`) are left out of the percentage and reported as "N images not checked" next to it, so coverage stays visible.
- `pinned`, `local` and `not_found` images are not counted either way.
- If replicas of one image disagree, the worst status wins: any `behind` makes it behind, otherwise any not-checked replica makes it not checked.

This applies to the device **Patches** tab percentage, the organization patch compliance percentage and compliant-device count, and the patch compliance CSV report. A device with a behind image and no missing OS patches is listed as needing updates and is not compliant. When an organization has container images, the CSV gains `stale_images`, `current_images` and `images_not_checked` rows.

Views filtered by severity, source or update ring exclude images, because images have no severity, source or approval. The security posture score, and therefore the existing **Patch compliance** monitor, is unaffected. Devices without workload inventory data show the same numbers as before.

sections.heading: Alert on out-of-date images
sections.text:
The **Container image currency** monitor (`container_image_currency`) is evaluated on the server from the stored image statuses. There is one alert subject per image repository and tag on a device.

| Setting | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Minimum days behind (`minDaysBehind`) | 0 to 365, default 7. The image alerts once it has been `behind` for at least this many days. |

- The clock starts when the image was first seen behind. A transient registry error does not restart it; a change of the local image does.
- The alert recovers when the image is `current`. Any other status is unknown: it neither alerts nor recovers.
- Pinned, locally built and `not_found` images are not monitored: there is nothing to compare.
- When the last container using an image is removed, its open alert resolves automatically. This happens in a complete inventory snapshot, when workload collection is turned off by policy, or when the runtime is uninstalled. Failed, incomplete or truncated snapshots never resolve alerts.

Every partner gets a partner-wide built-in monitor, **Container image out of date** (low severity, 7 days, 24-hour cooldown). Like the other built-in monitors it is not attached to any policy: attach it to a configuration policy to start evaluating. Only devices whose policy enables **Workload inventory** have data.

sections.heading: Not yet available
sections.text: Private-registry image checks and operator-triggered compose updates are deferred to a later release.

title: Architecture
description: How Breeze RMM components fit together: API server, web dashboard, Go agent, PostgreSQL, BullMQ job queue, TURN server, and multi-tenant hierarchy.

sections.heading: Multi-Tenant Hierarchy
sections.text:
Breeze uses a strict tenant hierarchy that isolates data at every level:

```
Partner (MSP)
  └── Organization (Customer)
        └── Site (Location)
              └── Device Group
                    └── Device
```

Every database query is scoped to the user's tenant context. A partner admin sees all their organizations; an org admin only sees their own.

sections.heading: API Server (Hono)
sections.text:
The API is a TypeScript application built with [Hono](https://hono.dev) running on Node.js >= 22.22.2. It handles:

- REST endpoints for all CRUD operations
- WebSocket connections from agents (telemetry, commands, terminal)
- WebSocket connections from browsers (real-time updates, terminal relay)
- JWT authentication with refresh tokens
- RBAC permission checks on every request

Key paths:
- `apps/api/src/routes/` — Route handlers
- `apps/api/src/middleware/` — Auth, rate limiting, tenant scoping
- `apps/api/src/services/` — Business logic
- `apps/api/src/db/schema/` — Drizzle ORM schema definitions

sections.heading: Web Dashboard (Astro + React)
sections.text:
The frontend is an [Astro](https://astro.build) SSR application with React Islands for interactive components:

- Device inventory and live status
- Remote terminal (xterm.js)
- Script execution and scheduling
- Alert management
- Discovery scanner results

sections.heading: Agent (Go)
sections.text:
A single Go binary (~8 MB) that runs as a system service:

- **Enrollment** — Registers with the API, receives a `brz_` bearer token
- **Heartbeat** — Sends system telemetry (CPU, memory, disk, network) every 60s
- **Commands** — Executes scripts, collects inventory, runs discovery scans
- **Terminal** — Spawns a PTY and streams I/O over WebSocket
- **File Transfer** — Bi-directional file transfer with the dashboard
- **mTLS** — Optional Cloudflare client certificate for mutual authentication

  The Go agent source is in `agent/` (not `apps/agent/`). Both directories exist but serve different purposes.

sections.heading: Database (PostgreSQL + Drizzle)
sections.text:
PostgreSQL 16 with Drizzle ORM for type-safe schema management:

- 30+ tables covering devices, users, organizations, alerts, scripts, audit logs
- Hand-written SQL migrations in `apps/api/migrations/`, applied with `pnpm db:migrate`
- Seed script with default roles, permissions, and alert templates

sections.heading: Job Queue (BullMQ + Redis)
sections.text:
Redis-backed job queue for async operations:

- Script execution scheduling
- Discovery scan dispatching
- Alert processing pipeline
- Agent command queuing

sections.heading: TURN Server (coturn)
sections.text:
A [coturn](https://github.com/coturn/coturn) TURN relay enables WebRTC remote desktop connections when direct peer-to-peer paths are blocked by NAT or firewalls:

- Runs with `network_mode: host` for efficient UDP handling and wide relay port range (49152–65535)
- Uses time-limited credentials generated from a shared secret (`TURN_SECRET`)
- The API distributes TURN credentials to viewers and agents via `GET /remote/ice-servers`

sections.heading: Reverse Proxy (Caddy)
sections.text:
Caddy handles TLS termination, compression, and routing:

- Auto-provisions certificates from Let's Encrypt
- Routes `/api/*` to the API server
- Routes everything else to the web dashboard
- Adds security headers (HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options)

sections.heading: Data Flow: Agent ↔ API
Security Layers
sections.text:
1. **Transport** — All traffic over HTTPS/WSS with auto-provisioned TLS
2. **Authentication** — JWT for users, SHA-256 hashed bearer tokens for agents
3. **Authorization** — RBAC with per-resource permissions
4. **Tenant Isolation** — Every query scoped to org context
5. **Rate Limiting** — Redis-backed sliding window (120 req/60s per agent)
6. **Audit Logging** — All mutating operations logged with actor, action, resource
7. **mTLS (optional)** — Cloudflare API Shield client certificates for agents

title: What is Breeze RMM?
description: Overview of Breeze RMM, an open-source remote monitoring and management platform for MSPs and IT teams, with its architecture and technology stack.

sections.text: Breeze is an open-source **Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM)** platform built for MSPs and internal IT teams. It's designed to scale to 10,000+ agents while staying fast, secure, and simple to operate.

sections.heading: Why Breeze?
sections.text:
**Lightweight Agent:**
    A single Go binary (~8 MB) that runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows. No runtime dependencies.

  **Real-time Visibility:**
    WebSocket-powered live telemetry, remote terminal, and file transfer — no polling delays.

  **Multi-Tenant by Design:**
    Partner → Organization → Site → Device Group → Device hierarchy, built into every query.

  **Security-First:**
    SHA-256 hashed agent tokens, optional Cloudflare mTLS, RBAC, audit logging, and rate limiting out of the box.

sections.heading: Architecture at a Glance
sections.text:
```
┌─────────────┐     HTTPS/WSS     ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Breeze Agent │ ◄──────────────► │           Breeze API (Hono)           │
│   (Go)       │                  │  ┌────────┐  ┌───────┐  ┌─────────┐  │
└─────────────┘                   │  │Postgres│  │ Redis │  │ BullMQ  │  │
                                  │  └────────┘  └───────┘  └─────────┘  │
┌─────────────┐     HTTPS         └──────────────────────────────────────┘
│  Dashboard   │ ◄──────────────►  Astro + React Islands (SSR)
│  (Browser)   │
└─────────────┘
```

| Layer | Technology |
|---|---|
| **Frontend** | Astro 5 + React Islands |
| **API** | Hono (TypeScript) on Node >= 22.22.2 |
| **Database** | PostgreSQL 16 + Drizzle ORM |
| **Queue** | BullMQ + Redis 7 |
| **Agent** | Go (cross-platform binary) |
| **Real-time** | WebSocket + HTTP polling |
| **Remote Access** | WebRTC (with optional TURN relay) |

sections.heading: Finding Settings
sections.text: The sidebar's **Settings** group lists only the screens most people use day to day: **Partner**, **Billing**, **Ticketing**, **Users** and **Integrations**. Everything else is one click further, under **More settings**, which opens the settings catalogue at `/settings`. The catalogue shows one card for every settings screen your role can open, grouped by area (Account & Access, Billing & Service Desk, Devices & Enrollment, Automation & Data, AI, Integrations), with a search box. Since v0.117.0 screens such as Roles, SSO, Access Reviews, Enrollment Keys, Custom Fields, Variables and Saved Filters live there rather than in the sidebar; their addresses are unchanged, so where these docs say **Settings → Roles**, open **More settings** and pick the card.

title: Prerequisites
description: Server hardware requirements and software needed to run Breeze RMM, including CPU, RAM, disk, and OS minimums plus Docker and Docker Compose setup.

sections.heading: Server Requirements
sections.text:
**Server sizing only:**
This table covers the Breeze **server** (API, web, PostgreSQL, Redis, and the reverse proxy). It says nothing about agent-side footprint on the machines you're monitoring, which is separate and much smaller.

| Resource | Floor | Baseline (small MSP) |
|---|---|---|
| **CPU** | 2 x86-64 vCPU | 4 vCPU |
| **RAM** | 4 GiB | 8 GiB |
| **Disk** | 20 GiB free in the install directory | 60 GiB SSD-backed, plus snapshot headroom |
| **OS** | Ubuntu 22.04+ / Debian 12+ | Ubuntu 24.04 LTS |
| **Network** | Public IP, ports 80/443 open, NTP | Static IP with DNS A record, TLS reverse proxy, NTP |

The **CPU / RAM / Disk Floor** values are what [`guided-setup.sh`](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/blob/main/scripts/guided-setup.sh) checks before install: below them it warns and, without an explicit "continue anyway" (defaulted to no, including in unattended `--yes` runs), the install stops. They're a warning threshold, not a tested capacity limit. The OS and Network rows are general recommendations — the script doesn't check them.

The **CPU / RAM / Disk Baseline** values are a real-world small-MSP data point, contributed via [#3930](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/issues/3930): a two-person MSP settled on 4 vCPU / 8 GiB RAM / 60 GiB SSD, plus extra headroom for snapshots. The jump from the 20 GiB disk floor reflects PostgreSQL, Redis's append-only file, container images, logs, upgrade image churn, and (on ZFS) snapshots all competing for the same volume — 20 GiB leaves little margin for any of that.

Breeze does not publish arm64 server images — GHCR images are amd64 only. On Apple Silicon, use `docker-compose.override.yml.local-build` to build native arm64 images instead (see [Docker Deployment](/deploy/environment/#docker-deployment)).

**No per-agent sizing formula:**
There isn't yet enough controlled data to turn "N agents" into a hardware number. Validate your sizing against actual agent count, event volume, retention window, remote-control usage, and backup policy, and scale up if you see resource pressure.

Redis in particular ships with a `256mb` default `maxmemory` and a `noeviction` policy (see [`REDIS_MAXMEMORY`](/deploy/environment/#docker-deployment)) — job data queues rather than getting silently dropped, but a fleet outgrowing the default will need it raised, or writes start failing. If you have real-world sizing data for your fleet size, [open an issue](https://github.com/LanternOps/breeze/issues/new) — we'd like to build this table out with more data points.

sections.heading: Docker & Docker Compose
sections.text:
Breeze runs entirely in Docker containers. Install Docker Engine with the Compose plugin:

  **Ubuntu/Debian:**
```bash
    curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh
    sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
    # Log out and back in, then verify:
    docker compose version
```

  **macOS:**
```bash
    # Install Docker Desktop from https://docker.com/products/docker-desktop
    # Or via Homebrew:
    brew install --cask docker
```

sections.heading: Node.js & pnpm (Development Only)
sections.text:
Node.js and pnpm are **not required for standard Docker deployments** — the API container handles database migrations automatically on startup via `AUTO_MIGRATE=true` (the default).

You only need these tools if you are doing local development or managing migrations manually:

```bash
# Install Node.js >= 22.22.2 (pinned to 22.23.2 in .nvmrc)
curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_22.x | sudo -E bash -
sudo apt-get install -y nodejs

# Install pnpm
npm install -g pnpm@10
```

sections.heading: Git
sections.text:
```bash
sudo apt-get install -y git
```

sections.heading: DNS Configuration
sections.text:
Point your domain to your server's public IP:

```
A   breeze.yourdomain.com    → 203.0.113.10
```

Caddy will automatically provision a TLS certificate from Let's Encrypt once DNS resolves.

sections.heading: Optional: Go Toolchain
sections.text:
Only needed if building the agent from source (pre-built binaries are available):

```bash
# Go 1.26.10+
wget https://go.dev/dl/go1.26.10.linux-amd64.tar.gz
sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.26.10.linux-amd64.tar.gz
export PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/go/bin
```

sections.heading: Firewall Rules
sections.text:
Ensure these ports are accessible:

| Port | Protocol | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **80** | TCP | HTTP → HTTPS redirect (Caddy) |
| **443** | TCP | HTTPS (web UI, API, agent WebSocket) |
| **3478** | TCP/UDP | TURN server (coturn — required only if using WebRTC remote desktop) |
| **49152–65535** | UDP | TURN media relay port range (coturn — required only if using TURN) |

All other services (PostgreSQL, Redis, Prometheus, Grafana) bind to `127.0.0.1` and are **not** exposed publicly.

title: Quickstart
description: Get Breeze RMM running in minutes with guided or manual setup, then reach the dashboard and enroll your first agent with an enrollment token.
headings: Reaching the dashboard from another machine

sections.text: Get a working Breeze instance running with a single `docker compose up`.

sections.heading: Guided setup (recommended)
sections.text:
The guided installer downloads the templates, generates **every** required
secret in the right format, checks that the version you pick has published
container images, and starts the stack:

```bash
mkdir breeze && cd breeze
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lanternops/breeze/main/scripts/guided-setup.sh
bash guided-setup.sh
```

The installer accepts Breeze 0.112.0 or later, because release signatures only
cover the container images from 0.112.0 on. It refuses an older release unless
you pass `--allow-unverified-release`, which installs it from unverified image
tags.

On Linux the installer also offers to register a boot service (`breeze-rmm`) so
the stack comes back up on its own after a reboot. Accept it on a server you
want running unattended; you can install or update it later with
`bash guided-setup.sh --install-systemd`.

The installer pins the Breeze images by digest. To upgrade, download the
current `guided-setup.sh` again and run `bash guided-setup.sh --upgrade`, not
`docker compose pull`. Pulling fetches the release you already run, and older
copies of the script do not have `--upgrade`. See the
[Upgrade Guide](/deploy/upgrades/).

Prefer to configure `.env` yourself? The manual path is below.

  Installing on a **headless server**? Read
  [Reaching the dashboard from another machine](#reaching-the-dashboard-from-another-machine)
  before you start — `BREEZE_DOMAIN=localhost` only serves requests made from the
  Docker host itself.

sections.heading: Manual setup
sections.text:
1. **Download the compose file and environment template**

```bash
   mkdir breeze && cd breeze
   curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lanternops/breeze/main/docker-compose.yml
   curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lanternops/breeze/main/.env.example
   # Caddy config — the compose file bind-mounts this, so it must exist on disk first
   curl -fsSL --create-dirs -o docker/Caddyfile.prod https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lanternops/breeze/main/docker/Caddyfile.prod
   cp .env.example .env
```

     Don't skip the `docker/Caddyfile.prod` download. The compose file bind-mounts
     it into the `caddy` container; if the file isn't on disk when you run
     `docker compose up`, Docker silently creates `docker/Caddyfile.prod` as an empty
     **directory** and Caddy fails to start.

2. **Set your domain**

```bash
   # Domain (use "localhost" for local testing — see the headless note below)
   BREEZE_DOMAIN=localhost
   ACME_EMAIL=you@example.com
```

3. **Generate the secrets**

   `.env.example` ships placeholder values for every secret. Replace them
   **in place** — edit the existing line for each key rather than appending a
   second copy at the end of the file.

   This one-liner rewrites each placeholder with a fresh value:

```bash
   for key in JWT_SECRET SESSION_SECRET AGENT_ENROLLMENT_SECRET \
     APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY MFA_ENCRYPTION_KEY ENROLLMENT_KEY_PEPPER \
     MFA_RECOVERY_CODE_PEPPER METRICS_SCRAPE_TOKEN; do
     sed -i "s|^${key}=.*|${key}=$(openssl rand -hex 32)|" .env
   done

   # Must be canonical base64 decoding to >= 32 bytes, and must not reuse JWT_SECRET
   sed -i "s|^PARTNER_API_CURSOR_SIGNING_KEY=.*|PARTNER_API_CURSOR_SIGNING_KEY=$(openssl rand -base64 32)|" .env

   # Database and Redis. Redis auth is REQUIRED — the API refuses to start without it.
   POSTGRES_PASSWORD="$(openssl rand -base64 24 | tr -d '/+=')"
   REDIS_PASSWORD="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
   sed -i "s|^POSTGRES_PASSWORD=.*|POSTGRES_PASSWORD=${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}|" .env
   sed -i "s|^REDIS_PASSWORD=.*|REDIS_PASSWORD=${REDIS_PASSWORD}|" .env
   sed -i "s|^REDIS_URL=.*|REDIS_URL=redis://:${REDIS_PASSWORD}@redis:6379|" .env
```

   On macOS, use `sed -i ''` instead of `sed -i`.

     `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY` and `MFA_ENCRYPTION_KEY` must differ from each other,
     and `PARTNER_API_CURSOR_SIGNING_KEY` must not reuse `JWT_SECRET`. The loop
     above satisfies both. The authoritative list of every variable, its format,
     and whether it is required lives in
     [Environment Variables](/deploy/environment/).

     Never commit `.env` to version control. It contains secrets.

4. **Check the version pin**

   `.env.example` pins `BREEZE_VERSION` to a specific release. Confirm it is the
   one you want before starting:

```bash
   grep '^BREEZE_VERSION=' .env
```

   To upgrade later, follow the [Upgrade Guide](/deploy/upgrades/). With the
   digest-pinned image refs described below, changing `BREEZE_VERSION` alone
   does not change the images. Update the four refs with it, or run
   `guided-setup.sh --upgrade`.

     Pick a version that has **published container images**, which is not always
     the newest git tag — a release can be tagged before its images finish
     building. If you pin one that was never published, `docker compose up` fails
     with `not found`. The guided installer checks this for you.

   **Then fill in the image digests.** Since v0.112.0, `.env.example` ships the
   four `BREEZE_*_IMAGE_REF` lines as `@sha256:replace-with-signed-release-digest`
   placeholders, and `docker compose up` will not start until they name real
   images. The guided installer resolves them from the release's signed image
   inventory automatically; on the manual path, run the verifier script from the
   release and copy the four refs it emits into `.env` — see
   [Signed, digest-pinned image references](/deploy/production/#signed-digest-pinned-image-references-v01120-and-later).

5. **Start Breeze**

```bash
   docker compose up -d
```

   On first boot the API container automatically:
   - Runs database migrations
   - Seeds the default admin user
   - Starts the background job workers

6. **Verify**

```bash
   # Wait for API to be healthy (~30s on first boot)
   docker compose logs -f api --since 1m
```

   Once you see `Breeze API running`, open the dashboard:

   - **Dashboard**: `https://localhost` (accept the self-signed cert)
   - **Health check**: `curl -k https://localhost/health`

sections.heading: Reaching the dashboard from another machine
sections.text:
`BREEZE_DOMAIN` becomes Caddy's site address, and Caddy only answers requests
whose `Host` header matches it. With `BREEZE_DOMAIN=localhost` the ports are
published on all interfaces, but a browser on your laptop sends
`Host: 192.168.1.50`, which matches nothing — so a minimal/headless server
install has no reachable UI even though `curl -k https://localhost/health`
returns `OK` on the box itself.

Pick whichever fits:

- **SSH tunnel** — leave `BREEZE_DOMAIN=localhost` and forward the port:

```bash
  ssh -L 8443:127.0.0.1:443 user@your-server
  # then browse to https://localhost:8443
```

  A browser origin includes the **port**, so `https://localhost:8443` is a
  different origin from the `https://localhost` that the generated `.env`
  allows, and the API rejects sign-in requests coming from it. Pick one of:

```bash
  # Forward the SAME port — 443 is privileged, so run this as root
  sudo ssh -L 443:127.0.0.1:443 user@your-server
  # then browse to https://localhost
```

```bash
  # …or keep the high port and add the tunnel origin to .env on the server
  # (comma-separated, no spaces, no trailing paths)
  CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=https://localhost,https://localhost:8443
  docker compose up -d api
```

  The API now accepts same-origin requests on its own, so this entry is
  optional — a browser reaching Breeze through the tunnel is already treated as
  same-origin. It stays correct either way.

- **LAN address** — serve the machine's IP or hostname directly:

```bash
  BREEZE_DOMAIN=192.168.1.50
  PUBLIC_APP_URL=https://192.168.1.50
  DASHBOARD_URL=https://192.168.1.50
```

  Caddy cannot get a public certificate for a private address, so it serves its
  internal self-signed cert — accept the browser warning.

- **Internal domain** — a name that resolves only on your LAN or VPN, or a host
  whose ports 80 and 443 are not reachable from the internet:

```bash
  BREEZE_DOMAIN=breeze.mydomain.com
  PUBLIC_APP_URL=https://breeze.mydomain.com
  DASHBOARD_URL=https://breeze.mydomain.com
  CADDY_LOCAL_CERTS=local_certs
```

  Let's Encrypt cannot validate a name it cannot reach, so
  `CADDY_LOCAL_CERTS=local_certs` switches Caddy to its own internal CA instead.
  The guided installer asks this for you — *"Can Let's Encrypt reach this
  domain?"* — whenever you give it a domain that is not `localhost` or an IP.

  Browsers warn on every visit until that CA root is trusted on each client
  machine. Export it with:

```bash
  docker compose exec caddy cat /data/caddy/pki/authorities/local/root.crt
```

    `PUBLIC_APP_URL` still uses `https://` — the site is HTTPS either way, only
    the issuer changes. Leave `CADDY_LOCAL_CERTS` empty for any deployment
    Let's Encrypt *can* reach.

- **Real domain** — the production path. See
  [Production Deploy](/deploy/production/).

Whichever you choose, `PUBLIC_APP_URL` must be the URL users actually visit:
it is what agent installers and portal links are built from.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
**You are sent back to the login page with "session expired" right after signing in**
- Cause: the address in your browser's address bar is not an origin this server
  accepts. `CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` doesn't list it, or `PUBLIC_APP_URL` is set to
  a different address than the one you are visiting. Reaching a
  `BREEZE_DOMAIN=localhost` install through an SSH tunnel on a different port is
  the usual way to land here — the password was fine, the sign-in worked, and
  the token refresh that follows it is what got rejected.
- Confirm: open your browser devtools, go to the **Network** tab, and sign in
  again. `POST /api/v1/auth/refresh` returns **403** with the body
  `{"error":"Invalid request origin"}`. Newer Breeze builds also say so on the
  login page itself, naming the exact origin that was refused.
- Fix: browse to the address in `PUBLIC_APP_URL`, or add the address you are
  actually using to `CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` in `.env` (comma-separated, no spaces,
  no trailing paths) and restart the API with `docker compose up -d api`.

sections.heading: The browser shows ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR
sections.text:
Chrome reports `ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR` and Firefox `SSL_ERROR_INTERNAL_ERROR_ALERT`,
with no certificate warning you can click through. That is Caddy aborting the TLS
handshake with alert 80 (`internal_error`) because it holds no certificate for the
name you asked for. Confirm it from the Caddy log:

```bash
docker logs breeze-caddy 2>&1 | grep tls.obtain
```

`could not get certificate from issuer` there means the Let's Encrypt order for
`BREEZE_DOMAIN` failed. Let's Encrypt needs **public DNS pointing at this host and
ports 80 and 443 open from the internet** — an internal-only name, or a host behind
a firewall, can never pass validation.

Two ways out:

- Make the domain publicly resolvable and open 80/443 inbound, then restart Caddy
  so it retries the order.
- Or keep it internal and switch to Caddy's own CA — set
  `CADDY_LOCAL_CERTS=local_certs` in `.env` (see **Internal domain** above) and
  restart Caddy:

```bash
  docker compose up -d caddy
```

  An empty `CADDY_LOCAL_CERTS` is the default and is correct for every
  internet-reachable deployment. Only set it when the ACME order genuinely cannot
  succeed — an internal CA means every browser and agent must trust that root.

sections.heading: What's Running
sections.text:
| Container | Port | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `breeze-caddy` | 80, 443 | Reverse proxy + auto-TLS |
| `breeze-api` | 3001 (internal) | Hono API server |
| `breeze-web` | 4321 (internal) | Astro SSR dashboard |
| `breeze-portal` | 4322 (internal) | Customer portal, served under `/portal` |
| `breeze-postgres` | 5432 (internal) | PostgreSQL 16 database |
| `breeze-redis` | 6379 (internal) | Redis 7 (BullMQ + caching) |
| `breeze-worker` | — (internal) | Background job workers, split out from the API process (only with `--profile worker-split`) |
| `breeze-coturn` | 3478 (host) | TURN relay for WebRTC remote desktop (only with `--profile turn`) |

sections.heading: Next: Enroll Your First Agent
sections.text:
Download and install the Breeze agent on a device. `BREEZE_SERVER` must be the
URL of your Breeze server **as the target device can reach it** — not
`localhost`, which on the target device means the target device itself:

Easiest: open **Devices → Add Device**, switch to the **CLI Commands** tab, pick
a site, click **Generate token**, and copy the command shown for **Linux/macOS**
(or **Windows**). The Linux/macOS command looks like this — the dialog fills in
your real server URL and token:

```bash
# On the target device (Linux/macOS):
f="$(mktemp)" && { curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 -o "$f" "https://breeze.example.com/api/v1/agents/install.sh" && head -n1 "$f" | grep -q '^#!' || { echo "[ERROR] Could not fetch the Breeze installer from https://breeze.example.com — verify this machine has network access to your Breeze server." >&2; false; }; } && sudo bash "$f" --server "https://breeze.example.com" --token "<your-enrollment-token>"
```

The enrollment token is **required** — it identifies the organization and site.
If your server is configured with an org enrollment secret, the dialog appends it
as an **optional** extra gate alongside the token (never instead of it):
`--enrollment-secret "<your-enrollment-secret>"`. The installer also accepts the
equivalent `BREEZE_SERVER`, `BREEZE_ENROLL_TOKEN` and `BREEZE_ENROLLMENT_SECRET`
environment variables.

  Agents cannot enrol against a `localhost`-only install. Give the server a LAN
  address or a real domain first (see above) — the agent needs to reach it from
  wherever it runs.

See [Agent Installation](/agents/installation/) for detailed instructions per platform.

For production deployment with a real domain and monitoring, see [Production Deploy](/deploy/production/).

title: Infrastructure Alerts
description: Prometheus and Alertmanager rules that monitor the Breeze platform itself, covering API health, PostgreSQL, Redis, disk usage, and agent heartbeats.

sections.text:
These alerts monitor the Breeze platform itself -- API health, database, Redis, and disk usage. For alerts about your managed devices, see [RMM Alerts](/features/alerts/).

If you deploy the optional observability stack (`docker-compose.monitoring.yml`), Breeze supports infrastructure-level alerting through Prometheus and Alertmanager.

  In-app alerts monitor your managed devices. Infrastructure alerts (this page) monitor the Breeze servers, database, and queue. Most organizations use both.

sections.heading: Pre-Configured Infrastructure Alert Rules
sections.text: The file `monitoring/rules/breeze-rules.yml` ships with these rules:

sections.heading: API Alerts
sections.text:
| Alert | Severity | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| `HighErrorRate` | critical | Error rate > 5% for 5 minutes |
| `SlowResponseTime` | warning | P95 latency > 2s for 10 minutes |
| `APIServiceDown` | critical | API target down for 2 minutes |
| `EndpointLatencyHigh` | warning | Any endpoint P95 > 5s for 5 minutes |
| `High4xxRate` | warning | 4xx rate > 20% for 10 minutes |
| `DbPoolPermitsHeldByAbandonedTransactions` | warning | Abandoned pool permits (transactions abandoned at their database session-setup deadline or after the pool-acquire budget expired; see `[db-pool-acquire]` and `[db-wedged-backend]` logs) continuously present for 3 minutes (API or worker) |

sections.heading: Infrastructure Alerts
sections.text:
| Alert | Severity | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| `RedisDown` | critical | Redis exporter down for 2 minutes |
| `RedisMemoryHigh` | warning | Redis memory > 80% of max |
| `PostgresDown` | critical | Postgres exporter down for 2 minutes |
| `PostgresConnectionPoolSaturated` | warning | Connections > 80% of max |
| `DiskSpaceLow` | warning | Disk usage > 85% |

sections.heading: Business Alerts
sections.text:
| Alert | Severity | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| `NoAgentHeartbeats` | critical | Zero heartbeats received for 5 minutes |
| `AlertProcessingBacklog` | warning | Alert queue depth > 100 for 10 minutes |
| `BackupDispatchFailuresDetected` | warning | Backup, restore, or verification start failures in the last 15 minutes |
| `RestoreTimeoutsDetected` | critical | Restore command timeouts in the last 15 minutes |
| `ScheduledVerificationSkipsDetected` | warning | Scheduled backup verification runs skipped in the last hour |
| `CapacityMetricsMissing` | critical | One of the core capacity series (`http_requests_total`, `http_request_duration_seconds_count`, `agent_heartbeat_total`, `breeze_active_devices`) has no producer. This is a deadman guard: an absent series makes every alert built on it evaluate against an empty vector, which never fires — `up` alone can't catch this, since the scrape itself still succeeds. |
| `FleetGaugesStale` | warning | `breeze_active_devices` and the organization-count gauge haven't refreshed in over 5 minutes, or have never succeeded. These gauges hold their last value on a failed refresh, so a dead refresher otherwise looks like a perfectly stable fleet. |

sections.heading: Anomaly Detection Alerts
sections.text:
| Alert | Severity | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| `FailedLoginSpike` | warning | More than 50 failed logins in 5 minutes for one tenant — possible credential stuffing or brute force |
| `EnrollmentSpike` | warning | More than 100 agent enrollments in 10 minutes for one tenant — verify it matches an expected rollout before assuming a leaked enrollment key |
| `CommandDispatchSpike` | warning | More than 200 commands dispatched in 5 minutes for one tenant — possible compromised account fanning out commands |
| `AuthenticatorL4BasisDenied` | warning | A sustained non-zero rate of critical-tier (L4) approval denials on a given platform-bound basis for 15 minutes — technicians on that basis are stuck unable to approve privileged-access or destructive-action requests from mobile until they update the app and re-enroll. See [Approval Security](/features/approval-security/#enrolling-an-approver-device) for the "Not attested" badge this tracks. |

  These thresholds are deliberately coarse starting points — tune them once you have real production baselines. The `tenant` label collapses to a single series unless `METRICS_INCLUDE_ORG_ID` is enabled; the alerts still fire on the aggregate either way.

sections.heading: Alertmanager Routing
sections.text:
Alertmanager routes infrastructure alerts by severity. Edit `monitoring/alertmanager.yml` to configure receivers:

```yaml
route:
  receiver: default
  group_by: ['alertname', 'severity', 'job']
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h

  routes:
    - match:
        severity: critical
      receiver: critical-alerts
      group_wait: 10s
      repeat_interval: 1h

    - match:
        severity: warning
      receiver: warning-alerts

    - match_re:
        alertname: '^(Redis|Postgres|DiskSpace).*'
      receiver: infrastructure-alerts
```

When a critical alert fires, related warning alerts for the same alert name are automatically suppressed via inhibition rules.

sections.heading: Configuring Infrastructure Notification Channels
sections.text:
Uncomment and edit the receiver blocks in `monitoring/alertmanager.yml` to enable Slack, PagerDuty, or email for infrastructure alerts:

  **Slack:**
```yaml
receivers:
  - name: critical-alerts
    slack_configs:
      - api_url: 'https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR/WEBHOOK/URL'
        channel: '#alerts-critical'
        send_resolved: true
        title: '{{ .Status | toUpper }}: {{ .GroupLabels.alertname }}'
```

  **PagerDuty:**
```yaml
receivers:
  - name: critical-alerts
    pagerduty_configs:
      - service_key: 'YOUR_PAGERDUTY_SERVICE_KEY'
        severity: 'critical'
```

  **Email:**
```yaml
receivers:
  - name: warning-alerts
    email_configs:
      - to: 'ops@yourdomain.com'
        from: 'alerts@yourdomain.com'
        smarthost: 'smtp.yourdomain.com:587'
        auth_username: 'alerts@yourdomain.com'
        auth_password: 'password'
```

After editing, restart Alertmanager:

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.monitoring.yml restart alertmanager
```

sections.heading: Custom Infrastructure Alert Rules
sections.text:
Add custom Prometheus rules in `monitoring/rules/`:

```yaml
# monitoring/rules/custom-rules.yml
groups:
  - name: custom-alerts
    rules:
      - alert: HighAgentChurn
        expr: rate(breeze_device_enrollments_total[1h]) > 10
        for: 30m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "High agent enrollment rate"
          description: "More than 10 new enrollments per hour for 30 minutes"
```

Prometheus automatically picks up new rule files. Reload the config without restarting:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:9090/-/reload
```

title: Health Endpoints
description: Built-in health, readiness, and metrics endpoints for Breeze RMM, with load balancer, Docker, and Kubernetes probe setup and troubleshooting.
headings: Using Health Checks with Load Balancers

sections.text: Breeze exposes health check endpoints that let you verify whether the API and its dependencies are running. Use these with load balancers, container orchestrators, and uptime monitors to detect and respond to outages automatically.

sections.heading: Available Endpoints
sections.text:
| Endpoint | Purpose | Auth Required |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | Basic liveness -- is the API process running? | No |
| `GET /health/ready` | Full readiness -- database, Redis, and every required queue consumer runnable (alias: `GET /ready`) | No |
| `GET /ready` | Alias of `/health/ready` (same evaluator, same body) | No |
| `GET /health/live` | Kubernetes liveness probe (alias for `/health`) | No |
| `GET /metrics/scrape` | Prometheus-formatted metrics | Bearer token |

sections.heading: GET /health
sections.text:
Returns `200 OK` if the API process is alive. This endpoint does not check backend dependencies -- it only confirms the HTTP server is accepting connections.

```json
{
  "status": "ok",
  "version": "0.50.0",
  "uptime": 86400
}
```

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `status` | Always `"ok"` when the process is running |
| `version` | Current Breeze API version |
| `uptime` | Seconds since the process started |

sections.heading: GET /health/ready (alias: GET /ready)
sections.text:
Returns `200 OK` only when the database and Redis are reachable **and every
queue consumer this process is required to run is attached and connected**.
Returns `503 Service Unavailable` otherwise. Both paths are served by the same
cached evaluator (default 5 s cache, 3 s per-probe timeout; the two are clamped
so a failure or recovery is visible within 10 s). Both are tunable — see
[`READINESS_CACHE_TTL_MS` and `READINESS_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS`](/deploy/environment/#readiness-probe-tuning) —
though the defaults suit every deployment we know of.

**Healthy response (200):**

```json
{
  "ready": true,
  "db": true,
  "redis": true,
  "workers": true,
  "checkedAt": "2026-09-01T12:00:00.000Z",
  "consumerSummary": {
    "required": 113,
    "runnable": 113,
    "unavailable": 0,
    "optionalRunning": 1,
    "optionalDisabled": 3
  }
}
```

**Degraded response (503):**

```json
{
  "ready": false,
  "db": true,
  "redis": true,
  "workers": false,
  "checkedAt": "2026-09-01T12:00:05.000Z",
  "consumerSummary": {
    "required": 113,
    "runnable": 112,
    "unavailable": 1,
    "optionalRunning": 1,
    "optionalDisabled": 3
  }
}
```

If the evaluator itself fails, the body is `{ "ready": false, "db": null, "redis": null, "workers": null, "checkedAt": "...", "consumerSummary": null, "error": "readiness evaluation failed" }` with status 503 — `null`, not `false`, because the backends may be healthy.

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `ready` | Overall admission verdict; the status code follows it |
| `db` / `redis` | Live dependency probes (bounded by the probe timeout) |
| `workers` | `true` when worker initialization has completed and every required queue consumer is running with a connected Redis client |
| `checkedAt` | When this verdict was computed (it may be cached for up to the cache TTL) |
| `consumerSummary` | Aggregate counts only: `required`, `runnable`, `unavailable` (= required − runnable), `optionalRunning`, `optionalDisabled` |

Only aggregate counts are ever exposed. Consumer names, queue names, Redis
endpoints, transition timestamps, and error messages are internal and never
appear in this body. The counts depend on the process role (`BREEZE_ROLE`)
and on feature flags: an `api`-role process counts only the socket-owner
consumers it starts, a `worker`-role process only the global ones, and
consumers behind an off feature flag (`EVENT_DISPATCH_MODE`,
`BREEZE_AI_AGENTS_ENABLED`, `AUDIT_CHAIN_VERIFY_ENABLED`) are counted as
`optionalDisabled` rather than blocking readiness. The shared abuse-signals
consumer is required when either abuse signals or partner trust is enabled;
it is optional only when both are off. The numbers above are illustrative.

The optional `worker` container (Compose profile `worker-split`) serves its
own `/health/ready` on its `API_PORT`. When its readiness evaluator runs, the
body has the same fields plus `"role": "worker"`, and a 503 adds a single
`reason` of `db`, `redis`, or `workers-pending`. Three 503s bypass the
evaluator and carry only `{ "ready": false, "reason": ... }` with none of the
other fields: `shutting-down` (the process received SIGTERM),
`migrations-pending` (schema parity not yet confirmed), and `db` when the
evaluator itself throws.

  Use `/health` for liveness probes (restart the container if the process is dead) and `/health/ready` for readiness probes (stop sending traffic until dependencies recover). Do not put `/health/ready` in a Docker Compose `healthcheck:` for a service other containers `depends_on` — Compose turns it into a startup gate. The `worker` container is the one exception, because nothing depends on it. See `docs/operations/health-probes.md` in the repository.

sections.heading: GET /metrics/scrape
sections.text:
Prometheus-formatted metrics. Requires the `METRICS_SCRAPE_TOKEN` bearer token set in your environment.

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $METRICS_SCRAPE_TOKEN" \
  https://breeze.yourdomain.com/metrics/scrape
```

See [Observability Stack](/monitoring/stack/) for the full list of available metrics.

sections.heading: Using Health Checks with Load Balancers
sections.text:
Configure your load balancer to probe the health endpoints so unhealthy instances are automatically removed from rotation.

  **AWS ALB:**
```
Target group health check:
  Protocol: HTTP
  Path: /health/ready
  Healthy threshold: 2
  Unhealthy threshold: 3
  Timeout: 5 seconds
  Interval: 30 seconds
  Success codes: 200
```

  **Nginx:**
```nginx
upstream breeze_api {
    server api1:3001;
    server api2:3001;
}

server {
    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass http://breeze_api;
    }
}

# Passive health checks happen automatically.
# For active checks (Nginx Plus), add:
# health_check uri=/health/ready interval=30s fails=3 passes=2;
```

  **HAProxy:**
```
backend breeze_api
    option httpchk GET /health/ready
    http-check expect status 200
    server api1 api1:3001 check inter 30s fall 3 rise 2
    server api2 api2:3001 check inter 30s fall 3 rise 2
```

sections.heading: Docker Health Checks
sections.text:
Every container in the Breeze production stack has a built-in health check. Docker (and Docker Compose) use these to determine container status and trigger restarts.

| Container | Check Command | Interval | Start Period |
|---|---|---|---|
| API | `wget http://localhost:3001/health` | 30s | 40s |
| Worker (profile `worker-split`) | `wget http://localhost:3001/health/ready` | 30s | 60s |
| Web | `wget http://localhost:4321/` | 30s | 30s |
| PostgreSQL | `pg_isready` | 10s | 15s |
| Redis | `redis-cli ping` | 10s | 5s |
| Prometheus | `wget http://localhost:9090/-/healthy` | 30s | 10s |
| Grafana | `wget http://localhost:3000/api/health` | 30s | 30s |
| Alertmanager | `wget http://localhost:9093/-/healthy` | 30s | 10s |
| Loki | `wget http://localhost:3100/ready` | 30s | 10s |

Check container health status at any time:

```bash
docker compose ps
```

Look for `(healthy)`, `(unhealthy)`, or `(health: starting)` in the STATUS column.

sections.heading: Kubernetes Probes
sections.text:
If you deploy Breeze on Kubernetes, map the health endpoints to pod probes:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: breeze-api
    ports:
      - containerPort: 3001
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /health/live
        port: 3001
      initialDelaySeconds: 10
      periodSeconds: 15
      failureThreshold: 3
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /health/ready
        port: 3001
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
    startupProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /health
        port: 3001
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 5
      failureThreshold: 30
```

sections.heading: Key Metrics to Watch
sections.text:
These are the most important indicators of operational health. Monitor them in Grafana or your preferred tool.

| Metric | Healthy Range | What It Means |
|---|---|---|
| `/health/ready` status | 200 | All backend dependencies are reachable |
| `http_request_duration_seconds` P95 | < 2s | API response times are acceptable |
| `http_requests_total` 5xx rate | < 1% | Very few server errors |
| `redis_memory_used_bytes` | < 80% of max | Redis has headroom |
| `pg_stat_activity_count` | < 80% of `max_connections` | Database connection pool is not saturated |
| `breeze_active_devices` | Matches expected count | Agents are checking in |
| API `uptime` | Increasing | Process has not restarted unexpectedly |

sections.heading: /health returns non-200
sections.text:
The API process is not running or not reachable on port 3001.

1. Check if the container is running: `docker compose ps api`
2. Check container logs: `docker compose logs api --tail 50`
3. Verify the port binding: `docker compose port api 3001`
4. If the process is crash-looping, check for missing environment variables or database connection strings in the logs.

sections.heading: /health/ready returns 503
sections.text:
One or more backend dependencies are down.

1. Read the `db`, `redis`, and `workers` booleans in the response body. If only `workers` is `false`, `consumerSummary.unavailable` tells you how many required queue consumers are not running; check the API container logs for `[CRITICAL] Failed to initialize <worker>` lines and for Redis disconnects.
2. If `db` is failing:
   - Verify PostgreSQL is running: `docker compose ps postgres`
   - Test the connection manually: `docker compose exec postgres pg_isready`
   - Check for connection pool exhaustion: look at `pg_stat_activity_count` in Grafana
3. If `redis` is failing:
   - Verify Redis is running: `docker compose ps redis`
   - Test the connection: `docker compose exec redis redis-cli ping`
   - Check memory usage: `docker compose exec redis redis-cli info memory`
4. If `workers` is failing: verify Redis is healthy (a consumer that lost its Redis client reports not-ready until it reconnects), then restart the container if a `[CRITICAL] Failed to initialize` line names a worker — initialization failures are permanent for the process lifetime.

sections.heading: Containers showing (unhealthy)
sections.text:
1. Identify which container is unhealthy: `docker compose ps`
2. Check container logs: `docker compose logs <container> --tail 100`
3. If the container keeps restarting, look at the `start_period` -- it may be failing its health check before it finishes starting. Increase the start period in your compose override if needed.

  If Redis becomes unreachable, `/health` stays 200 (the process is alive) but `/health/ready` and `/ready` return 503 for as long as Redis is down — no queue consumer can run without it, so the process is deliberately withheld from admission rather than admitted with degraded background work. Features that depend on Redis -- rate limiting, BullMQ job queues, and real-time pub/sub -- recover automatically when Redis returns.

title: Observability Stack
description: Set up the Breeze observability stack: Prometheus scraping, Grafana dashboards, Loki log aggregation, Alertmanager, and key metrics to watch.
headings: Prometheus Is Not Scraping the API

sections.text:
Breeze includes an optional observability stack as a separate Docker Compose overlay (`docker-compose.monitoring.yml`). Enable it alongside the core stack to get full metrics, dashboards, log aggregation, and infrastructure alerting.

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.monitoring.yml up -d
```

sections.heading: Components
sections.text:
| Component | Port | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Prometheus** | 9090 (localhost) | Time-series metrics collection and alerting rules |
| **Grafana** | 3000 (localhost) | Dashboards and visualization |
| **Alertmanager** | 9093 (localhost) | Alert routing and notifications |
| **Loki** | 3100 (localhost) | Log aggregation and querying |
| **Promtail** | 9080 (localhost) | Log shipping from Docker containers to Loki |
| **Redis Exporter** | 9121 (internal) | Exports Redis metrics for Prometheus |
| **Postgres Exporter** | 9187 (internal) | Exports PostgreSQL metrics for Prometheus |

  All monitoring ports bind to `127.0.0.1` by default. Access Grafana and Prometheus via SSH tunnel or VPN -- they should not be exposed to the public internet.

sections.heading: Accessing Grafana
sections.text:
```bash
# Via SSH tunnel
ssh -L 3000:127.0.0.1:3000 user@your-server

# Then open http://localhost:3000
# Username: admin
# Password: (your GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD from .env)
```

  You can override the Grafana port with the `GRAFANA_PORT` environment variable. Similarly, `PROMETHEUS_PORT`, `ALERTMANAGER_PORT`, and `LOKI_PORT` let you change the other monitoring ports.

sections.heading: Pre-Built Dashboards
sections.text:
Breeze ships with a Grafana dashboard (`monitoring/grafana/dashboards/breeze-overview.json`) that is automatically provisioned. It includes these panels:

| Panel | What It Shows |
|---|---|
| **Service Status** | Up/down status of API, Redis, PostgreSQL, and other services |
| **Request Rate** | HTTP requests per second with breakdown by method |
| **Response Times** | P50, P95, and P99 latency over time |
| **Error Rate** | 4xx and 5xx response rates as percentages |
| **HTTP Status Distribution** | Breakdown of responses by status code |
| **Top Endpoints** | Most-used API endpoints by request volume |
| **Active Devices** | Count of agents with recent heartbeats |
| **Organizations** | Number of active tenants |
| **Redis Memory** | Memory usage, evictions, and hit rate |
| **PostgreSQL Connections** | Active connection count vs. max pool size |

Four panel groups shipped after the table above was originally written and aren't reflected in it:

| Panel | What It Shows |
|---|---|
| **Requests by Response Class** | Request rate broken down by status class over time, alongside the status-code pie chart |
| **Redis Operations** | Redis commands processed per second |
| **Active Alerts** | Count of currently open in-app alerts |
| **Agent Heartbeats** | Agent heartbeat rate over time |
| **Script Executions** | Script execution rate over time |
| **Backup Operations — Start Failures (24h)** | Backup, restore, or verification start failures in the last 24 hours |
| **Backup Operations — Restore Timeouts (24h)** | Restore command timeouts in the last 24 hours |
| **Backup Operations — Verification Skips (24h)** | Scheduled backup verification runs skipped in the last 24 hours |

sections.heading: Adding Custom Dashboards
sections.text:
