Managed PAM v2 follows the device's **effective organization policy**. `uac_interception_enabled` on the org's PAM config (or the resolved `pam` config-policy feature link, which takes precedence) must allow the agent to capture UAC events. With no opinion set anywhere, the global default is off.

The organization policy is authoritative for dormant elevation-account provisioning. On a normal Windows service agent, an enabled policy provisions the account after verified reconciliation and before admitting elevation requests, even when the local `agent.yaml` has `pam_enabled: false`. Provisioning failures remain retryable; failed reconciliation keeps PAM unavailable.

**`pam_enabled` controls local startup provisioning; it is not a local opt-out from organization PAM policy.** Setting it to `true` alone does not enable UAC interception without an enabled effective policy, and setting it to `false` does not block policy-driven provisioning. Support-mode agents do not provision the account.

On RD Session Hosts the agent runs its Windows helpers on demand. While UAC interception is enabled, it also keeps a SYSTEM helper in every signed-in session so the elevation dialog can appear. See [Windows Helper Lifecycle](/agents/helper/#windows-helper-lifecycle-always-on-vs-on-demand).

`PAM_ACTUATOR_ENABLED` gates the legacy `POST /api/v1/devices/:id/actuate-elevation` endpoint. It is not a kill switch for managed PAM v2. To disable policy-driven UAC interception, disable the effective organization's UAC-interception policy.

---

sections.heading: Separation of duties
sections.text:
The separation-of-duties property the system enforces today is **automation cannot self-grant**:

- An AI agent or Helper session **cannot sign off on the action it proposed** -- AI tool actions and unmatched UAC prompts always default to **pending**, waiting on a human (see [Decisioning chain and fail-safe behavior](#decisioning-chain-and-fail-safe-behavior)). Automation can never quietly relax its own approval, and an evaluator outage degrades to pending rather than to an auto-grant.

  **Human requester-vs-approver separation has been enforced since v0.82.0 (#1662).** For the `tech_jit_admin` flow, the requesting technician's user id is recorded on the request as `subjectUserId`, and the respond route rejects an APPROVE where the approver matches that `subjectUserId` with `403` (`Requester cannot approve their own elevation request`). Only APPROVE is blocked this way -- a self-DENY still grants nothing, so it remains allowed.

  `subjectUserId` is `null` only for the `uac_intercept` and `ai_tool_action` flows, where there is no single human requester to compare against: `uac_intercept` originates from an end-user OS prompt, and `ai_tool_action` originates from the AI agent or Helper. For those two flows the self-approval guard has nothing to compare and never fires -- rely on the automation-cannot-self-grant behavior below, approval reasons, and anomaly alerting for those paths instead.

Every approve, deny, and revoke is gated by:

- **Permission** -- the caller must hold the device execute permission.
- **Scope** -- organization, partner, or system scope, narrowed to the caller's allowed sites for site-restricted technicians.
- **MFA** -- the decision endpoints require a multi-factor-satisfied session. A caller without MFA receives `403`.

Decisions are made through a transactional compare-and-swap on the request's `pending` (or active) status, so when two approvers -- or an approver and the expiry reaper -- act on the same request at once, exactly one wins; a request can never be both approved and denied.

---

sections.heading: Decisioning chain and fail-safe behavior
sections.text:
When the agent reports a UAC observation, the control plane decides it before any human sees it:

1. **Software-policy bridge.** The device's winning software policy is consulted first: an allowlist match auto-approves, a blocklist match denies.
2. **PAM rules.** When no software policy binds, the org's enabled PAM rules run in priority order; the first match wins with its verdict (`auto_approve`, `auto_deny`, `require_approval`, or `ignore`).
3. **Org default verdict.** With no policy and no matching rule, the request falls to the org's configured **default verdict for unmatched elevations**. The default -- and the behavior when no configuration row exists -- is **require approval** (held pending for a human); an org may instead opt into **auto-deny**, failing unmatched elevations closed. An auto-deny here is a deliberate, configured decision, not an evaluator error.

This chain **fails safe**. If either evaluator *errors*, the request falls through to `pending` -- never to an auto-approval (regardless of the configured default verdict). Degrading a would-be blocklist denial to a pending row is preferable to dropping the observation, and an evaluator outage can never become a silent grant.

A rule must carry at least one identifying criterion; a rule scoped only by time window (or nothing) is rejected at the API, because it would match every elevation in the org -- catastrophic for an auto-approve verdict.

**When the device cannot act.** The agent reports the request first and then needs a SYSTEM helper in the requesting user's Windows session to show the dialog and handle `consent.exe`. If the agent gives up because no helper can run the flow in time (for example on a Remote Desktop session host whose session is disconnected, or a helper stuck in crash cooldown), it reports that it cannot act on the request. A request still waiting for a technician is closed as `expired`, so nobody can approve it, and the server then withdraws its mobile approvals. That withdrawal is best-effort (the agent retries a failed one for up to five minutes); a phone approval of a closed request is refused whether or not it has run. When the agent cannot tell, the request stays pending until the stale-request expiry. Under the Expired or All status filter, the requests list shows that the device could not act, with one of three reasons (no PAM helper available, the user's session unavailable, the PAM helper failed to start) and the agent's diagnostic message as a tooltip. A request already decided by policy keeps its status; the report is recorded on it for the audit trail.

---

sections.heading: Signer trust: CN matching vs. thumbprint pinning
sections.text:
Executable rules and signer groups can trust a binary by its Authenticode signer in two tiers of strength:

- **CN matching (weak, legacy).** A rule's `matchSigner` field -- or a bare-string entry in a signer group -- compares the candidate's certificate **Common Name** (e.g. "Microsoft Corporation") case-insensitively. The CN is a self-asserted display string on the certificate, not a cryptographic identity: an attacker who obtains or crafts a code-signing certificate whose CN matches or mimics a trusted vendor's name can get a malicious binary auto-approved by a rule or group keyed on CN alone. This class of attack was tracked as **issue #1776**.
- **Thumbprint pinning (strong).** A rule's `matchSignerThumbprint` field -- or a thumbprint-bearing entry in a signer group -- pins the certificate's **SHA-256 leaf-cert thumbprint**, a 64-character lowercase hex digest unique to the exact signing certificate. A look-alike certificate with a spoofed CN has a different key pair and therefore a different thumbprint; it cannot satisfy a thumbprint-pinned rule no matter how convincingly its display name is forged. `matchSigner` and `matchSignerThumbprint` AND together when both are set on a rule (maximum strength: exact certificate AND expected name); a signer-group entry may likewise pin a CN, a thumbprint, or both.

The matching engine described above is real and covered by tests, but it has nothing to match against yet on Windows:

**Not yet active in the agent:**
  The Windows agent does not extract an Authenticode signer at all today -- `decodeConsentRequest` in `agent/internal/etwlua/etwlua_windows.go` defers all WinTrust/CryptoAPI signer extraction, so every UAC event it reports carries a `null` signer CN and `null` thumbprint. A thumbprint-pinned rule fails closed against that `null` (see below), and a CN-only rule simply never matches either -- so **no signer-based rule, weak or strong tier, is enforceable in practice today.** Tracked as **issue #2082** (completes #1776). Once the agent emits a thumbprint, prefer thumbprint pins over CN-only rules for anything carrying an auto-approve verdict.

**Fail-closed guarantee.** A criterion is only ever satisfied when the candidate's data is present; absent data never satisfies a criterion, even when the rule negates it (see [Decisioning chain and fail-safe behavior](#decisioning-chain-and-fail-safe-behavior)). This applies to the thumbprint criterion without exception: if a binary's signer thumbprint cannot be determined -- because it is unsigned, or because the reporting agent predates thumbprint collection -- a rule or signer-group entry pinned to a thumbprint **never matches**. There is no silent fallback to CN-only matching in that case: a thumbprint-pinned rule that can't see a thumbprint fails closed rather than degrading to the weaker check.

**Constant-time comparison.** The thumbprint match is not a plain string comparison. The engine normalizes both the pinned and candidate thumbprints to lowercase, validates them as 64-character hex, and compares them with Node's `crypto.timingSafeEqual` -- a fixed-time byte comparison that does not short-circuit on the first mismatching byte. This closes the theoretical timing side-channel where an attacker able to submit binaries and measure decision latency might otherwise recover a valid thumbprint one byte at a time.

---

sections.heading: Offline rule enforcement and staleness
sections.text:
**Not yet active in the agent:**
  The HMAC-authenticated rule cache described below (`agent/internal/pam`) exists in the agent codebase but is not imported or invoked by anything today. Offline UAC observations are held in a separate on-disk queue (`agent/internal/etwlua/queue.go`) and posted to the API once connectivity returns; the agent does not currently enforce a locally cached ruleset while offline. Treat this section as a description of a built component awaiting wiring, not live behavior.

Once wired in, the agent would cache the PAM ruleset locally so it can keep enforcing while disconnected from the API. The cache is designed as an **HMAC-SHA256-authenticated JSON envelope**:

- The HMAC is the authoritative trust boundary. Tampering with the file on disk is detected on load, and a mismatch causes the agent to reject the rule body entirely.
- The HMAC key lives in a separately permissioned `keys/` subdirectory, not alongside the cache file, so a single ACL regression on the data directory cannot expose both the envelope and the key needed to forge a new one. On Windows the cache is additionally locked to a SYSTEM-and-Administrators-only DACL; on Unix it is mode `0600` under a `0750` parent.

Staleness is designed to be bounded by two thresholds keyed on the last successful sync:

| Threshold | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **24 hours** (stale) | The agent keeps enforcing the cached rules but raises a staleness alert. |
| **7 days** (refuse) | The agent refuses to hand back the cached ruleset at all. The policy layer must re-sync or fail closed rather than enforce ancient rules. |

  The staleness gate uses wall-clock time. A local-administrator attacker who can roll the system clock back can keep a stale envelope "fresh" indefinitely. The gate is designed to catch the *operational* failure mode -- "agent forgotten or connectivity broken for more than a week, rules need to fail closed" -- not to defend against an active local-admin adversary on the box. A monotonic last-seen-fresh watermark is tracked as a follow-up.

---

sections.heading: Audit guarantees
sections.text:
Every elevation produces an immutable chain of events on a dedicated ledger, separate from -- and in addition to -- the platform audit log:

- A `requested` event is written for every observation.
- Auto-decisions add an `approved` / `denied` event attributed to the deciding software policy or PAM rule.
- Human decisions add `approved`, `denied`, or `revoked` events attributed to the approver **by user**, with the supplied reason.
- Actuation, session start/stop, and command execution land as their own event types.
- A `device_unable` event records an agent's report that it cannot act on the request, with the reason category; when that closes a pending request, an `expired` event with cause `device_unable` follows it.

The ledger denormalizes the organization id and ties each audit row to its parent request with a **composite foreign key** `(elevation_request_id, org_id) -> elevation_requests(id, org_id)`. This is a structural guarantee that an audit row's tenant can never drift from its parent request's tenant, even under a logic bug. Because it inherits the platform's forced row-level security, an audit entry is only ever visible within its own tenant.

The **Audit** tab of the Privileged Access console renders this ledger -- filterable by status, flow, and date range, and exportable to CSV for compliance reporting. Each entry names the decider, so there is never ambiguity about who (or what rule) granted access.

sections.heading: Ownership changes
sections.text: An elevation request belongs to the organization that owned the device when it was made. Moving a device to another organization, or merging its organization into another, expires every elevation request on it that is still live and has not been actuated -- pending, approved and not yet used -- and writes an `expired` event to the ledger naming the ownership change as the cause. The departing organization's policy decided those requests; the receiving organization's policy decides any new ones. Evidence of actuations that already happened stays with the request and is never rewritten.

sections.heading: Evidence retention after a merge
sections.text:
When an organization is merged away while it still owns PAM evidence, Breeze keeps it as a held shell rather than deleting the chain, so the ledger stays verifiable. A nightly job deletes evidence from those held shells only -- never from a live organization -- once every row in the shell's chain is older than `PAM_EVIDENCE_RETENTION_DAYS` (default 400, never below 30). Set `PAM_EVIDENCE_RETENTION_ENABLED=false` to keep merged evidence indefinitely. See [Privileged Access Management](/features/pam/) for the operator view.

---

sections.heading: Windows Event Log
sections.text:
Console audit is authoritative, but an auditor reviewing the *endpoint* directly -- the usual Cyber Essentials / SOC workflow -- previously saw only that the dormant `~breeze_elev` account logged on (native events 4624/4672/4688), with no link back to the Breeze user who authorized it. Every actuation the agent performs on Windows also writes a structured event to the Application log under a dedicated source, so a SIEM can answer "who approved this elevation" without cross-referencing the console.

- **Source:** `Breeze-PAM` (distinct from the generic `BreezeAgent` source used for enrollment/bootstrap diagnostics, so PAM activity can be filtered on its own).
- **Event IDs:**

  | ID | Stage | Fires when |
  |----|-------|------------|
  | 1004 | Elevation actuated | The agent begins actuating an approved elevation request -- credential minted, before consent.exe injection or the token-launch. |
  | 1005 | Session ended | The actuation attempt completes, successfully or not. |
  | 1006 | Account demoted | `~breeze_elev` is removed from Administrators at the end of an actuation. Not written if the demote itself fails -- the log never claims a demote that didn't happen. |
  | 1007 | Self-heal demote at startup | Reserved for agent startup finding the dormant account still elevated from a prior crash. Not yet wired to a call site. |
  | 1008 | Actuation refused | The agent fail-closed refuses to actuate an otherwise-approved request (for example, an unresolved prior consent-prompt dismissal, #2610). |

- **Message body:** a fixed field template -- request ID, target path, target SHA-256, subject user, requested-by name, approved-by name and email, approved-at timestamp, window-end timestamp, risk tier, and matched PAM rule name -- so a SIEM rule can parse the same shape regardless of which event ID fired. Unset fields render as `-`.
- **Never included:** user ids, session tokens, or the elevation credential. Every identity field is a display name or email resolved server-side inside the same tenant-scoped request that queued the actuation (`POST /devices/:id/actuate-elevation`) -- the agent never holds or forwards a Breeze user id.
- **Windows only.** macOS/Linux elevation does not yet have a separate-account model to log against; unified-log/syslog parity is tracked alongside that work.
- **Not yet configurable.** The write is unconditional today -- there is no per-org toggle to silence it for orgs without a SIEM. A `writeEndpointEventLog` config-policy toggle is planned as a follow-up.

The same fields are also appended to the agent's own local `audit.jsonl` (a tamper-evident, SHA-256 hash-chained log file the agent keeps on disk, separate from the platform [audit log](/reference/audit-logs/)) under the existing `privileged_operation` event type, so the trail survives even where the Windows Event Log write is unavailable.

---

sections.heading: What PAM does and does not protect against
sections.text:
**PAM protects against:**

- **Standing local-administrator sprawl.** Endpoints carry no permanently privileged user account; admin exists only inside approved windows.
- **Credential exposure.** The elevation credential is minted, used, and destroyed on the endpoint and never transits the network or lands in a config file.
- **Automation self-grant.** AI tool actions and unmatched UAC prompts default to **pending** and wait on a human, so automation can never approve the action it proposed.
- **Human self-approval (`tech_jit_admin`).** The requesting technician's user id is recorded as `subjectUserId`, and the respond route rejects an approval where the approver matches it (since v0.82.0, #1662). See [Separation of duties](#separation-of-duties).
- **Replay of an approval.** Single-use actuation makes an approved request non-replayable.
- **Tenant cross-contamination.** Forced row-level security plus a composite-FK audit tie keep every request, rule, and audit entry inside its own organization.
- **Silent failure of the decision engine.** Evaluator errors fail safe to pending, never to auto-approve.

**PAM does not protect against:**

- **A compromised approver.** If an authenticated, MFA-satisfied operator approves a malicious request, PAM grants it. Mitigations are operational: approval reasons, requester history surfaced in the UI, per-tenant approval-rate limits, and anomaly alerting on approval-rate spikes. Treat approver accounts as the high-value identities they are.
- **Self-approval on the `uac_intercept` and `ai_tool_action` flows.** These flows don't record a single human requester (`subjectUserId` is `null`), so the self-approval guard has nothing to compare and never fires there. Automation self-grant is still blocked independently (see above). See [Separation of duties](#separation-of-duties).
- **Signer-spoofed binaries.** The signer-matching engine (CN and thumbprint) is real, but the Windows agent doesn't extract a signer yet, so no signer-based rule is enforceable today. See [Signer trust: CN matching vs. thumbprint pinning](#signer-trust-cn-matching-vs-thumbprint-pinning) (#2082).
- **An offline device enforcing stale or tampered rules.** The HMAC-authenticated rule cache with staleness thresholds is built but not yet wired into the agent's offline path. See [Offline rule enforcement and staleness](#offline-rule-enforcement-and-staleness).
- **An existing local-administrator adversary on the endpoint.** The dormant-admin self-heal assumes an attacker without prior SYSTEM/admin control (the offline staleness gate, once wired in, would make the same assumption -- see the caveat above). A box that is already fully compromised is outside PAM's threat model -- PAM is a privilege-*reduction* control, not endpoint EDR.
- **Third-party agent-stack interactions.** UAC-touching code interacts with whatever else is installed. There is a documented production-breaking deadlock between the N-able N-Central agent and `consent.exe` on idle or locked machines that hangs UAC prompts for 4-5 minutes. Validate PAM against the agent stack your customers actually run before enabling it broadly. See the [admin guide's operational notes](/features/pam/#operational-notes).
- **Non-Windows endpoints.** The dormant-admin lifecycle, secure-desktop injection, and UAC interception are Windows-only. On other platforms the elevation primitives are no-ops.

---

sections.heading: Platform-evolution and liability notes
sections.text:
- **Windows Administrator Protection / 24H2.** PAM's detection relies on the documented `Microsoft-Windows-LUA` ETW telemetry provider, which Microsoft extends (rather than replaces) for the Administrator Protection path. The injection path uses the supported SYSTEM-context route to the secure desktop.
- **CVE-2026-20824 (Credential UI hardening, Jan 2026).** Microsoft tightened which processes can request `uiAccess` and added input-source validation. The hardening targeted remote-input tools (TeamViewer, AnyDesk, RDP); SYSTEM-context injection on the secure desktop was not named as impacted. Breeze tracks the trajectory and validates the path empirically each Windows release.
- **E&O / SLA implications.** Because PAM lets the MSP grant administrator access, an erroneous or coerced approval can attribute blame to the MSP. This may warrant disclosure on the MSP's errors-and-omissions coverage and explicit carve-outs in MSP-customer SLAs. Flag PAM enablement in customer onboarding.

title: Secret Rotation
description: Rotation schedules and step-by-step procedures for Breeze RMM secrets, including the JWT secret, encryption keys, peppers, and database credentials.

sections.heading: Rotation Schedule
sections.text:
| Secret | Rotation Frequency | Impact of Rotation |
|---|---|---|
| `JWT_SECRET` / `JWT_SIGNING_KEYRING` | Every 90 days | None, if rotated via the keyring (see below); all active JWTs invalidated immediately if `JWT_SECRET` is rotated in legacy single-secret mode |
| `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Annually | Requires data re-encryption migration |
| `MFA_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Annually | Requires re-encryption migration; users locked out if skipped |
| `ENROLLMENT_KEY_PEPPER` | Annually | All unexpired enrollment keys, all outstanding installer links and every downloaded installer that has not enrolled yet invalidated |
| `MFA_RECOVERY_CODE_PEPPER` | Annually | All existing MFA recovery codes invalidated |
| `AGENT_ENROLLMENT_SECRET` | Every 90 days | Only affects new enrollments |
| `SESSION_SECRET` | Every 90 days | No session impact (session tokens are random, not derived from this secret); invalidates in-flight OAuth state and the legacy encryption-at-rest fallback that uses it |
| `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` | Every 90 days | Requires coordinated DB + app restart |
| `REDIS_URL` credentials | Every 90 days | Brief reconnection |
| `S3_ACCESS_KEY` / `S3_SECRET_KEY` | Every 90 days | None |
| `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` | Every 90 days | None (existing certs unaffected) |
| `TURN_SECRET` | Every 90 days | Active remote sessions may drop |
| `METRICS_SCRAPE_TOKEN` | Every 180 days | Brief gap in metrics collection |
| `RESEND_API_KEY` / SMTP password | Per provider policy | Brief notification gap |
| Twilio credentials | Per provider policy | Brief SMS notification gap |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | Per provider policy | AI assistant unavailable |
| User API keys | User responsibility | Immediate |

sections.heading: Rotating the JWT Signing Key
sections.text:
Zero-downtime rotation is done through `JWT_SIGNING_KEYRING`, a JSON map of `kid` (key ID) to secret, plus `JWT_ACTIVE_KID` to select which entry signs new tokens. Every other kid in the keyring stays verify-only, which is what lets a rotation drain safely.

1. Add a new `kid` alongside the current one in `JWT_SIGNING_KEYRING` (each secret must be at least 32 characters), but leave `JWT_ACTIVE_KID` pointed at the existing kid:
```bash
   # existing: JWT_SIGNING_KEYRING={"2026-05":"<current-secret>"}
   #           JWT_ACTIVE_KID=2026-05
   JWT_SIGNING_KEYRING={"2026-05":"<current-secret>","2026-08":"<new-secret-from-openssl-rand-base64-64>"}
   JWT_ACTIVE_KID=2026-05
```

2. Update `.env.prod` and restart the API. Both kids now verify incoming tokens; only `2026-05` signs new ones.

3. Flip `JWT_ACTIVE_KID` to the new kid and restart again:
```bash
   JWT_ACTIVE_KID=2026-08
```
   New tokens sign under `2026-08`; tokens already issued under `2026-05` keep verifying until they expire.

4. After one full refresh-token lifetime (7 days), remove the old kid from `JWT_SIGNING_KEYRING` and restart.

  `JWT_SECRET` is kept as a permanent verify-only fallback for tokens minted before `JWT_SIGNING_KEYRING` was first deployed (those carry no `kid` header) — it isn't part of the rotation cycle. There is no `JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS` variable; the keyring replaces that mechanism.

**Legacy single-secret mode:**
  If `JWT_SIGNING_KEYRING` is unset, `JWT_SECRET` alone signs and verifies tokens and no `kid` header is emitted. Rotating `JWT_SECRET` in that mode invalidates every existing access and refresh token immediately — plan for a full re-login, or switch to the keyring first for zero-downtime rotation.

sections.heading: Rotating App Encryption Key
sections.text:
Rotating `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY` without re-encrypting existing data will make all previously encrypted values (SSO client secrets, integration tokens, and from v0.121.0 backup destination credentials) permanently unreadable. The re-encryption script covers all of them.

1. Generate a new key:
```bash
   openssl rand -hex 32
```

2. Record the old key securely — you need it for the re-encryption migration

3. Run the re-encryption migration:
```bash
   OLD_ENCRYPTION_KEY=<old-key> \
   APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY=<new-key> \
   npx tsx scripts/re-encrypt-secrets.ts
```

4. Verify decryption of several records with the new key

5. Update `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY` in `.env.prod` to the new key

6. Restart the API:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml restart api
```

sections.heading: Rotating MFA Encryption Key
sections.text:
Rotating `MFA_ENCRYPTION_KEY` without re-encryption will lock out all users with MFA enabled. They would need admin intervention to disable and re-enable MFA.

1. Generate a new key:
```bash
   openssl rand -hex 32
```

2. Run a re-encryption migration targeting MFA secret columns (same approach as `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY`)

3. Update `MFA_ENCRYPTION_KEY` in `.env.prod`

4. Restart the API:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml restart api
```

sections.heading: Rotating Enrollment Key Pepper
sections.text:
`ENROLLMENT_KEY_PEPPER` is used for one-way hashing. Rotating it invalidates **all** unexpired enrollment keys. You must regenerate and redistribute them after rotation.

  It also invalidates **every outstanding installer link and downloaded installer** that has not enrolled yet. Installer tokens are stored as a hash keyed by this pepper, and unlike enrollment keys there is no legacy-pepper fallback for them. Re-issue installers after rotating.

1. Generate a new pepper:
```bash
   openssl rand -hex 32
```

2. Update `ENROLLMENT_KEY_PEPPER` in `.env.prod`

3. Restart the API:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml restart api
```

4. Regenerate enrollment keys and redistribute to anyone deploying new agents

sections.heading: Rotating MFA Recovery Code Pepper
sections.text:
`MFA_RECOVERY_CODE_PEPPER` is used for one-way hashing. Rotating it invalidates **all** existing MFA recovery codes. Users must generate new recovery codes.

1. Generate a new pepper:
```bash
   openssl rand -hex 32
```

2. Update `MFA_RECOVERY_CODE_PEPPER` in `.env.prod`

3. Restart the API:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml restart api
```

4. Notify users to regenerate their MFA recovery codes via Settings, or trigger a bulk regeneration as an admin

sections.heading: Rotating Agent Enrollment Secret
sections.text:
1. Generate a new secret:
```bash
   openssl rand -hex 32
```

2. Update `.env.prod` with the new `AGENT_ENROLLMENT_SECRET`

3. Restart the API

4. Update any deployment scripts or MDM policies with the new secret

  Existing enrolled agents are **not** affected by enrollment secret rotation. They authenticate using individual bearer tokens, not the enrollment secret. Only new enrollments require the updated secret.

sections.heading: Rotating Session Secret
sections.text:
1. Generate a new secret:
```bash
   openssl rand -base64 64
```

2. Update `SESSION_SECRET` in `.env.prod`

3. Restart the API:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml restart api
```

4. Active sessions are **not** invalidated — session tokens are random values, not derived from `SESSION_SECRET`. Rotation invalidates in-flight OAuth state (accounting and mailbox-connect authorization flows) and removes the old value as a legacy fallback key for secret encryption-at-rest.

sections.heading: Rotating Database Password
sections.text:
1. Generate a new password:
```bash
   openssl rand -base64 24 | tr -d '/+='
```

2. Update the password in PostgreSQL:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml exec postgres \
     psql -U breeze -c "ALTER USER breeze PASSWORD 'new-password';"
```

3. Update `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` and `DATABASE_URL` in `.env.prod`

4. Restart the API:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml restart api
```

  For zero-downtime rotation, create a second database user with identical permissions, switch the app to the new user, then drop the old user.

sections.heading: Rotating Redis Credentials
sections.text:
1. Set or update the Redis password:
```bash
   redis-cli CONFIG SET requirepass "new-redis-password"
   redis-cli -a "new-redis-password" CONFIG REWRITE
```

2. Update `REDIS_URL` in `.env.prod`:
```
   REDIS_URL=redis://:new-redis-password@localhost:6379
```

3. Restart the API and worker processes:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml restart api worker
```

  Existing jobs in BullMQ are not lost — they are persisted in Redis and will be processed after reconnection. If using Redis Sentinel or Cluster, update credentials on all nodes first.

sections.heading: Rotating S3 / Object Storage Credentials
sections.text:
1. Create a new access key pair in your S3/R2/MinIO console

2. Update `S3_ACCESS_KEY` and `S3_SECRET_KEY` in `.env.prod`

3. Restart the API:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml restart api
```

4. Verify by uploading and downloading a test file

5. Delete the old access key in your storage provider's console

  Objects already stored in the bucket are unaffected by credential rotation. No data is lost.

sections.heading: Rotating Cloudflare API Token
sections.text:
Only relevant if you have `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ZONE_ID` configured for mTLS certificate management.

1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to My Profile > API Tokens

2. Create a new token with the same permissions (Client Certificates: Edit for the relevant zone)

3. Update `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` in `.env.prod`

4. Restart the API:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml restart api
```

5. Verify by triggering a certificate enrollment or renewal

6. Delete the old token in the Cloudflare dashboard

  Existing mTLS certificates already issued to agents remain valid. Only new certificate operations (enrollment, renewal) require a valid API token.

sections.heading: Rotating TURN Secret
sections.text:
1. Generate a new secret:
```bash
   openssl rand -hex 32
```

2. Update `TURN_SECRET` in both the TURN server configuration and `.env.prod`

3. Restart the TURN server and the API:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml restart api turn
```

  Active remote desktop and terminal sessions using old TURN credentials will fail when those credentials expire (typically within a few minutes). Users can reconnect.

sections.heading: Rotating Metrics Token
sections.text:
1. Generate a new token:
```bash
   openssl rand -hex 32
```

2. Update `METRICS_SCRAPE_TOKEN` in `.env.prod`

3. Update the token file:
```bash
   echo "new-token" > monitoring/secrets/metrics_scrape_token
   chmod 600 monitoring/secrets/metrics_scrape_token
```

4. Restart API and Prometheus:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml restart api prometheus
```

  Prometheus will return `401` errors until its config is updated. There will be a brief gap in metrics collection but no data loss.

sections.heading: Rotating Email Provider Credentials
sections.text:
Covers `RESEND_API_KEY`, `SMTP_USER` / `SMTP_PASS`, and `MAILGUN_API_KEY`.

1. Rotate the credential in the provider's dashboard (Resend, Mailgun, or your SMTP provider)

2. Update the corresponding env var(s) in `.env.prod`

3. Restart the API:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml restart api
```

4. Verify by triggering a test notification (e.g., password reset email)

  Keep the old credential active until the new one is deployed. Notifications (password resets, alert emails) will fail between revocation of the old credential and deployment of the new one.

sections.heading: Rotating SMS Provider Credentials (Twilio)
sections.text:
Covers `TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID` and `TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN`.

1. In the Twilio console, generate a new Auth Token (or create a new API key pair)

2. Update `TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID` and/or `TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN` in `.env.prod`

3. Restart the API:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml restart api
```

4. Verify by triggering a test SMS alert

5. Revoke the old credential in the Twilio console

  MFA SMS messages and SMS-based alerts will fail between revocation of the old credential and deployment of the new one. Keep the old credential active until the new one is deployed.

sections.heading: Rotating Anthropic API Key
sections.text:
1. Generate a new API key in the [Anthropic console](https://console.anthropic.com/)

2. Update `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in `.env.prod`

3. Restart the API:
```bash
   docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml restart api
```

4. Revoke the old key in the Anthropic console

  AI assistant queries will fail between revocation of the old key and deployment of the new one. The rest of the platform is unaffected.

sections.heading: User API Keys
sections.text:
User-facing API keys are managed through the application, not through environment variables.

- **Individual rotation:** Users regenerate their API key via Settings > API Keys > Regenerate, or via `POST /api/v1/api-keys/:id/rotate` — this reissues the secret in place on the same key record (same id, scopes, and rate limit) and resets usage stats; it requires MFA
- **Admin revocation:** Admins can revoke any API key via the admin panel or `DELETE /api/v1/api-keys/:id`
- **Bulk revocation:** In a security incident, an admin can revoke all API keys; users must generate new ones

No environment variable changes or restarts are required. The old key is immediately invalidated upon regeneration.

sections.heading: Emergency Rotation
sections.text:
If you suspect any secret has been compromised:

1. **Rotate the compromised secret immediately** using the procedures above
2. **Check audit logs** for unauthorized access during the exposure window
3. **Rotate related secrets** — if `JWT_SECRET` was compromised, also rotate `SESSION_SECRET`; if database credentials leaked, also rotate `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY` in case encrypted data was exfiltrated
4. **Notify affected users** if their data may have been accessed
5. **File a post-incident report** documenting the timeline, impact, and remediation

  Never rotate all secrets simultaneously. Rotate one at a time and verify the system is healthy before moving on. Always test in staging first.

title: Trust Center attestation
description: Verify a published Trust Center page as a signed, machine-readable JWT, and rotate the keys that sign it.
headings: What it proves, and what it does not

sections.text:
Every published [Trust Center](/security/trust-center/) page that is current (evaluated in the last 24 hours) has a signed, machine-readable copy: a compact JSON Web Token (JWT) that carries the exact public payload the page renders. Insurer, auditor and procurement tooling can fetch it, verify the signature against the deployment's public keys, and read the same controls a person sees on the page.

While the page is current, it links to the copy in its footer ("Machine-readable, signed copy") and in its HTML head as `<link rel="alternate" type="application/jwt">`. A stale page shows no link, and its attestation URL answers `503` (see below).

sections.heading: What it proves, and what it does not
sections.text:
An attestation proves that **this Breeze installation computed this payload, for this page, at this time**. The signature binds the payload to the page URL and to the time of the last evaluation, so the token cannot be edited or replayed against another page without detection.

It does **not** prove that the organization is secure, compliant or certified. The payload is an evidence summary from Breeze telemetry, with the same limits as the page itself.

**Self-hosted installations:**
On a self-hosted installation, the operator controls both the telemetry and the signing key. The attestation is then a statement by that installation, not independent assurance. Treat it as evidence from the operator, not as a third-party audit.

sections.heading: Endpoints
sections.text:
| URL | Returns |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/v1/trust/attestation/<partner>/<org>` | The attestation for an organization page, as `application/jwt` |
| `GET /api/v1/trust/attestation/<partner>` | The attestation for a partner home page |
| `GET /api/v1/trust/attestation/jwks.json` | The public verification keys, as `application/jwk-set+json` |

All three are public, need no authentication and allow cross-origin reads (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, never with credentials). They are rate limited to 60 requests per minute per IP address.

| Response | When |
|---|---|
| `200` | The page is published and was evaluated in the last 24 hours. `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60` or less (never past the token's `exp`). |
| `404 {"error":"Not found","code":"NOT_FOUND"}` | The page does not exist, is not published, or cannot be served. The response is the same for every cause. |
| `503 {"code":"ATTESTATION_STALE"}` with `Retry-After: 3600` | The page has not been evaluated in the last 24 hours. No token is issued for a stale page. |
| `503 {"code":"SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE"}` | Attestation URLs: the installation has no active signing key, or no public URL configured (see [Self-hosting](#self-hosting)). JWKS: every key has been revoked, so there is nothing to publish. While there is no active key, the JWKS still answers `200` with the verify-only keys, so archived tokens keep verifying. |

Every response other than `200` is `Cache-Control: no-store`. The JWKS is `Cache-Control: public, max-age=600`.

sections.heading: The token
sections.text:
The JOSE header:

```json
{ "alg": "ES256", "kid": "trust-AbCdEf0123456789", "typ": "trust-attestation+jwt" }
```

The claims:

| Claim | Value |
|---|---|
| `iss` | The installation's origin, for example `https://breeze.example.com` |
| `sub` | The public page URL, for example `https://breeze.example.com/portal/trust/northwind/acme` |
| `iat` | When the token was signed (seconds since the epoch) |
| `exp` | The earlier of `iat + 1 hour` and `lastEvaluatedAt + 24 hours` |
| `jti` | A random UUID, unique per token |
| `trust.v` | `1` |
| `trust.payload` | The exact public payload the page renders, including its snapshot id |
| `trust.lastEvaluatedAt` | When Breeze last evaluated the page's controls (ISO 8601) |

There is no `aud` claim. The signature algorithm is always ES256 (ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256).

sections.heading: Verify a token
sections.text:
A correct verifier checks **all** of the following, not only the signature:

1. The signature, against a key from the installation's `jwks.json`, with the algorithm pinned to `ES256`.
2. `typ` is `trust-attestation+jwt`.
3. `iss` is the installation's origin that you expect.
4. `sub` is the page URL you expect.
5. `exp` has not passed.

The examples below use `https://breeze.example.com` and the page `northwind/acme`.

sections.heading: Node.js (`jose`)
Python (`PyJWT`)
sections.text:
```python
import jwt
import requests

origin = "https://breeze.example.com"
page = f"{origin}/portal/trust/northwind/acme"
jwks = jwt.PyJWKClient(f"{origin}/api/v1/trust/attestation/jwks.json")

token = requests.get(f"{origin}/api/v1/trust/attestation/northwind/acme", timeout=10).text
if jwt.get_unverified_header(token).get("typ") != "trust-attestation+jwt":
    raise ValueError("not a trust attestation")
claims = jwt.decode(
    token,
    jwks.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token).key,
    algorithms=["ES256"],
    issuer=origin,
    options={"require": ["iss", "sub", "iat", "exp"]},
)
if claims["sub"] != page:
    raise ValueError("attestation is for a different page")
```

sections.heading: .NET (`Microsoft.IdentityModel.JsonWebTokens`)
Archived tokens
Self-hosting
sections.text:
There is nothing to set up. The installation creates its signing key the first time an attestation or the JWKS is requested, and stores the private key encrypted with `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.

- Set `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_ID` so the encrypted key is bound to its database column (the same setting protects every other encrypted column).
- Set `DASHBOARD_URL` (or `PUBLIC_APP_URL`) to the public URL of your installation. The `iss` and `sub` claims come from it. In production, attestation answers `503` until one of them is set.

sections.heading: Rotating the signing key
sections.text:
Rotation is an operator task. The command runs from a Breeze source checkout (the API container image ships the compiled server only, not `scripts/`), with `DATABASE_URL`, `REDIS_URL`, `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY` and `APP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_ID` set to the production values:

```bash
pnpm --filter @breeze/api trust:signing-key list
pnpm --filter @breeze/api trust:signing-key prepare            # new key, published in the JWKS, not signing yet
# wait at least 10 minutes (the JWKS max-age) so caching verifiers have the new key
pnpm --filter @breeze/api trust:signing-key activate <kid>     # new key signs; the old key becomes verify-only
```

`activate` refuses a key prepared less than 10 minutes ago unless you pass `--force`. The previous key stays in the JWKS so tokens it signed keep verifying; its private key is destroyed.

**If a key is compromised**, revoke it and mint a replacement in one step:

```bash
pnpm --filter @breeze/api trust:signing-key revoke <kid> --replace
```

The revoked key leaves the JWKS at once. Verifiers that cache the JWKS stop trusting it within 10 minutes. Without `--replace`, revoking the active key leaves the installation with no signing key, and attestation answers `503` until you `prepare` and `activate` a new one: Breeze never creates a replacement on its own after a revoke.

Every command prints the keyset (key ids, statuses and dates, never key material) and writes an audit log entry `trust_signing_key.<command>`. After a change it tells the running API instances to reload the keyset; if it cannot (for example, Redis is unreachable), it says so, and each instance picks up the change within 60 seconds. A revoke also deletes the cached tokens the revoked key signed. The command exits non-zero if a committed change could not be audited or a revoke could not be announced, and says which.

title: Embed a Trust Center card
description: Show a compact, live security posture card from a published Trust Center page inside an iframe on websites you allow.
headings: The full page is never framable

sections.text: A published [Trust Center](/security/trust-center/) page can be shown on the customer's own website as a small card inside an `<iframe>`. The card is a summary that links out to the full page. Only the websites you list may display it.

sections.heading: What the embed shows
sections.text:
The card shows the same summary the public page header shows:

- the organization's logo and name
- "Security posture · verified by Breeze"
- the summary line (how many Breeze-verifiable controls are shown and how many are met)
- the date the page was last verified, and a "Verification paused" note when the page is stale (not evaluated in the last 24 hours)
- a **View the full trust page** link, which opens the full page in a new tab

The card never shows individual controls, documents, the method section or anything that is not already on the public page. It has no scripts and no forms.

sections.heading: Turn it on
sections.text:
1. Open the organization, then the **Trust Center** tab.
2. Find **Embed on your website**.
3. Add each website that will show the card, for example `https://www.example.com`, and select **Save websites**. Saving requires multi-factor authentication.
4. Copy the iframe snippet into the website's HTML.

```html
<iframe src="https://breeze.example.com/portal/trust/embed/<partner>/<org>" title="Security posture card" width="100%" height="160" loading="lazy" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin"></iframe>
```

Until at least one website is listed, the embed URL answers 404 and nothing can frame it.

**Reserved partner slugs:**
The embed lives at `/portal/trust/embed/…`, so the partner slug `embed` is reserved, alongside `preview` and `access`. A partner whose slug is one of these cannot publish a trust page, and a page already published under such a slug stops serving. Rename the partner slug to publish again.

sections.heading: Rules for allowed websites
sections.text:
Each entry is an exact **origin**: `https://`, a host name, and an optional port.

- `https` only. `http://` addresses are refused.
- No paths, queries or fragments (`https://www.example.com/about` is refused, not shortened).
- No wildcards (`https://*.example.com`), IP addresses, `localhost` or single-label host names.
- `www.example.com` and `example.com` are different websites; list both if both show the card.
- At most 10 websites per page.
- International domain names are stored in their punycode form (`https://bücher.example` is saved as `https://xn--bcher-kva.example`).

sections.heading: When changes take effect
sections.text:
The list is a live setting. It is not part of the published snapshot, so changing it needs no republish.

- Removing a website takes effect on the next load of the embed. The card and the embed responses are never cached (`Cache-Control: no-store`).
- A card that is already open in a visitor's browser stays until that visitor reloads the page.
- Unpublishing the page stops the embed everywhere on the next load.

sections.heading: Nested frames
sections.text: Browsers check every frame above the card, not only the one that contains it. If the website that shows the card is itself framed by another site, that outer site must be on the list too.

sections.heading: The full page is never framable
sections.text:
Only `/portal/trust/embed/...` can be framed. The full trust page, previews and gated-document links always answer with `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, and in production also with `frame-ancestors 'none'`.

**Local development:**
  The portal's development server drops the Content-Security-Policy header unless `CSP_STRICT_DEV=1` is set. Without that CSP the embed keeps `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, so it cannot be framed in local development. This is deliberate, so a missing CSP never leaves the card framable by anyone.

sections.heading: Behind your own reverse proxy
sections.text:
The portal sets the framing headers itself: `frame-ancestors` lists your websites and `X-Frame-Options` is removed. A proxy in front of Breeze that adds a second `Content-Security-Policy` to `/portal/trust/embed/` responses breaks the embed, because browsers enforce every CSP they receive. A proxy-added `X-Frame-Options: DENY` is ignored by modern browsers when `frame-ancestors` is present, but it still blocks the card in older browsers. Keep both off that path; see the note in [TLS and reverse proxies](/deploy/tls/#nginx-alternative).

**Prefer a badge?:**
  If you only need a small "verified by Breeze" link, the **Badge** section of the same tab gives you an image badge that works on any website, with no allowlist.

title: Customer editing of the trust page
description: Let a customer's admin contacts edit part of their trust page draft from the customer portal, preview it and withdraw it. You still publish.
headings: What a customer admin can change

sections.text:
A customer often knows details of its own trust page better than you do: who handles security questions, which website to link, which controls to leave off. Portal editing lets the customer's admin contacts change those details from the customer portal. **You keep publishing.** A customer edit changes the draft, and the public page shows it only after your next publish.

Editing is off for every organization until you turn it on.

sections.heading: Turn it on
sections.text:
1. Open **Organizations**, select the organization, and open **Settings → Customer Portal**.
2. Under **Portal features**, turn on **Customer trust page editing** and save. Saving requires MFA, like every portal setting.

"Enable all visibility" never turns this on. It grants a write permission, so you turn it on for one organization at a time.

sections.heading: Who can edit
sections.text:
A portal user can edit when all of these are true:

- The organization has **Customer trust page editing** turned on.
- The portal user's account is active and is linked to a contact.
- That contact holds the **admin** responsibility for the **whole organization**. An admin role limited to a site or a device group does not qualify.

Assign the admin responsibility in the organization's **Contacts**. Granting it here also means "this person may edit the trust page draft". A portal login without a contact (for example, one created by Microsoft Entra sign-in) never qualifies.

Breeze checks these conditions on every request, so removing the role or turning the setting off takes effect at once, even for a customer who is signed in.

For a qualifying user, the portal shows **Trust page** in its navigation. The page is at `/security/trust-page` in the customer portal.

sections.heading: What a customer admin can change
sections.text:
- The security contact email.
- The website link.
- Which controls are hidden on the public page.
- Whether the page shows coverage percentages.
- Whether the page shows the number of devices.

They can also open a **preview** of the draft. The preview link expires after 15 minutes.

sections.heading: What stays with you
sections.text:
- **Publishing.** The portal has no Publish button. Publishing still needs your MFA, your partner trust status and the customer's authorization.
- The introduction text, shared documents, the embed allowlist and the partner home page.
- Settings the draft inherits from your partner template. A customer edit sets an explicit value on the page for the field it changed. Fields the customer did not touch keep inheriting.

Each customer save increases the page's revision number. If you loaded the editor before the customer saved, your publish is refused with "This page changed since you loaded it". Reload, review the customer's change, then publish. A customer whose save collides with yours sees the same kind of message and reloads.

sections.heading: Withdrawal
sections.text:
Under **Withdraw the page**, a customer admin can select **Unpublish this page**, for example to withdraw consent. They confirm by typing the organization's name. The public page stops serving on the next request. The page keeps its draft, and only you can publish it again.

The withdrawal does not clear the customer authorization you recorded when you published, so you can publish the page again without recording a new one. Treat a withdrawal as a conversation to have with the customer before you republish; whether the authorization should be cleared is under review (#9255).

sections.heading: Audit
sections.text: Every customer action is recorded in the audit log with the portal user as the actor: `portal.trust_page.update` (with the changed field names and the new revision) and `portal.trust_page.unpublish`.

title: Trust Center questionnaire export
description: Download your published Trust Center page as questionnaire answers in CSV or JSON, for security questionnaires and insurer forms.

sections.text:
The Trust Center tab can export the answers your public page already gives as a spreadsheet-friendly **CSV** or a **JSON** file. Use it to fill in a customer or insurer questionnaire without retyping what the page says. It is an evidence summary computed by Breeze from device telemetry, **not a certification or attestation of compliance**.

Open the organization record, go to the **Trust Center** tab, and use the **Export questionnaire answers** buttons in the status card.

sections.heading: Published page only
sections.text: The export is built in your browser from the same published data the public page renders. It never includes more than the public page shows: hidden controls stay hidden, percentages and device counts appear only if the page shows them, and an unpublished page cannot be exported (the buttons are disabled). If you change the draft, publish first; the export follows what is live.

sections.heading: Columns
sections.text:
Each row is one control shown on the page, in page order: telemetry controls first, then declared controls.

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `control_id`, `category` | Stable control identifier and its category |
| `question` | Breeze's plain-English question for the control |
| `answer` | `Yes`, `Partially`, `No` or `Not assessed` |
| `status` | The page status (`met`, `attention`, `not_met`, `not_assessed`; declared controls use `current` or `expired`) |
| `reason` | Why a control is not assessed (for example `no_data`); `declaration_expired` for an expired declaration |
| `basis` | How the answer is known: "Continuously verified by Breeze RMM telemetry", or "Declared by … on …, expires …" |
| `devices_assessed`, `devices_eligible`, `percent` | Empty when the page hides percentages |
| `evidence_as_of` | When the evidence was last gathered |
| `framework_refs` | Framework references, for example `cis_v8 10.1; nist_csf_2 PR.PS` |
| `verification_paused` | `true` on every row when the page's evidence is stale |
| `page_url`, `snapshot_id`, `generated_at`, `published_at` | Where the page lives and which published version the row came from |

sections.heading: Answer mapping
sections.text:
- Met → `Yes`
- Needs attention → `Partially`
- Not met → `No`
- Not assessed → `Not assessed`, with the reason in `reason`
- A current declared control → `Yes`; an expired declaration → `Not assessed`

When the page's evidence is stale, the answers keep the last verified values and every row carries `verification_paused` = `true`. Check that column before relying on an answer.

Declared controls are statements made by a named person at your company. They are labeled as declared in `basis` and are never presented as measured.

sections.heading: JSON
sections.text: The JSON file carries the same rows plus the page metadata: `format` (`breeze-trust-questionnaire`), `version`, `pageUrl`, the organization name, `snapshotId`, `generatedAt`, `publishedAt`, `lastEvaluatedAt`, `stale`, the summary, the methodology and the disclaimer.

sections.heading: Spreadsheet safety
sections.text:
Every CSV cell is checked before it is written. A value that begins with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, a tab or a line break is prefixed with a single quote so Excel and Sheets treat it as text instead of running it as a formula.

Need a copy a third party can verify? The export is a convenience format. The signed attestation is the verifiable machine-readable copy; see [Trust Center signed attestation](/security/trust-center-attestation/).

title: Trust Center
description: Publish a public, telemetry-backed security page for each customer organization, with controls evaluated from live Breeze data.

sections.text: The Trust Center lets you publish a public page for an organization that summarizes its security posture from live Breeze telemetry. It is an evidence summary, **not a certification**. Manage it from the organization record, in the **Trust Center** tab.

sections.heading: What the page shows
sections.text:
- A set of security controls grouped by category, each marked Met, Needs attention, Not met, or Not assessed.
- Optional percentages, an optional device count, and an optional "Managed by" block naming your company.
- An introduction, a security contact email, and a website that you write.
- Documents you explicitly choose to share. Nothing is shared by default, and each document is confirmed before it is added.
- A "How this page is verified" section that states the method used.

sections.heading: What it never shows
sections.text:
- Device names, hostnames, users, IP addresses, or any other per-device detail.
- A single overall posture score. The page reports individual controls only.

sections.heading: How controls are evaluated
sections.text:
Each control is evaluated against the devices (or accounts) it applies to:

- **Eligible**: the units the control applies to.
- **Assessed**: eligible units that reported evidence inside the evidence window.
- **Passing**: assessed units that meet the control.

The rules are fixed and shown on the public page:

- Evidence older than **30 days** is not counted.
- A control is evaluated only when at least **80%** of eligible units were assessed (the coverage floor). Below that, it reads **Not assessed**, never 0%.
- A control reads Met at **95%** or higher, Needs attention at **80%** or higher, and Not met otherwise.

Controls are re-evaluated every hour while a page is published, and again when you publish. The hourly refresh re-reads the evidence only: your page settings, introduction, contact details and document list stay as they were at the last publish. Edits you save in the Trust Center tab reach the public page when you publish again. Removing a document from the page still takes it off the public page at the next refresh.

sections.heading: The Microsoft 365 MFA control
sections.text: One control, **MFA enforced (Microsoft 365 Conditional Access)**, is evaluated from the organization's Microsoft 365 connection rather than from devices. It reads Met when an enabled Conditional Access policy requires multi-factor authentication for all users on all cloud apps; report-only policies do not count. It needs a Microsoft 365 connection whose Conditional Access sync completed inside the evidence window. Without one, or when the tenant has no synced policies (security defaults and per-user MFA are not read), the control reads **Not assessed**, never Not met.

sections.heading: Who can publish
sections.text:
Publishing is limited to partners whose account is trusted. A new account must first earn trust, and a restricted account cannot publish. The Trust Center tab explains the reason when publishing is unavailable.

To publish or unpublish you need the `organizations:write` permission and a session with multi-factor authentication. Viewers without write permission can see the tab but cannot change it.

A page's public URL is built from the partner slug and the organization slug. Renaming either one changes the URL of every trust page built from it, and the old links stop working.

sections.heading: Customer authorization
sections.text:
When you publish a customer's page you must confirm that the customer authorized it and record who gave that authorization (name and role). Breeze stores the attestation with the date. A partner's own page needs no customer authorization, so only your own internal organization can be marked as the partner page.

The partner-page setting cannot be removed from a page that is live without a recorded customer authorization, and the partner page cannot be moved to another organization while the current one is live that way. Unpublish the page first. This keeps a page that was published as your own from staying live as a customer page nobody authorized.

sections.heading: Framework references
sections.text: Controls can show references to safeguards in frameworks such as CIS Controls v8 and the Essential Eight. These are indicative mappings, never a statement of compliance. Each public page carries the required attribution. CIS Controls are a registered trademark of the Center for Internet Security, Inc.

sections.heading: Declared controls
sections.text:
Some practices cannot be measured from telemetry, such as security awareness training, an incident response plan, vendor risk management, a data inventory, periodic access reviews, a backup and recovery plan, penetration testing and cyber insurance. You can **declare** these on the page.

- A declaration is a short statement (10 to 1000 characters) made by a named member of your team, on behalf of your company. You confirm that it is accurate and that you are authorized to make it. You can attach a document from the organization's library as evidence; the public page names it only when that document is also shared on the page.
- Declaring, re-declaring and withdrawing need the `organizations:write` permission and a session with multi-factor authentication, and each action is recorded in the audit log.
- The public page lists declared controls in their own section, labeled "Declared by *your company* on *date*". They never carry a Met or Not met status, and they are never counted in the number of controls met.
- Each declaration expires exactly **365 days** after it is made. Thirty days before it expires, users with `organizations:write` on the organization get an in-app notification and an email. An expired declaration stays on the public page, muted and marked "Declaration expired on *date*", until you withdraw it or publish again. A publish never carries an expired declaration forward, so re-declare it first to keep it on the page.
- A new or re-declared control appears on the public page when you publish again. A withdrawal and an expiry take effect at the next hourly refresh, without a publish.

sections.heading: Documents available on request
sections.text:
A linked document can be **Public** (anyone with the page link downloads it) or **Available on request**. A document on request is listed on the public page by title, with no download link. Changing a document's visibility asks you to confirm the disclosure again.

A visitor who wants it fills in a short request form: name, work email, company and the reason they need it. Then:

1. Breeze emails the visitor a confirmation link. The request reaches you only after they click **Confirm request** on that page. The link expires after 24 hours.
2. Users who can edit the organization get an in-app notification and an email. If you turn on **Create a ticket for each confirmed request** in the **Document access requests** section, Breeze also opens a ticket.
3. You approve or deny the request in the **Document access requests** section of the Trust Center tab. Approving requires multi-factor authentication. A denial emails the requester, with your note if you add one.
4. An approved requester is emailed a download link that works for **7 days**. It covers the documents offered on request on the published page at the moment you approved. **Resend link** emails a new link and the old one stops working; the 7 days do not restart. **Revoke** ends access immediately.

Requests open only while the page is published. Downloads stop if you unpublish the page, if the document is removed, deleted or replaced by a newer version, or if you switch it back to Public.

**Needs an email transport:**
Document requests depend on email: the visitor's confirmation link is how a request reaches you, and approvals and download links are emailed too. On an install with no email transport configured, no request can be confirmed. The **Approve** and **Resend link** toasts still say an email was sent on such an install (#9256).

sections.heading: Non-disclosure terms
sections.text: You can add non-disclosure terms in the **Document access requests** section. Requesters must accept them before they can send a request, and Breeze records the exact text each requester accepted. The terms are shown as plain text and reach the public page when you next publish.

sections.heading: Privacy and retention
sections.text: Access links are single-purpose and only ever appear after the `#` in the address, so they are never sent to a server in a URL or written to an access log. Breeze stores only a hash of each link. Requests (name, email, company, purpose) are deleted 365 days after their last status change, except for an approval that is still in force. Expired links are deleted after 30 days. Each request, confirmation, decision and download is recorded in the audit log.

sections.heading: Framework view
sections.text:
A trust page can map its controls to one or more security frameworks and show how many of each framework's safeguards have evidence behind them. For example: "Evidence shown for 12 of 106 safeguards (9 verified by Breeze telemetry · 3 declared by the provider)." A safeguard counts when a shown control that references it was assessed from telemetry, or when a current declared control references it. Expired declarations and controls that are not assessed are listed but not counted. This is a summary of evidence, not a statement of compliance, and the page never says a business is compliant with, certified to, or meets a framework.

Choose frameworks in the **Framework view** section of the Trust Center tab. **Use default** clears the page's own choice and falls back to the partner template, then the built-in default. The editor suggests Essential Eight for partners in Australia and Cyber Essentials for partners in the United Kingdom. The built-in default is NIST CSF 2.0 while the CIS setting below is off; with it on, the default becomes CIS Controls v8.

The CIS Controls v8 view requires `BREEZE_TRUST_CIS_FRAMEWORK_VIEW` (default off). Enabling it is an operator decision after CIS licensing is confirmed. While it is off, CIS cannot be selected and the framework view omits it; control cards still show their CIS references. See the [environment reference](/deploy/environment/).

sections.heading: Hardening safeguards
sections.text:
When the CIS Controls v8 view is enabled, the configuration hardening control gains a collapsed **Safeguards evidenced by hardening checks** list. Breeze maps each hardening check the agent runs, per operating system, to the CIS Controls v8 safeguards it supports, and evaluates each safeguard from the latest scan of every eligible device: a device passes a safeguard only when every mapped check that produced a result passed, and `not applicable` or errored checks do not count for or against it. Each safeguard then uses the same coverage floor and thresholds as every other control, so a safeguard with too little scan coverage shows as not assessed.

The list is partial by construction. Only some hardening checks map to a named safeguard, and a check with no mapping still counts toward the overall hardening pass rate. The public page shows safeguard identifiers, Breeze's own short descriptions and a status. It never shows the hardening checks' own titles or identifiers. The list appears only while `BREEZE_TRUST_CIS_FRAMEWORK_VIEW` is on, and it is not a statement of compliance.

sections.heading: Subprocessors, FAQ and history
sections.text:
Three optional blocks give buyers and auditors the context behind the controls. All three are drafted in the Trust Center tab and reach the public page only when you publish.

- **Subprocessors.** List the third parties that process data for your customer. **Add from detected tools** suggests the security products, backup service and Microsoft 365 connection Breeze already knows about, and you can add any others by hand (up to 50). A suggestion is only a prefill: review the purpose, location and website before you save. Websites must start with `https://`.
- **FAQ.** Up to 30 questions with short formatted answers (2,000 characters each), shown as expandable items. Answers are cleaned of scripts and unsupported formatting when you save and again every time the page is built.
- **Controls met over time.** Off by default. When on, the page shows a 90-day chart of how many controls were met. The chart is built from the page's earlier snapshots, so turning it on can show changes from before you enabled it. It shows change-points only (a point appears when the number changes at a re-evaluation) and does not claim every hour was verified. The setting follows the usual inheritance (page, then partner template, then default) and the Trust Center tab shows which one applies.

sections.heading: Partner defaults
sections.text:
Set defaults for every customer's page once, in **Settings → Partner → Trust Center**: which of the optional blocks show (percentages, device count, "Managed by", search indexing, the 90-day history), an introduction, the controls hidden by default and the framework view. A field you leave blank uses the Breeze default, and the form shows that default next to it.

Each organization's Trust Center tab shows where each setting comes from: **Set for this organization**, **Partner template**, or **Breeze default**. A value an organization sets for itself always wins. **Reset to inherited** removes that value so the organization follows your defaults again. For the introduction, choose between the partner template's introduction, no introduction, or a custom one.

Publishing freezes the values the page was published with. A later change to your defaults reaches a published page only when that page is published again.

A page that existed before partner defaults were introduced keeps the values it had, as settings of its own, so your new defaults do not change it. Use **Reset to inherited** on each such setting to adopt the partner template.

Changing the defaults needs the `organizations:write` permission, access to every organization in your partner account, and a session with multi-factor authentication. Partner users limited to selected organizations can view the defaults but not change them.

sections.heading: Languages
sections.text: The public page is shown in one of eight languages: English, Portuguese (Brazil), Spanish (Latin America), French (France), French (Canada), German, Italian and Turkish. The language is taken from your partner **Language** setting at the moment you publish and frozen with the page, so changing the setting later takes effect at the next publish. Breeze translates its own copy: section headings, control titles and descriptions, statuses and the verification method text. The non-English translations are machine-drafted. Text you wrote yourself, such as the introduction, FAQ answers and document titles, is shown as you entered it.

sections.heading: Badge
sections.text:
A published page offers a live status badge you can embed on your website. The badge links to the public page and goes dark when the page is unpublished.

Unpublishing takes effect immediately: the public link stops working and the badge goes dark. You can publish again at any time.

sections.heading: Self-hosting
sections.text:
Nothing to configure. Trust pages are served under `/portal/trust/...`, which your existing reverse-proxy rule for `/portal` already covers. The public API lives under `/api/v1/trust/`. Proxies that already forward `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-Host` (Caddy's default) need nothing; if yours strips them, canonical URLs fall back to the internal origin.

`PARTNER_TRUST_MODE` applies only to hosted installs; self-hosted installs skip the trust gate.
